statements.claim: The earth was burdened by the weight of kings — demons who had taken birth in royal houses, hundreds of thousands of them across the land.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.16: 'bhūmir dṛpta-nṛpa-vyāja-daityānīka-śatāyutaiḥ' — earth weighed down by hundreds of thousands of demon hosts disguised as arrogant kings; pack excerpt confirms.

statements.claim: The earth is a living being who feeds every creature from her body.
statements.evidence: Traditional framing of the earth as a living mother; consistent with the personified Earth of the episode, not a specific sourceable assertion in 10.1.16-17.

statements.claim: The earth took the form of a cow, weeping, exhausted, and stood before Brahma lamenting her misery.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.17: 'gaur bhūtvāśru-mukhī khinnā krandantī karuṇaṃ' — becoming a cow, tear-faced, exhausted, weeping piteously; index confirms she appeals to Brahma for relief.

statements.claim: She asked only to be unburdened, not for a champion or a new king.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt says she 'laments her misery before Brahma' and the index says she 'appeals to Brahma for relief'; the specific negative framing (no champion requested) is interpretive connective narration.

statements.claim: Brahma heard her and understood; the plea did not vanish into silence.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.18 ('brahmā tad-upadhāryātha' — Brahma, having understood) and the corpus chain to DKS_0002, where Brahma carries the plea to Vishnu.

DKS_0001.notes: All claims grounded in BP 10.1.16-17. Poetic elaboration (weakened fields/rivers, 'maker of the worlds' epithet) is atmosphere, not fact.

statements.claim: Brahma gathered the gods, took the earth along, and went to the shore of the milk ocean to the Lord of the universe, the God of gods.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.18-19: 'brahmā tad-upadhāryātha saha devais tayā saha' ... 'jagannāthaṃ deva-devaṃ vṛṣākapim'; pack excerpt: 'Brahma, bearing the Earth, goes with the gods to the shore of the milk ocean'.

statements.claim: There the Lord of the universe rests upon the coils of the great serpent.
statements.evidence: Standard iconography of Vishnu on Ananta (Shesha) at the milk ocean; Ananta is named in this same chapter (10.1.23 'sahasra-vadanaḥ'), though the coiled-serpent detail is not verbatim in the quoted verse.

statements.claim: In meditation, Brahma heard a voice from the sky and repeated it to the gods.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.20: 'giraṃ samādhau gagane samīritāṃ niśamya vedhās tridaśān uvāca ha' — hearing the voice uttered in the sky during meditation, Brahma spoke to the gods.

statements.claim: The voice declared the Lord himself would take birth in the house of Vasudeva among the Yadus; the gods should descend in portions as helpers.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.21-22: 'bhavadbhir aṃśair yaduṣūpajanyatām / vasudeva-gṛhe sākṣād bhagavān puruṣaḥ paraḥ'.

statements.claim: Ananta, the thousand-headed serpent, would come born as his elder, and Vishnu's Maya (the power by which the world is deluded) would walk beside him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.23-24: 'vāsudeva-kalānantaḥ sahasra-vadanaḥ svarāṭ' and 'viṣṇor māyā bhagavatī yayā sammohitaṃ jagat'.

statements.claim: The earth's burden had been known and resolved long before she came weeping to that shore.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.21: 'puraiva puṃsāvadhṛto dharā-jvaraḥ' — the earth's fever was already determined by the Person.

DKS_0002.notes: Fully grounded in BP 10.1.18-24. Serpent-coils iconography rated connective (standard tradition, named in-chapter).

statements.claim: Kamsa, the prince who had driven his sister's chariot with his own hands, stood over Devaki with a drawn sword after the wedding.
statements.evidence: Chariot-driving from BP 10.1.33 ('pathi pragrahiṇaṃ kaṃsam' — Kamsa holding the reins) via corpus-chain story DKS_0003; sword drawn: BP 10.1.34 and pack summary 'Kamsa draws his sword on his own sister'.

statements.claim: The voice on the road had said her eighth child would be his death.
statements.evidence: Corpus-chain story DKS_0003 pack: bodiless voice warns the eighth child of Devaki will slay him (BP 10.1.28-33; VP 5.1).

statements.claim: He had become the disgrace of his own line, a man without shame.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.34-35: 'sa khalaḥ pāpo bhojānāṃ kula-pāṃsanaḥ' ... 'nṛśaṃsaṃ nirapatrapam' — wicked defiler of the Bhoja race, cruel, shameless.

statements.claim: Vasudeva argued that death is born with the body, the soul follows karma helplessly, and the body is like a dream body or fire latent in wood.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.37-43: 'mṛtyur janmavatāṃ vīra dehena saha jāyate', 'dehī karmānugo 'vaśaḥ', dream-body and fire-in-wood similes (vv. 40, 42, 50).

statements.claim: He called Devaki his younger sister, a young girl, like a daughter, who had done no wrong.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.44: 'eṣā tavānujā bālā kṛpaṇā putrikopamā'.

statements.claim: Vasudeva, reasoning that the course of destiny is hard to turn, resolved to surrender each son to Kamsa to save Devaki's life, and the promise made Kamsa sheathe his sword.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.46-52: 'mṛtyur buddhimatāpohyo yāvad buddhi-balodayam / pradāya mṛtyave putrān mocaye kṛpaṇām imām', 'gatir dhātur duratyayā', 'prasanna-vadanāmbhojo'; pack excerpt: 'promising to hand over each son born to Devaki; at this Kamsa relents'.

DKS_0004.notes: Two opening callbacks (chariot, road-voice) rest on the preceding story DKS_0003's evidence (BP 10.1.28-33); rest grounded in BP 10.1.34-54. Tradition note (VP 5.1 variant) is acknowledged in the story metadata.

statements.claim: When Devaki bore her first son, Kirtiman, Vasudeva carried the newborn to Kamsa as promised.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.55-56: 'devakī sarva-devatā' ... 'kīrtimantaṃ prathamajaṃ kaṃsāyānakadundubhiḥ'.

statements.claim: Kamsa, moved by Vasudeva's truthfulness, said he had no fear from this child and returned the boy.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.58-60: 'dṛṣṭvā samatvaṃ tac chaureḥ satye caiva vyavasthitim' ... 'pratiyātu kumāro 'yaṃ na hy asmād asti me bhayam'.

statements.claim: The sage Narada came to Kamsa and told him the gods had already begun descending among the cowherds of Vraja like Nanda and in the houses of the Yadavas.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.61-63: 'nandādyā ye vraje gopā ... sarve vai devatā-prāyā' and 'etat kaṃsāya bhagavāñ chaśaṃsābhyetya nāradaḥ'.

statements.claim: Narada revealed that Kamsa himself had been slain by Vishnu in a former life.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.67: 'ātmānam iha sañjātaṃ jānan prāg viṣṇunā hatam'.

statements.claim: Kamsa had Devaki and Vasudeva seized, bound in chains, and shut away; he imprisoned his father Ugrasena, lord of the Yadus, Bhojas and Andhakas, and took the kingdom.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1.65-68: 'devakīṃ vasudevaṃ ca nigṛhya nigaḍair gṛhe' and 'ugrasenaṃ ca pitaraṃ yadu-bhojāndhakādhipam'; summary: 'kills every son she bears, one by one'.

statements.claim: Each child Devaki bore after the first was taken from her and destroyed.
statements.evidence: BP 10.1 summary ('kills every son she bears, one by one'); Harivamsha 1.57: 'destroy all the embryos of Devaki'; VP 5.1.

DKS_0005.notes: Fully grounded in BP 10.1.55-68 + Harivamsha/VP corroboration. 'Gathering like an army in the dark' is connective flourish.

statements.claim: After the night passed, Kamsa summoned his ministers in Mathura, pouring out his fear of the prophecy.
statements.evidence: BP 10.4.28: 'tasyāṃ rātryāṃ vyatītāyāṃ kaṃsa āhūya mantriṇaḥ'; 'before dawn' rendering of night's end is connective timing.

statements.claim: The ministers were the enemies of the gods (demons) in his court.
statements.evidence: BP 10.4.29: 'tam ūcur deva-śatravaḥ' — the enemies of the gods said to him.

statements.claim: They said the gods are battle-fearful: they cast away weapons, lose their chariots, and stand with folded palms, wretched and pleading.
statements.evidence: BP 10.4.31-35: 'devaḥ samara-bhīravaḥ', 'nyasta-śastrā divaukasaḥ', 'vismṛta-śastrāstrān virathān bhaya-saṃvṛtān', 'kṣema-śūrair ... asaṃyuga-vikatthanaiḥ'.

statements.claim: Yet the gods must not be neglected: like a small disease left untended, they will grow strong again.
statements.evidence: BP 10.4.36-37: 'tathāpi devāḥ sāpatnyān nopekṣyā iti manmahe / yathāmayo 'ṅge samupekṣito nṛbhir na śakyate rūḍha-padaś cikitsitum'.

statements.claim: Vishnu is the root of the gods, dwelling wherever eternal dharma stands; the gods live on the brahmanas, cows, Vedas, austerity, truth, self-control and tranquillity.
statements.evidence: BP 10.4.38-41: 'mūlaṃ hi viṣṇur devānāṃ yatra dharmaḥ sanātanaḥ', 'brāhmaṇān brahma-vādinaḥ / viprā gāvaś ca vedāś ca tapaḥ satyaṃ damaḥ śamaḥ'.

statements.claim: They counselled: slay the newborns in every city and village, root out the brahmanas, cows and Vedas, and starve the gods.
statements.evidence: BP 10.4.30, 39-41: 'pura-grāma-vrajādiṣu' and the root-out list; pack excerpt: 'persuade Kamsa to slay every infant in city and village, and to root out the brahmanas, cows and austerity'.

DKS_0006.notes: Fully grounded in BP 10.4.28-41. 'Some weep' is a mild amplification of the wretched/pleading description (connective).

statements.claim: From Mathura Kamsa sent forth demons who could assume any form, bidding them destroy the holy everywhere.
statements.evidence: BP 10.4.42-43: 'sandiśya sādhu-lokasya kadane kadana-priyān' — commanding the slaughter of the righteous; pack excerpt: 'Kamsa sends forth demons who can assume any form, bidding them slaughter the holy everywhere'.

statements.claim: The demons were of restless, grasping nature with minds clouded by darkness.
statements.evidence: BP 10.4.44: 'te vai rajaḥ-prakṛtayas tamasā mūḍha-cetasaḥ'.

statements.claim: They cut short life, scattered prosperity, smeared good names, trampled righteousness and turned blessings to ash.
statements.evidence: BP 10.4.45: 'āyuḥ śriyaṃ yaśo dharmaṃ lokān āśiṣa eva ca' — (destroying) life, prosperity, fame, righteousness, blessings.

statements.claim: Some fell upon the brahmanas and sages who protected infants and kept the rites alive; others watched the roads for young children.
statements.evidence: BP 10.4 summary ('massacre the sages' and infants' protectors'); VP 5.4: 'let every boy in whom there are signs of unusual vigour be slain without remorse'.

statements.claim: Kamsa himself withdrew into his palace and shut its doors, leaving the land to the demons.
statements.evidence: BP 10.4 excerpt: 'himself withdraws into his palace'; VP 5.4: 'Having issued these commands, Kansa retired into his palace'.

DKS_0007.notes: Fully grounded in BP 10.4.42-46 + VP 5.4. Atmospheric details (roads feeling wrong, door-knock fear) are connective.

statements.claim: The gods had already descended in portions — Dharma, Indra, the Wind, the sun, the twin celestial physicians, the priest of the gods, the Vasus and others — and it had not been enough.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.54: portions of Dharma, Indra, Pavana, the two Aswins, the sun, the priest of the gods, the eighth portion of the Vasus had descended; Narada declares the incarnations useless for the destruction of the kings.

statements.claim: Narada appeared in the assembly of the gods with a heavy heart and spoke to Vishnu.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.54: 'That immortal sage Nārada ... with a depressed heart said to Vishnu in the midst of the assembled gods'.

statements.claim: Narada's appearance: bright as fire, eyes like the rising sun, huge matted locks, raiment white as moon-rays, a vina kept like a companion, antelope skin, golden sacred thread, staff and water-pot.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.54: 'effulgent like fire, had eyes like the rising sun and had huge and all-spreading matted locks. He wore a raiment white like the rays of the moon ... carried a big Vina like a female companion ... antelope skin ... sacred thread made of gold. With a staff and Kamandalu in his hands'.

statements.claim: He loved the spark of a quarrel and could read the hidden cause of every dissension.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.54: 'always used to pick up quarrels ... capable of deciphering the secret cause of dissensions in this world'.

statements.claim: Narada said the incarnations of the gods were useless, the kings' quarrel would bear no fruit, and the work could not be accomplished without Narayana's own power — asking why Vishnu had not first sent a portion of his energy.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.54: 'useless have been the incarnations of the gods for the destruction of the kings ... this dissension of the kings will be productive of no fruit. Methinks their work cannot be accomplished without Nārāyana's Yoga' and 'why didst not thou send, first of all, a portion of thy energy to relieve the earth of her burden?'

statements.claim: He named Mathura on the bank of the Yamuna, ringed with prosperous villages, the old haunt of the demon Madhu and his son Lavana, terrors to all creatures, whose hosts had been slain by Vishnu in the old war and reborn as kings.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.54: 'There is a delightful city on the face of the earth by name Mathurā. It is situate on the bank of Yamunā and abounds in many prosperous villages. There was a great Dānava ... by name Madhu ... The great Dānava Lavana was Madhu's son ... a terror to all creatures' and the Daityas slain in the war of which Taraka was the root.

statements.claim: Vishnu resolved to go to the region of men, take a human form, destroy the demons headed by Kamsa, and be born among the cowherds, living happily with them.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.54 excerpt: 'Going to the region of men and assuming a human form I shall bring about the destruction of all those mighty demons headed by Kansa ... Being born as a milkman with them he will live there happily.'

DKS_0008.notes: Grounded in Harivamsha 1.54 (VP 5.1 hair-plucking variant noted in pack, not asserted here). 'A hundred lesser powers' is rhetorical amplification of the ~16 named divine portions — connective, not a specific count claim.

statements.claim: Devaki had been with child seven times; every child that had come from her had been dashed against a stone by Kamsa.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.59: 'Devaki conceived for seven times as described before. Kansa killed the Sargarbhas by dashing them against a stone, as soon as they came out.'

statements.claim: The embryo of Devaki's seventh conception was drawn out of her womb and carried into the womb of Rohini, Vasudeva's other wife.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.59: 'The embryo of the seventh conception was transferred to Rohini'; 1.54 (in DKS_0005 pack): 'take that eldest brother of mine in the seventh month and place him within Rohini's womb'.

statements.claim: At dead of night, while Rohini slept deeply, a discharge of blood came, she dreamed the embryo slipping away, and woke grieving.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.59: 'at the dead of night while Rohini was sleeping a sound sleep there took place a discharge of blood followed by an abortion. Rohini, in a dream, saw the falling of her embryo and when she awoke ... she was greatly pained on not seeing it.'

statements.claim: Rohini, lovely as the moon, was seized with grief; the goddess of sleep told her she had drawn the embryo from Devaki's womb into hers, and the son would be celebrated by the name Sankarshana.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.59: 'Vasudeva's wife Rohini, resembling the moon, was worked up with great anxiety; thereat the goddess of sleep said to her. "O fair one, I have extracted the embryo out of Devaki's womb and placed it in yours. Therefore this your son will be celebrated by the name of Sangkarshana"'.

statements.claim: The name Sankarshana means the one drawn out — carried from one mother into another.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.54: 'On account of his thus being taken away from the womb ... will pass ... by the name of Sangkarsana'; the story's etymological gloss matches this.

statements.claim: The child would one day be known as Balarama, the elder of the two brothers, born before the other.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.54: 'that moon-like elder brother of mine'; the pack index title: 'Devaki's Seventh Embryo Is Transferred to Rohini (Balarama Born)'; BP 10.1.23 (Ananta as elder).

statements.claim: Kamsa's servants kept watching in the prison, unaware; the eighth child would come soon after.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.59 notes Kamsa's servants watched Devaki's eighth conception with great care; the 'empty womb / watching and not knowing' framing is narrative connective tissue.

DKS_0009.notes: Grounded in Harivamsha 1.59 (with 1.54 command context). The 'Balarama' identification is the pack's own index framing.

statements.claim: Kamsa seized the newborn girl and meant to dash her against a stone, as he had done to Devaki's other children
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.59 (pack): 'Kansa killed the Sargarbhas by dashing them against a stone, as soon as they came out'; the girl was 'dashed her against a stone... was not crushed.'

statements.claim: The child slipped from his grip, cast off her human shape and rose into the air above the cell
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.59: 'casting off her human from... she... rose up in the sky.'

statements.claim: She stood clothed in dark blue, crowned and garlanded, her hair unbound
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.59: 'clad in a dark blue raiment... adorned with celestial garlands, pastes, and a shining crown she, with dishevelled hairs.'

statements.claim: She remonstrated with him, and told him the child who would destroy him was already born and was not this girl
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.59: 'remonstrating with Kansa' (passage then truncated); the goddess's announcement that his destroyer is already born is the canonical core of the episode and is presupposed by the pack's own summary of Kamsa's ensuing repentance.

statements.claim: A prophecy had promised that the eighth child of his sister Devaki would be his death, and he destroyed her children one by one, dashing each at birth
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.59: 'she conceived him for the eighth time for whom Kansa had killed her seven children' and 'killed the Sargarbhas by dashing them against a stone, as soon as they came out.'

statements.claim: The goddess rose from the stone and told him his destroyer was alive, hidden beyond his reach
statements.evidence: Same Harivamsha 1.59 episode: the girl-goddess, not crushed, remonstrates with Kamsa; her news that the destroyer is already born underlies Kamsa's shame and confession in the pack's summary.

statements.claim: Kamsa went to Devaki, threw himself at her feet and said 'I throw myself at your feet like a son. Be not offended with me.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Harivamsha 1.59): 'I throw myself at your feet like a son. Be not offended with me.'

statements.claim: Devaki forgave him, saying 'I forgive you for the sin you have committed by destroying my children.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Harivamsha 1.59): 'Devaki said:—"I forgive you for the sin that you have committed by destroying my children."'

statements.claim: Devaki told him he was not the true instrument of what had happened; Time itself had driven these events and no king or mother could have turned them aside
statements.evidence: Index summary: 'Devaki forgives him, saying Time alone is the instrument.' (passage truncated in pack, summary is the intended reading)

DKS_0010.notes: All claims supported; the goddess's speech and Devaki's Time-speech fall in the pack's truncated portion but are attested by the index summary and the excerpted dialogue.

statements.claim: The news came to Kamsa from the lips of the sage Narada, that he was to die at the hands of a child of his sister Devaki
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.57: 'Hearing from Nārada, the account of his death, Kansa, out of fear, began to hold counsels as to how he should destroy Devaki's embryo.'

statements.claim: The warning was not new, for a prophecy at Devaki's wedding had already promised it
statements.evidence: Backstory framing: the wedding prophecy is the corpus's established premise (stated in DKS_0010) but is not quoted in this pack; treated as connective reference to prior events rather than a new factual assertion.

statements.claim: He shut Devaki and Vasudeva in the palace prison, set warders over them, had the months counted from the first sign of a child, and had Vasudeva watched day and night by women and eunuchs, told nothing
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.57: 'Let Devaki, well guarded in the inner appartment by the warders... the women of my harem will count the months from the very first... Let Vasudeva too be kept unconsciously day and night... by eunuchs and women... Let no body disclose to him the secret.'

statements.claim: Kamsa said even an adverse destiny could be turned propitious by the right rites, medicines, care and devotion
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.57: 'Even an adverse destiny is made propitious by well employed mantras, properly administered medicines, care and devotion.'

statements.claim: The six demons, the Saragarbhas, were sons of Kalanemi and grandsons of Hiranyakashipu
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.57: 'Saragarbhas, the sons of Kālanemi... their grand-father Hiranyakasipu.'

statements.claim: They had won a boon from Brahma through hard penance: immunity from gods and men, from every weapon and every curse
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.57: boon to be 'unslayable by the gods, the huge Uragas, Yakshas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Chāranas, men and by the great Rishis... whose weapons are their curses.'

statements.claim: Hiranyakashipu cursed them for seeking the boon from Brahma rather than from him: they would be born from Devaki, one after another, and Kamsa would kill them
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.57: 'By your disregarding me and praying for a boon to the lotus-sprung Brahmā, you have become my enemies... you all six will be born in order from Devaki and Kansa will kill you.'

statements.claim: Kamsa would kill them while they were still in the womb
statements.evidence: Pack says they would be 'born in order from Devaki and Kansa will kill you' and, per Vishnu's words, 'They will be born of her womb and proceed to the abode of Death' - i.e. born first, then killed. Harivamsha 1.59 (same source book, quoted in the corpus) confirms: 'Kansa killed the Sargarbhas by dashing them against a stone, as soon as they came out.' Killing at birth, not in the womb.
statements.resolution: Corrected in story text via consolidation pass.

statements.claim: Vishnu went down into the nether regions where the six demons lay in a death-like sleep, entered their dreams, took hold of their vital breaths and gave them into the keeping of Sleep, commanding her to place them in Devaki's womb in order
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.57: 'repairing to the nether region Vishnu arrived... possessing death-like sleep. Thereupon entering into the body of the Saragarbhas in a state of dream... caught hold of their vital breaths and consigned them to the care of sleep... place them in order in the womb of Devaki.'

statements.claim: The first six would be born and pass on to the house of Death, and Kamsa's fear, believing it was averting fate, would only serve it
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.57: 'They will be born of her womb and proceed to the abode of Death. Kansa's efforts will be baffled and Devaki's labour will be crowned with success.'

statements.claim: In the seventh month of Devaki's seventh conception, Sleep was to lift the elder brother and set him in the womb of Rohini, Vasudeva's other wife; the child who would be known as Balarama (Sankarshana)
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.57: 'when my gentle portion will be conceived by Devaki in her seventh conception, take that eldest brother of mine in the seventh month and place him within Rohini's womb... will pass... by the name of Sangkarsana.'

statements.claim: Sleep herself, who would be called Yogamaya, was to be born on earth as the daughter of Yashoda, Nanda's wife
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.57: 'you will be conceived by Yashodā, the best of milk-women, the most beloved wife of Nanda'; Harivamsha 1.59: Yashodā 'conceived the goddess of sleep, begotten of a portion of Vishnu's energy.'

statements.claim: Vishnu entered the heart of Vasudeva, and from Vasudeva the Lord passed into Devaki, a portion of the divine taking its place in her womb
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.15-16 (the Lord enters Vasudeva's heart/mind); Vishnu Purana 5.2: 'Hari... became incarnate as the conception of the former princess.'

statements.claim: Devaki, carrying the support of the whole world, began to glow with a light that filled the prison
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.17-18: 'sa bibhrat pauruṣaṃ dhāma bhrājamāno yathā raviḥ... sā devakī sarva-jagan-nivāsa-nivāsa-bhūtā nitarāṃ na reje.'

statements.claim: Kamsa came to look on his sister and saw in her the presence of the very one who would destroy him, knew his death had come near, but stayed his hand
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.19-22: Kamsa sees her illumining the house and thinks 'this is Hari, the taker of my life'; 'he who lives by extreme cruelty is as good as dead'; 'from that most cruel intent he desisted.'

statements.claim: He reasoned the child, once born, would be easier to destroy than the mother who carried it
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.20-22 (Kamsa's deliberation against striking now; 'from that most cruel intent he desisted'); pack summary: 'Kamsa, though uneasy, refrains from harming her.'

statements.claim: He sat and lay down and stood and ate and walked the earth, waiting and watching her
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.23: 'āsīnaḥ saṃviśaṃs tiṣṭhan bhuñjānaḥ paryaṭan mahīm' (sitting, lying, standing, eating, wandering the earth).

corrections.original_sentence: For seeking that boon from Brahma rather than from him, their grandfather Hiranyakashipu had turned on them in fury and cursed them: they would be born from Devaki, one after another, and Kamsa would kill them while they were still in the womb.
corrections.suggested: For seeking that boon from Brahma rather than from him, their grandfather Hiranyakashipu had turned on them in fury and cursed them: they would be born from Devaki, one after another, and Kamsa would kill them as soon as they came into the world.

DKS_0011.notes: One CONTRADICTED claim: the pack (HV 1.57) has the six born first and then killed ('born in order from Devaki and Kansa will kill you'; 'born of her womb and proceed to the abode of Death'), and HV 1.59 describes dashing them against a stone as soon as they came out - the story's 'while they were still in the womb' is wrong. Everything else maps cleanly to BP 10.2.15-23 and HV 1.57.

statements.claim: Brahma and Shiva came down to the prison, and with them the sage Narada and a host of gods and seers
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.24: 'brahmā bhavaś ca tatraitya munibhir nāradādibhiḥ.'

statements.claim: They had come to praise what was hidden in Devaki's womb, and their words were addressed to the child rather than the mother
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.25-39 are the gods' hymns to the Lord in the womb; the address to Devaki comes only at the close (10.2.40).

statements.claim: They praised him as the source and the abode of truth itself, the one on whom all truth rests
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.25: 'satya-vrataṃ satya-paraṃ tri-satyaṃ satyasya yoniṃ nihitaṃ ca satye satyasya satyam.'

statements.claim: They called him the single root from which all existence grows, one tree with its two fruits and its many branches, its three roots and its several tastes, the one path through the world's turnings
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.26: 'ekāyano 'sau dvi-phalas tri-mūlaś catū-rasaḥ pañca-vidhaḥ ṣaḍ-ātmā' (one path/refuge, two fruits, three roots, four tastes, five kinds, sixfold self - the cosmic-tree simile of the commentators).

statements.claim: He is the origin of all things, the one who sustains them, and the grace that attends them
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.27: 'tvam eka evāsya sataḥ prasūtis tvaṃ sannidhānaṃ tvam anugrahaś ca.'

statements.claim: They said he had no cause to be born at all, and his coming could be explained only as play, taken up for the welfare of all that moves and all that stands still
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.38 ('na te 'bhavasyeśa bhavasya kāraṇaṃ vinā vinodaṃ') and 10.2.28 ('bibharṣi rūpāṇy... kṣemāya lokasya carācarasya').

statements.claim: Devotees cross the terrible ocean of birth and death on the boat of his lotus feet, while those who believe themselves free but turn away from him fall back into the world
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.29-31: 'bhavārṇavaṃ bhīmam... bhavat-padāmbhoruha-nāvam'; 'vimukta-māninas... patanty adho.'

statements.claim: Through pure goodness, by the rites of the Vedas, by discipline and by the stillness of meditation people come to honor him, and the one who only hears and repeats his auspicious names is not drawn again into the round of birth
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.33 ('sattvaṃ viśuddhaṃ... veda-kriyā-yoga-tapaḥ-samādhibhis tavārhaṇaṃ') and 10.2.36 ('śṛṇvan gṛṇan saṃsmarayaṃś ca cintayan nāmāni... na bhavāya kalpate').

statements.claim: They sang of his descents - the fish, the boar, the man-lion, the tortoise, the swan - and of forms taken among kings and sages and gods
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.39: 'matsyāśva-kacchapa-nṛsiṃha-varāha-haṃsa-rājanya-vipra-vibudheṣu kṛtāvatāraḥ.'

statements.claim: 'Fortunate are you, mother, for the Supreme Person rests in your womb. Do not fear the king of the Bhojas, who is near his end. Your son will be the protector of the Yadavas.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.40: 'diṣṭyāmba te kukṣi-gataḥ paraḥ pumān... mābhūd bhayaṃ bhoja-pater mumūrṣor goptā yadūnāṃ bhavitā tavātmajaḥ.'

statements.claim: The burden of the earth, grown too heavy, was about to be lifted, and the earth and heavens would be marked by his auspicious footprints
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.37: 'bhuvo bhāro 'panītas tava janmaneśituḥ... diṣṭyāṅkitāṃ tvat-padakaiḥ suśobhanair drakṣyāma gāṃ dyāṃ ca.'

statements.claim: Having sung his glories, they returned to their own world as quietly as they had come
statements.evidence: BP 10.2.41-42 close the hymn; pack summary: 'having sung his glories they return to heaven.'

DKS_0012.notes: All statements map to BP 10.2.24-42; the theological praises are faithful renderings of the Sanskrit verses.

statements.claim: Still lying where he had been born, the child took on a four-armed form with lotus-petal eyes, holding conch, discus, mace and lotus
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.8: 'catur-bhujaṃ śaṅkha-gadādy-udāyudham'; pack summary: 'holding conch, discus, mace and lotus.'

statements.claim: A crown of precious stone rested on his head, bright earrings hung from his ears, and his hair fell in a thousand shining locks
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.9: 'mahārha-vaidūrya-kirīṭa-kuṇḍala-tviṣā pariṣvakta-sahasra-kuntalam.'

statements.claim: Vasudeva's eyes widened with wonder; he bowed his head, folded his hands and praised the Lord he held as his son
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.10-11: 'vismayotphulla-vilocanaḥ... natāṅgaḥ kṛta-dhīḥ kṛtāñjaliḥ.'

statements.claim: Vasudeva praised the three colors he assumes: white that preserves, red that creates, dark that brings an age to its end
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.19: 'bibharṣi śuklaṃ... varṇam' (for sthitī), 'sargāya raktaṃ rajasopabṛṃhitaṃ', 'kṛṣṇaṃ ca varṇaṃ tamasā janātyaye.'

statements.claim: He is the one who creates, sustains and withdraws the three worlds by his own power, never touched by the qualities he sets in motion
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.18: 'tvatto 'sya janma-sthiti-saṃyamān... tvad-āśrayatvād upacaryate guṇaiḥ.'

statements.claim: The child could not be known through the senses but only through the discerning mind
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.16: 'bhavān buddhy-anumeya-lakṣaṇair grāhyair guṇaiḥ sann api tad-guṇāgrahaḥ.'

statements.claim: He had come down into his own house to protect the world
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.20: 'tvam asya lokasya vibho rirakṣiṣur gṛhe 'vatīrṇo 'si.'

statements.claim: The cruel Kamsa had already killed every child born before this one, and even now, hearing of this birth, he would be coming with weapons in his hands
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.21: 'ayaṃ tv asabhyas tava janma nau gṛhe śrutvāgrajāṃs te nyavadhīt... sa te 'vatāraṃ... śrutvādhunaivābhisaraty udāyudhaḥ.'

statements.claim: Devaki praised him as the unseen light, the changeless witness whom no name and no form can hold, the lamp that lights the soul itself, the abode of peace
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.23 ('rūpaṃ yat tat prāhur avyaktam ādyaṃ brahma jyotir nirguṇaṃ nirvikāram... sa tvaṃ sākṣād viṣṇur adhyātma-dīpaḥ') and 10.3.25 ('taṃ tveśānaṃ kṣema-dhāma prapadye').

statements.claim: 'May that wicked one never learn of your birth. Save us from the terrible son of Ugrasena. Hide this extraordinary form.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.28 ('janma te mayy asau pāpo mā vidyān'), 10.3.27 ('sa tvaṃ ghorād ugrasenātmajān nas trāhi'), 10.3.29 ('upasaṃhara viśvātmann ado rūpam alaukikam').

statements.claim: He recalled a time before this life when they had been a childless couple, set by Brahma to bring forth children, who turned from worldly pleasures and performed long austerities, living on fallen leaves and air, their minds held still
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.32-34: 'yuvāṃ vai brahmaṇādiṣṭau prajā-sarge... ajuṣṭa-grāmya-viṣayāv anapatyau... varṣa-vātātapa-hima-gharma-kāla-guṇān anu śīrṇa-parṇānilāhārāv upaśāntena cetasā.'

statements.claim: At the end he had appeared and offered a boon, and they asked for a son like himself, seeing no one in the world who could equal him in character and generosity
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.36-40: 'tadā vāṃ parituṣṭo 'ham... prādurāsaṃ varada-rāḍ... adṛṣṭvānyatamaṃ loke śīlaudārya-guṇaiḥ samam.'

statements.claim: He had been born to them once in that first life, and again as the son of Aditi born of Kashyapa; this third birth came with the same form, shown to them so they would remember
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.41-43: 'tayor vāṃ punar evāham adityām āsa kaśyapāt... tṛtīye 'smin bhave 'haṃ vai tenaiva vapuṣātha vām... prāg-janma-smaraṇāya.'

statements.claim: 'You have known me as your son and as the divine, again and again.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.44: 'yuvāṃ māṃ putra-bhāvena brahma-bhāvena cāsakṛt.'

statements.claim: Then he withdrew the dazzling form; the four arms, crown, earrings and thousand locks were gone, and an ordinary infant lay in Vasudeva's arms
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.45-46 (Śuka: the Lord then resumed the mortal aspect; pack summary: 'then becomes an ordinary infant again').

DKS_0014.notes: All statements match BP 10.3.8-45, including the past-births recollection (Aditi/Kashyapa, third birth).

statements.claim: Years afterward, Uddhava told the story from its true beginning
statements.evidence: BP 3.2.24-25 is Uddhava's recollection (pack summary: 'Uddhava said...').

statements.claim: The earth had grown heavy, could no longer bear what rested upon her, prayed, and the Lord agreed to descend to relieve her
statements.evidence: Pack summary: 'the Lord, prayed to by the earth, came to relieve her.'

statements.claim: He was born of Vasudeva and Devaki, born in a prison belonging to the Bhoja king, Kamsa
statements.evidence: BP 3.2.24: 'vasudevasya devakyāṃ jāto bhojendra-bandhane.'

statements.claim: Vasudeva, fearing Kamsa, carried the child away to the settlement of Nanda, into the pasture lands of Vraja
statements.evidence: BP 3.2.25: 'tato nanda-vrajam itaḥ pitrā kaṃsād vibibhyatā.'

statements.claim: He lived there eleven years, with Balarama through all of it, and his glory stayed concealed
statements.evidence: Pack summary: 'he dwelt in Nanda's Vraja for eleven years with Balarama, his glory concealed.'

statements.claim: No one in the settlement knew what they sheltered; the village saw only a cowherd's son
statements.evidence: Consistent with 'his glory concealed' in the pack; the village's ignorance is connective elaboration of that concealment.

DKS_0016.notes: Compact pack (BP 3.2.24-25 only); every concrete claim matches it.

statements.claim: Vasudeva had been set at liberty, and the first place he went was to the waggon of Nanda the cowherd
statements.evidence: VP 5.5: 'WHEN Vasudeva was set at liberty, he went to the waggon of Nanda.'

statements.claim: Nanda had come down from his pastures to the city on business, to pay the year's tribute, and had camped with his people and waggons
statements.evidence: VP 5.5: 'The yearly tribute has been paid to the king'; 'their goods being placed in their waggons.'

statements.claim: Vasudeva found Nanda rejoicing, for a son had been born to him in the night, and congratulated him on having a son in his old age
statements.evidence: VP 5.5: 'found Nanda there rejoicing that a son was born to him... congratulated him on having a son in his old age.'

statements.claim: Vasudeva urged Nanda not to tarry near the court once his business was settled, and to rise at once and set off for his own pastures
statements.evidence: VP 5.5: 'men of property should not tarry near the court, when the business that brought them there has been transacted. Why do you delay...? Up, Nanda, quickly, and set off to your own pastures.'

statements.claim: Vasudeva asked that the boy Rohini had borne him accompany Nanda and be brought up in his home as if he were Nanda's own son
statements.evidence: VP 5.5: 'let this boy, the son whom Rohiṇí has borne me, accompany you, and be brought up by you as this your own son.'

statements.claim: Nanda agreed; the cowherds loaded their goods into their waggons, their taxes paid, and returned to their village - Nanda setting out for Gokula with a son born to him in the night and Rohini's boy entrusted to his care
statements.evidence: VP 5.5: 'Accordingly Nanda and the other cowherds, their goods being placed in their waggons, and their taxes having been paid to the king, returned to their village'; chapter title: 'Nanda returns with the infants Krishṇa and Balaráma to Gokula.'

statements.claim: The boys themselves would remember none of it: not the city, nor the fear, nor the father who had arranged their going
statements.evidence: Reflective close; not asserted in VP 5.5 but plausible connective narration.

DKS_0017.notes: All claims track VP 5.5 nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: That night, in two households far apart, Devaki bore a son in the prison of Mathura and Yashoda bore a daughter among the cowherds of Vraja
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.59: 'Devaki gave birth to Vishnu and Yashodā to that daughter' in the same night ('In the auspicious midnight... Devaki gave birth to Vishnu and Yashodā to that daughter'); BP 10.3.50.

statements.claim: Vasudeva came to the cowherd settlement carrying his newborn son and found the cowherds sunk in sleep, no one awake to see him
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.50: 'nanda-vrajaṃ śaurir upetya tatra tān gopān prasuptān upalabhya nidrayā.'

statements.claim: He laid his son in Yashoda's bed, took up the girl-child born to her that night, and lifted her into his arms in his son's place
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.50: 'sutaṃ yaśodā-śayane nidhāya tat-sutām upādāya punar gṛhān agāt'; Harivamsha 1.59: 'Placing his son in her house against her knowledge he brought her daughter.'

statements.claim: He carried the girl back to the city and the prison and laid her down beside Devaki on her bed
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.51: 'devakyāḥ śayane nyasya vasudevo 'tha dārikām.'

statements.claim: He quietly took up again the chains that held him, so that nothing would seem to have changed
statements.evidence: Pack summary: 'returns to the prison, where he lays her beside Devaki and resumes his chains.'

statements.claim: Yashoda woke with no knowledge of what had happened; she did not realize what had been born to her that night, was never told, and the child would be her son
statements.evidence: BP 10.3.52: 'yaśodā nanda-patnī ca jātaṃ param abudhyata'; Harivamsha 1.59: 'against her knowledge.'

statements.claim: Neither of the two mothers would ever know the exchange
statements.evidence: Consistent with the pack (Yashoda 'did not realize'; Devaki later pleads for the girl as her own child in HV 1.59), though framed as narrative summary.

DKS_0019.notes: All claims match BP 10.3.50-52 and HV 1.59.

statements.claim: Nanda had the auspicious benedictions recited for his newborn son and performed the birth-rite in the proper way, with bathing and purification
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.1: 'vācayitvā svastyayanaṃ jāta-karmātmajasya vai'; 10.5.3: 'kālena snāna-śaucābhyāṃ saṃskārais tapasejyayā.'

statements.claim: At the proper time the priests and bards - sutas, magadhas and vandins - recited their verses of blessing
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.4: 'saumaṅgalya-giro viprāḥ sūta-māgadha-vandinaḥ.'

statements.claim: To the priests he gave a great number of adorned cows
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.2: 'dhenūnāṃ niyute prādād viprebhyaḥ samalaṅkṛte' (two hundred thousand adorned cows).

statements.claim: All of Vraja was swept and sprinkled; the doorways, courtyards and inner rooms of the houses were washed clean
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.5: 'vrajaḥ sammṛṣṭa-saṃsikta-dvārājira-gṛhāntaraḥ.'

statements.claim: The cattle - cows, bulls and young calves - were led out smeared with turmeric and oil and decked with cloth and ornaments
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.6-7: 'gāvo vṛṣā vatsatarā haridrā-taila-rūṣitāḥ mahārha-vastrābharaṇa-kañcukoṣṇīṣa-bhūṣitāḥ.'

statements.claim: The cowherd women, hearing that a son had been born to Yashoda, came in a bright procession with fresh kumkum, jeweled earrings and necklaces, garments of many colors and garlands, and blessed the child 'May he live long'
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.8-11: 'gopyaś cākarṇya muditā yaśodāyāḥ sutodbhavam'; 'nava-kuṅkuma-kiñjalka...'; 'sumṛṣṭa-maṇi-kuṇḍala-niṣka-kaṇṭhyaś citrāmbarāḥ... śikhā-cyuta-mālya-varṣāḥ'; 'tā āśiṣaḥ prayuñjānāś ciraṃ pāhīti bālake.'

statements.claim: All manner of instruments sounded through the settlement, for this was a great festival
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.12: 'avādyanta vicitrāṇi vāditrāṇi mahotsave.'

statements.claim: The cowherds, full of joy, sprinkled one another with curd, milk, ghee and water
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.13: 'gopāḥ parasparaṃ hṛṣṭā dadhi-kṣīra-ghṛtāmbubhiḥ.'

statements.claim: Nanda, generous-hearted, gave to everyone who came: clothes, ornaments and cattle, honoring each as was fitting
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.14-15: 'nando mahā-manās tebhyo vāso 'laṅkāra-go-dhanam tais taiḥ kāmair adīnātmā yathocitam apūjayat.'

statements.claim: He congratulated the blessed Rohini
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.16: 'rohiṇī ca mahā-bhāgā nanda-gopābhinanditā.'

statements.claim: It was said afterward that from that day Nanda's Vraja was rich in every way
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.17: 'tata ārabhya nandasya vrajaḥ sarva-samṛddhimān.'

statements.claim: Once a year, the chief of the cowherds had business in the royal city; Nanda of Gokula made the journey to Mathura to pay the tribute his people owed the crown.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.18: Nanda travels to Mathura to pay the yearly tax; index summary 'annual tribute'.

statements.claim: He traveled plainly with a few attendants and bullock carts, a road he knew well.
statements.evidence: No detail of attendants/carts in pack; generic travel framing consistent with the yearly tax errand.

statements.claim: In Gokula, only days before, a son had been born to him, and the rejoicing had not yet cooled in his house.
statements.evidence: Pack does not date the birth; corpus chain previous story is 'Nanda Celebrates the Birth of His Son' (DKS_0020); recent birth consistent with BP 10.5.22 greeting in next episode.

statements.claim: Vasudeva heard that Nanda had arrived and rose at once from where he sat and went out to meet him, sending no one ahead.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.19-20: vasudeva upaśrutya bhrātaraṃ nandam āgatam / taṃ dṛṣṭvā sahasotthāya.

statements.claim: He threw his arms around Nanda and held him close, as though life itself had returned to his body, all the long waiting ended in that embrace.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.20: dehaḥ prāṇam ivāgatam ('as if life had returned to his body'); index summary: 'Vasudeva joyfully embraces him as a brother'.

statements.claim: They were not brothers by blood; Nanda was a cowherd chief and Vasudeva a man of standing in Mathura.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.18-19: Nanda is chief of Gokula's cowherds (gopān gokula-rakṣāyāṃ), Vasudeva a Mathura noble; 'brother' is the source's own address (bhrātaram).

statements.claim: For a long moment the two men stood together in the street; the tribute, carts and accounts could wait.
statements.evidence: Atmosphere/scene-setting; no counter-evidence in pack.

statements.claim: Nanda was moved by the warmth, having expected the city to be all business and no welcome.
statements.evidence: Internal reflection framing; not asserted in pack but not contradicted.

DKS_0021.notes: Faithful to BP 10.5.18-20. The tribute errand, Vasudeva's sudden rising and life-returning embrace all match the Sanskrit; 'brothers' matches the source's bhrātaram address. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Vasudeva honored Nanda, seated him comfortably, and asked after his health with warmth.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.21: pūjitaḥ sukham āsīnaḥ pṛṣṭvānāmayam ādṛtaḥ.

statements.claim: Vasudeva said it was fortunate that Nanda, who for so many years had no child, now had a son to be the joy of his later years.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.22: diṣṭyā bhrātaḥ pravayasa idānīm aprajasya te.

statements.claim: The wheel of the world turns strangely; the friendship of dear ones does not stay fixed in a single spot, for each is carried by his own fortune.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.23-24: diṣṭyā saṃsāra-cakre 'smin vartamānaḥ punar-bhavaḥ / naikatra priya-saṃvāsaḥ suhṛdāṃ citra-karmaṇām.

statements.claim: He asked whether the cattle were free of disease and the water and grass plentiful; Nanda answered the herds were healthy and the pastures green.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.25: kaccit paśavyaṃ nirujaṃ bhūry-ambu-tṛṇa-vīrudham; Nanda's reply implied by his reassuring speech (10.5.28-29).

statements.claim: Vasudeva asked after his own two sons being raised in Nanda's care in Vraja, and after the mother who was with them.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.26: bhrātar mama sutaḥ kaccin mātrā saha bhavad-vraje.

statements.claim: A man's true wealth is not his goods but his friends, and through friends every aim a man holds in life is fulfilled.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.27: puṃsas tri-vargo vihitaḥ suhṛdo hy anubhāvitaḥ.

statements.claim: Nanda said the affairs of men are ruled by forces no one can fully foresee, and even a king's cruelty is the working of some unseen fate.
statements.evidence: BP 10.5.28-29 (śrī-nanda uvāca): nūnaṃ hy adṛṣṭa-niṣṭho 'yam adṛṣṭa-paramo janaḥ — men are governed by the unseen; the kingly-cruelty gloss matches the fate-flavored original and index summary.

statements.claim: Vasudeva urged Nanda not to linger in Mathura, saying great disturbances and evil omens were rising in Gokula and would not wait for his return.
statements.evidence: Index excerpt (BP 10.5.21-32): 'tells him not to linger, for great disturbances are rising in Gokula'.

statements.claim: Nanda did not argue; he gathered his men, hitched their carts, and set out at once for Gokula.
statements.evidence: Index excerpt: 'Nanda and his men hasten back with their carts.'

DKS_0022.notes: Faithful to BP 10.5.21-32. The seated greeting, the childless-years felicitation, the questions about cattle/water/grass and the hidden sons with their mother, the friends-as-wealth maxim, Nanda's fate speech, and the urgent warning all trace to the Sanskrit. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Kamsa, the king of Mathura, had not forgotten the child he feared; the prophecy had told him Devaki's child would one day take his life, and he had tried cages, guards and the sword.
statements.evidence: Not in the cited excerpt (BP 10.6.1-5); backstory framing from prior corpus episodes (Devaki prophecy, BP 10.1-4) consistent with kaṃsena prahitā in 10.6.1; not contradicted by the pack.

statements.claim: Putana was a demoness whose trade was children; wherever she went infants died, drawn to places where no protective hymn was chanted.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.1-2: pūtanā bāla-ghātinī / na yatra śravaṇādīni rakṣo-ghnāni sva-karmasu; index excerpt 'wandering among villages killing infants'.

statements.claim: She flew through the air from one settlement to the next, and one day rose into the air and turned toward Nanda's Gokula.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.3: sā khe-cary ekadotpatya pūtanā nanda-gokulam.

statements.claim: By her magic she took the form of a lovely woman — hair bound with fresh jasmine, waist slender, hips full, dressed in fine cloth, ears bright with ornaments, face framed in shining curls.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.4: keśa-bandha-vyatiṣakta-mallikā, bṛhan-nitamba-stana-kṛcchra-madhyamām, suvāsasaṃ, kalpita-karṇa-bhūṣaṇa, tviṣollasat-kuntala-maṇḍitānanām.

statements.claim: Her smiles and sidelong glances charmed the cowherd women, who took her for the goddess of fortune come to look upon her lord.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.5: valgu-smitāpāṅga-visarga-vīkṣitair mano harantīṃ vanitāṃ vrajaukasām; gopyaḥ śriyaṃ draṣṭum ivāgatāṃ patim.

statements.claim: The cowherd women welcomed her freely and showed her no suspicion; no one asked her name or turned her away.
statements.evidence: Implied by the gopis' being charmed and mistaking her for Śrī (10.6.5); not a separate asserted fact in the pack.

statements.claim: And somewhere in that village a child slept — the child Kamsa had sent her to find.
statements.evidence: Dramatic framing leading into the next episode (Putana's attack, BP 10.6.6-12); consistent with her mission (kaṃsena prahitā).

DKS_0023.notes: Faithful to BP 10.6.1-5. The child-killing demoness, the protective-hymn detail, the flight into Gokula, and the full physical portrait (jasmine hair, full hips, slender waist, fine clothes, ear ornaments, curls) plus the Śrī-goddess mistake all match the Sanskrit. The prophecy backstory is prior-canon framing, not a fabrication. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Putana's body, released from the lovely form, lay where she had fallen — so vast that as she fell she crushed the trees for a long stretch around her.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.13: patamāno 'pi tad-dehas tri-gavyūty-antara-drumān ('crushing trees within three gavyūti').

statements.claim: Her mouth gaped wide with teeth like the shafts of a plow; her nostrils opened like mountain caves; her eyes were deep pits.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.14-15: īṣā-mātrogra-daṃṣṭrāsyaṃ, giri-kandara-nāsikam, andha-kūpa-gabhīrākṣaṃ.

statements.claim: The cowherds and their women trembled at the sight and none would draw near.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.16: santatrasuḥ sma tad vīkṣya gopā gopyaḥ kalevaram.

statements.claim: Krishna lay playing on the corpse's chest, utterly unafraid.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.17: bālaṃ ca tasyā urasi krīḍantam akutobhayam.

statements.claim: Yasoda and Rohini came forward and gathered him up.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.18: yaśodā-rohiṇībhyāṃ tāḥ samaṃ bālasya sarvataḥ.

statements.claim: The women bathed the child first with cow's urine and then with the fine dust of the cow pen.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.19: go-mūtreṇa snāpayitvā punar go-rajasārbhakam.

statements.claim: Touching and sprinkling water, they passed their hands over each part of him — feet, hands, waist, heart, throat, head — and chanted protective invocations over each.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.20-21: gopyaḥ saṃspṛṣṭa-salilā aṅgeṣu karayoḥ pṛthak; the body-part litany (aṅghri... kaṭi... hṛt... kaṇṭha... mukha) in verse 21.

statements.claim: They invoked the discus-holder before him, the mace-holder behind, the bow and sword at his sides, the conch above, Garuda on the ground, and the Lord of all everywhere around.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.22: cakry agrataḥ saha-gado harir astu paścāt / tvat-pārśvayor dhanur-asī madhu-hājanaś ca / koṇeṣu śaṅkha urugāya upary upendras / tārkṣyaḥ kṣitau haladharaḥ puruṣaḥ samantāt.

statements.claim: They named every spirit that preys on children and bade them stay far away.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.26-28: ḍākinyo yātudhānyaś ca kuṣmāṇḍā ye 'rbhaka-grahāḥ... pūtanā mātṛkādayaḥ... bāla-grahāś ca ye.

statements.claim: Meanwhile Nanda and the other cowherds were on the road back from Mathura; they reached the village to find the great body and the child safe, and marveled.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.30: tāvan nandādayo gopā mathurāyā vrajaṃ gatāḥ.

statements.claim: They said surely he was a great sage or a master of yoga, to have come through such a thing untouched.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.31: nūnaṃ batarṣiḥ sañjāto yogeśo vā samāsa saḥ.

statements.claim: They took up axes, cut the vast body to pieces, carried the pieces away and set them alight.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.32: kalevaraṃ paraśubhiś chittvā tat te vrajaukasaḥ.

statements.claim: As the body burned, the smoke carried a fragrance like aloe — sweet and clean — for the demoness had been granted the reward of a mother.
statements.evidence: BP 10.6.33: dahyamānasya dehasya dhūmaś cāguru-saurabhaḥ; index summary: 'for she attained a mother's reward.'

DKS_0025.notes: Faithful to BP 10.6.13-33. The crushed trees (three gavyūti), plow-shaft teeth, cave nostrils, well-deep eyes, playing infant, cow-urine/dust bath, full body-part protective litany, weapon-holders invocation, child-spirits list, Nanda's return from Mathura, axe dismemberment, and aloe-fragrant smoke all match the Sanskrit; the mother's-reward gloss is the index summary's own reading. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: On the day of a certain child's birth-rites in Gokula, a loaded cart overturned for no reason anyone could see, with only an infant near it.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.4-7: set during the autthānika ceremony; ano... śiśor alpa-pravāla-mṛdv-aṅghri-hataṃ vyavartata; kathaṃ svayaṃ vai śakaṭaṃ viparyagāt.

statements.claim: Yasoda, Nanda's wife, had bathed and purified herself; brahmins had recited benedictions over her newborn son and been honored with gifts.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.4: nandasya patnī kṛta-majjanādikaṃ vipraiḥ kṛta-svastyayanaṃ supūjitaiḥ.

statements.claim: The women of Vraja had gathered for the rite of the child's first rising, and Yasoda moved among them greeting each one.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.5: autthānikautsukya-manā manasvinī samāgatān pūjayatī vrajaukasaḥ; 10.7.7: autthānike karmaṇi yāḥ samāgatāḥ.

statements.claim: In the press of it all the child was set down for a moment in the shade of a cart heaped with vessels.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.6: adhaḥ-śayānasya śiśor ('the child lying beneath'); laden cart implied by the scattered vessels (10.7.6-7, Harivamsha 'pitcher... broken').

statements.claim: He began to cry and kicked; one small foot, soft and tender as a new leaf, struck the underside of the cart.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.6: alpa-pravāla-mṛdv-aṅghri-hataṃ (struck by the tender, coral-soft foot); Harivamsha: 'raising up his legs he overturned the carriage with one of them... began to cry for milk.'

statements.claim: The cart overturned violently — wheels wrenched from the axle, shaft and yoke broken, vessels spilled and shattered.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.6 vyavartata; Harivamsha 1.61: 'The axles, the pitcher and the rod were all broken'; index excerpt: 'its wheels and axle broken and its vessels scattered.'

statements.claim: The crash brought Yasoda, the women of Vraja, and Nanda and the other men running; they stood astonished, asking how a cart could turn over by itself, with no wind and no animal near.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.7: dṛṣṭvā yaśodā-pramukhā vraja-striya... nandādayaś cādbhuta-darśanākulāḥ / kathaṃ svayaṃ vai śakaṭaṃ viparyagāt; Harivamsha: 'without any wind... without the fighting of the bulls.'

statements.claim: The cowherd boys and girls said the child did it, kicked it with his own foot, but the grown men shook their heads, dismissing it as child-talk.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.8-9: ūcur avyavasita-matīn gopān gopīś ca bālakāḥ / na te śraddadhire gopā bāla-bhāṣitam ity uta; Harivamsha 1.61: boys said 'this boy upsetting the carriage with his feet'; the milkmen 'placed no confidence in the words of the boys.'

statements.claim: Yasoda was afraid of the evil eye and of unkind influence drawn to a child who had been part of such a wonder; she gathered up her crying son.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.10: rudantaṃ sutam ādāya yaśodā graha-śaṅkitā (fearing a grasping influence/graha).

statements.claim: The cowherds, strong men all, set the cart upright again and gathered up what remained of its goods.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.11: pūrvavat sthāpitaṃ gopair balibhiḥ sa-paricchadam.

statements.claim: Nanda had the protective rites recited over his son with the words of the three Vedas, and brought out his finest cows adorned with cloth, garlands and gold, standing with a steady heart while blessings were spoken.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.12-16: sāmarg-yajur-upākṛtaiḥ; vācayitvā svastyayanaṃ nanda-gopaḥ samāhitaḥ; gāvaḥ sarva-guṇopetā vāsaḥ-srag-rukma-mālinīḥ; viprā mantra-vido yuktās tair yāḥ proktās tathāśiṣaḥ.

statements.claim: The story follows the Bhagavata's placement of the episode during the birth-rites (not the Harivamsha's river-bathing setting), as disclosed in the tradition_note.
statements.evidence: tradition_note: 'The Harivamsha sets this episode while Yasoda is away bathing at the river... the Bhagavata Purana places it during the child's birth-rites'; story matches the Bhagavata setting.

DKS_0026.notes: Faithful to BP 10.7.3-16 (primary), corroborated by Harivamsha 1.61 and Vishnu Purana 5.6. The birth-rites setting, tender-foot kick, shattered axle/yoke/vessels, everyone-runs astonishment, children's truth vs adults' disbelief, graha-fearing Yasoda, cart re-erection, and three-Veda rites with adorned cows all match. Variant-setting issue is correctly disclosed. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Yasoda sat with her son on her lap, dandling him and looking into his face.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.17: ekadāroham ārūḍhaṃ lālayantī sutaṃ satī.

statements.claim: Without warning the child grew heavy in her arms, so heavy she could hardly hold him; astonished, she set him down on the ground.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.18: bhūmau nidhāya taṃ gopī vismitā bhāra-pīḍitā.

statements.claim: A dry, violent wind tore through the lanes of Gokula, lifting dust and grit in a spinning wheel.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.20: gokulaṃ sarvam āvṛṇvan muṣṇaṃś cakṣūṃṣi reṇubhiḥ; 10.7.23: khara-pavana-cakra-pāṃśu-varṣe (fierce wind-wheel raining dust).

statements.claim: This was Trinavarta, a demon in the service of Kamsa, sent by his master in the shape of a whirlwind to do what the king could not.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.19: daityo nāmnā tṛṇāvartaḥ kaṃsa-bhṛtyaḥ praṇoditaḥ; index summary 'Kamsa's servant Trinavarta, in the form of a whirlwind, snatches the child away.'

statements.claim: The spinning dust filled the whole settlement and stole the light and sight of everyone in it; for a moment Gokula went dark and no one could see the person beside them.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.20-22: muṣṇaṃś cakṣūṃṣi reṇubhiḥ; muhūrtam abhavad goṣṭhaṃ rajasā tamasāvṛtam / nāpaśyat kaścanātmānaṃ paraṃ cāpi vimohitaḥ.

statements.claim: When the dust began to settle, Yasoda looked for her son and he was gone; she searched the spot and his path but the wind had scoured the ground clean, and she could not find him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.23: suta-padavīm abalāvilakṣya mātā ('the mother, unable to trace her son's path').

statements.claim: The other women of Gokula came running with tears on their faces, for the village's dearest child had been taken.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.24: ruditam anuniśamya tatra gopyo bhṛśam anutapta-dhiyo 'śru-pūrṇa-mukhyaḥ.

statements.claim: High above the blinded village the whirlwind rose with its small captive, believing it was carrying out the errand it had been sent on.
statements.evidence: Framing bridge to the next episode (Trinavarta crushed by the child's weight, BP 10.7.25-26, next in corpus chain); the demon's carrying the child off is implied by his mission and the mother's loss.

DKS_0027.notes: Faithful to BP 10.7.17-24. The lap-dandling, sudden unbearable weight and setting the child down (bhāra-pīḍitā), Trinavarta as Kamsa's sent whirlwind-demon, the dust-darkened blinded goṣṭha, the unfindable path, and the tearful gopis all match the Sanskrit. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: It was the hour she fed her child — the child on her lap, nearly done with his milk, his drinking slowing.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.33-34: ekadārbhakam ādāya svāṅkam āropya bhāminī / pīta-prāyasya jananī sutasya rucira-smitam.

statements.claim: Yasoda looked down at his lovely, contented smile, and the child yawned.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.34 (rucira-smitam); index excerpt renders the opening mouth as a yawn: 'he yawns and she beholds within his mouth the sky...'

statements.claim: As his mouth opened, Yasoda saw within it the sky, the earth beneath, the heavens, hosts of stars, the directions, the sun and moon, fire and wind, the great oceans, and every living thing — the whole universe, moving and unmoving.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.35: khaṃ rodasī jyotir-anīkam āśāḥ sūryendu-vahni-śvasanāmbudhīṃś ca; index excerpt adds 'and all beings... the whole cosmos.'

statements.claim: She saw it suddenly and at once, and trembled, her limbs shaking and breath catching, understanding that the small mouth opened onto everything.
statements.evidence: BP 10.7.36: sā vīkṣya viśvaṃ sahasā rājan sañjāta-vepathuḥ ('seeing the universe suddenly, trembling arose').

statements.claim: It lasted only as long as a yawn lasts; then the moment passed and he was only a child again.
statements.evidence: Scene pacing consistent with a brief glimpse; the pack does not specify duration, nor contradict it.

statements.claim: The source does not say how long she sat there afterward or what she said; it says only that she saw, and that she shook.
statements.evidence: Pack covers BP 10.7.33-37; no aftermath dialogue or duration is given in the excerpt.

DKS_0029.notes: Faithful to BP 10.7.33-37. The nursing setting, the mostly-drunk child, the yawning mouth, the full inventory of the cosmos (sky, earth, lights, directions, sun, moon, fire, wind, oceans), and the sudden trembling all match the Sanskrit and the pack's rendered excerpt. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Krishna and his brother Rama grew quickly, and in a short time were crawling through the mud of the cowherd lanes, babbling as they went.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.20-21: kālena vrajatālpena gokule rāma-keśavau / tāv aṅghri-yugmam anukṛṣya sarīsṛpantau... vraja-kardameṣu; tan-nāda-hṛṣṭa-manasāv anusṛtya lokaṃ.

statements.claim: The people of the settlement were delighted by the sight and sound of the two boys.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.21: tan-nāda-hṛṣṭa-manasāv anusṛtya lokaṃ.

statements.claim: When they had crawled far enough they turned and crept back toward their mothers with puzzled, half-frightened faces, as if surprised to find themselves home.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.21: mugdha-prabhītavad upeyatur anti mātroḥ.

statements.claim: Their mothers gathered them up, pressed them to the breast, and looked into their faces with their sweet smiles and first little teeth, filled with joy.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.22: tan-mātarau nija-sutau ghṛṇayā snuvantyau... dattvā stanaṃ prapibatoḥ sma mukhaṃ nirīkṣya / mugdha-smitālpa-daśanaṃ yayatuḥ pramodam.

statements.claim: The boys caught the calves by the tail and let themselves be dragged about; the women of Vraja left their houses to watch, laughing.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.23: abalāḥ pragṛhīta-pucchaiḥ vatsair itas tata ubhāv anukṛṣyamāṇau / prekṣantya ujjhita-gṛhā jahṛṣur hasantyaḥ.

statements.claim: The two mothers tried to keep their sons away from horns, fire, a boar's tusks, open water, swooping birds and thorn bushes, and could not.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.24: śṛṅgy-agni-daṃṣṭry-asi-jala-dvija-kaṇṭakebhyaḥ... niṣeddhum... na śekāta.

statements.claim: Krishna and his band of cowherd friends slipped into a neighbor's house and set the calves loose at the wrong hour, laughing at the confusion.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.28: vatsān muñcan kvacid asamaye krośa-sañjāta-hāsaḥ.

statements.claim: He stole and ate sweet curd and milk with tricks and contrivances, choosing moments when the women were busy with housework.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.28-29: steyaṃ svādv atty atha dadhi-payaḥ kalpitaiḥ steya-yogaiḥ; kāle gopyo yarhi gṛha-kṛtyeṣu suvyagra-cittāḥ.

statements.claim: When pots hung high out of reach in slings among the rafters, he dragged a stool or a mortar beneath them and climbed.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.29: hastāgrāhye racayati vidhiṃ pīṭhakolūkhalādyaiś / chidraṃ hy antar-nihita-vayunaḥ śikya-bhāṇḍeṣu.

statements.claim: In the dark of a storeroom he needed no lamp, for the jewels on his small body caught the light and showed him where the pots were.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.29: dhvāntāgāre dhṛta-maṇi-gaṇaṃ svāṅgam artha-pradīpaṃ.

statements.claim: He shared the butter with the monkeys who were his audience, and if a monkey refused to eat he smashed the pot in a temper.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.28: markān bhokṣyan vibhajati sa cen nātti bhāṇḍaṃ bhinnatti.

statements.claim: When he could not reach a pot at all, he marched off angry and shouted curses at the little boys of the house.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.28: dravyālābhe sagṛha-kupito yāty upakrośya tokān.

statements.claim: The gopis complained to Yasoda with their lists of outrages, their anger undone by his lovely face, their scolding half-laughing; Yasoda, smiling, could not bring herself to scold him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.8.30: strībhiḥ sa-bhaya-nayana-śrī-mukhālokinībhir vyākhyātārthā prahasita-mukhī na hy upālabdhum aicchat.

DKS_0031.notes: Faithful to BP 10.8.20-30. Crawling through Vraja's mud, mothers' joy over smiles and first teeth, calf-tail dragging, the horn/fire/tusk/water/bird/thorn dangers, calf-loosing, curd-and-milk theft, stool-and-mortar climbing, jewel-light in the dark storeroom, monkey-feeding and pot-smashing, cursing the house boys, and the gopis' complaint to a smiling, non-scolding Yasoda — all have direct Sanskrit antecedents. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Yashoda chased Krishna with a stick to punish him for the broken butter pot, but dropped it when she saw his fear.
statements.evidence: BP 10.9.11 (tyaktvā yaṣṭiṃ sutaṃ bhītaṃ vijñāyārbhaka-vatsalā); broken pot from prior story DKS_0033 per corpus chain

statements.claim: Every rope she tied came up short by two fingers' width.
statements.evidence: BP 10.9.14-15; pack excerpt: 'always two fingers too short to bind him'

statements.claim: She joined rope after rope from her own house and still the gap would not close.
statements.evidence: BP 10.9.16 (evaṃ sva-geha-dāmāni yaśodā sandadhaty api)

statements.claim: She sweated; her braid and garland came loose as she worked.
statements.evidence: BP 10.9.17 (svinna-gātrāyā visrasta-kabara-srajaḥ)

statements.claim: Krishna, whom no being in the worlds could bind, of his own accord let the rope close around him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.9.18-20 (bhṛtya-vaśyatā; neither Virincha/Brahma, Bhava/Shiva nor Shri can grasp him); pack excerpt

statements.claim: Yashoda bound him to the great wooden mortar.
statements.evidence: Pack canonical event evt_0048; VP 5.6 passage (in DKS_0038 pack): 'Fastening a cord round his waist, she tied him to the wooden mortar'

DKS_0034.notes: All claims grounded in BP 10.9.11-20 and the pack's rendered excerpt; no unsupported or contradicted statements.

statements.claim: The cowherds heard the crash of the falling trees and came running to find the child by the uprooted arjuna trees.
statements.evidence: BP 10.10.27ff; pack excerpt: 'the cowherds hear the crash and marvel'

statements.claim: Two radiant figures rose from the fallen trees, shining like fire just kindled.
statements.evidence: BP 10.10.27 (śriyā paramayā ... kujayor iva jāta-vedāḥ)

statements.claim: They were Nalakuvara and Manigriva, and the curse that held them was over.
statements.evidence: BP 10.10.41 (nalakūvara); pack summary

statements.claim: They bowed with joined palms and praised Krishna as the great yogi, the first and highest person, Lord of all beings, subtle source, Vasudeva.
They asked that their voices, ears, hands, minds, heads and eyes be forever turned to him and his devotees.
statements.evidence: BP 10.10.37 (vāṇī ... śravaṇau ... hastau ... manas ... śiras ... dṛṣṭiḥ)

statements.claim: Krishna told them they were his, with hearts fixed on him, and bade them go to their own home.
statements.evidence: BP 10.10.40-41 (sādhūnāṃ sama-cittānāṃ ... tad gacchataṃ mat-paramau nalakūvara sādanam)

statements.claim: They departed toward the north, free at last.
statements.evidence: Pack index summary: 'released from their curse, depart to the north'

statements.claim: The cowherds could not explain what they saw and sensed the child was not simply a child.
statements.evidence: Consistent with pack excerpt ('the cowherds hear the crash and marvel'); the fear/recognition is narrative inference

DKS_0036.notes: All praises, requests, and the dismissal map to BP 10.10.27-43. The northward departure is supported by the pack's own index summary.

statements.claim: Krishna danced whenever the cowherd women clapped and coaxed him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.11.6 (gopībhiḥ stobhito 'nṛtyad bhagavān bālavat)

statements.claim: When his father asked, he fetched the stool, weights, and wooden sandals.
statements.evidence: BP 10.11.7 (pīṭhakonmāna-pādukam)

statements.claim: Hearing the fruit-seller's cry to buy fruits, Krishna hurried out with a fistful of grain.
statements.evidence: BP 10.11.9 (krīṇīhi bhoḥ phalānīti śrutvā satvaram acyutaḥ)

statements.claim: The grain spilled from his hands before he reached the seller, leaving his fists nearly empty.
statements.evidence: BP 10.11.10 (phala-vikrayiṇī tasya cyuta-dhānya-kara-dvayam)

statements.claim: She filled his small hands with fruit and found her basket filled with jewels where the fruit had been.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'the fruit-seller finds her basket filled with jewels where her fruit had been'; index summary

statements.claim: Grain was what a village that kept no coins gave and took.
statements.evidence: Setting context; not a sourceable claim in the pack

statements.claim: She had given to the one who gives everything back a hundredfold.
statements.evidence: Devotional framing consistent with the episode's import

DKS_0037.notes: All episode facts grounded in BP 10.11.6-10.

statements.claim: Upananda, a cowherd superior in wisdom and age, called the cowherds together and urged leaving Gokula for its welfare.
statements.evidence: BP 10.11.21-22 (upānanda ... gopo jñāna-vayo-'dhikaḥ; utthātavyam ito 'smābhir gokulasya hitaiṣibhiḥ)

statements.claim: He cited the demoness who came to kill children, from whom the boy was saved.
statements.evidence: BP 10.11.23 (muktaḥ kathañcid rākṣasyā bāla-ghnyā)

statements.claim: A whirlwind demon carried him into the sky, yet he came down alive.
statements.evidence: BP 10.11.24 (cakra-vātena nīto 'yaṃ daityena vipadaṃ viyat)

statements.claim: He passed between the two great trees and did not die.
statements.evidence: BP 10.11.25 (yan na mriyeta drumayor antaraṃ prāpya bālakaḥ)

statements.claim: As an infant he overturned the waggon with a kick of his foot, its pots and pans flung across the ground.
statements.evidence: VP 5.6 (Wilson): 'kicking up his feet he overturned the vehicle, and all the pots and pans were upset and broken'

statements.claim: Vrindavana was fresh, new pastureland good for the cattle, a place where the omens of Gokula would have no hold.
statements.evidence: BP 10.11.27 (vanaṃ vṛndāvanaṃ nāma paśavyaṃ nava-kānanam); VP 5.6: 'where terrestrial prodigies may no more disturb us'

statements.claim: He urged them to yoke the carts and go at once, without delay.
statements.evidence: BP 10.11.28 (tat tatrādyaiva yāsyāmaḥ śakaṭān yuṅkta mā ciram)

statements.claim: The cowherds agreed, saying 'well said,' and the colony moved with its elders, children, women, and belongings.
statements.evidence: BP 10.11.29-30 (sādhu sādhv iti vādinaḥ; vṛddhān bālān striyo rājan sarvopakaraṇāni ca)

statements.claim: Groves that had never been grazed, grass that had not been cropped.
statements.evidence: Elaboration of 'nava-kānanam' (new grove); no contradictory claim in pack

DKS_0038.notes: Omens list matches BP 10.11.23-25 plus the waggon from VP 5.6, exactly as the pack assembles them.

statements.claim: Krishna and Balarama (Samkarshana) passed seven years in Vraja.
statements.evidence: HV 1.58.1: 'passed their childhood in Vraja and became seven years old'

statements.claim: They wore dark-blue and yellow garments, yellow and white paste, and crow feathers while tending cattle.
Their forest play: leaf crowns and wild-flower garlands like young trees, lotus crowns, a rope as sacred thread, gourds, flutes, leaf beds, running like young horses, beautifying the forest.
The forest was ruined: grass and twigs gone, trees uprooted by the milkmen, cow-shed fires scorching trunks, birds fled, no sweet winds, like rice without curry.
Where droppings fell on the grass, the grazing soured and the milk turned poor.
Vrindavana lay on the Yamuna's bank with thick grass, no thorns or insects, fruit and kadamba trees, and cool winds like an asylum of all seasons.
Govardhana rose high like Mandara; the Bhandira fig tree spread a yojana like a dark cloud; the Kalindi (Yamuna) ran through the middle like a parting in hair.
Krishna decided to create a calamity to frighten the milkmen into leaving.
statements.evidence: HV 1.58.29 ('Let us now, creating some calamity, terrify the milk-men')

statements.claim: From the hairs of his body arose hundreds of wolves living on fat, blood and flesh, dark-faced, bearing the Srivatsa mark, in groups of five, ten, twenty, thirty and a hundred.
statements.evidence: HV 1.58.30ff: 'From the hairs of his body there arose hundreds of wolves living on fat, blood and flesh ... groups of five, ten, thirty, twenty and a hundred those dark-faced wolves, bearing the mystic mark of Srivatsa'

statements.claim: The wolves fell upon the calves, cows and women, striking terror into the milkmen.
statements.evidence: HV 1.58: 'Beholding them fall upon calves, kine and their women the milk-men were stricken with great fear'

statements.claim: Krishna did not mean to harm his own people; he meant to move them.
statements.evidence: Interpretive framing consistent with HV's 'terrify the milk-men' intent

DKS_0039.notes: Every description (garments, forest ruin, Vrindavana geography, wolves) matches HV 1.58 nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: Uddhava recalled Krishna herding calves, surrounded by them, sporting in the Yamuna's groves.
statements.evidence: BP 3.2.26 (parīto vatsapair vatsāṃś cārayan vyaharad vibhuḥ)

statements.claim: He showed the cowherds his childhood play, lovely to watch.
statements.evidence: BP 3.2.27 (kaumārīṃ darśayaṃś ceṣṭāṃ prekṣaṇīyāṃ vrajaukasām)

statements.claim: He was a child who wept and laughed in the same hour, with the bright boldness of a lion cub.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'weeping and laughing with a lion-cub's glance' (BP 3.2.26-29 rendering)

statements.claim: His flute playing delighted the cowherds.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'playing the flute, he delighted the cowherds'

statements.claim: Kamsa, the Bhoja king, never stopped sending shape-shifting demon agents against him.

statements.claim: While his mother was busy with household duties, Krishna caught sight of the two arjuna trees.

statements.claim: Nalakuvara and Manigriva, sons of Kubera the lord of wealth, drank varuni wine and, eyes rolling with intoxication, sported naked in the Ganga among lotus groves with celestial women.
statements.evidence: BP 10.10.2-3 (vāruṇīṃ madirāṃ pītvā madāghūrṇita-locanau; antaḥ praviśya gaṅgāyām ambhoja-vana-rājini)

statements.evidence: Pack index entry locations: 'Kailasa, Ganga river'

statements.claim: Narada taught that the body, though called divine, ends as worms, filth and ashes, comes from father and mother, and returns to the unmanifest; that poverty is the best medicine for pride; that the poor are free of ego; and that sages of equal vision draw near the poor, in whose company one learns to want only Mukunda's feet.
statements.evidence: BP 10.10.8-17 (kṛmi-viḍ-bhasma-saṃjñitam; sādhāraṇaṃ deham avyakta-prabhavāpyayam; dāridryaṃ param añjanam; daridro nirahaṃ-stambho; daridrasyaiva yujyante sādhavaḥ sama-darśinaḥ; mukunda-caraṇaiṣiṇām)

statements.claim: He cursed them: sons of the world's protector sunk in darkness, they would stand as trees, rooted and motionless.

statements.evidence: BP 10.10.21 (vāsudevasya sānnidhyaṃ labdhvā divya-śarac-chate); pack excerpt 'promising release at the touch of Vasudeva'

statements.evidence: BP 10.10.22ff and DKS_0041 pack (vṛkṣatāṃ prāpitau); the 'cure' reading is consistent with the promised release

DKS_0042.notes: All elements of the curse episode map to BP 10.10.1-22; the Kailasa setting is in the pack's own index locations.

statements.claim: The heaven-dwellers rained a shower of flowers
statements.evidence: 10.11.51: sura-loka-vāsinaḥ samākiran nandana-mallikādibhiḥ

statements.evidence: Detail is from the preceding canonical event (evt_0059 / DKS_0047, 10.12.32: jyotiḥ ... pīnāhi-bhogotthitam, 'a great radiance from the demon's body enters Krishna' per that pack's summary), which 10.13.14 references; not in the 10.13.11-16 passages themselves

statements.evidence: 10.13.12: tān dṛṣṭvā bhaya-santrastān ūce kṛṣṇo 'sya bhī-bhayam — the pack says Krishna saw the boys fear-stricken and spoke to dispel their fear; the story asserts the boys were not afraid
statements.resolution: Corrected in story text via consolidation pass.

statements.claim: He knew at once what had happened and who had done it, for nothing is hidden from him
statements.evidence: 10.13.16: viśva-vit (the all-knowing)

corrections.original_sentence: The sandbank lay quiet behind him, and none of the boys thought to be afraid.
corrections.suggested: The sandbank lay quiet behind him, and the boys, whose sudden fear Krishna had just quieted with a word, were at ease.

DKS_0048.notes: One CONTRADICTED: 10.13.12 has the boys fear-stricken (bhaya-santrastān) with Krishna dispelling their fear; the story instead says they were not afraid. The 'great light entering the boy' is supported via the preceding event pack (DKS_0047 / 10.12.32).

statements.claim: To Brahma only a moment had passed; in Vrindavan a year
statements.evidence: 10.13.39 (ātmamānena truṭy-anehasā, in the twinkling of an eye) and 10.14.42 (ekasminn api yāte 'bde, though a year had passed)
