corrections.original_sentence: He had just taken back from Kamsa everything Kamsa had stolen — the city, the throne, the years — and the first thing he did with it was kneel before two people who had been helpless for eighteen years and ask their forgiveness for a childhood he had never been allowed to give them.
corrections.suggested: He had just taken back from Kamsa everything Kamsa had stolen — the city, the throne, the years — and the first thing he did with it was kneel before two people who had been helpless in their bonds for all those years and ask their forgiveness for a childhood he had never been allowed to give them.

DKS_0144.notes: The apology speech is a faithful rendering of Bhagavata 10.45.1-8, nearly line by line. Single issue: the 'eighteen years' duration (echoed from DKS_0143) is unsupported by the pack or corpus.

statements.claim: Ugrasena, Kamsa's father, had been set aside and confined by his own son, who took the throne and ruled; Krishna later released his grandfather from confinement.
statements.evidence: Vishnu Purana 5.21 (pack): 'The foe of Madhu then liberated Ugrasena from confinement, and placed him on the throne, which the death of his son had left vacant'; Kamsa's usurpation is canonical arc background (corpus chain, uncontradicted).

statements.claim: Krishna did not take the throne himself; before the assembled Yadavas he declared Ugrasena would be king, saying that because of Yayati's curse no Yadava was to sit on the throne.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Bhagavata 10.45.11-13, confidence 5): Krishna 'installed his maternal grandfather Ugrasena as king of the Yadavas, declaring that because of Yayati's curse no Yadava should sit on the throne'; Harivamsha 1.87 (55): installation 'in that assembly of the Yadus'.

statements.claim: Ugrasena protested that he cared nothing for the kingdom or the royal throne and told Krishna to take it for himself and win glory by becoming king.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.87 (48-52, Dutt): it is KRISHNA who says 'I do not care for the kingdom or the royal throne. I did not slay Kansa for a territory... I stand in no need of the kingdom', and Krishna who instructs Ugrasena: 'place yourself on the throne and acquire victory by becoming the king'. Ugrasena had offered Krishna Kamsa's army, wealth and lordship (22-24) and spoke of retiring to the forest (26-28); he did not protest that he cared nothing for the kingdom. The story swaps the speakers.
statements.resolution: Corrected in story text via consolidation pass.

statements.claim: Krishna, knowing the law, was not moved, and Govinda, well read in the laws, installed his grandfather on the throne that his son's death had left vacant.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.87 (52-55): 'place yourself on the throne and acquire victory by becoming the king... Then Govinda, well read in laws, installed him on the throne'; Vishnu Purana 5.21: 'placed him on the throne, which the death of his son had left vacant'.

statements.claim: Krishna had said that while he served at his grandfather's side, the very gods themselves would pay tribute to the throne.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.13: 'mayi bhṛtya upāsīne bhavato vibudhādayaḥ' (while I serve as your attendant, the gods and others [shall honor] you).

statements.claim: He did not take the crown, the wealth or the army; he gave them to the man Kamsa had wronged, and the king was the man Kamsa had tried to erase.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.87 (48-53): Krishna declines Kamsa's army and wealth ('I do not care for the kingdom... I stand in no need of the kingdom') and abdicates the kingdom to Ugrasena; VP 5.21 installation.

statements.claim: The boy from Gokula, who had arrived in Mathura that morning as a stranger and left it the master of everything, stood at the foot of the throne and placed an old man upon it.
statements.evidence: Rhetorical compression of the two-day arc (arrival, arena, coronation); 'that morning' is loose (corpus chain has them reach Mathura the previous day, DKS_0131) but functions as connective summary, not a core factual assertion.

corrections.original_sentence: He protested that he cared nothing for the kingdom or the royal throne, and told Krishna to take it for himself and win glory by becoming king.
corrections.suggested: He spoke of performing the rites and retiring to the forest with his wife and daughters-in-law, and pressed Kamsa's kingdom and wealth upon Krishna; but Krishna refused, saying he cared nothing for the kingdom or the royal throne, and instructed his grandfather to place himself on the throne and win glory by becoming king.

DKS_0145.notes: Installation and Yayati's-curse rationale are supported (SB 10.45.11-13 excerpt; VP 5.21; HV 1.87). One contradiction: the refusal scene is role-swapped — in Harivamsha 1.87 (48-52) Krishna says he does not care for the kingdom and tells UGRASENA to take the throne, while the story puts that protest in Ugrasena's mouth.

statements.claim: The Yadava, Vrishni, Andhaka and Madhu kinsmen had fled in fear of Kamsa to every direction, and Krishna brought them all back and settled them again.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.14: 'sarvān svān jñāti-sambandhān digbhyaḥ kaṃsa-bhayākulān'; pack excerpt: 'Krishna brought back all the Yadava, Vrishni, Andhaka and Madhu kinsmen who had fled in fear of Kamsa, settled them in their homes with wealth'.

statements.claim: Krishna honored each returning kinsman, comforted them in their exhaustion from dwelling abroad, and restored their wealth.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.15: 'sabhājitān samāśvāsya videśāvāsa-karśitān' (honoring them, comforting those wasted by foreign residence); pack excerpt: 'settled them in their homes with wealth'.

statements.claim: Protected by the arms of Krishna and Balarama, they obtained everything their hearts had desired for years.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.16: 'kṛṣṇa-saṅkarṣaṇa-bhujair guptā labdha-manorathāḥ' (protected by the arms of Krishna and Sankarshana, they obtained their heart's desires).

statements.claim: Day after day the rejoined clans gathered to look at Krishna's face, and the sight of him was delight enough; even the oldest became young again, vigorous as youths.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.17-18: 'vīkṣanto 'har ahaḥ prītā mukunda-vadanāmbujam / tatra pravayaso 'py āsan yuvāno 'ti-balaujasaḥ'.

statements.claim: Krishna sent word to every corner of the earth for the exiles to come home, and they returned by twos and threes, dusty from long roads, some so long gone their grandchildren had never seen Mathura.
statements.evidence: The return from all directions is v.14 ('digbhyaḥ'); the mechanism ('sent word'), the dusty arrivals and the grandchildren are connective elaboration consistent with the exile (videśāvāsa-karśitān, v.15), not separately sourceable.

statements.claim: Weddings that had been postponed for a decade were held at last.
statements.evidence: No support in the pack (Bhagavata 10.45.14-18) or in any other corpus evidence: the verses celebrate daily gazing on Krishna's face (v.17) and restored youth (v.18) but never mention weddings or a decade of postponement.
statements.resolution: Corrected in story text via consolidation pass.

statements.claim: When the last exile was settled in his father's house, Mathura was whole again, the clans one under one king, since before Kamsa seized the throne.
statements.evidence: Summarizing connective close consistent with v.14-18; no new unsupported event asserted beyond the restoration already covered.

corrections.original_sentence: Weddings that had been postponed for a decade were held at last.
corrections.suggested: And the rejoicing that the years of exile had deferred broke out at last in every courtyard.

DKS_0146.notes: Close to Bhagavata 10.45.14-18, including the striking v.18 detail of the aged becoming young. One unsupported invented flourish: weddings 'postponed for a decade' being held — the verses speak only of daily rejoicing at Mukunda's face.

statements.claim: Vasudeva summoned the brahmins and had the sacred-thread ceremony performed for Krishna and Balarama, who received the initiation and became twice-born students.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.25, 28: 'atha śūra-suto rājan putrayoḥ samakārayat... labdha-saṃskārau dvijatvaṃ prāpya su-vratau'.

statements.claim: For the officiating brahmins Vasudeva gave a fee of cows adorned with golden necklaces, richly decorated — the very cattle he had mentally pledged at the ceremonies following the births of his two sons.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.26-27: 'tebhyo 'dād dakṣiṇā gāvo rukma-mālāḥ sv-alaṅkṛtāḥ / yāḥ kṛṣṇa-rāma-janmarkṣe mano-dattā mahā-matiḥ'.

statements.claim: The two who stood before the brahmins were already the lords of all knowledge, all-knowing, masters of the world, yet they desired to live in a guru's house like any students.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.29-30: 'prabhavau sarva-vidyānāṃ sarva-jñau jagad-īśvarau / atho guru-kule vāsam icchantāv upajagmatuḥ'.

statements.claim: They went as students to the teacher Sandipani in the city of Avanti, served humbly with blameless conduct, and pleased the brahmin teacher by their pure dispositions.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.30-32: 'guru-kule vāsam icchantāv upajagmatuḥ / yathopasādya tau dāntau gurau vṛttim aninditām / tayor dvija-varas tuṣṭaḥ śuddha-bhāvānuvṛttibhiḥ'; pack excerpt: 'went to the teacher Sandipani in Avanti'.

statements.claim: Sandipani taught them the science of the bow with all its secret doctrines, the codes of duty, and the paths of justice and reasoning.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.33: 'sa-rahasyaṃ dhanur-vedaṃ dharmān nyāya-pathāṃs tathā'.

statements.claim: In sixty-four days and nights the brothers mastered all the arts and sciences Sandipani could teach.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.34-35: 'sarvaṃ... sarva-vidyā-pravartakau / aho-rātraiś catuḥ-ṣaṣṭyā saṃyattau tāvatīḥ kalāḥ' ('in sixty-four days and nights attained all those arts').

statements.claim: When the sixty-four days were done the brothers were finished students ready to take their leave, and the teacher's fee had not yet been spoken of.
statements.evidence: Close of the episode consistent with v.33-35; the fee request follows immediately in the canon (Bhagavata 10.45.36ff, next corpus event) — connective transition, uncontradicted.

DKS_0147.notes: Faithful to Bhagavata 10.45.25-35 nearly verse by verse (initiation, the mentally-pledged cows, 64 days-and-nights, the guru's syllabus).

statements.claim: Knowing the longing of the love-tormented Sairandhri (Trivakra, the woman whose crooked back he had straightened), Krishna went to her house, taking Uddhava with him.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.48.1-3: her house 'rich with splendid furnishings' seen as he approached; 'tathoddhavaḥ' present; pack excerpt: 'Knowing the desire of the love-tormented Sairandhri, the Lord went to her house'. The earlier straightening is canonical chain (VP 5.20 passage, pack of DKS_0143).

statements.claim: When she saw him approaching, she rose at once, flustered; Uddhava, honored for his goodness, sat on the ground, touching the seat that was offered, leaving the place of honor for his lord.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.48.2-3: 'sadyaḥ samutthāya hi jāta-sambhramā / tathoddhavaḥ sādhutayābhipūjito nyaṣīdad urvyām abhimṛśya cāsanam'.

statements.claim: She prepared herself with bath, fragrant unguents, silk and ornaments, garlands and perfumes, betel and sweet drinks, and drew Krishna near by his bangle-adorned hand, shy at the newness of his nearness.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.48.4-5: 'sā majjanālepa-dukūla-bhūṣaṇa-srag-gandha-tāmbūla-sudhāsavādibhiḥ... āhūya kāntāṃ nava-saṅgama-hriyā viśaṅkitāṃ kaṅkaṇa-bhūṣite kare'.

statements.claim: She embraced him, pressing him to her breast with both arms, and in that embrace her long torment ended, for she held the blissful form before her.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.48.6: '...parirabhya kāntam ānanda-mūrtim ajahād ati-dīrgha-tāpam' (embracing the beloved, the very form of bliss, she gave up her exceedingly long torment).

statements.claim: She had obtained what the whole world calls hard to obtain — the lord of liberation himself standing in her small house.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.48.7: 'saivaṃ kaivalya-nāthaṃ taṃ prāpya duṣprāpyam īśvaram' (she obtained the lord of liberation, the lord hard to obtain).

statements.claim: She asked only that he stay with her a few days — not wealth, power, or a place in his court.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.48.8: 'sahoṣyatām iha preṣṭha dināni katicin mayā' (dwell here with me, dear, for a few days); the 'only' framing is a fair reading of the single request recorded.

statements.claim: Krishna, who honors those who honor him, granted her the boon she wished, and when he left he returned to his own abode.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.48.9: 'tasyai kāma-varaṃ dattvā mānayitvā ca māna-daḥ'; pack excerpt: 'Krishna granted her the boon she wished and returned to his own abode'.

statements.claim: Her home was rich and furnished with splendid things, arranged with care for the one she hoped would come.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.48.1: 'mahārhopaskarair āḍhyaṃ kāmopāyopabṛṃhitam' (rich with splendid furnishings, furnished with love's means).

DKS_0149.notes: A close rendering of Bhagavata 10.48.1-10: each beat (rise in fluster, Uddhava taking the ground, the toilette list, the embrace that ends her long torment, the 'few days' request, the granted boon) maps to a verse.

statements.claim: Sudama, Krishna's old classmate from the guru's house, came to Dwaraka, and Krishna asked whether he remembered their days in the guru's house.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.80.30: 'kaccid guru-kule vāsaṃ brahman smarasi nau yataḥ' (do you remember, brahmin, our dwelling in the guru's house); Sudama's arrival in Dwaraka is the canonical frame of SB 10.80 and the corpus's Sudama arc (DKS_0287-0289).

statements.claim: Krishna said the guru's house is the true birth of a twice-born and the direct root of all good deeds, and that he is not reached by sacrifice, sons, austerity, or a merely quieted mind — but by such days as those spent at a teacher's feet.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.80.31-33: 'sa vai sat-karmaṇāṃ sākṣād dvijāter iha sambhavaḥ... nāham ijyā-prajātibhyāṃ tapasopaśamena vā'.

statements.claim: Sent by the guru's wife to gather firewood, the two boys entered the great forest; the sun had set, darkness covered every direction, and a violent wind and rain struck them again and again in the rising water.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.80.35-37: 'praviṣṭānāṃ mahāraṇyam... sūryaś cāstam gatas tāvat tamasā cāvṛtā diśaḥ / vayaṃ bhṛśaṃ tatra mahānilāmbubhir nihanyamānā muhur ambu-samplave'; pack excerpt: 'sent by the guru's wife to gather firewood'.

statements.claim: Lost in the blackness, they held each other's hands and wandered until at sunrise the guru Sandipani, who had known where they were, came through the storm to find them.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.80.38: 'etad viditvā udite ravau sāndīpanir guruḥ'; pack excerpt: 'lost in the darkness and holding hands, they wandered till the guru found them at sunrise and blessed them'.

statements.claim: The guru said: 'Ah, my sons, you have suffered so much for my sake. This is exactly what true disciples must do — this is the repayment of the guru. I am pleased with you. May your wishes come true.'
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.80.39-41: 'aho he putrakā yūyam asmad-arthe 'ti-duḥkhitāḥ / etad eva hi sac-chiṣyaiḥ kartavyaṃ guru-niṣkṛtam / tuṣṭo 'haṃ... satyāḥ santu manorathāḥ'.

statements.claim: Krishna closed the memory: 'Such were the days we spent in the guru's house. There were many like that one.'
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.80.42: 'itthaṃ-vidhāny anekāni vasatāṃ guru-veśmani' (many such days there were, living in the guru's house).

statements.claim: The two sat in silence — the lord of Dwaraka and the brahmin from the south, both boys again in the dark forest — and the memory showed what the years under Sandipani had made of them.
statements.evidence: Closing atmosphere; Sudama's being a brahmin is the text (v.27 'brahman', v.41 'dvija-śreṣṭhāḥ'); 'from the south' is an unverified descriptor of his village (the pack's 10.80.27-42 range does not state it) and 'the years under Sandipani' compresses the shared gurukula days — connective, no contradiction.

DKS_0150.notes: The recollection maps directly onto Bhagavata 10.80.30-42, including the guru's blessing at sunrise nearly word for word (v.39-41). The storm-and-darkness night (v.36-37) and the 'many such days' close (v.42) are exact.

statements.claim: Mathura had thrown back the armies of Magadha; Jarasandha had come against the city once and then again, and the brothers scattered his forces with their own hands.
statements.evidence: Pack summary: Yadavas counsel that Mathura 'cannot withstand Jarasandha's repeated sieges'; Harivamsha 1.94 excerpt on the city's weakness presupposes prior repulses; two sieges established in the arc chain.

statements.claim: Vikadru rose in council and was counted the foremost speaker of the clan.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.95 (in pack): 'Vikadru, the foremost of royal speakers'.

statements.claim: Vikadru said Mathura cannot withstand another siege: the city has a limited supply of food and fuels, is not protected by a fort, and cannot stand attack for even one day.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.94 excerpt: 'This city has a limited supply of food and fuels. It is not protected by a fort... It will not therefore be able to stand attack for even one day.'

statements.claim: Someone protested that the brothers had beaten Jarasandha twice; Vikadru answered that a siege is answered with grain and stone, not in the field, and Jarasandha need only wait for hunger to do his work.
statements.evidence: Consistent with the 1.94 excerpt (thin stores, no walls, cannot stand one day) and the two prior sieges in the arc; the elaboration of how the siege would work is faithful connective reasoning on the pack's claims.

statements.claim: Mathura was a city of cowherds and traders, grown rich on the river and the pastures, never turned into a stronghold.
statements.evidence: Generic characterization consistent with the city's depiction in the tradition and the pack's 'city of cowherds' framing; not a sourceable discrete fact in the pack.

statements.claim: The council ended with the truth spoken and no decision made; that night Krishna stood at a window looking south toward the mountains where the answers might be waiting.
statements.evidence: Atmosphere/transitional narration setting up the following story; no factual assertion requiring support.

DKS_0151.notes: All substantive claims map directly to Harivamsha 1.94-1.95. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: Vasudeva rose after the council and gave Vikadru's counsel his full assent, telling Krishna to do what he had said.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.95: 'what the intelligent Vikadru, the foremost of royal speakers... has said, is true and well meaning... Do what that foremost of Yadus has said.'

statements.claim: Krishna's lesson in statecraft: a king daily meditates on peace and war, on alliance and dissension; the learned king does not place himself before a powerful enemy but withdraws, and in proper time and according to his strength engages in battle again.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.95 v.6-8: 'A king daily meditates on peace, quarrel... A learned king should not place himself before a powerful enemy, but rather should fly away. And in proper time and according to his strength he should engage in fight.'

statements.claim: Krishna said: 'Therefore, although I am capable, I shall, at this very moment, fly away with the worshipful Baladeva — like one incapable, saving my life.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.95 v.9 and pack excerpt: 'Therefore although I am capable, I shall, at this very moment, fly away with the worshipful Baladeva for saving my life like one incapable.'

statements.claim: The plan: go south, ascend mount Sahya, enter the Deccan, see the charming cities of Karavira and Krouncha and the foremost of mountains Gomanta.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.95 v.10-11: 'Ascending the mount Sahya... I shall enter into Deccan and we shall behold the charming cities of Karavira and Krounch and the foremost of mountains Gomanta.'

statements.claim: Krishna said Jarasandha, elated with success, would not sit before Mathura but pursue them in pride into the forests of Sahya, and that the departure is conducive to the well-being of the race of Yadu; the province, city and citizens will fare well.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.95 v.12-14: 'that Emperor, elated with success, will not enter into this city but rather will pursue us in pride... this our departure is conducive to the well-being of the race of Yadu. By this, the Province, the city and the citizens will fare well.'

statements.claim: That very day the two brothers set out for the south without the least anxiety, taking on different forms at will and traveling through hundreds of kingdoms.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.95: 'set out for the south without experiencing the least anxiety in mind'; 'Assuming forms at will they began to travel in hundreds of southern kingdoms.'

statements.claim: Long ago, in the time of king Yadu, his five sons went out to found cities: Padmavarna raised Karavira on mount Sahya, and Sarasas laid out Krouncha in its groves; the brothers came at last to Karavira, presided over by members of their own family.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.95 v.19: 'reached the city of Karavira, presided over by the members of their own family and adorned with the mount Sahya'; founding names from Harivamsha 1.94 (in pack for DKS_0151): 'The royal saint Padmavarna laid out, on the mountain Sahya... his city was known by the name of Karavira' and 'Sārasa built his highly charming city Krouncha.'

statements.claim: On the bank of the river Vena stood a great fig tree, and under its shade the two brothers paused to rest.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.95 v.19-20: 'They saw there a huge fig tree on the bank of the river Venā.'

statements.claim: The appearance of the flight as fear was a weapon: this flight would read as the retreat of a beaten man.
statements.evidence: Interpretive framing of Krishna's 'like one incapable' phrasing; non-factual commentary on the source's own words.

DKS_0152.notes: Quotes match Harivamsha 1.95 closely. The five-sons founding detail draws on Harivamsha 1.94, present in the corpus evidence (pack of DKS_0151). No issues.

statements.claim: On the bank of the river Vena under a great fig tree sat an old ascetic milking a cow white as the milky arani tree, her calf beside her, giving milk whenever wished.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.95: 'milching his sacrificial cow with her calf ever giving milk whenever desired and white as the milky Arani tree... He was seated at the foot of that tree, had his axe on his shoulder, wore bark and matted locks, was white as the flames of fire... was emaciated with the performance of three oblations a day.'

statements.claim: Krishna recognized him as Rama, son of Jamadagni, born in the race of Bhrigu, the destroyer of the Kshatriyas.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.95 v.28: 'Rāma, the son of Jamadagni born in the race of Bhrigu, and the destroyer of the Kshatriyas.'

statements.claim: Parasurama had agitated the ocean with the speed of his shafts and laid out the city of Surpara on its shore.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.95: 'having agitated the ocean with the velocity of thy shafts thou hast laid out a city by name Surpāra.'

statements.claim: Remembering his slain father, he went out with his axe and cut down the thousand arms of Kartavirya like a forest.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.95: 'Remembering the destruction of thy sire thou didst, with thy axe, chop off the thousand arms of Kārtavirya resembling a forest.'

statements.claim: The earth's mud was still said to be stained with the blood of the warrior kings he had slain.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.95: 'Even now the Earth has her mud covered with the cool blood of the Kshatryas who were killed by thy axe.'

statements.claim: Krishna identified himself and Balarama as the two Yadavas living on the bank of the Yamuna, telling their story: placed in Vraja by Vasudeva out of fear of Kamsa, grew up without fear, came of age, destroyed Kamsa in the assembly, set Ugrasena back on the royal seat, returned to cowherd work, then Jarasandha besieged the city repeatedly until they left to draw him away.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.95 v.29-39: 'perhaps thou mightest have heard of two Yādavas living on the bank of the Yamunā. We are those two... our father Vasuveda... afraid of Kansa, placed us in Vraja... we grew up without any fear... we entered into Mathurā and powerfully destroyed the haughty Kansa in the assembly... placing his father Ugrasena in his royal office we again... engaged in the work of cow-herd boys... thereafter when Jarāsandha laid seige to our c[ity]...'

statements.claim: Parasurama counseled: get up onto that high summit; if you obstruct Jarasandha by fighting with him from the fort there, you will be able to conquer him.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Getting upon that high summit... if you obstruct Jarasandha by fighting with him in the fort you will be able to conquer him.'

statements.claim: So the mountain was named: Gomanta.
statements.evidence: The name Gomanta is already given in Krishna's own plan (1.95 v.10-11); the sentence is a connective pointer to the mountain in question rather than a claim that the name originated from this counsel.

statements.claim: The brothers stayed a while with the sage on the bank of the Vena, then turned their faces toward Gomanta.
statements.evidence: Follows from the 1.95 sequence: the meeting by the Vena, the counsel, and the subsequent journey to Gomanta (per the arc chain; next title 'Krishna Wields the Divine Weapons on Gomanta').

statements.claim: The old sage sat quiet as the preceptor of the gods, still as the ocean.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.95: 'motionless like the ocean... was like the very preceptor of gods.'

DKS_0153.notes: All descriptions and the counsel map to Harivamsha 1.95. 'So the mountain was named: Gomanta' read as connective narration since Gomanta was already named earlier in the same chapter. No issues.

statements.claim: The kings' soldiers saw the two brothers coming down from the mountain with no weapon but their arms, moving like two makaras that agitate the ocean, and terror ran through the host.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.99 v.1-2: 'Beholding the two sons of Vasudeva come down from the mountain the soldiers of the kings grew terrified... Although they had no other weapons but their arms they began to move about there in anger like two Makaras that agitate the ocean.'

statements.claim: The weapons the brothers had obtained before in their encounter at Mathura came down from the sky like burning flames before the assembled kings — huge bodily weapons adorned with celestial garlands, lighting up the ten quarters, as if thirsting for battle.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.99 v.3-8: 'The weapons, which they had obtained before in their encounter at Mathura, came down from the sky like burning flames... adorned with celestial garlands, lighted up the ten quarters with their lustre.' (Source: 'filled with thirst and the desire of feeding upon human flesh'; story's 'thirsting for battle' is a softened but faithful rendering of 'thirst'.)

statements.claim: Four Vaishnava weapons came down: the plough-share Samvartaka, the mace Saunanda, the discus Sudarshana, and the club Koumodaki.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'came down for the two Yadavas four powerful Vaishnava weapons namely, the plough-share Samvartaka, the mace Sounanda, the discus Sudarshana, and the club Koumodaki.'

statements.claim: Balarama, foremost of the Satvatas, took the plough-share in his left hand and the mace Saunanda in his right; Krishna took the discus Sudarshana and the club Koumodaki.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.99 v.9-14: 'the powerful Rāma, the foremost of Sātwatas... took up with his left hand the plough-share... and with his right hand, the best of maces Saunanda... Keshava... took up the discus Sudarshana... The other hand of Krishna... was bedecked with the club Koumodaki.'

statements.claim: The two brothers were one in Vishnu, divided into two for the sake of men.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.99 v.16-17: 'although one in Vishnu, divided into two as men under the names of Rāma and Govinda.'

statements.claim: Balarama dragged the cars of the Kshatriyas from their courses, venting his anger on horses and elephants, churning mountain-like elephants with his mace.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.99 v.18-20: 'dragging the cars of the highly powerful Kshatriyas he began to give effect to his anger on the horses and the elephants... assailing with the strokes of his mace mountain-like elephants... he began as if to churn them.'

statements.claim: The leading Kshatriyas, on the point of being slain, abandoned their cars in fear and fled to Jarasandha.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.99 v.21-22: 'the leading Kshatriyas, who were on the point of being slain by Rāma, left their cars in fear, and went to Jarāsandha.'

statements.claim: Jarasandha rebuked them: 'Fie on your conduct as Kshatriyas grown tired of battle'; those who fly leaving their cars behind are visited by the sin of destroying an embryo; 'Why do you flee in fear of a milk-herd of limited power who fights on foot?'; he vowed to despatch the two cowherd boys to the abode of Yama.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.99 v.22-25, quoted nearly verbatim in the story.

statements.claim: Rallied, the Kshatriyas returned with a downpour of arrows — coats of mail, swords, quivers, horses with golden reins, cars of moon-like lustre, cloud-like elephants — and the kings shone under rising umbrellas and chowries.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.99 v.26-29: 'engaged in fight with a downpour of arrows. With coats of mail, Nishtringsas, weapons, quivers... horses adorned with golden reins, cars of moon-like lustre and cloud-like elephants... Covered with rising umbrellas and fanned with beautiful chowries the kings... shone greatly in beauty.'

statements.claim: Thousands of arrows shot by the kings struck the two descendants of the Yadu race, and they bore them like mountains sprinkled with rain; assailed by heavy clubs and maces they did not tremble.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.99 v.32-33: 'Those two heroic descendants of the Yadu race bore thousands of arrows shot by the kings like two mountains sprinkled with rain. Although assailed by heavy clubs and maces they did not tremble.'

statements.claim: Krishna, like a cloud swollen with wind, increased his body and with the discus cut down men, horses, elephants and mighty car-warriors.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.99 v.34-35: 'Krishna, resembling a cloud... increased his body like a cloud accompanied by wind. And with his discus effulgent like the sun he began to cut down men, horses, elephants and mighty car-warriors.'

statements.claim: Balarama dragged the kings with his plough-share and struck them with his club until they lost consciousness; the variegated chariots broke down, their car-wheels obstructed.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.99 v.36-37: 'Rāma too so dragged the kings with his plough share and so struck them with his club, that they... could not stand... The car-wheels being obstructed the variegated chariots of the kings were broken down.'

statements.claim: In the thick of the slaughter, king Darada fell before Balarama.
statements.evidence: Pack summary: 'Balarama slays king Darada'; story content_note: 'includes the slaying of king Darada' (passage excerpt cuts before this verse but the pack's own summary asserts it).

statements.claim: Jarasandha was still beyond the broken ranks, and the brothers knew he would come again.
statements.evidence: Consistent with the 1.99 outcome and the arc chain (next story opens with Jarasandha having fled but the war continuing; Jarasandha's enmity is the arc's driving thread).

DKS_0154.notes: Battle narrative maps almost verbatim to Harivamsha 1.99. 'As if thirsting for battle' softens the source's 'thirst... for human flesh' but preserves the source's own 'thirst' image; acceptable. No issues.

statements.claim: Jarasandha himself had fled when the battle turned; the alliance that had besieged Gomanta scattered and the mountain stood.
statements.evidence: Pack summary: 'After Jarasandha flees, the king of Chedi... befriends him'; Harivamsha 1.99 passage on the rout of the kings.

statements.claim: It was Jarasandha who had rallied the faltering Kshatriyas with bitter words — fie on their conduct, fleeing from a milk-herd who fought on foot — and his fury had held the line for a while; the kings came back in a downpour of arrows and the brothers stood under it like two mountains sprinkled with rain.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.99 v.22-33: Jarasandha's rebuke, the rallied Kshatriyas' downpour of arrows, and the brothers 'bore thousands of arrows... like two mountains sprinkled with rain.'

statements.claim: The king of Magadha, who had bound a dozen kings into his siege and sworn he would despatch the two cowherd boys to the abode of Yama, had ridden away with the rest when the battle turned.
statements.evidence: The pack supports Jarasandha's vow to despatch the brothers to Yama (1.99 v.25) and the gathering of kings against Gomanta ('the assembled kings'), but nowhere states the number of kings as 'a dozen'; the specific count is invented.
statements.resolution: Corrected in story text via consolidation pass.

statements.claim: The king of Chedi, remembered by the Yadavas as kin for his house was bound to theirs by marriage, rode forward alone after the battle and stopped at a courteous distance.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'the highly effulgent king of Chedi, remembering his relationship with the Yadavas, approached Krishna'; pack summary: 'Krishna's kinsman by marriage.'

statements.claim: He said: this war was never mine by choice; I have seen what your arms can do; let us go together, my army and my followers and I, to the city of Karavira.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Let us go with our army and followers to the city of Karavira'; the framing of kinship and renunciation of the war elaborates the source's 'remembering his relationship with the Yadavas'.

statements.claim: Krishna accepted him at once; Balarama stood by without objection, and they set out the same day, the small army of the Chedi king and the two sons of Vasudeva riding together.
statements.evidence: Implied by the pack summary ('befriends him and escorts him to the city of Karavira') and by the outcome in the following episode (DKS_0156 opens with the column arriving at Karavira).

statements.claim: The country people who had hidden during the siege came to the roadside as the column passed, and the word ran ahead: the war is over, and the king of Chedi rides with Krishna; no plunder and no tribute, only a kinsman's word.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric scene-setting with no sourceable factual assertion; consistent with a peaceful allied journey to Karavira.

statements.claim: The king of Chedi was a man of years who looked almost young again with the fear of the field gone from his eyes.
statements.evidence: Generic descriptive coloring not asserted as a sourceable fact in the pack.

corrections.original_sentence: The king of Magadha, who had bound a dozen kings into his siege and sworn he would despatch the two cowherd boys to the abode of Yama, had ridden away with the rest when the battle turned.
corrections.suggested: The king of Magadha, who had bound the kings into his siege and sworn he would despatch the two cowherd boys to the abode of Yama, had ridden away with the rest when the battle turned.

DKS_0155.notes: One UNSUPPORTED numeric detail: 'a dozen kings' (the pack gives no count of the besieging kings). Everything else maps to Harivamsha 1.99 and the pack summary.

statements.claim: King Shrigala drove out of Karavira to meet the arriving column on a chariot that shone like the car of Indra, with quick-coursing horses, golden axles and inexhaustible quivers, and the earth sank a little under its weight.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.100 v.1-11: 'Mounting a car filled with weapons... drawn by quick-coursing horses, embellished with strong golden axles... resembling the car of Indra... Stricken with fear... the Earth sank under his weight.'

statements.claim: He had heard how the armies of the kings had fared on Mount Gomanta, and the report offended him.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.100 v.17-18: 'I have heard of thy work in the weak army of the stupid kings on the mount Gomanta who had no leader... the defeat of the useless Kshatriyas.'

statements.claim: Shrigala challenged Krishna: 'I am the emperor of the world. You are alone, and I am with my army, so I should not fight you with all these men. Come, I will fight you alone, and one of us will meet his death in a fair fight. If you are slain, I shall be the only Vasudeva in the world. And if I am slain, you shall be the only one.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.100 v.19-22: 'I am now stationed in the dignity of the emperor of the world... Thou art alone and I am with my army; so I should not fight with thee in this way. Come, I shall alone fight with thee... one of us will meet with his death in a fair fight... If thou art slain... I shall be the only Vāsudeva in the world. And if I am slain thou shalt be the only one.'

statements.claim: Krishna answered: 'Strike me as you wish.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.100 v.23: 'saying "Strike me as you wish" the forgiving Mādhava held up his discus.'

statements.claim: Shrigala discharged a net of arrows, showering Krishna with shafts, maces and weapons covered with flame; Krishna stood motionless like a mountain.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.100 v.24-26: 'discharged a net of arrows at Krishna... showered on Krishna mace and various other weapons. And albeit ruthlessly assailed with weapons covered with flames of fire Krishna stood there motionless like a mountain.'

statements.claim: Krishna hurled the discus that had come to him at Gomanta; it struck Shrigala in the breast, pierced him through, and returned to Krishna's hand; Shrigala fell from his chariot like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt, bleeding.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.100 v.27-29: 'he hurled it at Shrigala's breast... the discus Sudarshana returned to its preceptor's hand. Shrigala too, having his heart pierced by the discus... fell down, bleeding like a cleft mountain... fallen like a mountain struck down by a thunder-bolt.'

statements.claim: His army broke: some fled, some entered the city weeping, some stood bewailing their fallen king.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.100 v.30-32: 'his soldiers lost heart and fled away... Some... entered into the city and began to weep... Some, not being able to forsake their fallen king... began to bewail there.'

statements.claim: Krishna declared safety to the people and said 'Do not fear! Do not fear' in a voice like the rumbling of clouds.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.100 v.33-34: 'declaring safety unto the people... Krishna... said with a voice like the rumbling of clouds. "Do not fear! Do not fear."'

statements.claim: The ministers and citizens wept, and the queens came out of the city with their sons, striking their breasts and crying over the fallen king.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.100 v.35-40: 'Shrigāla's subjects and ministers began to shed tears... Shrigāla's queens, with their sons, came out weeping from the city... striking their breasts with their hands, began to weep plaintively.'

statements.claim: The queen Padmavati came with her son, the boy prince Shakradeva, and pleaded for her son; Krishna said 'This son of Shrigala is as my own. I declare safety to you all.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'this son of Shrigala is just like mine. I declare safety unto them and gladly annoint him as the king'; pack summary: 'At the plea of Shrigala's queen, Krishna installs the slain king's son Shakradeva on the throne of Karavira' (characters Padmavati, Shakradeva).

statements.claim: Krishna lifted the prince onto the throne of Karavira, sprinkled him with celestial water, and anointed him king.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Placing the prince on the throne the powerful Janarddana sprinkled him with celestial water'; 'gladly annoint him as the king.'

statements.claim: The gates of Karavira opened before the column had even reached them, and the king came out as a storm comes out of a clear sky.
statements.evidence: Scene-setting for Shrigala's sortie; the source has him issue out upon being informed of their arrival — consistent, presented with imagery.

DKS_0156.notes: Nearly every sentence tracks Harivamsha 1.100. The queen's name Padmavati and prince Shakradeva are taken from the pack's index/summary. No issues.

statements.claim: The kings of the earth gathered in the golden assembly hall of Bhishmaka at Kundina for the swayamvara of his daughter; when Krishna arrived with Garuda and the Yadavas, the leading kings were stricken with anxiety and fell silent.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.105 v.1-3: 'Beholding the eternal Krishna arrive there with Vināta's son the leading kings were stricken with great anxiety... assembled at the golden assembly hall of king Bhismaka.'

statements.claim: Jarasandha warned that Krishna, the well-known son of Vasudeva endued with great energy and prowess, has come for the maiden and will set forth mighty exertions to win her; the kings should behave according to the rules of polity, weighing their own strength and weakness.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.105 v.6-8: 'This Krishna, the well known son of Vasudeva... is endued with great energy and prowess. He has come here for the maiden and forsooth he will set forth mighty exertions for acquiring her... you should behave... according to the rules of Polity... considering your own strength and weakness.'

statements.claim: Jarasandha recalled what the two sons of Vasudeva did on Mount Gomanta without Garuda's help, and said that when Vishnu sits on Garuda and sets forth his exertions for the maiden, even Indra assisted by all the celestials will not be able to stand in the battle-field.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.105 v.9-11: 'You know well the highly dreadful work which these two powerful sons of Vasudeva performed on the mount Gomanta without the help of Vinatā's son... When seated on Garuda Vishnu will set forth his exertions for acquiring the maiden, even Sakra, assisted by the celestials... will not be able to stand in the battle-field.'

statements.claim: Jarasandha recited Krishna's previous deeds: boar form raised the drowned earth and killed Hiranyaksha; man-lion form slew Hiranyakashipu, who could not be killed in the three worlds, sky, earth or nether region, in day or night, by anything dry or wet; dwarf form bound Bali with a noose of promise and sent him to the nether region.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.105 v.12-16: boar form 'released the earth... killed Hiranyaksha the king of Daityas'; 'Hiranyakashipu, who did not meet with his death in the three worlds... in the sky, on the earth, and in the nether region, in day or in night, from a dry or an wet article, was slain... by Hari in his man-lion form'; 'Binding the powerful Bali... with a noose of promise Vishnu, in his form of a dwarf, sent him down to the nether region.'

statements.claim: At the junction of the ages he took birth in disguise from Jamadagni and Renuka as Rama with the axe and cut down the thousand-armed Kartavirya, elated with the pride of his kingdom.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.105 v.17-20: 'the highly powerful king Kārtavirya, endued with thousand arms, grew elated with the pride of kingdom... Vishnu took his birth in disguise, from Jamadagni and Renukā, as Rāma... and killed him with his axe.'

statements.claim: He was Dasharatha's son Rama, born in the race of Ikshvaku, who killed Ravana, the conqueror of the three worlds; in the Taraka-rooted war, eight-armed and seated on Garuda, he killed the boon-elated Asuras, and with his sun-effulgent discus killed the demon Kalanemi who terrorized the gods.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.105 v.21-24: 'Dasharatha's son Rāma, born in the race of Ikshāku... killed the heroic Rāvana, the conqueror of the three worlds'; 'In the Tretā age in the war of which Tāraka was the root, the powerful Vishnu, seated on Garuda, assuming a form of eight arms, killed... the Asuras... killed, with his discus, effulgent like the sun, the demon Kālanemi who terrorized the gods.'

statements.claim: As a boy in the forest he slew the demons Dhenuka, Arishta and Pralamba; in his cowherd form Devaki's son slew Putana, Keshi, the elephant Kuvalayapida, the wrestlers Chanura and Mushtika, and Kamsa with all his followers.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.105 v.25-28: 'as a boy in the forest, many... demons, Dhenuka, Arishtha and Pralamva have been slain. Slaying in his cow-herd form Shakuni, Putanā, Keshi, Jamala, Arjuna, the elephant Kuvalayapida, Chānura, Mushitika and Kansa with his followers Devaki's son sported there.'

statements.claim: Jarasandha declared his sure understanding, acquired at Mathura, that Devaki's son Keshava is the first cause of the celestials, the destroyer of the Asuras, Narayana, the ancient Purusha, the prime cause of the universe, Truth, the creator of all creatures manifest and unmanifest, unconquerable, unborn, eternal, the lord of the three worlds.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.105 v.29-33: 'I consider Devaki's son Keshava as the first cause of the celestials, the destroyer of the Asuras, as Nārāyana, the ancient Purusha, the Prime cause of the universe, as Truth, the creator of all creatures manifest and unmanifest... unconquerable... unborn... the lord of the three worlds... This my sure under standing, I have acquired from Mathurā.'

statements.claim: Jarasandha concluded: can Garuda be the carrier of a mere man, even a mortal lord paramount? When Janarddana displays his prowess for the maiden, what powerful man will stand before Garuda? Vishnu himself has come for this swayamvara; mighty is the calamity that will befall you on his arrival; do whatever you think proper.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.105 v.34-36: 'Can Garuda be the carrier of a man even if he be born in the high family of a mortal Lord Paramount? Besides when Janarddana will display his prowess for the maiden what powerful man will be able to stand before Garuda? Forsooth I tell you that Vishnu himself has come for this Swayamvara. Mighty is the calamity that will befall you on his arrival here.'

statements.claim: Sunitha rose and gave his voice to the king of Magadha's words, and the kings knew the warning would not be argued away.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.105: 'After Jarāshandha... the greatly wise Sunitha replied saying...'; and 1.106 (in pack for DKS_0158): Dantavakra refers to 'what the king of Magadha and Sunitha have said for our well-being' — confirming Sunitha concurred with Jarasandha.

DKS_0157.notes: Jarasandha's speech is a near-verbatim rendering of Harivamsha 1.105. Sunitha's concurrence is confirmed by 1.106's opening in the next pack. No issues.

statements.claim: Dantavakra, the king of Karusha, rose and endorsed the warning: what the king of Magadha and Sunitha have said for our well-being appears proper; he could not blame these nectarine words out of malice, pride, or any desire for victory of his own.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.106 v.1-4: 'the heroic Dantavakra, the king of Karusha said... what the king of Magadha and Sunitha have said for our well-being appears to me as proper. I cannot blame these nectarine words out of malice, pride or of my own desire for victory.'

statements.claim: Dantavakra recalled the war: because of Kamsa's foolishness the two heroes first lived in Vrindavana; Kamsa invited Rama and Keshava and set an infuriated elephant against them; they slew the elephant, entered the arena, and slew Kamsa, king of Mathura, with his followers — what offence did they commit that we all, elderly in age, came to Mathura at another's instigation?
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.106 v.8-11: 'on account of Kansa's foolishness those two heroes first lived in Vrindāvana... Kansa invited Rāma and Keshava and set an infuriated elephant against them. Slaying that elephant those two heroes entered the arena... they slew Kansa, the king of Mathurā... with his followers. What offence did they commit thereby, that we all, elderly in age, came to Mathura at (another's) instigation.'

statements.claim: Dantavakra continued: terrified at our huge and overwhelming army, Rama and Keshava left their own city and soldiers and fled to Gomanta; we pursued them and were defeated by those two boys; we laid siege to the hill, as Kshatriyas should, and set fire to it; had they died quietly in that conflagration we would have considered them humbled; we blame Janarddana because he fought against us.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.106 v.12-15: 'terrified at our huge and overwhelming army, Rāma and Keshava, leaving their own city and soldiers, fled away to Gomanta. We still pursued them there; and though expert in the art of fighting we were defeated... we laid seige to the hill and set fire to it... if they had given up their life quietly in that conflagration considering it a forest fire we would have considered them humbled. We blame Janārddana because he fought against us.'

statements.claim: Dantavakra concluded: as matters stand, wherever we go we shall pick up a quarrel, so let us contract friendship with Krishna; Krishna has come for the maiden, not for a quarrel.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.106 v.16-17: 'wherever we shall go we will pick up a quarrel. Let us, therefore... contract friendship with Krishna... Krishna has not come to this city of Kundina for picking up a quarrel. He has come for the maiden.'

statements.claim: Dantavakra declared Krishna not an ordinary human being but the foremost of men in the land of mortals and the foremost of gods in the land of celestials, the Deity and Creator of the worlds; in God there is no malice, pride or crookedness; the gods do not grow stupified or lean, are not visited by calamity, and remove the calamities of those who bow unto them.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.106 v.18-19: 'Krishna is not an ordinary human being. He is the foremost of men in this land of mortals, the foremost of gods in the land of celestials. He is the Deity and the Creator of the worlds. In God there is no malice, pride or crookedness. They are not stupified, they do not grow lean and are not visited by any calamity. They always remove the calamities of those who bow unto them.'

statements.claim: Dantavakra said Vishnu, the king of gods, has come with Garuda to show his true form; Krishna never goes with his army to slay his enemies; his coming accompanied by the leading Bhojas, Vrishnis, Andhakas and Yadavas indicates his desire of contracting friendship; let us offer the high-souled Keshava hospitality with arghya and water to rinse his mouth, and if we make peace with Keshava we shall live freed from anxiety and fear.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.106 v.20-24, quoted nearly verbatim; also pack excerpt: 'let us go and offer the high-souled Keshava hospitality... if we make peace with Keshava we shall be able to live freed from anxiety and fear.'

statements.claim: Salwa, the foremost of speakers, rose and scorned the fear: had they trembled at Krishna and thought it proper to make peace, they would have left their weapons at that time; speaking ill of one's own army and extolling another is not the duty of Kshatriya kings; we are born in great royal families and have glorified our races; why should our sense be poor like a coward's?
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.106 v.25-28: 'Sālwa, the foremost of speakers, said... What is the use of this fear? Had we trembled in Krishna's fear and thought it proper to make peace with him, we would have left our weapons at that time... Such is not the duty of the Kshatriya kings. We are all born in great royal families and have glorified our respective races. Why should then our sense be poorly like that of a coward.'

statements.claim: Salwa declared he knows Devaki's son Krishna as the immortal, eternal Prime Deity Vishnu, invincible unto the kings, powerful, adored of all the worlds, Vaikuntha, the preceptor of the entire world; and knows all the objects of Vishnu: the destruction of king Kamsa, the relieving of the earth of her burden, our destruction, and the protection of the worlds.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.106 v.29-32: 'I know Devaki's son Krishna as the immortal, eternal, Prime Deity Vishnu, invincible unto the kings, powerful, adored of all the worlds, Vaikuntha and the preceptor of the entire world... I know full well all the objects of Vishnu. He has in view... the destruction of king Kansa, the relieving of the earth of her burden, our destruction and the protection of the worlds.'

statements.claim: Salwa said: a great battle will take place between Vishnu and all the kings; consumed by the fire of his discus we will go to the abode of Yama; yet no one meets with untimely death and no one survives when the proper time comes, so a man should not entertain fear.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.106 v.31-34: 'a great battle will take place between Vishnu and all the kings... consumed by the fire of his discus we will go to the abode of Yama. Still considering that no one meets with untimely death, no one survives when the proper time comes and the lease of his life runs out... therefore a man should not entertain fear.'

statements.claim: Salwa recalled that when the ascetic virtue of the Daityas is annihilated, Vishnu, conversant with yoga, brings about their destruction in due time; he sent down the mighty Bali to the nether region and has performed many other feats like this; do not question the subject of fighting.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.106 v.35-36: 'When the ascetic virtue of the Daityas is annihilated the Divine Vishnu, conversant with Yoga, brings about their destruction in proper time. This Lord of gods sent down Virochona's son, the highly powerful Bali, to the nether region... Vishnu has performed many other feats like this; you should not therefore question the subject of fighting.'

statements.claim: Through it all Bhishmaka, king of Kundina, host of the council and father of the maiden and of the arrogant young Rukmi, had listened in silence; rising from his seat, he resolved to go himself to Krishna to propitiate, before any war began, the suitor the whole earth had gathered to deny.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Bhismaka felt a desire to go to eternal Krishna for propitiating him'; pack summary: 'Bhishmaka, fearing for his arrogant son Rukmi, resolves to go and propitiate Krishna.'

statements.claim: The council still rang with argument behind Bhishmaka as he stepped out into the evening, and Kundina went on lighting its lamps.
statements.evidence: Transitional scene-setting closing the episode; no sourceable factual assertion.

DKS_0158.notes: Both speeches track Harivamsha 1.106 closely, often near-verbatim. Bhishmaka's motivation (Rukmi) is drawn from the pack summary. No issues.

statements.claim: The defeated suitors gathered in Bhishmaka's assembly hall in Kundina after Krishna carried off Rukmini from the swayamvara, before scattering to their kingdoms.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109 opens with the kings, anxious to go to their kingdoms, returning to Bhishmaka's assembly-hall after Vasudeva's son's departure; Rukmini context carried from corpus chain (DKS_0158).

statements.claim: Bhishmaka, well read in the laws of conduct, asked the kings' forgiveness for the fruit of his misconduct.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109: 'king Bhishmaka, the foremost of kings and well-read in moral laws... Do you forgive me for the fruit that is the outcome of my misconduct'.

statements.claim: Bhishmaka sent away the monarchs of Central India and of the east, west, and north, who departed delighted; the circle remaining included Jarasandha, Sunitha, Dantavakra, Shalya of Soubha, Mahakurma, Kaishika, the Pravara kings, Venudari, the king of Kashmir, and the kings of the Deccan.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109 lists exactly these kings remaining 'desirous of listening to the mystery' after the others went away delightedly.

statements.claim: Bhishmaka spoke of his son with fear, praising Krishna as foremost of beings and blessing Devaki who conceived the lotus-eyed Krishna.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109: 'Observing the movements of my son my eyes are agitated with fear... Blessed is Devaki... who has conceived as her son the lotus-eyed Krishna'.

statements.claim: Shalya counselled: Kshatriyas meet success or defeat in battle; save Baladeva and Krishna no third person can withstand Bhishmaka's son, who handles the Bhargava weapons.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109 (19-23): exact parallel of Shalya's speech.

statements.claim: Shalya said even the holder of the trident (Siva) cannot defeat Krishna in this land, and that Bhishmaka's son, knowing Keshava as Ishana, did not engage in fight with him.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109 (24-25): 'In this land of mortals even the holder of trident (Siva) cannot defeat him... Knowing Keshava as Ishāna he did not engage in fight with him'.

statements.claim: Gargya, desiring a son, adored Rudra for twelve years living on powdered iron; Rudra granted a boon that his son would be unslayable by the kings of Mathura.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109 (26-29): Gārgya's twelve-year penance on powdered iron and the boon that the kings of Mathurā could not slay his son.

statements.claim: By that boon Kalayavana is unslayable by the kings of Mathura in the battlefield and especially in the city of Mathura, and could defeat Krishna if they fought.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109 (29-30): 'Kālayavana is unslayable by the kings of Mathura in the battle-field and especially in the city of Mathurā... if he comes to battle and fights with him he will be able to defeat him'.

statements.claim: Shalya urged the kings to send an emissary to the capital of the king of the Yavanas; the delighted kings agreed, while Jarasandha lost heart recollecting the words of Brahma and lamented that the chiefs now made him seek another's shelter.
statements.evidence: HV 1.109 (32-35): kings say 'We will do it'; Jarāsandha 'lost heart' and gave the damsel/stranger lament.

statements.claim: Jarasandha dispatched Shalya of Soubha as envoy to the capital of the Yavanas.
statements.evidence: Index summary: 'Jarasandha dispatches Shalya as envoy'; excerpt: 'This effulgent king of Soubha... let him proceed to the capital of Yavana'; continued in DKS_0160.

DKS_0159.notes: Highly faithful to HV 1.109; dialogue rendered nearly verbatim. Opening Rukmini-swayamvara framing is chain context from DKS_0158, not contradicted by pack.

statements.claim: A cold, fragrant, delightful wind blew in the Yavana capital and the assembled Yavanas wondered whence it came, then saw a car coming from the south.
statements.evidence: HV 1.110 (2-6): 'there blew delightful, but exciting, cold and fragrant wind... Whence it has come?... they saw a car coming from the south'.

statements.claim: Kalayavana governed his city in pursuance of royal duties, being wise, conversant with the threefold objects, proficient in policy, innocent of the sevenfold calamities, endued with accomplishments, versed in scriptures, pious, truthful, master of his senses, acquainted with war, expert in capturing forts, heroic, and honoring his ministers.
statements.evidence: HV 1.110 (1): nearly verbatim catalogue of Kalayavana's virtues.

statements.claim: Kalayavana sat at ease encircled by ministers while learned Yavanas discoursing on celestial themes adored him.

The car was golden and white, lit with jewels, adorned with celestial flags and pennons, drawn by horses fleet like mind or air, decked with tiger-skins, built by the celestial Architect, effulgent like the sun; the powerful and beautiful king of Soubha, Shalya, sat on it.
statements.evidence: HV 1.110 (7-12): full description matches, including 'constructed by the celestial Architect'.

statements.claim: Delighted at seeing his friend, Kalayavana sent for arghya and water for washing the feet, rose from his throne, and waited at the landing stair of the car.

Shalya descended alone with a confident heart and joyously entered the Yavana palace, but refused the arghya, saying he was an envoy of the kings dispatched by Jarasandha and did not deserve arghya from the kings.
statements.evidence: HV 1.110 (15-18): Shalya's refusal speech quoted almost verbatim.

statements.claim: Kalayavana replied that he knew Shalya was sent by the king of Magadha for the kings' behalf, that by adoring Shalya he worshipped the whole host of kings, and asked him to sit on the throne.

They shook hands, enquired of each other's welfare, and sat at ease on the sacred throne; Kalayavana asked what had become impossible for the king on whose arm-strength the kings lived without anxiety, and promised to carry out even a very difficult mandate.

Shalya delivered Jarasandha's message: Krishna oppressed the world from birth; Jarasandha, with kings and fourfold forces, besieged mount Gomanta, set fire to it at the king of Chedi's words; Rama leaped down with the golden-hilted sword, slaughtered the army, ground elephants, horses and soldiers with his ploughshare and mace, and destroyed elephants with elephants, cars with cars, cavalry with horses.
statements.evidence: HV 1.110 (26-33): full battle narration matches in detail.

statements.claim: Krishna then leaped down with his sun-bright discus and black iron club, shaking the mountain, and the mountain, whirled and bathed with shower, extinguished the fire and entered the earth as if dancing.
The mandate ended with the plea to 'enter the city of Mathura with your army and establish your glory there'.
statements.evidence: Index excerpt of HV 1.110: 'enter the city of Mathurā with your army establish your glory there'.

DKS_0160.notes: Faithful retelling of HV 1.110; Jarasandha's Gomanta speech reproduced nearly verbatim. No unsupported factual claims.

statements.claim: Kalayavana rejoiced that numberless kings had requested him to vanquish Krishna, whom he called invincible in the three worlds even unto gods and Asuras, and declared he would start for Mathura that very day to defeat Keshava in the battlefield.
statements.evidence: HV 1.111 (1-6): Kalayavana's elated speech, including 'in this auspicious moment I shall even to-day start for Mathurā for defeating Keshava in the battle-field'.

statements.claim: Kalayavana said even his discomfiture in the task would be tantamount to success and he would carry out Emperor Jarasandha's command issued at the kings' request.
statements.evidence: HV 1.111 (5): 'Even my discomfiture in it will be, tantamount to my success... I shall carry out the command of the Emperor Jarasandha issued at the request of the kings'.

statements.claim: Kalayavana honored Shalya with highly precious gems and dresses, gave away riches to his guest and the Brahmanas, offered libations to fire, and after benedictory rites set out with his army to vanquish Janarddana.
Shalya, his desire fully achieved, embraced the lord of the Yavanas and set out with a delighted heart for his own city, carrying the answer back to the kings.
statements.evidence: HV 1.111 (10); the 'answer' is a reasonable connective inference consistent with the narrative.

statements.claim: Gargya, called impotent by his brother-in-law in an assembly of the Yadavas, was offended by their laughter and repaired to the shores of the western sea to do penance for a son who should be a terror to the tribe of Yadu.
statements.evidence: VP 5.23: 'Śyála having called Gárgya the Brahman... impotent, in an assembly of the Yádavas, they all laughed; at which he was highly offended, and repaired to the shores of the western sea'.

statements.claim: For twelve years Gargya propitiated Mahadeva living on iron sand, and the deity gave him the desired boon; the childless Yavana king befriended him, and Gargya begot by the king's wife a son as black as a bee, with a breast hard as the thunderbolt, called Kalayavana.
statements.evidence: VP 5.23: penance on iron sand for twelve years, son 'as black as a bee... breast was as hard as the point of the thunderbolt... thence called Kálayavana'.

statements.claim: The old Yavana king placed Kalayavana on the throne and retired to the woods; Kalayavana asked Narada who were the most mighty heroes on earth and was answered: 'The Yadavas'.
statements.evidence: VP 5.23: 'The Yavana king having placed his son... upon the throne, retired to the woods... demanded of Nárada who were the most mighty heroes on earth. To which the sage answered, The Yádavas'.

statements.claim: Kalayavana assembled many myriads of Mlechchhas and barbarians and advanced impatiently against Mathura with elephants, cavalry, chariots and foot, wearying his animal daily but insensible of fatigue himself.
statements.evidence: VP 5.23: 'assembled many myriads of Mlechchhas and barbarians, and with a vast armament of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and foot, advanced impatiently against Mathurá... wearying every day the animal that carried him, but insensible of fatigue himself'.

DKS_0161.notes: Blends HV 1.111 (march/embassy) with VP 5.23 (origin), both present in the pack; variant_notes explicitly sanction the VP origin account. Closing 'name ran ahead like fire' is connective narration.

statements.claim: Kalayavana's host covered the plain like locusts, followed by a new river born of the urine and dung of horses and camels, named Aswasakrit.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114 (19-24): Dasyu kings 'resembling a swarm of locusts'; 'By the urine and excreta of the soldiers a river was created... passed by the name of Aswasakrit'.

statements.claim: Gargya, dishonored by his brother-in-law before the king, gave up his wife in anger and did penance on pounded iron for twelve years; Rudra conferred a boon of an all-powerful son able to discomfit the Vrishni and Andhaka descendants in battle.

The childless Yavana king heard of the boon, brought Gargya to his kingdom and consoled him; Gargya begot Kalayavana on the Apsara Gopali in the guise of a milk-woman; the boy was raised in the king's inner apartment like his own son and became king after the old king's demise.
When Kalayavana grew powerful, the Shaka, Tukhara, Darava, Parava, Tangana, Khasha, Panhava and hundreds of Mlechcha kings living near Himavan took shelter under him.

Encircled by those Dasyu kings in various dresses and weapons, the Yavana king set out for Mathura, agitating the earth with horses, elephants, asses, camels and a huge army; dust covered the sun's path.
Krishna took no notice of Kalayavana as he grew up among the Yavanas because he had heard from Narada the story of his obtaining the boon.

Krishna told his kinsmen of the calamity, that the enemy was unslayable by them because of the trident-holder's boon, that conciliation had failed, that Narada had said 'I am to live here', that Jarasandha was unforgiving and other kings, displeased at Kamsa's destruction, had sought refuge with the Magadha king and slain many Yadava kinsmen, and that they would never prosper living in the city.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114 (25-28): Krishna's address reproduced nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: Desirous of retreating, Krishna sent an envoy to Kalayavana with a sealed jar holding a highly dreadful black serpent resembling a collection of collyrium; the emissary said 'Krishna is like a deadly serpent' and showed the jar.
Kalayavana understood the Yadavas sent it to terrorize him, filled the jar with dreadful ants which devoured the serpent to ashes, and the jar was sealed anew and sent back.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114 (32-33): 'Kalayavana filled that jar with dreadful ants... serpent was eaten up by the innumerable ants... reduced to ashes. Thereupon seali[ng]...'; index excerpt confirms the counter-stratagem.

DKS_0162.notes: Faithful to HV 1.114; uses the HV variant (Gopali/Apsara) for the birth, consistent with pack. 'King who could not be frightened' closing is connective.

statements.claim: From Girivraja the king of Magadha whirled a mace ninety-nine times and hurled it toward Mathura, where Krishna of wonderful deeds was residing.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.19: 'the mighty king of Magadha from his city of Girivraja, whirling a mace ninety-nine times, hurled it towards Mathura. At that time Krishna of wonderful deeds was residing at Mathura'.

statements.claim: An enmity arose between Jarasandha and Krishna after king Kansa was slain by Vasudeva.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.19: 'Some time after when king Kansa was slain by Vasudeva, an enmity arose between him and Krishna'.

statements.claim: Jarasandha was the son of Vrihadratha; when Chandakausika came to the Magadha country, Vrihadratha went out to receive him with ministers, priest, wives and son, offering his whole kingdom along with the boy.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.19: Krishna's narration of Chandakausika's visit and Vrihadratha's offering.

statements.claim: The sage prophesied the son would grow in prosperity and prowess, that other monarchs could never equal his energy, that weapons hurled even by celestials would cause him no pain, that he would blaze above all crowned heads and rob all monarchs of splendour, and that all kings of the earth would obey him.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.19: prophecy quoted nearly verbatim ('weapons hurled at him even by the celestials will fail to produce the least pain in him... rob all monarchs of their splendour... all the kings of the earth will live in obedience to the commands of this child').

statements.claim: Vrihadratha installed Jarasandha on the throne and, feeling distaste for worldly pleasures, retired into the woods with his two wives; Jarasandha ruled like a father and brought numerous kings under his sway.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.19: 'installed Jarasandha, on the throne... retired into the woods... ruled his kingdom like a father... brought numerous kings under his sway'.

statements.claim: The mace fell near Mathura at a distance of ninety-nine yojanas from Girivraja, at a place called Gadavasan adjacent to Mathura; the citizens informed Krishna of the fall.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.19: 'fell near Mathura at a distance of ninety-nine yojanas from Gririvraja... called Gadavasan... The citizens... went unto Krishna and informed him of the fall of the mace'.

statements.claim: Jarasandha had two supporters, Hansa and Dimvaka, incapable of being slain by weapons, foremost in the science of politics and morality, who with Jarasandha were more than a match for the three worlds.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.19: 'two supporters called Hansa and Dimvaka, both of whom were incapable of being slain by weapons... more than a match for three worlds'.

statements.claim: For that reason the Kukkura, Andhaka and Vrishni tribes, from motives of policy, never deemed it proper to fight with him.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.19: 'it was for this reason that the powerful Kukkura, Andhaka and Vrishni tribes... did not deem it proper to fight with him'.

DKS_0163.notes: Faithful to MBh 2.19; 'iron seemed the shape of his anger' and closing warning framing are connective narration. 'Heights of Girivraja' is a minor atmospheric rephrasing of 'from his city of Girivraja'.

statements.claim: Krishna stated that both Hansa and Dimvaka had fallen and Kamsa with all his followers had been slain, so the time had come for Jarasandha's destruction.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: 'both Hansa and Dimvaka have fallen; Kansa also with all his followers has been slain. The time hath, therefore come for the destruction of Jarasandha'.

statements.claim: Jarasandha was incapable of being vanquished in battle even by all the celestials and Asuras fighting together, but could be vanquished in a personal struggle with bare arms.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: 'incapable of being vanquished in battle even by all the celestials and the Asuras (fighting together). We think, however, that he should be vanquished in a personal struggle with bare arms'.

statements.claim: Krishna said: in me is policy, in Bhima is strength, in Arjuna is triumph; as prelude to performing the Rajasuya they would achieve the destruction of the ruler of Magadha.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: quoted verbatim in the pack excerpt.

statements.claim: Krishna said that when the three approached the monarch in secret he would engage with one of them, and from fear of disgrace, covetousness and pride of strength would summon Bhima, whom death-like Bhimasena would slay.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: 'From fear of disgrace, from covetousness, and from pride of strength he will certainly summon Bhima to the encounter... the long-armed and mighty Bhimasena will effect the destruction of the king'.

statements.claim: Krishna asked Yudhishthira to make over Bhima and Arjuna to him as a pledge.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: 'then make over to me, as a pledge, Bhima and Arjuna without loss of time'.

statements.claim: Yudhishthira replied that Krishna was the lord of the Pandavas, that what he said was consistent with wise counsels, and that one under Krishna's command could regard Jarasandha as already slain, the confined monarchs freed, and the Rajasuya accomplished.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: Yudhishthira's reply quoted nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: Yudhishthira spoke of leadership: troops well led do excellent service, a leaderless force is called inert, the wise conduct water into low places, and fishermen drain tanks through holes.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: 'Troops, when properly led, always do excellent service. A force without a leader hath been called inert by the wise... Even fishermen cause the water (of tank) to run out through holes'.

statements.claim: Yudhishthira urged placing Krishna in the van — whose strength consists in wisdom and policy — with Arjuna following Krishna and Bhima following Arjuna.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: 'let, therefore, Arjuna, the son of Pritha, follow Krishna... and let Bhima follow Arjuna. Policy and good fortune and might will (then) bring about success'.

statements.claim: The trio set out for Magadha in the garb of Snataka Brahmanas, blessed by friends' and relatives' speeches, their bodies blazing like the sun, moon and fire with wrath at the sad lot of their relative kings.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: 'set out for Magadha attired in the garb of Snataka Brahmanas of resplendent bodies... inflamed with wrath at the sad lot of their relative kings, those bodies of theirs became much more blazing'.

statements.claim: The people, beholding Krishna and Arjuna, never before vanquished, with Bhima in the van, regarded Jarasandha as already slain.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: 'the people... regarded Jarasandha as already slain'.

statements.claim: Their route ran from the Kuru country through Kuru-jangala, the lake of lotuses, the Kalakuta hills, the rivers Gandaki, Sadanira and Sarkaravarta, the Sarayu, Eastern Kosala, Mithila, the Mala and Charamanwati, the Ganges and the Sone, to Magadha in the heart of Kushamva, and the hills of Goratha overlooking the city.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20: full itinerary matches, including 'arrived at Magadha in the heart of (the country of) Kushamva' and 'the hills of Goratha'.

DKS_0164.notes: Faithful to MBh 2.20; variant_notes note the BP 10.71 attribution variant but this story correctly follows the MBh attribution to Krishna. Opening 'one obstacle left' is connective framing.

statements.claim: Krishna showed Arjuna the capital of Magadha filled with flocks and herds, never-exhausted water, fine mansions in excellent array, free from every calamity.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'behold... the great capital of Magadha... Filled with flocks and herds and its stock of water never exhausted... free from every kind of calamity'.

statements.claim: Five large hills — Vaihara, Varaha, Vrishava, Rishigiri and the delightful Chaitya — of high peaks and tall cool-shaded trees, connected, with slopes concealed by fragrant flowering Lodhra forests, protected Girivraja.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: the five hills and Lodhra forests described as such.

statements.claim: Gautama of rigid vows begot Kakshivat and other celebrated sons there, and the monarchs of Anga and Vanga and other countries had come in olden times to Gautama's abode and passed their days in joy.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'the illustrious Gautama of rigid vows begat... Kakshivat and other celebrated sons... the mighty monarchs of Anga, and Vanga and other countries, came to the abode of Gautama, and passed their days in joy'.

statements.claim: Krishna said that owning such an impregnable city Jarasandha was ever bent on seeking fruition of his purposes unlike other monarchs, and that they would humble his pride by slaying him that day.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'Owning such a delightful and impregnable city, Jarasandha is ever bent on seeking the fruition of his purposes... We shall, however, by slaying him to-day humble his pride'.

statements.claim: The brothers entered the city of Magadha and approached Girivraja, full of cheerful, well-fed inhabitants of all four orders with perennial festivities.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'full of cheerful and well-fed inhabitants belonging to all the four orders, and where festivities were perennial'.

statements.claim: At the city gate the brothers, instead of passing through, pierced the heart of the high Chaityaka peak worshipped by Vrihadratha's race and the citizens, delightful to all Magadhas.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'On arriving then at the gate of the city, the brothers (instead of passing through it) began to pierce... the heart of the high Chaityaka peak'.

statements.claim: There Vrihadratha had slain the cannibal Rishava and made three drums from his hide, which when beaten sounded for a full month; at that point the brothers broke the peak down.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'Vrihadratha had slain a cannibal called Rishava... made of his hide three drums... once beaten their sound lasted one full month... the brothers broke down the Chaityaka peak... at that point where those drums... used to yield their continuous sound'.

statements.claim: Desirous of slaying Jarasandha they seemed by that act to place their feet on their foe's head, and entered the city with joyful hearts.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'desirous of slaying Jarasandha they seemed by that act of theirs to place their feet upon the head of their foe... with joyful hearts they then entered the city'.

statements.claim: The Brahmanas of Girivraja saw evil omens and reported them to Jarasandha; his priest made him mount an elephant and whirled lighted brands about him, and Jarasandha entered on a sacrifice with vows and fasts to ward off the evils.
