statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'the learned Brahmanas residing within the city saw many evil omens... the priest making the king mount an elephant whirled lighted brands about him... entered upon the celebration of a sacrifice, with proper vows and fasts'.

statements.claim: Unarmed, with bare arms as their only weapons, the brothers entered the capital in the guise of Brahmanas, beheld the shops full of edibles and floral wreaths, snatched garlands forcibly from the flower-vendors, and passed along the public road.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'the brothers unarmed... entered the capital in the guise of Brahmanas... snatched forcibly from the flower-vendors the garlands they had exposed for sale'.

statements.claim: Decked in garlands and ear-rings, arms besmeared with sandal paste like sala trunks, they entered Jarasandha's abode like Himalayan lions; the Magadha people wondered at the elephant-like heroes, and the bulls among men passed through three crowded gates to the king.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: all similes and details match ('like Himalayan lions eyeing cattle-folds... arms... looked like the trunks of sala trees... passing through three gates that were crowded with men').

statements.claim: Jarasandha rose in haste and received them with water for the feet, honey and the Arghya ingredients, gifts of kine and other respects, saying 'Ye are welcome'; both Arjuna and Bhima remained silent.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'rising up in haste received them with water to wash their feet with, and honey and the other ingredients of the Arghya--with gifts of kine... Ye are welcome!... both Partha and Bhima remained silent at this'.

DKS_0165.notes: Faithful to MBh 2.21. 'All his rites could not undo what the portents promised' is connective interpretation, not a factual assertion.

statements.claim: Jarasandha rose in haste and received the three Brahmanas with water to wash the feet, honey and the other Arghya ingredients, gifts of kine and other respects, saying 'Ye are welcome'.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21 (also quoted in this pack): 'rising up in haste received them with water to wash their feet with, and honey and the other ingredients of the Arghya--with gifts of kine... Ye are welcome'.

statements.claim: Both of his two younger guests (Bhima and Arjuna) remained silent.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'both Partha and Bhima remained silent at this'.

statements.claim: Jarasandha came to the meeting amid ill omens: Brahmanas of Girivraja had seen evil signs and reported them, his priest made him mount an elephant and whirled lighted brands, and he entered on a sacrifice with vows and fasts.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'the learned Brahmanas residing within the city saw many evil omens which they reported to Jarasandha... the priest making the king mount an elephant whirled lighted brands about him... entered upon the celebration of a sacrifice, with proper vows and fasts'.

statements.claim: The three strangers had passed along the public road past shops full of edibles and floral wreaths and snatched garlands from the flower-vendors; the Magadha people wondered at them, and they passed through three crowded gates to the king.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: repeated details match (shops, garlands, three gates, elephant-like heroes with sala-trunk arms).

statements.claim: Krishna spoke for the three: 'O king of kings, these two are now in the observance of a vow. Therefore they will not speak. Silent they will remain till midnight. After that hour they will speak with thee.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (MBh 2.21): 'And addressing the monarch Krishna said,--O king of kings these two are now in the observance of a vow. Therefore they will not speak. Silent they will remain till midnight After that hour they will speak with thee!'

statements.claim: Whatever questions Jarasandha might wish to ask would have to wait until the night hour.
statements.evidence: Inference from the vow-of-silence explanation; consistent with the source, not a new factual claim.

DKS_0166.notes: Faithful to MBh 2.21; recap material repeats pack details. Closing meditation on the waiting court is connective narration.

statements.claim: Krishna showed Arjuna the great capital of Magadha as the three brothers approached: filled with flocks and herds, its water never failing, adorned with fine mansions in excellent array, free from every kind of calamity, and said 'We shall, however, by slaying him today, humble his pride.'
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21 (Ganguli): Vasudeva's speech to Partha is nearly verbatim, including 'We shall, however, by slaying him to-day humble his pride.'

statements.claim: The five hills of Girivraja — Vaihara, Varaha, Vrishava, Rishigiri and the delightful Chaitya — seemed jointly to protect the city; Chaitya was worshipped by the citizens and by the royal line of Vrihadratha.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: hills named exactly; Chaitya 'worshipped by the race of Vrihadratha, as also by the citizens'. The 'fingers of a cupped hand' simile is connective imagery.

statements.claim: Instead of entering by the gate, the brothers tore down the Chaityaka peak at the point where the great drums of Vrihadratha used to sound — drums which, once beaten, sounded for a full month.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: arriving at the gate the brothers (instead of passing through it) broke down the high Chaityaka peak worshipped by the Magadhas, at the point where Vrihadratha's drums (made from the cannibal Rishava's hide) 'once beaten their sound lasted one full month'.

statements.claim: In the guise of Brahmanas, bare arms as their only weapons, the brothers walked the crowded streets past shops of edibles and wreaths, snatched garlands from the flower-vendors, their sandal-smeared arms like the trunks of sala trees, passed through three crowded gates proudly like Himalayan lions eyeing cattle-folds, and the people of Magadha wondered much at the giants.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: every element near-verbatim (guise of Brahmanas, bare arms as only weapons, garlands snatched from flower-vendors, sala-trunk arms, three crowded gates, Himalayan lion simile, the Magadhas' wonder).

statements.claim: Within the city the learned Brahmanas had seen evil omens and reported them to Jarasandha; his priest made the king mount an elephant and whirled lighted brands about him, and the king began a sacrifice with proper vows and fasts to ward off the portents.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: near-verbatim sequence.

statements.claim: Jarasandha rose up in haste and received the strangers with water for the feet, honey and the ingredients of the arghya, and gifts of kine, bidding them welcome; Bhima and Arjuna remained silent.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.21: 'Jarasandha rising up in haste received them with water... honey and the other ingredients of the Arghya--with gifts of kine... Ye are welcome'; 'both Partha and Bhima remained silent'. Krishna speaking for them is carried from the chain (DKS_0166).

statements.claim: After the welcome Jarasandha censured the guests for coming into his city by no proper gate.
statements.evidence: Pack index summary: 'When Jarasandha censures the disguised guests for entering by an improper gate'; the passage itself truncates just as Jarasandha addresses them, and Krishna's reply presupposes the question.

statements.claim: Krishna answered: 'These are the rules of the ordinance... an enemy's abode should be entered through a wrong gate and a friend's abode through the right one... this also is our eternal vow that having entered the foe's abode for the accomplishment of our purpose, we accept not the worship offered to us.'
statements.evidence: Pack source excerpt (MBh 2.21) quotes the reply near-verbatim.

statements.claim: The brothers' refusal of the offered worship meant the king's courteous welcome was over: they had declared themselves his enemies, and what remained was the purpose for which they had come (slaying him).
statements.evidence: The 'untouched water and gifts' are a visual dramatization of the vow just quoted (we accept not the worship offered); the framing of the exchange as a declaration of enmity is narrative consequence, not a new sourced fact.

DKS_0167.notes: Highly faithful to MBh 2.21; Krishna's reply quoted nearly verbatim. The passage's hermitage digressions (Gautama, Nagas) are omitted without distortion.

statements.claim: Jarasandha asked why the guests, whom he had never injured even on careful scrutiny, regarded him, an innocent man, as a foe, demanding a true answer 'for this is the rule followed by the honest.'
statements.evidence: MBh 2.22: Jarasandha's opening speech is near-verbatim (the source's vocative 'ye Brahmanas' is dropped, as their disguise is not yet broken in the story).

statements.claim: Krishna replied that he came not of his own will: a certain person at the head of a royal line had sent him and his companions; and that Jarasandha had brought many Kshatriyas of the world as captives to his city — a wicked wrong by which he could not regard himself innocent.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.22: 'there is a certain person of the head of a (royal) line... At his command have we come against thee. Thou hast brought, O king, many of the Kshatriyas of the world as captives (to thy city.) Having perpetrated that wicked wrong how dost thou regard thyself as innocent?'

statements.claim: Krishna said the captive kings were being treated with cruelty and kept for sacrifice to the god Rudra; slaughter of human beings as sacrifice unto the gods is never seen, and Jarasandha was addressing persons of his own order as animals fit for sacrifice (to god Sankara).
statements.evidence: MBh 2.22: near-verbatim, including 'slaughter of human being as sacrifice unto the gods is never seen... sacrifice unto god Sankara...' and Rudra as the intended recipient.

statements.claim: Krishna revealed their identity: 'Know that we are certainly not Brahmanas. I am Hrishikesha, otherwise called Sauri, and these two heroes among men are the sons of Pandu. O king of Magadha, we challenge thee. Fight standing before us. Either set free all the monarchs, or go thou to the abode of Yama.'
statements.evidence: MBh 2.22: quoted nearly verbatim (source spells 'Hrishesha').

statements.claim: Krishna spoke of warriors dying in open fight attaining heaven as the sure consequence — the triumph won by Indra through vanquishing the Asuras — and of kings Damvodhava, Kartavirya, Uttara and Vrihadratha who met destruction with all their forces for disregarding their superiors; valour dwells in every man, so Jarasandha should cast off superiority and pride before his equals.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.22: content near-verbatim (heaven as the certain consequence of death in battle, Indra's triumph over the Asuras, the four ruined kings, 'Valour dwelleth in every man').

statements.claim: Jarasandha answered unshaken: he never made a captive of a king without first vanquishing him; all the monarchs in his city were defeated in open war; it is the Kshatriya duty to bring others under sway by prowess and treat them as slaves; having gathered the monarchs for sacrifice he would not liberate them from fear; he offered combat — troops against troops, or alone against one, two or three.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.22: Jarasandha's reply near-verbatim; the passage truncates mid-sentence at 'or against two, or against three' but the pack summary and corpus render the same challenge.

statements.claim: The lord Sauri, ever devoted to truth, keeping in view the command of Brahma and remembering that the ruler of Magadha was destined to be slain in battle by Bhima and not by a descendant of Madhu, desired not to slay the king himself; he drew back his own hand and left the king to Bhima.
statements.evidence: Pack source excerpt (MBh 2.22): 'the lord Sauri ever devoted to truth ... keeping in view the command of Brahma and remembering that the ruler of Magadha was destined to be slain in battle by Bhima and not by the descendant of Madhu (Yadavas), desired not to slay himself king Jarasandha.'

statements.claim: Krishna alone would have been more than a match for the king of Magadha, and the strength of the descendants of Madhu could have ended the matter there and then.
statements.evidence: Rhetorical framing of Krishna's restraint; the pack states only that he desired not to slay Jarasandha (the sentiment that he could have is implied, not stated).

statements.claim: The son of Pandu stepped forward to meet Jarasandha, and the long duel began — a fight in which Krishna took no part because this death was destined to be Bhima's.
statements.evidence: Bridge to the ensuing fight: the pack passage truncates at Jarasandha's reply, but the duel follows directly from the excerpt's statement that Jarasandha was destined to be slain by Bhima; the 'long duel' itself is not narrated in the quoted excerpt.

DKS_0168.notes: Faithful to MBh 2.22; Krishna's and Jarasandha's speeches nearly verbatim. All claims check out; no contradictions with the pack.

statements.claim: Muchukunda, waking after sleeping through the turning of eras, walked out into the daylight and, beholding men of diminished stature, knew that the Kali age had arrived.
statements.evidence: VP 5.24 (Wilson): 'beholding men of diminutive stature, now first knew that the Kali age had arrived.'

statements.claim: Muchukunda praised Krishna as the sovereign of all things, the eternal lord, Hari, and Krishna granted his wish, promising: 'Go to whatever celestial regions you wish... When you have fully enjoyed all heavenly pleasures, you shall be born in a distinguished family, retaining the recollection of your former births; and you shall finally obtain emancipation.'
statements.evidence: VP 5.24: the boon speech is quoted nearly verbatim; the opening clause 'Thus praised by the wise Muchukunda' underlies the story's 'praised by the wise'.

statements.claim: Muchukunda prostrated himself before the lord of the world, went out from the cave, and departed to Gandhamadana, the shrine of Nara-Narayana, to perform penance.
statements.evidence: VP 5.24: 'prostrated himself before Achyuta, the lord of the world, Muchukunda, went forth from the cave... departed to Gandhamádana, the shrine of Narańáráyańa, to perform penance.'

statements.claim: In time it came about exactly as Krishna had promised: Muchukunda enjoyed the celestial regions, was born again in a distinguished family with his memory of former births intact, and at last obtained emancipation.
statements.evidence: Proleptic closing consistent with the boon Krishna states verbatim in the passage; the pack's excerpt does not itself narrate the later fulfillment (which the corpus chain places ahead of this point).

statements.claim: Krishna, having destroyed his enemy by stratagem, returned to Mathura, took captive Kalayavana's army — rich in horses, elephants and cars — conducted it to Dwaraka and delivered it to Ugrasena; the Yadu race was relieved of all fear of invasion.
statements.evidence: VP 5.24: near-verbatim ('Krishńa having by this stratagem destroyed his enemy, returned to Mathurá, and took captive his army, rich in horses, elephants and cars, which he conducted to Dwáraká, and delivered to Ugrasena, and the Yadu race was relieved from all fear of invasion').

statements.claim: Balarama, hostilities having ceased, went to Nanda's cow-pens desiring to see his kinsmen, and conversed with the herdsmen and their women with affection and respect: the elders embraced him, he embraced the younger ones, and with those of his own age he talked and laughed; the cowherds made him many kind speeches.
statements.evidence: VP 5.24: near-verbatim, including the embrace pattern and the cowherds' kind speeches to Halayudha.

statements.claim: Some gopis spoke to Balarama with the affectation of anger and jealousy, asking after Krishna — 'Is all well with the fickle and inconstant Krishna?... Does the volatile swain, the friend of an instant, amuse the women of the city by laughing at our rustic efforts (to please him)? Does he ever think of us...? Will he not come here once again to see his mother?' — and adding 'Father, mother, brother, husband, kin, what have we not abandoned for his sake?... it is a different tale to tell for him without us, and for us without him.'
statements.evidence: VP 5.24: gopis' speech is near-verbatim, including the rhetorical questions and the closing lament.

statements.claim: Balarama carried the gopis' message back with him when he left the cow-pens.
statements.evidence: Closing connective; the passage ends with the gopis' speeches and does not narrate Balarama's departure or what he carried back.

DKS_0169.notes: Faithful retelling of VP 5.24 (Wilson); dialogue near-verbatim. The story's one forward-looking fulfillment sentence is consistent with the quoted boon.

statements.claim: Kamsa's widows Asti and Prapti, daughters of Jarasandha, came to their father's court and told him of their widowhood; grief and anger rose in Jarasandha.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.1-2 (pack rendering): 'Kamsa's widows Asti and Prapti went to their father Jarasandha and told him of their widowhood; enraged...'; HV 1.89: Jarasandha heard of Kamsa's death from his two daughters and was worked up with anger.

statements.claim: Jarasandha owed Kamsa a debt: the dead king had been his son-in-law and ally — the son of Ahuka who, chaining his own father, ruled Mathura depending on Jarasandha's help and disregarding the Yadavas; and when the vicious-souled Kamsa was slain by Rama and Krishna, Ugrasena, encircled by the Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas, became king in his place.
statements.evidence: HV 1.89: near-verbatim, including Kamsa chaining his father, ruling 'depending on Jarāsandhā's (help) and disregarding the Yadavas', the debt Jarasandha wished to pay, and Ugrasena's accession 'encircled by Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas'.

statements.claim: Kamsa had been the one man who held the Yadava race in check while Jarasandha gathered the world's kings into his prisons.
statements.evidence: Kamsa's check on the Yadavas is inferred from HV 1.89 (he ruled with Jarasandha's backing, disregarding the Yadavas); Jarasandha's imprisonment of captive kings is carried from the corpus chain (MBh 2.22, DKS_0168 pack: 'many of the Kshatriyas of the world as captives').

statements.claim: Resolved to make the earth free of Yadavas and burning like fire in anger, Jarasandha made every possible arrangement and started for Mathura in no time.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.1-2 (pack rendering: 'he resolved to make the earth Yadava-free'); HV 1.89: 'burning like fire in anger... making every possible arrangement the king of Magadha started for Mathurā... to slay all the Yadus.'

statements.claim: All the highly energetic warrior kings defeated and subjugated by Jarasandha's prowess, and all his friends, relatives, kinsmen and allies, followed him with their own armies, eager to please him, out of jealousy toward Janardana.
statements.evidence: HV 1.89: 'All the highly energetic warrior kings who were defeated and subjugated by Jarāsandha's prowess, all those who were his friends, relatives, kinsmen and allies, encircled by their own armies, followed Jarāsandha with a view to please him... out of jealousy towards Janārddana.' The 'fear' motive added in the story is a connective gloss on their subjugation.

statements.claim: Among the kings who followed were Dantavakra of Karusha, the powerful king of Chedi, the king of Kalinga, Bhishmaka and his son Rukmi, the kings of Anga and Vanga, of Koshala, Kashi and Dasharna, Bhagadatta the lord of the Yavanas, Suvala of Gandhara, and Duryodhana with the other sons of Dhritarashtra.
statements.evidence: HV 1.89: the roster is listed nearly verbatim (Dantavakra the king of Karusha, king of Chedi, king of Kalinga, Bhishmaka, his son Rukshmi, kings of Anga and Vanga, kings of Koshala, Kashi and Dashārna, Bhagadatta the lord of Yavanas, Suvala the king of Gāndhāra, Duryodhana and other sons of Dhritarāshtra).

statements.claim: The allied host entered the province of Shurasena, a country abounding in barley and fuel, and the command went out for the armies of the united kings to lay siege on all sides to the city of Mathura.
statements.evidence: HV 1.89: 'Entering the province of Shurasena, abounding in barley and fuels, they all... laid siege to Mathurā'; HV 1.90 excerpt: 'Let the armies of the kings united lay siege on all sides to this city.'

statements.claim: Twenty-three akshauhinis — counted in soldiers, horses, chariots and elephants — surrounded Mathura.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.3 (Sanskrit: akṣauhiṇībhir viṃśatyā tisṛbhiś cāpi saṃvṛtaḥ = surrounded by twenty-three akshauhinis) and v.7 (bhaṭāśva-ratha-kuñjaraiḥ). Note: HV 1.89 counts six divisions at the outset; the story follows its primary source (BP) at the siege.

statements.claim: Krishna saw that host like an overflowing sea and reflected long — the blessed Hari, kāraṇa-mānuṣaḥ, one whose humanity is an instrument for his work in the world.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.4-5 (Sanskrit): 'nirīkṣya tad-balaṃ kṛṣṇa udvelam iva sāgaram / cintayām āsa bhagavān hariḥ kāraṇa-mānuṣaḥ'. The gloss of kāraṇa-mānuṣaḥ follows standard commentary.

statements.claim: The fires of the besieging host burned through the first night, and Krishna was still thinking, because he had come to act in human ways and a human king must first decide what he is willing to do.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric close; Krishna's reflection is sourced (v.5) but the night-fires and the 'human ways' deliberation are narrative framing of that reflection.

DKS_0170.notes: Faithful blend of BP 10.50.1-5 (primary) with HV 1.89/1.90 roster and siege details. HV's six-division figure vs BP's twenty-three akshauhinis is a source variant; story follows BP. VP 5.22's 'eighteen times' variant not asserted here.

statements.claim: Jarasandha had come to avenge his son-in-law Kamsa, resolved to leave no Yadava alive — the twenty-three divisions camped around Mathura like a sea overflowing its banks.
statements.evidence: Recap carried from the immediate chain: BP 10.50.1-5 (DKS_0170 pack): widows' report, rage, 'make the earth Yadava-free', twenty-three akshauhinis; the 'sea overflowing its banks' simile is BP 10.50.4 verbatim.

statements.claim: Reflecting on the host, Krishna thought: 'I will destroy this force... this weight that has been heaped upon the earth. It was to remove the earth's burden that I came down; and for the protection of dharma, another form of mine is ever maintained.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.6-9 (Sanskrit): haniṣyāmi balaṃ hy etad bhuvi bhāraṃ samāhitam... etad-artho 'vatāro 'yaṃ bhū-bhāra-haraṇāya me / anyo 'pi dharma-rakṣāyai dehaḥ saṃbhriyate mayā.

statements.claim: Out of the empty air above Mathura two chariots descended, bright as the sun, each with its driver at the reins and carrying ancient divine weapons — bows, quivers, maces, armor — coming of their own accord, unsummoned.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.10-11 (Sanskrit): ākāśāt sūrya-varcasau... āyudhāni ca divyāni purāṇāni yadṛcchayā; pack rendering: 'two chariots with the splendor of the sun descended from the sky with drivers and ancient divine weapons'. yadṛcchayā = spontaneously, grounding 'of their own accord'.

statements.claim: Krishna turned to Balarama: 'Look, Arya... Calamity has come upon the Yadavas, who look to you. It was for this that we two were born — to bring ease to the good.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.12-13 (Sanskrit): paśyārya vyasanaṃ prāptaṃ yadūnāṃ tvāvatāṃ prabho / etad-arthaṃ hi nau janma sādhūnām īśa śarma-kṛt.

statements.claim: The brothers armed themselves and the two chariots rolled out through the gates of Mathura, out onto the open ground between the walls and the enemy host.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.14 (Sanskrit): daṃśitau rathinau purāt (the two, armed, chariot-borne, from the city). The citizens running into the streets are connective colour.

statements.claim: Krishna's chariot was driven by Daruka; as the wheels cleared the gate he raised the great conch to his lips and blew it once, the sound rolling across the plain between city and camps.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.15 (Sanskrit): śaṅkhaṃ dadhmau vinirgatya harir dāruka-sārathiḥ — Hari, whose charioteer was Daruka, having gone out, blew his conch.

statements.claim: Terror entered the hearts of the Magadha king's forces and the allied kings' ranks at the conch's sound.
statements.evidence: Pack rendering of BP 10.50.6-15: 'Krishna blew his conch and terror entered the enemy's hearts.' The trembling soldiers' vignette is elaboration of that terror.

statements.claim: Two chariots stood before the greatest army of the age, and for a moment the army did not move; then the battle began.
statements.evidence: Closing bridge to DKS_0172; the pause before battle is dramatic connective consistent with the narrative flow, not a sourced beat.

DKS_0171.notes: Faithful to BP 10.50.6-15 (primary, Sanskrit verses rendered accurately); opening recap and closing bridge are connective. Daruka's role and the 'of their own accord' detail both match the Sanskrit.

statements.claim: Seeing the brothers come, Jarasandha shouted abuse — insults for Krishna, and for Balarama a challenge: if he had any courage, to come and fight, summoning his fortitude.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.16-17 (Sanskrit): tāv āha māgadho vīkṣya he kṛṣṇa puruṣādhama... tava rāma yadi śraddhā yudhyasva dhairyam udvaha — the Magadha addresses Krishna with abuse (puruṣādhama) and dares Rama to fight with fortitude.

statements.claim: On the towers, terraces and gates of Mathura, the city's women gathered to watch and swooned, overcome with grief at the sight of the enormous host.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.20 (Sanskrit): striyaḥ purāṭṭālaka-harmya-gopuraṃ samāśritāḥ sammumuhuḥ śucārditaḥ — women, resorting to the city's ramparts, palaces and gates, swooned, afflicted with grief.

statements.claim: Krishna's arrows streamed out without pause or gap, like a wheel of fire burning in an unbroken circle; elephants with split foreheads fell, horses fell with necks severed, chariots were smashed.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.21-23 (Sanskrit): nirantaraṃ yadvad alāta-cakram (without interval, like a wheel of fire); nirbhinna-kumbhāḥ kariṇo nipetur (elephants with split frontal lobes fell); aśvāḥ śara-vṛkṇa-kandharāḥ (horses with necks severed by arrows).

statements.claim: Jarasandha's army was an ocean, dark and without a shore, one no one could have crossed; the one who waded into it, though he fought in mortal form, was not measured by mortal measure.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.27-28 (Sanskrit): balaṃ tad aṅgārṇava-durga-bhairavaṃ duranta-pāraṃ... tathāpi martyānuvidhasya varṇyate — the army like a frightful, uncrossable ocean, yet the crossing is described of him who conforms to mortal ways.

statements.claim: In the sky, out of sight of the armies, gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, saints and Yakshas gathered from all quarters to watch, and the field shone under their gathered light like the night sky lit with luminaries.
statements.evidence: HV 1.92 (in pack): 'there came there from all quarters thousands and thousands of gods Gandharvas, Siddhas, Saints and Yakshas. Shining greatly in their effulgence the battle-field looked like welkin covered with luminous bodies.'

statements.claim: In the middle of it all Balarama sought out Jarasandha, who had spent his chariot, horses and charioteer and stood chariotless on the field; with his army slain and allies gone, the king was bound with ropes by the Vrishni soldiers.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.29-30 (Sanskrit): jagrāha virathaṃ rāmo jarāsandhaṃ mahā-balam (Rama seized the chariotless, mighty Jarasandha); badhyamānaṃ hatārātiṃ pāśair vāruṇa-mānuṣaiḥ (being bound with divine and human ropes after his enemies were slain); v.33 hateṣu sarvānīkeṣu (all his armies slain).

statements.claim: Balarama seized Jarasandha the way a lion seizes a lion, by the shoulders, so that the king hung helpless in his grip.
statements.evidence: The lion-seizing-lion simile is in the pack excerpt (BP 10.50.29), but the 'by the shoulders' grip and 'hung helpless' are dramatizing gestures of the same supported seizure; no source specifies the body part.

statements.claim: Krishna stayed the binding: 'The Magadha is not to be slain... He will gather forces again.' He spoke to the captive with words of pure and plain meaning, and released him.
statements.evidence: Pack rendering of BP 10.50.16-41 (Krishna stayed the binding, 'The Magadha is not to be slain; he will gather forces again'); v.32 vākyaiḥ pavitrārtha-padair (with words of pure meaning). HV 1.92 corroborates the sparing via the celestial voice (the king of Magadha is not to be slain by Rama).

statements.claim: Released by the two lords of the world, Jarasandha stood in shame — a shame softened by being counted worthy of such handling by the heroes — then turned and walked off the field, and no one stopped him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.31 (Sanskrit): sā mukto loka-nāthābhyāṃ vrīḍito vīra-sammataḥ — released by the two lords of the world, ashamed, approved/held worthy by heroes.

statements.claim: The people of Mathura poured out through the gates to meet Krishna, free of their fever and carried on a wave of joy; conches and kettledrums (dundubhis, bheris, turyas) sounded from the walls; the streets were sprinkled with water and adorned with banners; women on the rooftops showered the returning chariots with garlands, curds and unbroken rice.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.35-38 (Sanskrit): māthurair upasaṅgamya vijvarair muditātmabhiḥ; śaṅkha-dundubhayo nedur bherī-tūryāṇy anekaśaḥ; sikta-mārgāṃ hṛṣṭa-janāṃ patākābhir abhyalaṅkṛtām; nicīyamānaḥ... mālya-dadhy-akṣatāṅkuraiḥ (showered with garlands, curds and unbroken grains).

statements.claim: The weapons that had come down from the sky for the battle were seen no more, as if they had never been.
statements.evidence: HV 1.92: 'And all the weapons that came down from the welkin also disappeared.'

statements.claim: Seventeen times after that day Jarasandha came again to Mathura, each time with an army reckoned in akshauhinis, and seventeen times the Vrishnis, by Krishna's splendor, destroyed his host and sent him home.
statements.evidence: BP 10.50.40-41 (Sanskrit): evaṃ saptadaśa-kṛtvas tāvaty akṣauhiṇī-balaḥ / akṣiṇvaṃs tad-balaṃ sarvaṃ vṛṣṇayaḥ kṛṣṇa-tejasā — seventeen times, with an army of that many akshauhinis, the Vrishnis destroyed his whole force by Krishna's splendor. (VP 5.22's 'eighteen times' is a variant the story does not use; BP is the primary source.)

statements.claim: The king who had sworn to leave no Yadava alive was spared by the very men he had come to destroy — spared, as he himself suspected, for a purpose none of them could yet see.
statements.evidence: Closing suspense-framing: the sparing and its purpose (Jarasandha's eventual death by Krishna's own means) are sourced (BP 10.50.31; HV 1.92 divine voice), but the attribution of suspicion to Jarasandha himself is the narrator's gloss, not in the sources.

DKS_0172.notes: Faithful to BP 10.50.16-41 with HV 1.92 corroboration; Sanskrit verses rendered accurately (wheel-of-fire arrows, lion seizure, seventeen attacks, celebration scene). The single embellished gesture (seizure 'by the shoulders') is connective.

statements.claim: Gargya, preceptor of the Andhaka and Vrishni races, had kept the vow of celibacy all his life — he had a wife but had never known her — and his brother-in-law mocked him before the king and named him impotent.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114: 'The high-minded Gārgya was the preceptor of both the Andhaka and Vrishni races. He always observed the vow of celibacy; and although he had a wife he did not know her... this brother-in-law described him as impotent before the king.'

statements.claim: Stung by the dishonor, Gargya left the city, gave up thought of his wife, and for twelve years lived on pounded iron and worshipped Mahadeva the trident-holder, until the god granted a boon: an all-powerful son who would discomfit the descendants of the Vrishni and Andhaka races in battle.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114: 'having been thus dishonored in the city of Ajitanjaya and giving up his desire of being united with his wife... living on pounded iron for twelve years he worshipped Mahādeva, the holder of trident. For this Rudra conferred on him a boon that he would obtain an all powerful son who would be able to discomfit in battle the descendants of the Vishni and Andhaka races.'

statements.claim: The sonless king of the Yavanas heard of the boon, brought Gargya to his own kingdom and set women (milk-women) to attend on him; the Apsara Gopali, taking the form of a milk-woman, conceived through him; the child was Kalayavana, raised in the palace like the king's own son, and he reigned when the king died.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114: 'The king of Yavanas had no son. Hearing of the boon... the king brought him over to his own kingdom... engaged the milk-women to attend him... an Apsara, Gopāli by name, conceived that dreadful and undecaying embryo through Gārgya... brought up in the inner appartment, like his son... after the demise of the lord of Yavanas Kalyavana became king.'

statements.claim: The kings of the Shakas and Tukharas, the Daradas, Paravas and Tanganas, the Khashas and Panhavas — hundreds of mlechcha kings from the lands near the great mountains — took shelter under Kalayavana.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114: 'Shaka, Tukhāra Darava, Parava, Tangana, Khasha, Panhava and hundreds of Mlechcha kings, living near Himavan, took shelter under him.' (Story's spellings follow the VP 5.23 variant roster of the same kings.)

statements.claim: When Kalayavana finally marched on Mathura, his host covered the earth like a swarm of locusts and the dust raised by his soldiers hid the path of the sun.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114: 'Encircled by those Dasyu kings resembling a swarm of locusts... the king of Yavanas set out for Mathura... The path of the sun was covered with the dust raised by the soldiers.'

statements.claim: Krishna, having heard from Narada the story of the boon, had never met the Yavana head-on; now he told his kinsmen the calamity that had befallen the Vrishnis and Andhakas — the enemy could not be slain by them because of the trident-holder's boon; he had tried conciliation and the rest but the proud king wanted battle; Narada had told him 'You are to live here'; Jarasandha did not forgive and the kings sheltering under him were displeased over Kamsa's death; they would never prosper if they stayed in Mathura.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114: Krishna's speech to his kinsmen is near-verbatim ('Great is the calamity... enemy is unslayable by us on account of the boon... I employed all other means as conciliation etc... he wishes for battle worked up with pride. 'I am to live here:' this Nārada said to me... The emperor Jarāsandha is not forgiving... on account of the distruction of Kansa, have been displeased... we will never acquire prosperity if we live in this city.'); the 'never met head-on' derives from 'took no notice of Kālayavana... because he had heard from Narada the story of his obtaining the boon'.

statements.claim: Krishna sent an envoy to Kalayavana with a sealed jar containing a dreadful black serpent, saying 'Krishna is like a deadly serpent'; Kalayavana, understanding the threat, filled the jar with innumerable sharp-beaked ants, which devoured the serpent and reduced it to ashes.
statements.evidence: HV 1.114: near-verbatim (black serpent 'resembling a collection of collyrium' sealed in a jar; the envoy's words; Kalayavana filling the jar with dreadful ants that ate the serpent and reduced it to ashes).

statements.claim: Kalayavana knew Krishna by the marks Narada had described — the chest marked with Shrivatsa, the Kaustubha jewel on his neck, the ever-glad face, the pure smile — and, certain no other could be he, ran at him; Krishna turned and fled toward the cave though the Yavana shouted 'Flight is not proper for one born in the Yadu clan!'
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.1-8 (Sanskrit): śrīvatsa-vakṣasaṃ... kaustubhāmukta-kandharam... nitya-pramuditaṃ... su-kapolaṃ śuci-smitam; lakṣaṇair nārada-proktair nānyo bhavitum arhati; iti niścitya yavanaḥ prādravad taṃ parāṅ-mukham; palāyaṇaṃ yadu-kule jātasya tava nocitam.

statements.claim: Inside the mountain cave Kalayavana found a man lying asleep, laughed — 'This one has led me far... and now lies here like a virtuous man, pretending to sleep' — and, certain it was Krishna, kicked him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.9 (Sanskrit): nanv asau dūram ānīya śete mām iha sādhu-vat; VP 5.23: 'concluded it must be Krishńa, and kicked him'; pack rendering: 'the fool kicked the sleeping man thinking him Krishna'.

statements.claim: The sleeper — Muchukunda — had been asleep for a very long time; slowly he opened his eyes, and the angry glance that fell on the Yavana burned Kalayavana to ashes in a moment.
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.10-11 (Sanskrit): sa utthāya ciraṃ suptaḥ śanair unmīlya locane... dṛṣṭi-pātena; VP 5.23: 'casting on him an angry glance, the Yavana was instantly consumed, and reduced to ashes'; HV 1.114: 'he looked at the Yavana king with angry eyes. As soon as he was eyed, the king of Yavanas was all ablaze.' The motives imputed to the glance (anger at being woken/kicked) are connective glosses on the sourced angry glance.

statements.claim: Krishna entered the cave only after being pursued by an army that no one in the world could defeat, and the pursuit was exactly what he intended.
statements.evidence: The flight before the pursuing Yavana is sourced (BP 10.51.5-6: the Yavana ran at him, feeling him within reach at every step), but 'the pursuit was exactly what Krishna intended' is narrative inference from the luring stratagem.

DKS_0173.notes: Faithful blend of HV 1.114 (Gargya origin, tribal kings, serpent ruse — near-verbatim), BP 10.51.1-11 (recognition marks, cave pursuit) and VP 5.23 (kick and burning glance). All named tribes and details check out against the pack.

statements.claim: The sleeper was Muchukunda, son of Mandhata, of the Ikshvaku line — a king of an age long since passed.
statements.evidence: Pack rendering of BP 10.51.12-20: 'Muchukunda, son of Mandhata of the Ikshvaku line, guarded the gods in battle against the asuras.'

statements.claim: Long ago, when the gods fought the asuras, the hosts of heaven led by Indra asked this mortal king to stand guard for them; Muchukunda fought for the gods in their war and guarded them through battles longer than the lives of ordinary men.
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.13-15 (Sanskrit): sa yācitaḥ sura-gaṇair indrādyair ātma-rakṣaṇe (he was asked by the hosts of gods led by Indra for their own protection). The 'battles longer than ordinary lives' is dramatization of the ages-long guard duty summarized in the pack.

statements.claim: When the war was over, the gods released him, telling him gently that the world he had left was gone: his kingdom, with its enemies cut down, no longer waited for him, and his sons, queens, kinsmen, ministers and counselors were all gone; 'Time is mightier than the mighty' and 'The Blessed Lord is the immutable sovereign.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.16-18 (Sanskrit): nara-lokaṃ parityajya rājyaṃ nihata-kaṇṭakam / sutā mahiṣyo bhavato jñātayo 'mātya-mantrinaḥ / kālo balīyān balināṃ bhagavān īśvaro 'vyayaḥ — leaving the world of men, your kingdom with its thorns cut down; your sons, queens, relatives, ministers and counselors; time is mightier than the mighty; the Blessed Lord is the immutable Sovereign.

statements.claim: The gods offered Muchukunda a boon, as promised: 'Choose whatever you wish... Ask anything except liberation — that is not ours to grant.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.19 (Sanskrit): varaṃ vṛṇīṣva bhadraṃ te ṛte kaivalyam adya naḥ — choose a boon, good fortune to you, except kaivalya (liberation), which is not ours to give. The 'as promised' is a connective reference to the gods' earlier undertaking.

statements.claim: Muchukunda bowed to the gods and asked for sleep — not for a night or a season, but to lie down in the earth and sleep without waking, undisturbed, until the proper time came round for him to wake; the gods granted it and he lay down in the cave and slept.
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.20 (Sanskrit): evam uktaḥ sa vai devān abhivandya mahā-yaśāḥ (thus addressed, the greatly glorious one bowed to the gods) — continuing in the pack's rendering: 'he chose sleep as his boon and lay in the cave'; his sleeping through ages is carried from DKS_0173 (BP 10.51.10, ciraṃ suptaḥ).

statements.claim: The years turned to ages and ages to yugas while Muchukunda slept: kingdoms rose and fell, Mathura was besieged and delivered, and a king came to his cave and was burned to ash at his feet.
statements.evidence: Recap-connective: the burned king is Kalayavana (DKS_0173, BP 10.51.10-11) and Mathura's siege and deliverance are the chain events of DKS_0170-72 (BP 10.50); the yuga-scale passing of time is framing consistent with the ages-long sleep.

statements.claim: The gods asked Muchukunda to guard them because he was strong and because a king of the Ikshvaku line who gave his word kept it.
statements.evidence: Motivation added by the narrator; the pack states only that he was asked (yācitaḥ) to guard the gods, not why.

statements.claim: When Muchukunda woke, he understood without being told that the one who had woken him was not the one who had kicked him, and he opened his mouth to ask who the stranger was.
statements.evidence: Scene-setting connective leading into the next beat (DKS_0175); consistent with the previous story's events (BP 10.51.1-11, VP 5.23) but not itself a sourced fact.

DKS_0174.notes: Faithful to BP 10.51.12-20; the boon offer and the gods' speech match the Sanskrit closely. Backstory recaps and closing scene-setting are connective. Subtitle matches the pack summary.

statements.claim: Muchukunda woke to find a heap of ashes at the cave's mouth, where the one who had pursued Krishna into the mountain had been consumed by his own wickedness.
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.21 ('yavane bhasma-sān nīte') and 10.51.32 ('so 'pi bhasmī-kṛto nūnam ātmīyenaiva pāpmanā' - reduced to ashes by his own sin); pursuit context from corpus chain (DKS_0174).

statements.claim: Before him stood a young man dark as a laden rain cloud, dressed in yellow silk, four-armed, radiant, wearing a garland of forest flowers (Vaijayanti), with a smile of pure affection.
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.22-24: ghana-śyāmaṃ pīta-kauśeya-vāsasam, catur-bhujaṃ rocamānaṃ, vaijayantyā mālayā, sānurāga-smitekṣaṇam.

statements.claim: Muchukunda, senses worn by his long vigil, asked whether he was the fire/lord of fire, the best of the three lords of the worlds, whose splendor he could not bear to look upon.
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.25-33: cira-prajāgara-śrānto nidrayāpahatendriyaḥ; 'kiṃ svit tejasvināṃ tejo... vibhāvasuḥ'; 'trayāṇāṃ puruṣarṣabham'; 'tejasā te 'viṣahyeṇa... draṣṭuṃ na śaknumaḥ'.

statements.claim: Krishna said he had measured the dust of the earth through many births and known the deeds of all three times; Kalanemi, Kamsa, Pralamba and other haters of the good had been slain for the relief of the world; and he had entered the cave for Muchukunda's sake, offering any boon.
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.36-42: rajāṃsi vimame... uru-janmabhiḥ; kāla-trayopapannāni; kālanemir hataḥ kaṃsaḥ pralambādyāś ca sad-dviṣaḥ; so 'haṃ tavānugrahārthaṃ guhām etām upāgataḥ; varān vṛṇīṣva.

statements.claim: Muchukunda reflected that he had once conquered the circle of the directions and sat on an excellent throne honored by kings, and that the king's body is only a jar of clay that ends as ordure, worms and ashes.
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.47-50: kalevare ghaṭa-kuḍya-sannibhe; kalevaro viṭ-kṛmi-bhasma-saṃjñitaḥ; nirjitya dik-cakram... varāsana-sthaḥ sama-rāja-vanditaḥ.

statements.claim: Muchukunda declared he desired no boon but the service of Krishna's feet, counting the kingdom's falling away as Krishna's grace, renouncing all blessing that binds, and asking only for refuge.
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.52-56: sat-samāgamaḥ; rājyānubandhāpagamo yadṛcchayā; na kāmaye 'nyaṃ tava pāda-sevanād... varaṃ; visṛjyāśiṣaḥ... guṇānubandhanāḥ; abhayam ṛtam aśokaṃ pāhi.

statements.claim: Krishna answered that Muchukunda's not being tempted by the boons was his true wakefulness, that the undisciplined devotion of breath and mind does not reach him, that he should wander the earth with his mind fixed on Krishna; and that in his next birth he would be born a brahmana, friend of all beings, and attain Krishna alone.
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.58-62 (apramādāya; prāṇāyāmādibhiḥ; vicarasva mahīṃ... mayy āveśita-mānasaḥ; janmany anantare... sarva-bhūta-suhṛttamaḥ); brahmana rebirth + attaining him alone per pack index summary of 10.51.21-62.

statements.claim: Muchukunda rose from the cave floor and walked out a wanderer; the long sleep of the king of the Ikshvakus was over.
statements.evidence: BP 10.51.60 (wander the earth) and 10.51.30 (aikṣvākāḥ); closing connective framing consistent with the grant.

DKS_0175.notes: Faithful rendering of BP 10.51.21-62. 'Young man' and 'golden throne' are minor ornamental details; no unsupported or contradicted factual claims found.

statements.claim: Jarasandha marched on Mathura again with an immense army, unable to forgive that the city sheltered the two brothers and had turned him back before.
statements.evidence: BP 10.52.1-13 pursuit episode; prior repeated defeats per arc (BP 10.70.29: broken eighteen times; corpus chain of Jarasandha sieges).

statements.claim: Krishna had already sent the city's wealth - herds and treasure - away with men he had chosen.
statements.evidence: BP 10.52.5: nīyamāne dhane gobhir nṛbhiś cācyuta-coditaiḥ (wealth carried away with cows and men at Acyuta's command).

statements.claim: Seeing the enemy's rush, Krishna and Balarama abandoned the abundant wealth and fled on foot as if terrified.
statements.evidence: BP 10.52.6-8: vihāya vittaṃ pracuram abhītau bhīru-bhīta-vat; palāyamānau tau dṛṣṭvā māgadhaḥ prahasan balī.

statements.claim: Exhausted, they climbed Mt. Pravarshana and hid among its rocks and trees; Jarasandha's men found no trace of them, and the king set the mountain on fire.
statements.evidence: BP 10.52.9-11: śrāntau tuṅgam āruhatāṃ girim; girau nilīnāv... nādhigamya padam; dahyamāna-taṭāt; mountain and fire-setter per pack summary.

statements.claim: From the burning slope the brothers leapt eleven yojanas, unseen by Jarasandha and his followers, and returned to their sea-girt city.
statements.evidence: BP 10.52.11-12: utpatya tarasā dahyamāna-taṭād ubhau; alakṣyamāṇau ripuṇā sānugena; 'eleven yojanas' and 'sea-girt city' per pack summary.

statements.claim: Jarasandha returned believing the brothers had burned in his fire and told the story of their destruction, satisfied with a false victory.
statements.evidence: BP 10.52.13: so 'pi dagdhāv iti mṛṣā manvāno bala-keśavau.

statements.claim: The whole pursuit - the flight, the hill, the fire - had been shaped deliberately: the brothers chose to be thought dead so Jarasandha would stop pursuing.
statements.evidence: Index summary 'feign flight from Jarasandha'; BP 10.52.7 bhīru-bhīta-vat (like men afraid) supports the feigned character of the flight.

statements.claim: Jarasandha told his generals that this time there would be no third campaign.
statements.evidence: Character bravado/dialogue; no sourceable campaign count in the pack (canonical 'eighteen times' defeats belong to the arc, BP 10.70.29).

DKS_0176.notes: Solid rendering of BP 10.52.1-13; 'no third campaign' is rhetorical villain dialogue, not a sourced count - noted but not treated as a factual error.

statements.claim: In Krishna's assembly at Dwaraka, with brahmanas seated, a man of unprecedented appearance was admitted and bowed to Krishna with joined palms.
statements.evidence: BP 10.70.20-22: brāhmaṇāḥ... āsīnā brahma-vādinaḥ; puruṣo 'pūrva-darśanaḥ; namaskṛtya kṛṣṇāya... kṛtāñjaliḥ.

statements.claim: The man reported that Jarasandha had forcibly imprisoned the kings who refused to submit during his conquest of the directions - twenty thousand of them - in his fortress at Girivraja.
statements.evidence: BP 10.70.23 (ye ca dig-vijaye tasya sannatiṃ na yayur nṛpāḥ); 'twenty thousand of them in Girivraja' per pack summary of 10.70.20-30.

statements.claim: The captive kings' message: the strong cut short the weak's hopes in this world; a king's happiness is only a dream depending on others, carried in bodies ever afraid; they take refuge in Krishna from the terror of the world, and his feet remove the sorrow of those who bow - free them from the bond of Magadha, where Jarasandha holds them with the strength of ten thousand elephants, like a lion penning sheep.
statements.evidence: BP 10.70.25-28: balavān... jīvitāśāṃ sadyaś chinatti; svapnāyitaṃ nṛpa-sukhaṃ para-tantram; śaśvad-bhayena mṛtakena dhuraṃ vahāmaḥ; praṇata-śoka-harāṅghri-yugmo; baddhān viyuṅkṣva magadhāhvaya-karma-pāśāt; ayuta-mataṅgaja-vīryam; mṛga-rāḍ ivāvīḥ.

statements.claim: The kings reminded Krishna that Jarasandha had been broken eighteen times in battle by Krishna with his discus raised, and yet still swells with pride and oppresses Krishna's people.
statements.evidence: BP 10.70.29: dvi-nava-kṛtva udātta-cakra bhagno mṛdhe... ūḍha-darpo... yuṣmat-prajā rujati.

statements.claim: The kings said Krishna descended into the world for the protection of the good and the restraint of the wicked, and asked him to ordain an end to it.
statements.evidence: BP 10.70.26: sad-rakṣaṇāya khala-nigrahaṇāya kalayāvatīrṇaḥ; tad vidhehi (10.70.29).

statements.claim: The messenger's words left the assembly still; twenty thousand prisoners hung on Krishna's answer.
statements.evidence: Closing scene-setting; the messenger's relay (dūta uvāca at 10.70.30) frames the speech as delivered at court.

DKS_0177.notes: Accurate to BP 10.70.20-30; the speech is correctly framed as the messenger relaying the captive kings' words (dūta uvāca). No issues.

statements.claim: Uddhava counselled that the Rajasuya is the imperial rite to be performed by one who has conquered the circle of the directions, and that Jarasandha, who holds twenty thousand kings at Girivraja, stands across that path.
statements.evidence: BP 10.71.2: yaṣṭavyam rājasūyena dik-cakra-jayinā; captivity of the kings per BP 10.70 (corpus chain); plan framed in Uddhava's voice per variant note (BP attribution).

statements.claim: One deed serves two ends: bring Jarasandha down and the directions lie open for the sacrifice and the captive kings go free.
statements.evidence: BP 10.71.3 (asmākaṃ ca mahān artho hy etenaiva bhaviṣyati) and 10.71.9 (jarāsandha-vadhaḥ kṛṣṇa bhūry-arthāyopakalpate); pack summary: 'defeating Jarasandha serves both purposes'.

statements.claim: Jarasandha's strength equals ten thousand elephants, and he cannot be conquered even with a hundred akṣauhiṇīs.
statements.evidence: BP 10.71.4-5: nāgāyuta-samo bale; mā śatākṣauhiṇī-yutaḥ.

statements.claim: He could only be met in single combat - a duel of two chariots - and the one man who could match him was Bhima.
statements.evidence: BP 10.71.5-6: dvai-rathe sa tu jetavyaḥ; brahma-veṣa-dharo gatvā taṃ bhikṣeta vṛkodaraḥ.

statements.claim: Bhima would go to Girivraja disguised as a brahmana and beg for the duel, and Jarasandha - proud of his strength - would grant it, to be slain before Krishna.
statements.evidence: BP 10.71.6; pack summary ('request single combat, and slay him before Krishna'); Jarasandha's pride granting the challenge consistent with 10.72.29-31 outcome.

statements.claim: The women of the captive courts, the gopis, the daughter of Janaka, and the sages who found refuge in Krishna sing of the enemy's fall and their release; all who look to Krishna await this deed.
statements.evidence: BP 10.71.8: gāyanti te viśada-karma gṛheṣu devyo rājñāṃ sva-śatru-vadham ātma-vimokṣaṇaṃ ca; gopyaś ca... janakātmajāyāḥ... munayo vayaṃ ca.

statements.claim: Krishna accepted the plan: Bhima in a brahmana's guise, Krishna and Arjuna there to see it through, the quarrel ending on a field of single combat.
statements.evidence: BP 10.71.6 plan + 10.72.15 execution (bhīmaseno 'rjunaḥ kṛṣṇo brahma-linga-dharās trayaḥ jagmur girivrajaṃ), per corpus chain.

DKS_0178.notes: Matches BP 10.71.1-10. 'One direction that never bowed' is a rhetorical gloss on Jarasandha's unconquered status; no issues.

statements.claim: Yudhishthira was preparing the Rajasuya and Krishna departed Dwaraka for Indraprastha, entrusting the city to Balarama and mounting his Garuda-bannered chariot.
statements.evidence: BP 10.71.11-13 (athādiśat prayāṇāya; Garuda banner and Balarama per pack summary); Rajasuya purpose per 10.71.1-10 and 10.72.1-15 (corpus chain).

statements.claim: He set out surrounded by an immense army - chariots, horsemen, elephants, foot soldiers - while mridangas, bheris, the deep anaka, conches and gomukha horns resounded.
statements.evidence: BP 10.71.13: ratha-dvipa-bhaṭa... mṛdaṅga-bhery-ānaka-śaṅkha-gomukhaiḥ praghoṣa-ghoṣita-kakubho nirakramat; 10.71.16 (army with banners, weapons, armor).

statements.claim: Behind the army came the women of the palace - Krishna's wives with their children and attendants - in gilded palanquins, followed by trains of oxen, camels, mules, asses, buffaloes and she-elephants carrying household goods.
statements.evidence: BP 10.71.12 (sva-varodhān sa-sutān sa-paricchadān), 10.71.14 (nṛ-vāji-kāñcana-śibikābhir... sahātmajāḥ patim anu), 10.71.15 (naroṣṭra-go-mahiṣa-kharāśvatary-anaḥ kareṇubhiḥ parijana-vāra-yoṣitaḥ).

statements.claim: The sage Narada met them, was honored by Krishna, bowed, and rose through the sky carrying Krishna in his heart.
statements.evidence: BP 10.71.17: munir yadu-patinā sabhājitaḥ praṇamya taṃ hṛdi vidadhad vihāyasā.

statements.claim: Krishna sent a royal messenger ahead to the kings whose lands the road crossed, so that no ruler would mistake the army for an invasion.
statements.evidence: BP 10.71.18-19: rāja-dūtam uvācedaṃ bhagavān prīṇayan girā; ity uktaḥ prasthito dūto yathā-vad avadan nṛpān (the courtesy/signal reading is a fair gloss on the messenger's mission).

statements.claim: The route ran through Anarta, the dry country of Sauvira, the wastes of Maru, and Vinashana, then crossed the Drishadvati and the Sarasvati.
statements.evidence: BP 10.71.20-21: ānarta-sauvīra-marūṃs tīrtvā vinaśanaṃ hariḥ; tato dṛṣadvatīṃ tīrtvā... sarasvatīm.

statements.claim: Everywhere they passed, towns emptied into the streets and local kings rode out to greet Krishna and ride part of the way with him.
statements.evidence: Atmosphere consistent with the herald's advance notice (10.71.19) but not detailed in the verses.

DKS_0179.notes: Faithful to BP 10.71.11-21 including the exact route names. Departure purpose (Rajasuya summons) is supported by the surrounding 10.70-10.72 context in the corpus chain.

statements.claim: Bhima slew Jarasandha in single combat outside the city, in a duel long enough to shatter two great maces.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.32-43: Jarasandha took a second mace and went out of the city (nirjagāma purād bahiḥ); the two maces were pulverized (gade... cūrṇī-babhūvatuḥ) before Bhima split him (10.72.40-43).

statements.claim: Krishna installed Jarasandha's son Sahadeva as lord of the Magadhas before the assembled court and elders.
statements.evidence: Pack summary of BP 10.72.45: 'Krishna installs Jarasandha's son Sahadeva as lord of the Magadhas'.

statements.claim: Krishna released the kings Jarasandha had held captive in Girivraja, who came out into the light after long captivity.
statements.evidence: Pack summary of BP 10.72.45: 'releases the kings who had been held captive by Jarasandha'; the story's note that the old text gives the release a single line matches the single-verse citation.

statements.claim: Jarasandha had not held the kings for ransom but had gathered them with the intent of offering them as a sacrifice to Rudra.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.22 (carried in corpus chain pack DKS_0182): Krishna charges Jarasandha with bringing the Kshatriyas of the world as captives 'to offer them as sacrifice unto the god Rudra'; captivity itself per BP 10.70.23-28. (The BP-only excerpt of 10.72.45 shows imprisonment and release without the motive, which the MBh source in the same arc supplies.)

statements.claim: The kingdom of Magadha was handed back to its own line - a son of Jarasandha's on the throne - rather than destroyed, and the kings were freed with no conditions asked.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.45 (installation of the son + release of the kings as one act); no conditions appear in the source; closing interpretation consistent with it.

statements.claim: With Jarasandha dead and the kings freed, the last obstacle on the road to the Rajasuya was gone.
statements.evidence: Arc: the Rajasuya plan required conquering the directions (BP 10.71.1-10) and proceeds thereafter in the corpus chain.

DKS_0180.notes: The Rudra-sacrifice motive is sourced from MBh 2.22 (same arc, pack DKS_0182) rather than the BP 10.72.45 excerpt alone - noted for the record; both sources are part of this corpus's evidence set for the episode.

statements.claim: Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna, disguised as brahmanas, went to Girivraja and presented themselves at Jarasandha's house at the hour of hospitality, asking alms as suppliants from afar.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.15-17: brahma-linga-dharās trayaḥ jagmur girivrajaṃ; atithya-velāyāṃ gṛheṣu; rājan viddhy atithīn prāptān arthino dūram āgatān; MBh 2.20 (garb of Snataka Brahmanas).

statements.claim: They came on a plan Krishna had argued and Yudhishthira had accepted: Jarasandha, unbeatable in open battle even by all the celestials, could be vanquished only in personal combat.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20 (in this pack): Krishna's speech to Yudhishthira and Yudhishthira's assent; 'incapable of being vanquished in battle even by all the celestials and the Asuras... should be vanquished in a personal struggle with bare arms'.

statements.claim: The road was long: from the country of the Kurus through Kuru-jangala, past the lake of lotuses and the hills of Kalakuta, across the Gandaki and the Sarayu, through the eastern lands and past Mithila, then across the Ganges and the Sone, until the hills of Goratha rose before the city of Magadha, filled with cattle and grain and water.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.20 (quoted in pack): 'set out from the country of the Kurus, passed through Kuru-jangala... lake of lotuses... hills of Kalakuta... crossing the Gandaki... Sarayu... Eastern Kosala... Mithila... crossed the Ganges and the Sone... hills of Goratha, they saw the city of Magadha... filled with kine and wealth and water.'

statements.claim: Jarasandha was a king famed for giving, of whom it was said he would part with anything a guest asked, even his own head.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.26: dadāmy ātma-śiro 'pi vaḥ; pack summary: 'the generous king, famed for giving even his own head to suppliants'.

statements.claim: Studying their voices, bearing and the marks on their arms, Jarasandha recognized these as royal men wearing a brahmana's guise.
statements.evidence: Pack summary of BP 10.72.14-26: 'recognizing them by their voices and marks'; BP 10.72.22: rājanya-bandhavo hy ete brahma-liṅgāni bibhrati; bowstring scars are the warrior mark read from 'marks'.

statements.claim: He reflected on Bali - who gave the earth to Vishnu in a dwarf brahmana's guise and lost his kingdom but kept his fame - and on Harishchandra, Rantideva, Shibi, a hunter and a pigeon, who won eternal honor with perishable bodies by giving.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.19-20, 23-24: hariścandro rantideva uñchavṛttiḥ śibir baliḥ; vyādhaḥ kapoto bahavo hy adhruveṇa dhruvaṃ gatāḥ; baler... kīrtir... vipra-vyājena viṣṇunā; dvija-rūpiṇe... mahīm prādād.

statements.claim: His answer was large: choose whatever you desire, and I will give it - even my very head.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.26: ity udāra-matiḥ prāha kṛṣṇārjuna-vṛkodarān; he viprā vriyatāṃ kāmo dadāmy ātma-śiro 'pi vaḥ.

DKS_0181.notes: Excellent fidelity: route details match MBh 2.20 nearly verbatim; generosity exemplars and the 'even my head' promise match BP 10.72. No issues.

statements.claim: Krishna asked for battle - single combat, man to man - declaring they were warriors who had come desiring war, then named Bhima (Vrikodara, son of Pandu), his brother Arjuna, and himself Krishna, their cousin and Jarasandha's enemy.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.27-28: yuddhaṃ no dehi rājendra dvandvaśo... rājanyā nānya-kāṅkṣiṇaḥ; asau vṛkodaraḥ pārthas tasya bhrātārjuno hy ayam; anayor mātuleyaṃ māṃ kṛṣṇaṃ jānīhi te ripum; MBh 2.22: 'I am Hrishesha otherwise called Sauri, and these two heroes... sons of Pandu'.

statements.claim: Krishna charged Jarasandha with bringing the Kshatriyas of the world here as captives to offer in sacrifice to Rudra - human slaughter never seen among the virtuous - and bade him set the kings free or go to the abode of Yama.
statements.evidence: MBh 2.22 (in pack): 'Thou hast brought... many of the Kshatriyas of the world as captives... seekest to offer them as sacrifice unto the god Rudra!... The slaughter of human being as sacrifice unto the gods is never seen... Either set free all the monarchs, or go thou to the abode of Yama.'

statements.claim: Jarasandha laughed aloud and answered that he could not recollect ever having wronged the three, and that he never made a captive of a king not first vanquished in fair war - every man in his prison had been beaten in battle, the law of his order being to bring others under sway by prowess.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.29 (jahāsoccaiḥ); MBh 2.22: 'I do not recollect if I ever acted injuriously towards ye... I never make a captive of a king without first vanquishing him... bring others under sway by the exhibition of prowess and then to treat them as slaves.'

statements.claim: Jarasandha refused to fight Krishna, taunting him as a coward who had abandoned his own city of Mathura and fled to the sea.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.30: na tvayā bhīruṇā yotsye... mathurāṃ sva-purīṃ tyaktvā samudraṃ śaraṇaṃ gataḥ.

statements.claim: He judged Arjuna no match, but Bhima his equal in age and strength - the fight he wanted - so he gave Bhima a great mace, took a second for himself, and walked out through the city gates to the level ground outside the walls.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.31-33: ayaṃ tu vayasātulyo... arjuno na bhaved yoddhā bhīmas tulya-balo mama; ity uktvā bhīmasenāya prādāya mahatīṃ gadām dvitīyāṃ svayam ādāya nirjagāma purād bahiḥ; samekhale (level arena) at 10.72.33.

statements.claim: Bhima followed him out, with Krishna and Arjuna behind, as the city of Girivraja gathered to see the strongest man of Magadha meet his challenger.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.32-33 (the duel is joined in public on the level ground outside the city); crowd-gathering is connective framing consistent with a public duel before witnesses.

DKS_0182.notes: Blends BP 10.72.27-32 and MBh 2.22 accurately; the two sources' elements (BP's short reveal/laugh/taunt, MBh's fuller accusation and defense) are combined without contradiction. No issues.

statements.claim: Jarasandha, the king of Magadha, and Bhima, the second of the Pandava brothers who had come with Krishna and Arjuna, faced each other with maces on the open ground outside Girivraja.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.33: 'tataḥ samekhale vīrau saṃyuktāv itaretaram'; pack excerpt: 'the two heroes clash outside the city'; Jarasandha as lord of Magadha and the three challengers are the episode's established frame (10.72.44 'magadheśvare'; corpus chain from DKS_0182).

statements.claim: When Krishna revealed who they were and demanded the duel that would settle the old feud, Jarasandha looked the three over and chose Bhima.
statements.evidence: Corpus-chain story DKS_0182 ('Krishna Reveals Their Identities and Challenges Jarasandha', BP 10.72.19-32) establishes the challenge and Jarasandha's choice of Bhima; the pack's verses 33-38 begin mid-duel, presupposing that selection.

statements.claim: The champions circled in wide, intricate patterns, turning now left, now right, like wrestlers reading each other's feet.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.34: 'maṇḍalāni vicitrāṇi savyaṃ dakṣiṇam eva ca' (varied circles, left and right); pack excerpt: 'circling in intricate patterns like wrestlers'.

statements.claim: Their great maces shattered under the force of the blows until each champion was left holding a ruined staff.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.36: the maces hurled with arm-force were crushed to powder ('cūrṇī-babhūvatuḥ'); pack excerpt: 'their clubs shatter under the force of their blows'.

statements.claim: Dropping the ruined weapons, they fell on each other with bare hands, striking with fists hard as iron, the sound harsh and rolling like the crash of a thunderbolt.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.37: 'kruddhau sva-muṣṭibhir ayaḥ-sparaśair apiṣṭām ... nirghāta-vajra-paruṣas tala-tāḍanotthaḥ' (enraged, they crushed each other with iron-touching fists; the sound harsh as a thunderbolt); pack excerpt: 'striking with fists hard as iron, the sound like thunder'.

statements.claim: Neither man gave ground; they were matched in skill, matched in strength, and every advantage seized was answered before it could be pressed.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.38: 'sama-śikṣā-balaujasoḥ' (equal in skill, strength and valor); pack excerpt: 'the fight of the equal champions remains indecisive'.

statements.claim: The great duel remained unfinished — not for lack of fury, but because fury alone could not break the balance between the two.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'yet the fight of the equal champions remains indecisive'; BP 10.72.38 (equal skill, strength, valor) — the story's framing is a direct restatement.

statements.claim: Only one person on that field knew the duel could not end this way: Krishna, who had come to end a threat, watched with patience.
statements.evidence: Foreshadowing of the sequel (evt_0264: Krishna signals Bhima — BP 10.72.39-40, where Krishna is said to know the enemy's birth and death and the means); the inner-state gloss here is narrative bridge, not a pack assertion for this episode.

statements.claim: Jarasandha had ruled that city for years on a strength no one had ever matched; the choice of Bhima was that of a man who wants to break the strongest one first.
statements.evidence: His might and kingship are the arc's premise (DKS_0182 chain; 10.72.44 'magadheśvare'), but 'for years' and the motive attribution are unsourced connective coloring.

DKS_0183.notes: Duel narrative follows BP 10.72.33-38 almost point by point (circling, shattering clubs, iron fists, indecision). Atmosphere (dust field, evening light, 'like a thunderbolt') is figurative, not factual.

statements.claim: Everyone who watched understood the duel had no end in it: Bhima and Jarasandha were too evenly matched, and both too proud to stop.
statements.evidence: Recap of the indecisive equal-champion duel of DKS_0183 (BP 10.72.38); the 'proud' motive gloss and crowd reaction are connective narration.

statements.claim: Krishna knew something no one else on the field knew: Jarasandha could never be killed by the ordinary means of war.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.39: 'śatror janma-mṛtī vidvāñ jīvitaṃ ca jarā-kṛtam' (knowing the enemy's birth, death and that his life was made by Jara); pack excerpt: 'Knowing his enemy's birth and death'.

statements.claim: Jarasandha had been born in two halves, and the demoness Jara had joined the halves together; the joining was what gave him life.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.39: 'jīvitaṃ ca jarā-kṛtam' (his life was made by Jara); the two-halves birth is the corpus's established backstory referenced by the pack index ('Knowing Jarasandha's birth secret') and the preceding arc.

statements.claim: A body so put together could not be felled by any blow, however mighty; it could only be undone along the seam where it had been joined.
statements.evidence: Interpretive logic tying the birth secret (10.72.39) to the prescribed means; pack excerpt says Krishna, 'wishing to show Bhima the means', splits a twig — the seam-vulnerability explanation is the standard reading but not a literal pack sentence.

statements.claim: While the champions circled, Krishna bent down, picked up a twig and, in Bhima's sight, snapped it in two and let the halves fall; Bhima understood.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.40-41: 'sañcintyārī-vadhopāyaṃ bhīmasyāmogha-darśanaḥ' and 'tad vijñāya mahā-sattvo bhīmaḥ' (Bhima, understanding); pack excerpt: 'splits a twig in two as a sign. Bhima understands'.

statements.claim: Bhima dropped low, caught Jarasandha by one leg and pinned the other foot to the earth with his own, then heaved with all his strength.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.42: 'ekam pādaṃ padākramya dorbhyām anyaṃ pragṛhya saḥ' (pressing one foot with his foot, grasping the other with both arms).

statements.claim: Bhima tore the joined king apart along the seam of his birth — from leg and thigh through loins, hip and back, up to the shoulders — and the lord of Magadha was killed at last.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.43-44: 'eka-pādoru-vṛṣaṇa-kaṭi-pṛṣṭha-stanāṃsake' (limb-by-limb seizure from foot to shoulder) and 'nihate magadheśvare'; pack excerpt: 'tearing him apart kills him'.

statements.claim: A great cry of lamentation rose up and rolled over the city: the lord of Magadha was dead.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.44: 'hāhā-kāro mahān āsīn nihate magadheśvare' (a great cry of lamentation arose when the lord of Magadha was slain); the spread 'from the field to the streets' is mild connective extension.

statements.claim: Bhima stood over the body of the man he could not have beaten in a fair fight and understood what Krishna had shown with the twig: some enemies are defeated not by the hardest blow but by being known truly.
statements.evidence: Reflective coda drawing on the equal, indecisive duel (10.72.38) and Krishna's knowledge of the birth secret (10.72.39); moral gloss, not a sourceable event.

DKS_0184.notes: Core sequence (twig-signal, foot-pin, tearing apart, lamentation) matches BP 10.72.39-44 closely. 'Seam of birth' wording is standard interpretive gloss of the tearing method.

statements.claim: For years Jarasandha had sealed conquered kings inside a prison carved into the rock at Girivraja; after he fell in the duel, Krishna opened the prison.
statements.evidence: Pack index title/summary: 'Twenty thousand eight hundred freed kings emerge from the mountain prison'; BP 10.73.1 ('kṣut-kṣāmāḥ ... saṃrodha-parikarśitāḥ' — wasted by hunger and confinement) and the Jarasandha arc establish the rock prison; release follows his death (10.72-73 sequence).

statements.claim: Twenty thousand eight hundred kings came out, hardly recognizable — hunger had eaten the flesh from their bodies and long confinement had worn them thin.
statements.evidence: Pack title/summary: 'Twenty thousand eight hundred freed kings'; BP 10.73.1: 'kṣut-kṣāmāḥ śuṣka-vadanāḥ saṃrodha-parikarśitāḥ' (emaciated by hunger, withered-faced, worn thin by confinement).

statements.claim: Krishna stood before them dark and four-armed, marked with Srivatsa, his eyes like the heart of a lotus; his lotus hands held mace, conch and discus; a jewel blazed at his throat; a garland of wildflowers hung over his shoulders.
statements.evidence: BP 10.73.2-4: 'śrīvatsāṅkaṃ catur-bāhuṃ padma-garbhāruṇekṣaṇam / padma-hastaṃ gadā-śaṅkha-rathāṅgair upalakṣitam / bhrājad-vara-maṇi-grīvaṃ nivītaṃ vana-mālayā'.

statements.claim: The kings drank him in — breathing as if through their noses, reaching as if with their arms — and the weariness of captivity dissolved in the joy of seeing him; then one after another they bowed and pressed their heads to his feet.
statements.evidence: BP 10.73.5-6: 'jighranta iva nāsābhyāṃ rambhanta iva bāhubhiḥ / kṛṣṇa-sandarśanāhlāda-dhvasta-saṃrodhana-klamāḥ'; pack excerpt: 'bow at his feet in gratitude'.

statements.claim: They spoke not of revenge: 'We do not resent the king of Magadha. A ruler swollen with the pride of power does not find what is good for him; such men mistake a mirage for a pool of water. We were the same — our fortunes blinded us and we fought each other for conquest. You have shaken those fortunes away. What is a kingdom to this body that falls and suffers and ends? Teach us the way to your lotus feet.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.73.8-14: 'nainaṃ nāthānusūyāmo māgadhaṃ ... rājyaiśvarya-madonnaddho na śreyo vindate nṛpaḥ / mṛga-tṛṣṇāṃ yathā bālā manyanta udakāśayam / ... ta eva kṛṣṇādya ... vicālitāḥ śriyaḥ / ... na rājyam mṛga-tṛṣṇi-rūpitaṃ dehena śaśvat patatā rujāṃ bhuvā / taṃ naḥ samādiśopāyaṃ yena te caraṇābjoyoḥ'.

statements.claim: With a single voice they praised him: Krishna, Vasudeva, Hari, the Supreme Self.
statements.evidence: BP 10.73.15: 'kṛṣṇāya vāsudevāya haraye paramātmane'.

statements.claim: Krishna answered: 'It is well that you have resolved rightly, you who speak the truth. Haihaya fell, and Nahusha, and Vena, and Ravana, and Naraka. Know that this body and everything born of it come to an end. Return to your people and carry on their line, taking happiness and sorrow, birth and death as they come, indifferent to the body, content in yourselves, firm in your vows.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.73.18-22: 'diṣṭyā vyavasitaṃ bhūpā bhavanta ṛta-bhāṣiṇaḥ / haihayo nahuṣo veṇo rāvaṇo narako 'pare / ... dehādy utpādyam anta-vat / santanvantaḥ prajā-tantūn sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ bhavābhavau / udāsīnāś ca dehādāv ātmārāmā dhṛta-vratāḥ'. 'Pride undid them all' is a connective gloss of the chapter's mirage/pride theme (v.9-10).

statements.claim: He turned to Sahadeva and had the kings bathed, fed fine food and dressed in fresh garments and ornaments; Mukunda himself honored them; chariots yoked with good horses and decked with jewels and gold were brought, and the kings were lifted onto them.
statements.evidence: BP 10.73.24-27: 'saparyāṃ kārayām āsa sahadevena / bhojayitvā varānnena su-snātān samalaṅkṛtān / te pūjitā mukundena rājāno mṛṣṭa-kuṇḍalāḥ / rathān sad-aśvān āropya maṇi-kāñcana-bhūṣitān'.

statements.claim: So the twenty thousand eight hundred kings were freed from their long hardship by Krishna and rode home; when they reached their people, they told them everything — the years of darkness, the duel, and the dark four-armed figure who had waited in the light.
statements.evidence: BP 10.73.28-29: 'ta evaṃ mocitāḥ kṛcchrāt kṛṣṇena su-mahātmanā / jagaduḥ prakṛtibhyas te mahā-puruṣa-ceṣṭitam' (freed from hardship by Krishna, they told their subjects the deeds of the great Person).

DKS_0185.notes: Follows BP 10.73.1-29 closely, including the 20,800 count (pack title/summary), Krishna's form, the kings' no-resentment speech, Krishna's exemplar list (Haihaya/Nahusha/Vena/Ravana/Naraka) and the Sahadeva-led honoring. Emotive framing ('medicine', 'dull eyes bright again') is atmosphere.

statements.claim: Krishna addressed the Yadus in assembly at Mathura: born there and brought up in Vraja, their griefs ended and enemies defeated, but hostilities with the kings and battle with Jarasandha had begun; Mathura was limited and an enemy could enter too easily; a crore of princes and soldiers crowded together would breed dissension; it was time to lay out a city elsewhere.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (1-7): 'This Mathurā city is the abode of the Yadus: we too were born here and brought up in Vraja. However all our griefs have disappeared and the enemies have been defeated. Now our hostilities with the kings and battle with Jarāsandea have commenced ... the city of Mathurā is very limited and the enemies can easily enter it ... if one Koti of princes and infantry live here jointly there is every possibility of a dissension cropping up amongst them'.

statements.claim: The Yadavas answered with one delighted voice: 'Krishna, do what you think proper for us all.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (9): 'Hearing it all the Yādavas delightedly said:—"O Krishna, do what thou deemst proper for the behoof of all these people"'.

statements.claim: The Vrishni elders consulted and spoke openly of the danger: Jarasandha was destined to be unslayable by them and his power very great; his soldiers were so many that the Yadus could not destroy them even in a hundred years.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (10-11): 'Our enemy the king Jarāsandha has been destined as unslayable by us. And his power is also very great ... so great is the number of his soldiers that we shall not be able to bring about their destruction even in hundred years'.

statements.claim: Word came that Jarasandha was marching on Mathura with Kalayavana at his side and a great, irrepressible army behind him, and the Yadavas resolved to retreat.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (12-13): 'the emperor Jarāsandha, along with Kālayavana was proceeding towards Mathurā with his army ... Having heard of the approach of Jarāsandha and Kālayavana with that highly irrepressible huge army the Yadavas thought of retreating'.

statements.claim: Krishna rose in the assembly and said: 'Today is an auspicious day. We leave Mathura this very day, with our army and our followers.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (14): '"To day is an auspicious day. So we shall, even this very day, issue out of Mathura along with our army and followers"'.

statements.claim: They left the city headed by Vasudeva, with wives in the chariots and elephants under burdens, carrying wealth, kinsmen and friends — golden chariots, infuriated elephants, horses trotting with gold on their harnesses; they set out toward the west with Vasudeva and the elders guiding the army from the front, and marched until the ocean rose on the horizon.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (15-20): 'the Yadavas, headed by Vasudeva, along with their wives, cars and elephants, set out ... went on with their wealth, kinsmen, friends, golden chariots, infuriated elephants and trotting horses decorated with gold ... set out for the west ... Stationed in front, Vasudeva and other ... guided the army'; they then 'reached the bank of the ocean'.

statements.claim: The shore was variegated with creepers, rich in coconut trees, covered with ketaki, palmyras and climbing vines, and the Yadavas looked around as if they had stepped into a celestial region.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (21-24): 'It was variegated with creepers, abounded in coconut trees ... was covered with Ketaki trees, palmyras, Pannages and vines. Having secured such a picturesque site the Yadavas were highly delighted as if they had arrived at the celestial region'.

statements.claim: Krishna searched the shore and found an extensive tract on the bank of the ocean with coppery soil mixed with gravel, well suited for beasts of burden, carrying every favorable mark, as if presided over by the Goddess of Prosperity, fanned by the sea breeze and watered by the ocean.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (24-29): 'Searching for a site where he would lay out a city Krishna ... saw an extensive tract of land situated on the bank of the ocean.
