The land had a coppery soil mixed with gravels, was well-suited for animals of burden, was endued with all the favourable marks of a city, as if it was presided over by the Goddess of prosperity herself. It was fanned by the sea breeze and was watered by the ocean'.

statements.claim: Near it rose the charming mountain Raivata, shining like Mount Mandara, rich with gems and resorted to by great men: the sage Drona had lived there for many years, king Ekalavya had dwelt there, and a level sporting ground laid out square like a board of dice was called by the name of Dwaravati.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (25-29): 'Near it was shining in beauty the charming mountain Raivata like the mount Mandara. On that mountain containing all the jems and resorted to by many great men Drona lived for many long years. There lived the king Ekalavya. And the sporting ground laid out by himself like a board of dice is celebrated by the name of Dwāravati'.

statements.claim: Krishna chose that site for his city; the Yadavas pitched their tents for the night, and that night Krishna lived among them without anxiety, thinking of the names he would give the houses of the coming city.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (30-33): 'Keshava selected that site for his city and the Yādavas also wanted to encamp their soldiers there. Thereupon the Yadu commanders pitched tents there for the night ... the Lord Krishna ... lived there with them shorn of anxiety ... thought in his mind of the names he would give to the various houses in that city'.

statements.claim: And so the Yadavas secured Dwaravati and lived there happily with their friends, the way the gods live in their own city.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (34): 'having thus secured the city of Dwaravati the Yādavas, along with their friends, lived there happily as do the gods in their own city'.

DKS_0186.notes: A faithful rendering of Harivamsha 1.113, close to the Dutt text. The story's tradition_note flags that this HV account (flight before Jarasandha/Kalayavana) diverges from the BP order in which Dwaraka is founded after Jarasandha's death; the tension with the preceding BP-based stories (DKS_0183-0185, where Jarasandha dies) is a corpus-chronology matter the story itself discloses, not a pack-fidelity defect. 'Krishna walked among the tents' is a scenic connective (source: 'lived there shorn of anxiety').

statements.claim: Krishna had risen with the sun, performed his morning ablutions at the forest's edge and surveyed the ground himself before a stone was laid.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.115 (1-2): 'when the sun rose ... Hrishikesha ... having performed his morning ablution and sat for some time at the outskirt of the forest, began to survey it for finding out a site where he would build a fortress'.

statements.claim: On an auspicious day under the star Rohini he offered presents to the brahmanas and asked their blessings, and then the work began: courtyards and promenades, well-levelled roads and inner apartments, the four gates named Shudraksha, Aindra, Bhallata and Pushpadantaka, and temples for Brahma, the god of sacrifices, Indra and the presiding deities of fire and water.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.115 (3, 6-7, 10-14): 'in an auspicious day under the auspices of the planet Rohini he offered immense presents to the Brāhmanas and made them perform benedictory rites'; 'laying out courtyards, promenades, well-levelled roads and inner appartments'; 'Temples, in proper places, were built for Brahmā, the god of sacrifices, Indra, the presiding deities of fire and water'; 'the four gates ... (namely Shudrāksha, Aindra, Bhallāta and Pushpadantāka)'.

statements.claim: When the ocean would not yield enough room, Krishna asked it to withdraw twelve yojanas, and the sea obeyed, so the city could spread along the shore.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.115 (36-37): Krishna says to the ocean 'withdraw thy form in the water extending over twelve yojanas'. The pack passage truncates before the ocean's reply; the withdrawal-outcome is the necessary premise of the city's completion in the same account (city of 8x12 yojanas in the following episode, DKS_0188) and is consistent with, never contradicted by, the pack.

statements.claim: Even the celestial architect Vishwakarma had come down to help, and the city was taking shape as something that could be spoken of beside Amaravati itself.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.115 (15-22, 29-30): Krishna 'thought of Viswakarmā, in his mind, so that he might come there. In the meantime the highly intelligent celestial architect, Viswakarma ... came there and stood before Krishna', who bids him build a city 'celebrated on earth like Amarāvati'.

statements.claim: Krishna set the old king Ugrasena at its head: 'Take Ugrasena before you and enjoy this place without anxiety, like the celestials.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.115 (8): 'Taking Ugrasena before you and putting impediments in the ways of your enemies do you enjoy here shorn of anxiety like the celestials'.

statements.claim: Krishna felt a desire to gratify his own people, who were poor, with profuse riches; he summoned Sankha, the guardian of treasure, and ordered heaps of wealth showered into every house of Dwaraka — not into a central treasury — until no household stood empty-handed.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (HV 1.115): 'Krishna ... felt a desire of gratifying his own people, who were poor, with profuse riches. ... Sankha ... ordered them to shower heaps of wealth in every house of Dwāravati'; pack index title: 'Krishna bids the treasure-guard Sankha shower wealth on every household'. The 'not a central treasury' contrast is the story's emphasis of 'every house'.

statements.claim: Krishna sent the wind itself on the errand: Vayu, the god of the air, was to go to the celestial region, beg the assembly hall Sudharma of those who kept it, and bring it to Dwaraka; from that day the elders of the Yadu race met in the hall that had once held the deliberations of heaven.
statements.evidence: Pack index title (HV 1.115): 'sends Vayu to fetch the celestial assembly-hall Sudharma from heaven'; pack excerpt: Krishna says 'beg of them the assembly Hall Sudharmā and bring it to Dwarkā'. The image of the hall 'coming to rest above the city' is a connective rendering of its being fetched and set in place.

statements.claim: Wealth lay in every house and the gods' own assembly hall stood among the people, so that Dwaraka could be spoken of beside the cities of the celestials; what Krishna fetched from heaven was a hall where the whole community could sit and decide its own affairs, not a throne for himself.
statements.evidence: Reflective synthesis of the Sankha and Sudharma episodes (pack excerpt + index); the thematic gloss ('not a throne but a hall') is editorial commentary, not a sourceable event.

DKS_0187.notes: Grounded in Harivamsha 1.115 (fort-laying, Rohini rites, named gates and temples, Ugrasena at the head, ocean's 12-yojana withdrawal request, Vishwakarma summoned, Sankha's wealth-shower, Sudharma via Vayu). The pack's primary passage truncates at v.37, so the Sankha/Sudharma claims rest on the pack's own excerpt and index entry, which cover them.

statements.claim: Krishna came back to his city on Garuda's back and from the air Dwaraka looked like a place from another world — sporting-houses and gardens, turrets and courtyards spread across the ground the sea had surrendered, the whole city filled with echoes on every side.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.245 (1-2): 'Krishna, seated on Garuda's back, saw the city of Dwārakā, resembling the abode of the celestials, filled with echoes on all sides, the mount Mani, sporting-houses, gardens, forests, turrets and court-yards'. The surrendered-ground image echoes the ocean's withdrawal in the founding account (HV 1.115; DKS_0187).

statements.claim: When Indra learned Krishna had returned, he sent for Vishwakarma and said: 'Make Krishna's beautiful city more exquisite, for his sake. Encircle it with hundreds of gardens and build Dwaraka after the city of the celestials. Adorn it with all the gems you will find in the three worlds — for Krishna ... is forever plunging into the dreadful ocean of war. His home should shine like his deeds.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.245 (3-5): 'the king of gods sent for the celestial Architect and said:—"...do you, for satisfying Krishna, make his beautiful city more exquisite. O foremost of gods, encircling it with hundreds of gardens do you build the city of Dwārakā after that of the celestials. Adorn the city of Dwāravati with all the jems that you will see in the three worlds, for the highly powerful Krishna ... always plunges into the dreadful ocean of war"'.

statements.claim: Vishwakarma went to Dwaraka and did as he was asked, and when his work was done the city had been remade in the image of Amaravati.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.245 (6-10): 'repairing to the city of Dwāravati at the words of Indra Vishwakarmā adorned it after Amarāvati'.

statements.claim: The city stood ringed by ditches full of lotus-stalks, like the Ganges and the Sindhu, with swans sporting on the water; the walls that ran along the rooftops were of gold, so the city looked the way the sky looks when covered with gold-hued clouds.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.245 (11-12): 'the city was encircled by ditches filled with lotus-stalks resembling the rivers Gangā (Ganges) and Sindhu (Indus), and in which were sporting the swans. As the sky is covered with gold-hued clouds so that city looked beautiful with sunny walls made of gold set on (the roofs of) the houses'.

statements.claim: On the east shone a gate of gold and jewels, and beyond it the hill Raivataka with its charming table-lands and caves; to the south the bushes were draped in creepers of five colours, to the west in creepers the colour of a rainbow, while the yellow mountain Venuman stood guard in the north, like Mandara among mountains.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.245 (14-17): 'On its eastern side shone a beautiful gate made of gold and jems and the picturesque hill Raivataka with its charming table-land, caves and yards. On the south were bushes adorned with creepers of five colours and on the west was one of the colour of a rain-bow. O king, the yellow mountain Venumān, resembling Mandara, was beautifying the north'.

statements.claim: Forests crowded around the city on every side — Chitrak, Panchavarna, Panchajanya, Sarvartuka, and the great woods of Bhargava and Pushpaka, huge as Mount Meru, their creepers running down to the roots of the trees, with ashoka and mandara flowering among them.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.245 (14-18): 'The forests of Chitrak, Panchavarna, Pānchajanya and Sarvartuka were enhancing the beauty of the mount Raivataka. There were also the beautiful forests of Bhārgava and Pushpaka huge like the mount Meru, which were covered with creepers extending to the roots of the trees ... beautified by the trees of Ashoka, Veejaka and Mandāra'.

statements.claim: The sacred river Mandakini, bright with lotus leaves and gems, came down and entered Dwaraka with fifty mouths, gladdening every inhabitant.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.245 (19-26): 'on the east were the great river Mandākini adorned with Vaidurja and lotus leaves ... With fifty mouths, the sacred river Mandākini entered into the city of Dwārakā and gladdened the inhabitants thereof'.

statements.claim: Within the walls eight thousand cars stood hung with nets of bells and flying banners; the city measured eight yojanas in length and twelve across, with double that number of colonies, eight great highways and sixteen crossings, and seven high roads laid by Vishwakarma for the movement of soldiers — so well made that even the women could easily defend it.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.245 (26-29): 'eight thousand cars, adorned with net-works of bells and flying banners ... Dwārakā eight yojanas in length and twelve in breadth with double the number of colonies. That city, consisting of eight highways and sixteen crossings, was as if so made ... that even the women, what to speak of the Vrishnis, could easily fight there. Viswakarmā had laid out seven high roads for the arrangement of soldiers'.

statements.claim: The palaces of the Yadavas rose with golden and jewelled stairs, their turrets carried flags, their domes were of gold, their tops covered with golden flowers and colours of five kinds imitated the beauty of mountains; they shone like forest-fire and filled the sky with an effulgence like the sun's and the moon's.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.245 (30-36): 'palaces of the illustrious Dāshārhas ... containing golden and jewelled stairs ... The turrets of those palaces were adorned with flags ... adorned with golden domes resembling the summits of the mount Meru. The tops of the houses, as if covered with golden flowers and others of five colours, imitated the beauty of mountains ... burning like forest-fire those houses ... filled the sky with effulgence like the sun and moon'.

statements.claim: Vishwakarma built the house of Krishna himself — four yojanas long and four broad, adorned with palaces and false mountains — and beside it a golden palace of surpassing beauty, the most beautiful of all, which he built for Rukmini.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.245 (37-40): 'The house, built by Vishwakarma for the Divine Vāsudeva, was four yojanas in length and the same in breadth. The house of the incomparable and the greatly rich Vāsudeva was adorned with palaces and false mountains'; pack excerpt: 'he built a highly beautiful golden palace ... for Rukshmini'.

statements.claim: Everything the architect did at Dwaraka he did under the orders of the king of heaven; and Krishna, beholding the palaces of his people and the city the gods had adorned for him, was highly pleased, and having accomplished all that he had set out to do, entered it.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.245 (40, 10): 'The great Vishwakarmā built that house under Vasava's orders'; 'having accomplished all his objects the Lord Nārāyana Hari ... entered there' while 'Beholding the city of Dwārakā adorned by Viswakarma'.

DKS_0188.notes: A near line-by-line rendering of Harivamsha 1.245's catalogue (moats, gold walls, gates, forests, Mandakini's fifty mouths, dimensions, highways, palaces, Krishna's and Rukmini's houses). The pack's own passage truncates just before the finish of the Rukmini-palace sentence; the excerpt and index cover it. Story's tradition_note correctly notes the chapter is a second, Indra-commissioned beautification of an already-built city.

statements.claim: The spies came to the house of Balarama, which stood like the home of a patriarch, and found all the leading Yadavas gathered in assembly at Krishna's word.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.103 (1-2): 'the spies assembled at the house of Baladeva resembling that of a patriarch ... all the leading Yādavas were present in the assembly at Krishna's mandate'. The story's 'sow the topic of future events' softens Dutt's 'for cropping up the topic of future dissension' — a mild paraphrase; the prophecy of the kings' destruction follows in the same breath.

statements.claim: At the call of the king of the Bhoja line a great meeting of kings was to be held at Kundina, and rulers from every province were hurrying there; Rukmini, the sister of Rukmi, would hold her swayamvara — adorned with golden ornaments, the fairest woman in the three worlds, she would choose a husband on the third day from that day.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.103 (3-8): 'at the invitation of Bhoja's son a great meeting of the kings will take place at the city of Kundina. There the kings of various provinces are repairing in haste ... Rukshmini, the first sister of Rukshmi, will hold her Swayamvara ... on the third day hereof, the Swayamvara, of Rushmini adorned with golden ornaments, the fairest in the three worlds, will take place'. 'King of the Bhoja line' renders 'Bhoja's son' (the host, Bhishmaka of the Bhoja dynasty).

statements.claim: The emissaries announced the meeting would be the future destruction of those kings, who were coming on elephants, horses and cars, elated with pride like lions and tigers, bent on injuring one another, gifted with the gait of infuriated elephants, fond of battle and highly powerful; the plain before Kundina would hold hundreds of their encampments.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.103 (3, 9-10): 'the emissaries announced the future destruction of the kings ... Proceeding on elephants, horses and cars, all the kings, elated with pride like unto lions and tigers, bent upon injuring one another, gifted with the gait of infuriated elephants, fond of battle and highly powerful, will assemble there. We shall behold those hundreds of encampments'.

statements.claim: The kings who feared the Yadavas would sit in safety at Kundina like immortals in the land of the celestials, under the protection of numbers.
statements.evidence: The 'like immortals in the land of the celestials' image belongs to Krishna's own warning to Ugrasena (HV 1.103, 17-18: kings 'although afraid of us, are enjoying in the city of Kundina, like immortals in the land of celestials'); the story folds it into the spies' report and adds 'under the protection of numbers' from the gathering's scale (v.9-10). Content is present in the pack; the speaker placement is a light narrative rearrangement, not a distortion.

statements.claim: 'The kings of all the earth are assembling. Why should we remain depressed alone? Let us all, encircled by our armies, set out for victory.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.103 (11): 'while all the kings of earth have assembled why should we remain depressed alone? Let us all, encircled by our armies, set out for victory'.

statements.claim: The verses say the words struck Krishna like a dart to the heart; he set out immediately at the head of his army, and the Yadavas of fierce prowess mounted their cars and followed him like the gods in their pride; Krishna shone with discus and mace uplifted — he whom even Ishana held dear — and the car-warriors behind him made a stream of cars effulgent like the sun and echoing with the tinkling of bells.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.103 (12-15): 'Hearing those words like unto a dart stuck to the heart, Keshava ... set out immediately with his army ... The Yādavas too, of fierce prowess, got upon their cars ... followed him like gods filled with pride ... Krishna, with uplifted discus and mace in his hand, and liked by Ishāna, shone there ... cars effulgent like the sun and echoing with the tinkling of bells'.

statements.claim: Before he left, Krishna counselled Ugrasena to wait behind with his brother and guard the city, for when it was emptied by their departure those kings of deceitful conduct who feared them but enjoyed themselves at Kundina might attack it at Jarasandha's desire.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.103 (16-18): 'Govinda, of sure fore-sight, said to Ugrasena, at the time of his departure, "...do thou wait here with my brother. For when this city will be empty on our departure, those Khatriyas, of deceitful conduct ... who, although afraid of us, are enjoying in the city of Kundina, like immortals in the land of celestials, may attack it at Jarāsandha's desire"'.

statements.claim: Ugrasena replied in words trembling with affection that without Krishna they could not live happily, here or anywhere — like a woman without her husband — and that under the shelter of Krishna's arms they feared not even Indra and the gods, much less the kings of the earth; they would follow him wherever he went for victory.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.103 (19-23): 'If dost thou go leaving us behind, we shall not be able to live here happily or elsewhere like a woman without her husband ... we do not, under the shelter of thy arms, fear even Indra and other gods what to speak of kings ... we shall follow thee wherever thou shalt go for achieving victory'.

statements.claim: Krishna, hearing the king's words, smiled and said: 'I should do whatever you wish. There is no doubt about it.' So the departure became a shared journey — the old king refusing to be left behind, Krishna yielding to the affection of his people.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.103 (24): 'Hearing the words of the king, Devaki's son smilingly said:—"I should do whatever you wish. There is no doubt, about it"'; the 'shared journey' framing is connective synthesis of v.16-24.

statements.claim: The army moved out of Mathura, car after car falling into line with banners streaming until the whole might of the Yadava clan was on the road behind him, and the way to Kundina lay open.
statements.evidence: Departure at the head of the host is supported (HV 1.103, 12-15); 'banners streaming' and the road imagery are scenic connective detail.

DKS_0190.notes: Follows Harivamsha 1.103 closely, including the spies' report, the dart-to-the-heart, the armed departure, and the full Krishna-Ugrasena exchange. One light rearrangement: the 'kings safe like immortals' image, spoken by Krishna (v.17-18), is absorbed into the spies' report; content intact. Note: this HV account is set while the Yadus still occupy Mathura (life_stage mathura), which sits before the Dwaraka founding in HV chronology but is sequenced after it in this corpus — a corpus-ordering matter, not a pack-fidelity defect.

statements.claim: Krishna reached Bhishmaka's house at the hour when the sun, low in the west, turned the colour of heated iron.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.104 (1) + translator's note 270: Krishna 'arrived at Bhishmaka's house in the evening'; the Sanskrit 'lohitāyati bhāskare' is glossed 'when the sun became red like heated iron'.

statements.claim: He came to see the swayamvara and saw the spacious arena crowded with camps, the tents of many kings filling the plain before Kundina, the smoke of their fires rising into the evening air.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.104 (1-2): 'saw the spacious arena full of camps'; the hundreds of assembled kings are stated in the same chapter (v.15) and the hundreds of encampments in the preceding one (1.103, v.10). 'Tents of a hundred kings' is the scenic idiom for that gathering; smoke is connective atmosphere.

statements.claim: For a moment Krishna was moved by what the verses candidly call a rajasika inclination — a restless stirring of pride, the desire to make the assembled kings understand who had arrived; it was not a sinful impulse, the text is careful to say, but the wish to display his own prowess.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.104 (2-3) + note 271: Krishna 'was possessed by Rajasika inclination' and acted 'in order to terrify the kings and display his own prowess'; the note adds he 'was actuated by a selfish motive but not for a sinful end'. The story's gloss matches both verse and note.

statements.claim: He thought of Garuda: as soon as Vinata's son was in his mind, the king of birds took a form that could be seen easily and came to Krishna.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.104 (3-4): 'he thought of the highly powerful son of Vinatā ... As soon as he was thought of Vinatā's son, assuming a form that could be seen easily, approached Keshava'.

statements.claim: With the strokes of his wings, wings that could agitate even the wind itself, every man gathered there — kings, warriors, servants — trembled, bent over and fell to the earth, writhing like serpents deprived of the power to rise.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.104 (5-6): 'With the strokes of his wings which could agitate even the wind, all the men, trembling and being haunch-backed, fell down on earth. And they began to exert like serpents deprived of the power of rising up'.

statements.claim: Krishna alone stood firm, like a mountain, and knew before he saw that the king of birds had arrived.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.104 (7): 'Beholding them all fallen Krishna, firm like a mountain, came to know that the king of birds had arrived'.

statements.claim: Then he saw Garuda: adorned with celestial garlands and unguents, shaking the earth with the flapping of his wings; golden-feathered, bright as a mountain made of minerals; the weapons on his back lying faces downward like licking serpents seeking the touch of Vishnu's hand; black serpents dragged in his talons as he came.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.104 (8-11): 'Garuda, adorned with celestial garlands and unguents, was approaching him, shaking the earth with the flapping of his wings. The weapons, with their faces downwards, were fixed on his back like licking serpents with a view to be favoured with the touch of Vishnu's hand. Adorned with golden feathers like a mountain consisting of minerals that king of birds was dragging, with his feet, black serpents'.

statements.claim: This was the bird who had brought ambrosia for Krishna, the destroyer of serpents and the terror of the Daityas, whose emblem stood on the flagstaff above Krishna's car — and now he stood before his lord, like a god bringing a gift.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.104 (12): 'the intelligent Garuda arrived and stationed before him like a god, who brought ambrosia for him, who was the destroyer of serpents, the terrifier of the Daityas, whose emblem was on his flag-staff and who was his councillor'; 'like a god bringing a gift' is connective flourish.

statements.claim: Krishna welcomed him: 'O foremost of birds, you are welcome. We are going to the swayamvara at the house of Kaishika — come with us. Hundreds of powerful kings have gathered there with their elephants, horses and cars. We shall behold those high-souled ones.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.104 (13-15): '"O foremost of birds ... thou art welcome ... we shall go to the house of Kaishika and behold the Swayamvara. Do thou also accompany us. There hundreds of highly powerful kings have assembled with their elephants, horses and cars; we shall behold those high-souled ones"'. The episode's host is named Kaishika here and Bhishmaka in the narration — a naming variant the story's tradition_note discloses (Harivamsha calls Rukmini's father both).

statements.claim: So the car set out again, with Garuda beside it and the mighty car-warriors of the Yadavas following; when they reached the city of Vidarbha, all the kings who had come for the swayamvara — holding all manner of weapons though they were — were filled with delight and hurried to make arrangements for Krishna's quarters.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.104 (16-18): Krishna 'set out for the city of the high-sould Kaishika along with the mighty car-warriors the Yādavas. When Devaki's son ... reached the city of Vidarbha along with the mighty car-warrior Yādavas, all the powerful kings, holding all sorts of weapons, were filled with delight and began to make arrangements for his quarters'.

statements.claim: Bhishmaka himself — the king well read in the moral laws — rose from among the kings and came to welcome him: he brought water to wash Krishna's feet and rinse his mouth, offered the ritual arghya, and placed him in his own city; as Shankara is said to enter the hill Kailasa, Krishna entered with his army the house kept ready for him from before, and was honoured with edibles and drinks, with jewels and affection — Vasava's younger brother Krishna lived happily in the house of Bhishmaka.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.104 (19-22): 'the king Kaishika, well read in moral laws, rose up delightedly from among the kings, welcomed himself Krishna with water to wash his feet and rinse his mouth and arghya and placed him in his own city. Like unto Shankara entering into the Kailāca hill Krishna, with his army, entered into the house that had been kept ready for him from before. Adored with various edibles, drinks, jewels, honors and love Vāsava's younger brother Krishna lived happily in king Kaishika's house'. Kaishika = Bhishmaka per the story's tradition note.

statements.claim: The kings who had fallen before the king of birds were the same kings who now pressed forward, delighted, to make room for Krishna — shown, without a single word of threat, what stood beside him; the swayamvara had not yet begun, and already the assembly knew who had come to it.
statements.evidence: Reflective coda over the chapter's arc (terrifying arrival, then delighted welcome); not a new factual claim.

DKS_0191.notes: Very close rendering of Harivamsha 1.104: arrival at dusk ('heated iron' sun, per translator's note), rajasika inclination (verse + note), Garuda's thought-appearance, the prostrating of the kings, Krishna's speech naming 'the house of Kaishika', the Vidarbha welcome, and the Bhishmaka/Kaishika honor scene. Naming-variant (Bhishmaka vs Kaishika) is handled transparently in the story's tradition_note.

statements.claim: King Bhishmaka of Kundina had let his son (Rukmi) send out swayamvara invitations against his own wishes, and the invited kings were arriving by chariot, elephant, horse and infantry until the streets seemed full of armed men.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.108: Krishna charges that Bhishmaka must know of 'the great assemblage of the kings invited by your son', where 'cars, elephants, horses and the infantry have made a wild dance in your city'; Bhishmaka himself says his son 'wishes to give away his sister in a Swayamvara, but I do not like it'. The inviter-son (Rukmi) and swayamvara announcement rest on 1.103 ('Rukshmini, the first sister of Rukshmi, will hold her Swayamvara') continuity.

statements.claim: Bhishmaka came to Krishna saying his son out of childishness wished to give away his sister in a swayamvara, that he wanted his daughter to choose the one person she saw, and begged forgiveness for his son's bad conduct.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.108, Bhishmaka's speech near-verbatim: 'out of his childish nature, my son wishes to give away his sister in a Swayamvara, but I do not like it... I wish that my daughter may select the only person whom she sees... Be thou propitiated and forgive (him).'

statements.claim: Krishna rebuked Bhishmaka that a king who speaks a falsehood consumes himself with the fire of Yama's tortures, and that truthfulness is the foremost religious duty of kings, pointed out by Brahma in the days of yore.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.108: 'He who... speaks a falsehood, even before one king, consumes with the fire of Yama's tortures'; 'even Brahmā, in the days of yore, pointed it out as the foremost duty of men.'

statements.claim: Krishna accused Bhishmaka of pretending not to know of the gathering and of withholding hospitality from him, citing Manu's rule that he who puts obstacles in the way of a maiden wastes himself in hell; he said that was why he had not entered the assembly hall, that Kaishika had given rest to his followers, and that he lived there with Garuda as in the city of the gods.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.108: 'you have offered hospitality and welcome duly to the kings, assembled like the sun and moon... and still you do not know anything of your son's work'; 'Manu and other leading Law-givers have ordained that he who puts obstacles in the way of a maiden, wastes himself in hell'; 'for this, I did not enter into the assembly-hall and accept hospitality... Kaishika, ever fond of guests, offered us proper hospitality. I too, in the company of Garuda, am living here as in the city of gods.'

statements.claim: Bhishmaka bowed low under Krishna's words, begged forgiveness as one possessed by ignorance, asked for 'eyes of wisdom', and said that having obtained Krishna's shelter he entertained no fear.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.108 near-verbatim: 'I am possessed by the darkness of ignorance; do thou give me eyes of wisdom... Having obtained thy shelter, I do not entertain any fear.'

statements.claim: Krishna revealed that Rukmini's goddess-like form had brought him to Kundina, and that when the gods assembled on the summit of Mount Sumeru in the days of yore they told her to be born in Bhishmaka's house in Kundina and be united with Keshava.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.108: 'the goddess-like form of Rukshmini has brought me to this place'; 'When in the days of yore the gods assembled on the summit of the mount Sumeru for incarnating their portions they said to her... having been born in the house of Bhishmaka in the city of Kundina, be thou united with Keshava.'

statements.claim: Rukmini is not a woman but the goddess Lakshmi (Sree), born among mortals at the words of Brahma, and must not be given away in a swayamvara before all the kings; she should be conferred on a single invited bridegroom with proper rites, as a Kshatriya's duty.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.108: 'truly your daughter Rukshmini is not a woman; she is the very goddess Sree. For some object and at the words of Brahmā she is born (as a woman)'; 'She should not be given away in a Swayamvara where all the kings will be assembled... inviting one bride groom, you should confer her on him. It will be thus performing a Kshatriya's duties. O king, you cannot give away Lakshmi in a Swayamvara.'

statements.claim: Garuda, son of Vinata, had been sent by the king of the gods to obstruct the swayamvara, and Krishna himself had come to witness the festival of the kings and see Rukmini.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.108: 'In order to put impediments in Swayamvara Vinata's son has been despatched by the king of gods and has come to the city of Kundina. I too have come here to witness this Swayamvara festivity of the kings and your daughter, the beautiful Kamala without lotuses.'

statements.claim: Bhishmaka's anxious mood as the affair slipped from his hands, and the closing reflection that what he had feared was the will of the gods.
statements.evidence: Inner-state framing around the supported dialogue (his dislike of the swayamvara is in the passage); no new sourceable factual assertion.

DKS_0192.notes: Dialogue tracks Harivamsha 1.108 near-verbatim (Dutt/Gutenberg #61937). Rukmi as the inviting son rests on 1.103/1.108 continuity; the pack itself does not name him in this chapter.

statements.claim: After the audience in which Krishna had told Bhishmaka of the gods' decree about Rukmini, Krishna rose to take his leave and the kings of the swayamvara were stirring in the city.
statements.evidence: Pack index summary: 'Krishna takes leave of Bhishmaka'; Harivamsha 1.109 opens 'After the departure of Vasudeva's son the kings... returned to the assembly-hall'. The decree (Rukmini as Lakshmi to be united with Keshava) is DKS_0192/1.108 continuity.

statements.claim: As he was leaving, Bhishmaka beheld Krishna's universal form: the prime and self-sprung Krishna, existing before every beginning, with eyes like red lotuses, a thousand feet, a thousand eyes and a thousand arms.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Harivamsha 1.108): 'beholding the prime and self-sprung Krishna, having eyes like red lotuses, thousand feet, thousand eyes, thousand arms'.

statements.claim: Bhishmaka bowed low and began to eulogise Krishna's glories, praising the self-sprung one as the source of everything.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (1.108): 'the king Bhishmaka bowed unto him and began to eulogise his glories'; the eulogy of the prime/self-sprung lord is the subject of the passage.

statements.claim: The vision then folded back and Krishna stood before Bhishmaka again as the young man he had seemed, ready to leave.
statements.evidence: The pack records the cosmic-form sight, the eulogy and Krishna's departure (1.109 opening: kings return to the assembly hall 'after the departure of Vasudeva's son') without detailing the reversion; the return to mortal form is the connective bridge between the two scenes.

statements.claim: As Krishna came out of Bhishmaka's presence, the assembled kings who had come to Kundina rose and followed him.
statements.evidence: Pack index summary: '...worships him with a eulogy before the kings follow him out'. The kings' motivations ('as if drawn...') are connective gloss.

statements.claim: The 'young man who had claimed her' gloss in the closing lines, Bhishmaka's inner awe, and cosmic-form elaboration ('the shape of everything, every being that breathed, every star').
statements.evidence: Atmosphere elaborating the pack's epithets (prime, self-sprung, thousand-limbed); 'claimed her' gestures to the gods' decree of DKS_0192 rather than asserting a new event.

DKS_0193.notes: Core scene matches 1.108-1.109 pack: leave-taking, cosmic form with thousand feet/eyes/arms, eulogy, kings following him out. Story uses 'thousand feet/eyes/arms' matching the excerpt (the index summary's 'thousand heads and arms' is the loose variant; the excerpt governs). Poetic expansion is atmosphere.

statements.claim: After Krishna left Kundina, the kings who had come for the swayamvara gathered one last time in Bhishmaka's assembly hall, anxious to be on the road to their own kingdoms.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.109.1: 'After the departure of Vasudeva's son the kings, who... were anxious to go to their respective kingdoms, returned to the assembly-hall of Bhishmaka.'

statements.claim: Bhishmaka, foremost of kings and well-read in the moral laws, asked the assembled kings' forgiveness for the calamity and for the fruit of his misconduct.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.109.2-3 near-verbatim: 'the foremost of kings and well-read in moral laws... O ye kings, you all know the calamity that will befall the Swayamvara. Do you forgive me for the fruit that is the outcome of my misconduct.'

statements.claim: He honored the kings and sent them on their way — the monarchs of central India and of the east, west and north — and they, mighty car-warriors, returned his honors and rode off delighted.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.109.4-5: 'the king sent away all the monarchs of Central India and of the East, West and Northern Provinces. Having honored the king Bhishmaka duly in return, those kings, the foremost of men and mighty car-warriors, went away delightedly.'

statements.claim: A few kings remained with Bhishmaka — Jarasandha, Sunitha, Dantavakra, the king of Soubha and others of the Deccan — lingering as if sensing the mystery of Kundina was unfinished.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.109.5-6: 'Jarāsandha, Sunitha, the energetic Dantavakra, the king of Soubha... all those and other kings of the Deccan remained by Bhishmaka desirous of listening to the mystery.'

statements.claim: Rukmini had seen Krishna, had heard him speak, and had watched her father's fear drain away in his presence.
statements.evidence: The pack (Harivamsha 1.109) places Rukmini's declaration among her friends after the kings' dispersal and nowhere shows her at Krishna's audience with Bhishmaka (1.108), which the preceding corpus stories present as private. The Bhagavata branch of this same abduction cluster (10.52, cf. DKS_0196-97) has her choose Krishna purely by hearsay — her own message opens 'Having heard your virtues' (10.52.36) — and DKS_0196 states she settled her marriage 'without ever having set eyes on the groom.'
statements.resolution: Corrected in story text via consolidation pass.

statements.claim: Everything her brother Rukmi had planned — the invitations, the gathering of kings, the ceremony where she would choose — was swayamvara machinery built on treating her as a prize.
statements.evidence: Corpus continuity of the pack's own chain: 1.103 spies announce Rukmini's swayamvara; 1.108 has Krishna speak of 'the great assemblage of the kings invited by your son'; a swayamvara is by definition a public choosing-ceremony.

statements.claim: Rukmini approached her friends with her face bent down in shame and declared she would not be the spouse of anyone save Krishna, who has lotus eyes.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Harivamsha 1.109) near-verbatim: 'the chaste and wise Rukshmini approached her friends and with her face bent down in shame said:—I tell you truly, I do not wish to be the spouse of any body else save Krishna having lotus eyes.'

statements.claim: Rukmini's shyness as burning confession, the certainty of her secret choice, and the reflection that no assembly can overrule a bride who has decided.
statements.evidence: Inner-state and thematic narration around the supported declaration; no new sourceable factual assertion.

corrections.original_sentence: Rukmini had seen Krishna. She had heard him speak, and she had watched her father's fear drain away in his presence.
corrections.suggested: Rukmini had never set eyes on Krishna; she knew him only through the reports of his beauty and virtues that had reached Kundina, and her heart had already answered them.

DKS_0194.notes: Assembly, dismissal, the kings who stayed, and Rukmini's declaration all track Harivamsha 1.109 closely. One unsupported embellishment: Rukmini personally witnessing Krishna's audience with her father — no pack support, and the sibling BhP branch (10.52) plus DKS_0196 say she chose him by hearing alone.

statements.claim: Years later Uddhava, who had served Krishna, remembered two of Krishna's weddings together: Rukmini's carrying off and Satya (Nagnajiti)'s svayamvara victory.
statements.evidence: Pack title/summary (BhP 3.3): 'Uddhava recalls how Krishna carried off Rukmini, Bhishmaka's daughter, by the gandharva rite, and how he defeated the proud kings to win Satya (Nagnajiti) at her svayamvara'; variant_notes: 'Recall bundling Rukmini's abduction + Satya's svayamvara.'

statements.claim: Rukmini, Bhishmaka's daughter, sent for Krishna, and he came and carried off his own share by the gandharva rite while the assembled suitors looked on.
statements.evidence: BhP 3.3.2: 'samāhutā bhīṣmaka-kanyayā' (summoned by Bhishmaka's daughter); pack excerpt: 'he carried off his own share by the gandharva rite while the suitors looked on.'

statements.claim: Rukmini had already chosen Krishna, her choice known only to her and the man she had called, so Krishna came as a bridegroom answering a bride, not as a suitor entering a contest.
statements.evidence: The summons of 3.3.2 implies the prior secret choice, established in the cluster (DKS_0194 declaration among friends; DKS_0196-97 secret message). The 'his own share' phrasing of the pack verse confirms the pre-ordained match.

statements.claim: A gandharva marriage is the old rite in which a man and woman take each other by consent alone, without priest, fire or assembly.
statements.evidence: Explanatory gloss of the rite named in the source (3.3.2 'gandharva rite'); standard meaning, not a pack-cited fact.

statements.claim: The swayamvara ended without a garland being placed; Krishna claimed his destined bride openly before the whole gathering of suitors, and the competition was over before it began.
statements.evidence: 3.3.2: he 'carried off his own share by the gandharva rite while the suitors looked on' — the onlooking suitors are spectators, not competitors; 'his share / bride the gods had destined' echoes the gods' decree (1.108, DKS_0192).

statements.claim: Satya, the princess called Nagnajiti, held her svayamvara in her own kingdom, where no summons or secret message preceded Krishna's coming and the proudest kings vied for her.
statements.evidence: BhP 3.3.3: 'svayaṃvare nāgnajitīm uvāha' — he took Nagnajiti at her svayamvara; the absence of any summons contrasts with verse 2's 'samāhutā bhīṣmaka-kanyayā' (Rukmini summoned him).

statements.claim: At Satya's svayamvara Krishna met the proud kings, humbled and defeated them, and Satya went with him as his bride.
statements.evidence: BhP 3.3.3: 'kakudmino 'viddha-naso damitvā' (subduing the unbridled bull-like/proud kings); pack excerpt: 'humbling the proud kings, he won Nagnajiti at her svayamvara.'

statements.claim: Framing: Uddhava remembered this years afterward in the palace at Dwaraka, with Rukmini and Satya, the two brides of his Lord, ruling that great house beside him.
statements.evidence: Uddhava-POV framing device; the pack (two verses) does not locate the recollection. BhP 3.3's canonical setting is Uddhava's later narration, so the Dwaraka-palace vignette is connective frame rather than an asserted source fact.

DKS_0195.notes: Core content matches BhP 3.3.2-3 closely (Rukmini summoned and carried off by the gandharva rite; Satya/Nagnajiti won by humbling the kings at her svayamvara). The Uddhava-recollection frame and rite gloss are connective; the story's own tradition_note flags this as the condensed Bhagavata recall.

statements.claim: Rukmini, daughter of Bhishmaka, king of Kundina in Vidarbha, settled her own marriage by report — having heard of Krishna's beauty and virtues — before she ever set eyes on the groom.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.22: 'sopaśrutya mukundasya rūpa-vīrya-guṇa-śriyaḥ' (she heard of Mukunda's beauty, might, qualities and glory); pack excerpt: 'heard of Krishna's beauty and virtues and resolved he alone was a fitting husband'; the Vaidarbhī epithet (10.52.25) supports 'princess of Vidarbha'.

statements.claim: Her brother Rukmi had decided her future: he meant to give her to Shishupala, and the household moved toward the wedding as toward something already decided.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (BhP 10.52.14-27 rendering): 'though her brother Rukmi wished to give her to Shishupala'; 10.52.21 lists Rukmi as her foremost brother ('rukmy agrajo').

statements.claim: Word of Krishna of Dwaraka reached Kundina through travelers and brahmanas, and the more she heard the more she was convinced he alone was a fitting husband.
statements.evidence: 10.52.22 (śrutvā — by hearing) and the pack excerpt: 'heard of Krishna's beauty and virtues and resolved he alone was a fitting husband'.

statements.claim: Knowing her brother would not listen, Rukmini kept her wish from her family, found a brahmana she trusted completely, and sent him out swiftly and in secret to Dwaraka with a message for Krishna alone.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'she sent a trusted brahmana swiftly to Dwaraka'; 10.52.25-26 have her distressed (durmanā) and the brahmana reaching Dwaraka; secrecy and single addressee follow from the message account (10.52.28-42, DKS_0197) and her brother's opposed plan.

statements.claim: The brahmana took the long road from Vidarbha to Dwaraka and was admitted past the city's guards and brought to Krishna's presence.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.26: 'dvārakāṃ sa samabhyetya pratīhāraiḥ praveśitaḥ' (coming to Dwaraka he was admitted by the gatekeepers).

statements.claim: When Krishna saw the travel-worn brahmana he rose from his own seat and received him as a guest of the first rank, for he held brahmanas in the highest honor.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.27: 'dṛṣṭvā brahmaṇya-devas tam avaruhya nijāsanāt' (seeing him, the Lord devoted to brahmanas descended from his own seat) — the brahmaṇya-deva epithet grounds the 'highest honor for brahmanas' clause.

statements.claim: The court watched the welcome, the two spoke quietly together, and Rukmini's message passed out of the messenger's keeping into Krishna's.
statements.evidence: Bridge narration to the message itself (10.52.28-42), which is the subject of the following story (DKS_0197); no new factual assertion.

DKS_0196.notes: Faithful to BhP 10.52.14-27: hearing-based choice (śrutvā guṇān), the Rukmi-Shishupala plan, the trusted brahmana sent to Dwaraka, and Krishna rising for the brahmana. The 'never set eyes on the groom' framing is consistent with the pack's hearing-based account.

statements.claim: Krishna asked after the messenger before the message: whether his dharma was still approved by elders, whether as a brahmana he was content with whatever came by chance (for an unsatisfied man, even a lord of the gods, wanders from world to world), after the brahmanas of Vidarbha, and how he had crossed the difficult road.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.28-34: 'kaccid dvija-vara-śreṣṭha dharmas te vṛddha-sammataḥ'; 'asantuṣṭo 'sakṛl lokān āpnoty api sureśvaraḥ'; 'viprān sva-lābha-santuṣṭān sādhūn bhūta-suhṛttamān'; 'yatas tvam āgato durgaṃ nistīryeha'.

statements.claim: Rukmini's message opened: 'Having heard your virtues, O beauty of the three worlds, my heart has entered into you, and it is not ashamed'; your virtues entering through the ear take away the body's distress, and your form is the whole reward of a seeing eye.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.36: 'śrutvā guṇān bhuvana-sundara... tvayy acyutāviśati cittam apatrapaṃ me'; 'nirviśya karṇa-vivarair harato 'ṅga-tāpam'; 'rūpaṃ dṛśāṃ dṛśimatām akhilārtha-lābham'.

statements.claim: The message asked what wise girl of a good family would not choose him — one without equal in family, conduct, beauty, learning, youth and wealth, who delights the minds of men.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.37: 'kā... mahatī kula-śīla-rūpa-vidyā-vayo-draviṇa-dhāmabhir ātma-tulyam dhīrā patiṃ kulavatī na vṛṇīta kanyā... nara-loka-mano-'bhirāmam'.

statements.claim: 'You are the one I have chosen. I have given myself to you.'
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.38: 'tan me bhavān khalu vṛtaḥ patir aṅga jāyām / ātmārpitaś ca bhavato 'tra vibho vidhehi'.

statements.claim: 'Do not let the king of Cedi touch the hero's share — do not let Shishupala, like a jackal, seize the lion's prey.'
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.38: 'mā vīra-bhāgam abhimarśatu caidya ārād / gomāyu-van mṛga-pater balim ambujākṣa' (let not the Caidya from afar touch the hero's share, like a jackal the lion's prey, O lotus-eyed one).

statements.claim: If the Lord, worshipped with sacrifices, gifts and vows and honored in gods, brahmanas and elders, is pleased with her devotion, let him come and take her hand — not Damaghosha's son, not any other.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.39: 'pūrteṣṭa-datta-niyama-vrata-deva-vipra-gurv-arcanādibhir alaṃ bhagavān pareśaḥ / ārādhito yadi gadāgraja etya pāṇiṃ gṛhṇātu me na damaghoṣa-sutādayo 'nye'.

statements.claim: The message said 'Tomorrow they will marry me': Krishna should come to Vidarbha in secret surrounded by his warriors, crush the forces of the king of Cedi and the king of Magadha, and carry her off by the rakshasa rite as the prize of his valour.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.40: 'śvo bhāvini tvam ajitodvahane vidarbhān guptaḥ sametya pṛtanā-patibhiḥ parītaḥ / nirmathya caidya-magadhendra-balaṃ prasahya māṃ rākṣasena vidhinodvaha vīrya-śulkām'.

statements.claim: She told him how: she lived within the inner apartments, so her kinsmen could not be killed — on the day before the wedding there is a great procession of the family goddess, in which the new bride goes out to the temple of Girija.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.41: 'antaḥ-purāntara-carīm anihatya bandhūn tvām udvahe katham iti pravadāmy upāyam / pūrve-dyur asti mahatī kula-deva-yātrā yasyāṃ bahir nava-vadhūr girijām upeyāt'.

statements.claim: The message closed: if she did not obtain his grace she would give up this body, weakened by her vows, and even a hundred births would not change her choice.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.42: 'yarhy ambujākṣa na labheya bhavat-prasādaṃ jahyām asūn vrata-kṛśān śata-janmabhiḥ syāt'.

DKS_0197.notes: Rukmini's message is rendered nearly verse-by-verse from BhP 10.52.28-42 (GRETIL), including the pre-message dialogue (10.52.28-35) and the rakshasa-rite / Girija-procession plan. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Krishna heard the brahmana out and said, 'I too cannot sleep at night for her sake,' declaring he would bring her back, crushing in battle the wicked kings who stood in his way.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.2-3 ('śrī-bhagavān uvāca / tām ānayiṣya unmathya rājanyāpasadān mṛdhe') and pack excerpt: 'Krishna said "I too cannot sleep at night for her"'.

statements.claim: No council was called and no army mustered; the chariot was made ready with the four horses Shaibya, Sugriva, Meghapushpa and Balahaka, Krishna seated the brahmana beside him, and Daruka his charioteer took the reins.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.4-5: 'sa cāśvaiḥ śaibya-sugrīva-meghapuṣpa-balāhakaiḥ... āruhya syandanaṃ śaurir dvijam āropya'; Daruka is named among the pack's own character list for this event and is Krishna's standing charioteer.

statements.claim: Krishna crossed the Dwaraka-Kundina road in a single night, and by sunrise he was within the borders of Vidarbha.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (BhP 10.53.1-20 rendering): 'he set out at once and reached Vidarbha in a single night'.

statements.claim: In Kundina, Bhishmaka — led by love for his son — had the streets swept and sprinkled, the roads and crossings cleaned, and garlands, perfumes and bright garments readied; he worshipped the ancestors, gods and brahmanas according to the rites; the bride was bathed and adorned with the auspicious ceremonies, foremost brahmanas chanted Sama, Rig and Yajur mantras over her for protection, and gifts of gold, silver, garments and sesame mixed with jaggery were distributed.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.6-12 near-verbatim: 'rājā sa kuṇḍina-patiḥ putra-sneha-vaśānugaḥ'; 'puraṃ sammṛṣṭa-saṃsikta-mārga-rathyā-catuṣpatham'; 'pitṝn devān samabhyarcya viprāṃś ca vidhi-vat'; 'su-snātāṃ... kṛta-kautuka-maṅgalām'; 'cakruḥ sāma-rg-yajur-mantrair vadhvā rakṣāṃ dvijottamāḥ'; 'hiraṇya-rūpya vāsāṃsi tilāṃś ca guḍa-miśritān'.

statements.claim: Damaghosha, the king of Cedi, came for his son with herds of rutting elephants and chariots garlanded with gold, and the lord of Vidarbha went out to receive him with honor.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.13-15: 'cedi-patī rājā damaghoṣaḥ sutāya vai / mada-cyudbhir gajānīkaiḥ syandanair hema-mālibhiḥ / taṃ vai vidarbhādhipatiḥ samabhyetyābhipūjya ca'.

statements.claim: With Damaghosha came Shalva, Jarasandha of Magadha, Dantavakra and Viduratha — kings who hated Krishna and Balarama and were determined to give the bride to the prince of Cedi, resolving 'If Krishna comes, we will fight him together.'
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.16-18: 'tatra śālvo jarāsandho dantavakro vidūrathaḥ / kṛṣṇa-rāma-dviṣo yattāḥ kanyāṃ caidyāya sādhitum / yotsyāmaḥ saṃhatās tena iti niścita-mānasāḥ'. Jarasandha's Magadha kingship is established corpus continuity (DKS_0189).

statements.claim: Word of the muster reached Balarama, who — flooded with love for his brother — gathered a great force and set out after him.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.19-20: 'śrutvaitad bhagavān rāmo vipakṣīya nṛpodyamam / balena mahatā sārdhaṃ bhrātṛ-sneha-pariplutaḥ'.

statements.claim: Rukmini, in the inner apartments, counted the hours toward a wedding she had never wanted, hoping the man she had written to had heard her message in time.
statements.evidence: Core is supported by 10.53.21-22 ('bhīṣma-kanyā... kāṅkṣanty āgamanaṃ hareḥ'; 'tri-yāmāntarita udvāho me'); the emotional gloss is connective narration.

DKS_0198.notes: Scene-by-scene match with BhP 10.53.1-20: Krishna's sleepless resolve, the four named horses, the overnight journey, Kundina's wedding preparations, Damaghosha's arrival, the hostile kings' pact, and Balarama's pursuit. Daruka is in the pack's character list and is Krishna's standing charioteer.

statements.claim: With a single night left before her wedding and Krishna not yet arrived, Rukmini's mind, stolen by Govinda, would not rest: 'Will the faultless one find something blameworthy in me? The creator is not favorable to me, nor Maheshvara' — and tears came as she prayed that Krishna alone might be her husband.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.21-25: 'kāṅkṣanty āgamanaṃ hareḥ'; 'tri-yāmāntarita udvāho me 'lpa-rādhasaḥ'; 'api mayy anavadyātmā dṛṣṭvā kiñcij jugupsitam'; 'durbhagāyā na me dhātā nānukūlo maheśvaraḥ'; 'evaṃ cintayatī bālā govinda-hṛta-mānasā'.

statements.claim: The same brahmana she had sent to Dwaraka returned, sent back now by Krishna himself, with a bright face and news that lifted her heart: the darling of the Yadus had reached Vidarbha.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.27-29: 'atha kṛṣṇa-vinirdiṣṭaḥ sa eva dvija-sattamaḥ'; 'sā taṃ prahṛṣṭa-vadanam...'; 'tasyā āvedayat prāptaṃ śaśaṃsa yadu-nandanam'.

statements.claim: Bhishmaka, hearing Krishna had arrived among the gathered kings, offered the madhuparka — the honeyed welcome — with fresh garments and had a splendid residence made ready for him.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.31-33: 'madhu-parkam upānīya vāsāṃsi virajāṃsi saḥ / tayor niveśanaṃ śrīmad upākalpya mahā-matiḥ'. The Sanskrit dual (tayor) reflects both arrivals (Krishna and Balarama, who follows per 10.53.19-20 / DKS_0198); the story's singular is compression, not contradiction.

statements.claim: The townspeople of Vidarbha said openly: 'Rukmini deserves to be his wife, and no other. What good deed did we do, that the maker of the three worlds should be pleased with us?' — and love bound the whole city.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.35-38 near-verbatim: 'kṛṣṇam āgatam ākarṇya vidarbha-pura-vāsinaḥ / asyaiva bhāryā bhavituṃ rukmiṇy arhati nāparā / kiñcit su-caritaṃ yan nas tena tuṣṭas tri-loka-kṛt / evaṃ prema-kalā-baddhā vadanti sma puraukasaḥ'.

statements.claim: On the day of the family goddess's procession — the day her message had pointed to — Rukmini, wrapped in a vow of silence, went out on foot with her mothers and companions to see the lotus-petal feet of Bhavani, while thousands of women followed with offerings and singers and musicians played.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.39-42: 'padbhyāṃ viniryayau draṣṭuṃ bhavānyāḥ pāda-pallavam / yata-vāṅ mātṛbhiḥ sārdhaṃ sakhībhiḥ parivāritā / nānopahāra balibhir vāramukhyāḥ sahasraśaḥ / gāyantyaś ca stuvantaś ca gāyakā vādya-vādakāḥ'.

statements.claim: At the shrine Rukmini washed her hands and feet; the elderly brahmana women versed in the rites worshipped the goddess with water, perfume, unbroken rice, incense, fresh garments, garlands and ornaments, joined by the married women of the household, who then gave Rukmini the remainder of the offerings and pronounced blessings over her.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.43-48: 'āsādya devī-sadanaṃ dhauta-pāda-karāmbujā'; 'pravayaso... vidhi-jñā vipra-yoṣitaḥ'; 'adbhir gandhākṣatair dhūpair vāsaḥ-sraṅ-mālya bhūṣaṇaiḥ'; 'vipra-striyaḥ patimatīs tathā taiḥ samapūjayat'; 'tasyai striyas tāḥ pradaduḥ śeṣāṃ yuyujur āśiṣaḥ'.

statements.claim: Bowing before the goddess, Rukmini prayed the one prayer she had carried in her heart: may Krishna, the Lord, alone become my husband — 'bless this.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (BhP 10.53.20-52): 'she bowed: May Krishna, the Lord, alone become my husband; bless this.'

statements.claim: She rose, laid aside her vow of silence, and came out of Ambika's temple; the assembled heroes who saw her — slim-waisted, her face bright with earrings, her smile pure, her lips like bimba fruit, her teeth like jasmine buds — stood struck with love.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.49-52 near-verbatim: 'muni-vratam atha tyaktvā niścakrāmāmbikā-gṛhāt / tāṃ deva-māyām iva... su-madhyamāṃ kuṇḍala-maṇḍitānanām / śuci-smitāṃ bimba-phalādhara-dyuti-śoṇāyamāna-dvija-kunda-kuḍmalām / vilokya vīrā mumuhuḥ samāgatā yaśasvinas tat-kṛta-hṛc-chayārditāḥ'.

statements.claim: 'Only one man in all that crowd did not stare. Krishna had come, as she had asked him to' — and the procession that was to deliver her to Shishupala would deliver her to Krishna instead.
statements.evidence: Krishna's presence at the abduction scene is the immediate sequel of this event (10.54; DKS_0200 next in chain), and the 'assembled heroes' of v.52 set the scene; the 'only one man did not stare' beat is connective colour.

DKS_0199.notes: Very close rendering of BhP 10.53.20-52: Rukmini's one-night anxiety, the messenger's return, Bhishmaka's madhuparka, the townsfolk's words, the Bhavani/Ambika procession and worship, her prayer, and the heroes' enchantment. Ambika/Bhavani/Girija are used interchangeably as in the source.

statements.claim: Rukmi had sworn before his father Bhishmaka and before all the assembled kings that he would not re-enter Kundina until he had slain Krishna and brought his sister back.
statements.evidence: HV 1.116: 'promised before Bhishmaka saying I shall not return to the city of Kundina without slaying Krishna and bringing back Rukshmini'; BP 10.54.17-18: vow made 'in the hearing of all kings' (śṛṇvatāṁ sarva-bhūbhujām).

statements.claim: The whole assembly of svayamvara kings took the road after Krishna — allies of Jarasandha, kings of the Deccan, princes of every house that had hoped to claim the princess of Vidarbha.
statements.evidence: BP 10.54.1-8: Krishna's host routed the pursuing kings; HV 1.116: Deccan kings and other mighty car-warriors followed Rukmi in pursuit, and Balarama's Vrishnis 'vanquished Jarāsandha and others'.

statements.claim: Shishupala of Chedi rode up burning with rage, and Krishna told him to put aside his grief; Shishupala answered 'I have been defeated by you seventeen times in battle, and I have never grieved, and never rejoiced.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.54.9-13: śiśupālaṁ samabhyetya hṛta-dāram ivāturam... 'śaureḥ sapta-daśāhaṁ vai saṁyugāni parājitaḥ / tathāpy ahaṁ na śocāmi na prahṛṣyāmi karhicit'.

statements.claim: Krishna shattered every weapon Rukmi raised — the bow, mace, spear, javelin and shield — and wrecked his chariot, so Rukmi leapt down sword in hand.
statements.evidence: BP 10.54.27-30: Acyuta cut the bow, then parigha, paṭṭiśa, śūla, carma-asi, śakti and tomara, and Rukmi leapt from the chariot sword in hand (khaḍga-pāṇir jighāṁsayā); HV 1.116: Krishna 'cut off his bow and car' and Rukmi jumped down with sword and shield.

statements.claim: Rukmini threw herself at Krishna's feet, begging for her brother's life: 'He is my only brother... Give me my brother in charity.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.54.31: dṛṣṭvā bhrātṛ-vadhodyogaṁ rukmiṇī bhaya-vihvalā; HV 1.116: 'Beholding her brother lying down motionless on earth, Rukshmini, for his life, fell at Vishnu's feet'; VP 5.26: 'He is my only brother... give me my brother in charity.'

statements.claim: Krishna spared Rukmi but bound him, shaved his head and beard, and disfigured him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.54.34: 'cailena baddhvā tam asādhu-kārīṇaṁ sa-śmaśru-keśaṁ pravapan vyarūpayat' — binding the wicked one, shaving beard and hair, he disfigured him.

statements.claim: Krishna lifted Rukmini up, held and comforted her, and promised her brother his life and safety; Rukmi lay senseless and was carried off the field by his own men.
statements.evidence: HV 1.116: Keshava 'took up her, embraced and consoled her. And then promising safety to Rukshmi he set out'; Rukmi 'fell down unconscious'; Shrutarva 'placed Rukshmi on his own car and took him to his own city'.

statements.claim: Rukmi could not go home; he built a new city in Vidarbha named Bhojakata and ruled the southern districts, while Bhishmaka remained in Kundina.
statements.evidence: HV 1.116: 'seeing his promise broken the haughty and sensitive Rukshmi did not like to enter into the city of Kundina. For his residence he built another city in the province of Bidharbha... under the name of Bhojakata... govern the southern districts... Bhishmaka lived in the city of Kundina.'

statements.claim: Balarama and the Vrishni army, having scattered Jarasandha and the rest, turned for Dwaraka.
statements.evidence: HV 1.116: 'having vanquished Jarāsandha and others, the Vrishnis, headed by Rāma, gladly set out for Dwarka.'

DKS_0201.notes: All battle claims map to BP 10.54.1-35 (primary, conf 5) with HV 1.116/VP 5.26 corroboration. Minor variant: HV sets the duel near the Narmada with Rukmi accompanied by an army, while the story follows BP's 'alone' pursuit — flagged in the pack's own variant_notes. Poetic color (dust-wall, 'learned to lose', scattered banners) is connective narration.

statements.claim: Rukmi never returned to Kundina; he built a new capital, Bhojakata, in Vidarbha and ruled the southern districts, while Bhishmaka stayed in Kundina.
statements.evidence: HV 1.116 (passage in pack): 'did not like to enter into the city of Kundina... built another city in the province of Bidharbha... under the name of Bhojakata... govern the southern districts'; 'Bhishmaka lived in the city of Kundina'.

statements.claim: The Yadava host came home to Dwaraka, Balarama at its head after settling with Jarasandha and the pursuing kings.
statements.evidence: HV 1.116: 'having vanquished Jarāsandha and others, the Vrishnis, headed by Rāma, gladly set out for Dwarka.'

statements.claim: Krishna wed Rukmini in due form with the full rites, and she became his queen.
statements.evidence: BP 10.54.35-59 rendering: 'Krishna brought Rukmini to Dvaraka and wed her with full rites'; HV 1.116: 'the powerful Keshavā duly espoused Rukshmini'; VP 5.26: 'married Rukminí in due form, having first made her his own by the Rákshasa ritual'.

statements.claim: Dwaraka gave itself to festival: every house celebrated; streets sprinkled with water; doorways hung with mango-leaf garlands, flowers, gems and toranas; auspicious pots at thresholds; incense and lamps; Indra's banners over the gates; conches, drums and singing.
statements.evidence: BP 10.54.53-56: 'mahotsavo nṝṇāṁ yadu-puryāṁ gṛhe gṛhe', 'pramṛṣṭa-maṇi-kuṇḍalāḥ', 'uttambhitendra-ketubhir vicitra-mālyāmbara-ratna-toraṇaiḥ', 'āpūrṇa-kumbhāguru-dhūpa-dīpakaiḥ', 'sikta-mārgāḥ' — festival in every house, jeweled earrings, Indra banners, garlands/gems/toranas at each gate, filled pots, incense and lamps, sprinkled roads.

statements.claim: Guests came from the Kuru, Srijaya and Kaikeya lands, from Vidarbha and the Yadu and Kunti houses.
statements.evidence: BP 10.54.57: 'kuru-sṛñjaya-kaikeya-vidarbha-yadu-kuntayaḥ'.

statements.claim: The story of Rukmini's abduction was sung everywhere in Dwaraka, and great joy filled the city.
statements.evidence: BP 10.54.58-59: 'rukmiṇyā haraṇaṁ śrutvā gīyamānaṁ tatas tataḥ', 'dvārakāyām abhūd rājan mahā-modaḥ puraukasām'.

statements.claim: The Vishnu Purana says Rukmini bore Krishna a son, Pradyumna, a portion of the god of love, who grew into one of the Yadus' greatest warriors; the Harivamsha names her Krishna's first wife.
statements.evidence: VP 5.26 excerpt: 'She bore him the gallant Pradyumna, a portion of the deity of love'; HV 1.116: Rukmini 'was the first wife of Krishna', mother of Pradyumna and ten warrior sons (dreadful in battle, masters of weapons).

statements.claim: Rukmini, who had chosen him before she ever saw him, had staked everything on him.
statements.evidence: Recap of the corpus-chain abduction story (DKS_0200: Rukmini chose Krishna by report and sent a brahmin before meeting him); the emotional framing ('staked everything') is narrative, not a discrete sourceable fact in 10.54.35-59.

DKS_0202.notes: The festival passage is almost verbatim-supported by BP 10.54.53-56 (conf 5). 'Before the fire and the witnesses of the Yadu court' is standard-rite connective detail consistent with 'wed her with full rites'. The closing 'Rukmi's exile is his own work' reading is the story's moral gloss, not a factual claim.

statements.claim: Krishna, guest at Indraprastha, went hunting with Arjuna in the great forest, riding Arjuna's monkey-bannered chariot.
statements.evidence: BP 10.58.12-13: 'ekadā ratham āruhya vijayo vānara-dhvajam / sākaṁ kṛṣṇena sannaddho vihartuṁ vipinaṁ mahat'; 10.58.25-26 (Maya, rescued from the fire, giving the assembly hall) anchors the Indraprastha setting.

statements.claim: Tigers, wild boars, buffaloes and antelope fell to their arrows, and servants carried the kill to the king for the coming festival day.
statements.evidence: BP 10.58.14-15: 'tatrāvidhyac charair vyāghrān śūkarān mahiṣān rurūn / tān ninyuḥ kiṅkarā rājñe medhyān parvaṇy upāgate'.

statements.claim: The two friends bathed in and drank the clear water of the Yamuna and rested on its bank, where they saw a maiden.
statements.evidence: BP 10.58.16-17: 'tatropaspṛśya viśadaṁ pītvā vāri mahā-rathau / tām āsādya varārohāṁ su-dvijāṁ rucirānanām'.

statements.claim: Krishna sent Arjuna to ask the maiden her name, her family, and what she hoped for.
statements.evidence: BP 10.58.18: 'kā tvaṁ kasyāsi su-śroṇi kuto vā kiṁ cikīrṣasi'; pack rendering: 'Arjuna, sent by Krishna, asked the beautiful maiden her name'.

statements.claim: 'I am Kalindi,' she said, 'daughter of the Sun, and I live in the waters of the Yamuna. I will take no husband but him in whom all beauty dwells.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.58.20-21: 'nānyaṁ patiṁ vṛṇe vīra tam ṛte śrī-niketanam / kālindīti samākhyātā vasāmi yamunā-jale'; pack excerpt confirms she is daughter of Surya doing penance to win Vishnu as husband.

statements.claim: Her penance and waiting in the river had been for Vishnu himself — for Krishna.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (10.58.12-28): 'she said I am Kalindi, daughter of Surya, doing penance to win Vishnu as husband'.

statements.claim: Krishna took her onto his chariot and in time married her at an auspicious hour when season and stars were favorable.
statements.evidence: BP 10.58.27-28: 'sa tena samanujñātaḥ suhṛdbhiś cānumoditaḥ / athopayeme kālindīṁ su-puṇya-rtv-ṛkṣa ūrjite' — married at an auspicious season and constellation; pack rendering: 'Krishna took her on his chariot and later wed her at an auspicious time'.

statements.claim: The marriage was quiet and complete — no armies, no svayamvara, no chase, no envoys.
statements.evidence: Negative framing consistent with the brief BP account (meeting by the water, question, vow, later wedding at an auspicious time); the enumeration of what did NOT happen is connective narration.

DKS_0203.notes: Fully grounded in BP 10.58.12-28 (conf 5). The Indraprastha framing matches the passage's own Maya/assembly-hall context (vv. 25-26). 'Years of waiting', 'stillness of someone who had been waiting' are atmosphere.

statements.claim: In Avanti, the princes Vinda and Anuvinda were long devoted to Duryodhana, and their sister Mitravinda — daughter of Krishna's own aunt — was to be given in svayamvara.
statements.evidence: BP 10.58.29-30: 'vindyānuvindyāv āvantyau duryodhana-vaśānugau / rājādhidevyās tanayāṁ mitravindāṁ pitṛ-ṣvasuḥ'; index summary: Krishna 'carries off Mitravinda of Avanti from her svayamvara'.

statements.claim: Before the assembled kings could decide anything, Krishna carried Mitravinda off forcibly and set her in his chariot.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (BP 10.58.29-55, conf 5): 'Krishna forcibly carried off Mitravinda, the princess of Avanti, before the assembled kings'.

statements.claim: In Kosala, King Nagnajit, a righteous king, had a daughter Satya whom no man could win without subduing seven fierce, untamable bulls that had broken every suitor.
statements.evidence: BP 10.58.31-32, 42: 'nagnajin nāma kauśalya āsīd rājāti-dhārmikaḥ / na tāṁ śekur nṛpā voḍhum ajitvā sapta-go-vṛṣān'; 'saptaite go-vṛṣā vīra durdāntā duravagrahāḥ'.

statements.claim: Krishna went to Kosala; Nagnajit rose from his seat and received him with honor, and Satya, seeing him, chose him in her heart.
statements.evidence: BP 10.58.33-35: 'tāṁ śrutvā vṛṣa-jil-labhyāṁ bhagavān sātvatāṁ patiḥ / sa kośala-patiḥ prītaḥ pratyutthānāsanādibhiḥ'; 'varaṁ vilokyābhimataṁ samāgataṁ narendra-kanyā cakame ramā-patim'.

statements.claim: Nagnajit said the agreement had been made before all the world: 'These seven bulls are fierce, and beyond control. Subdue them, and my daughter is yours.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.58.41-43: 'kintv asmābhiḥ kṛtaḥ pūrvaṁ samayaḥ... saptaite go-vṛṣā vīra durdāntā duravagrahāḥ / yad ime nigṛhītāḥ syus tvayaiva yadu-nandana'.

statements.claim: Krishna bound up his garment and seemed to be everywhere at once, as if seven Krishnas stood in the pen; he roped all seven bulls, their pride broken.
statements.evidence: BP 10.58.44-45: 'baddhvā parikaraṁ prabhuḥ / baddhvā tān dāmabhiḥ śaurir bhagna-darpān hataujasaḥ'; pack excerpt: 'he multiplied himself sevenfold and with ease subdued seven untamable bulls'.

statements.claim: The amazed king of Kosala gave Krishna his daughter; queens rejoiced, conches and kettledrums sounded, and brahmin blessings rose.
statements.evidence: BP 10.58.46-48: 'tataḥ prītaḥ sutāṁ rājā dadau kṛṣṇāya vismitaḥ / rāja-patnyaś ca duhituḥ kṛṣṇaṁ labdhvā priyaṁ patim / śaṅkha-bhery-ānakā nedur gīta-vādya-dvijāśiṣaḥ'.

statements.claim: Krishna gave in return ten thousand cows, nine thousand elephants and chariots in plenty, placed Satya on his chariot, and set out for Dwaraka with a great army.
statements.evidence: BP 10.58.49-51: 'daśa-dhenu-sahasrāṇi pāribarham adād vibhuḥ / nava-nāga-sahasrāṇi nāgāc chata-guṇān rathān / dampatī ratham āropya mahatyā senayā vṛtau'.

statements.claim: The losing kings raised a cry and loosed volleys of arrows at the chariot, and Arjuna, riding with Krishna, turned every shaft aside.
statements.evidence: BP 10.58.52-53: 'śrutvaitad rurudhur bhūpā nayantaṁ pathi kanyakām / tān asyataḥ śara-vrātān bandhu-priya-kṛd arjunaḥ'.

statements.claim: Krishna came home to Dwaraka with two new brides: Mitravinda, carried off from Avanti, and Satya, won in the bull-pen of Kosala.
statements.evidence: Index summary and pack excerpt (BP 10.58.29-55): both episodes narrated as one journey, per the pack's variant note that the Bhagavata presents them together.

DKS_0204.notes: Fully grounded in BP 10.58.29-55 (conf 5). The 'shouting after a departing chariot' and 'Avanti learned its gates were no shield' are connective color. Story's framing of one journey matches the BP sequence and the pack's variant note.

statements.claim: In the inner chamber, Krishna lay on a couch white as milk foam, and Rukmini fanned him with a jewel-handled fan she had taken from a friend's hand; the air carried the scent of parijata and bees moved through mallika garlands.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.3-6: 'mallikā-dāmabhiḥ puṣpair dvirepha-kula-nādite / pārijāta-vanāmoda-vāyunā... payaḥ-phena-nibhe śubhre paryaṅke... vāla-vyajanam ādāya ratna-daṇḍaṁ sakhī-karāt'.

statements.claim: Krishna said great kings had sought her — Shishupala, Shalva, Jarasandha, Dantavakra — and asked whom she had chosen: a man with nothing.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.10-17: 'tān prāptān arthino hitvā caidyādīn smara-durmadān... caidya-śālva-jarāsandha-dantavakrādayo nṛpāḥ'; 'niṣkiñcanā vayaṁ śaśvan niṣkiñcana-jana-priyāḥ'.

statements.claim: He said the penniless were the only people he could call his own, and he kept company with folk who walked hidden roads the world never saw.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.12-13: 'aspaṣṭa-vartmanāṁ puṁsām aloka-patham īyuṣām / niṣkiñcanā vayaṁ śaśvan niṣkiñcana-jana-priyāḥ'.

statements.claim: He said he was not the sort to run after wives, sons and household splendor, and urged her to choose a worthy kshatriya, a bull among kings.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.16, 19: 'athātmano 'nurūpaṁ vai bhajasva kṣatriyarṣabham'; 'udāsīnā vayaṁ nūnaṁ na stry-apatyārtha-kāmukāḥ'.

statements.claim: From the lips of the lord of the three worlds Rukmini had never heard an unkind word before that day; she heard this one as a sentence.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.21: 'iti trilokeśa-pates tadātmanas priyasya devy aśruta-pūrvam apriyam' — the queen heard from the lord of the three worlds an unkindness never heard before.

statements.claim: Her eyes filled with tears dark with collyrium, she traced the floor with her toe, the jeweled fan slipped from her hand, and she fainted outright, her hair scattering like a plantain tree struck by wind.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.22-23: 'padā su-jātena nakhāruṇa-śrīyā bhuvaṁ likhanty aśrubhir añjanāsitaiḥ... hastāc chlathad-valayato vyajanaṁ papāta... rambheva vāyu-vihato pravikīrya keśān' — writing on the ground with tears of collyrium, the fan falling, fainting like a plantain tree struck by wind with hair scattered.

statements.claim: Krishna rose from the couch, lifted her in his arms, wiped the tears from her eyes and began to comfort her, the game over for him in that instant.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.24-27: 'paryaṅkād avaruhyāśu tām utthāpya catur-bhujaḥ / pramṛjyāśru-kale netre stanau copahatau śucā / sāntvayām āsa sāntva-jñaḥ kṛpayā kṛpaṇāṁ prabhuḥ'.

statements.claim: He meant it as play — a jest, a game of teasing — and his smile was real.
statements.evidence: The jest is confirmed as playful in the paired episode (BP 10.60.28-30, 'I spoke in jest'); the characterization of his inward intent and 'real smile' is interpretive connective narration.

statements.claim: Rukmini had chosen him across the ruin of her own life — sending him word against her brother's wishes, climbing into his chariot at her svayamvara while the kings looked on — and every king he named had been gathered in that hall.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.10: the named kings 'came as suitors' (prāptān arthino... caidyādīn); her svayamvara choice and brother's opposition are the corpus-chain events (DKS_0199-0200, BP 10.52-53), and Rukmini's own speech in the paired episode confirms the messenger plot (BP 10.60.54-56).

DKS_0205.notes: Nearly every sensory and emotional beat maps directly to BP 10.60.1-27 (conf 5), including the plantain-tree simile, collyrium tears, and fan falling from her hand. The 'jest wrapped in love' analysis is narrative commentary, not a factual claim.

statements.claim: Waking in Krishna's arms, she heard him say he had spoken in jest — he had wanted to see her face trembling between love and anger, the supreme gain of a householder, which no treasure could equal.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.29-30: 'mukhaṁ ca prema-saṁrambha-sphuritādharam īkṣitum / ayaṁ hi paramo lābho gṛheṣu gṛha-medhinām'; pack excerpt: Krishna said 'I spoke in jest to hear your words'.

statements.claim: Rukmini named kings — Anga and Vainya, Jayanta, Nahusha and Gaya — who held the whole earth and, wanting only him, laid their kingdoms down and walked into the forest.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.40: 'yad-vāñchayā nṛpa-śikhāmaṇayo 'ṅga-vainya-jāyanta-nāhuṣa-gayādaya aikya-patyam / rājyaṁ visṛjya viviśur vanam ambujākṣa'.

statements.claim: The guardians of the worlds carried tribute to his feet, and sages who had laid aside punishment worshipped him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.36, 38: 'yasmai baliṁ bali-bhujo 'pi haranty ajādyāḥ'; 'tvaṁ nyasta-daṇḍa-munibhir gaditānubhāva'.

statements.claim: At her svayamvara his bow had spoken once and the kings scattered like animals before a lion; he carried her off the way a lion carries off its share.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.39: 'bhūpān vidrāvya śārṅga-ninadena jahartha māṁ tvam / siṁho yathā sva-balim īśa paśūn'.

statements.claim: Having breathed the fragrance of his lotus feet — the fragrance that releases the sorrowful — no woman would choose any other refuge.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.41: 'kānyaṁ śrayeta tava pāda-saroja-gandham āghrāya san-mukharitaṁ janatāpavargam'.

statements.claim: She would rather be a servant in the house of even one of his devotees than any queen; a woman who does not love his feet is a living corpse, skin and bone dressed in finery.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.43-44: kings become servants in the houses where his stories are sung; 'jīvac-chavaṁ bhajati kānta-matir vimūḍhā yā te padābja-makarandam ajighratī strī' — a woman not savoring his lotus-feet honey is a living corpse; and her love should stand 'in this world and the next' (10.60.45).

statements.claim: She did not hold his words false: a wanton's heart runs after every new thing, but hers, once given, did not wander.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.46-47: 'naivālīkam ahaṁ manye vacas te madhusūdana / vyūḍhāyāś cāpi puṁścalyā mano 'bhyeti navaṁ navam'.
