statements.claim: Krishna praised her faithfulness: at her own wedding she had ignored the gathered kings and sent a brahmin to him in secret; she had never complained of her brother's enmity for fear of wounding him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.54-55: 'sva-vivāha-kāle prāptān nṛpān na vigaṇayya raho-haro me prasthāpito dvijaḥ'; 'bhrātur virūpa-karaṇaṁ yudhi nirjitasya... duḥkhaṁ samuttham asaho 'smad-ayoga-bhītyā naivābravīḥ kim api'.

statements.claim: Those who seek him only for the gifts of marriage are poor in fortune even when rich; her devotion was of the kind that frees a soul from the world.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.52-53: 'māṁ prāpya māniny apavarga-sampadaṁ vāñchanti ye sampada eva tat-patim / te manda-bhāgā niraye 'pi ye nṛṇām'; 'mayi tvayā kṛtānuvṛttir bhava-mocanī'.

statements.claim: As Krishna lived with Rukmini, so he dwelt in the homes of his other wives — the Lord of the universe, in each house simply a husband at home.
statements.evidence: BP 10.60.58: 'tathānyāsām api vibhur gṛheṣu gṛhavān iva'.

DKS_0206.notes: Fully grounded in BP 10.60.28-58 (conf 5); Krishna's reference to Rukmi's death 'at the dice-gathering' (10.60.55) is a source-internal chronology note, not an error in this story. The closing peace imagery is connective.

statements.claim: The wedding of Aniruddha, Krishna's grandson, to Rukmi's granddaughter was held in peace in Rukmi's city of Bhojakata, Rukmi having swallowed his old enmity with Krishna.
statements.evidence: HV 1.118: Aniruddha, son of Pradyumna (Keshava's son), wed Rukshmavati, Rukmi's granddaughter, celebrated with great festivity; 'Rukshmi used always to show rivalry with Krishna; still... he cast off his enmity'.

statements.claim: After the ceremony, the Kalinga king and the gathered kings — the king of Ashmaka, Rukmi's son Shrutarva, Chanura, Kratha, Anshuman, Jayatsena and Deccan princes — urged Rukmi, an expert at dice, to play against Balarama, who loved the game though he played it like a cowherd.
statements.evidence: HV 1.118: 'the liberal king of Ashmaka, Venudāri, Rukshma's son Shrutarvā, Chānura, Krātha, Angshuman, the highly powerful king of Kalinga, Jayatsena... chiefs of Deccan spoke secretly to Rukshmi: You are an expert in dice...'; BP 10.61.26-27: 'kāliṅga-pramukhā nṛpāḥ... anakṣa-jño hy ayaṁ rājann api tad-vyasanaṁ mahat'.

statements.claim: The hall had golden pillars, a flower-strewn floor sprinkled with sandal water, and golden seats.
statements.evidence: HV 1.118: 'entered into a beautiful hall with golden pillars and its floor covered with flowers. And it was sprinkled with sandal water... sat upon golden seats.'

statements.claim: Rama joined gladly, saying he was only sporting; the wagers climbed from a hundred coins to a thousand to ten thousand, until Rukmi set a stake of a hundred thousand and Rama matched it and lost, his anger rising like the sea at high tide.
statements.evidence: HV 1.118: Rāma gladly said 'See I am sporting'; betted from ten to a thousand gold coins and was repeatedly defeated. BP 10.61.28-30: 'śataṁ sahasram ayutaṁ rāmas tatrādade paṇam / tato lakṣaṁ rukmy agṛhṇād glahaṁ tatrājayad balaḥ / manyunā kṣubhitaḥ śrīmān samudra iva parvaṇi'.

statements.claim: Mastering his wrath, Rama calmly offered one final wager of everything on a single throw; this time, though Rukmi cheated, Rama won — the game was fair.
statements.evidence: BP 10.61.31: 'taṁ cāpi jitavān rāmo dharmeṇa chalam āśritaḥ' — Rama won that too by righteousness though (Rukmi) resorted to fraud; HV 1.118: 'although a master of anger... controlling his passions, calmly said: My next bet is one hundred koti' and Rukshmi was 'rightly defeated by Rāma'.

statements.claim: A voice from the sky declared the stake had been won by Balarama and by Balarama alone.
statements.evidence: BP 10.61.32: 'tadābravīn nabho-vāṇī balenaiva jito glahaḥ'; VP 5.28 (pack excerpt note) and pack rendering confirm the heavenly voice.

statements.claim: Rukmi, urged on by the kings, refused to hear it and jeered: 'Cowherds who live in the forest know nothing of dice.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.61.33-34: 'tām anādṛtya vaidarbho duṣṭa-rājanya-coditaḥ / naivākṣa-kovidā yūyaṁ gopālā vana-gocarāḥ'.

statements.claim: The Kalinga king laughed loudest, showing every tooth; Balarama seized him, dashed him to the floor and struck the teeth out of his head.
statements.evidence: HV 1.118: 'Hearing it the king of Kalinga, delightedly and showing his teeth, laughed aloud'; 'he struck down the teeth of the Kalinga king'; BP 10.61.36: 'kaliṅga-rājaṁ tarasā gṛhītvā daśame pade'.

statements.claim: The kings who had mocked him he broke where they stood — arms, thighs, skulls — until the flower-strewn hall ran red.
statements.evidence: BP 10.61.37: 'anye nirbhinna-bāhūru-śiraso rudhirokṣitāḥ' — others with broken arms, thighs and heads, drenched in blood.

statements.claim: Rukmi he struck down dead with his iron club; Krishna said nothing, good or ill, because the dead man was Rukmini's brother.
statements.evidence: BP 10.61.38: 'nihate rukmiṇi śyāle nābravīt sādhv asādhu vā'; pack rendering: 'Balarama struck him down with his club, and Krishna said nothing, fearing to wound Rukmini'; weapon variant (club vs dice-board) noted in pack variant_notes (HV/VP).

statements.claim: The wedding party placed Aniruddha and his bride in the finest chariot and left for Dwaraka that night.
statements.evidence: BP 10.61.39: 'tato 'niruddhaṁ saha sūryayā varaṁ rathaṁ samāropya yayuḥ kuśasthalīm' — placing Aniruddha with his bride on a fine chariot, they went to Kusasthali (Dwaraka).

DKS_0207.notes: Fully grounded in BP 10.61.26-39 (conf 5) with HV 1.118 corroboration. 'Same night' is connective timing (BP does not specify). Story's earlier wager ladder follows BP (100/1000/10000, then a lakh); HV uses different figures (10→1000, then a koti) — a source-number variant the pack itself preserves, not an error.

statements.claim: Years afterward, when Draupadi asked Krishna's queens how each had come to marry him, Lakshmana answered with a story about a fish.
statements.evidence: BP 10.83.16-38 (pack): 'Asked by Draupadi how Krishna married them, Lakshmana recounts that her father arranged a svayamvara with a fish target'; 10.83.17 'śrī-lakṣmaṇovāca'.

statements.claim: On the way, Krishna had married Bhadra, daughter of his aunt Srutakirti, given to him by her brothers.
statements.evidence: BP 10.58.55: 'śrutakīrteḥ sutāṁ bhadrāṁ upayeme pitṛ-ṣvasuḥ'; pack excerpt: 'Krishna wed Bhadra, daughter of his aunt Srutakirti, given by her brothers'.

statements.claim: In Madra, the king proclaimed a svayamvara for his daughter Lakshmana with a fish target that no archer could see directly, only its reflection in the water below; the king who strung the bow and pierced the fish would win her.
statements.evidence: BP 10.83.17-18, 23: 'matsyaḥ pārthepsayā kṛtaḥ'; 'matsyābhāsaṁ jale vīkṣya jñātvā ca tad-avasthitim' — the fish's semblance seen in the water; 10.58.56: Lakshmana, daughter of the king of Madra.

statements.claim: The kings of the earth came; some could not string the bow at all, and the kings of Magadha, Ambashta and Cedi, the strongest, strung it but every arrow they loosed at the reflection missed.
statements.evidence: BP 10.83.21-23: 'ādāya vyasṛjan kecit sajyaṁ kartum anīśvarāḥ / sajyaṁ kṛtvāpare vīrā māgadhāmbaṣṭha-cedipāḥ / matsyābhāsaṁ jale vīkṣya jñātvā ca tad-avasthitim'.

statements.claim: Krishna took up the bow, which bent in his hands, glanced once at the fish in the water, and with a single arrow brought the fish down; celestial drums and shouts of victory sounded from the sky and earth.
statements.evidence: BP 10.83.24-26: 'rājanyeṣu nivṛtteṣu bhagna-māneṣu māniṣu / tasmin sandhāya viśikhaṁ matsyaṁ vīkṣya sakṛj jale / divi dundubhayo nedur jaya-śabda-yutā bhuvi'.

statements.claim: Lakshmana entered the arena with chiming anklets, holding a garland of golden-gleaming jewels and a shy smile, and set the garland on Krishna's shoulder; conches, drums and bheris answered.
statements.evidence: BP 10.83.27-29: 'tad raṅgam āviśam ahaṁ kala-nūpurābhyāṁ padbhyāṁ pragṛhya kanakojvala-ratna-mālām... sa-vrīḍa-hāsa-vadanā... aṁse 'nurakta-hṛdayā nidadhe sva-mālām'; 'mṛdaṅga-paṭahāḥ śaṅkha-bhery-ānakādayaḥ'.

statements.claim: As the old verse puts it, he carried off the fair daughter of Madra the way Garuda seizes nectar from the gods.
statements.evidence: Pack tradition note and BP 10.58.56 rendering: 'he carried off Lakshmana, the fair daughter of the king of Madra, from her svayamvara like Garuda seizing nectar'.

statements.claim: The losing kings surged to stop him on the road; Daruka lifted Lakshmana into the chariot drawn by four fine horses, and Krishna cut down arms, legs and necks with arrows from Sharnga until the road lay open.
statements.evidence: BP 10.83.30-34: 'māṁ tāvad ratham āropya haya-ratna-catuṣṭayam / dārukaś codayām āsa kāñcanopaskaraṁ ratham / te 'nvasajjanta rājanyā niṣeddhuṁ pathi kecana / te śārṅga-cyuta-bāṇaughaiḥ kṛtta-bāhv-aṅghri-kandharāḥ'.

statements.claim: He entered Dwaraka like the sun entering its home, through gates hung with banners; and the king of Madra honored the guests Krishna had left behind with serving women, wealth, elephants, chariots and horses.
statements.evidence: BP 10.83.35-37: 'samāviśat taraṇir iva sva-ketanam' (entered like the sun its own abode); 'pitā me pūjayām āsa suhṛt-sambandhi-bāndhavān / dāsībhiḥ sarva-sampadbhir bhaṭebha-ratha-vājibhiḥ'.

statements.claim: Lakshmana ended her story: 'We are only servants in the home of that self-satisfied Lord.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.83.38: 'ātmārāmasya tasyemā vayaṁ vai gṛha-dāsikāḥ' — we are verily the house-servants of that self-delighting (ātmārāma) Lord.

DKS_0208.notes: Fully grounded in BP 10.58.55-57 + 10.83.16-38 (both conf 5). 'A marriage of kinsmen, arranged and blessed' glosses Bhadra's account per the pack. Closing reflection on Lakshmana's words is connective commentary.

statements.claim: Prasena rode out of Dwaraka wearing the Syamantaka jewel and was not seen alive again; the Vrishnis and Andhakas suspected Krishna of stealing it
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 vv.27-29: adorned with the jewel Prasena went a-hunting and was slain by a lion; hearing of his death the Vrishni and Andhaka families entertained suspicions against Krishna because they knew he had a fancy for that jewel.

statements.claim: The Syamantaka came to Dwaraka as a gift of the sun and produced gold in the palaces of the Vrishnis and Andhakas, brought timely rain, and kept disease away
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 vv.19-25: Vivaswan took the jewel from his neck and gave it to the king; the jewel produced gold in the palace of the Vrishnis and Andhakas, the god of rains poured in due season, and there was no fear of disease.

statements.claim: Satrajit, having received the jewel, gave it in delight to his brother Prasena, who wore it everywhere
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 v.24: the king Satrajit, with great delight, conferred the peerless jewel Syamantaka on his brother Prasena.

statements.claim: Krishna desired the jewel but, though capable, never took it by force or stealth
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 v.26: Govinda grew desirous of the jewel; although capable he did not take it by force or pilfer it.

statements.claim: A lion slew Prasena in the forest for the jewel; a bear slew the lion, took the jewel, and carried it into its den
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 vv.27-28: Prasena was slain by a wild lion for the Syamantaka; killing that lion a highly powerful bear took the jewel and entered into his den.

statements.claim: Knowing himself innocent, Krishna resolved 'I must bring the jewel' and set out with his followers, searching the mountains Rikshavan and Vindhya until stricken with fatigue
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 vv.29-34: Krishna, thinking himself innocent, resolving 'I must bring the jewel', followed Prasena's footsteps with his followers and ransacked the mountains Rikshavan and Vindhya until stricken with fatigue.

statements.claim: Krishna found Prasena and his dead horse but no jewel, and near them the lion killed by the bear, the truth surmised from the footsteps
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 vv.33-34: he saw Prasena and his horse killed there without the jewel, and the lion killed by the bear; it was surmised by the footsteps, and he followed them to the bear's den.

statements.claim: From inside the den a nurse was playing with the jewel with Jamvavan's son, saying 'Do not weep; the lion killed Prasena and he has been killed by Jamvavan; this Syamantaka belongs to you'
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 vv.35-36: a nurse was giving play with the jewel to Jamvavan's son, saying 'Do not weep'; the nurse said the lion killed Prasena, he was killed by Jamvavan, and the Syamantaka belonged to the boy.

statements.claim: Krishna left the Yadavas with Baladeva at the den's mouth and entered silently with the Sharnga bow, wrestling Jamvavan for twenty-one days
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 vv.37-40: keeping the Yadavas with Baladeva at the mouth of the den and displaying a beautiful form and voice, Krishna with the Sharnga bow entered; Govinda wrestled with Jamvavan for twenty-one days.

statements.claim: The Yadavas headed by Baladeva returned to Dwaraka and announced that Krishna had been slain
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 v.40: after Krishna entered the den all the Yadavas, headed by Baladeva, returned to Dwaraka and announced that he had been slain.

statements.claim: The clan had whispered that Krishna stole the jewel, and the rumor now went around that he was dead
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 vv.29,40: the families suspected Krishna of the theft because of his fancy for the jewel; the Yadavas announced he had been slain.

DKS_0209.notes: All named events, characters, places, and the nurse's dialogue match Harivamsha 1.38. Opening riding-out imagery and crowd reactions are connective atmosphere. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Krishna had recovered the Syamantaka and conferred it on Satrajit, whose daughter Satyabhama was his wife
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 v.1 (jewel Krishna conferred on Satrajit was stolen) plus episode continuity (DKS_0215 pack, BP 10.56 v.43: Krishna married Satyabhama; HV 1.39 v.2 notes Akrura always wished for Satyabhama).

statements.claim: Shatadhanwa, a kinsman of the Bhoja line, slew Satrajit at dead of night, took the jewel, and made a present of it to Akrura, who exacted a promise of secrecy and swore to stand by Shatadhanwa, saying all Dwaraka was under his control
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 vv.3-5: Shatadhanwa slew Satrajit at the dead of night, took the jewel and gave it to Akrura, who made him promise never to reveal its whereabouts and said 'If Krishna attacks you I shall follow you; the whole of Dwarka is under my control.'

statements.claim: Akrura had long desired Satyabhama and the jewel
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 v.2: Akrura always wished to have the beautiful Satyabhama and, on opportunity, desired to possess the jewel.

statements.claim: Satyabhama, grieving, came to her husband, told him what Shatadhanwa had done, and stood weeping by his side
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 vv.6-7: on her father being slain, Satyabhama repaired to her husband, communicated what had been perpetrated by Shatadhanwa of the Bhoja race, and stood by his side shedding tears.

statements.claim: Krishna told Balarama that Prasena was killed by a lion and Satrajit slain by Shatadhanwa, that he was master of the jewel, and urged mounting the chariot to slay the Bhoja and recover the Syamantaka
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 vv.9-11: Krishna told his elder brother Haladhar 'Prasena has been killed by a lion and Satrajit has been slain by Shatadhanwa; I am the master of the jewel Syamantaka; get on your car and after slaying the Bhoja Syamantaka will be ours.'

statements.claim: In the terrible encounter with Krishna, Akrura, though capable, out of wickedness did not help Shatadhanwa
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 vv.12-13: a terrible encounter arose; Akrura, beholding both enraged, though capable, out of wickedness did not help the son of Hridika.

statements.claim: Fearful, Shatadhanwa fled on his mare Vijnatahridaya, which could cover a hundred yojanas, fighting Krishna as he fell back until the mare, spent with exhaustion and misery, died
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 vv.14-17: stricken with fear Shatadhanwa fled; his mare Vijnatahridaya could go a hundred yojanas and with her he fought Krishna; after a hundred yojanas, on account of the exhaustion and misery of the mare, her vital breaths went up to the sky.

statements.claim: Krishna told Balarama to wait, saying he would go on foot and carry away the jewel himself
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 v.18: Krishna said to Rama 'Wait here; I have seen the wretched plight of the mare; going on foot I shall carry away the jewel Syamantaka.'

statements.claim: Krishna killed Shatadhanwa on the way to Mithila but the jewel was not on him, and he returned with empty hands
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 v.19: going on foot, Krishna killed Shatadhanwa on the way to Mithila and did not see Syamantaka.

statements.claim: Balarama demanded the jewel, Krishna said he had not got it, and Balarama, exclaiming 'Fie on you', said he forgave him as his brother, was going away, and had nothing to do with him or the Vrishnis of Dwarka, then entered Mithila
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 vv.20-23: Balarama said 'Give me the jewel'; Krishna said 'I have not got it'; Rama, filled with anger, repeatedly exclaimed 'Fie on you', said 'I forgive you because you are my brother; I go away; I have nothing to do with you or other Vrishnis of Dwarka', and entered the city of Mithila.

statements.claim: The king of Mithila honored Balarama with presents after his heart, and Duryodhana received from Balabhadra the most excellent instruction in the use of clubs
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 vv.23,28: Rama was honored with all becoming presents after his heart by the king of Mithila; the king Duryodhana received from Balabhadra the most excellent instructions in the use of clubs.

statements.claim: The mighty car-warriors of the Vrishni race with Krishna propitiated Balarama and brought him back to Dwaraka
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 v.29: propitiating Balarama, all the mighty car warriors of the Vrishni race and the high-souled Krishna brought him back to the city of Dwarka.

DKS_0210.notes: Faithful to Harivamsha 1.39 including quoted speeches. Emotional color (Akrura 'watched from nearby', the quarrel 'began over a jewel neither brother was holding') is connective framing, not asserted fact. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: After Akrura's departure from Dwarka with the Andhakas, Indra (Pakashasana) withheld rain and drought devastated the whole country
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 vv.30-31: after the departure of Akrura, Pakashasana did not pour rain and the whole country was devastated by drought.

statements.claim: Krishna neglected Akrura in a feat of dissension among his kinsmen, and Akrura left with the Andhakas
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 v.30: the foremost of men Akrura, with Andhakas, left Dwarka; Krishna, in a feat of dissension amongst his kinsmen, neglected him.

statements.claim: The Kukuras and Andhakas propitiated Akrura when the country was devastated by drought
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 v.32: when the whole country was devastated by drought, the Kukuras and Andhakas began to propitiate Akrura.

statements.claim: When the liberal Akrura returned to Dwarka, the thousand-eyed Indra began to pour showers on the bank of the ocean
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 v.33: when the liberal Akrura returned to Dwarka, the thousand-eyed Indra began to discharge showers on the bank of the ocean.

statements.claim: To please Krishna, Akrura gave him his sister Sushila in marriage
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 v.34: in order to please Krishna, the intelligent Akrura gave him in marriage his sister Sushila.

statements.claim: Guessing by his riches and liberality that the Syamantaka was with Akrura, Krishna told him in the midst of an assembly that the jewel was in his keeping, asked him to give it and not cheat him, and said the anger that possessed him sixty years before was now ended
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 v.35: guessing by his riches and liberality that Syamantaka was with Akrura, Janarddana said to him in the midst of an assembly 'The jewel is in thy possession; give it to me; do not cheat me; the anger that possessed me sixty years before is now ended.'

statements.claim: Akrura kept the stolen jewel hidden and his riches had grown on the secret
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 vv.1-5,25: Akrura held the jewel stolen by Shatadhanwa and bound Shatadhanwa to secrecy; he devoted jewels to sacrifices and Krishna guessed the jewel by Akrura's riches and liberality.

statements.claim: Krishna suspected where the jewel lay before Akrura left; the estrangement broke open and Krishna did not call him back
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 v.25 (Akrura, on account of the jewel, took protective measures) and v.30 (Krishna neglected Akrura); the story's ordering is a narrative synthesis the pack does not contradict.

statements.claim: Whether the jewel passed back into Krishna's hands that day is not recorded in the sources
statements.evidence: The pack's passage is truncated at v.35 and its excerpt records only the return, the rain, and the words spoken; the story's hedge matches the available evidence.

DKS_0211.notes: Drought description (cracked earth, failing wells, thin herds) is generic elaboration of the pack's 'whole country devastated by draught' - connective narration. Akrura 'foremost of the Vrishnis' rests on the pack's 'foremost of men Akrura' and his Vrishni identity in the lineage. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Satrajit wore the jewel at his throat and shone so brightly that people seeing him from afar had their sight dimmed and mistook him for the sun-god
statements.evidence: BP 10.56 vv.3-7: wearing the jewel on his neck he shone like the sun; people seeing him from afar had their sight dimmed by his splendor and thought the sun was coming; excerpt: 'the people of Dvaraka mistook him for the sun-god.'

statements.claim: The jewel was the Syamantaka, given to Satrajit by the sun, who was his friend
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 vv.12-16,19: the sun was Satrajit's friend as valuable as his life; at the ocean bank the lord Vivaswan appeared and took from his neck the peerless jewel Syamantaka and gave it to him; BP 10.56 excerpt: pleased with his devotee Satrajit, Surya gave him the jewel.

statements.claim: Satrajit asked the sun for the jewel with which he lights the worlds
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 vv.17-21: the king said 'Thou hast appeared before me as a friend but what special favour have I got' and 'O lord, it behoveth thee to confer upon me this jewel with which thou dost always light the worlds.'

statements.claim: The people followed Satrajit through the city thinking the sun was going
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 vv.22-23: holding the jewel the king entered his own city; all the people followed him thinking that the sun was going.

statements.claim: Wearing it Satrajit shone like the sun, and the jewel yielded eight loads of gold each day and warded off all calamity
statements.evidence: BP 10.56 v.10 and excerpt: 'dine dine svarna-bharan astau sa srjati' (daily it produces eight loads of gold); the jewel yielded eight loads of gold daily and warded off all calamity; Satrajit shone like the sun.

statements.claim: In the older telling, gold welled up in the palaces of the Vrishnis and Andhakas and the rains came in their season
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 v.25: the jewel produced gold in the palace of the Vrishnis and Andhakas and the god of rains poured in due season.

statements.claim: Krishna grew desirous of the jewel but, though capable, did not take it by force or steal it
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 v.26: Govinda grew desirous of the peerless jewel; although capable he did not take it by force or pilfer it.

statements.claim: In time Satrajit, delighted, conferred the jewel on his brother Prasena, who wore it wherever he went
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 v.24: the king Satrajit, with great delight, conferred the peerless jewel Syamantaka on his brother Prasena.

DKS_0212.notes: Blends BP 10.56 (eight loads of gold, sun-mistake) and Harivamsha 1.38 (ocean-bank worship, gift dialogue) as the pack does; both variants are cited in the story. Crowd color (children crying out, elders shading eyes) is connective. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Krishna asked Satrajit for the jewel and the covetous Satrajit refused
statements.evidence: BP 10.56 v.11 and excerpt: though Krishna asked for the jewel, the covetous Satrajit refused (BP: he was asked by Shauri for the jewel).

statements.claim: Prasena, Satrajit's brother, went hunting wearing the jewel and was slain by a lion together with his horse; the lion was in turn slain by the bear Jambavan, who took the jewel
statements.evidence: BP 10.56 vv.12-13 and HV 1.38 vv.27-28: a lion, killing Prasena together with his horse, took the jewel; the lion was in turn slain by Jambavan (BP excerpt); HV: killing the lion, a highly powerful bear took the jewel and entered his den.

statements.claim: The jewel was made a plaything for the bear-king's child in the cave
statements.evidence: BP 10.56 v.14: the jewel was made a plaything (kridanaka) for the child in the cave; HV 1.38 v.35: a nurse was giving play with the jewel to Jamvavan's son.

statements.claim: The city whispered that Krishna had killed Prasena for the jewel
statements.evidence: BP 10.56 v.15 and excerpt: the people whispered that Krishna had indeed killed the jewel-necked one who went to the forest (Prasena).

statements.claim: Knowing himself innocent, Krishna resolved 'I must bring the jewel' and set out with his followers, following tracks through the Rikshavan and Vindhya mountains until weary
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 vv.29-34: knowing their suspicion and thinking himself innocent, Krishna, resolving 'I must bring the jewel', followed Prasena's footsteps with his followers, ransacking the mountains Rikshavan and Vindhya until stricken with fatigue; he saw Prasena and his horse dead and the lion killed by the bear, surmised by the footsteps.

statements.claim: Krishna found Prasena and his horse dead with no jewel, the lion nearby slain by the bear, and followed the trail to the bear's den
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 vv.33-34: he saw Prasena and his horse killed there without the jewel, and near Prasena the lion killed by the bear; following the footsteps he searched for the den of the running bear.

statements.claim: From inside the den the nurse spoke of the plaything jewel to the child, saying 'The lion killed Prasena, and the lion was killed by Jambavan; do not weep - this Syamantaka belongs to you'
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 vv.35-36: a nurse was giving play with the jewel to Jamvavan's son, saying 'Do not weep'; the nurse said the lion killed Prasena and was killed by Jamvavan, and the Syamantaka belonged to the boy.

statements.claim: Krishna left Balarama and the Yadavas at the den's mouth and entered alone with his bow
statements.evidence: HV 1.38 vv.37-38: keeping all the Yadavas with Baladeva at the mouth of the den and displaying a beautiful form and voice, Krishna with the Sharnga bow silently entered.

DKS_0213.notes: Faithful blend of BP 10.56.11-15 (Satrajit's refusal, rumor) and HV 1.38 (mountains, nurse's words, Baladeva at the den). 'His own cub' is an animal idiom for Jamvavan's son in the pack. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: The people of Dwaraka, not seeing Krishna emerge from the cave, thought him dead, and Devaki and Rukmini grieved
statements.evidence: BP 10.56 vv.32-33: the people did not see the exit of Shauri who had entered the cave; Devaki, Rukmini, and Anakadundubhi grieved.

statements.claim: The grieved citizens of Dwaraka cursed Satrajit, blaming his refusal
statements.evidence: BP 10.56 v.34: the grieved Dvaraka dwellers cursed Satrajit; the reason (his refusal sending Krishna after the jewel) is the citizens' speech, consistent with the episode.

statements.claim: Krishna returned as if risen from the dead, with the jewel restored and his bride Jambavati, the bear king's daughter
statements.evidence: BP 10.56 v.36: they found Krishna come back as if from death; pack index/summary: 'Krishna returns with the jewel and Jambavati'; excerpt: 'Krishna returned with the jewel and his bride.'

statements.claim: Krishna summoned Satrajit to an assembly in the king's presence, recounted the whole affair, and restored the Syamantaka to Satrajit
statements.evidence: BP 10.56 v.37: summoning Satrajit in the assembly in the king's presence; excerpt: Krishna recounted all in the assembly and restored the Syamantaka to Satrajit; HV 1.38 excerpt: he handed over Syamantaka to Satrajit in an assembly of the Satwatas.

statements.claim: Satrajit took the jewel with his face bowed, deeply ashamed
statements.evidence: BP 10.56 v.38: he, greatly ashamed, took the jewel with his face downward.

statements.claim: Satrajit resolved to give Krishna his daughter Satyabhama, a jewel among women, together with the jewel, as reparation
statements.evidence: BP 10.56 vv.39-42: reflecting on the wrong he had done, Satrajit decided 'I shall give my daughter, a jewel among women, and the jewel itself.'

statements.claim: Krishna married Satyabhama according to the rites but refused the jewel, saying 'We do not accept the jewel, O king'
statements.evidence: BP 10.56 vv.43-44: Bhagavan married Satyabhama according to the rites and said 'We do not accept the jewel, O king.'

statements.claim: Krishna told the story of Prasena, the lion, the bear, and the wrestle with Jambavan in the den, and the bear king yielded the jewel and his daughter
statements.evidence: BP 10.56 v.14 (jewel made a plaything for the child in the cave) and the episode's cave-wrestle sequence (DKS_0214 cluster); pack summary: 'clears his name in open assembly.'

statements.claim: Krishna had gone to clear his name, not to own the jewel
statements.evidence: BP 10.56 v.15 (rumor blamed Krishna for Prasena's death) and v.44 (he refuses the jewel); consistent with his refusing the jewel when offered.

DKS_0215.notes: Follows BP 10.56.32-44 closely (grief, curses on Satrajit, assembly before the king, ashamed Satrajit, Satyabhama + jewel offered, marriage, jewel refused) with HV corroboration. Satrajit's inner reasoning (paragraphs on shame turning to resolution) is connective psychology matching BP vv.39-42. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Krishna was away from Dwaraka, visiting the elders of the Kuru court, when the plan was made
statements.evidence: BP 10.57 v.1 lists his visits to Bhishma, Kripa, Vidura, Gandhari, and Drona (Hastinapura elders); excerpt: 'While Krishna was away, Akrura and Kritavarma urged Satadhanva...'

statements.claim: Akrura and Kritavarma instigated Satadhanva to seize the jewel, claiming Satrajit had broken his word and scorned them after promising a jewel among women
statements.evidence: BP 10.57 vv.2-4: having obtained the opportunity, the two spoke to Satadhanva - 'he who, having promised us the jewel of a maiden, scorned us' - and the wicked one, his mind corrupted by those two, slew Satrajit.

statements.claim: Akrura had long wished for Satyabhama and desired the jewel once it came to Satrajit's keeping
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 v.2: Akrura always wished to have the beautiful Satyabhama and, as soon as he got an opportunity, desired to possess the valuable jewel.

statements.claim: Satadhanva, of the Bhoja line, slew the sleeping Satrajit at night and made off with the Syamantaka
statements.evidence: BP 10.57 excerpt: 'the wicked Satadhanva slew the sleeping Satrajit and made off with the Syamantaka'; HV 1.39 v.3: having slain Satrajit at the dead of night, Shatadhanwa took away the jewel.

statements.claim: The women of the house cried out like orphans
statements.evidence: BP 10.57 v.5: the women, wailing, cried out like orphans.

statements.claim: Satadhanva carried the jewel to Akrura, who made him swear never to reveal where it had gone and promised in return: 'If Krishna attacks you, I will follow you; the whole of Dwaraka is now under my control'
statements.evidence: HV 1.39 vv.3-5: Shatadhanwa made a present of the jewel to Akrura, who made him promise never to give out that the jewel was in his possession and said 'If Krishna attacks you I shall follow you; the whole of Dwarka is now under my control.'

DKS_0216.notes: Clean merge of BP 10.57.1-5 (Kritavarma+Akrura instigation, broken-promise motive, sleeping victim, wailing women) with HV 1.39 (Bhoja lineage, gift to Akrura, oath). Envy framing and the two men 'believing themselves the cleverer' are connective. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Satyabhama found her father Satrajit slain in the night with the Syamantaka gone, and cried out 'Father, father!', feeling herself slain along with him
statements.evidence: BP 10.57 v.6 and excerpt: Satyabhama, seeing her father slain, was afflicted with grief and wailed 'father, father, I am slain.'

statements.claim: Her husband Krishna was far away in Hastinapura, the city of the elephant
statements.evidence: BP 10.57 v.7: she went to Gajasahvaya (Hastinapura, the elephant-named city) where Krishna was; BP 10.57 v.1 (Krishna visiting the Kuru elders).

statements.claim: Satyabhama placed her father's body in a great vat of oil before leaving
statements.evidence: BP 10.57 v.7: having placed the dead body in a vat of oil (taila-dronim), she went to Hastinapura; the preservation purpose is standard connective.

statements.claim: She told Krishna everything and stood weeping by his side
statements.evidence: BP 10.57 v.7 and excerpt: she went to Hastinapura to tell Krishna; HV 1.39 v.7 (episode continuity): stricken with grief and standing by his side she began shedding tears.

statements.claim: Hearing the news, Krishna wept with Balarama, following the ways of human beings
statements.evidence: BP 10.57 v.8: hearing it, the two lords (Krishna and Balarama), following the ways of human beings (nri-lokatam), grieved; excerpt: 'who, hearing it, wept with Balarama.'

statements.claim: Krishna and Balarama mourned as a son-in-law and a brother mourn
statements.evidence: BP 10.57 v.8 (they followed human ways in grief); Krishna is Satyabhama's husband (BP 10.56 v.43) and thus Satrajit's son-in-law; elaboration of the source's nri-lokatam.

DKS_0217.notes: Faithful to BP 10.57.6-8 (oil-vat detail, Gajasahvaya, wailing, the two lords following human ways) corroborated by HV 1.39.7 (weeping at Krishna's side). Emotional rendering (riding 'as though the news would spoil in her keeping', the closing vow) is connective. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Satadhanva fled on his mare Vijnatahridaya, which could carry him a hundred yojanas without rest, pursued by Krishna and Balarama seeking the Syamantaka jewel.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39: Satadhanva's mare 'by name Vijnātāhridayā' could go over a distance of a hundred Yojanas, and with her he fled from Krishna; pack index: 'Krishna pursues and beheads Satadhanva near Mithila but finds no jewel'.

statements.claim: Satrajit was slain at night and the jewel Krishna had once bestowed on Satrajit was gone from his home.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39: 'having slain Satrājit at the dead of night the highly powerful Shatadhanwā took away the jewel'; also 'the peerless jewel which Krishna conferred on Satrājit' — same source confirms Krishna had earlier given the gem to Satrajit.

statements.claim: Krishna and Balarama mounted their chariot and gave chase at once, determined to run the killer down before he could reach a friendly court.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata Purana 10.57.18: 'garuḍa-dhvajam āruhya rathaṃ rāma-janārdanau' — Rama and Janardana mounted the Garuda-bannered chariot in pursuit; Harivamsha: Satadhanva 'stricken with fear took to his heels' when Krishna returned.

statements.claim: After a hundred yojanas the mare failed in a grove on the approach to Mithila and stood motionless, her strength spent.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata Purana 10.57.19: 'mithilāyām upavane visṛjya patitaṃ hayam' — the fallen horse abandoned in a grove at Mithila; Harivamsha: 'Having travelled over a distance of a hundred Yojanas Shatadhanwa found her motionless'; Krishna speaks of 'the wretched plight of the mare'.

statements.claim: Krishna told Balarama to wait, went forward on foot with the discus, and struck down Satadhanva on the outskirts of Mithila.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39: Krishna said 'Wait here... Going on foot I shall carry away the jewel Swyamantaka', then 'going on foot, Achyuta... killed Shatadhanwa on the way to Mithila'; Bhagavata 10.57.20 (padātis... tigma-neminā — on foot, with the sharp-rimmed discus) and pack summary: beheaded him with his discus.

statements.claim: Krishna searched the body and the fallen man's garments but found no jewel on Satadhanva.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.57 summary: 'searching him found no jewel'; Harivamsha 1.39: 'Having slain the highly powerful Bhoja king he did not see Swyamantaka'.

statements.claim: Balarama demanded the jewel — 'Give me the jewel' — and when Krishna answered 'I have not got it', Balarama angrily cursed him, declared he would go away and have nothing more to do with him or the Vrishnis of Dwaraka.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39 (vv.20-22): 'seeing Krishna return Balarāma said to him "Give me the jewel"'... 'Krishna said: "I have not got it." Thereat Rama was filled with anger. Repeatedly exclaiming "Fie on you, Fie on you"... "I forgive you because you are my brother. May you farewell. I go away. I have nothing to do with you or other Vrishnis of Dwārkā."'

statements.claim: Balarama entered Mithila, where King Janaka rose and received him with honor and gifts, and he stayed there for months, during which Duryodhana received from him instruction in the use of the mace.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.57.24-25: Janaka 'sahasotthāya' (rose suddenly) with pleased mind and honored him; 'uvāsa tasyāṃ katicin mithilāyāṃ samā' (stayed some months in Mithila); Harivamsha 1.39: 'the king Duryodhana received from Balabhadra the most excellent instructions in the use of clubs'.

statements.claim: Krishna returned to Dwaraka alone, the murderer punished and the jewel still lost.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.57.26: 'keśavo dvārakām etya' — Krishna returned to Dwaraka (Balarama having remained in Mithila); no jewel was found, per index summary.

DKS_0218.notes: Every factual beat matches Bhagavata 10.57.9-25 and Harivamsha 1.39 (Dutt). Location phrasing harmonizes both sources ('grove on the approach to Mithila' / killed 'near Mithila'). 'Bent on avenging... and recovering the jewel', 'the same discus that had ended the lives of greater demons' and the closing suspense about the jewel's whereabouts are connective framing, not sourceable assertions.

statements.claim: The rains stopped when Akrura left Dwaraka and returned when he came back, as the Kukuras and Andhakas observed.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39 (vv.30-33): after Akrura's departure 'Pākashasana did not pour rain' and the country was devastated by drought; 'When the liberal Akrura returned to Dwārkā the thousand-eyed Indra began to discharge showers'; the Kukuras and Andhakas propitiated Akrura.

statements.claim: Krishna, returned from Mithila, saw that the slain Satadhanva received the funeral rites due to a kinsman.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata Purana 10.57.27: 'tataḥ sa kārayām āsa kriyā bandhor hatasya vai' — he caused the rites of the slain kinsman to be performed.

statements.claim: The night Satrajit was slain the jewel passed from Satadhanva into Akrura's keeping, bound by a vow that its hiding would never be revealed.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.57.35: 'nanu dāna-pate nyastas tvayy āste śatadhanvanā' (was it not deposited with you by Satadhanva?); Harivamsha 1.39 (vv.3-4): Satadhanva took the jewel 'and made a present of it to Akrura', who secured a promise that it would never be given out that the jewel was in Akrura's possession.

statements.claim: Akrura's own prosperity betrayed him: he gathered jewels and goods for a lavish sacrifice men called the Akrura Yajna and entered a vow of armor as though expecting danger.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39 (vv.24-27): Akrura 'entered into the initiation-like coat of mail for protecting himself', 'devoted most excellent jewels and various other articles to the performance of sacrifices', and 'that sacrifice... was called the Akrura Yajna'.

statements.claim: Before the assembly Krishna spoke to Akrura gently: was the jewel not entrusted to him by Satadhanva? Satrajit had no son, so the gem would pass to his daughter's sons, yet no one else could hold it — let Akrura show it to the kinsmen and bring peace to the house.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.57.35-38 near-verbatim: 'nanu dāna-pate nyastas tvayy āste śatadhanvanā / satrājito 'napatyatvād gṛhṇīyur duhituḥ sutāḥ / tathāpi durdharas tv anyais tvayy āstāṃ su-vrate maṇiḥ / darśayasva mahā-bhāga bandhūnāṃ śāntim āvaha'.

statements.claim: Akrura produced the Syamantaka; Krishna showed it to the assembled kinsmen, and the suspicion clinging to him since Satrajit's death dissolved.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.57.39-40: Akrura, won over by these gentle words, showed the jewel 'syamantakaṃ darśayitvā jñātibhyo raja ātmanaḥ' (showing it to the kinsmen, [wiping] his own stain); Harivamsha: 'gave him the jewel in the midst of the assembled Satwatas'.

statements.claim: Krishna returned the jewel to Akrura, giving it up with a delighted heart.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39: 'Hari, the repressor of enemies, returned it to him with a delighted heart'; Bhagavata index summary: 'then returned the jewel to Akrura'.

statements.claim: Balarama was brought home from Mithila by the car-warriors of the Vrishni race, Krishna among those who fetched him, and the brothers were reconciled.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39: 'propitiating Balarāma all the mighty car warriors of the Vrishni race and the high-souled Krishna brought him back to the city of Dwārkā'.

statements.claim: Akrura, confirmed in Krishna's friendship, gave his own sister Sushila to Krishna in marriage.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39: 'in order to please Krishna the intelligent Akrura gave him in marriage his sister Sushilā'.

DKS_0219.notes: One nuance: the pack (Harivamsha) has Akrura extract the vow of secrecy FROM Satadhanva ('he made Shatadhanwā promise that he would never give out that the jewel was in his possession'), whereas the story's summary sentence has Akrura himself sworn to the fleeing thief; the substance — a pact of secrecy over Akrura's possession, kept until Krishna exposed it — is supported by both sources, so not counted as a contradiction. The rain motif, Akrura Yajna, assembly speech, jewel's return, and Sushila marriage are all directly grounded.

statements.claim: A wind bearing celestial fragrance blew over Dwaraka and flowers fell from a clear sky as the Yadavas sat at their daily business in the great assembly hall Dasharha.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.120 (vv.23-25): the assembly-hall 'celebrated by the name of Dāshārha' with huge golden door-ways, where 'the leading members of the Vrishni and Andhaka races, headed by Rāma and Krishna, used to carry on their daily transactions'; 'there blew the wind carrying celestial fragrance and there was a downpour of flowers'.

statements.claim: The king of the gods descended on his white elephant Airavata, the celestials gathered about him.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.120 (vv.26-27): 'Vāsava was seen, seated on a white elephant and encircled by the gods'; Vishnu Purana 5.29: 'ŚAKRA... came mounted on his fierce elephant Airávata to visit Śauri at Dwáraká'.

statements.claim: Rama and Krishna went out with King Ugrasena and the chiefs of the Vrishni and Andhaka houses to receive Indra, who embraced them in order of age and rank, entered the hall and accepted the offerings of hospitality.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.120 (vv.28-31): 'Rāma, Krishna and the king Ugrasena, with other leading Yādavas went out and welcomed the king of gods... the king of gods embraced Janārddana, Baladeva, the king Ahuka and then the other Yādavas, in order of age and rank... adored by Rāma and Krishna he entered into that magnificent assembly-hall... duly accepted arghya and other articles of hospitality'.

statements.claim: Indra touched Krishna's face with his hand — the auspicious countenance of his younger brother.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.120 v.32: 'Then touching the auspicious countenance of his younger brother (Krishna) with his hand the highly powerful Vāsudava addressed to him the following consoling words'.

statements.claim: Indra listed the oppressors Krishna had slain: Arishta, Dhenuka, Chanura, Mushtika, Kesin, Kamsa, Kuvalayapida, and the child-killer Putana, by whose fall the three worlds were preserved and the gods received their share of sacrifices.
statements.evidence: Vishnu Purana 5.29: 'Arisht́a, Dhenuka, Cháńúra, Musht́ika, Keśin... have all been slain by thee. Kansa, Kuvalayápíd́a, the child-destroying Putaná, have been killed by thee... By thy valour and wisdom the three worlds have been preserved, and the gods, obtaining their share of the sacrifices... enjoy satisfaction'.

statements.claim: Naraka, son of the Earth and king of Pragjyotisha, had grown swollen with a boon granted by Brahma.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.120 v.34: 'Elated with the boon conferred on him by Brahmā the great Asura Naraka has foolishly stolen the ear-rings of Aditi'; Vishnu Purana 5.29: 'The son of the earth, called Naraka, who rules over the city of Prágjyotisha'.

statements.claim: Naraka had stolen Aditi's nectar-dripping earrings, Varuna's umbrella which no water can wet, and the jewel-crest of Mount Mandara; he had carried off 16,100 maidens of gods, saints, demons and kings, wearing a single braid, and shut them in a house on Mount Mani; and he now demanded Indra's elephant Airavata.
statements.evidence: Vishnu Purana 5.29: 'He has taken away the umbrella of Varuńa, impermeable to water, the jewel mountain crest of Mandara, and the celestial nectar-dropping earrings of my mother Adití; and he now demands my elephant Airávata'; Harivamsha 1.120 (vv.12-14): 'sixteen thousand and one hundred chaste maidens, wearing a single braid of hairs, were brought... The powerful Bhouma made a house for them on the mount Mani'.

statements.claim: Naraka was unslayable by any creature but not by Krishna, and Garuda, capable of ranging anywhere and assuming any strength, would bear him to the demon's city.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.120 (vv.36-37): 'This Vinatā's son Guruda, highly powerful, capable of ranging anywhere and of assuming any strength... will take thee there. O Upendra, Bhumi's son, Naraka, is unslayable by all creatures. Do thou soon kill that sinful one and come back'.

statements.claim: Krishna smiled gently, rose from his throne, took Indra by the hand and thought of Garuda, who appeared; Krishna seated Satyabhama on his back, mounted behind her, and flew to Pragjyotisha.
statements.evidence: Vishnu Purana 5.29: 'the divine Hari gently smiled, and, rising from his throne, took Indra by the hand: then wishing for the eater of the serpents, Garud́a immediately appeared; upon whom his master, having first seated Satyabhámá upon his back, ascended, and flew to Prágjyotisha'.

statements.claim: Razor-edged nooses defended the demon's walls, and four guardians — Hayagriva, Nisunda, Panchanada, and Muru with his thousand sons — kept watch.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.120 (vv.18-19): 'He had four gate-keepers, dreadful in battle, namely Hayagriva, Nisunda, Panchanada and the great Asura Muru with his thousand sons'; Vishnu Purana 5.29: 'The environs of Prágjyotisha were defended by nooses, constructed by the demon Muru, the edges of which were as sharp as razors'.

statements.claim: Indra mounted Airavata and, in the sight of all Dwaraka, returned to the abode of the gods.
statements.evidence: Vishnu Purana 5.29: 'Indra mounted his elephant, and, in the sight of the inhabitants of Dwáraká, went to the abode of the gods'.

DKS_0220.notes: Both sources (Harivamsha 1.120, VP 5.29) fully ground the episode. Minor spatial nuance: Harivamsha says the Dasharha hall itself 'extended over a yojana and had huge golden door-ways'; the story attaches the yojana dimension to its courtyard — cosmetic, not counted. Krishna's 'thought of Garuda' compresses VP's 'wishing for' Garuda. The maidens' number (16,100, single braid) and Mount Mani detail come from Harivamsha; the theft list from VP, as the pack notes.

statements.claim: Krishna came to Mount Raivataka with Rukmini for the festival closing the vow she had undertaken; his sons and brothers had been sent ahead by Narada's arrangement, and his sixteen thousand wives came in splendor befitting their rank.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.4-7): Krishna 'once went to the mount Raivataka with Rukshmini' because 'there was to take place a great festival on the day of the termination of Rukshmini's vow'; 'according to Narada's command, Vāsudeva's sons and brothers had already been sent there'; 'The sixteen thousand wives of the intelligent Madhava with splendour befitting their rank, had gone there'.

statements.claim: Krishna gratified the twice-born, beggars, those practicing religious rites and all who sought his well-being, and at the termination of the fasting honored Rukmini, daughter of Bhishmaka, before them all.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.8-11): 'the lord of subdued senses, conferred on the twice-borns all their desired-for objects, as well as on the beggars, on those who always practise religious rites and on all those who sought his well-being... At the termination of the fasting, the Lord highly honored his beloved spouse Rukshmini, the daughter of Bhishmaka'.

statements.claim: The ascetic Narada arrived while Krishna sat with Rukmini encircled by the other queens; Krishna received him with rites laid down in the scriptures, and Narada gave him a single Parijata flower.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.12-14): 'Krishna, sat on a seat with Rukshmini encircled by his other wives when the ascetic Nārada arrived... duly adored him with rites laid down in the Scriptures... Nārada... gave him a Pārijata flower'.

statements.claim: Because Rukmini sat beside him, Krishna gave her the flower; following his hint she set it in her hair and was doubly beautified by it.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.15-17): 'Bhoja's daughter Rukshmini was by him, so Hari gave her that Parijata flower. Taking that lovely flower and following Krishna's hint, that blameless lady... put it on her head... was doubly beautified by that celestial flower'.

statements.claim: Narada described the flower's powers: it never withers; it gives wished-for fragrance for one year; heat and cold as desired and juices of every taste; whatever flowers she longs for; root of good luck and piety keeping the mind from evil paths; whatever color she wishes; thin or plump at her will; dispels unwholesome smell; serves as a lamp at night; garlands of Santanaka flowers and undecaying clothes; mastery over hunger, thirst and exhaustion; songs with musical instruments; and it leaves her when one full year is complete, the Creator having invested it with such a character.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.20-32) enumerates each power in the same order: never withers (20), wished-for fragrance for one year (21), heat/cold and juices (22), whatever flowers wished (24), root of good luck and piety, no evil path (25), color assumed, thin or plump (26), dispels unwholesome smell, lamp at night (27), Santanaka garland and undecaying clothes (28), mistress of hunger, thirst, exhaustion and decrepitude (29), songs with instruments (30), departs on completion of one full year (31), Creator's character (32).

statements.claim: Even the wives of the gods — Uma, Aditi, Sachi, Savitri and Sri herself — wear such flowers, and for them too the flower's stay lasts no more than a year.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.33-35): Uma (beloved spouse of Mahadeva, Himalaya's daughter), 'Aditi... Sachi, Savitri, the mother of gods and the goddess Sree too, always use this flower. Even for the wives of the gods and the leading celestial Vasus... its period of duration does not exceed more than a year'.

statements.claim: Narada declared Rukmini the foremost and most beloved among the sixteen thousand wives of Vasudeva.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 pack excerpt: 'among the sixteen thousand wives of Vāsudeva, I consider thee as the foremost and the most beloved.'

DKS_0221.notes: The whole episode is a close rendering of Harivamsha 1.122 (Dutt). 'Mount Raivataka had never seen such a gathering' and the mood-shift of the closing lines are connective narration; the flower's powers, the one-year rule, the goddess list and Narada's declaration all track the source verse-by-verse.

statements.claim: Satyabhama's maids brought word-for-word news of the Raivataka festival: Krishna had come with Rukmini for the ceremony ending her vow, gratified the twice-born and others, and at the end of the fasting honored Rukmini, the daughter of Bhishmaka, before all his sixteen thousand wives.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.4-11): the same festival account (Krishna came with Rukshmini for the vow's termination, gratified twice-borns/beggars/rite-practitioners, sixteen thousand wives present, honored Rukshmini at the fasting's end), here recapitulated as the report that reaches Satyabhama.

statements.claim: Narada gave Krishna a single Parijata flower, which Krishna passed to Rukmini at his side; she set it in her hair, and the flower's powers included never withering, a year of wished-for fragrance, heat and cold at will, lamplight at night, any desired color, Santanaka garlands and undecaying clothes, and songs at a wish.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.14-16, 20-32): flower given to Krishna and passed to Rukshmini; Narada enumerates the same powers.

statements.claim: The goddesses of heaven — Sachi, Aditi, Savitri, Uma — wore such flowers, but even for them the flower's stay lasted no more than a year.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.33-35): Uma, Aditi, Puloma's daughter Sachi, Savitri, the mother of gods and Sree always use this flower; 'even for the wives of the gods... its period of duration does not exceed more than a year'.

statements.claim: Satyabhama, proud on the foundation of being the wife Krishna loved best, could not bear the accession of such good fortune to the other wife of her husband.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 pack excerpt: 'the highly proud Satyabhāma... could not bear the accession of such a good fortune unto the other wife of her husband.'

statements.claim: Worked up with anger like the flame of fire, Satyabhama cast off her ornaments where she stood and retired to the lonely apartment of anger, where she sat in the midst of her handmaids.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 pack excerpt: 'Worked up with anger like the flame of fire... she entered into the lonely apartment of anger'; Harivamsha 1.123 v.6 confirms she was 'inside the apartment of anger in the midst of her handmaids'.

DKS_0222.notes: Fully grounded in Harivamsha 1.122-123. 'Rukmini... his first wife' compresses the source's 'beloved spouse' — acceptable as she is the wife honored at the festival. 'The room kept in the mansion for exactly such a mood, as if the palace itself expected this of its queens' and the closing suspense line are interpretive connective narration.

statements.claim: While Narada still sat with Rukmini praising the flower, Krishna noticed Satyabhama's absence and left the festival under some pretext.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 v.1: 'Finding the sage (Narada) seated with Rukshmini, the high-souled Keshava that knower of all things, set out under some pretext (for the mansion of Satyabhama)'.

statements.claim: Krishna went quickly toward the spacious mansion on the Raivataka hills that Vishvakarma himself had built for Satyabhama, walking slowly and with fear, aware that she, dearer to him than his own vital breaths, was under jealous resentment.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 (vv.2-4): 'the spacious mansion of Satyabhama that was built on the delightful Raivataka hills by Visvakarma himself'; 'he was aware that the daughter of Satrajit, his beloved queen—she dearer to him than his own vital breaths—had been under the influence of jealous resentment'; 'the slayer of Madhu proceeded with slow steps, and with greater fear'.

statements.claim: Krishna left Pradyumna to entertain and attend upon Narada, told his servant Daruka to wait at the gate, and entered the palace alone.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 v.5: 'Engaging Pradyumna to entertain and attend upon Narada and telling his servant Daruka "Wait at the gate," he entered into the palace of Satyabhama'.

statements.claim: From a distance Krishna watched her jealous gestures in the apartment of anger: sighing hot and frequently, a derisive laugh at a lotus nipped with her nails, figures drawn with her toe, deep thought with her face on her left palm, sandal smeared on her breast then cruelly thrown aside, and rising from and falling back into her bed.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 (vv.6-11): 'sighing hot and frequently'; 'laughing a derisive laugh mixed with sighs at the lotus... nipping with her nails'; 'describing figures on the ground with the tip of her toe slightly bent'; 'face resting on the lotus of her left palm'; 'take the delightful sandal from the hands of her maids, smear it on her breast and then again cruelly throw it aside'; 'rise from her bed and fall into it again and again'.

statements.claim: When she laid her head on her pillow with her veil over her face, Krishna, commanding the maids by signs not to announce him, approached with faltering steps, took up the fan and fanned slowly while laughing gently.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 (vv.12-14): 'as the daughter of Satrajit laid her head on her pillow, previously covering it with her veil, Janardanna thought "This is my opportunity"... by (manual) signs commanding the handmaids not to announce his presence, he approached Satyabhama with faltering steps. Taking up the fan and standing by her side, he then began to fan slowly and laugh gently'.

statements.claim: His contact with the Parijata flower perfumed him with a divine, supernatural, rare fragrance; Satyabhama uncovered her face and asked what it was, questioned her maids without glancing at him, and the maids knelt speechless with palms joined; she wondered whether the earth had emitted the scent, then her glance fell on Kesava.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 (vv.15-20): 'perfumed in consequence of his contact with the Pārijāta flower, diffused there a divine, super-natural and rare fragrance'; she 'uncovered her face, and said "What is this?"... without bestowing a glance on her godly husband, began to question her maids'; maids 'could not say anything, and kneeling down... with palms joined together'; she wondered if it were 'one of her excellent emissions' of the earth; 'her glance suddenly lighted on Kesava that creator of the worlds'.

statements.claim: She said 'Ah! right', her eyes dimmed with tears, pouting and sighing she turned her downcast countenance away, and with brows contracted in a frown and face on her palms told Hari, 'Thou lookest beautiful', as tears of jealous passion flowed like dew from lotus petals.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 (vv.21-24): "She said 'Ah! right,' and then suddenly her eyes became dimmed with tears... pouting and herself sighing... turned her down-cast countenance away... contracting her brows in a disapproving frown and placing her face on her palms, she said to Hari with her eyes upraised, 'Thou lookest beautiful'. Tears of jealous passion began to flow down from her eyes, like drops of dew falling from a pair of lotus-petals'."

statements.claim: Krishna approached in haste, held her tears in his hands, wiped the tears falling on her breast, and asked why tears flowed, why she wore plain white garments rather than those sprinkled with safflower and gold-dust, white being the dress of ladies worshipping the gods.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 (vv.25-30): 'approached her in haste and held them in her hands... wiping off with his hands those tears that were falling on her breast, that wearer of the mark of Srivatsa... spoke'; questions on tears (27), and garments 'sprinkled with safflower and gold-dust... white garments which ladies do not like to wear except at the time of worshipping the gods' (29-30).

statements.claim: Krishna protested: 'Just as flame is in fire, so my love resides in thee, and thee only.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 pack excerpt: 'Just as flame is in fire ... so my love resides in thee and thee only.'

DKS_0223.notes: A faithful, nearly scene-by-scene rendering of Harivamsha 1.123 (Dutt). The commentary that he watched 'the theater of a woman who wanted to be angry at the one man she loved' is connective interpretation; all described gestures, the fragrance beat, the dialogue and the final protest are in the source passage.

statements.claim: Krishna entreated Satyabhama on his life to reveal the cause of her grief, saying her sorrow seemed to burn through all his limbs.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 (vv.1-3): 'sorrow seems to burn through all my limbs... I entreat thee, on my life, to reveal to me the cause of thy grief'.

statements.claim: Satyabhama spoke of her honor and prosperity established by Krishna in days gone by and famous in the world, and that being most beloved among his wives had prompted her pride.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 (vv.5-6): 'it was thy ownself that established my honor and prosperity... That I am most beloved of thee among all thy wives—is what prompted me to raise my head with pride above all others'.

statements.claim: She said her maids had told her she had been laughed at by her co-wives and others, that the Parijata flower Narada gave Krishna had been given to her dear one, totally neglecting her, an unmistakable expression of regard.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 (vv.7-9): 'to-day I have been laughed at by my rival (co-wives) and by other people... I hear that the Parijata flower that Nārada gave thee, thou hast given to thy dear one, totally neglecting my (poor) self... thou hast given unmistakable expression to—by presenting her with that best of all precious things'.

statements.claim: She accused: Narada eulogized her in Krishna's presence and he was gratified; if the sage had his reasons, why was the name of this unfortunate one uttered in that connection?
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 (vv.10-11): 'Narada also eulogised her in thy presence, and thou surely wert also gratified having heard that eulogy... why was it that the name of this unfortunate one was uttered in that connection?'

statements.claim: She said if she must repent for tasting the sweet liquor of his love she would rather have nothing to do with it, asked his permission, and declared she could not have believed even in a dream that he would honor another above her.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 (vv.12-13): 'if I am to repent for having tasted the (sweet) liquor of thy love, it is better I should have nothing to do with it? Be kindly pleased to accord me thy permission... I could not have believed even in my dream, that thou hast honored some body else more than myself'.

statements.claim: She charged that perhaps Narada had conceived a love for her rival but her grief was Krishna's presence in the scene, and that dishonored she no longer desired to live, her source of protection having become her source of fear.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 (vv.14-16): 'It may be that the sage Narada of incomparable powers has conceived a love for her (Rukshmini), but O lord, the cause of my grief in this, is thy presence in the scene... thus dishonored, I do not desire to live any longer. My source of protection has been turned to-day into my source of fear'.

statements.claim: She recalled his earlier assurance, 'O daughter of Satrajit, know that there is no wife of mine dearer to me than thyself', and asked what had become of it.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 v.22: 'Thou didst tell me in days gone by,—'O daughter of Satrajit, know that there is no wife of mine dearer to me than thyself'—What of that assurance! Or who cares to remember it!'

statements.claim: She called him a cheat and knave, fickle, deceiving and partial to her rival, claiming to have read his secret thoughts by his articulations and features, his tongue honeyed but too guileful.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 (vv.25-26): 'I did not know thee hence-before to be so much of a cheat and a knave; but now I have come to know thee as fickle, deceiving, and partial to my rival... I have read thy innermost and secret thoughts, O thief, by thy articulations and thy features and signs... it is thy tongue only that is honeyed, but thou art too guileful'.

statements.claim: Krishna consoled her, saying the sage Narada of unimpeachable deeds gave the flower to Rukmini out of generous feeling or regard for her to please Krishna — but he did not give it with his own hands.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 (vv.27-28 and passage): 'know me to be thine entirely... in order to please me the sage Narada of unimpeachable deeds gave that Parijata flower to her (Rukshmini) in my presence, merely out of generous feelings or regard for her; (but I did not give it with my own hands)'.

statements.claim: Krishna vowed: 'What to speak of a single flower — I shall fetch that best of all trees, the Parijata tree itself, from the gardens of paradise, and keep it in thy mansion... this shall be my foremost concern.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 pack excerpt: 'What to speak of a single flower, I shall fetch that best of all trees namely the Parijata tree itself, from the gardens of paradise, and keep it in thy mansion.'... 'so be it, then; this shall be my foremost concern.'

DKS_0224.notes: Satyabhama's long speech and Krishna's consolation track Harivamsha 1.124 (Dutt) closely, nearly verbatim in places. The closing paragraph ('the whole tree it had come from, uprooted and planted in her own courtyard') is connective summary — the source promise is to fetch the tree and keep it in her mansion; no discrepancy counted.

statements.claim: Narada was preparing to take his leave when Krishna stopped him with an errand to heaven.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 v.1: 'finding that the sage Nārada was desirous of departing, spoke to him thus'.

statements.claim: Krishna asked Narada to go to heaven, interview the courtiers of the slayer of Tripura, and remind Pakasasana (Indra) of their ancient brotherly love, as a request, not a command.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 (vv.2-3): 'having repaired to heaven and there interviewed the courtiers of that intelligent slayer of Tripura... remind Pakasasana of all our ancient brotherly love that thou knowest—inform him not as my command but as my request'.

statements.claim: Krishna's message described the Parijata as the tree created by Kasyapa in days gone by for Aditi's happiness, bestowing religious merit and unbounded prosperity, given as a gift by the very virtuous goddesses in fulfillment of their vows; his wives, hearing of it, desired to give it away in turn for merit and for his gratification, so Indra should send it down to Dwaraka, to be restored to heaven after the ceremony of presentation.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 (vv.4-8): the Pārijāta tree 'which the illustrious and virtuous Kasyapa... created in days gone by for the sake of Aditi's happiness, that most excellent of all trees that bestows religious merit, and unbounded prosperity... given... by the very virtuous goddesses in fulfilment of their vows... my wives also hearing of the presentation of that tree, desire to give it away... Ask him therefore to send down to Dwarvati that best of all trees the Pārijāta; and it shall be restored to heaven after the ceremony of presentation is over'.

statements.claim: Krishna added that Narada should exert himself to persuade Indra, which would bring into prominence his ambassadorial abilities.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 (vv.9-10): 'thou shalt also so put forth thy endeavours that the lord of the immortals be persuaded to give over the excellent Parijata tree... this will also bring into prominence what ambassadorial abilities thou dost possess'.

statements.claim: Narada agreed to carry the message but said he was sure Indra would never part with the Parijata tree.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 (vv.11-12): 'Very well,—I shall thus speak to the lord of the gods... but I am sure he will never part with the Parijata tree'.

statements.claim: Narada recalled that the gods and Danavas had obtained the Parijata by churning the ocean with the Mandara mountain; the creator had wanted to take the tree away with Mandara, and Indra personally entreated Mahadeva, saying it was Sachi's sporting tree; Mahadeva granted the boon and did not bring the Parijata to the Mandara.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 (vv.13-17): 'The Danavas and the gods obtained this Parijata tree by throwing the Mandara mountain into the waters of the ocean... Sakra personally going to Sankara told him:—'This is Sachi's sporting tree, and may be allowed to remain in her gardens'... Mahadeva granted him the boon saying 'Let it be so then'... he did not also bring the Parijata tree to... the Mandara mountain'.

statements.claim: To please Uma, Hara created on the dales of the Mandara a self-luminous forest of Parijata trees extending over four miles, into which neither sun, moon nor wind could penetrate, where heat and cold reigned at the pleasure of the mountain's daughter; none could enter it but the god and goddess, their followers, and Narada himself; the Parijatas showered gems and jewels at a mere thought, and Shiva's attendants enjoyed the forest with his permission.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 (vv.18-23): 'Hara, in order to please his wife Umā, created on the dales of the Mandara mountain a forest of the Parijata trees extending over full four miles... neither the rays of the sun, nor the cool beams of the moon, nor even the breaths of the wind can penetrate... self-luminous, and heat and cold reign there at the pleasure of the mountain's daughter... Excepting the mighty god and goddess and their followers and myself... nobody... can enter that charming wood... the Pārijātas shower all kinds of best gems and jewels... as soon as they are merely thought of... troops of the illustrious attendants of Siva, also enjoy that beautiful forest'.

statements.claim: Narada told how the Daitya Andhaka, puffed up by a boon, transgressed into that forest and was slain by Hara, though ten times as powerful as Vritra and incapable of being slain by any created being.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 (vv.27-28): 'a mighty and dreadful Daitya of cruel motives by name Andhaka, who was puffed up with arrogance through the virtues of a boon... ventured to transgress into that forest... He was slain by... Hara, although he was ten times as powerful as Vritra and incapable of being slain by any created being'.

statements.claim: Narada concluded that the thousand-eyed Indra would never give the tree, obtained with such great difficulty, since it bestows all desires on Sachi and fulfills Indra's own wishes.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 (vv.29-30): 'the thousand eyed god Indra will never give thee, the Pārijāta tree obtained with great difficulty. That best of trees always bestows on the goddess Sachi all her desires, as well as... it fulfils the wishes of the highly powerful Indra'.

statements.claim: Krishna answered: if the lord of the immortals does not give the Parijata tree at Narada's request, he will hurl his mace at his breast.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 pack excerpt: 'If that lord of the immortals do not give the Parijata tree at thy request, I shall then hurl my mace at his breast.'

DKS_0225.notes: The entire message, Narada's recollection of the churning and of Shiva's Parijata forest on Mandara, the Andhaka anecdote, and the closing ultimatum are grounded in Harivamsha 1.125 (Dutt). 'As if the promise required the one thing no man could simply take' and the closing framing of plea-plus-warning are connective narration.

statements.claim: In the court of heaven, the sage Narada stood before Indra, the king of the gods, carrying Krishna's request for the Parijata tree
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.127 (Dutt): the whole chapter is Narada relaying Krishna's demand to Indra and Indra's answer ('Narada's Advice and Indra's Answers').

statements.claim: The Parijata bloomed in Indra's own pleasure garden, the Nandana forest, and its blossoms were said to scent the very air of heaven
statements.evidence: 1.127 does not name the garden; the Nandana pleasure-park identification is corroborated by HV 1.220 elsewhere in the corpus, and 'said to scent' is hedged atmosphere.

statements.claim: Krishna expected indulgence because he was Indra's younger brother, and he sent his words with courtesy
statements.evidence: HV 1.127: 'I am the younger brother of Indra and therefore I claim indulgence at his hands.'

statements.claim: Neither gods nor Gandharvas, rakshasas nor asuras, nor the foremost of serpents would turn Krishna from his pledge
statements.evidence: HV 1.127: 'Neither the gods, nor the Gandharvas, nor the Rakshas, nor the Asuras, nor the foremost of the Pannagas, will succeed in attempting to thwart me out of my pledge.'

statements.claim: If Indra refused when asked in friendship, Krishna would come to heaven and hurl his mace at the breast of the king of the gods, where Sachi lays fragrant ointments
statements.evidence: HV 1.127: 'If Purandara thus requested by thee in a conciliatory manner does not give the Parijata tree to me, then will I hurl my mace at the breast of Purandera on which Sachi besmears fragrant ointments.'

statements.claim: Indra had forgiven Krishna again and again, remembering only that Krishna was his brother
statements.evidence: HV 1.127: 'Krishna committed many acts offensive and insulting to me; I did put up with them all only remembering that he is my brother.'

statements.claim: When the Khandava forest burned, Krishna drove Arjuna's chariot and kept Indra's rain clouds away, letting the fire rage on
statements.evidence: HV 1.127: 'On the occasion of the burning of the Khandava forest when he drove Arjuna's chariot, he prevented my clouds from extinguishing the raging conflagration.'

statements.claim: In lifting Govardhana Krishna acted against Indra's interests by setting aside the worship owed to the lord of rain
statements.evidence: HV 1.127: 'He committed an act unpleasant and inimical to my interests by lifting up the Govardhana mountain.' (The worship-motivation is connective gloss on the established episode.)

statements.claim: Asked to help Indra against Vritra, Krishna answered that he was impartial and looked equally on all creatures, so Indra slew Vritra with the strength of his own arms
statements.evidence: HV 1.127: 'he replied to me saying—I am impartial and look equally upon all creatures. Then I slew Vritra with the help of the strength of my own arms.'

statements.claim: In every war between gods and asuras Krishna fought as his own will pleased, ignoring the authority of the king of heaven
statements.evidence: HV 1.127: 'when ever war breaks out between the gods and the Asuras Krishna always fights as it pleases his sweet will (ignoring my authority altogether).'

statements.claim: Narada had tried to turn Krishna from this course, showing him reason after reason, but Krishna paid heed to none
statements.evidence: HV 1.127: 'I showed him numerous reasons (for not taking down the Parijata tree), but he paid no heed whatever to them... still his mind did not change.'

statements.claim: Narada counselled Indra that it was better to allow the Parijata to be transplanted to Dwaraka than to let a quarrel split the house of heaven
statements.evidence: HV 1.127: 'it seems to me better to allow the Parijata to be transplanted to Dwarka.' (The 'quarrel splitting the house' is framing.)

statements.claim: Kashyapa and Aditi, parents of the brothers, had gone into the waters on a sojourn, and the matter should rightly have been laid before them
statements.evidence: HV 1.127: 'Our father, the almighty Kasyapa, together with our mother Adity has gone for a sojourn into the waters. This matter ought to be laid before them.'

statements.claim: Krishna had abused his elder brother, at the urging of his wife
statements.evidence: HV 1.127: 'my brother Krishna... has, through the instigation of his wife, abused me his elder brother.'

statements.claim: Indra cried 'Fie on women, and fie on the influence of arrogance, when even Vishnu, instigated by his wife, insults me this day'
statements.evidence: HV 1.127: 'fie on women, and fie on the influence of arrogance, in as much as... even Vishnu, instigated by his wife, has this day insulted me.'

statements.claim: Brahma and the parents had taught that there is no friend like a brother, and a well-behaved brother is dearer than thousands of sons
statements.evidence: HV 1.127: 'Brahma told me... that a well-behaved and wise brother is to me esteemed more than thousands of sons and wives... there is no friend like the brothers.'

statements.claim: The asuras fought Indra because they were not his brothers; only a brother could wound him so
statements.evidence: HV 1.127: 'The Danavas of sinful propensities fight with me because they are not my brothers.' ('Only a brother could wound him so' is connective.)

statements.claim: Indra would not begin a rupture among kin; the matter should be set before the parents on their return
statements.evidence: HV 1.127: 'a rupture among our relatives is remote from my thoughts... This matter ought to be laid before them.'

statements.claim: Indra's final answer: 'Until I am conquered in a battle by Krishna, the wielder of the discus, I will not part with the Parijata tree... tell Achyuta that I am prepared for the quarrel'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (HV 1.127): 'Until I am conquered in a battle by the wielder of the discus Krishna, I will not, O foremost of sages, part with the Parijata tree... tell Achyuta that I am prepared for the quarrel.'

statements.claim: Narada bowed and left the court of heaven carrying the challenge back to Dwaraka, while Indra sat waiting for the brother who had promised to come
statements.evidence: Departure and waiting are scene-setting; the chapter excerpt ends with Indra's speech and does not narrate Narada's exit.
