statements.evidence: HV 1.238 (10-12): 'By that boon he got what he wanted and the great Asura Vajranabha lived in the city of Vajra... millions of demons lived in that city of Vajra, in his garden and in many charming branch cities... healthy, well-fed and contented.'

statements.claim: Elated by pride in his boon, Vajranabha told Indra: 'All the three worlds are the common property of the high-souled sons of Kashyapa. I wish to govern the three worlds. If you do not approve of my proposal, give me battle.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 (13-15), near-verbatim quotation of the source.

statements.claim: Indra consulted Brihaspati and answered that their father, the ascetic Kashyapa, was engaged in a sacrifice and would do what is fair after its termination.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 (16-17): 'Mahendra... consulted with Vrihaspati and said... our father, the ascetic Kashyapa, is now engaged in a sacrifice. After its termination he will do what is fair.'

statements.claim: Vajranabha carried the same demand to Kashyapa, who repeated Indra's words and told him to return to Vajra, live self-controlled, and wait for the sacrifice to end.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 (18-19): 'Kashyapa said what the king of gods had communicated... O son, go now to the city of Vajra and live there controlling yourself. After the termination of the Yajna I will do what is fair.'

statements.claim: Indra went secretly to Dwaraka and told Krishna everything Vajranabha had said.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 (20): 'Mahendra went to the city of Dwaravati... and communicated secretly to Vasudeva what Vajranabha had said.'

statements.claim: Krishna answered: 'My father's horse-sacrifice is at hand. When it is over, I will kill Vajranabha. But even the wind cannot enter his city unless he wishes it, so we will find our own way in.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 (20-23): 'the horse-sacrifice of Vasudeva is now at hand. After its termination I will kill Vajranabha... even the wind cannot enter into his city if Vajranabha does not wish it. At a convenient hour we will concert measures for entering there.' (Vasudeva is Krishna's father, so 'my father's horse-sacrifice' is accurate.)

statements.claim: During the horse-sacrifice the actor Bhadra pleased the assembled sages with his art and was asked to pray for a boon.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 (26-27): 'During the celebration of Vasudeva's sacrifice an actor, by name Bhadra, pleased the great saints with his beautiful acting. The leading Munis then asked him to pray for a boon.'

statements.claim: Prompted by Krishna's wish and as if urged by the goddess of learning, Bhadra asked to range freely over the earth and sky, to be slain by no creature mobile or immobile, to assume any form, never to be touched by age, and to find the sages always pleased with him.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 (28-32): 'as desired by Krishna and as if urged on by the goddess of learning, prayed for the following boon... may I range over the earth consisting of seven insular continents... range all over the sky... be not slain by all creatures mobile and immobile. May I assume any form... May not decrepitude overtake me and may the Munis always remain pleased with me.' (The story's list is selective, omitting the first boon about the food of the twice-born — not contradictory.)

statements.claim: The Munis said 'So be it,' and Bhadra wandered the cities of the demon kings performing, coming to Dwaraka on every festival day where the Yadavas received him.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 (33-35): 'the Munis said So be it... He began to show his performances in the cities of the Danava kings... On the occasion of every Parva, that great actor... used to come to Dwaraka adorned with the Yadavas.'

statements.claim: In heaven Indra told the swans — his brothers, begotten by Kashyapa, though carriers of the gods and the pious — of the great duty of killing the enemies of the gods.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 (36-37): 'Sakra... said to Dhartarashtra swans: O celestial birds, although you are the carriers of the gods and the pious, still you are our brothers on account of your being begotten by Kashyapa... Now the great duty of killing the enemies of the gods awa...' (source text truncated at this point but matches).

DKS_0243.notes: Grounded in HV 1.238. 'No enemy had ever been known to pass those walls' is rhetorical connective framing of the wind-proof city. Boon list summarized selectively but accurately.

statements.claim: The troupe's fame ran ahead of them in the lands of the demons, and the Asuras welcomed the actor with presents of jewels.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 (3-4): 'arriving there, the actors too, heard of before, excited their curiosity... With great delight they welcomed the actor with presents of jewels.'

statements.claim: In the city of Supura the citizens were so enchanted they begged for more.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 (5): 'the actor, who had obtained the boon, pleased highly the citizens of Supura with his dancing.' The delighted response is supported; 'begged for more' is an embellishment of their enthusiasm.

statements.claim: The troupe's newest players were Pradyumna, Gada, Shamba and other Yadava heroes in costumes, led by Bhadra, the actor granted the boon to wander the three worlds.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 (15-16): 'the Daityas, living in branch cities, took the Yadavas, disguised as actors, to the charming city of Vajra'; Bhadra's world-ranging boon is from HV 1.238 (29-32).

statements.claim: Vajranabha, having heard of the marvellous actors, sent a messenger to bring the actor in.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 (14): 'the king of Daityas had already heard of it. Now pleased he sent a messenger to bring the actor.'

statements.claim: The demons of the branch cities brought the troupe to Vajra, lodged them in a house built by the celestial architect, and supplied needed articles by the hundred.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 (15-17): 'the Daityas, living in branch cities, took the Yadavas... to the charming city of Vajra. For their accomodation, a beautiful house, built by the celestial architect, was offered, and necessary articles, by hundreds, were given them.'

statements.claim: Vajranabha set up a beautiful pavilion and made a festival with the actors; his family's women watched from behind a screen where they could see all, while he sat with his kinsmen.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 (18-20): 'having set up a beautiful pandal the great Asura, Vajranabha, made a great festival with the actors... having kept the women of his family behind a screen at a place from which they could see all, the great Asura himself sat with his kinsmen.'

statements.claim: First the instruments — bells, flutes, drums — then the women of the troupe sang the celestial Gandharva song Chhalikya, the music the Yadavas had brought down from heaven.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 (21-23): 'They first played various tunes on musical instruments, as Kansya, Venu, Muraja etc. Afterwards the women, brought by the Bhaimas, sang the Gandharva song Chhalikya'; its celestial origin is the corpus chain (DKS_0241: 'Krishna Brings the Celestial Chhalikya Song to the Yadavas').

statements.claim: They sang the descent of the Ganga in seven scales and three modes, in the raga Vasanta and its kin, and the Asuras rose again and again to please the actors.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 (24-25): 'with seven scales, Gandhara and others, three Gramas, and with Ragas, Vasanta and others, they sang sweetly the song of the sacred discension of Ganga... Asuras rose up again and again and pleased the actors.'

statements.claim: They performed the Ramayana: the birth of Vishnu for the destruction of Ravana, and how the sage Rishyashringa was brought to King Dasharatha.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 (6-7): 'They gave a performance of the great epic Ramayana: the birth of the incomparable Vishnu for the destruction of the king of Rakshasas (Ravana). How Lomapada and Dasharatha had brought for Shanta, the Muni Rishwashringa.' The story's phrasing compresses the well-known episode (Rishyashringa fetched, later serving Dasharatha's sacrifice) without contradicting it.

statements.claim: The demons were startled that actors could so resemble Rama, Lakshmana and Bharata, and repeatedly rose to give away necklaces of gold and vaidurya, bracelets and cloths.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 (8-13): 'the actors so perfectly personated the characters of Rama, Lakshmana, Shatrughna, Bharata... that even the elderly Danavas were startled... they repeatedly rose up, expressed their appreciation and gave away charming necklaces of gold and Vaidurja, bracelets and cloths.'

statements.claim: Pradyumna, in actor's guise, conducted the prologue with Gada and Shamba, and Rukmini's son sang the hymn of the Ganga's descent with beautiful gestures.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 (26): 'the powerful Pradyumna, who had assumed the guise of an actor, Gada and Shamva conducted the Nandi. After the termination of the Prologue Rukshmini's son sang the hymn, accompanied with beautiful gestures, of the descension of Ganga.' (Pradyumna is Rukmini's son — consistent.)

statements.claim: In the drama Rambhabhisara, Shura played Ravana, Monovati Rambha, Pradyumna Nalakuvara and Shamba his jester; by illusion the Yadavas conjured the scene of Kailasha and acted Nalakuvara cursing Ravana and consoling Rambha.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 (27-30): 'they began the performance of the drama Rambhabhisara, Shura acted the part of Ravana, Monovati represented Rambha, Pradyumna Nalakuvara and Shamva his Vidushaka. By their illusory powers the Yadavas represented the scene of Kailasha. They acted how the wicked Ravana was imprecated by Nalakuvara... and how Rambha was consoled.'

statements.claim: The Danavas gave costly garments, jewelled necklaces, sky-going cars, celestial elephants, sandal, aguru and scents, and the gem Chintamani which grants all that is thought of — until the demon lords were deprived of their riches and jewels, their women too.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 (31-37): 'They gave them costly apparels, jewelleries, necklaces set with costly jems... cars ranging in the sky, elephants coursing in the etherial region, cool and celestial sandal, Agura, and other scents and the valuable jem Chintamani which gives all that is thought of. Giving away presents in this way at every scene those Danavas were deprived of their riches and jewels. Even the women of the Danava-Chiefs shared the same fate.' ('Treasuries ran dry' is the source's 'deprived of their riches' rendered vividly.)

statements.claim: Behind the screen Prabhavati received Suchimukhi's message: she had gone to Dwaraka, seen Pradyumna secretly, told him of Prabhavati's love, and he had appointed this evening to meet her — for the Bhaimas never speak untruth.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 (38-41): 'Prabhavati's friend Suchimukhi said to her... I had gone to the charming city of Dwaraka... I saw Pradyumna there secretly and told him about your love for him... Pleased he has appointed this evening for meeting you... the Bhaimas never speak an untruth; verily to-day you will meet your love.' (Suchimukhi is the goose addressed in the following verse.)

DKS_0244.notes: Grounded in HV 1.240. 'The city of Vajra was impossible to enter / even the wind could not pass unless willed' rests on HV 1.238 (23), carried by the corpus chain. Only flourish: Supura citizens 'begged for more'. Performance details map 1:1 to the source.

statements.claim: After Kashyapa's sacrifice ended, the gods and Asuras returned to their habitations.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 (1): 'After the termination of the sacrifice of Kashyapa... the gods and Asuras repaired to their respective habitations.'

statements.claim: Vajranabha went to Kashyapa to set the conquest of the three worlds in motion and received a warning.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 (2): 'After the end of the sacrifice Vajranabha too, desirous of conquering the three worlds, went to Kashyapa who told him...'

statements.claim: Kashyapa's warning: Sakra is the eldest and foremost, endued with ascetic power, devoted to the Brahmanas, grateful, king of the whole world, refuge of the good and pious, ruling because he works for the well-being of all creatures; Vajranabha will not vanquish him but will himself be killed, as one who rouses a serpent is destroyed in no time.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 (3-6), near-verbatim: 'Sakra is the eldest of you all and the foremost in accomplishments... Because he is engaged in the well-being of all creatures he has obtained this sovereignty over the world. O Vajranabha, you will not be able to vanquish him but yourself will be killed. As one who excites the anger of a serpent meets with his own destruction, so you will in no time be destroyed.'

statements.claim: Vajranabha refused his father's counsel, saluted Kashyapa, and began arrangements, gathering kinsmen, warriors and friends, first setting out to conquer the region of the celestials.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 (7-9): 'as a man, desirous of meeting with death... does not take medicine so Vajranabha did not approve of the words of Kashyapa. Having saluted Kashyapa... he collected his kinsmen, warriors, and friends. He first set out for conquering the region of the celestials.'

statements.claim: Indra and Upendra had sent the swans, birds begotten by Kashyapa and brothers of the gods, to bring about Vajranabha's destruction.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 (10): 'the highly powerful deities Indra and Upendra had sent the Swans there for bringing about Vajranabha's destruction'; their Kashyapa-begotten brotherhood is from HV 1.238 (36-37).

statements.claim: Learning from the swans that Vajranabha was marching, the Yadavas worried: Vajranabha will be killed by Pradyumna, but Vajranabha's daughter and Sunabha's daughters, their devoted wives, are all with child and near delivery.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 (11-14): 'the high-souled... Yadus thus consulted... Forsooth Vajranabha will be killed now by Pradyumna. But Vajranabha's daughter and Sunabha's daughters are their devoted wives. They are all enciente and the time for their delivery is near at hand.'

statements.claim: The gods promised through the swans: you will have beautiful sons like Kama, who even in the womb will master the Vedas with their auxiliaries, grow to youth at once, and master every future topic and scripture.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 (15-17), near-verbatim.

statements.claim: In Vajra, Prabhavati bore Pradyumna a son, omniscient and youthful like his father; after a month Chandravati bore Chandraprabha, resembling Gada; and Gunavati bore Gunavan — all youthful and omniscient.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 (19-21): 'Prabhavati gave birth to a son, omniscient and youthful after his father. The son Chandraprabha, resembling Gada, whom Chandravati gave birth to after a month... Gunavati too gave birth to a similiarly beautiful son by name Gunavan, youthful and omniscient.'

statements.claim: The boys mastered every shastra and moved about the palace turrets, shown to the Daityas by the desire of Indra and Upendra.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 (22-23): 'These Yadu boys began to grow up... mastering all the Shastras. They used to move about on the turrets of the palaces and at the desire of Indra and Upendra they were seen (by the Daityas).'

statements.claim: The Daityas stationed in the sky told Vajranabha, who cried 'Arrest them who have trespassed into my house'; soldiers guarded all quarters amid cries to seize and kill them, and the mothers wept.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 (24-27): 'As soon as they saw them the Daityas, stationed in the sky... communicated it to Vajranabha... Vajranabha said: Arrest them who have trespassed into my house... the soldiers guarded all the quarters... exclamations, Arrest them speedily kill them. Hearing it the mothers, fond of sons, began to weep in fear.'

statements.claim: Pradyumna reassured them: so long as we are alive and firm, the Daityas can do nothing to us.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 (28-29), near-verbatim.

statements.claim: Pradyumna told Prabhavati her father, uncles, brothers and kinsmen waited with clubs; for her sake they deserve respect, but the time is dreadful — if they endure they die, if they fight they succeed — and asked her to consult her two sisters, being under her orders.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 (30-33), near-verbatim.

statements.claim: Prabhavati, kneeling and weeping with hands on her forehead, urged him to take up arms: if he survives he will see his wife and sons; remember the honourable Rukmini and Aniruddha; a great rishi booned her a blameless life, no widowhood and living sons, and she hopes his words will not be falsified; she rinsed her mouth and placed a sword in his hands.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 (34-38): 'Placing her hands on her forehead and kneeling down Prabhavati, weeping, said... take up your arms and protect yourself. If you yourself survive you will see your wife and sons. Remember the honarable Vaidarbhi and Aniruddha... the great and intelligent Rishi had conferred on me the boon that I would lead a blameless life for ever, would not be a widow and my sons would live... Saying this and rinsing her month... handed over a sword to Rukshmini's son.' (Vaidarbhi = Rukmini.)

DKS_0245.notes: Grounded in HV 1.243 with near-verbatim dialogue. The opening's 'went home to prepare' before visiting Kashyapa is a light connective reordering of verse 2 (he goes to Kashyapa straight after the sacrifice).

statements.claim: From Garuda's back Krishna saw his own house of hundreds of palaces, the sable-hued palace, with a million white jewelled pillars, a gate of gems lustrous as fire and golden seats set here and there.
statements.evidence: HV 1.246 (1-8): 'saw his own house consisting of hundreds of palaces. He saw there a million of white jewelled pillars, a gate with jems lustrous like fire and a number of effulgent golden seats placed here and there... sable-hued palace.'

statements.claim: For his court a great palace entirely of gold with crystal pillars was made, ringed by lakes full of lotuses and fragrant red lotuses, maddened peacocks and coels, with golden and jewelled stairways.
statements.evidence: HV 1.246 (5-6): 'a huge palace had been made entirely of gold with crystal pillars. He also saw beautiful and big lakes, with its water full of lotuses and fragrant red lotuses resorted to by maddened peacocks and coels, with golden and jewelled stairs.'

statements.claim: Viswakarma enclosed the whole with stone walls a hundred yards high girded with ditches, on a plot half a yojana on every side, measured against Indra's palace.
statements.evidence: HV 1.246 (7-8): 'That house was encircled by Viswakarma with stone walls hundred yards high which were girt with ditches. After the measurement of Indra's palace the celestial Architect had built that house on a plot of land measuring half a yojana on all sides.'

statements.claim: Krishna blew the Panchajanya: the sound made his enemies' hairs stand erect, stirred the ocean, resounded through the sky, and seemed most wonderful.
statements.evidence: HV 1.246 (9-10): 'He then blew his conch the sound of which made the hairs of his enemies stand erect. At that sound the ocean was greatly agitated and the sky resounded. Indeed it appeared very wonderful... Hearing the sound of Panchajanya conch-shell...'

statements.claim: At the conch's sound and the sight of Garuda, the Kukuras and Andhakas were freed from sorrow; beholding Keshava shining like the sun with conch, discus and club, the citizens beat trumpets, blew bugles and raised leonine shouts.
statements.evidence: HV 1.246 (10-13): 'Hearing the sound of Panchajanya conch-shell and seeing Garuda all the members of the Kukura and Andhaka families were freed from sorrow. Beholding Keshava effulgent like the sun, with conch-shell, discus, and club in his hands, seated on Garuda, the citizens attained to an excess of joy. Thereupon they began to beat trumpets, blew bugles and set up leonine shouts.'

statements.claim: Beholding the slayer of Madhu, the Kukuras, Andhakas and other Dasharhas approached him with great delight.
statements.evidence: HV 1.246 (13): 'beholding the slayer of Madhu the Kukuras, Andhakas and other Dasharhas began to approach him with great delight.'

statements.claim: King Ugrasena, placing Vasudeva before him, repaired to Vasudeva's palace with conches and trumpets; Devaki, Rohini and Ahuka's wives moved about with joy.
statements.evidence: HV 1.246 (14-15): 'Placing Vasudeva before him and accompanied with the sound of conch-shells and trumpets, the king Ugrasena repaired to Vasudeva's palace. Devaki, Rohini and Ahuka's wives began to move about with joy in their own houses.'

statements.claim: Hari, whom Indra and the other gods serve, arrived at the appointed house; alighting at the entrance he showed respect to the Yadus and, honored by Balarama, Ahuka, Gada and Pradyumna, entered his residence with the mountain of jewels.
statements.evidence: HV 1.246 (16-18): 'Hari whom serve Indra and other gods, arrived at the appointed house. Having got down at the entrance... showed proper respect to all the Yadus. And himself honored by Rama, Ahuka, Gada, Pradyumna and others he entered into his residence with the mountain of jewels.'

statements.claim: Rukmini's son Pradyumna carried in the Parijata, the tree most favourite of Indra; by its power the heroes saw the beauty of their own persons and delighted.
statements.evidence: HV 1.246 (19-20): 'Rukshmini's son Pradyumna himself took to the house the Parijata the most favourite of Indra's trees. By the power of the Parijata the heroes saw the beauty of their own persons and attained to great delight.'

statements.claim: Eulogized by the Yadu chiefs, Krishna entered the house Viswakarma built, placed the jewel-mountain in his inner apartment, and with the Vrishnis worshipped and planted the Parijata in its proper place.
statements.evidence: HV 1.246 (21): 'Thus eulogized by the delighted Yadu chiefs Krishna entered into the house constructed by Viswakarma. Having placed that mountain of jems with summits in his inner appartment Achyuta... united with the Vrishnis, worshipped the celestial tree Parijata and planted it in its proper place.'

statements.claim: With his kinsmen's permission Krishna honored all the maidens brought from Naraka's house with raiments, ornaments, maid-servants, riches and objects of enjoyment; they had already been received by Devaki, Rohini, Revati and Ahuka's wives.
statements.evidence: HV 1.246 (22-24): 'obtaining the permission of his own kinsmen Keshava... honored all the maidens he had brought from Naraka's house with raiments, ornaments, maid-servants, riches and objects of enjoyment. Those maidens had already been received honourably by Devaki, Rohini, Revati and Ahuka's wives.'

statements.claim: By his good fortune Satyabhama ruled over all the females, while Rukmini, Bhishmaka's daughter, was in charge of the relatives, and Krishna allotted each woman her own house, tank and garden.
statements.evidence: HV 1.246 (25-28): 'By his good luck Satyabhama ruled over all the females, and Bhishmaka's daughter Rukshmini was in charge of the relatives. Krishna allotted to each of those women, separate houses, tanks, and gardens.'

DKS_0246.notes: Grounded in HV 1.246, nearly scene-by-scene. Final paragraph (Parijata 'changing the air of the city', jewel-mountain 'like a promise kept') is connective close on supported elements. 'Dwarka'/'Dwaraka' spelling variance only.

statements.claim: Balarama, Rohini's son, grew dreadful like Kala at the end of a cycle, drew enemies close with his ploughshare and ground them with his mace.
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (65-66): 'when Rohini's son engaged in the battle his form grew dreadful like Kala, as if desirous of consuming all, at the end of a cycle. Ranging in the battle-field the highly powerful Baladeva... drew the enemies with his plough-share and grinded them with his mace.'

statements.claim: Pradyumna thwarted the fighting Danavas with his arrows; Krishna, dark as a mass of collyrium, blew his conch and fought in many ways with conch, discus and club.
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (67-68): 'The highly powerful Pradyumna... thwarted the fighting Danavas with his arrows. Blowing his conch-shell Janarddana, the holder of conch-shell, discus and club, resembling a mass of collyrium, fought in many ways.'

statements.claim: Garuda struck the Daityas with his wings and mutilated them with beak and nails, despatching them to Yama's abode; overpowered by those four heroes the Asura army fled.
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (69-70): 'Having struck the Daityas with his wings and mutilated them with his nails and beak the intelligent son of Vinata despatched them to the abode of Yama. Thus assailed with a downpour of arrows and overpowered by those four heroes the dreadful army of the Asuras fled away.'

statements.claim: Seeing his host routed, Rudra's follower Jvara, the fever-demon, came walking to the field sighing like a maniac; he had three legs, three heads, six arms, nine faces and a consuming weapon, like Yama himself.
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (71-72): 'Rudra's follower, Jvara, came walking to the battle-field sighing again and again like a maniac. He had three legs, three heads, six arms, nine faces and a consuming weapon and was like Yama himself.'

statements.claim: He roared like thousands of muttering clouds, yawned and dozed, hairs erect, eyes filthy; making his face terrible, he told the wielder of the ploughshare he would not return with his life.
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (73-75): 'He roared like thousands of muttering clouds, sighed and yawned repeatedly, was dozing, had his hairs erect and eyes filthy... Why are you elated with the pride of your strength? Do you not see that I have come to the battle-field? Wait a few moments. While you have come before me in the battle-field you will not return with your life.'

statements.claim: Smiling and showing a fist dreadful as the fire of dissolution, Jvara ran at Balarama, who wheeled in thousands of circular ways so the demon found no opening.
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (76): 'smiling and showing his fist dreadful like the fire of dissolution Jvara ran towards Halayudha. Rohini's son however began to move about so quickly in thousands of circular ways that Jvara could not find an opportunity.'

statements.claim: Jvara's consuming weapon struck Balarama's breast, fell onto Mount Sumeru shattering it into pieces, and the remnant left on his breast began to consume Krishna's elder brother.
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (77-78): 'hurled his consuming weapon which fell on his breast. Dropping on the summit of the mount Sumeru from Rama's breast that burning weapon shattered it into pieces. Krishna's elder brother was however being consumed by the remnant that was left on his breast.'

statements.claim: Sighing and yawning ceaselessly, eyes dilated, hairs erect, senses bewildered, almost losing consciousness, Balarama cried to Krishna: 'I am being consumed... How shall I be saved?'
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (79-84): 'His eyes were dilated, hairs stood erect and all his senses were bewildered... almost losing consciousness Haladhara said to Krishna:—O Krishna, O large-armed Krishna, O thou the giver of protection, I am being consumed, nay I am being consumed completely. How shall I be saved?'

statements.claim: Krishna smiled, said 'No fear', and embraced his brother, who was thereby saved from being burnt.
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (84): 'Krishna... smilingly said:—No fear. Saying this he embraced Halayudha. He was then saved by loving Krishna from being burnt.'

statements.claim: The slayer of Madhu, highly angered, told Jvara: 'Come and fight with me. Show me the full extent of your strength and power in this battle.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (84): 'Having saved Rama from being consumed the slayer of Madhu, Vasudeva, highly angered, said to Jvara:—O Jvara, come and fight with me. Show to me the extent of your strength and power in this battle.'

DKS_0247.notes: Grounded in HV 1.270 (Sonitpura battlefield per pack index; story leaves the field unnamed). Opening and closing lines are connective framing of supported battle events.

statements.claim: Recap: Jvara came to protect the routed Asura army; his burning weapon fell on Balarama's breast and consumed him; Krishna saved his brother with an embrace and the fire went out.
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (70-84), fully present in this pack: 'with a view to protect them Rudra's follower, Jvara, came walking to the battle-field... hurled his consuming weapon which fell on his breast... Krishna's elder brother was however being consumed... he embraced Halayudha. He was then saved by loving Krishna from being burnt.'

statements.claim: Krishna challenged Jvara to show the extent of his strength and power in the battle.
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (84): 'O Jvara, come and fight with me. Show to me the extent of your strength and power in this battle.'

statements.claim: Jvara, three-legged, three-headed, six-armed, nine-faced, follower of Rudra, discharged his great burning weapon with his right hand at Krishna's body; Krishna felt the burning for a few moments and then the fire went out.
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (85-86): 'Jvara, with his right hand, discharged his great burning weapon on Krishna's body. At this the powerful Krishna, the foremost of strikers, experienced a burning sensation for a few moments. Immediately after the fire was put out.' ('The way fire dies when it meets what it cannot consume' is connective imagery.)

statements.claim: Jvara, with serpent-like long arms, struck Krishna on the neck and dealt a blow on his breast; a great encounter followed between the fever-demon and the foremost of men.
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (87-89): 'Jvara, with his serpent-like long arms, struck Krishna on the neck and then dealt a blow on his breast. Thus there took place a great encounter, in the battle-field, between Jvara and the highly energetic Krishna the foremost of men.'

statements.claim: The sound of their striking arms was like thunder striking a mountain summit.
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (89): 'The sound of the stricking of arms caused by Krishna and Jvara in that highly dreadful battle was like that of a thunder striking a mountain summit.'

statements.claim: In the midst of the fight were heard words as if one fighter instructed the other: 'Do not strike this way. Strike this way.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (90): 'Occasionally was heard Do not strike in this way: you should do it in this way.'

statements.claim: The Lord of the Universe, under the guise of a man, as if thinking he would come to an end, ground the sky-ranging, golden-adorned Jvara with his arms in a fearful struggle.
statements.evidence: HV 1.270 (91-93): 'that Lord of the Universe, under the guise of a man, thinking that he would come to an end, grinded the sky-ranging Jvara adorned with golden ornaments with his arms.' (The pestle-and-mortar simile and 'strength ran out like water from a broken jar' are narrative imagery for the grinding, which the source records.)

statements.claim: The two fought for a moment, and Krishna threw the broken Jvara down upon the earth, believing the field was won.
statements.evidence: HV 1.271 (1) (corpus-chain next event, in DKS_0249's pack): 'Considering Jvara, assailed with his arms, dead Krishna... threw him down on the surface of the earth.' Consistent with the close of 1.270.

statements.claim: Released from the crushing embrace, the fever-demon did not flee but entered Krishna's body.
statements.evidence: HV 1.271 (2): 'Released from his arms, Jvara, of incomparable energy, did not leave Krishna's body but entered into it.' (Presented here as cliffhanger leading to DKS_0249.)

DKS_0248.notes: Grounded in HV 1.270, with the closing possession taken from the immediately following HV 1.271 (canonical next event). 'Field emptied around them' is connective. 'Two most powerful beings... strokes that would have felled armies' is rhetorical amplification of the source's language, not a new fact.

statements.claim: Considering Jvara dead from the grinding of his arms, Krishna threw him down on the earth, but released from his grip the fever-demon of incomparable energy entered Krishna's body.
statements.evidence: HV 1.271 (1-2): 'Considering Jvara, assailed with his arms, dead Krishna... threw him down on the surface of the earth. Released from his arms, Jvara, of incomparable energy, did not leave Krishna's body but entered into it.'

statements.claim: Possessed by fever, Krishna's movements slackened; he repeatedly supported himself by touching the ground, was possessed by sleep, his steps slackened, hairs stood erect, and he sighed and yawned repeatedly.
statements.evidence: HV 1.271 (3-4): 'Possessed by Jvara (fever) of incomparable energy Krishna had his movements slackened and repeatedly supported himself by touching the ground. He was possessed by sleep, his steps were slackened and his hairs stood erect. He repeatedly sighed and yawned.'

statements.claim: The great Yogin, victor of enemy cities, regained his natural state only after a long time.
statements.evidence: HV 1.271 (5): 'the great Yogin Krishna, the victor of the enemy's cities, regained his natural state after a long time.'

statements.claim: Knowing himself possessed, Krishna created from his own energy a dreadful second Jvara, terrible to all creatures, for the destruction of the first.
statements.evidence: HV 1.271 (6-8): 'knowing himself possessed by Jvara Purosottama created another for its destruction. With his energy... created a dreadful Jvara, highly terrible unto creatures.'

statements.claim: The created fever seized the first Jvara by force, dragged him out of Krishna's body, and presented him before his maker — the fever was driven out by fever itself.
statements.evidence: HV 1.271 (8-9): 'Catching hold, by force, of the former Jvara the one, created by Krishna, presented it before him. Having thus driven out that Jvara from his body through one created by him...'

statements.claim: The angry Krishna struck Jvara down and was about to tear him to pieces; bewildered, Jvara cried 'O Janardana, it behooves you to protect me!'
statements.evidence: HV 1.271 (10): 'the highly powerful and angry Vasudeva struck him down on the ground and was about to tear him into pieces. Thereat Jvara, bewildered, said O Janarddana, it behoveth thee to protect me.'

statements.claim: An invisible voice from the sky commanded: 'O Krishna... the delight of the Yadavas, do not kill this Jvara. O sinless one, he is worthy of being protected by you.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.271 (11-12): 'an invisible voice was heard in the sky:—O Krishna, O large-armed Krishna, the enhancer of the delight of the Yadavas, do not kill this Jvara. O sinless one, he is worthy of being protected by thee.'

statements.claim: Hari, lord of the past, future and present, great preceptor of the world, let Jvara go.
statements.evidence: HV 1.271 (12): 'Thus addressed Hari, the lord of the past, future and present and the great preceptor of the world let Jvara off.'

statements.claim: Jvara prostrated with bent head at Krishna's feet and asked the boon that he alone be the fever in this world, with no other flourishing beside him.
statements.evidence: HV 1.271 (13-15): 'prostrating himself with bent head at Hrishikesha's feet Jvara said... I pray from thee for this boon only that I may be the only Jvara in this world and no one else may flourish.'

statements.claim: Krishna granted it: it is proper to confer a boon on one who prays; as before Jvara will be the only fever, and he whom Krishna created will dissolve into him.
statements.evidence: HV 1.271 (16-18): 'It is proper to confer a boon on one who prays for it. Besides you have sought my protection... As before you will be the only Jvara. May he, whom I have created, dissolve in me.'

statements.claim: Krishna told Jvara how he would range through the world, and promised that whoever, having saluted Krishna, attentively reads this account of the great battle will be freed from fever.
statements.evidence: HV 1.271 (19-28, 33-35): Krishna instructs how Jvara will range spread among creation mobile and immobile, and 'the man, who having saluted me, will attentively read this account of prowess displayed only by our arms in the great battle, will be freed from fever.'

statements.claim: Jvara, delighted, said 'So be it' and, saluting his master, left the battlefield.
statements.evidence: HV 1.271 (36-37): 'the highly powerful Jvara said:—So be it. Having thus obtained the boon and promised, Jvara, saluting Krishna, left the battle-field.'

DKS_0249.notes: Grounded in HV 1.271 with near-verbatim boon exchange. 'As everything made from him returns to him' is theological connective gloss on the created Jvara dissolving into Krishna. The story omits the detailed four-part division of fever among creatures — an omission, not a distortion.

statements.claim: An invisible voice spoke out of the sky and halted the killing: 'do not kill this Jvara. He is worthy of being protected by you.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (12): 'an invisible voice was heard in the sky:—"O Krishna... do not kill this Jvara... he is worthy of being protected by thee"'.

statements.claim: The war was between Krishna and the thousand-armed king Vana, Shiva's devoted servant, and Shiva's creatures fought for Vana — among them Jvara, the fever, who had been created by Hara.
statements.evidence: Arc context of ch. 271-272 (pack chain): Vana is Shiva's protégé whom Shiva defends; Jvara himself says 'Formerly I had been created by Hara the slayer of Tripura' (1.271.29-32).

statements.claim: Jvara entered Krishna's body: Krishna's movements slackened, his steps grew heavy, his hair stood on end, he yawned and sighed without cease and supported himself with one hand on the ground until, after a long time, the great yogi recovered.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (1-5): 'Released from his arms, Jvara... entered into it. Possessed by Jvara Krishna had his movements slackened... his hairs stood erect. He repeatedly sighed and yawned... supported himself by touching the ground... regained his natural state after a long time'.

statements.claim: Krishna created a second, more dreadful Jvara from his own energy, which seized the original by force and dragged it from Krishna's body.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (6-12): 'Purosottama created another for its destruction... created a dreadful Jvara, highly terrible unto creatures. Catching hold, by force, of the former Jvara... presented it before him... driving out that Jvara from his body'.

statements.claim: Krishna threw Jvara down on the earth and was about to tear him into pieces.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (11-12): 'the highly powerful and angry Vāsudeva struck him down on the ground and was about to tear him into pieces'.

statements.claim: Krishna, the lord of the past, present and future and the great preceptor of the world, let Jvara go; Jvara prostrated with bent head and asked to be the only Jvara in the world.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (13-18): 'Hari, the lord of the past, future and present and the great preceptor of the world let Jvara off. Thereupon prostrating himself with bent head... Jvara said... I may be the only Jvara in this world and no one else may flourish'.

statements.claim: Krishna granted the boon and said the counter-Jvara he had created would dissolve in him.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (17-18): 'May you fare well... You will have what you are praying for. As before you will be the only Jvara. May he, whom I have created, dissolve in me'.

statements.claim: Krishna instructed Jvara to divide into three parts — four-legged animals, immobile objects, human beings — with a fourth portion of the third part living among birds, appearing among mankind every day, after two, three and four days.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (19-28): 'divide yourself into three parts. With one do you possess the four-legged animals, with the second the immobile objects and with the third the human beings. And with the fourth portion of your third part you will always live in the midst of the birds... appearing every day, after two days, three days and four days you are to live amongst mankind'.

statements.claim: In trees Jvara would live as the insect and blight that withers leaves, in fruits as Aturya, in lotuses as frost, in the earth as drought/desert, in water as Neelika, in peacocks as the crest, in mountains as mineral, in cows as Khoraka.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (25-27): 'In trees you will live in the shape of an insect and the disease that withers up the leaves... in the fruits... like Aturya disease; in the lotuses like frost, in the earth like a desert, in the water like Neelikā, in the peacocks like the growing of the tuft, in the mountain like mineral and in the cows like Khoraka'.

statements.claim: With Jvara's sight and touch animals would lose their lives; only gods and men could withstand him.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (27-28): 'With your very view and touch the animals will be shorn of their lives. Only gods and men will be able to withstand you'.

statements.claim: Jvara saluted Krishna, said he was created by Hara the slayer of Tripura and, vanquished in battle, had become Krishna's servant.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (29-32): 'blessed I am for thy giving me soverignty over all creatures... Formerly I had been created by Hara the slayer of Tripura... Now vanquished by thee in battle I have become thy servant. Thou art now my master'.

statements.claim: Krishna declared that a man who salutes him and attentively reads the account of the great battle will be freed from fever; Jvara assented and left the battlefield.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.271 (33-37): 'the man, who having saluted me, will attentively read this account... will be freed from fever... Jvara... saluting Krishna, left the battle-field'.

DKS_0250.notes: Close to verbatim rendering of Harivamsha 1.271. 'The great battle came to a halt' and 'frost melts into the morning' are connective imagery; no unsupported facts.

statements.claim: Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna, riding Garuda like three fires, dispersed the Danava army with a downpour of arrows, and fire consumed thousands of Danavas.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (1-5): 'riding quickly Vinatā's son, those three (heroes), stationed in the battle-field like three fire-gods... Seated on Garuda's back those highly powerful three heroes assailed and dispersed the Dānava army with a downpour of arrows... consumed thousands of Dānavas'. The trio is Krishna, Baladeva and Pradyumna (1.274: Kartikeya 'drove towards Krishna, Baladeva and Pradyumna').

statements.claim: The survivors scattered, dropping coats of mail, swords, daggers, darts, leathern protectors and axes.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (6-8), Vana's speech enumerates exactly these abandoned items.

statements.claim: Vana shouted his fleeing soldiers back, appealing to their Daitya birth and life with Hara; the Danavas fled anyway, and only the Pramathas stood firm.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (6-11): Vana's rallying words given; 'the Dānavas, beside themselves with fear, paid no heed to them and fled away. Of the soldiers remaining there only the Pramathas stood firm'.

statements.claim: Kumbhanda, Vana's powerful minister and friend, also appealed to the Danavas in vain.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (12): 'Kumbhānda, Vāna's powerful minister and friend' makes the appeal; the Danavas flee before he finishes.

statements.claim: Seeing his soldiers routed, Shiva's eyes reddened with anger, and to protect Vana he stood on his lustrous car; Kartikeya ascended a car burning like fire; Rudra's car drawn by lions, devouring the sky, came like the full moon freed from clouds.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (12-17): 'Siva... had his eyes reddened with anger. And in order to protect Vāna, he stood on his lustrous car... Kumāra too ascended a car burning like... Powerful Rudra, ascending a car drawn by lions... looked like the full-moon freed from clouds'.

statements.claim: The car was surrounded by ghosts with faces of lions, tigers, serpents, horses, camels, asses, peacocks, rams, cats and sheep, variously dressed in bark or animal skins, some dwarfish and grim-visaged, blowing conch-shells and bugles, standing around Shankara.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (17-28): full catalog of the ghostly host given, including 'faces of lions... tigers... serpents... horses... camels... asses... peacocks... rams... cats... sheep', 'put on lion and tiger skins', 'blew conch-shells and bugles', 'stood encircling Shankara'.

statements.claim: Krishna rode Garuda to meet Rudra's car; Hara struck him with hundreds of winged arrows and Hari answered with the weapons given by Indra.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (29-31): 'Krishna, riding Garuda, proceeded to the battle-field... Hara... struck him in anger with hundreds, of winged arrows... Hari too, irate, took up most excellent weapons given by Indra'.

statements.claim: The duel shook the earth, terrified the elephants, scattered mountain summits, set the quarters ablaze, drew inauspicious cries from jackals, and Indra rained blood and fire-brands over the rear of Vana's army.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (32-37): 'the earth shook and the elephants trembled... mountains were covered with the water of streams; some had their summits scattered... quarters, sky and earth were as if all ablaze... dreadful-looking jackals began to emit inauspicious cries... Indra began to send down showers of blood and fire-brands'.

statements.claim: Brahma, knowing Rudra had entered battle, came encircled by celestials; Apsaras, Gandharvas, Yakshas, Vidyadharas, Siddhas and Charanas watched from the sky.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (33-37): 'the Grandfather... came there encircled by the celestials. The Apsaras, Gandharvas, Yakshas, Vidyadharas, Siddhas, and Chāranas, stationed in the sky, began to witness that encounter'.

statements.claim: Vishnu discharged Indra's weapon at Rudra; Hara answered with his dreadful fiery weapon; Krishna and the three other heroes were entirely covered with arrows.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.272 (37+): 'Vishnu discharged Indra's weapon at Rudra... Hara discharged the highly dreadful fiery weapon... Krishna and the three other heroes were entirely covered with arrows'.

DKS_0251.notes: 'Half of Vana's army was running, and the rest was burning' is a rhetorical opener (pack: fire consumed thousands, soldiers fled). 'Fire kindled by Krishna's discus': source passage names the fire as engendered by Krishna's arrows, though discus, plough-share and arrows were all used in the same assault — treated as connective detail, core claim (fire consuming thousands) supported. Closing 'sky turned the colour of the end of the world' is atmosphere.

statements.claim: After Krishna and Rudra retired from the field the battle continued, with Kartikeya (Guha) driving his car at Krishna, Baladeva and Pradyumna and striking them with hundreds of sharpened arrows.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (1-4): Janamejaya asks how the battle continued after the two retired; 'Stationed on the car brought by Kumbhānda, Guha (Kārtikeya) drove towards Krishna, Baladeva and Pradyumna and struck them with hundreds of dreadful and sharpened arrows'.

statements.claim: The three heroes, bathed in blood, fought like three fires; Kartikeya countered their three weapons (from Wind-god, Fire-god and Indra) with Shaila, Varuna and Savitri, but the Yadavas devoured all his weapons by illusion.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (4-8): 'Bathed in blood those three gods, like unto three fires, fought with Kumara... he, too, with three weapons, counteracted them and struck the Yadavas with three other weapons, namely Shaila, Vāruna and Sāvitri. They however, devoured, by virtue of their illusory powers, all the weapons'.

statements.claim: Guha, burning with effulgence and biting his lips, took up the dreadful Brahmashira weapon, blazing like a thousand suns and destructive of the world; creatures lost consciousness and the universe bewailed.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (8-12): 'Guha... took up the dreadful weapon Brahmashira... endued with the effulgence of a thousand suns and destructive of the world... the creatures lost their consciousness through its warmth... the whole universe bewailed'.

statements.claim: Keshava raised his discus, which clouded the lustre of the Brahmashira as clouds cover the sun, leaving it shorn of power and energy.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (9-12): 'Keshava, the slayer of Keshi, took up his discus... so that discus... clouded... that of Brahmashira weapon... shorn of its lustre, power and energy'.

statements.claim: Kartikeya hurled the golden, bell-set Sakti like the fire of dissolution; it flew into the sky, yawned and moved as if to slay Krishna; the gods feared Krishna would be consumed.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (13-16): 'He then discharged... that celestial burning Sakti set with bells... it went up into the sky, yawned and moved about with great force as if desirous of slaying Krishna... the gods... said—"Perhaps Krishna will be consumed"'.

statements.claim: Madhava shouted as if remonstrating and struck the Sakti down to the ground; 'Well done' rose from all sides and Indra with the celestials sent up a leonine shout.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (16-21): 'the highly powerful Mādhava shouted and as if remonstrating struck it down on the ground... arose from all sides exclamations "Well done! Well done!" And Vāsava together with the celestials sent up a leonine shout'.

statements.claim: As Krishna was about to discharge his discus, the beautiful goddess Kottavi, at Mahadeva's mandate, came naked to protect Kumara; Lamva, her eighth portion, stood between them like a golden Sakti.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (22-25): 'When Krishna... was about to discharge his discus, the beautiful Kottavi, at the mandate of Mahādeva, came there naked for protecting Kumāra. The eighth portion of the goddess, Lamvā, intervened between them like a beautiful golden Sakti'.

statements.claim: Krishna was baffled, told Kottavi to fly away, and she refused to put on her cloth for Kumara's protection; Krishna told her to take Guha away and, beholding the naked goddess, put away his discus.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (25-31): 'Krishna was baffled and said... "Fly away soon..."... Kottavi did not put on her cloth for protecting Kumāra... "Take Guha with you and fly away soon..."... beholding that naked goddess... the Lord Hari put away his discus'.

statements.claim: The goddess brought Guha before Hara; seeing Kartikeya released, Vana felt the urge to fight Madhava himself; his ghosts, Yakshas and soldiers fled, only Pramathas remained, and Vana marched out with his Daitya commanders while priests performed benedictory rites.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.274 (28-37): 'the goddess brought Guha before Hara... Vāna came to that place. When he saw Guha released... he felt an inclination for fighting himself with Mādhava... the ghosts, Yakshas and Vāna's soldiers fled away... only Pramathas remained there... his priests and other elderly persons... performed benedictory ceremonies'.

DKS_0252.notes: Faithful rendering of Harivamsha 1.274; no unsupported or contradicted claims found.

statements.claim: Vana shouted his boast: Krishna would not escape alive to Dwaraka; being of eight arms he could not fight Vana's thousand arms, which would multiply into a million.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (36-44): Vana's taunt given nearly verbatim: 'You will not escape from me to-day alive to Dwarakā... being of eight arms how you will be able to fight with me who have a thousand arms?... multiply into a million'.

statements.claim: Vana's words travelled like the dreadful waves of an ocean raised by wind, and his angry eyes shone like two suns rising.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (45-48): 'Vāna was thus roaring his words as if travelled all over like the dreadful waves of an ocean raised by the wind... his eyes, filled with anger, shone like two suns rising in the firmament'.

statements.claim: Narada laughed aloud from the palace top, as if sundering the sky, and moved about on his yoga seat, curious to see the battle.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (45-48, 66-76): 'Nārada so laughed aloud that as if the sky was sundered in twain. Seated on a Yoga seat that ascetic, filled with curiosity, moved about on all sides'; later he is 'sitting on the highest top of the palace'.

statements.claim: Krishna replied that heroes do not vaunt, that victory is not won by words, and bade Vana fight and be defeated.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (46-51): Krishna's speech given nearly verbatim, including 'The heroes do not vaunt thus... If by words victory is accomplished in a battle, you would have been no doubt victorious'.

statements.claim: Vana covered Krishna with burning arrows, parighas, nisthringsas, clubs, tomars, shaktis, maces and pattishas; proud thousand-armed Vana fought easily against eight-armed Keshava.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (52-58): 'Vāna, with great care, covered Krishna with burning arrows. With Parighas, Nisthringsas, clubs, Tomaras, Saktis, maces and Pattishas he completely covered Keshava... Although having eight-arms Keshava... fought with thousand-armed Vāna'.

statements.claim: The son of Bali (Vana), enraged at Krishna's superior training, discharged the celestial great weapon Brahma had created for Hiranyakashipu; darkness shrouded the quarters, dreadful omens appeared, and everything passed beyond perception.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (59-62): 'Bali's son was greatly worked up with anger. He then discharged that celestial great weapon... which Brahmā, by his ascetic powers, had formerly created for Hiranyakashipu. When that weapon was shot off all the quarters were enshrouded with darkness... everything was beyond the range of perception'.

statements.claim: The Danavas applauded Vana with 'Well done', the gods cried 'Alas', a dreadful rain of burning arrows fell, and wind, storm and clouds did not move while Keshava was burnt.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (60-62): 'The Dānavas applauded Wāna, saying "Well done! Well done!" and words of exclamations by the gods as "Alas!"... A dreadful downpour of burning arrows was caused... wind, storm or clouds did not move'.

statements.claim: Krishna took up Indra's weapon like inevitable death; the darkness was shorn away, the fire extinguished, the Danavas lost heart, and the gods laughed and roared like lions.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (63-65): 'the divine slayer of Madhu took up Indra's weapon like unto inevitable death... all the worlds were shorn of darkness, the fire was extinguished and the Dānavas completely lost their hearts... the gods began to laugh and roar like lions'.

statements.claim: With thunderbolt-like arrows from the Sarnga bow Krishna sundered Vana's car with horses and standards, then stripped off his crown, coat of mail, bow and shield, struck him on the breast with winged arrows, and Vana swooned.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (78-87): 'with arrows, like unto thunderbolts, shot off his Srānga bow Keshava sundered Vāna's car, with horses and standards, into pieces... separated from Vāna's person his highly lustrous crown, coat of mail, bow and shield... struck him on the breast with winged arrows. Cut to the very quick Vāna lost his consciousness and swooned away'.

statements.claim: Narada rose up clapping from the palace top, blessing his life for witnessing Damodara's prowess and urging Krishna to destroy Diti's son Vana.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (88-95): 'Nārada, who was sitting on the highest top of the palace, rose up with clapping and said "O great fortune!... wonderful prowess of Dāmodara... Destroy soon Diti's son Vāna"'.

statements.claim: The standards themselves fought — the gods' and Danavas' horses clashed, and Garuda and the peacock struck each other with wings, beaks and talons until Garuda seized the peacock's head.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (97-101): 'their standards, encountering each other, fought; so did the horses of the Devas and Dānavas. When Garuda and the peacock fought they struck each other with wings, beaks and talons... Garuda... caught hold of the peacock's head with his beaks'.

DKS_0253.notes: Near-verbatim to Harivamsha 1.275 (vv. 36-101). Pack passage is truncated after the peacock fight ('struck him wi[...]'); story's ending (seizing the peacock's head) matches the visible text.

statements.claim: The war had come to Sonitpura because Krishna's grandson Aniruddha had been carried away from Dwaraka and bound with serpent-nooses in Vana's palace.
statements.evidence: Arc background confirmed in Harivamsha 1.276 (pack of DKS_0256): 'The heroic Aniruddha being taken away stealthily the city of Dwārakā is filled with anxiety... waiting, bound with serpents, in the female appartment'; Aniruddha is Pradyumna's son, hence Krishna's grandson.

statements.claim: Garuda and the great peacock of Vana's banner fought in the air, striking with wings, beaks and talons, until the eagle caught the peacock's head in his beak.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (97-101): 'When Garuda and the peacock fought they struck each other with wings, beaks and talons... Garuda... caught hold of the peacock's head with his beaks'.

statements.claim: Vana rose again (the second time that day) after his chariot, horses and standards had been shattered by Krishna's Sarnga bow and his crown, mail, bow and shield lay scattered; he came on with a thousand armed hands.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (82-87, continued after truncation per evt_0356 summary): the car is sundered and arms stripped by Sarnga arrows (vv. 82-87); the canonical summary for evt_0356 has Krishna and Vana facing off again when the goddess intercedes.

statements.claim: Vana roared the boast again ('You will not escape me alive to Dwaraka... Being of eight arms, how will you fight me, who have a thousand?... arms multiply into a million') and Krishna answered that heroes do not vaunt.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (36-51): the full boast and Krishna's reply are in the pack passage (same chapter as this story's event).

statements.claim: Vana loosed the great weapon Brahma had created for Hiranyakashipu, darkening all quarters; Krishna took up Indra's weapon, dispelling the darkness; Vana then buried Krishna under maces and spears, and Krishna felled him with winged arrows so that he lost consciousness.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (59-65, 78-87): the Brahma-for-Hiranyakashipu weapon, its darkness, Indra's weapon counter, the maces/pattishas barrage and the winged-arrow swoon are all in the pack passage.

statements.claim: Narada rose up clapping on the palace roof, hailing Damodara's prowess and urging the destruction of Diti's son Vana.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.275 (88-95): Narada's praise from the palace top given in the pack passage.

statements.claim: When the discus was in Krishna's hand, the goddess Kottavi (Lamva) stepped between them unclothed, saying she had conferred a boon on Vana to protect him and would not see it broken.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt for evt_0356 (Harivamsha 1.275): 'Lamvā... appeared naked before Vasudeva... said:—"...I conferred on him a boon saying that I would protect him"'.

statements.claim: Krishna vowed to cut off Vana's thousand arms but spare his life — Vana would live with only two arms; the discus then cut off the arms, and Vana stood alive with two, the boon and vow both honoured.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt for evt_0356 (Harivamsha 1.275): Krishna said 'I will forsooth cut off to-day his thousand arms... Your son will live even if Vāna has two arms'; index summary: 'Krishna vows to cut off Vana's thousand arms, leaving only two, while sparing his life'.

statements.claim: Shiva, who had once promised Vana his protection, was watching the battlefield.
statements.evidence: Lead-in to evt_0357 (pack excerpt, Harivamsha 1.275): Mahadeva says 'I have promised Vāna protection'; DKS_0255 recounts the intercession.

DKS_0254.notes: Story opens by re-narrating the tail of the ch. 275 duel (boast, Brahma/Indra weapons, winged-arrow swoon, Narada's praise) that DKS_0253 already covered — the shared pack passage is truncated so the arm-cutting scene itself is supported only by the index/excerpt summary of evt_0356, which the story matches. No contradicted or unsupported claims.

statements.claim: Vana stood with only two hands left after his thousand arms fell; Krishna's discus was poised to end him when Shiva spoke.
statements.evidence: Follows evt_0356 (arms cut to two, life spared pending Shiva's plea) and evt_0357 excerpt: Krishna says 'I withdraw my discus. At thy request Vāna will live'.

statements.claim: Shiva said he had promised Vana protection long ago, that Vana had worshipped him, and bade Krishna desist and let him live.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Harivamsha 1.275): 'Mahadeva said:—"...I have promised Vāna protection... desist"'.

statements.claim: Krishna withdrew his discus, saying: 'I withdraw my discus... At your request, Vana will live.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Harivamsha 1.275): 'Krishna... "I withdraw my discus. At thy request Vāna will live"'.

statements.claim: Nandi, Shiva's bull, bade Vana dance before the lord, and the two-armed Vana danced; Shiva was pleased and told Vana to ask a boon.
statements.evidence: Index summary evt_0357: 'the armless Vana, bidden by Nandi, dances before Shiva and receives boons'; pack excerpt: 'Vāna... began to dance... Mahādeva... said:—"I am pleased with you... pray for a boon"'.

statements.claim: The boons made Vana Mahakala, chief of the Pramathas, Shiva's chosen attendant, and he left in the company of Rudra.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.276 (opening, in pack of DKS_0256): 'Having thus obtained a number of boons Vāna was highly pleased. And having attained to the dignity of Mahākala he went with Rudra'; index summary evt_0357: 'becoming the Pramatha chief Mahakala'.

DKS_0255.notes: Story honestly flags that the sources do not set down Vana's exact request in full — consistent with the pack (excerpt + index give the dance, the boon and the Mahakala outcome; ch. 275 passage itself is truncated before this scene). 'Nandi at Shiva's side', murmurs and dust settling are connective. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: The war began when Usha, daughter of Vana, carried away Aniruddha, Krishna's grandson, who was bound with serpent-nooses in her father's palace.
statements.evidence: Arc background; Harivamsha 1.276 passage (this pack): 'The heroic Aniruddha being taken away stealthily the city of Dwārakā is filled with anxiety... waiting, bound with serpents, in the female appartment'; the Usha-Aniruddha match is the arc of the corpus chain.

statements.claim: The serpents binding Aniruddha left his body like arrows the moment Garuda's shadow fell; Aniruddha saluted Krishna, Balabhadra, Garuda and his father Pradyumna, and Usha saluted bashfully.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.276 (8-17): 'Seeing Garuda, all the huge serpents... at once left him... dropped on the ground as arrows... Aniruddha saluted the highly powerful and illustrious Balabhadra... bowed unto the great Garuda... approached his father Pradyumna and saluted him. Ushā too... with bashfulness she also bowed'.

statements.claim: Narada asked Krishna to celebrate a marriage acquired by prowess for Aniruddha and to see the exchange of jokes between the bridal parties; the wedding was celebrated with Apsaras cutting jokes and Gandharvas singing.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.276 (18-28): Narada's request quoted; 'the Apsaras began to cut diverse jokes with him. The Gandharvas sang melodious and auspicious songs and the Apsaras danced'.

statements.claim: Krishna gave Vana's kingdom to Kumbhanda, who had asked only for safety, and promised him protection.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.276 (24-28): Kumbhānda seeks refuge; Krishna: 'You will now become the king of this kingdom. I confer this kingdom on you. Live you for ever under my protection'.

statements.claim: Kumbhanda told Krishna that Vana had cows in Varuna's keeping whose nectar-like milk makes a man highly powerful, invincible in battle and immortal.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.276 (34-35): 'Vāna has some cows in charge of Varuna. They give nectar-like milk, drinking which a man becomes highly powerful and invincible in battle'; pack excerpt: 'the kine of Vāna... drinking whose milk a man becomes immortal'.

statements.claim: The celestial kine were sought for Satyabhama; Krishna, his mind filled with joy, set out at once; Baladeva, Krishna, Pradyumna and Aniruddha mounted Garuda, who rose uprooting trees and shaking the earth.
statements.evidence: Index summary evt_0359: 'Seeking Vana's celestial kine in Varuna's charge for Satyabhama'; Harivamsha 1.276 (35, 97-100): 'Hari's mind was filled with joy... Baladeva, Krishna, the highly powerful Pradyumna and energetic Aniruddha sat on Garuda's back. Uprooting the trees and shaking the earth, Garuda... went on'.

statements.claim: Varuna's army came out to keep the kine and was routed by the high-souled Keshava.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Harivamsha 1.276): 'Varuna's... army... were all routed by the high-souled Keshava'.

statements.claim: Varuna loosed the Varuna-weapon and the sea rose against Krishna; Krishna met it with the Vaishnava weapon, and with its energy the water itself was ablaze, consuming the Varuna-weapon.
statements.evidence: Index summary evt_0359: 'Krishna routs Varuna's army and battles Varuna, whose Varuna-weapon is consumed by Krishna's Vaishnava weapon'; pack excerpt: 'with the energy of Vaishnava weapon that water was ablaze'.

statements.claim: Weaponless and ruined, Varuna still did not yield the cows.
statements.evidence: Consistent with evt_0360 (next story): Varuna pleads that he promised Vana never to give away the kine — the pack excerpt of DKS_0257 quotes his refusal.

DKS_0256.notes: Opening paragraphs recap the Aniruddha rescue/wedding from the same ch. 276 passage (supported). 'City had fallen' and battle-shore description are connective. Satyabhama motive comes from the index summary, not the (truncated) passage body — noted but treated per the summary as intended reading.

statements.claim: Varuna stood in his ruined domain with his army routed and his great weapon consumed, yet still refused to surrender the cows.
statements.evidence: Continuation of evt_0359 (pack excerpt: Varuna's army routed by Keshava, Varuna-weapon consumed by Vaishnava weapon) plus evt_0360 excerpt: Varuna refuses to give away the kine.

statements.claim: Varuna said he had promised Vana long ago that if he lived he would never give the kine away, and would not break his word even to save himself.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Harivamsha 1.276): 'Varuna said... "I had formerly promised, that if alive I would never give away these kine"'.

statements.claim: Krishna, honouring Varuna's truthfulness, released the cows and Varuna, saying: 'You are truthful... Therefore, to please you, I let Vana's cows go free. And you too are released.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Harivamsha 1.276): 'Krishna... said:—"...you are truthful and therefore for pleasing you I let loose Vāna's cows. And you too are released"'.

statements.claim: The battle ended in a kept promise rather than conquest.
statements.evidence: Frame commentary over the supported resolution; the pack records the release but not this editorializing.

statements.claim: Krishna, Baladeva, Pradyumna and Aniruddha returned to Dwaraka on Garuda, and the celestial kine came to graze in the fields of the Yadava capital, where the rejoicing citizens welcomed them home.
statements.evidence: Index summary evt_0360: 'Krishna... releases both Varuna and the cows and returns to Dwarka amid the rejoicing citizens'; Harivamsha 1.276: the same four ride Garuda back (v. 97-100); kine settling in Dwarka follows the Satyabhama motive of evt_0359.

statements.claim: The tale of the fallen thousand arms, the dance before Shiva and the burning sea spread through the city.
statements.evidence: Recap of earlier events (evt_0356/0357/0359), all pack-supported; framing only.

DKS_0257.notes: Krishna's dialogue and Varuna's plea are near-verbatim from the pack excerpt. The story's reconciliation (release the cows yet they come to Dwarka) goes slightly beyond the excerpt, which records only the release and the return; consistent with the intended reading (kine sought for Satyabhama, evt_0359 index). Citizens' rejoicing, lamps and children are connective.

statements.claim: Narakasura, called Bhauma, son of the earth goddess, had grown until his body seemed to fill the heavens and the world cowered in his shadow.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.5 (pack excerpt): 'Seeing the son of the earth-goddess who devoured the heavens, he slew him' (Sanskrit: sutaṃ mṛdhe khaṃ vapuṣā grasantaṃ ... dharitryā).

statements.claim: He carried off the princesses of the earth, daughters of kings, and shut them away in his citadel of Pragjyotisha, beyond mountains, water and fire.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.6: 'the princesses seized by Bhauma' (nara-deva-kanyāḥ kujena); Pragjyotisha as Naraka's stronghold and its mountain/fire/water defenses are established in the same cluster (BP 10.59.2-5).

statements.claim: The kings who had tried to win the princesses back had broken themselves against those walls and gone home defeated.
statements.evidence: No specific failed rescue by kings is in the pack; generic amplification of the captivity's hopelessness (cf. Harivamsha 1.121: 'nobody... could take them away').

statements.claim: It was Krishna who finally went against the demon; the son of the earth met the friend of the distressed, and the earth could not save him; the demon was struck down and with his fall the captivity ended.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.5-6: Krishna slew the earth-goddess's son; Hari is named 'friend of the distressed' (ārta-bandhum) and the seized princesses, seeing him, rose and chose him.

statements.claim: Seeing Hari, the sixteen thousand princesses came out of their prisons and of their own will chose him, asking to be his.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.6: seeing Hari the friend of the distressed, they rose and chose him (cf. BP 3.3.6 in canto-3 passage: utthāya sadyo jagṛhuḥ).

statements.claim: In one moment, in their many houses, he took their hands - the giving of the hand, the vow of marriage, in every home at the same instant.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.7: 'he took their hands in one moment in their many houses' (āsāṃ muhūrta ekasmin nānāgāreṣu yoṣitām).

statements.claim: In time each of those houses filled with ten sons, children who carried their father's likeness.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.8: 'begetting ten sons in each' (ekaikasyāṃ daśa daśa, per fuller canto-3 passage) and ātma-tulyāni = offspring like himself.

statements.claim: Uddhava remembered and told this afterward to the court of Dwaraka whenever asked about the war in the north.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.5-8 is Uddhava's own narration (excerpt opens 'Uddhava said').

statements.claim: The princesses entered Dwaraka as rescued captives and became the mothers of its future; the city filled with sixteen thousand households.
statements.evidence: Consistent with the maidens being sent to Dvaraka (BP 10.59.35); the forward-looking flourish is framing, not a pack claim.

DKS_0258.notes: Recall-bundled story (BP 3.3) fully tracks the pack; all substantive claims supported. 'Sixteen thousand' matches the round canonical count.

statements.claim: Garuda flew to heaven bearing the umbrella of Varuna, the jewel mountain and Krishna on his back, going lightly as if in sport.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30 (Wilson): 'GARUD́A, laden with the umbrella of Varuńa and the jewel mountain, and bearing Hrishikeśa on his back to the court of Indra, went lightly, as if in sport, along.'

statements.claim: At the portals of Swarga Krishna blew his conch and the gods came out to meet him bearing respectful offerings.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30: 'When they arrived at the portals of Swarga, Hari blew his shell; on which the gods advanced to meet him, bearing respectful offerings.'

statements.claim: Aditi, mother of Indra and of the gods, had once kept the earrings that Narakasura had torn away; Krishna bowed before her with Indra beside him, placed the earrings back in her hands and told her the demon was dead.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30: Krishna went to 'the palace of the mother of the gods, whose turrets resembled white clouds; and on beholding Adití, paid his respects to her, along with Śakra; and, presenting to her her own earrings, informed her of the destruction of the demon Naraka.'

statements.claim: Aditi's hymn: the lotus-eyed remover of all fear; the eternal, universal, living soul; origin of all beings; evening, night and day; earth, sky, air, water and fire; mind, intellect and individuality; Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva; gods and demons and serpents, men and beasts and trees, the vast and the minute, composed of gathered atoms.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30 hymn, near-verbatim (lotus eyes; removest all fear; eternal, universal, and living soul; origin of all beings; evening, night, day; earth, sky, air, water, fire; mind, intellect, individuality; forms called Brahmá, Vishńu, and Śiva; gods, Daityas, Punnagas, men, animals, trees; all bodies composed of aggregated atoms).

statements.claim: Beyond every perceptible shape is a form no eye can rest on, which she could only glimpse and name; the illusion beguiling those who think 'I am, this is mine' is woven by him, and only worshippers cross it to freedom.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30: 'nor do I know that form of thine, which is beyond perception'; notions 'I am--this is mine' are delusions of the mother of the world originating in his active agency; 'Those men who... diligently worship thee, traverse all this illusion, and obtain spiritual freedom.'

statements.claim: It is a fault to ask small things of one who could give everything - like asking a wish-fulfilling tree for a rag to cover one's nakedness.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30: 'It is the fault of the impure acts of the unrighteous (to proffer such idle requests to one able to confer such more important benefits), like asking for a rag to cover one's nakedness from the tree that bestows whatever is solicited.'

statements.claim: Krishna asked Aditi for her blessing; she granted that while he dwells among mortals, first among men, he shall be invincible to gods and demons alike.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30: 'Mother goddess, do thou shew favour unto me, and grant me thy blessing.' ... 'whilst thou dwellest amongst mortals, the first of men, thou shalt be invincible by gods or demons.'

statements.claim: Satyabhama, accompanied by Indra's queen, asked Aditi's blessing and was promised she would never suffer decay nor loss of beauty, becoming the refuge of all loveliness.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30: 'Satyabhámá, accompanied by the queen of Indra, addressed Adití... thou shalt never suffer decay, nor loss of beauty: thou shalt be the asylum of all loveliness.'

statements.claim: Indra conducted Krishna and Satyabhama through Nandana and the pleasant gardens of the gods, where the golden Parijata tree that had risen from the churned ocean stood.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30: 'Indra then respectfully saluted Janárddana... and conducted him and Satyabhámá through Nandana and other pleasant gardens of the gods; where Keśava... saw the Párijáta tree... produced when the ocean was churned for ambrosia: the bark was of gold, and it was embellished with young sprouting leaves of a copper colour.'

statements.claim: Far below the clouds, the walls of the demon's citadel still stood, unbroken and waiting.
statements.evidence: No pack support, and it conflicts with the source sequence: the pack passage has Krishna already laden with the umbrella of Varuna and the jewel mountain 'recovered from the demon's hoard' at Pragjyotisha and announcing Naraka's destruction - i.e., Naraka was slain at his stronghold and the hoard recovered BEFORE the earrings reached heaven (cf. VP 5.29-30; BP 10.59.22-37). The line also contradicts this story's own opening ('recovered from the demon's hoard').
statements.resolution: Corrected in story text via consolidation pass.

corrections.original_sentence: and far below the clouds, in the land of men, the walls of the demon's citadel still stood, unbroken and waiting.
corrections.suggested: and far below the clouds, in the land of men, the demon's conquered city lay still, its stolen hoard already scattered back toward its owners.

DKS_0259.notes: Body of the story is near-verbatim VP 5.30 (hymn, blessings, gardens). One issue: the closing transition line asserts the citadel of Pragjyotisha was still standing at the time of the heaven visit, but the earrings were recovered from that citadel after Naraka's fall - the war was already over when they were returned to Aditi.

statements.claim: Narakasura broke into the hoard of heaven, carrying off Varuna's umbrella, Aditi's earrings and the jewel mountain Amara, and the gods could not recover them; Indra came to Krishna with his complaint.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.1-5 (pack excerpt): 'Indra, robbed of his umbrella, earrings and the Amara hill, complained to Krishna.'

statements.claim: Krishna did not summon an army; he took Satyabhama with him, mounted Garuda and went to Pragjyotisha himself.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.2: 'sa-bhāryo garuḍārūḍhaḥ prāg-jyotiṣa-puraṃ yayau' (with his wife, mounted on Garuda, he went to the city of Pragjyotisha).

statements.claim: Pragjyotisha was ringed with mountains, weapon-forts, belts of fire and water, and the snares of Mura, so that nothing that came near ever came back out.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.3-5 rendering names the mountain, weapon-fort, fire/water and Mura-pasha defenses; 'nothing came back out' is hyperbole consistent with the defenses never having been breached.

statements.claim: Krishna broke the mountains with his mace and took the weapon-forts with arrows.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.3: 'gadayā nirbibhedādrīn śastra-durgāṇi sāyakaiḥ' (he split the mountains with his mace, the weapon-forts with arrows).

statements.claim: He cut the fire and water with his discus and severed the snares of Mura with his sword.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59 (pack rendering): 'the fire and water with his discus, and Mura's nooses with his sword.'

statements.claim: The sound of the conch Panchajanya broke the great engines of the city and the hearts of the proud men who served them, terrible as the thunder that ends an age.
