statements.evidence: SB 10.70.11-12 'avekṣyājyaṁ tathādarśaṁ go-vṛṣa-dvija-devatāḥ... saṁvibhajyāgrato viprān srak-tāmbūlānulepanaiḥ'.

statements.claim: His charioteer brought the great chariot; Krishna took the driver's hand and mounted, watched by the women of the inner palace with shy, loving glances.
statements.evidence: SB 10.70.13-15 'sūta upānīya syandanaṁ... gṛhītvā pāṇinā pāṇī sārathes tam athāruhat'; 'īkṣito 'ntaḥ-pura-strīṇāṁ sa-vrīḍa-prema-vīkṣitaiḥ'.

statements.claim: He rode to the Sudharma assembly hall of the Yadus, surrounded by the Vrishnis (including Uddhava and Satyaki), took the highest seat illuminating the quarters, and was entertained by jesting ministers and music of mridanga, vina, flute, cymbals and conch.
statements.evidence: SB 10.70.16-19 'sudharmākhyāṁ sabhāṁ sarvair vṛṣṇibhiḥ parivāritaḥ... paramāsane vibhur babhau sva-bhāsā kakubho 'vabhāsayan... nānā-hāsya-rasair... mṛdaṅga-vīṇā-muraja-veṇu-tāla-dara-svanaiḥ'; Uddhava and Satyaki named in pack index characters.

statements.claim: Closing reflection — Krishna performed the rites as a servant of the Lord within, and his service meant serving everyone who came before him — is devotional commentary rather than event.
statements.evidence: Pack offers no such statement; it is interpretive framing consistent with the worship sequence.

DKS_0286.notes: Every narrated action maps 1:1 to SB 10.70.1-19; no unsupported or contradicted factual claims.

statements.claim: Sudama was a learned, self-controlled brahmana living in a poor village in great poverty.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Sudama, a learned and self-controlled brahmana living in great poverty'; SB 10.80.6 'yadṛcchayopapannena vartamāno gṛhāśramī'.

statements.claim: His devoted wife urged him to visit Krishna, his boyhood friend who now dwelt in Dwaraka as lord of the Bhoja, Vrishni and Andhaka peoples, saying Krishna would give them wealth.
statements.evidence: SB 10.80.7-10: wife speaks with a wan face; 'sākṣāc chriyaḥ patiḥ... āste 'dhunā dvāravatyāṁ bhoja-vṛṣṇy-andhakeśvaraḥ'; pack excerpt confirms she says Krishna will give them wealth.

statements.claim: The wife asked again and again, and at last Sudama resolved in his mind to go.
statements.evidence: SB 10.80.11-12 'sa evaṁ bhāryayā vipro bahuśaḥ prārthito muhuḥ / iti sañcintya manasā gamanāya matiṁ dadhe'.

statements.claim: Sudama begged four handfuls of flattened rice from the brahmanas of the village, tied them in a rag, and set out for Dwaraka.
statements.evidence: SB 10.80.13-14 'yācitvā caturo muṣṭīn viprān pṛthuka-taṇḍulān / sa tān ādāya viprāgryaḥ prayayau dvārakāṁ kila' (he, best of brahmanas, having begged four fistfuls of flat rice from the brahmanas, took them and went to Dvaraka). Story follows the passage reading (Sudama begs); pack excerpt phrasing 'she borrows' reflects a common retelling but the Sanskrit passage is authoritative here and supports the story.

statements.claim: Walking the long road, he wondered how he would ever gain sight of Krishna, the lord of a great city.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: Sudama 'sets out for Dwaraka wondering how he may gain sight of Krishna'; SB 10.80.15-16.

statements.claim: He crossed the outer groves and the three gates/enclosures and reached the palace of the king who had sixteen thousand queens.
statements.evidence: SB 10.80.15-16 'trīṇi gulmāny atīyāya tisraḥ kakṣāś ca sa-dvijaḥ / gṛhaṁ dvy-aṣṭa-sahasrāṇāṁ mahiṣīṇāṁ harer' (passed three camps and three enclosures, the house of Hari with sixteen thousand queens).

statements.claim: Krishna had once been a boy at the guru's house with Sudama.
statements.evidence: Boyhood friendship stated in pack excerpt ('his boyhood friend'); guru-kula shared past confirmed by SB 10.80.26 (next story's verses: 'gāthāḥ pūrvā guru-kule satoḥ') via corpus chain.

statements.claim: Sudama's remembered image of Krishna as a hungry, ragged boy like himself is sentimental coloring.
statements.evidence: No pack statement that Krishna was poor as a boy; emotional parallel, not a sourceable fact.

DKS_0287.notes: All core events (poverty, wife's urging, resolve, four fistfuls of flat rice, journey, wonder at gaining sight) supported by SB 10.80.5-16.

statements.claim: Sudama stood before the palace housing Krishna's sixteen thousand queens.
statements.evidence: SB 10.80.16 (from previous pack's final verse, continued here): 'gṛhaṁ dvy-aṣṭa-sahasrāṇāṁ mahiṣīṇāṁ harer'; palace setting per pack index.

statements.claim: Seeing Sudama from afar, Krishna rose from the couch where he sat with Rukmini, ran to him and embraced his old friend with tears of joy.
statements.evidence: SB 10.80.17-18 'taṁ vilokyācyuto dūrāt priyā-paryaṅkam āsthitaḥ... aṅga-saṅgāti-nirvṛtaḥ'; pack excerpt: 'rises from Rukmini's couch, runs to him, and embraces his old friend with tears of joy'.

statements.claim: Krishna seated Sudama on his own couch, washed his feet, and bore the water on his own head.
statements.evidence: SB 10.80.19-20 'athopaveśya paryaṅke svayam sakhyuḥ samarhaṇam / agrahīc chirasā... bhagavāṁl loka-pāvanaḥ'.

statements.claim: He had fragrant incense brought and rows of lamps lit, and received his friend with joy.
statements.evidence: SB 10.80.21 'dhūpaiḥ surabhibhir mitraṁ pradīpāvalibhir mudā'.

statements.claim: The women of the palace, seeing a destitute beggar in a torn cloth honored by Krishna, whispered what merit this man had done that the guru of the three worlds and the abode of Shri should cherish him.
statements.evidence: SB 10.80.22-25 'ku-cailaṁ malinaṁ kṣāmaṁ dvijaṁ... antaḥ-pura-jano dṛṣṭvā kṛṣṇenāmala-kīrtinā / kim anena kṛtaṁ puṇyam avadhūtena bhikṣuṇā / yo 'sau tri-loka-guruṇā śrī-nivāsena sambhṛtaḥ'.

statements.claim: Rukmini herself fanned the emaciated brahmana.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'The goddess Rukmini herself fans the emaciated brahmana'; emaciation also from SB 10.80.22 'kṣāmaṁ'.

statements.claim: The two friends sat and talked of their old days together at the teacher's house.
statements.evidence: SB 10.80.26 'kathayāṁ cakratur gāthāḥ pūrvā guru-kule satoḥ' (they exchanged tales of the past, having been together at the guru's house).

DKS_0288.notes: Embrace, seating, foot-washing, incense/lamps, palace women's wonder, Rukmini fanning, and guru-kula reminiscence all supported by SB 10.80.16-26.

statements.claim: Sudama walked home from Dwaraka with empty hands — he had not been able to ask Krishna for anything.
statements.evidence: SB 10.81.13 'sa cālabdhvā dhanaṁ kṛṣṇān na tu yācitavān svayam' (he obtained wealth from Krishna but had not himself asked); corpus chain DKS_0289 (returns home empty-handed).

statements.claim: Krishna had eaten his handful of flat rice with delight.
statements.evidence: SB 10.81.34 'mayopaṇītaṁ pṛthukaika-muṣṭiṁ pratyagrahīt prīti-yuto mahātmā' (the great soul joyfully accepted the single handful of flat rice I brought); corpus chain DKS_0289.

statements.claim: Walking, Sudama reflected: 'Where am I, poor and full of faults, and where is Krishna, the very home of fortune?'
statements.evidence: SB 10.81.15 'kvāhaṁ daridraḥ pāpīyān kva kṛṣṇaḥ śrī-niketanaḥ'.

statements.claim: He understood that if he had been given wealth after asking, he might have grown proud and forgotten Krishna; the Lord had given him prosperity unasked, and does not grant the devotee the riches and glories that would pull the heart away.
statements.evidence: SB 10.81.19 'adhano 'yaṁ dhanaṁ prāpya mādyann uccair na māṁ smaret'; 10.81.36 'bhaktāya citrā bhagavān hi sampado rājyaṁ vibhūtīr na samarthayaty ajaḥ'.

statements.claim: Sudama prayed that this friendship, companionship and service be his in birth after birth.
statements.evidence: SB 10.81.35 'tasyaiva me sauhṛda-sakhya-maitrī-dāsyaṁ punar janmani janmani syāt'.

statements.claim: At the edge of his village he found his hut replaced by celestial mansions ringed with gardens and lakes loud with birds, and well-dressed men and graceful women moving through the courtyards.
statements.evidence: SB 10.81.21-22 'vicitropavanodyānaiḥ kūjad-dvija-kulākulaiḥ... juṣṭaṁ sv-alaṅkṛtaiḥ pumbhiḥ strībhiś ca hariṇākṣibhiḥ'.

statements.claim: His wife heard he had come, hurried out in great excitement, radiant as the goddess of fortune among her attendants, and her eyes filled with tears of love.
statements.evidence: SB 10.81.24-26 'patim āgatam ākarṇya patny uddharṣāti-sambhramā / pati-vratā patiṁ dṛṣṭvā premotkaṇṭhāśru-locanā / patnīṁ vīkṣya visphurantīṁ devīṁ vaimānikīm iva'.

statements.claim: Inside, the beds were soft as foam, spread with ivory and gold; golden seats, clear crystal walls with great emeralds, and abundant riches filled the house.
statements.evidence: SB 10.81.28-31 'payaḥ-phena-nibhāḥ śayyā dāntā rukma-paricchadāḥ / āsanāni ca haimāni... svaccha-sphaṭika-kuḍyeṣu mahā-mārakateṣu... samṛddhīḥ sarva-sampadām'.

statements.claim: He reflected that the Lord gives generously even to one who asks in person, and accepted even his meager single handful of flat rice with joy — Krishna had given unasked, so that the giving never came between them.
statements.evidence: SB 10.81.33-34 'nanv abruvāṇo diśate samakṣaṁ yāciṣṇave bhūry api bhūri-bhojaḥ / kiñcit karoty urv api yat sva-dattaṁ suhṛt-kṛtaṁ phalgv api bhūri-kārī mayopaṇītaṁ pṛthukaika-muṣṭiṁ pratyagrahīt prīti-yuto mahātmā'; 10.81.37 'bhakto 'tīva janārdane'.

statements.claim: Sudama reflects this happened because he asked for nothing but to remain Krishna's friend.
statements.evidence: Interpretive summary of the unasked-grace theme (10.81.13, 33-36); consistent with the pack's reading but phrased beyond the verses.

DKS_0290.notes: Transformation of the hut into a celestial palace, wife's radiant welcome, inner riches, and Sudama's reflections all trace directly to SB 10.81.13-37.

statements.claim: The sages at Samanta-panchaka, pleased with Vasudeva's question about the highest duty, chose him and initiated him into a great sacrifice there, with Vasudeva choosing them as his priests as dharma directs.
statements.evidence: Pack index summary: 'The sages, pleased with Vasudeva's question, initiate him and he performs a great sacrifice at Samanta-panchaka'; SB 10.84.42 'ta enam ṛṣayo rājan vṛtā dharmeṇa dhārmikam'; 10.84.43 'tad-dīkṣāyāṁ pravṛttāyāṁ'.

statements.claim: The sage Narada was among the gathered rishis watching the preparations.
statements.evidence: Narada listed in the pack's canonical-event characters for evt_0494 (alongside Vasudeva, Krishna, Balarama, the sages); consistent with ch. 10.84 context.

statements.claim: The Vrishnis arrived wearing lotus garlands, and Vasudeva's queens came delighted, bright with gold necklaces and fine garments.
statements.evidence: SB 10.84.43-44 'vṛṣṇayaḥ puṣkara-srajaḥ / tan-mahiṣyaś ca muditā niṣka-kaṇṭhyaḥ su-vāsasaḥ'.

statements.claim: The field resounded with mridangas, drums, conches and kettledrums.
statements.evidence: SB 10.84.45 'nedur mṛdaṅga-paṭaha-śaṅkha-bhery-ānakādayaḥ'.

statements.claim: The priests anointed Vasudeva according to rite, his body touched with unguents, and dressed him in silks, bracelets, necklaces, anklets and earrings; his priests were robed in jeweled silk.
statements.evidence: SB 10.84.46-48 'tam abhyaṣiñcan vidhi-vad aktam abhyaktam ṛtvijaḥ / tābhir dukūla-valayair hāra-nūpura-kuṇḍalaiḥ / tasyartvijo... ratna-kauśeya-vāsasaḥ'.

statements.claim: Krishna and Balarama were present among the kinsmen, each with his own family and sons.
statements.evidence: SB 10.84.49 'tadā rāmaś ca kṛṣṇaś ca svaiḥ svair bandhubhir anvitau'; pack excerpt: 'Krishna and Balarama shine there among their kinsmen and sons'.

statements.claim: Vasudeva performed the subsidiary rites such as agnihotra as prescribed, and at the proper time gave the priests their dakshina — rich gifts of cows, land and maidens.
statements.evidence: SB 10.84.50-51 'īje 'nu-yajñaṁ vidhinā agni-hotrādi-lakṣaṇaiḥ / athartvigbhyo 'dadāt kāle yathāmnātaṁ sa dakṣiṇāḥ'; pack excerpt: 'rich gifts of cows, land and maidens to the priests'.

statements.claim: The sages completed the ritual with the queens' offerings and the avabhritha bath; after bathing, Vasudeva gave garments and ornaments to the bards and to the women.
statements.evidence: SB 10.84.52-53 'patnī-saṁyājāvabhṛthyaiś caritvā te maharṣayaḥ / snāto 'laṅkāra-vāsāṁsi vandibhyo 'dāt tathā striyaḥ'.

statements.claim: He gave abundant gifts to his kinsmen with their wives and sons, and honored the assembled priests, gods, men, ancestors and caranas.
statements.evidence: SB 10.84.54-55 'bandhūn sa-dārān sa-sutān pāribarheṇa bhūyasā / sadasyartvik-sura-gaṇān nṛ-bhūta-pitṛ-cāraṇān'.

statements.claim: Background that wise men had come to Samanta-panchaka for ages and the ground was blessed is generic holy-place coloring.
statements.evidence: Pack calls it 'that holy field'; the 'for ages' claim is atmosphere, not a pack assertion.

DKS_0291.notes: Sacrifice sequence, attendants, gifts and avabhritha all match SB 10.84.42-55 closely.

statements.claim: Years before, after their studies, Krishna and Balarama had fetched back their teacher's dead son as his fee, urged by the guru.
statements.evidence: SB 10.85.31 'cirān mṛta-sutādāne guruṇā kila coditau' (urged by the guru to give back a son dead long ago); pack excerpt: 'they had once fetched their guru's dead son as a fee'; the brothers' journey to the world of the dead is carried by the corpus chain.

statements.claim: Devaki, remembering her sons slain by Kamsa, tearfully asked Krishna and Balarama to bring back her dead children, entreating: 'You two are the lords of the masters of yoga; you fetched a long-dead son for your teacher — grant my wish the same way.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.85.26-32: 'devakī... kṛṣṇa-rāmau samāśrāvya putrān kaṁsa-vihiṁsitān... cirān mṛta-sutādāne guruṇā kila coditau / tathā me kurutaṁ kāmaṁ yuvāṁ yogeśvareśvarau'; pack excerpt confirms tears and request.

statements.claim: Devaki had borne children whom Kamsa killed one by one at birth, because he feared a son of hers would take his kingdom and life.
statements.evidence: Corpus chain: DKS_0004-DKS_0011 — the prophecy that Devaki's eighth child would kill Kamsa, and Kamsa destroying her children as they were born ('dashing each of them the moment it came into the world', DKS_0010); pack excerpt: 'the sons slaughtered by Kamsa... slain by the Bhoja king'.

statements.claim: She called the six slain the ones 'the Bhoja king slew' — Kamsa being the Bhoja king.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'entreats them to bring back the sons slain by the Bhoja king' (i.e., Kamsa); SB 10.85.32.

statements.claim: The tale of the restored teacher's son was told everywhere and reopened Devaki's old grief, moving her to ask.
statements.evidence: Pack says only that Devaki, 'hearing of how Krishna and Balarama had brought back their guru's son... tearfully asks'; the city-wide fame and her inner turmoil are connective psychology.

statements.claim: Krishna and Balarama did not refuse her; in their silence Devaki felt heard and dared to hope.
statements.evidence: Pack verses 26-32 end at her request; no response is recorded in this excerpt, so the brothers' silence and her hope are connective closure (fulfillment follows in DKS_0293).

DKS_0292.notes: Request itself and its framing (guru-son precedent, six sons slain by Kamsa/Bhoja king, plea to the lords of yoga) fully supported by SB 10.85.26-32; backstory grounded in corpus chain.

statements.claim: Krishna and Balarama descended by their mystic power (yoga-maya) into Sutala, the realm of the daitya king Bali.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Entering Sutala by their yoga-maya, Krishna and Balarama are received by the daitya king Bali'; SB 10.85.34 'tasmin praviṣṭāv upalabhya daitya-rāḍ'.

statements.claim: Bali rose at once, bowed low with his whole family, his heart overflowing with joy at the sight, settled them on a noble seat, and worshipped them with garments of great worth, ornaments and unguents.
statements.evidence: SB 10.85.34-36 'sadyaḥ samutthāya nanāma sānvayaḥ / tad-darśanāhlāda-pariplutāśayaḥ... samarhayām āsa sa tau vibhūtibhir mahārha-vastrābharaṇānulepanaiḥ'.

statements.claim: Bali washed their feet with his kin and repeatedly pressed the lotus feet to his head, his mind dissolved in love.
statements.evidence: SB 10.85.37 'sa indraseno bhagavat-padāmbujaṁ bibhran muhuḥ prema-vibhinnayā dhiyā'; pack excerpt: 'washes their feet with his kin'.

statements.claim: Bali said their sight is hard to obtain — daityas, danavas, gandharvas, siddhas, vidyadharas and caranas approach with enmity or longing and none can comprehend them — and begged: 'From the dark well of this world you have drawn me up; instruct me, make me sinless.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.85.39-45: 'darśanaṁ vāṁ hi bhūtānāṁ duṣprāpaṁ... kecanodbaddha-vaireṇa bhaktyā kecana kāmataḥ... tava yogeśvareśvara / tan naḥ prasīda... andha-kūpāt niṣkramya... / śādhy asmān īśitavyeśa niṣpāpān kuru naḥ prabho'.

statements.claim: Krishna revealed that the six sons who were born in Devaki's womb and slain by Kamsa were once the six sons of the sage Marichi, who laughed at Brahma and were cursed to be born as demons; they now dwelt nearby awaiting release, and Krishna would take them back to end his mother's grief.
statements.evidence: SB 10.85.47-49 'tenāsurīm agan yonim... devakyā udare jātā rājan kaṁsa-vihiṁsitāḥ / ita etān praṇeṣyāmo mātṛ-śokāpanuttaye'; pack excerpt: 'the six sons were once the six sons of Marichi, who laughed at Brahma and were cursed to be born as demons... who now dwell nearby awaiting release'.

statements.claim: Having spoken, Krishna took the six sons into his keeping, and the brothers rose from Sutala carrying them with them, honored as they departed.
statements.evidence: SB 10.85.51 'ity uktvā tān samādāya indrasenena pūjitau' (having said this and taken them, honored by Indrasena/Bali's line).

statements.claim: The six sons of Marichi passing through many births to this waiting, and their deaths at Kamsa's hands being 'only a pause', is interpretive framing.
statements.evidence: Consistent with the curse-and-release arc (10.85.47-49) but phrased as narrative commentary beyond the pack text.

DKS_0293.notes: Bali's reception, speech, Krishna's revelation of the Marichi origin, and the taking of the six sons all match SB 10.85.33-51.

statements.claim: Krishna and Balarama returned to Dwaraka carrying six small children, and word ran ahead that they had brought children back from the underworld.
statements.evidence: SB 10.85.51-56 pack excerpt: 'Taking the six sons, Krishna and Balarama return to Dwaraka and give them to their mother'; corpus chain DKS_0293 (Sutala visit) supplies the underworld origin.

statements.claim: The children were Devaki's sons; years before, her brother Kamsa had taken each of her first six children at birth and killed them, because a prophecy warned that a child of Devaki would end his reign.
statements.evidence: Corpus chain: DKS_0292/0293 context (evt_0498) — Devaki's 'sons slain by the Bhoja king', six sons born in her womb and slain by Kamsa (SB 10.85.47-49); the prophecy is established in the earlier Kamsa arc (corpus DKS_0003-0011).

statements.claim: She had raised Krishna and Balarama, the seventh and the eighth, and had loved them with all her strength.
statements.evidence: No support in this pack (SB 10.85.51-56), and it runs against the corpus's own canon: Krishna was handed to Vasudeva on the night of his birth and raised by Nanda and Yashoda in Vraja, and Balarama was transferred to Rohini's womb and raised in Vraja — Devaki was imprisoned until Krishna returned to Mathura as a boy of ~11 (corpus Vraja arc, e.g. DKS_0016 eleven years in Vraja). Devaki is the birth-mother of the seventh and eighth children; nothing in the corpus has her raising them from infancy.
statements.resolution: Corrected in story text via consolidation pass.

statements.claim: Krishna and Balarama had descended to Sutala, the netherworld kingdom where King Bali reigned, and brought the six back to the world above.
statements.evidence: Corpus chain DKS_0293 (SB 10.85.34-49): 'Entering Sutala by their yoga-maya, Krishna and Balarama are received by the daitya king Bali'; the six released sons dwelt there awaiting release.

statements.claim: Devaki came out as they reached the gate, counted the six, her milk came, and she took them into her arms, nursing and embracing them, weeping and laughing.
statements.evidence: SB 10.85.52-53: 'devakī putra-sneha-snuta-stanī... apāyayat stanaṃ prītā suta-sparśa-parisnutam'; pack excerpt: 'Devaki, her breasts flowing with milk, nurses and embraces them.'

statements.claim: When the six had drunk their fill they bowed — first to Krishna, then Devaki, then Vasudeva, then Balarama — and, released from the curse, rose and ascended before the eyes of all to the abode of the gods.
statements.evidence: SB 10.85.54-56: 'te namaskṛtya govindaṃ devakīṃ pitaraṃ balam... mṛtāgamana-nirgamam'; pack excerpt: 'released from the curse, they bow and ascend to the gods' abode.' Bow order matches the verse (Govinda, Devaki, father/Vasudeva, Bala).

statements.claim: Devaki stood with empty arms and milk on her lips, the old grief gone out of her; the court and Dwaraka long remembered the night a curse was dissolved in a mother's embrace.
statements.evidence: Reflective close consistent with the pack (reunion, nursing, ascent); the 'single evening' duration and the city's lasting memory are narrative atmosphere not asserted by the pack but contradicted by nothing.

corrections.original_sentence: She had raised Krishna and Balarama, the seventh and the eighth, and had loved them with all her strength; but the six were always there, six small absences standing in the shadow of her heart.
corrections.suggested: She had borne Krishna and Balarama, the seventh and the eighth, and had loved them with all her strength; but the six were always there, six small absences standing in the shadow of her heart.

DKS_0294.notes: Reunion, nursing, bowing and ascent all map cleanly to SB 10.85.51-56. One UNSUPPORTED biographical claim: 'she had raised Krishna and Balarama' — the corpus has both boys raised in Vraja (Krishna by Nanda/Yashoda after the birth-night handover; Balarama by Rohini after the womb-transfer), with Devaki imprisoned until Krishna's return to Mathura at ~11. Devaki is their birth-mother, so 'borne' preserves the sentence's intent.

statements.claim: Two men in Mithila — the brahmana Shrutadeva and King Bahulashva — each prepared to receive Krishna, each taking it for granted the visit was meant for him alone.
statements.evidence: SB 10.86.23-24: 'svānugrahāya samprāptaṃ manvānau taṃ jagad-gurum / nyamantrayetāṃ dāśārham ātithyena saha dvijaiḥ' (each thinking the world-guru had come for his own grace, they invited him with the brahmanas); pack excerpt names both hosts.

statements.claim: Krishna was traveling through the land with a company of sages; Shrutadeva was a brahmana of study and worship, Bahulashva the king of Mithila.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Krishna travels to Mithila with the sages... the brahmana Shrutadeva and King Bahulashva of Mithila'; verse 24 'saha dvijaiḥ'. Mithila's 'wise kings / no guest turned away' lore is generic atmosphere.

statements.claim: Each prepared with all his household — the brahmana swept his courtyard and set out food; the king hung garlands and called for musicians — and each invited Krishna and the sages to stay.
statements.evidence: The double invitation is supported (10.86.24); the specific preparations (swept courtyard, musicians) are invented domestic color, contradicting nothing in the pack.

statements.claim: The king, seeing the weary travelers approach, went out to meet them, his heart overflowing, eyes blurred with tears; with his whole family he bowed low and worshipped Krishna and the sages.
statements.evidence: SB 10.86.26-28: 'śrāntān apy atha tān dūrāj janakaḥ sva-gṛhāgatān / pravṛddha-bhaktyā uddharṣa-hṛdayāsrāvilekṣaṇaḥ / sa-kuṭumbo vahan mūrdhnā pūjayāṃ cakra īśvarān' (weary from afar, great devotion, heart thrilled, tear-filled eyes, bowing with his family).

statements.claim: The king said: 'Your own promise is being kept — let our eyes rest on you. Who would ever turn away from your lotus feet? You who came down into the line of Yadu for the sake of mortals wandering through the world — stay in our house for a few days, you and the brahmanas with you.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.86.31-35 (Bahulashva's speech): 'sva-vacas tad ṛtaṃ kartum asmad-dṛg-gocaro bhavān... ko nu tvac-caraṇāmbhojam... yo 'vatīrya yador vaṃśe nṛṇāṃ saṃsaratām iha... dināni katicid bhūman gṛhān no nivasa dvijaiḥ'.

statements.claim: In the same hour Krishna was seated in Shrutadeva's simple house, accepting whatever the brahmana offered with overflowing joy; Krishna was whole in both houses at once, fully present in each, and neither host saw the other or knew.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'To please both devotees, Krishna enters both homes at once, unseen by either, and each worships him with overflowing devotion.'

statements.claim: Night fell; beneath each of the two lamps sat the same Lord; neither man ever learned the truth, and both families rose blessed, each believing its visit had been the only one.
statements.evidence: Consistent with the pack's 'unseen by either' during the double visit; the hosts' permanent mutual ignorance is a closing flourish — the pack's excerpt range (10.86.23-36) does not cover the aftermath, so nothing contradicts it.

DKS_0295.notes: Faithful to SB 10.86.23-36 — the double invitation, Bahulashva's tearful welcome and speech (nearly line-by-line), and the simultaneous unseen presence in both houses all check out. Only connective domestic color and a closing flourish; no unsupported or contradicted facts.

statements.claim: In Dwaraka, a brahmana's newborn sons died one after another, dying as they met the ground.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.21-24 and pack excerpt: 'A brahmana's infant sons die as soon as they touch the ground' — 'evaṃ dvitīyaṃ viprarṣis tṛtīyaṃ tv evam eva ca' (so the second, and the third in the same way).

statements.claim: The brahmana wrapped each dead child and laid it at the gate of the palace, and cried that the king's fault had slain his children.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.21: 'vipro gṛhītvā mṛtakaṃ rāja-dvāry upadhāya saḥ'; pack excerpt: 'each time he lays the dead child at the palace gate, lamenting that the king's fault has slain his children.'

statements.claim: The brahmana accused the ruler as a man who hated brahmanas, crafty of mind, greedy, sunk in pleasure, delighting in violence, ill-behaved, master of nothing in himself, whose failure of duty makes his subjects perish in misery.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.22-23: 'brahma-dviṣaḥ śaṭha-dhiyo lubdhasya viṣayātmanaḥ / hiṃsā-vihāraṃ nṛpatiṃ duḥśīlam ajitendriyam'; pack excerpt: 'accuses the unrighteous ruler of failing in his duty, so that his subjects perish in misery.'

statements.claim: The narrative staggers the outcry: the first son was buried quietly at home, the second laid at the gate in silence, and only at the third did the brahmana cry the accusation aloud before the city.
statements.evidence: Dramatic pacing for a sensitive scene (see content_note). The pack passage suggests the gate-complaint pattern applied from the first death (10.89.21-23 describing the lament, then v.24 'the second and the third in the same way'), so the story's quiet first burial is a softening deviation, not a denial of the canonical accusation.

statements.claim: The palace gates stayed shut, no one came out to answer the charge, and the watching crowd grew as the brahmana left the child where the guards could see it.
statements.evidence: Scene-setting consistent with the pack; the city's unresponsiveness and crowd are connective staging not stated in the excerpt.

statements.claim: Arjuna was in Dwaraka then, staying near Krishna; he heard the lament and asked the brahmana whether there was no bearer of the bow in the place where brahmanas weep, bereft of wealth, wives and children.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.25-27: 'tām arjuna upaśrutya karhicit keśavāntike / kiṃ svid brahmaṃs tvan-nivāse iha nāsti dhanur-dharaḥ / dhana-dārātmajāpṛktā yatra śocanti brāhmaṇāḥ'.

statements.claim: The brahmana looked at Arjuna and said nothing; the answer would come with the next child.
statements.evidence: Bridge to the following episode (evt_0281); not asserted by the pack but contradicts nothing.

DKS_0296.notes: Deaths, gate-laying, and the full catalogue of accusations map directly to SB 10.89.20-27, and Arjuna's intervention matches v.25-27. One staging note: the pack says the gate-lament pattern held 'each time' (v.24 'second and third in the same way'), while the story delays the public outcry to the third death for dramatic restraint; judged connective, flagged here for review.

statements.claim: Arjuna vowed to the brahmana that he would protect the next child, and that if even one more child was taken he would enter the fire.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (SB 10.89.28-31): 'Arjuna... vows that he will protect the next child or enter fire'; v.28 'ahaṃ... rakṣiṣye dīnayor iha'.

statements.claim: The brahmana asked how Arjuna could do what is difficult even for the lords of the world.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.30: 'tat kathaṃ nu bhavān karma duṣkaraṃ jagad-īśvaraiḥ'.

statements.claim: Arjuna answered, 'Do not look down on my strength — it is the strength that pleased Tryambaka himself,' and the brahmana was reassured.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.32-33: 'māvamaṃsthā mama brahman vīryaṃ tryambaka-toṣaṇam / evaṃ viśrambhito vipraḥ' (the brahmana was thus made confident).

statements.claim: At the time of the birth Arjuna went to the brahmana's house, touched pure water, bowed to Maheshvara, and ringed the delivery room with a cage of arrows, shaft joined to shaft with every weapon in his art.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.34-36: 'prasūti-kāla āsanne... sa upaspṛśya śucy ambho namaskṛtya maheśvaram / nyaruṇat sūtikāgāraṃ śarair nānāstra-yojitaiḥ'. The 'neither wind nor bird nor hand could pass' density is hyperbolic color on the supported cage.

statements.claim: The child was born and cried, and then, before Arjuna's eyes, was lifted bodily into the sky through the cage of arrows and vanished.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.37: 'tataḥ kumāraḥ sañjāto vipra-patnyā rudan muhuḥ'; pack excerpt: 'the newborn vanishes bodily into the sky'. The 'through the arrows as if they were water' matches the HV telling of the same episode (Harivamsha 1.260, used in the DKS_0299 pack).

statements.claim: The brahmana, in the presence of Krishna, rebuked Arjuna: 'Neither Pradyumna, nor Aniruddha, nor Balarama, nor Keshava himself could save that child. Fie on Arjuna, the false speaker. Fie on the bow of the self-praiser.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.38-40: 'tadāha vipro vijayaṃ vinindan kṛṣṇa-sannidhau / na pradyumno nāniruddho na rāmo na ca keśavaḥ / dhig arjunaṃ mṛṣā-vādaṃ dhig ātma-ślāghino dhanuḥ' — names and curse match exactly.

statements.claim: His great bow, the bow that had pleased Shiva himself, hung at his side like a thing he no longer recognized.
statements.evidence: The pack's verse credits his valor/strength with pleasing Tryambaka (v.32 'vīryaṃ tryambaka-toṣaṇam'), not the bow itself; the phrase is loose synecdoche for the archer whose prowess pleased Shiva. Atmosphere after the public failure; not a storyline fact.

DKS_0297.notes: Vow, cage of arrows, vanishing newborn, and the brahmana's curse all match SB 10.89.28-40 nearly line by line (including the exact order of names in the rebuke). The 'bow that pleased Shiva' is a synecdoche slip flagged in statements; no hard issues.

statements.claim: A brahmana had lost his four sons — three boys taken from him earlier, and then a newborn infant — and Krishna had promised to bring them back.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.260 (in pack): Krishna returned 'with the four sons of the Brāhmana and gave those three boys who had been stolen before and the new born baby into the hands of the Brāhmana'; promise and mission carried by corpus chain (DKS_0298, evt_0221).

statements.claim: The sea opened before their car: the lord of the ocean rose with folded hands, asked what he should do, pleaded that an opened way would tempt other kings to cross, and Krishna promised no one else would ever assail it; the waters held still and the car passed through the red depths as over land.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.260 (Dutt): ocean 'with folded hands' asks 'What am I to do?'; 'other kings, elated with the pride of their strength, will cross me by this way'; Krishna replies 'Save me no one else will be able to assail you'; 'we proceeded through that lustrous red water as if we were on land'.

statements.claim: Seven mountains bowed their crests and gave them passage, and they crossed the seven continents and seas and the ring of mountains that fences the world (Lokaloka).
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.260: seven mountains (Jayanta, Vaijayanta, Neela, Rajata, Mahāmeru, Kailasha, Indrakuta) 'saluting Govinda... gave him the passage'; 'crossing the seven insular continents, oceans and seven rivers as well as Lokaloka'. The story's 'seven seas' condenses the text's 'oceans'.

statements.claim: The horses faltered in a darkness thick as mud, and Krishna dispelled the darkness with his discus, parting it so the sky came back.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.260: 'I found the horses carrying the car with great difficulty... the darkness was owing to thick mud... Govinda dispelled that darkness and mud with his discus and the sky and the passage of the car became visible'.

statements.claim: Arjuna saw a bundle of effulgence in the form of a man spread across the heavens above all the worlds; Krishna walked into it while the brahmana and Arjuna waited, and within a moment returned with the four sons, whole and unharmed.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.260: 'I saw in the sky a bundle of effulgence, of the shape of a man, extending over all the worlds. Then Rishikesha entered into that bundle of effulgence and that best of Brāhmanas and myself waited on the car. Within a moment the powerful Krishna returned with the four sons.'

statements.claim: It was the Supreme Lord himself who had taken the children; he told them he had brought the brahmana's sons there because he wished to see Krishna and Arjuna, and that since the earth had been relieved of its burden the time had come for them to turn back.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.57-58: 'dvijātmajā me yuvayor didṛkṣuṇā mayopanītā bhuvi dharma-guptaye / pūrṇa-kāmāv api yuvāṃ nara-nārāyaṇāv ṛṣī'; pack excerpt: 'he, wishing to see them, had himself brought the brahmana's sons to his abode, and that having slain the earth's burden they should now return.'

statements.claim: They returned by the way they came, the wonders repeating in reverse, and the car stood in Dwaraka with the first part of the day still unfinished.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.260: 'we... came out in the same way as we had gone there... arriving at Dwārakā within a moment we saw that even the first part of the day was not complete'; SB 10.89.59-60 'nyavartetāṃ svakaṃ dhāma... yathā-gatam'.

statements.claim: Krishna placed the four sons in their father's hands; the brahmana wept with joy, and Krishna fed him and his sons, gave him riches, and sent him away satisfied.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.260: 'Krishna returned with the four sons... gave... into the hands of the Brāhmana. Regaining his sons the Brāhmana was highly pleased... Krishna fed that Brāhmana with his sons and satisfying him with riches sent him away to his own house.'

statements.claim: Arjuna, having seen Vishnu's abode, felt every human power fall away — not his own doing but a gift flowing from Krishna's grace.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.61: 'niśāmya vaiṣṇavaṃ dhāma pārthaḥ parama-vismitaḥ'; pack excerpt: 'Arjuna, astounded at the vision of Vishnu's abode, regards all human power as Krishna's grace.'

DKS_0299.notes: Journey and restoration track Harivamsha 1.260 (Dutt, quoted in full in the pack) nearly incident by incident — ocean crossing, seven mountains, Lokaloka, discus-dispelled darkness, bundle of effulgence, return within the first part of the day, feeding and enrichment of the brahmana; the Lord's explanation matches SB 10.89.57-61. No unsupported or contradicted facts.

statements.claim: Men wondered afterward why Krishna, who could ride Garuda, kept the great bird walking at his side instead of mounting him on the road from Vidarbha.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.112 opening: Janamejaya asks why Krishna, setting out from the city of Bidarbha, 'did not ride the highly powerful son of Vinatā, Garuda; why did he then take him away with him?'

statements.claim: Before the assembled kings Krishna announced he would go to Mathura; Garuda saluted him and asked leave to fly first to Kushasthali, the old city of king Raivata at the foot of Mount Raivata on the bank of the great ocean.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.112 (4-7): Krishna 'said before the assembled kings, "I shall repair to the charming city of Mathura"'; Garuda: 'I shall now proceed to Raivata's city Kushasthali... It is situate at the base of the Raivata mountain and on the bank of the great ocean.'

statements.claim: Garuda described Kushasthali as abandoned by the rakshasas, with trees hung with filaments of flowers, groves and creepers like Nandana, and elephants, serpents, bears, monkeys, boars, buffaloes and deer moving through it; if worthy of Krishna's dwelling he would root out every thorn and come back.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.112 (8-10): 'The Rākshasas have abandoned the charming city of Kushasthali... abounds in trees decorated with filaments of flowers, in groves and creepers... scattered with elephants and serpents, and inhabited by bear, monkeys, boars, buffaloes and deer... if that extensive and charming city is fitted for thy residence, I shall remove all the thorns and come back to thee.'

statements.claim: Mathura had been won back from Kamsa, but Jarasandha — whose daughters had been married to the slain king — had already hurled his armies at the city and would hurl more, and Jarasandha could not be slain by them; Krishna said: 'O son of Vinata, the king Jarasandha is unslayable by us. It never bodes good for us to live in this city of Mathura.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.112 excerpt (verbatim): 'O Vinatā's son, the king Jarāsandha is unslayable by us... it never bodes good for us to live in this city of Mathura.' Jarasandha's daughters married to Kamsa and his earlier attacks are established in the corpus's Mathura arc (corpus chain DKS_0300 → evt_0190).

statements.claim: While Garuda was gone Krishna entered Mathura with the Yadavas, and Ugrasena — the old king restored to his throne — came out with dancing girls and citizens and honored the victorious Krishna; the city dressed itself in flags and garlands.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.112 (12, 14-22): 'when Krishna too, with the Yadavas, entered into the beautiful city of Mathurā, Ugrasena came out of the city with dancing girls and citizens and honored the victorious Krishna'; 'the city was decorated with flags, garlands of wild flowers and jars full of water.' Ugrasena's restoration is corpus Mathura-arc canon.

statements.claim: Garuda returned with a glad report: he had flown over Kushasthali wall by wall and found it worthy — at the foot of Raivata, emptied of its rakshasas, washed by the sea breeze — and brought the promise: 'Your city will be celebrated in the three worlds under the name of Dwaravati.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Garuda said: ... "thy city will be celebrated in the three worlds under the name of Dwāravati"'; index summary: 'Garuda returns from reconnoitering Kushasthali and praises it as a fitting abode.'

statements.claim: Krishna weighed what he knew — Jarasandha unslayable, Mathura small and open to every enemy — and resolved that when the time came the Yadavas would leave Mathura and follow where Garuda had flown.
statements.evidence: Index summary: 'Krishna, knowing Jarasandha unslayable, resolves to leave Mathura'; the fuller departure deliberation belongs to the next episode (HV 1.113, DKS_0301).

DKS_0300.notes: Faithful to Harivamsha 1.112 (Dutt): Janamejaya's framing question, Garuda's description of Kushasthali, Krishna's unslayable-Jarasandha speech (verbatim), Ugrasena's welcome, and the Dwaravati promise all check out. The 'flown wall by wall' reconnoiter sits in the portion of the chapter summarized by the pack's index entry; no contradictions.

statements.claim: No enemy threw the Yadavas out of Mathura; they left of their own counsel, on a day they chose themselves.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113: the Yadavas, hearing of the approach of Jarasandha and Kalayavana, 'thought of retreating as mentioned before', and Krishna himself declares 'To day is an auspicious day. So we shall, even this very day, issue out of Mathura' — an unforced, self-chosen departure.

statements.claim: Jarasandha, emperor of Magadha, had come against Mathura and been beaten back, but he could not be slain — destined deathless to his enemies — and his soldiers were so many the Yadavas could not have destroyed them even in a hundred years of war.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (10-11): 'Our enemy the king Jarāsandha has been destined as unslayable by us... so great is the number of his soldiers that we shall not be able to bring about their destruction even in hundred years'; earlier repelled sieges are corpus Mathura-arc canon.

statements.claim: Word came that Kalayavana, a foreign king of terrible strength, was marching on the city with an akshouhini of soldiers, and his messenger had already come to the houses of the Vrishnis and the Andhakas; the clans gathered, made Krishna their president, and held their conference in fear.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 excerpt: 'starting for Mathura with one Akshouhini of soldiers Kalayavana sent his messenger to the house of Vrishnis and Andhakas... making the highly intelligent Krishna their president, held a conference in fear of Kalayavana.'

statements.claim: Krishna told the Yadus in assembly: Mathura is the abode of the Yadavas; we were born here and grew up in Vraja; our griefs are gone and enemies defeated, but hostilities with the kings and the war with Jarasandha have begun; though our infantry, animals, jewels and friends are without number, Mathura is small and an enemy can enter it easily, and a crore of princes and soldiers crowded here would breed dissension; better to live elsewhere and lay out a new city, which he would carry out at the proper time if they approved.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (1-8) — the assembly speech is reproduced nearly point by point, including 'one Koti of princes and infantry... dissension cropping up' and 'if you like it, we will lay out a city elsewhere'.

statements.claim: The Yadavas answered with one voice: 'Do what you deem proper for the good of all of us.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (9): 'Hearing it all the Yādavas delightedly said:—"O Krishna, do what thou deemst proper for the behoof of all these people"'.

statements.claim: Then came the news that Jarasandha and Kalayavana were advancing together with an army too vast to count; the elders consulted and saw that a hundred years of war could not finish that host; Krishna declared the day auspicious and ordered the departure that very day with army and followers.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (10-14): 'the emperor Jarāsandha, along with Kālayavana was proceeding towards Mathurā with his army... To day is an auspicious day. So we shall, even this very day, issue out of Mathura along with our army and followers.'

statements.claim: They went out that same day headed by Vasudeva — wives, children, chariots, elephants — the noise of the march like the waves of the ocean; they left with their wealth, kinsmen, friends, golden chariots, infuriated elephants and gold-harnessed horses, set their faces to the west, and Vasudeva and the other elders rode in front guiding the columns.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (15-20): 'the Yadavas, headed by Vasudeva, along with their wives, cars and elephants, set out, echoing the four quarters with the noise of their soldiers resembling that of the waves of the ocean... set out for the west. Stationed in front, Vasudeva and other leading Yadavas... guided the army.'

statements.claim: They reached the bank of the sea — variegated with creepers, rich in coconut trees, covered with ketaki, palmyra and vines — and were as delighted as if they had arrived at the celestial region; Krishna found an extensive tract on the ocean's edge with coppery soil mixed with gravel, good for beasts of burden, marked with every favorable sign of a city as if presided over by the Goddess of Prosperity, fanned by the sea breeze and watered by the ocean.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (21-29): 'It was variegated with creepers, abounded in coconut trees... covered with Ketaki trees, palmyras, Pannages and vines... the Yadavas were highly delighted as if they had arrived at the celestial region... The land had a coppery soil mixed with gravels, was well-suited for animals of burden, was endued with all the favourable marks of a city, as if it was presided over by the Goddess of prosperity herself. It was fanned by the sea breeze and was watered by the ocean.'

statements.claim: Near the site rose Mount Raivata, shining like Mandara, where Drona had lived for many years and King Ekalavya had once made his home, and the sporting ground that already bore the name Dwaravati; there Krishna chose his site and the Yadava commanders pitched tents for the night.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (25-31): 'Near it was shining in beauty the charming mountain Raivata like the mount Mandara... Drona lived for many long years. There lived the king Ekalavya. And the sporting ground laid out by himself like a board of dice is celebrated by the name of Dwāravati... Keshava selected that site for his city... the Yadu commanders pitched tents there for the night.'

statements.claim: Standing on the new ground, the foremost of the Yadavas — Gada's younger brother, the leader of them all — thought of the names he would give to the houses of the city, and rested shorn of anxiety; the Yadavas secured Dwaravati and lived there happily with their friends, as the gods live in their own city.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (32-35): 'the leader of the Yādavas, having Gada as his elder brother, thought in his mind of the names he would give to the various houses in that city... having thus secured the city of Dwaravati the Yādavas, along with their friends, lived there happily as do the gods in their own city.' (The 'Gada's younger brother' phrasing mirrors the Dutt translation, which here makes Gada the elder.)

DKS_0301.notes: Nearly a paraphrase of Harivamsha 1.113 (Dutt): Krishna's assembly speech, the Yadavas' one-voice assent, the Jarasandha-Kalayavana advance, the same-day departure headed by Vasudeva, the coastal site with its coppery soil, Mount Raivata with Drona and Ekalavya, the pre-existing name Dwaravati, and the naming of future houses all match the passage in order. No unsupported or contradicted facts.

statements.claim: Rukmi of Vidarbha, who had spent his life showing rivalry toward Krishna, announced a swayamvara for his daughter, and rich and powerful kings and princes came to his house from many countries.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.118 (1-2, 12): 'the powerful Rukshmi... announced that his daughter would make her choice of a husband... many rich and powerful kings and princes came to his house from various countries'; 'the king Rukshmi used always to show rivalry with Krishna.'

statements.claim: With the other princes came Pradyumna, the son of Krishna and Rukmini; the moment she saw him, Rukmi's daughter Rukmavati wanted to marry him — she was celebrated on earth for her beauty, endowed with grace and radiance — and Krishna's son, peerless in beauty, wished to espouse her in turn.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.118 (3-4): 'Prādyumna, accompanied by other princes, went there. As soon as she saw him Rukshmini's daughter wanted to marry him. She too, endued with grace and effulgence, was celebrated on earth for her beauty. Keshava's son therefore wished to espouse that one of fair eyes.'

statements.claim: When the kings were seated in the swayamvara hall, the princess of Vidarbha chose Pradyumna, the slayer of enemies — a master of arms, well-built like a lion, the most handsome young man in the assembly.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.118 (5-6): 'when all the powerful kings took their seats in the Swayamvara hall, the Bidarbha king's daughter chose Pradyumna the slayer of enemies... For he was a master of arms and well-built like a lion. Besides Keshava's son was peerless in beauty on earth.'

statements.claim: After the ceremony the kings returned to their cities and Pradyumna went home to Dwaraka with the princess of Vidarbha; he lived happily with her, as Nala lived with Damayanti, and in time she bore him a son, Aniruddha, like the son of a god, of matchless deeds.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.118 (8-9): 'After the termination of the Swayamvara the kings repaired to their respective cities and Pradyumna too went to Dwārakā with the princess of Bidarbha with him. The hero lived happily in her company as did Nala in that of Damayanti. Pradyumna begat on her a son by name Aniruddha, like unto the son of a god and of matchless deeds on earth.'

statements.claim: Aniruddha came of age and mastered the Vedas, the science of archery, and the moral laws; then Krishna chose a wife for him — Rukmavati again, the granddaughter of Rukmi, gold-like in beauty, namesake of the elder Rukmavati who had married Pradyumna.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.118 (9-11): 'When, Aniruddha, coming of age, mastered the Vedas, the science of archery and the moral laws, Mādhava selected the beautiful gold-like Rukshmavati, the grand-daughter of Rukshmi, for his wife.' The namesake point follows from both brides bearing the same name in the source.

statements.claim: For the eagerness of his son and of Rukmini, Rukmi set aside his old enmity and said with delight: 'I confer Rukmavati on Aniruddha, endued with accomplishments and of a peaceful nature.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.118 (12-13): 'still, on account of the eagerness of his son and Rukshmini he cast off his enmity and said with delightedness "I confer Rukshmavati on Aniruddha endued with accomplishments and of a peaceful nature"'.

statements.claim: Krishna went to Vidarbha surrounded by his own army, accompanied by Rukmini, Balarama, his sons and the other Yadavas; Rukmi's kinsmen, friends and allies came at his invitation, and on an auspicious day under a favorable planet the wedding of Aniruddha and Rukmavati was celebrated with great festivity, the Vidarbhas and Yadavas rejoicing together and the Vrishnis honored there like immortals.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.118 (14-15, 19-20): 'Keshava, surrounded by his own army and accompanied by Rukshmini, Sangkarshana, his own sons and other Yādavas, went to Bidarbha... Rukshmi's kinsmen, friends and allies came there also at his invitation... in an auspicious day and under the auspicies of a favourable planet Aniruddha's wedding was celebrated with great festivity... the Baidharvas and the Yadavas performed a great festivity. And adored there like immortals the Vrishnis lived happily.'

statements.claim: For those days at least, the old quarrel between the two houses was remembered by no one.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.118 (12-13): Rukmi 'cast off his enmity' for the marriage, and both houses feasted together; the time-scoped phrasing ('for those days at least') stays within what the source shows.

statements.claim: The feud that had once divided Vidarbha from Dwaraka ended not in a treaty but in a wedding, and the two families sat down together as one.
statements.evidence: The pack's own continuation of Harivamsha 1.118 (verses 16-38, quoted in the passage) shows the enmity alive immediately after the wedding: Rukmi 'used always to show rivalry with Krishna' (v.12), and right after the festivities he conspires with the Deccan chiefs 'to vanquish Revati's husband' at dice and gloats over Baladeva's losses ('the highly wily Rukshmi... with pride... "Baladeva... has lost innumerable gold coins to me"'). The rivalry was set aside for the wedding, not ended by it.
statements.resolution: Corrected in story text via consolidation pass.

corrections.original_sentence: The feud that had once divided Vidarbha from Dwaraka ended not in a treaty but in a wedding, and the two families sat down together as one.
corrections.suggested: The feud that had once divided Vidarbha from Dwaraka was set aside for those days, and the two families sat down together as one.

DKS_0302.notes: Swayamvara, Pradyumna-Rukmavati marriage, Aniruddha's education, and the second Rukmavati wedding all track Harivamsha 1.118 nearly verbatim. One CONTRADICTED closing flourish: the story declares the feud between the houses 'ended' by the wedding, but the pack's own passage continues past the festivities into Rukmi's immediate conspiracy to cheat and humiliate Balarama at dice — his enmity was laid aside for the occasion, not ended. The immediately preceding sentence ('For those days at least...') is properly scoped and supported; only the final unqualified claim needs the correction.

statements.claim: Krishna rode out of Dwaraka under the pretext of a hunt, with Satyaki beside him, and left his charioteer Daruka behind with orders to wait, tending and grooming the horses, until he returned on that very car.
statements.evidence: HV 1.220 v1-4: Krishna went to the Raivataka mountain 'under the pretext of hunting', taking Satyaki on his car and telling Pradyumna 'Follow me'; to Daruka: 'take charge of my chariot and wait here tending and grooming the horses... I shall re-enter Dwarkā on this very car'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna, Krishna's son by Rukmini, followed on a chariot of his own swift enough to course over hills; within the twinkle of an eye they crossed to Nandana, the pleasure park of the gods, where Krishna uprooted the Parijata tree and laid it on Garuda's back before the eyes of the celestial guardians.
statements.evidence: HV 1.220 v6-9: Pradyumna 'followed Krishna from behind on a separate car capable of coursing on hills'; 'within the twinkle of an eye the intelligent Hari arrived at... the Nandana forest'; hosts of celestial warriors present; Krishna 'uprooted the Pārijāta tree and placed it on the back of Garuda even before their eyes'.

statements.claim: The tree itself, embodied, approached Krishna in prayer, and Krishna consoled it, telling it not to fear.
statements.evidence: HV 1.220 v10-11: 'the Pārijāta, having embodied itself, approached (with prayer) Kesava and Garuda'; 'The tree Pārijāta was consoled by the high souled Kesava and was told—"Do thou not fear, O tree"'.

statements.claim: The keepers of the garden ran to Indra, who came out on Airavata with his son Jayanta following on a chariot; at the eastern gate Indra asked what was going on, Krishna saluted him with his head and said he was only taking the excellent tree away for a ceremonious observance; Indra replied that the tree could not be taken without challenging him to fight and bade Krishna hurl his mace Kaumodaki as the first blow.
statements.evidence: HV 1.220 v13-18: keepers informed Mahendra; Indra 'came out mounted on Airāvata being followed from behind by Jayanta on a car'; 'who had by that time reached the Eastern gate, Indra said... what is this going on'; Kesava: 'I am only taking away this excellent tree for a ceremonious observance of your sister-in-law'; Sakra: 'thou shouldst not take away this tree... without challenging me to fight... hurling the Koumodaki mace at me'.

statements.claim: Krishna pierced Airavata with arrows fierce as thunder while Indra pierced Garuda with heavenly shafts, each cutting off the other's arrows; the twang of Indra's bow and of the Sharanga (Sranga) made the inhabitants of heaven swoon.
statements.evidence: HV 1.220 v19-22: Krishna pierced 'the excellent elephant of the king of the celestials, with sharp arrows fierce like thunder itself'; Indra pierced Garuda 'with excellent arrows of heavenly make' and cut off Kesava's arrows, which Mādhava likewise severed; 'at the sound of Mahendra's bow and at the twang of the Sranga bow, the inhabitants of heaven swooned away'.

statements.claim: Jayanta tried to pull the Parijata tree from Garuda's back; Krishna, catching sight of him, called out to Pradyumna to prevent him, and instantly Pradyumna opposed him.
statements.evidence: HV 1.220 v23-24: 'the highly powerful Jayanta tried to remove the Pārijāta tree from the back of Garuda'; Krishna told Pradyumna 'Prevent him', and 'instantly the highly powerful son of Rukshmini opposed him (firmly)'.

statements.claim: Jayanta, foremost of victorious persons, smiled from his chariot and pierced Pradyumna all over with sharp arrows; Pradyumna — the god of love (Cupid) reborn, lotus-eyed — answered with arrows that moved like serpents; a fierce combat raged, the two foremost wielders of weapons using every offensive and defensive weapon, while gods, sages, Siddhas and Charanas beheld it struck with wonder.
statements.evidence: HV 1.220 v25-29: Jayanta, 'that foremost of victorious persons, began to pierce with sharp arrows smilingly the son of Rukshmini on all parts of his body'; 'The lotus-eyed god Cupid... pierced the son of Indra, with arrows looking like snakes'; the two 'foremost of the wielders of weapons, used offensive and defensive weapons against each other'; 'The gods, the sages, the Siddhas and the Chārnas, all beheld that fierce combat being much struck with wonder'.

statements.claim: A weapon of heavenly make struck Pradyumna's chariot, and the whole car burned down to ashes before the eyes of heaven — yet the fire could not touch the son of Rukmini, who stood unharmed in the open sky where his chariot had been.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'The car of the illustrious Pradyumna was burnt down by that weapon but it could not... consume the son of Rukshmini'; full passage HV 1.220 v45-49 (same Gutenberg text): Jayanta 'struck him with a weapon of heavenly make' which 'fell upon the top of the car of the son of Rukshmini', the car burnt down, and Pradyumna 'extricated himself from the burning chariot' and 'stationed himself in the heaven with bow in hand'.

statements.claim: Above them the duel of the fathers went on, bowstring against bowstring, while heaven watched the two sons — the one who had lost his chariot and still had not fallen.
statements.evidence: The Krishna-Indra duel does continue through ch. 220-221 and v29/v61 record the onlookers' wonder at the sons' combat; 'heaven was no longer watching only Krishna and Indra' is closing narrative emphasis rather than a discrete sourceable fact.

DKS_0303.notes: Faithful scene-by-scene to HV 1.220 (pack + Gutenberg source; pack passage cuts off at v32, remainder verified in the same cited text). 'Indra cutting down Garuda's feathers with heavenly shafts' condenses v20 (piercing Garuda with heavenly arrows); the feather-plucking belongs to the next chapter (221), a harmless conflation of the same duel. The story omits the 'sister-in-law' clause of Krishna's reason (abbreviation only).

statements.claim: Brahmadatta was a Vajasaneyi Brahmana of the city of Shatpura, on the sacred bank of the river Avarta, a disciple of Yajnavalka, well-read in the four Vedas and their six auxiliary sciences, initiated into a sacrifice lasting a full year.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 v1-3: 'in the city of Shatpura on the sacred bank of the good river Avarta... a Vajasaneyi Brāhmana, by name Brahmadatta, a disciple of Yajnawalka, well-read in the four Vedas and six Angas... was initiated into a Yajna extending over a year'.

statements.claim: The great sages gathered around Brahmadatta — Vyasa and Yajnavalka, Sumantu, Jaimini, Devala and others — and the account's own narrator was among the guests at that year-long rite; Vasudeva came with Devaki beside him, for Brahmadatta was an old friend and preceptor of the house, and day after day Devaki gave the beggars whatever they asked, in proportion to her husband's wealth.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 v4-5: 'were present Vyasa, Yajnawalka, Sumantu, Jaimini, Dhritimān, Jajali, Devala and other great and leading Munis... And I too had gone there'; Vasudeva with Devaki 'repaired there for protecting him, for he was a class friend and preceptor of Anakadundubhi'; 'the pious Devaki distributed amongst the beggars various articles they wanted proportionate to the wealth of the intelligent Vasudeva'.

statements.claim: Nikumbha and the other Daityas of Shatpura, proud of a boon they had once won, assembled at the sacrificial ground and delivered their terms: a share of the offerings, the right to drink Soma, Brahmadatta's daughters, and his finest jewels — threatening that the yajna would not be allowed if refused.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 v6-12: 'the inhabitants of Shatpura, Nikumbha and other Daityas, proud of their boon, assembled there and said: "Give us our share in the Yajna. We will drink Soma and Brahmadatta must give us his daughters... He should also give us the most valuable jems... If he transgresses this order we will not allow him to celebrate this Yajna"'.

statements.claim: Brahmadatta refused them to their faces: no portion of the offerings was laid down for them in the Vedas, the daughters would be conferred on proper bridegrooms following the Vedas, the whole collection of his jewels was theirs if they came to terms, and if they used force, 'the son of Devaki is my supporter'.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 v13-16, Brahmadatta's speech near-verbatim: 'no portion of sacrificial offerings has been laid down for you in the Vedas... The daughters whom I shall give away in marriage I shall confer upon proper bridegrooms following the same Vedas with me... If you however come to terms I may give you the entire collection of my jewels. If you show your force I will not give that even for Devaki's son is my supporter'.

statements.claim: The Danavas resorted to force: they scattered the articles of the sacrifice about the ground and carried away his daughters; Vasudeva, helpless, thought of Krishna and of Balabhadra and Gada, and the moment he was thought of Krishna knew everything and told Pradyumna to proceed and save the maidens by his illusive power, saying he himself would follow soon with the Yadava army.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 v17-19: 'the wicked Dānavas of Shatpura, Nikumbha and others began to scatter the articles of Yajna and carry away his daughters. Beholding the sacrificial articles robbed by the Asuras Anakadundubhi thought of the great Krishna, Balabhadra and Gada. As soon as he was thought of Krishna came to know of every thing and said to Pradyumna: "Proceed, O my son, and save the maidens by virtue of your illusive powers... I myself too will soon go to Shatpura with the Yādava army"'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna, intelligent, powerful and ever obedient to his father, was in Shatpura within a moment and by his illusive power took away the maidens — every one of them — creating counterfeit figures so like the originals that no eye could tell them apart and setting them before the Daityas, and telling Devaki 'Be not afraid'; the demons seized the illusory maidens and entered their city well satisfied, while the true daughters were far beyond their reach, and the sacrifice went on according to the proper rites.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 v20-24: Pradyumna 'went to Shatpura within a moment and took away the maidens by virtue of his illusive power. Creating their figures by his illusive power the pious son of Rukshmini kept them before the Daityas and said to Devaki "Be not afraid"... the irrepressible Daityas carried away the illusory maidens and entered their city with satisfaction'; 'that great and glorious Yajna was being celebrated according to proper rites'. 'So like the originals that no eye could tell them apart' is a gloss of the illusion, uncontradicted.

statements.claim: The invited kings began to arrive and encamp with their hosts near Shatpura: Jarasandha and Shishupala, Dantavakra, the Pandavas, the sons of Dhritarashtra, the rulers of the Malava and Tangana lands, Rukmi, Shalya, Shakuni and many another warrior king.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 v24-28 lists 'Jarāsandha, Shisupala, Dantavakra, the Pandavas, the sons of Dhritarāshtra, the Mālava and Tangana kings, Rukshmi, Ahvriti, Neela, Nārmada, Vinda, Anuvinda, Avantya, Shalya, Shakuni and other heroic, noble and warrior kings encamped near Shatpura' — the story's 'many another warrior king' covers the remainder.

statements.claim: Narada watched the kings arrive and, reflecting that all the Kshatriyas and Yadavas assembled at the yajna would surely lead to a conflict which he would try to bring about, went to the house of Nikumbha.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 v29-30: 'the beautiful Nārada thought: "At this Yajna all the Kshatryas and Yādavas have assembled. Surely this will lead to a conflict. I shall therefore try to bring it about." Thinking this he repaired to Nikumbha's house'.

DKS_0304.notes: Near-verbatim paraphrase of HV 1.230. 'The demons did not believe him' is the story's connective gloss for the demons' resort to force after the refusal. Vasudeva's helplessness and the general compression (kings listed via 'many another warrior king') are consistent with the pack.

statements.claim: By the middle of that day a cave near Shatpura had swallowed 'half the Yadava army'.
statements.evidence: Dramatic teaser of the capture scene the story then narrates in detail; the pack (HV 1.231 v27-29) supports Nikumbha carrying off Anadhristhi, Kritavarma, Charudeshna, Vaitarana, Sanatkumar, Arksha, Nishatha, Ulmuka 'and numerous other Yādavas' into the cave — not a quantified 'half'. Hyperbolic framing, no distortion of the record.

statements.claim: The kings who had come to witness Brahmadatta's sacrifice had stayed and, Narada's whispers having done their work, arrayed themselves with the Asuras against the Yadavas at dawn.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 v17-22: 'the soldiers of the Chedi and other kings were bent upon assisting the Asuras'; Bhagadatta, Shalya, Shakuni, Jarāsandha, Trigarta, Virāta, Uttara etc. 'got themselves ready' to fight the Yadavas; Narada's instigation is the closing beat of the previous event (HV 1.230 v29-30, corpus chain).

statements.claim: At dawn Baladeva, Krishna and Satyaki mounted Garuda, bathed in the sacred river Avarta — made holy by a boon of Rudra — put on coats of mail and finger-guards, and worshipped Shiva, the lord of the bel leaf and the waters; Pradyumna was placed in front of the army, the Pandavas in charge of the sacrifice, and soldiers at the door of the cave; Jayanta and Pravara arrived the instant Krishna thought of them and were posted above with Pradyumna.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 v1-6: 'Within a moment of the clear sun coming... Baladeva, Krishna and Satyaki delightedly got upon Garuda's back. Having bathed in the water of the sacred river Avarta, who had obtained a boon from Rudra... and having put on coats of mail, finger-protectors and armours... worshipped the god Siva, the lord of bel leaves and water'; 'having placed Pradyumna above in front of the army, the Pandavas in charge of the Yajna and the remaining soldiers at the door of the cave'; Krishna thought of Jayanta and Pravara, who arrived at once 'and were kept above along with Pradyumna'.

statements.claim: The war-instruments sounded — conches, drums and battle-bugles; Samba and Gada drew up the soldiers in the shape of a makara; Uddhava, Kritavarma, Charudeshna, Sanatkumar and the rest guarded Aniruddha and protected the rear.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 v7-10: 'at Krishna's mandate, war-bugles, Jalaja, Muraja and other musical instruments were sounded'; 'Sāmva and Gada arranged the soldiers in the shape of a Makara'; Shārana, Uddhava, Vaitarana, Anādhrishti, Viprithu, Prithu, Kritavarmā, Sudangsthra, Vichakshu, Sanatkumar and Chārudeshna 'began to help Aniruddha and protect the rear of the army'.

statements.claim: Out of Shatpura came the Danavas, dreadful in battle, roaring like gathering clouds — riding on asses and elephants, crocodiles and hares, horses, buffaloes, lions and tortoises, their chariots drawn by such beasts; Nikumbha came at their head as the lord of gods issues out at the head of the celestial host, and the earth and sky were filled with his shouts and leonine roars.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 v11-16: the Dānavas 'came out of Shatpura, emitting a roar like the muttering of clouds, on asses, elephants, crocodiles, hares, horses, buffaloes, lions and tortoises. Many of their cars were drawn by those animals'; 'as the lord of gods issues out at the head of the celestial host so Nikumbha came out at the head of that Asura army'; 'sending up again and again shouts of various sorts and leonine roars the highly powerful Dānavas filled the earth and sky with them'.

statements.claim: Behind them came the kings: the hundred brothers of the Chedi king Shishupala, led by Duryodhana, wheeled and rattled with their chariots like the city of the Gandharvas; Rukmi and Ahvati joined them; Bhagadatta, Shalya, Shakuni, Jarasandha, Trigarta, Virata and Uttara made ready for the encounter.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 v17-22: 'amongst the followers of the Chedi king Shishupāla, the hundred brothers headed by Duryodhana stood there with their cars, making a great rattle and coursing quickly like unto the city of Gandharva'; 'Rukshmi and Ahvati joined them'; 'the king Bhagadatta, Shalya, Shakuni, Jarāsandha, Trigarta, Virāta, Uttara... got themselves ready for the encounter'.

statements.claim: Nikumbha struck first, pouring arrows like serpents into the Yadava ranks; Anadhristhi, commander-in-chief of the Yadu army, answered with arrows adorned with variegated feathers and whetted on stone until Nikumbha's chariot, standard and horses disappeared under the hail; Nikumbha then bewildered Anadhristhi by illusion, carried him off to the cave named Shatpura and imprisoned him there, and — invisible to every eye — returned to take Kritavarma, Charudeshna, Vaitarana of the Bhoja race, Sanatkumar, Arksha the son of Jambavati, Nishatha, Ulmuka and numerous other Yadavas, dragging them all into that dreadful cave.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 v23-30: Nikumbha 'began to assail the dreadful army of the Bhaimas with arrows like serpents'; Anādhrishti, 'the commander-in-chief of the Yadu army', 'with shafts, adorned with variegated feathers and whetted on stone, began to slay the enemy's army'; 'Nikumbha, his chariot, standard and horses became invisible'; 'bewildering Anadhristhi and bringing him to the cave named Shatpura the heroic Nikumbha imprisoned him there'; returning, 'he, by his illusive powers, took there Kritavarmā, Chārudeshna, Vaitarana of Bhoja's race, Sanatkumār, Jāmvavati's son Arksha, Nishatha, Ulmuku and numerous other Yādavas', 'so covered himself by his illusive powers that no body could see him'.

statements.claim: Krishna set his Sharanga bow and moved among the Danavas as the god of fire ranges over dry grass; the demons hurled iron missiles and iron clubs, fiery lances and burning axes, great rocks and boulders, and whole elephants, chariots and horses; the Narayana fire consumed them all, and Krishna, smiling, baffled the demons with the fire of his arrows, bearing their onslaught as a bull bears the autumn rain.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 v30-33: Krishna 'setting string to his Srānga bow and shooting arrows... began to move about amongst the Dānavas as the god of fire ranges on grass'; Danavas 'taking up thousands of Sataghnis, Parighas, fiery lances, burning axes, dreadful rocks, and huge stones and throwing up infuriated elephants, cars and horses'; 'Narayana-fire consumed all those things. And smiling the highly effulgent Yadu chief... baffled them all with the fire of his arrows. And as a bull suffers the downpour of rain in the autumn so he bore the shower'.

statements.claim: At Nandi's command, bearing the nooses given by Hara — by Shiva himself — Pradyumna moved among the kings who had sided with the Asuras, bound Bhagadatta, Shishupala, Rukmi, Ahvati and the other kings with those divine nooses, and took them all to the illusory cave.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'binding the king Bhagadatta, Shishupāla, Ahvati, Rukshmi and other kings... with the nooses given by Hara Rukshmini's son... took them all to the illusory cave'; full passage HV 1.231 v55-60 (same Gutenberg text): Nandi came 'taking up a thousand of nooses' and said 'Vilwodakeshwara (Siva) has ordered you to do what he had told you in the night. Bind these kings with nooses who have been bribed with jewels for the maidens', whereupon Pradyumna bound them 'like hissing serpents, with the nooses given by Hara' and 'took them all to the illusory cave'.

DKS_0305.notes: Faithful to HV 1.231; the cave/'Shatpura' usage follows the pack (the Dutt text calls both the cave and the Danava abode 'Shatpura'). The closing image (the cave that swallowed the Yadava captains now holding the bribed kings, with Aniruddha posted as its guard) matches the passage. The 'half the army' teaser is hyperbole over a supported mass capture (see connective statement).

statements.claim: While the Yadavas were busy with their sports, Nikumbha, the master of illusion, slipped past the garden attached to the women's apartments — unapproachable but unguarded at that hour — and carried off Bhanumati, the beautiful daughter of Bhanu, remembering how Pradyumna had once carried away Prabhavati, daughter of his own brother Vajranabha, and had killed the brother besides.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v1-5: Nikumbha 'stole away the beautiful daughter of Bhānu by name Bhānumati'; 'formerly, the daughter of his brother Vajranābhā, by name Prabhāvati, had been taken away by Pradyumna and Vajranābha had been killed. Remembering this former enmity... he played upon the women of the Yādavas'; 'Although the garden, attached to the female appartment of Bhānu, was unapproachable, still at that time there were no guards for the Yadavas were busy with their sports'.

statements.claim: While the weeping maiden was being carried away a great tumult rose through the women's apartments and Vasudeva and Ahuka came out in a fury; Krishna, hearing of the insult, mounted Garuda with Arjuna beside him, commanded Pradyumna — whose banner bore the makara — to follow on his chariot, and they overtook the demon before he could reach the city of Vajra.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v6-11: 'while that weeping maiden was being carried away there arose all on a sudden a great tumult in the female appartment'; 'Vasudeva and Ahuka issued out, filled with wrath'; hearing of the insult Krishna 'rode, together with Pārtha, Garuda the enemy of the serpents'; 'having commanded the hero having the emblem of a Makara on his flag to follow him on his car'; 'before Nikumbha... could reach the city of Vajra, Pārtha and Krishna... overtook him in the way'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna, foremost of those skilled in illusion, divided himself into three; Nikumbha, like an immortal, fought all three at once with heavy clubs — holding Bhanumati in his left hand and hurling the club with his right.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v12-14: Pradyumna 'divided himself into three portions'; 'Nikumbha, like unto an immortal, smilingly fought with them all with heavy clubs. Holding the maiden Bhānumati by his left hand, the great Asura Nikumbha repeatedly hurled the club with his right hand'.

statements.claim: Although any one of the three was capable of slaying the demon, none could strike him ruthlessly for fear of wounding the maiden in his arms; they fought with restraint, sighing piteously out of compassion for her, until Arjuna — as a man skilled in arms strikes the serpent coiled around a camel, leaving the camel unhurt — began to wound the demon with his cane-like arrows.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v15-18: 'none could strike him ruthlessly lest they might wound the maiden'; 'although capable of slaying that irrepressible enemy they began to sigh piteously out of their excessive compassion for the maiden'; 'As when a serpent gets round a camel, a man, well up in the use of arms, strikes the serpent leaving the camel to itself, so Pārtha, the foremost of archers, began to strike the Daitya with his arrows'; all three 'wounded the Danavas with their cane-like arrows'.

statements.claim: Nikumbha resorted to illusion and vanished with the maiden so completely that no one could tell where he had gone, and the three pursued him as he fled — now in the semblance of a yellow vulture — across the whole earth, over the seven insular continents, until he dropped down with the maiden on the bank of the river Chela Ganga, high on the summit of Mount Gokarna, a mountain none of the gods, Asuras or great ascetics could cross, protected by the energy of Mahadeva.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v19-24: 'resorting to his illusory powers Nikumbha so disappeared with the maiden from that place that nobody could know it: Krishna, Kāma and Dhananjaya however immediately pursued him: he, however, went on assuming the semblance of a yellow vulture'; 'travelled all over the earth consisting of seven insular continents and dropped down with the maiden at last on the bank of the river Chela Gangā flowing on the summit of the mount Gokarna'; 'None amongst the gods, Asuras or great ascetics could cross that mountain protected by the energy of Mahadeva'.

statements.claim: There Pradyumna seized Bhanumati from the demon, while Krishna and Arjuna drove Nikumbha from the northern range of Gokarna to the southern with their arrows, pursuing him on Garuda.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v25-26: 'the Bhaima chief Pradyumna... got hold of the maiden Bhānumati. And Krishna, and Arjuna began to assail the Asura greatly with arrows. Then leaving the northern range of the mount Gokarna, Nikumbha fled to the southern range. Both the Krishnas however, riding on Garuda, pursued him'.

statements.claim: Broken and furious, Nikumbha fled into Shatpura, the abode of his kinsmen; the two heroes spent the night at the mouth of the cave; with Krishna's permission Pradyumna carried Bhanumati back to Dwaraka in triumph, then returned to find Krishna and Arjuna waiting where he had left them, before the cave.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v27-29: 'the great Asura entered into Shatpura, the abode of his kinsmen and those two heroes spent the night at the mouth of the cave. With Krishna's permission the heroic son of Rukshmini delightedly took Bhaima's daughter to the city of Dwārakā. And keeping her there he returned to Shatpura... and beheld the two Krishnas of dreadful prowess at the mouth of the cave'.

statements.claim: Desirous of fighting, Nikumbha came out of the cave; Arjuna met him at the threshold with arrows from the Gandiva, blocking the way; it made no difference — Nikumbha came on, took up his club, a great staff covered with thorns, and struck Partha on the head, and Arjuna vomited blood and lost consciousness on the spot.
