statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v31-34: 'desirous of fighting the highly powerful Nikumbha came out of the cave... Dhananjaya, with arrows shot off his Gandiva bow, obstructed the thorough-fair. In spite of it Nikumbha... came out, took up his club covered with thorns and struck Pārtha on his head. Thus assailed... Pritha's son vomitted blood and lost his consciousness'.

statements.claim: The master of illusions smiled and, with an unseen stroke of the same club, struck the heroic son of Rukmini — the foremost of those skilled in illusion — on the head, and Pradyumna fell senseless beside his friend; then Govinda, the king of Dwaraka, seized his club Kaumodaki and ran toward Nikumbha.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v34-35 and pack excerpt: 'The Asura, master of illusions, smilingly struck the heroic son of Rukshmini, the foremost of those conversant with illusions... Wounded on the head with that unseen stroke of the club the heroic Pradyumna lost his consciousness'; excerpt: 'Govinda... took up his club Koumodaki and ran towards Nikumbha'.

DKS_0306.notes: Chapter title of HV 1.237 is itself 'Nikumbha Carries Away Bhanumati'; the story opens with the aftermath (the cave duel) then backtracks to the abduction — every scene maps to the pack's verses. Pack passage truncated mid-sentence at v34; the finale is confirmed by the pack's excerpt line.

statements.claim: The city of Vajra belonged to the Asura king Vajranabha, who had practised long austerities on the summit of Mount Sumeru until Brahma himself appeared and offered him a boon; Vajranabha asked for two things: that no god should ever be able to kill him, and that he should possess the city of Vajra — a city where even the air could not easily enter, ringed with gardens, with many branch cities, rich in peerless jewels, granting every wish before the wish was even spoken — and Brahma granted both.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 v5-9: Vajranābha 'practised hard austerities on the summit of the mount Sumeru'; 'the Divine Brahmā... asked him to pray for a boon'; he 'prayed for two boons that even the gods might not kill him, and that he might get the city Vajra where even the air cannot easily enter, which gives every sort of desired-for objects even when they are not thought of, which has gardens encircled by walls, many branch cities, and peerless jems of every description'.

statements.claim: Millions of Asuras, enemies of the gods, took refuge with Vajranabha and lived in Vajra's gardens and branch cities, healthy, well-fed and content, safe under the shelter of the boon.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 v11-12: 'seeking refuge with that great Asura who had obtained this boon, millions of demons lived in that city of Vajra, in his garden and in many charming branch cities... the enemies of the gods lived there, healthy, well-fed and contented'.

statements.claim: Elated by his good fortune, Vajranabha went to Indra and announced that the three worlds were the common property of all the high-souled sons of Kashyapa alike — he wished to govern them, and if Indra did not approve he could give battle; Indra consulted Brihaspati, and the two chose to wait, since their father Kashyapa was in the middle of a great sacrifice and would do what was fair when it ended; Vajranabha carried the same answer to Kashyapa himself, who sent him home with the same promise.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 v13-19: Vajranābha told Indra 'all the three worlds are the common properties of all the high-souled sons of Kashyapa. I therefore wish to govern the three worlds. If you... do not approve of my proposal, give me battle'; Mahendra 'consulted with Vrihaspati', answering 'our father, the ascetic Kashyapa, is now engaged in a sacrifice. After its termination he will do what is fair'; Kashyapa told Vajranabha the same and sent him back to the city of Vajra.

statements.claim: Indra came secretly to Dwaraka and told Krishna everything; Krishna answered that the horse-sacrifice of Vasudeva, his father, was at hand and that once it was over he would kill Vajranabha, adding honestly that even the wind could not enter the city if Vajranabha did not wish it, and that they would find a way in at the right hour.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 v20-23: 'Mahendra went to the city of Dwāravati... and communicated secretly to Vāsudeva what Vajranābha had said'; Janārddana: 'O Vāsava, the horse-sacrifice of Vasudeva is now at hand. After its termination I will kill Vajranabha... even the wind cannot enter into his city if Vajranābha does not wish it. At a convenient hour we will concert measures for entering there'.

statements.claim: During the horse-sacrifice itself, an actor named Bhadra so delighted the great saints that they invited him to ask for a boon; prompted by Krishna and as if urged on by the goddess of learning, he asked to roam freely over the seven continents of the earth and through the sky with nothing to obstruct him, to be strong and unharmed by any creature moving or still, to take whatever form he pleased, that age might never touch him, and that the sages might always be pleased with him — and the Munis said 'So be it'.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 v26-32: Bhadra 'pleased the great saints with his beautiful acting. The leading Munis then asked him to pray for a boon'; he prayed 'as desired by Krishna and as if urged on by the goddess of learning': 'may I range over the earth consisting of seven insular continents... without any obstruction, range all over the sky... be gifted with strength and be not slain by all creatures mobile and immobile. May I assume any form I like... May not decrepitude overtake me and may the Munis always remain pleased with me'; 'the Munis said "So be it"'. (The story omits the first request — to become the food of all twice-born — an omission, not an error.)

statements.claim: From that day the immortal-looking actor ranged over the whole earth, performing in the cities of the Danava kings, in Uttarakuru, Bhadrashva, Ketumala and the island of Kalamra, and on every festival day he came back to Dwaraka, where the Yadavas welcomed him.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 v33-35: 'That immortal-like one began to range all over the earth... He began to show his performances in the cities of the Dānava kings, in Uttarakura, Bhadrāshwa, Ketumāl and the island of Kalāmra. On the occasion of every Parva, that great actor... used to come to Dwarakā adorned with the Yadavas'.

statements.claim: Indra called the Dhartarashtra swans — celestial birds and his own brothers, since both gods and swans are begotten by Kashyapa — and told them the great duty of killing the enemies of the gods awaited them; they were to keep the counsel secret, go to the city of Vajra, where no one else could enter, and range in the tanks of the king's inner palace; there Vajranabha's daughter Prabhavati — fair as moonlight, the jewel of the three worlds, kept by her friends for a swayamvara — was to be won by hearing of the family, beauty, character and accomplishments of the high-souled Pradyumna; they were to carry her words to Pradyumna and bring back his, reporting to Indra and to his younger brother Krishna at Dwaraka every day.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 v36-50 (pack excerpt + Gutenberg source; pack passage cut at v37): Sakra to the Dhārtarāshtra swans: 'you are our brothers on account of your being begotten by Kashyapa... don't divulge the counsel'; 'going to the most excellent city of Vajranabha where no one else can enter you should range in the tanks of his inner appartment'; 'Vajranābha has a jewel of a daughter, peerless in beauty, in the three worlds, by name Prabhāvati who is fair like the rays of the moon... her friends have kept that beautiful and chaste maiden for Swayemvara'; 'Do you describe to her the various accomplishments, family, beauty, character, and age, of the high-souled Pradyumna'; 'take carefully her news to Pradyumna and return with his message to her'; 'you should communicate to me and to my younger brother Krishna at Dwāravati daily what happens there'.

statements.claim: Indra told the swans that the Danavas — elated by the pride of Brahma's boon — could not be slain by the gods; their destruction had to come from the sons of the gods, from Pradyumna and his brothers; and since the actor Bhadra had obtained the boon of entering the city, the Yadavas would enter Vajra in his guise.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 v51-52 (pack excerpt + Gutenberg source): 'Those Dānavas, elated with the pride of the boon conferred by Brahmā, are not to be slain by the gods. So their destruction in the battle-field should be brought about by Pradyumna and other sons of gods. An actor, Bhadra by name, has of late obtained the boon (of entering into his city). So the Yadavas, headed by Pradyumna, will enter into Vajranābha's city in his guise'.

statements.claim: So the swans rose into the sky and turned toward a city no army could approach, carrying a message that would open it from within — through the heart of the king's own daughter.
statements.evidence: Closing frame condensing the mission (chapter 239 opens with the celestial swans going to the city of Vajra); 'no army could approach' restates v40's 'where no one else can enter', and the courtship of Prabhavati is the mission per v43-47.

DKS_0307.notes: Every element of the story — including Indra's full speech to the swans — matches HV 1.238 v36-54. The pack's own passage cuts off mid-speech at v37 ('[...]'); the remainder was verified in the same cited Gutenberg translation (chapter CCXXXVIII), and the pack's excerpt line independently confirms the speech's gist. The opening 'beyond the seven continents' is atmospheric color (the city's kingdom is later placed by Mount Sumeru, ch. 244).

statements.claim: Vajranabha's orders went ahead of the troupe: the Asuras of his cities were to give the actors the finest rooms, treat them as guests, and press jewels and fine raiment upon them; the actor who had won the sages' boon reached the dependent city of Supura and so delighted its citizens with his dancing that they welcomed him with presents.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v1-5: king Vajranābha ordered the Asuras of their cities: 'Give them most excellent rooms... Treat them as guests, give them various jewels and various raiments which please people'; 'Receiving the order of their Chief they did all this... With great delight they welcomed the actor with presents of jewels... the actor, who had obtained the boon, pleased highly the citizens of Supura with his dancing'.

statements.claim: The company staged the Ramayana — the birth of Vishnu for the destruction of Ravana, and how the kings Lomapada and Dasharatha brought the young sage Rishyashringa to Shanta — personating Rama, Lakshmana, Shatrughna and Bharata so perfectly that even the oldest Danavas were startled and spoke again and again of the resemblance; the delighted Danavas rose from their seats, applauded, and threw down necklaces of gold and vaidurya, bracelets and cloths, and the actors praised each Asura house in verse, in the order of its family and birth.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v6-13: 'They gave a performance of the great epic Rāmāyana: the birth of the incomparable Vishnu for the destruction of the king of Rakshasas (Ravana). How Lomapāda and Dasharatha had brought for Shānta, the Muni Rishwashringa'; 'the actors so perfectly personated the characters of Rāma, Lakshmana, Shatrughna, Bharata... that even the elderly Dānavas were startled and spoke repeatedly of the similarity'; the Asuras 'repeatedly rose up, expressed their appreciation and gave away charming necklaces of gold and Vaidurja, bracelets and cloths'; 'the actors, with separate slokas, eulogised the Asuras in order of their family and birth'.

statements.claim: The news reached the city of Vajra; Vajranabha, who had heard of the famous actor long before, sent a messenger, and the Daityas of the branch cities conducted the disguised Yadavas into the great city itself, lodging them in a beautiful house built by the celestial architect; Vajranabha raised a great pavilion, made a festival of the players, gave them profuse jewels after they had rested, and — keeping the women of his family behind a screen — sat with his kinsmen to watch the play.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v14-20: 'the inhabitants of the dependant cities communicated to Vajra nābha the arrival of the beautiful actors... pleased he sent a messenger to bring the actor'; 'the Daityas, living in branch cities, took the Yadavas, disguised as actors, to the charming city of Vajra'; 'a beautiful house, built by the celestial architect, was offered'; 'having set up a beautiful pandal the great Asura, Vajranābha, made a great festival with the actors. After they had been relieved of toil... Vajranābha gave profuse jems and requested them to begin the play'; 'having kept the women of his family behind a screen... the great Asura himself sat with his kinsmen'.

statements.claim: Dressed as actors, the young men of the Yadava house began the performance: first the music of kamsya, venu and muraja; then the women of the troupe sang the Gandharva song Chhalikya, sweet to ear and mind; and with the seven scales, the three gramas and the ragas of spring they sang the song of the sacred descent of the Ganga, so that the Asuras rose again and again in pleasure.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v21-25: 'dressing themselves as actors, and arranging for the concert the Bhaimas... went on with the performance. They first played various tunes on musical instruments, as Kansya, Venu, Muraja etc. Afterwards the women... sang the Gandharva song Chhalikya, delightful to the mind and ears. Then with seven scales, Gāndhāra and others, three Grāmas, and with Rāgas, Vasanta and others, they sang sweetly the song of the sacred discension of Ganga... Asuras rose up again and again and pleased the actors'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna, Gada and Shamba — all in the guise of actors — conducted the nandi, the opening benediction, and Rukmini's son sang the hymn of the Ganga's descent with graceful gestures; then came the drama Rambhabhisara, in which Shura played Ravana, Monovati played Rambha, Pradyumna played Nalakuvara and Shamba played the jester, the Yadavas by their illusory powers conjuring the very scene of Kailasa, where the angry Nalakuvara cursed Ravana and comforted Rambha.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v26-30: 'the powerful Pradyumna, who had assumed the guise of an actor, Gada and Shāmva conducted the Nāndi. After the termination of the Prologue Rukshmini's son sang the hymn, accompanied with beautiful gestures, of the descension of Gangā. Afterwards they began the performance of the drama Rambhābhisara, Shura acted the part of Rāvana, Monovati represented Rambhā, Pradyumna Nalakuvara and Shāmva his Vidushaka. By their illusory powers the Yādavas represented the scene of Kailāsha... how the wicked Rāvana was imprecated by Nalakuvara, worked up with anger and how Rambhā was consoled'.

statements.claim: Scene by scene the delighted Danavas showered the stage with costly garments, jewelled necklaces, sky-cars, celestial elephants, cool sandal and aloe scents, and at last the Chintamani, the gem that grants every wish — giving so freely at every scene that they drained their own treasuries, the women of the Asura chiefs among them.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v31-37: 'They gave them costly apparels, jewelleries, necklaces set with costly jems, beautiful balloons, cars ranging in the sky, elephants coursing in the etherial region, cool and celestial sandal, Agura, and other scents and the valuable jem Chintāmani which gives all that is thought of. Giving away presents in this way at every scene those Dānavas were deprived of their riches and jewels. Even the women of the Danava-Chiefs shared the same fate'.

statements.claim: Prabhavati's friend Suchimukhi, the goose, came to the princess and said she had gone secretly to Dwaraka, seen Pradyumna there, and told him of her love; he was pleased and had appointed this evening for meeting her — 'the Yadavas never speak an untruth. Truly, today you will meet your love'; Prabhavati's heart leapt, and she asked the goose to stay in her room that night, saying that with her beside her she feared nobody and wished to see Krishna's son.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v38-44: Suchimukhi: 'I had gone to the charming city of Dwārakā... I saw Pradyumna there secretly and told him about your love for him... Pleased he has appointed this evening for meeting you... the Bhaimas never speak an untruth; verily to-day you will meet your love'; Prabhāvati: 'to-day wait in my room and sleep here. If you live by me I do not fear any body. With you I wish to see Keshava's son'.

statements.claim: That evening a fragrant garland, thick with bees, was carried to the princess's chamber and set down near Prabhavati; hidden among the bees was Pradyumna, who had taken the form of one of them; as dusk turned to evening the other bees flew away one by one, and the one that remained, the hero of the Yadava house, slowly settled on Prabhavati's ear.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v49-53 + pack excerpt: 'seeing a fragrant garland filled with bees carried for Prabhāvati, the highly powerful... hero, Pradyumna... sat there on assuming the form of a bee. That garland, covered with black-bees, was taken by the maid servants to the inner appartment and kept near Prabhāvati... when gradually evening set in, the other bees fled away. Then having none to follow him the heroic Bhaima chief slowly sat on Prabhāvati's ear'.

statements.claim: The full moon rose, and Prabhavati, whose limbs burned and whose mouth had gone dry, confessed to the goose the strange fever of loving a man she had only heard of — 'I have not seen him, and still my limbs burn' — and then the bee at her ear was no bee at all: the guest promised for the evening had come, and that night the long-pining lovers met.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v54-62: 'beholding the highly charming full moon arise... Prabhāvati... said to the goose, "O friend, my limbs are burning, my mouth is being dried up... I have not seen him—I have wanted him after only hearing of him—still my limbs are burning"'; the meeting follows in HV 1.241 v1-3 (same source): Pradyumna tells the goose 'in the guise of a black-bee, I have come here... Let her do what she likes to do with me', and appears in his own form — consistent with the corpus-chain next beat and the pack's stated scope ('the long-pining lovers meet by night').

DKS_0308.notes: Very faithful to HV 1.240, verse by verse through the whole festival and courtship. The pack's passage cuts off at v43 ('[...]'); the remainder (v44-62, bee scene) is confirmed verbatim in the same cited Gutenberg translation and by the pack's excerpt line. The closing 'lovers met at last' stops short of the marriage in ch. 241 — within scope, no error.

statements.claim: When the great sacrifice of the sage Kashyapa ended, gods and Asuras went back to their own habitations, and Vajranabha — still set on conquering the three worlds — went to his father to press his claim; Kashyapa warned him that Indra was the eldest of them all and foremost in accomplishments, strong by nature, devoted to the Brahmanas, grateful, the king of the whole world and the refuge of the good, holding his sovereignty because he worked for the well-being of all creatures — Vajranabha could not vanquish him and would be killed, as one who rouses a serpent meets his own destruction.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v1-6: 'After the termination of the sacrifice of Kashyapa... the gods and Asuras repaired to their respective habitations'; Vajranābha, 'desirous of conquering the three worlds, went to Kashyapa', who said: 'Sakra is the eldest of you all and the foremost in accomplishments: he is endued with great ascetic powers, is strong by nature, devoted to the Brāhmanas, grateful, the king of the whole world and the refuge of the good and the pious. Because he is engaged in the well-being of all creatures he has obtained this sovereignty... you will not be able to vanquish him but yourself will be killed. As one who excites the anger of a serpent meets with his own destruction, so you will in no time be destroyed'.

statements.claim: As a dying man lets pass the medicine that could save him, Vajranabha let the warning pass; he saluted his father and went home to gather kinsmen, warriors and friends, and his first march was against the celestial region itself.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v7-9: 'as a man, desirous of meeting with death... does not take medicine so Vajrānābha did not approve of the words of Kashyapa. Having saluted Kashyapa... he began to make arrangements for conquering the three worlds... collected his kinsmen, warriors, and friends. He first set out for conquering the region of the celestials'.

statements.claim: At that very time Indra and Krishna had sent their swans into the city of Vajra to bring about the Asura's ruin; hearing the swans' intelligence, the Yadava heroes consulted together: 'Vajranabha will be killed now, and by Pradyumna. But Vajranabha's daughter and Sunabha's two daughters are the devoted wives of our house, and all three are with child, near their time. What should we do?'
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v10-14: 'the highly powerful deities Indra and Upendra had sent the Swans there for bringing about Vajranābha's destruction'; the Yadus consulted: 'Forsooth Vajranābha will be killed now by Pradyumna. But Vajranābha's daughter and Sunābha's daughters are their devoted wives. They are all enciente and the time for their delivery is near at hand. What should we do now?' (Sunabha's two daughters, Chandravati and Gunavati, are identified in HV 1.241 v33-34.)

statements.claim: The two gods answered through the swans: 'Have no fear. Your sons will be beautiful as Kama and complete in every accomplishment; even in the womb they will master the Vedas with their auxiliaries. They will spring at once to youth, and they will be masters of every scripture.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v15-17: 'No fear: you will have beautiful sons like Kāma endued with all accomplishments; even when in the womb they will master all the Vedas with their auxilliaries. Your sons will at once grow to youth and they will be masters of all future topics and various scriptures'.

statements.claim: In time Prabhavati bore a son, omniscient and youthful as his father; a month later Chandravati bore Chandraprabha, the very image of Gada; and Gunavati bore Gunavan, beautiful and equally omniscient — the three boys grew swiftly, mastering every shastra, and played along the high turrets of the palaces, where the Daityas posted in the sky could see them and carried the news straight to Vajranabha, who was already preparing his war against heaven.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v19-24: 'Prabhāvati gave birth to a son, omniscient and youthful after his father. The son Chandraprabha, resembling Gada, whom Chandravati gave birth to after a month... Gunavati too gave birth to a similiarly beautiful son by name Gunavān'; the boys 'began to grow up... mastering all the Shastras. They used to move about on the turrets of the palaces and at the desire of Indra and Upendra they were seen (by the Daityas)... As soon as they saw them the Daityas, stationed in the sky, respectfully communicated it to Vajranābha who was desirous of conquering the celestial region'.

statements.claim: 'Arrest them,' said Vajranabha, 'those who have trespassed into my house'; at his order soldiers closed every quarter of the city and the cry went up on all sides — 'Arrest them — kill them'; the young mothers, who loved their sons, wept in fear, and Pradyumna steadied them: 'While we are alive and firm, you need not fear. The Daityas will not be able to touch us.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v25-29: Vajranābha: 'Arrest them who have trespassed into my house'; 'the soldiers guarded all the quarters... there arose on all sides exclamations, "Arrest them speedily kill them"'; 'the mothers, fond of sons, began to weep in fear. Pradyumna encouraged them, saying: "So long we are alive and firm you need not fear... The Daityas will not be able to do any thing to us"'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna laid the whole choice before Prabhavati: her father, uncles, brothers and all her kinsmen were waiting with clubs in their hands and for her sake deserved respect and honor, but the time was dreadful and the Danava kings meant to kill them — if they bore it they would die, if they fought they would succeed; he asked her to consult with her two sisters, saying they were under her orders.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v30-33: Pradyumna to Prabhāvati: 'your father, uncles, brothers kinsmen and other relatives are waiting with clubs in their hands. For you they deserve our respect and honor. But the time is very dreadful. The Dānava kings, desirous of killing us, will fight with us. If we bear it we shall have to die. If we fight we will meet with success. Consult with your two sisters and tell us what we should do for we are now under your orders'.

statements.claim: Prabhavati knelt, weeping, her hands on her forehead, and urged Pradyumna to take up his arms and protect himself, so that he would see his wife and sons; she bade him remember Rukmini and Aniruddha and save himself from the peril, trusting the boon of the great rishi, effulgent as sun and fire, that she would lead a blameless life, never be a widow, and that her sons would live.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v34-38: 'Placing her hands on her forehead and kneeling down Prabhāvati, weeping, said: "O descendant of Yadu... take up your arms and protect yourself. If you yourself survive you will see your wife and sons. Remember the honarable Vaidarbhi and Aniruddha and save yourself from this peril... the great and intelligent Rishi had conferred on me the boon that I would lead a blameless life for ever, would not be a widow and my sons would live... the words of the Rishi, effulgent like the sun and fire, will not be falsified"'. (Vaidarbhi = Rukmini, the princess of Vidarbha — the story's 'Rukmini' is the same person.)

statements.claim: She rose, rinsed her mouth, and took up a sword; the jewel of a woman placed it in Pradyumna's hands, saying 'Acquire victory'; bending low, Pradyumna bowed his head to the blade and accepted it with joy; and Chandravati, delightedly, gave a sword to Gada, and Gunavati gave another such weapon to the mighty Shamba.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt + HV 1.243 v39-41: Prabhāvati 'handed over a sword to Rukshmini's son... saying, "Acquire victory"'; full text: 'Bending low his head and bowing unto it the virtuous souled Pradyumna delightedly accepted the sword offered by his devoted wife. Chandravati delightedly gave to Gada one Nishtringsha and Gunavati gave another such weapon to the highly powerful Shāmva'.

DKS_0309.notes: Faithful to HV 1.243 v1-41 (pack passage complete through v38; the sword-giving beat v39-41 is confirmed by the pack excerpt line and the same Gutenberg text). The pack and story are in exact agreement throughout, including the rishi's boon and the arming of Gada and Shamba by Sunabha's daughters.

statements.claim: While the cries of 'Arrest them, kill them' still rang through the city of Vajra, Pradyumna, by his power of illusion, created a celestial car and made Ananta, the thousand-headed serpent, foremost of his class, its charioteer.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Pradyumna... created a car with his Māyā. He made the thousand-headed Nāga Ananta... his charioteer'; HV 1.243 v42-44 (same Gutenberg text): Pradyumna 'created a car with his Māyā. He made the thousand-headed Nāga Ananta, the foremost of their class, his charioteer'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna told his kinsmen to hold the ground and fight the Danavas below while he took the battle to the sky, and the soldiers sent to seize the trespassers found a household already in arms.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v42-44: Pradyumna said to Hansaketu, 'remain here with Shāmva and fight with the Dānavas. I will fight in the sky, protecting all the quarters' — the story's 'his kinsmen' is a fair generalization (the source names one addressee), and the arrest order of the preceding verses (v25-27) is the 'trespassers' context.

statements.claim: Like fire running over dry grass, Pradyumna swept through the midst of the Asura army, gladdening Prabhavati as he rode; crescent-shaped arrows, dreadful as serpents — some sharp-headed, some blunt — streamed from his bow into the ranks of the sons of Diti; the Asuras, resolute and maddened with battle fury, struck back with every weapon, but he cut off arms decked with armlets and heads without number, until severed heads and bodies covered the earth; Indra and the gods watched the battle of Daityas and Yadavas with pleasure, and the Daityas who turned upon Gada and Shamba met their destruction like boats in a mighty ocean.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v45-51: 'As fire ranges on grass, so he, ascending that best of cars, and gladdening Prabhāvati, began to move about in the midst of the Asura army. With crescent-shaped arrows, dreadful like serpents, some with sharp heads and some blunt he began to assail the sons of Diti'; 'the Asuras too, resolute and maddened with battle fury... struck the lotus-eyed son of Kamala's lord. Krishna's son cut off the arms of some decked with Keyuras and the heads of many... filled the surface of the earth. The king of gods, the victor of armies, along with the gods, began to witness with pleasure the battle between the Daityas and Bhaimas. The Daityas, who ran after Gada and Sāmva, met with destruction like a boat in a mighty ocean'.

statements.claim: Sensing that the Asura king's ascetic merit had run out, spirits (Bhutas) entered the city wherever they pleased, and the Asuras who had lived well-fed and safe behind their king's boon found their walls meaning nothing.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v57: 'Thinking "His ascetic virtue is gone and this wicked one is to be killed by the Yadavas" the Bhutas entered wherever they liked'.

statements.claim: With the permission of Brahma, Krishna sent his own car to Gada, with Matali's son to drive it; Indra sent his elephant Airavata to Shamba, with the twice-born Pravara riding it; and the celestial youth Jayanta came to stand at Pradyumna's side — after which Pradyumna and Jayanta pressed through the very palaces of the city, destroying the Asuras with a net of arrows, so that no corner of Vajra was safe from them.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v52-58: 'Hari, the lord of gods... sent his own car to Gada and asked Mātali's son Suvarchhā to become its driver. The Lord Indra sent his Airāvata to Shāmva and engaged Pravara to ride it. He sent Jayanta as an assistant to Rukshmini's son'; '(with the permission of Brahmā... Sakra... had sent there the car driven by Mātali's son and the Airāvata with the celestial youth Jayanta and the best of the twice-born Pravara)'; 'Gradually entering into their palaces the highly powerful Pradyumna and Jayanta began to destroy the Asuras with a net-work of arrows'. NB the Dutt text itself credits the car to Hari in v52 and to Sakra in v55-56 and v59-60; the story mirrors both attributions, so neither is an error.

statements.claim: In the midst of the slaughter Pradyumna called to Gada that Indra had sent the car, that Matali's son was its driver and that the elephant ridden by Pravara was for Shamba; that there was a great worship of Rudra at Dwaraka that day, and when it ended Krishna himself would come the next day, and by his orders they would kill the sinful Vajranabha together with his kinsmen; and he warned that they must take care that Vajranabha did not kill them and their sons, for the destruction of one's own sons is worse than one's own death — they should protect their sons by every means.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v59-64: Pradyumna to Gada: 'the king of gods has sent for you this car with the horses. The highly powerful son of Mātali is its driver. This elephant Airāvata, ridden by Pravara, has been sent for Shāmva... there will be a great Pujā of Rudra at Dwārakā to-day. After its termination the highly powerful Hrishikesha will come here to-morrow. According to his orders we will kill this sinful Vajranābha together with his kinsmen... we should so carefully concert measures that he may not kill us with our sons. The destruction of one's own sons in this world is more than his death. Therefore the learned should protect their sons by all means'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna then multiplied himself by his illusory power into millions of forms and dispelled the darkness the Daityas had cast over the field; wherever an enemy turned there Krishna's son stood, so that creatures seemed to see him in every foe, and the king of gods was pleased to see the destroyer of enemies everywhere at once.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v65-67: Pradyumna 'made, by his illusory power, millions of his own self and dispelled the dreadful darkness created by the Daityas. Seeing him... the king of gods was highly pleased. As the Divine soul lives in all human souls so the creatures saw Krishna's son in every one of the enemies'.

statements.claim: All through the night the battle raged; when Jayanta went down to the Ganga that issues from Vishnu's foot for his evening prayers, Pradyumna fought the Daityas alone, and when Pradyumna in his turn recited his evening prayers in the celestial Ganga, Jayanta alone held the host — and when dawn came, three in every four of the Asuras lay dead.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v68-70: 'The highly powerful son of Rukshmini thus fighting the night elapsed and three fourths of the Asuras were killed'; 'when Jayanta repaired to the Ganges issuing from Vishnu's feet for reciting his evening prayers, Krishna's son fought alone with the Daityas. And afterwards when Pradyumna recited his evening prayers in the etherial Gangā the highly powerful Jayanta alone fought with the Daityas'; pack excerpt: 'three fourths of the Asuras were killed'.

statements.claim: At sunrise the field was still: the army that had marched out to conquer heaven lay broken around the city, and only its king remained — untouched, at the center of the ruin, waiting.
statements.evidence: Closing transition to the next episode: three-fourths of the Asuras slain and the night battle ended are supported (v68); that Vajranabha alone remained 'untouched' is cliffhanger emphasis — he is indeed still alive and duels Krishna's son at sunrise in ch. 244.

DKS_0310.notes: The whole battle scene of HV 1.243 lies beyond the pack's visible passage (which cuts off mid-sentence at v38-39, '[...]'); every story beat was verified against the pack's excerpt line plus the same cited Gutenberg translation (chapter CCXLIII). The car-to-Gada attribution varies between Hari and Sakra within the Dutt text itself (v52 vs v55-56/59-60) — the story faithfully mirrors the source and its own dialogue is consistent. The pack index ('Indra sends his own car...') is a coarse paraphrase of the same dual-attribution passage.

statements.claim: Krishna came to the war riding Garuda, the king of birds and enemy of serpents, who crosses the sky swifter than wind, and went to Indra in the etherial region where he blew his conch Panchajanya, increasing the fear of the Daityas.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (Dutt): 'the deity Hari came there riding on Garuda, the enemy of the serpents... went to Sakra in the etherial region (2). Coming near Vasava, the lord Krishna duly blew the conch Panchajunya which increased the fear of the Daityas'; pack locations: 'sky over city Vajra'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna, hearing the conch, came to his father Keshava, who told him 'Speedily kill Vajranabha' and then 'Go there on Garuda's back'; saluting Indra and Krishna, Pradyumna mounted Garuda and went.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244: 'Hearing that sound Pradyumna... came near His father Keshava who said to him "Speedily kill Vajraalbha"... "Go there on Garuda's back". Saluting the foremost of celestials Indra and Upendra he did so.' (Upendra = Krishna; the story reads this as saluting Indra and his father.)

statements.claim: Seated firmly on Garuda, the heroic Pradyumna, well read in the use of all weapons, struck Vajranabha, wounding him on the breast with a club; Vajranabha lost consciousness and, bewildered like one dead, vomited blood again and again.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244: 'the heroic Pradyumna, well read in the use of all weapons, struck Vajranabha... wounded on the breast with a club... lost consciousness; and bewildered like one dead he vomitted blood again and again.'

statements.claim: Pradyumna, irrepressible in battle, told the fallen Vajranabha 'Be consoled', and Vajranabha, regaining consciousness, praised him — 'Well done, mighty Yadava; by your prowess you have become an illustrious enemy of mine; now is the time for me to strike you in return; wait here firmly.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (10-11): 'Thereat Krishna's son, irrepressible in battle, told him "Be consoled"... "Well done! Oh highly powerful Yadava. By your prowess you have become an illustrious enemy of mine. Now is the time for me to strike you in return; wait here firmly."'

statements.claim: Roaring like a hundred clouds, Vajranabha hurled a huge club adorned with bells, which struck Pradyumna on the forehead; Pradyumna vomited blood and lost consciousness.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (12-13): 'roaring like a hundred clouds the king of Daityas discharged... a huge club adorned with bells... wounded sorely on his forehead with that club... Pradyumna, vomitted blood and lost his conciousness.'

statements.claim: Seeing his son fall, Krishna blew his Panchajanya conch 'as if consoling his son', and at its sound Pradyumna revived and stood up.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (14): 'Seeing it the divine Krishna, the slayer of his enemies, blew his Panchajanya conch as if consoling his son. At the sound of that Panchanjanya... the highly powerful Pradyumna revived and stood up.'

statements.claim: Beholding Pradyumna revived, all the worlds were delighted — especially Indra and Krishna.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (15): 'beholding Pradyumna consoled, all the worlds especially Indra and Keshava were greatly delighted.'

statements.claim: Atmosphere: the conch blast made the air hold still, the Daityas 'remembered what followed it', and Pradyumna waited for the sound 'the way a son waits for his father's voice in a crowd'.
statements.evidence: Non-factual framing and imagery around the source's events; no factual assertion requiring a source.

DKS_0311.notes: Close paraphrase of Harivamsha 1.244 (Dutt). Every narrative beat — Garuda ride, Panchajanya blast, 'Be consoled' exchange, club wound, conch revival, universal delight — matches the passage. No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Recap: both warriors had been struck down and both had risen — Vajranabha from the breast wound, Pradyumna from the forehead blow, revived by his father's conch.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (same passage in pack): Vajranabha wounded on the breast then revived; Pradyumna wounded on the forehead, revived by Panchajanya.

statements.claim: Recap of the prior event: Pradyumna had ridden against the asura host with the serpent Ananta yoked to his celestial car, devastating their ranks while Indra sent his own car, his elephant Airavata and his son Jayanta to aid the Yadavas.
statements.evidence: Prior canonical event per corpus chain (DKS_0310): 'Pradyumna creates a celestial car with the thousand-headed serpent Ananta as charioteer and devastates the Asura host, while Indra sends his own car, Airavata and Jayanta to aid the Yadavas.'

statements.claim: According to Krishna's desire, his discus — set with thousands of sharpened axles and destructive of the Daityas — came through the air into his son's hand.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (16): 'according to Krishna's desire his discus, set with thousands of sharpened axles and destructive of the Daityas, came into the hand of his son.'

statements.claim: Saluting Indra and Krishna, Pradyumna discharged the discus, which separated Vajranabha's head from his body before the very presence of the Daityas.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (16-18): 'Saluting the high souled Indra and Upendra he discharged it... that discus, discharged by Narayana's son, separated Vajranabha's head from his body before the very presence of the Daityas.'

statements.claim: Sunabha, dreadful and taking delight in battle, was killed by Gada on the battlefield although he was very careful.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (19): 'The dreadful Sunabha, bent upon killing his enemies and taking delight in battles, was killed by Gada in the battle-field although he was very careful.'

statements.claim: Shamba, the aggrandiser of his enemies, with sharpened arrows sent the remaining enemies of the immortals into the family of Yama — i.e., despatched them.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (20): 'With sharpened arrows Shamva, the aggrandiser of his enemies, converted... the enemies of the immortals into the family members of Yama.'

statements.claim: Nikumbha, after Vajranabha's destruction, fled in fear of Narayana to the far city of Shatpura.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (21): 'After the destruction of the great Asura Vajranabha, Nikumbha, in fear of Narayana, fled to the city of Shatpura.'

statements.claim: Krishna and Indra came down to the city of Vajra, consoled the boys and old persons stricken with fear, and established peace there.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (22-23): 'the two high-souled Haris came down to the city of Vajra... Having consoled the boys and old persons stricken with fear those two foremost of celestials established peace there.'

statements.claim: Atmosphere/reflection: the pause before the discus, the sky imagery, and the closing thought that the young warrior 'began to understand what it meant to be trusted with such a weapon'.
statements.evidence: Non-factual framing around supported events.

DKS_0312.notes: Faithful retelling of Harivamsha 1.244 (the discus slaying, Gada/Shamba/Nikumbha coda, and descent to pacify Vajra). No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Recap: Vajranabha was dead, slain by the discus in Pradyumna's hand; his army scattered; Nikumbha had fled to the far city of Shatpura; the boys and old people of Vajra had been consoled by Krishna and Indra.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (16-23): discus severs Vajranabha's head; Nikumbha flees to Shatpura; the two Haris come down to Vajra, console boys and old persons, establish peace.

statements.claim: Following Brihaspati's advice, Indra and Krishna consulted together about the present and the future and divided Vajranabha's conquered kingdom into four parts.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (24): 'following Vrihaspati's advice and consulting (with him) about the present and future (arrangements) the highly powerful and great Indra and Upendra divided Vajranabha's kingdom into four parts.'

statements.claim: The kingdom was divided into four parts: one fourth to Jayanta's son Vijaya, one fourth to Pradyumna's son, one fourth to Shamba's son, and the remaining fourth to Gada's son Chandraprabha.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (25-26): 'one-fourth of that kingdom, gained by conquest, was given to Jayanta's son Vijaya, one-fourth to Pradyumna's son, one-fourth to Shamva's son and the remaining one-fourth to Gada's son Chandraprabha.'

statements.claim: Vijaya, the son of Indra's son Jayanta, was a boy of the divine line who could already range through the upper (etherial) region.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (31): 'Vijaya, from before, could range in the etherial region.'

statements.claim: The four koti villages and one thousand prosperous branch cities like the town of Vajra were divided into four parts, as were warm clothing, deerskins, cloths and jewels, and Indra and Krishna took pleasure in giving it all away.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (27-28): 'with great pleasure Sakra and Keshava divided into four parts also the four koti villages and one thousand prosperous branch cities like the town of Vajra... also divided, into four parts, various warm clothings, deer-skin, cloths and jewels.'

statements.claim: Before the assembled Rishis, Indra and Krishna anointed the four young kings, pouring the water of the Ganga that issues from Vishnu's feet, with the music of celestial bugles.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (29-30): 'those heroic kings... were annointed there before the Rishis by the gods Sakra and Krishna with the water of Ganga issuing from Vishnu's feet, accompanied with the music of celestial bugles.'

statements.claim: Madhava's (Krishna's) descendants learned to range the etherial region through virtues inherited from their mothers, and would travel by the etherial way between the celestial region and Dwaraka, the city protected by the Bhaimas.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (31 and Indra's speech): 'Madhava's descendants, on account of the virtues inherited from their mother, practised it also'; 'They will acquire practice of going to the celestial region and Dwaraka protected by the Bhaimas through the etherial way.'

statements.claim: Indra told Jayanta: 'O heroic victor of armies, it behoves you to protect all these kings. One of them is a perpetuator of my race, the other three are born in the family of Keshava. By my command none amongst creatures will be able to kill them. Give them elephants born of the quarter-elephants, horses from the race of Ucchaisrava, and chariots built by the celestial architect.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.244 (Indra's speech, as rendered in pack): 'O heroic victor of armies, it behoves you to protect all these kings... one is a perpetuator of my race and the other three are born in the family of Keshava. By my command none amongst creatures will be able to kill them... Give them... elephants born from those of the quarter, horses born from the race of Ucchaisrava and chariots constructed by the celestial Arch[itect].'

statements.claim: Reflection: 'four shares are still one realm under a single protection', and the four young kings receive what they did not have to win.
statements.evidence: Non-factual framing; the underlying facts (division into four, Indra's protection) are supported.

DKS_0313.notes: Faithful to Harivamsha 1.244 (24-31 + Indra's speech to Jayanta). All four recipients, the shares, the division of villages/cities/goods, the anointing, and Indra's boon match the passage. No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Recap: Naraka, the son of the earth (Bhumi), had been slain; the maidens kept in his inner apartments were freed; the summit of Mount Mani had been uprooted and brought; the riches collected. Krishna told the Yadavas 'You are the masters of all these things', and the Bhojas, Andhakas and Vrishnis, their hair standing erect in joy, worshipped him.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.248 (Dutt): 'by virtue of your ascetic power... Bhumi's son Naraka has been slain. Many beautiful maidens have been released from his inner appartment and the summit of the mount Mani has been uprooted and brought here... You are now the masters of all these things... the Bhojas, Andhakas and Vrishnis, having their hairs stand erect in joy, worshipped Janarddana.'

statements.claim: The wives of the Dasharhas and of Ahuka came to the hall; the seven queens of Vasudeva, headed by Devaki and the beautiful-faced Rohini, saw Balarama and Krishna seated at ease.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.248 (7-8): 'the wives of the Dasharhas and Ahuka, filled with joy, repaired to the Hail for seeing Krishna. The seven queens of Vasudeva, headed by Devaki and the beautiful-faced Rohini saw the large-armed Rama and Krishna seated at ease.'

statements.claim: First the queens saluted Rohini, then Balarama and Krishna rose and saluted Devaki; the goddess shone among her two lotus-eyed sons as Aditi, mother of the gods, shines among Mitra and Varuna.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.248 (9-10): 'Having saluted first Rohini Rama and Krishna afterwards saluted Devaki. As Aditi, the mother of gods, looks beautiful in the company of Mitra and Varuna so the goddess shone in the company of her two lotus-eyed-sons.'

statements.claim: The illusory daughter of Yashoda — born at the very same moment as Krishna, and for whose sake he slew Kamsa with his relatives — appeared before Krishna and Balarama.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.248 (11-13): 'the illusory daughter of Yashoda, whom the people describe as one and without any parts, with whom... Krishna... was born at the same moment and for whom he slew Kansa with his relatives, appeared before Krishna and Rama.'

statements.claim: Until then she had been adored in the Vrishni family and brought up and maintained like a daughter; known to the world as the irrepressible Yoga maiden, one and without parts, born for the protection of Keshava, whom she guarded with her goddess-like celestial body, the Yadavas worshipped her with joy.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.248 (13-14): 'Up to this time she was being adored in the Vrishni family and was being brought up and maintained like a daughter. She, whom the people of the world know as the irrepressible Yoga maiden... was born for the protection of Keshava. Because she protected Keshava with her goddess-like celestial body the Yadavas used to worship her with great pleasure.'

statements.claim: Krishna approached her as a man goes to a beloved female friend and held her by the hand; Balarama also held her hand, embraced her and smelt her head.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.248 (16-17): 'Madhava approached her, like unto a man his beloved female friend and held her by the hand. The highly powerful Rama too held her by his right hand, embraced her and smelt her head.'

statements.claim: The Vrishni women saw her standing between her two brothers Balarama and Krishna, like the goddess Shree with golden lotuses in her hands seated on a lotus, showered her with fried paddy and flowers, and returned to their quarters.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.248 (18-19): 'The Vrishni women then saw her between her two brothers Rama and Krishna like unto the goddess Sree, with golden lotuses in her hands and seated on a lotus too. They then showered fried paddy and diverse flowers and repaired to their respective quarters.'

statements.claim: The Yadavas spent that time praising Krishna's wonders and honoring him, and Madhava, the enhancer of the joy of the citizens, lived on happily among his people.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.248 (20-21): 'speaking highly of the wonderful deeds of Janarddana and honoring him the Yadavas sat delightedly... Madhava, the enhancer of the joy of the citizens, began to live there happily with them.'

statements.claim: Soon after, the sage Narada came to the meeting at the order of the king of the gods, ready to tell the assembled Vrishnis the story of Krishna's boyhood — 'another telling'.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.248 (22-25): 'the worshipful saint Narada, according to the order of the king of gods, came to Janarddana at the meeting... said to the Vrishnis... hear now of all the heroic deeds which Krishna... has performed from his boyhood.'

statements.claim: Scene-setting: the women of the hall fell quiet as she passed and 'some of them had not seen her since she was a child'; the hall watched in silence.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric embellishment not asserted in the pack (the pack instead stresses she was brought up within the Vrishni family); vague, non-sourceable framing of the reunion.

DKS_0314.notes: Faithful to Harivamsha 1.248 (Narada Describes the Feat of Krishna): Naraka recap, the queens' visit, Rohini/Devaki salutations, Yogamaya's appearance, Krishna and Balarama's greeting, the Shree simile, and Narada's arrival all match. No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Kama (Cupid) of firm vows, to kill Shamvara, took birth from Rukmini — the incarnation of Lakshmi — and Vasudeva as their beautiful son Pradyumna.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251 (2): 'Kama (Cupid) of firm vows, in order to kill Shamvara, took his birth from Rukshmini, the incarnation of Lakshmi, and Vasudeva as his beautiful son Pradyumna.'

statements.claim: On the seventh day at dead of night Shamvara stole the week-old infant from the lying-in room and carried him to his own city; Krishna, who followed celestial Maya, knew everything and did not kill the Danava at that time.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251 (3-4): 'On the seventh day at dead of night Kalashamvara stole away that infant son of Krishna from the lying-in room... Krishna, who followed the celestial Maya, knew every thing and therefore he did not kill at that time the Danava... As if urged on by Death the great Asura stole away Krishna's son... took him to his own city.'

statements.claim: Shamvara had no children, and he gave the stolen baby to his wife Mayavati as though he were her own son.
statements.evidence: The pack (HV 1.251, 5-7) states the childless one was Mayavati — 'His beautiful and accomplished wife Mayavati... had no offspring so that Danava... gave over that son of Vasudeva to her like his own' — and the same Harivamsha account (1.252; DKS_0316/0317 packs) has Shamvara send his hundred sons against Pradyumna, so Shamvara was not childless.
statements.resolution: Corrected in story text via consolidation pass.

statements.claim: Mayavati, seeing the infant, was filled with joy, her hair stood erect, and she gazed at him repeatedly with delight, recollecting that in a life before this one he had been her favourite husband — Kama, reduced to ashes long ago by the trident-bearing god (Shiva) stricken with sorrow for Sati.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251 (8-11): 'Seeing him she was filled with joy and her hairs stood erect: she looked at him repeatedly with delight... she recollected that he was her favourite husband... He was formerly reduced to ashes by the divine trident handed deity stricken with sorrow for Sati. Now he has been seen by me in another birth.'

statements.claim: Thinking 'being his wife and knowing him as my husband, how can I give him milk and address him as my son?', Mayavati handed the baby to a nurse; informed by the nurse, Pradyumna grew up believing Mayavati was his mother.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251 (12-14): '"However, being his wife and knowing him as my husband how can I give him milk and address him as my son?"... Mayavati handed over the baby to the nurse and soon reared him up... Informed by the nurse and out of ignorance Rukshmini's son knew Mayavati as his mother.'

statements.claim: Mayavati instructed the growing boy in all forms of illusion; he became a young man of striking beauty, an expert in the use of all sorts of weapons and quick to read those around him.
statements.evidence: Mostly HV 1.251 (15-16): she 'instructed him in all forms of illusion'; he 'looked highly beautiful, became an expert in the use of all sorts of weapons'. The closing clause generalizes the source's narrower 'in deciphering the movements of women' into 'quick to read the hidden intentions of the people around him' — a loose paraphrase, not a material distortion.

statements.claim: Mayavati, assuming the semblance of a beautiful woman, tempted him with her gestures; Pradyumna drew back, asking why she cast off a mother's feeling and behaved perversely — 'Women's minds flicker like lightning. Am I not your son? Tell me the secret of what you are doing.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251 (16-23): 'Mayavati, assuming the semblance of a beautiful woman, sought the company of her beloved consort and tempted him with her gestures... "Why do you, casting off your maternal feelings, behave in this perverse way?... The nature of women is fickle like lightning... Am I not then your son?... I wish to learn the secret of this from you."'

statements.claim: In a solitary place Mayavati revealed: 'You are not my son, and Shamvara is not your father. You are the son of Vasudeva and Rukmini, a prince of the Vrishnis. On your seventh night, when you were a helpless baby in the lying-in chamber, my husband stole you away.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251 (24-29): '"You are not my son, nor Shamvara is your father... you are the delightful son of Vasudeva and Rukshmini. After your birth on the seventh day you were brought here. When you were a helpless baby in the lying-in chamber you were stolen by my powerful husband."'

statements.claim: Mayavati told him his mother mourns him 'like a cow separated from her calf', and his father — mightier than Indra (Shakra), with the emblem of Garuda on his flag — does not even know he is alive; and she sought him as her lover because she did not give birth to him.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251 (28-33): 'Stricken with sorrow for a son like you your mother is bewailing like a cow estranged from its calf... your father, having the emblem of Garuda on his flag, and more powerful than even Shakra himself, does not know it... I seek you as my lover, because I have not given birth to you.'

statements.claim: Pradyumna, who had mastered all forms of illusion, was worked up with anger and resolved: 'Shall I cower here, afraid of the wretch who stole the infant son of Keshava? I will do what makes him angry — I will break his standard and call him out; when he comes to meet me I will kill him in battle and return to Dwaraka.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251 (34-38): 'Pradyumna... had mastered all forms of illusion. So... worked up with anger, he... called Shamvara. He said: "Alas shall I remain here fearing that wicked-souled Danava who has stolen away the infant son of Keshava? How may that sinful wretch become angry?... I should do what excites his anger... I will strike down the wonderful standard... If he comes to know of the spoliation of his standard Shamvara will surely come out. I will then kill him in battle and return to Dwaraka."'

statements.claim: Frame: 'the boy who was called Shamvara's son had believed it all his life... Both were lies, and the night he learned the truth, the lying ended in fire.'
statements.evidence: Metaphorical framing of the supported revelation scene; no factual assertion.

corrections.original_sentence: Shamvara had no children, and he gave the stolen baby to his wife Mayavati as though he were her own son.
corrections.suggested: Mayavati had no children of her own, and Shamvara gave the stolen baby to his wife as though he were her son.

DKS_0315.notes: One CONTRADICTED: the story transfers the childlessness to Shamvara ('Shamvara had no children'), whereas the pack (HV 1.251) says it was Mayavati who had no offspring — and the same source has Shamvara send his hundred sons against Pradyumna (HV 1.252; corpus chain). Everything else — the theft on the seventh night, Mayavati's recognition of Kama, the confession, and Pradyumna's resolve — is faithful.

statements.claim: Recap: Pradyumna had come to Shamvara's city as a stolen child, carried out of Dwaraka on his seventh night, and had been raised as a prince of the demon house; Mayavati had just told him he was the son of Vasudeva and Rukmini.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251 (2-7, 24-33) as given in the pack: the infant stolen from the lying-in room on the seventh day and reared in Shamvara's city; Mayavati's confession that he is Vasudeva and Rukshmini's son. Corpus chain previous title confirms.

statements.claim: Pradyumna resolved not to slip away secretly but to provoke Shamvara into an open fight: 'I will strike down the wonderful standard at his gate, the jeweled standard with the lion, standing like Mount Sumeru itself. When Shamvara learns that his banner lies broken, he will come out to me. I will kill him in battle, and I will go home.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251: 'With my sharpened spear I will strike down the wonderful standard with a flying pennon having the emblem of a lion which stands like the mount Sumeru on his gate. If he comes to know of the spoliation of his standard Shamvara will surely come out. I will then kill him in battle and return to Dwaraka.'

statements.claim: Mayavati had trained him in every form of illusion, and he had become expert in the use of all sorts of weapons.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251 (15-16): Mayavati 'instructed him in all forms of illusion'; Pradyumna 'became an expert in the use of all sorts of weapons.'

statements.claim: Pradyumna strung his bow, took up arrows and struck down the jeweled standard, so that the great pole came down across the gate and the lion emblem lay in the dust.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251 (end of passage): 'the large-armed Pradyumna stringed his bow, took up arrows and struck down that jewel of a standard.' The fall of the emblem across the gate is scene-setting consistent with the striking-down.

statements.claim: Word of the standard's spoliation reached Shamvara; filled with anger he ordered his hundred sons to go and kill Rukmini's son: 'Go quickly... and kill Rukmini's son.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (HV 1.251): 'Hearing of the spoliation of his standard... Shamvara, filled with anger, ordered his sons... "do you soon kill Rukshmini's son"'; number confirmed by corpus-chain next title ('Pradyumna Slays the Hundred Sons of Shamvara').

statements.claim: His father Krishna's banner bore the emblem of Garuda and he was mightier than Indra himself.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251 (Mayavati's speech): 'your father, having the emblem of Garuda on his flag, and more powerful than even Shakra himself.'

statements.claim: Atmosphere: the standard 'seemed to hold up the sky', travelers 'measured the city by it', the pole 'came down across the gate like a falling tree', and 'the silence after the crash was the loudest thing in the city'.
statements.evidence: Descriptive colour around the supported striking-down of the lion standard; no sourceable factual assertion.

DKS_0316.notes: Faithful to Harivamsha 1.251: the resolve, the lion-emblazoned jeweled standard standing like Mount Sumeru, the striking-down, and Shamvara's angry dispatch of his sons all match. No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: A great hair-stirring encounter took place between Rukmini's son and the sons of Shamvara, who in anger showered on Pradyumna arrows, spears, axes, javelins and maces all at once; Pradyumna, angered, struck each of them with five arrows.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.252 (1-3): 'in anger those great Daityas began to shower simultaneously on Pradyumna arrows, Saktis, Parashwadhas, Tomara's, Kuntas, Bhushundis and maces... Krishna's son too, worked up with anger, struck them in the battle each with five arrows shot off his bow.'

statements.claim: The resolute Asuras set up a net-work of weapons to kill Pradyumna, who killed the ten highly powerful sons of Shamvara.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.252 (4-6): 'those resolute Asuras, exceedingly wroth, set up a net-work of weapons for killing Pradyumna... He then killed the ten highly powerful sons of Shamvara.'

statements.claim: Pradyumna next cut off Chitrasena's head with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla).
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.252 (6): 'the powerful son of Keshava soon cut off Chitrasena's head with a Bhalla.'

statements.claim: The remaining sons of Shamvara united against him, running and shooting arrows, and Pradyumna cut off their heads as if in sport; having thus slain all one hundred sons of Shamvara — all good bowmen — he stood in the battlefield desirous of fighting.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.252 (7-10): 'the remaining sons of Shamvara... began to run taking up and discharging arrows... The highly powerful son of Krishna... cut off their heads, as if in sport. Having thus slain one hundred sons of Shamvara, all good bow men, he stood in the battle field desirous of fighting.'

statements.claim: Hearing of the death of his hundred sons, Shamvara was filled with wrath; he asked his charioteer to get ready his car, and the charioteer saluted him touching the ground with his head, brought the car and asked the soldiers to get ready.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.252 (10-11): 'Hearing of the death of his hundred sons Shamvara was filled with wrath. He asked his charioteer to get ready his car. Receiving the order of the king the charioteer saluted him touching the ground with his head and brought the car there, and asked the soldiers to get ready soon.'

statements.claim: The car was drawn by a thousand bears, tied with ropes of snakes, coated with tiger-skin, adorned with a network of small bells, painted with stars and adorned with gold, with ten stairs, flags bearing the figures of lions, wooden fenders and iron axles, high like the summit of Mount Mandara, bedecked with chowries and golden standards.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.252 (11-16): 'It was drawn by a thousand bear and tied with the ropes of snakes. It was coated with tiger-skin, adorned with a net-work of small bells... It had ten stairs... was painted with stars and adorned with gold. It had a huge standard... embellished with flags having the figures of lions painted on them. It had wooden fenders around it and iron axles. It was high like the summit of Mandara, was bedecked with beautiful chowries... adorned with golden standards.' (The pack additionally says the car was 'filled with wolves', which the story omits — an omission, not a distortion.)

statements.claim: As if urged on by Death, Shamvara, putting on golden armour and taking up his bow and arrows, set out with his soldiers and four ministers — Durdhara, Ketumali, Shatruhanta and Pramardana — and an army of two hundred chariots, ten thousand elephants, eight thousand horses and ten lakh foot soldiers.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.252 (17-22): 'As if urged on by Death, Shamvara, putting on a golden armour and taking up his bow and arrows, set out for battle accompanied by his soldiers and four ministers. Encircled by his ministers, Durdhara, Ketumali, Shatruhanta and Pramarddana... When with two hundred cars, ten thousands elephants, eight thousand horses and ten lakhs of infantry Shamvara set out...'

statements.claim: Portents appeared: cranes uttered hideous yells, firebrands fell, jackals yelled, vultures sat on the standards desirous of the Danavas' blood, headless figures dropped on his car, the moon was eclipsed (possessed by Rahu) and encircled by its disc, his left hand and eye danced, the horses slackened, Indra sent a shower of blood mixed with live coals and cinders, and the reins slipped from the charioteer's hands.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.252 (23-32): 'The cranes began to emit hideous yells... fire-brands... began to fall down. The jackals yelled... vultures sat on the tops of the standards desirous of drinking the blood of the Danavas. Headless figures were seen dropping on his car... The moon was possessed by Rahu (eclipsed) and encircled by its disc. His left hand and eye danced presaging some calamity and the horses... became of slackened speed... Indra began to send down a shower of blood mixed with live coals and cinders... reins slipped off the hands of the charioteer.'

statements.claim: Shamvara, filled with anger, paid no attention to the portents and proceeded to slay Pradyumna; the earth shook at the sound of bugles, conch-shells and drums, and terrified beasts and birds fled; Pradyumna, bent on slaying his enemy, waited in the battlefield.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.252 (32-33): 'But Shamvara, filled with anger, paid no attention to those portends and proceeded for slaying Pradyumna. Thereat the earth shook at the sound of bugles, conch-shells... Overwhelmed with terror... beasts and birds fled away on all sides. Krishna's son, however, bent on slaying his enemy, waited in the battle-field.'

statements.claim: Frame: Pradyumna 'stood untouched among the fallen' and 'the field was quiet except for the wind moving in the fallen flags'.
statements.evidence: The pack says Pradyumna stood 'desirous of fighting' after the slaughter; 'untouched' and the quiet-field image are battlefield atmosphere consistent with the account, which never has the hundred sons wound him.

DKS_0317.notes: Dense, faithful rendering of Harivamsha 1.252: five arrows each, ten sons, Chitrasena's head, the hundred bowmen slain, Shamvara's wrath, the full chariot description, the four ministers, army numbers and the omen catalogue all match the Dutt text. No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Shamvara, encircled by soldiers, struck Pradyumna with thousands of arrows; Pradyumna, displaying quick-handedness, cut those arrows off before they could reach him, and bending his bow shot arrows so that there was none in the army who was not struck.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.252 (34-38): 'Shamvara... struck Pradyumna with thousands of arrows. He, however, displaying quick-handedness, cut those arrows off before they could reach him. And bending his bow he shot arrows that there was none in the army who was not struck with one.'

statements.claim: Shamvara's men, assailed, returned to him in fear; beside himself with anger, Shamvara ordered his four ministers — Durdhara, Ketumali, Shatruhanta and Pramardana — 'At my command, go and strike my enemy's son. Do not neglect him; kill him at once. A danger ignored at its beginning grows like a disease — leave this boy alone and he will ruin us all.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.252 (38-42): 'Beholding his men take to their heels, Shamvara, beside himself with anger, ordered his ministers. "At my mandate do ye proceed and strike my enemy's son. Do not neglect him but kill him at once. If neglected he will ultimately ruin us like a disease disregarded in the beginning."'

statements.claim: Filled with anger and obeying Shamvara's command, the ministers drove their chariots out showering arrows; Pradyumna, the enhancer of Rukmini's delight, quickly took up his bow and struck Durdhara with twenty-five arrows, Ketumali with sixty-three, Shatruhanta with seventy and Pramardana with eighty-two; the angered ministers then covered him with a downpour of their own arrows.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.252 (43-49): 'Obeying Shamvara's command and filled with anger the ministers drove their cars showering arrows... The highly powerful Pradyumna, the enhancer of the delight of Rukshmini, in anger, struck Durdhara with twenty-five arrows, Ketumali with sixty three, Satruhanta with seventy and Pramarddana with eighty two. Thereat filled with anger the ministers covered Pradyumna with a downpour of arrows.'

statements.claim: Pradyumna shot an arrow at the breast of the short-lived Durdhara and the minister fell; before the eyes of the whole army he cut off Ketumali's head; the heart of the mighty Shatruhanta was cut out; and Pramardana was crushed down with Pradyumna's club.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (HV 1.252): 'he shot it at the breast of the short-lived Durdhara... with it before all he cut off Ketumali's head... the heart of the highly powerful Shatruhanta was cut off... Kama... crushed down Pramarddana with that club.'

statements.claim: The demon army — which had watched its hundred princes and now its four greatest warriors die — could bear no more: the soldiers fled the field in terror, abandoning their king and banners, and the rout was total.
statements.evidence: The pack's index entry for this event states the outcome as 'Pradyumna slays the four Danava ministers... one by one, and their army flees in terror'; the physical details (weapons thrown down, banners abandoned) are consistent dramatic rendering of that rout.

statements.claim: Frame: his mother was far away in Dwaraka, unaware that the son she had mourned for years was on a field in the demon country; and 'the omens that had darkened Shamvara's march were fulfilled at last'.
statements.evidence: Narrative frame consistent with the pack (mother bewailing like a cow estranged from its calf, HV 1.251; the omen catalogue of HV 1.252); no independent factual assertion.

statements.claim: Scene-setting: the ministers' bodies lay in a ring around Pradyumna with their chariots wrecked and flags trailing in the dirt, and the field emptied 'like a tide going out'.
statements.evidence: The pack confirms the ministers were slain from their cars and the army fled; the specific wrecked-chariot and trailing-flag imagery is descriptive colour beyond the excerpted text.

DKS_0318.notes: Faithful to Harivamsha 1.252 (second half): Shamvara's arrow volley, the counter-volley, the command to the ministers, the exact arrow counts (25/63/70/82), and the four distinct deaths (arrow to Durdhara's breast, Ketumali's head, Shatruhanta's heart, Pramardana crushed by club) all match the pack. No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Shamvara tells his charioteer: "take my car to the enemy soon. With arrows I will kill him who has done me wrong."
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.253 (Dutt): "filled with anger Shamvara said to his charioteer:—'O hero, do you soon take my car to the enemy. With arrows I will kill him who has done me wrong.'"

statements.claim: Pradyumna, son of Krishna and Rukmini, is the baby Shamvara had snatched away and meant to destroy, now grown to manhood.
statements.evidence: Passage 1.253: Shamvara laments "Why did I not kill him in his infancy?" while addressing him as "son of Rukshmini"; corpus chain (DKS_0318) covers his abduction and the slaying of Shamvara's four ministers.

statements.claim: Pradyumna had already cut down Shamvara's four chief ministers until the army fled from him.
statements.evidence: Corpus chain previous title (DKS_0318): "Pradyumna slays the four Danava ministers — Durdhara, Ketumali, Shatruhanta and Pramardana — one by one, and their army flees in terror."

statements.claim: Pradyumna's first golden shaft cut to Shamvara's vitals, and the demon reeled, clutched the reins and lost consciousness, recovering a few moments later.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "That arrow cutting to his very vitals, Shamvara... was greatly bewildered. And holding the reins of the car he lost consciousness. Regaining his consciousness a few moments after..."

statements.claim: Shamvara loosed seventy sharpened arrows; Pradyumna's seven shafts cut all seventy into seven parts before they reached him; then seventy winged arrows and a thousand more hid the sun.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "struck Krishna's son with seventy sharpened arrows. Pradyumna, with seven shafts, cut off those arrows into seven parts... And with seventy sharpened winged arrows he struck Shamvara... with a thousand beautiful winged arrows... the sky was so enshrouded by darkness that even the sun was not visible."

statements.claim: Shamvara dispelled the arrow-darkness with his thunderbolt and showered arrows on Pradyumna's car, which Pradyumna sliced to pieces by light-handedness.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "Seeing it Shamvara dispelled that darkness with his thunderbolt and showered arrows on Pradyumna's car... Pradyumna too, displaying light-handedness, cut off those arrows into many pieces with his knotty shafts."

statements.claim: Shamvara's illusory trees were burned to ash by fiery weapons; his downpour of stones was swept away by airy weapons.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "Shamvara, by his illusory powers, showered trees... destroyed them all by discharging fiery weapons. When all the trees were reduced to ashes Shamvara made a downpour of stones which Pradyumna removed from the battle-field by means of airy weapons."

statements.claim: Shamvara hurled illusory lions, tigers, bears, monkeys, horses, camels, asses and cloud-like elephants, which the Gandharva weapons cut to pieces.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "throwing on Pradyumna's car lions, tigers, bears, monkeys, horses, camels, asses and cloud-like elephants. Kāma however, with Gandharva weapons, cut them off into many pieces."

statements.claim: Shamvara raised illusory elephants with sixty heads each, ridden by expert drivers; Pradyumna's illusory lions destroyed them as the sun sends away the night.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "He showered youthful, well-decked elephants with sixty heads each... ridden by expert drivers... as the sun sends away the night so the illusory lions, created by the intelligent son of Rukshmini, destroyed the illusory elephants."

statements.claim: Pradyumna checked the Sunmohini Maya (the creation of the architect Maya) with his weapon of consciousness.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "Shamvara... created Sunmohini Māyā... the creation of Maya, discharged by Shamvara, the powerful Pradyumna obstructed it with his Sanjnā (consciousness) weapon."

statements.claim: Pradyumna's eight-legged sharabhas pursued Shamvara's illusory lions as the wind scatters clouds.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "Pradyumna took up Gandharva weapons and created Sharabhas... having eight legs, claws and teeth, pursued the lions. As the wind scatters clouds so those Sharabhas... pursued the lions."

statements.claim: Shamvara's inner doubt: "Alas! How stupid I am. Why did I not kill him in his infancy?... Only the dread illusion of serpents, taught to him by the great god Hara, remains."
statements.evidence: 1.253: Shamvara's thought quoted almost verbatim: "Alas! How stupid I am. Why did I not kill him in his infancy?... The dreadful illusion of serpents, which the great god Hara, the destroyer of Asuras, instructed me in, is only known to me."

statements.claim: Serpents full of burning venom fettered Pradyumna with his car, horses and charioteer; garudas appeared at his mere thought and destroyed them.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "Shamvara displayed that illusion of serpents full of burning venom, which fettered Pradyumna with his car, horses and charioteer... As soon as the high-souled Pradyumna thought of it Garudas began to move about and destroy the venomous serpents."

statements.claim: Gods and asuras cried "Well done! Well done! O mighty-armed son of Rukmini, the illusion is dispelled by you, and we are pleased."
statements.evidence: 1.253: "the gods and Asuras, eulogising him said 'Well done! Well done! O mighty-armed son of Rukshmini. On account of the illusion being dispelled by you we have been pleased.'"

statements.claim: Shamvara's remaining weapon was the golden club conferred by goddess Uma, able to dispel all illusion and kill all asuras, with which he had already sent many demons to Yama.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "the goddess Umā conferred that on me and said... this club which can dispell all forms of illusion and kill all the Asuras. I have with this club despatched to the abode of Yama..."

DKS_0319.notes: All events, dialogue and weapon sequence match Harivamsha 1.253 nearly verbatim. Poetic flourishes ("rode it like a storm", "In the end it was the arrows that gave out first") are connective narration; the club-ending dovetails with the passage's closing lines.

statements.claim: Narada, sent by Indra, descended from the sky to Pradyumna on the battlefield — an ascetic with matted locks, a vina and a face bright as fire.
statements.evidence: Pack index: "Sent by Indra, Narada reminds Pradyumna of his former birth as Kama"; Harivamsha 1.257 describes Narada "covered entirely with matted locks and with the Vinā in his hand... effulgent like fire".
