statements.claim: With the deed done, Pradyumna turned toward the city of his father, Dvaraka, where his mother was still waiting.
statements.evidence: VP 5.27 (in pack): 'he proceeded to his father's house, where he alighted, along with Máyávatí, in the inner apartments'; closing lines are connective continuity into the next story.

DKS_0337.notes: Story's tradition_note on the VP's numbered illusions (seven foiled, eighth mastered and turned back) matches the pack's VP excerpt verbatim. The framed beheading (crown and earrings) is the pack reading, not an invention.

statements.claim: Pradyumna descended from the sky into the inner palace of Dvaraka, escorted and showered with flowers by praising celestials, landing in the inner quarters with a woman (Mayavati) at his side.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.24-25: 'ākīryamāṇo divi-jaiḥ stuvadbhiḥ kusumotkaraiḥ / antaḥ-pura-varaṃ...'; Harivamsha 1.255: 'descended from the sky with Māyāvati at the inner appartment of Keshava'.

statements.claim: He was dark as a rain cloud, wrapped in yellow silk, his face like a lotus, dark curls at his temples; the women of the palace found his resemblance to their lord uncanny.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.26-28: 'jalada-śyāmaṃ pīta-kauśeya-vāsasam / sv-alaṅkṛta-mukhāmbhojaṃ nīla-vakrālakālibhiḥ'; the resemblance motif is Rukmini's own later reflection (v32, sārūpya with the bearer of Sharnga).

statements.claim: Rukmini looked at him long and wondered who this jewel among men was, whose lotus-eyed son he could be, how he had come to resemble the bearer of the Sharnga bow so exactly — whether he was the child she had carried.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.29-33: 'ko nv ayam nara-vaidūryaḥ kasya vā kamalekṣaṇaḥ / mama cāpy ātmajo naṣṭo nīto yaḥ sūtikā-gṛhāt / kathaṃ tv anena samprāptaṃ sārūpyaṃ śārṅga-dhanvanaḥ / sa eva vā bhaven nūnaṃ yo me garbhe dhṛto 'rbhakaḥ'.

statements.claim: She spoke aloud, half to herself: blessed is the woman whose son is such a beautiful boy — resembling Kama himself, just entering the first stage of youth; had death not carried her baby away, her Pradyumna would have been of this age by now.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.255 (in pack): 'Blessed is that woman whose son is such a beautiful, long-lived boy resembling Kāma and just ushered into the first stage of youth... if the powerful Death had not carried him away my baby Pradyumna would have been of this age by this time.'

statements.claim: The marks of the Vrishni line were on him; his face and hair were the face and hair of Narayana.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.255 (in pack): 'you are a prince of the Vrishni family; from the marks of your body you look like Janārddana without his discus. Your face and hairs resemble those of Nārāyana.'

statements.claim: Krishna, who knew everything, said nothing and let the moment ripen.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.34-35: 'evaṃ mīmāṃsamaṇāyāṃ vaidarbhyāṃ devakī-sutaḥ / vijñātārtho 'pi bhagavāṃs tūṣṇīm āsa janārdanaḥ'.

statements.claim: Narada came and told the whole story — the theft from the lying-in room, the casting into the sea, the fish, the demon's kitchen, the woman who raised the boy, the slaying of Shambara — and the palace filled with wonder and joy.
statements.evidence: Pack rendered excerpt (BP 10.55.24-39): 'when Narada told the whole tale, Rukmini, Devaki and Vasudeva embraced the couple in joy'; Harivamsha 1.255 has Krishna entering 'hearing from Nārada of the destruction of Shamvara'. 'As he so often did when a tale needed telling' is connective color.

statements.claim: Then Devaki and Vasudeva came, and Krishna and Balarama, and the palace women; Pradyumna saluted his mother and Govinda and bowed to Balarama; Krishna raised his eldest son, embraced him and smelt his head.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.37: 'devakī vasudevaś ca kṛṣṇa-rāmau tathā striyaḥ'; Harivamsha 1.255: 'Having saluted his mother and Govinda Pradyumna bowed unto Haladhara. Thereupon raising up Pradyumna... Keshava... embraced him and smelt his head.'

statements.claim: Krishna presented the young woman to Rukmini as Rati, beloved of Kama, wife of her son and their eldest daughter-in-law in all but name, who had raised him and brought him home; Rukmini raised her daughter-in-law, set her on her lap and embraced her.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.255 (in pack): Krishna: 'Know her as Rati, the beloved consort of Kāma... this auspicious and chaste lady is the wife of your son... She is our eldest daughter-in-law and deserves our affection'; 'Rukshmini... raised up her daughter-in-law adorned with gold, placed her on her lap and embraced her.'

statements.claim: Dvaraka celebrated Pradyumna as one returned from the dead, and Rukmini led her son and daughter-in-law by the hand to her own rooms.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.38: 'naṣṭaṃ pradyumnam āyātam ākarṇya dvārakaukasaḥ' with pack excerpt ('Dvaraka celebrated him as one returned from the dead'); Harivamsha 1.255: 'Rukshmini took her son who had returned with his wife to her own room'.

DKS_0338.notes: Rukmini mourning 'like an osprey over an empty nest' restates the kurarī simile of BP 10.55.14 from the preceding event — consistent corpus continuity.

statements.claim: Rukmi of Bhojakata gave his granddaughter Rocana (his son's daughter) in marriage to Aniruddha, Krishna's grandson (Rukmi's own daughter's son).
statements.evidence: BP 10.61.24: 'dauhitrāyāniruddhāya pautrīṃ rukmy ādadād dhareḥ' (Rukmi gave his son's daughter to Aniruddha, Hari's daughter's son); pack excerpt names Rocana; VP 5.28: 'he betrothed the maiden (who was his son's daughter) to the son of his own daughter (her cousin Aniruddha)'.

statements.claim: Rukmi still nursed enmity against Krishna over an old humiliation.
statements.evidence: BP 10.61.22: 'yady apy anusmaran vairaṃ rukmī kṛṣṇāvamānitaḥ' (though Rukmi, humiliated by Krishna, remembered his enmity). The 'grudge nursed for years / old humiliation' framing is the pack's own rendering of this verse.

statements.claim: Setting his grudge aside for his sister Rukmini's sake, Rukmi agreed to the match; Krishna had asked for Rocana's hand for Aniruddha.
statements.evidence: Pack rendered excerpt (BP 10.61.19-26): 'Though he still nursed enmity against Krishna, Rukmi, to please his sister Rukmini, gave his granddaughter Rocana in marriage to Aniruddha'; VP 5.28: 'Keśava demanded in marriage for him the granddaughter of Rukmin'.

statements.claim: Aniruddha was the son of Pradyumna, whom Rukmi's daughter had chosen at her swayamvara years before; he was known as powerful and gallant, fierce in fight, the tamer of his foes.
statements.evidence: VP 5.28 (in pack): 'The heroic Pradyumna was chosen for her lord, at her public choice of a husband, by the daughter of Rukmin; and he had by her the powerful and gallant prince Aniruddha, who was fierce in fight, an ocean of prowess, and the tamer of his foes.'

statements.claim: Rukmini, Balarama, Krishna and a train of Yadavas journeyed to Bhojakata for the wedding, and the city made ready with garlands and celebration.
statements.evidence: BP 10.61.25: 'tasminn abhyudaye rājan rukmiṇī rāma-keśavau' (at that festival Rukmini, Rama and Kesava [went]); VP 5.28: 'Ráma and other Yádavas attended Krishńa to Bhojakat́a, the city of Rukmin.' Decorations/gifts are generic wedding color.

statements.claim: Aniruddha and Rocana were cousins through both lines of Rukmi's blood — the daughter's son and the son's daughter — and the wedding joined the divided families.
statements.evidence: VP 5.28 (in pack): Rocana is Rukmi's 'son's daughter', Aniruddha 'the son of his own daughter'; both lines descend from Rukmi. The reconciliation-at-the-wedding reading matches BP's 'to please his sister Rukmini'.

statements.claim: The Yadavas rode the road that Rukmi had once sworn no one from Dvaraka would travel again.
statements.evidence: No source records any such oath; it is rhetorical heightening of the well-supported long feud and humiliation (BP 10.61.22), not an asserted, checkable event — treated as scene-setting rather than a sourceable fact.

statements.claim: When the celebrations ended the party from Dvaraka rode home, the two families were one again, and the wedding at Bhojakata would be remembered as the day the quarrel ended.
statements.evidence: The pack's own VP 5.28 passage shows the celebration ending otherwise: right after the wedding, Kalinga and other kings incited Rukmi to a dice game with Balarama ('he engaged Balaráma at a game of dice in the palace... Halayudha, galled by the broad laughter of the Kalinga prince, and the contemptuous speech of Rukmin, was exceedingly angry'), and the VP chapter header in the pack states: 'Balaráma beat at dice, becomes incensed, and slays Rukmin and others.' The feud thus did not end at this wedding — it ended in Rukmi's death during it.
statements.resolution: Corrected in story text via consolidation pass.

corrections.original_sentence: When the celebrations ended and the party from Dvaraka rode home, the two families were one again — joined at last by the very thing that had once divided them, and the wedding at Bhojakata would be remembered afterward as the day the quarrel ended.
corrections.suggested: But the old quarrel had not run its course: before the celebrations were over, Kalinga and other kings goaded Rukmi into a dice game with Balarama, and when Rukmi's taunts roused the enraged Balarama the wedding ended in blood, with Rukmi slain — remembered not as the day the quarrel ended but as the day it claimed him.

DKS_0339.notes: The story stops before the dice episode (its cited BP range 10.61.19-26 ends just before it), but the pack itself carries the VP account of the dice quarrel and its header ('Balaráma beat at dice, becomes incensed, and slays Rukmin and others'), so the closing claim of a peaceful, permanent reconciliation at this very wedding contradicts the pack.

statements.claim: Bana, son of Bali, always devoted to Shiva, ruled over the pleasant city of Shonitapura and had a thousand arms given him by the god.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.2-3, 7: 'tasyaurasaḥ suto bānaḥ śiva-bhakti-rataḥ sadā / śoṇitākhye pure ramye sa rājyam akarot purā'; 'doḥ-sahasraṃ tvayā dattaṃ'.

statements.claim: Bana had begun to find his thousand arms a burden — there were only so many weapons a man could hold — and his pride had grown until he believed no enemy was worthy of him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.7: 'doḥ-sahasraṃ tvayā dattaṃ paraṃ bhārāya me 'bhavat' (the thousand arms you gave have become a great burden to me). The psychologizing of his pride is connective narration consistent with v5 'vīrya-durmadaḥ' (mad with pride of valor) and v9-10 (Shiva angry, Bana delighted).

statements.claim: Bana stood before Shiva and addressed him: 'I bow to you, Mahadeva, teacher and lord of the worlds. The thousand arms you gave me have become a burden; they itch for battle, and I wish to test them against the great elephants that guard the quarters of the world.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.6-8: 'namasye tvāṃ mahā-deva lokānāṃ gurum īśvaram / doḥ-sahasraṃ tvayā dattaṃ paraṃ bhārāya me 'bhavat / kaṇḍūtyā nibhṛtair dorbhir yuyutsur dig-gajān aham'.

statements.claim: Shiva grew angry at the pride of his worshipper and declared: 'When your banner falls, then your pride will be humbled, in battle with a rival worthy of you.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.9: 'tac chrutvā bhagavān kruddhaḥ ketus te bhajyate yadā'; pack rendered excerpt: 'Shiva declared that when Bana's flag fell, his pride would be humbled in battle with a peer.'

statements.claim: Bana heard a promise in the warning and went home delighted, imagining the battle to come and never wondering what kind of battle would humble his pride.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.10: 'ity uktaḥ kumatir hṛṣṭaḥ sva-gṛhaṃ prāviśan nṛpa' (thus addressed, the foolish one, delighted, entered his house). The final image of the banner over the gates is connective scene-setting.

DKS_0340.notes: 'Eldest son of Bali' follows the pack's index entry and excerpt. Shiva as 'the refuge of his devotees, kind to those who love him' renders BP 10.62.4 ('śaraṇyo bhakta-vatsalaḥ').

statements.claim: Usha, daughter of Bana, king of Shonitapura, woke calling for a man she had never seen — 'where are you, my beloved?' — after dreaming of a dark, lotus-eyed youth.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.11-12, 15: 'tasyoṣā nāma duhitā svapne prādyumninā ratim... kvāsi kānteti vādinī'; 'dṛṣṭaḥ kaścin naraḥ svapne śyāmaḥ kamala-locanaḥ'.

statements.claim: The dream had been promised her: having seen Parvati sporting with Shiva, Usha wished for such a husband, and the goddess told her that he who appeared to her in a dream on the twelfth night of the bright fortnight of Vaishakha would be her lord.
statements.evidence: VP 5.32 (in pack): 'Ushá, the daughter of Báńa, having seen Párvatí sporting with her lord, Śambhu, was inspired with a wish for similar dalliance. The beautiful Gaurí... said... He who shall appear to you, princess, in a dream on the twelfth lunation of the light half of Vaiśákha, he will be your husband.'

statements.claim: Her friend Chitralekha, daughter of Bana's minister Kumbhanda — skilled in painting and a yogini — found her pining and asked: 'Whom do you seek, fair-browed one? What is the desire in your heart?'
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.13-14, 21: 'bāṇasya mantrī kumbhāṇḍaś citralekhā ca tat-sutā / kaṃ tvaṃ mṛgayase su-bhru kīdṛśas te manorathaḥ'; 'citralekhā... yoginī'.

statements.claim: Usha answered that she sought a man seen in a dream, dark, with lotus-petal eyes, whose lips she longed to taste — but she could not name him or his home.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.16: 'tam ahaṃ mṛgaye kāntaṃ pāyayitvādharaṃ madhu' (I seek him as my lover, having drunk the honey of his lips). The inability to name him follows from the dream (v11-12).

statements.claim: Chitralekha painted the gods, gandharvas, siddhas, charanas and the serpents of the deep, and then, among the great houses of men, the Vrishnis — and the face of Krishna himself, and after it his grandson Aniruddha, son of Pradyumna.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.18-20: 'ity uktvā deva-gandharva siddha-cāraṇa-pannagān / manujeṣu ca sā vṛṣṇīn śūram ānakadundubhim / aniruddhaṃ vilikhitaṃ...'. The verse names the Vrishnis and the hero Anakadundubhi (Vasudeva) before Aniruddha; listing Krishna's face among the Vrishni portraits is a natural connective rendering of 'the Vrishnis' (he is the line's foremost figure), and Usha's recognition falls on Aniruddha as in the source.

statements.claim: Seeing Aniruddha's portrait Usha cried 'This is he! This is he!' and then dropped her gaze, her cheeks burning with shame at her secret; Chitralekha, the yogini, recognized the youth as Krishna's grandson.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.20-21: 'aniruddhaṃ vilikhitaṃ vīkṣyoṣāvāṅ-mukhī hriyā / citralekhā tam ājñāya pautraṃ kṛṣṇasya yoginī' (seeing painted Aniruddha, Usha lowered her face in shame; the yogini Chitralekha knew him as Krishna's grandson); VP 5.32: 'This is he! this is he!'

statements.claim: Dvaraka was a city so far from Shonitapura that it might have been another world, with no road leading from Usha's chambers to it.
statements.evidence: The distance and impossibility are the story's framing of the abduction to come (next story, BP 10.62.21-25); no source quantifies the distance. Not asserted as a checkable fact.

DKS_0341.notes: Story follows the BP opening (dream first) while weaving in the VP's Parvati-promise frame, exactly as its tradition_note says the sources relate — both frames are present in the pack.

statements.claim: Chitralekha set out from Shonitapura, crossed the distance to Dvaraka, and by her yogic power found Aniruddha (Pradyumna's son) asleep on a beautiful couch in his inner chamber and carried the sleeping prince back to Shonitapura.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.21-22: 'citralekhā tam ājñāya pautraṃ kṛṣṇasya yoginī / tatra suptaṃ su-paryaṅke prādyumniṃ yogam āsthitā' (knowing him, the yogini, employing her power, [brought] Pradyumna's son who slept on a fine couch). The one-night crossing and 'he did not wake' are connective elaboration of the yogic transport; the pack's own excerpt says she 'flew to Dvaraka'.

statements.claim: Usha, overjoyed at seeing the youth of her dream, dressed him in the finest garments, wound garlands about him, set scents, incense and lamps burning about him, and placed him in the seat of honor in her chambers.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.23-24: 'sā ca taṃ sundara-varaṃ vilokya muditānanā / parārdhya-vāsaḥ-srag-gandha-dhūpa-dīpāsanādibhiḥ' (beholding the handsome youth, her face joyful, [she honored him] with supremely valuable garments, garlands, fragrance, incense, lamps and seats).

statements.claim: Aniruddha came to live hidden in the innermost women's quarters of Bana's palace, and day after day passed with no one perceiving it, while Usha's love grew.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.25: 'gūḍhaḥ kanyā-pure śaśvat-pravṛddha-snehayā tayā' (hidden in the maidens' quarters, with her love ever increasing).

statements.claim: The guards at every outer gate made the inner chambers where no man was permitted the safest walls in the city.
statements.evidence: Why the secret held is not detailed in BP 10.62.21-25 beyond 'hidden in the maidens' quarters'; the guarded-women's-quarters logic is connective framing consistent with the verse.

statements.claim: But eyes in the palace were beginning to notice the strangeness, and the days of the hidden love were numbered.
statements.evidence: Foreshadowing of the next corpus event (Bana captures and binds Aniruddha, per pack corpus chain and BP 10.62.26ff), phrased as narrative tease, not an asserted sourceable fact.

DKS_0342.notes: The story follows the BP version (sleeping prince carried by yogic power) and flags the Harivamsha variant (awake, Gandharva marriage) in its tradition_note — both present in the pack (BP passage + Harivamsha 1.266 excerpt).

statements.claim: Guards in Shonitapura discover an unknown young man in the king's inner apartments and report it to the king.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.26-28: the guards report to the king that his daughter has been enjoyed by a Yadava hero ('yadu-vīreṇa bhujyamānāṃ hata-vratām'); VP 5.33: 'The guards of the inner apartments discovering him there with Ushá, reported it to the king.'

statements.claim: Usha is the daughter of Bana, king of Shonitapura, and Aniruddha is the son of Pradyumna and grandson of Krishna.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.27-30 ('duhituḥ... kāmātmajam'), index entry and corpus chain; HV 1.266 identifies 'Pradyumna's son' Aniruddha and Usha as Vāna's daughter.

statements.claim: Usha had dreamed of a handsome young prince and fallen in love with the dream; the goddess's boon promised she would marry the man she saw.
statements.evidence: HV 1.266 (in pack): Usha chose Aniruddha 'on account of the boon given by the goddess', and Chitralekha tells him 'Ushā whom you saw in a dream and married'; background beat of DKS_0342 (corpus chain).

statements.claim: Her friend Chitralekha, skilled in the arts of illusion, brought Aniruddha from Dwaraka to Usha, and the two were united in the palace.
statements.evidence: HV 1.266: Chitralekha uses Tamasik illusion to carry Aniruddha to Shonitapura; VP 5.33: 'a female, possessed of magic faculties, conveyed him'; BP 10.62.26 confirms the secret union.

statements.claim: Bana, son of Bali, rushes in fury to the women's quarters and finds his daughter at dice with Aniruddha.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.29-31: 'tataḥ pravyathito bāṇo duhituḥ śruta-dūṣaṇaḥ... dīvyantam akṣaiḥ' — Bana, agitated at his daughter's defilement, sees him dicing with her; HV/VP agree.

statements.claim: Aniruddha is described as beautiful beyond compare, dark as a rain cloud, lotus-eyed, saffron-clad, with Usha's red kumkuma on his chest where she had leaned.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.30-31: 'bhuvanaika-sundaraṃ śyāmaṃ piśaṅgāmbaram ambujekṣaṇam... tad-aṅga-saṅga-stana-kuṅkuma-srajam' — world's one beauty, dark, saffron-clad, lotus-eyed, kumkuma from her breasts' contact on his body.

statements.claim: Aniruddha scatters the guards like a great boar scattering dogs, whereupon Bana binds him with serpent-nooses so he cannot move.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.33-34: he strikes the guards creeping like dogs 'śūkara-yūthapaḥ' (like a boar-leader) and 'taṃ nāga-pāśair... babandha ha' (bound him with serpent-nooses); HV: chained with serpents; VP: serpent bonds. The story's living-serpent framing follows BP (its own tradition_note flags the HV serpentine-shafts variant).

statements.claim: Kumbhanda counsels that the prince should not be slain; Aniruddha is handed over to the guards and kept bound, and Bana withdraws to his own apartments.
statements.evidence: HV 1.266: Kumbhānda said 'He does not deserve to be slain', Aniruddha is 'handing over... to the guards', and Vāna 'repaired to his own palace'; VP 5.33: Bana (having tried to kill the prince) 'followed the counsel of his minister' and captured him by magic.

statements.claim: The hidden union will bring war: someone in Dwaraka will count the children of the house of Yadu and find one missing.
statements.evidence: Foreshadowing bridge; Narada's report to the Yadavas and the count of the missing prince belong to the next episode (BP 10.63.1, DKS_0344), not asserted in this pack.

DKS_0343.notes: Faithful to BP 10.62.26-34 with HV 1.266/VP 5.33 support. The 'thrown into a cell' locale is the corpus's own framing (also DKS_0346/0347) — no pack source places him in a cell, and HV 1.276 has him remain bound in the women's apartment until release; judged a narrative setting choice, not a sourced fact error.

statements.claim: Narada tells the Yadavas that Aniruddha has been taken and is Bana's prisoner in Shonitapura.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.1: 'nāradāt tad upākarṇya vārtāṃ baddhasya karma ca' (hearing from Narada the news of the bound one); VP 5.33: 'Nárada came to them, and told them that he was the prisoner of Báńa... in Śońitapura.'

statements.claim: Pradyumna, Satyaki, Gada and Samba, with twelve full armies, besiege Shonitapura, breaking its parks, ramparts, towers and gateways.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.2-4: 'pradyumno yuyudhānaś ca gadaḥ sāmbo... akṣauhiṇībhir dvādaśabhiḥ... bhajyamāna-purodyāna-prākārāṭṭāla-gopuram' — twelve akṣauhiṇīs; parks, ramparts, towers (aṭṭāla) and gateways (gopura) being broken.

statements.claim: Bana is a devotee of Shiva, and for his sake Shiva takes the field with his son Skanda beside him and his strange hosts around him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.5: 'bāṇārthe bhagavān rudraḥ sa-sutaḥ pramathair vṛtaḥ' (Rudra with his son, surrounded by pramathas, for Bana's sake); HV 1.272: Kumāra (Skanda) also mounts a car; the attendant hosts (bhūta, pramatha, guhyaka) appear in BP 10.63.9-10.

statements.claim: The battle was dreadful, hair-raising and wonderful beyond mortal experience.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.6: 'āsīt su-tumulaṃ yuddham adbhutaṃ roma-harṣaṇam' — exceedingly tumultuous, wonderful, hair-raising.

statements.claim: The demon commanders Kumbhanda and Kupakarna hurl themselves at Balarama.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.7: 'kumbhāṇḍa-kūpakarṇābhyāṃ balena saha saṃyugaḥ' (engagement of Kumbhanda and Kupakarna with Bala[rama]); they later fall struck by the muṣala, Balarama's weapon (BP 10.63.15 in DKS_0345 pack).

statements.claim: Riding Garuda, Krishna and the Yadava heroes disperse the Danava army with arrow-fire; the Danavas flee despite Bana's rallying cry ('born in the race of the Daityas'), and only the pramathas hold their ground.
statements.evidence: HV 1.272: the three heroes on Garuda disperse the Dānava army with a downpour of arrows; fire from Krishna's arrows consumes thousands of Dānavas; Vāna shouts 'Born in the race of the Daityas why do ye... fly away?'; the Dānavas flee nonetheless and 'only the Pramathas stood firm'.

statements.claim: Shiva, eyes reddened with anger to protect Bana, mounts his great car drawn by lions and ringed by howling ghosts — with faces of tigers, serpents and horses, blowing conches, some in bark with matted locks — a car that seemed to devour the sky.
statements.evidence: HV 1.272: 'Siva... had his eyes reddened with anger. And in order to protect Vāna, he stood on his lustrous car... drawn by lions... as if devouring the sky'; the ghost-train with faces of tigers/serpents/horses, blowing conch-shells, some 'put on bark', some with 'matted locks', is described in the same passage.

statements.claim: Shiva looses the Brahma, wind, fire and Pashupata weapons; Krishna answers each with a match — Brahma answered by Brahma, the wind-weapon by the mountain-weapon — then Vishnu's Indra-given weapon flies at Rudra's car, Shiva's fiery weapon covers the heroes, the Varuna weapon quenches the fire, and the Vaishnava weapon routs the bhutas, yakshas and asuras.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.11-12 + pack summary: 'Krishna countered Shiva's Brahma, wind, fire and Pashupata weapons with matching astras' (brahmāstrasya brahmāstram, vāyavyasya pārvatam); HV 1.272: 'Vishnu discharged Indra's weapon at Rudra... Hara discharged the highly dreadful fiery weapon... Vāsudeva took up Vāruna weapon... fire... extinguished... Mādhava discharged his Vaishnava weapon... all the Bhutas, Yakshas and Asuras... fled on all sides.'

statements.claim: Brahma himself came with the celestials, and Apsaras, Gandharvas, Siddhas and Charanas crowded the sky to watch, while the earth was scorched, the mountains shaken and the quarters ablaze.
statements.evidence: HV 1.272: the Grandfather (Brahmā) came encircled by the celestials; Apsaras, Gandharvas, Siddhas and Chāranas witnessed the encounter; 'the quarters, sky and earth were as if all ablaze', mountains were covered with streams and their summits scattered.

statements.claim: Neither Shiva nor Krishna had yielded, and the duel would end only by a yawn.
statements.evidence: Foreshadowing bridge to DKS_0345; the pack's verses end with the weapons still exchanged (BP 10.63.1-12; HV 1.272 breaks off mid-passage), and the Jrimbhana-astra resolution belongs to BP 10.63.13.

DKS_0344.notes: Combines BP 10.63.1-12 and HV 1.272 as the pack itself does; both agree on the core weapon-exchange sequence. HV's 'Krishna and the three other heroes were covered with arrows' vs the story's 'three Yadava heroes' is negligible compression.

statements.claim: Krishna looses the Jrimbhana weapon, the astra of yawning, and strikes Shiva in the midst of his wrath; the god gapes uncontrollably, sinks down in his car and can no longer fight.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.13: 'mohayitvā tu giriśaṃ jṛmbhaṇāstreṇa jṛmbhitam' (stupefying Girisha, made him yawn with the Jrimbhana astra); VP 5.33: 'Hara, overcome with incessant gaping, sat down in his car, and was unable longer to contend with Krishńa.'

statements.claim: Krishna's army falls on Bana's host and breaks it utterly.
statements.evidence: Pack's rendered BP excerpt (10.63.13-20): 'Krishna, stupefying Shiva with the Jrimbhana weapon, slew Bana's army'.

statements.claim: Skanda tries to hold his father's cause together but, bloodied under Pradyumna's arrows from every side, takes to flight.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.14: 'skandaḥ pradyumna-bāṇaughair ardyamānaḥ samantataḥ' (Skanda tormented on all sides by Pradyumna's arrow-floods); VP 5.33: 'Kártikeya, wounded... took to flight.'

statements.claim: Kumbhanda and Kupakarna, the demon commanders, are struck down and fall.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.15: 'kumbhāṇḍa-kūpakarṇaś ca petatur muṣalārditau' (Kumbhanda and Kupakarna fell, struck by the muṣala).

statements.claim: Seeing his army shattered, Bana in fury seizes five hundred bows at once and shoots at Krishna; the discus in Krishna's hand cuts all five hundred bows down together.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.16-18: 'viśīryamāṇam sva-balaṃ dṛṣṭvā bāṇo 'ty-amarṣitaḥ / dhanūṃṣy ākṛṣya yugapad bāṇaḥ pañca-śatāni vai / tāni ciccheda bhagavān dhanūṃsi yugapad dhariḥ' — Bana drew five hundred bows at once and Hari cut them all simultaneously.

statements.claim: Kotara, Bana's mother, comes onto the field and stands before the conqueror with her hair unbound and without a veil, offering her own dignity so her son may live.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.19: 'tan-mātā koṭarā nāma nagnā makta-śiroruhā' — his mother Kotara, naked, with hair unbound; pack summary: she 'stood naked before Krishna to save her son's life'. The story's 'hair unbound and without a veil' is a modest rendering of nagnā (naked); same gesture, deliberate softening, not a substantive divergence.

statements.claim: Krishna turns his face aside and will not look upon her; the lingering ghostly hosts take the sign and flee, and the slaughter stops.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.20-21: 'tatas tiryaṅ-mukho nagnām anirīkṣan gadāgrajaḥ' (face averted, not looking at the naked one) and 'vidrāvite bhūta-gaṇe' (the host of bhūtas scattered).

statements.claim: Bana himself still stands, his thousand arms still his own; the discus has not yet done its work.
statements.evidence: Bridge to DKS_0346: in the BP sequence the arm-cutting (10.63.30-48) follows the Kotara/Fever episodes (10.63.19-29), so the line is chronologically consistent but is narrative scene-setting rather than a sourced event in this pack's verses.

DKS_0345.notes: Ordering matches BP 10.63.13-20 exactly (Jrimbhana, Skanda, Kumbhanda/Kupakarna, five hundred bows, Kotara). Only handling of note: BP's 'naked' rendered as 'hair unbound and without a veil' — an age-appropriate softening flagged above, kept as SUPPORTED since the act (unveiling/self-exposure to shield her son) is intact.

statements.claim: Bana boasts to Krishna: 'You will not escape me alive today. I have a thousand arms, and you have eight — how will you fight me? You will see my thousand arms multiply into a million.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.275: 'Wait! Wait! You will not escape from me to-day alive... being of eight arms how you will be able to fight with me who have a thousand arms?... You will see to-day my thousand arms... multiply into a million.'

statements.claim: Narada, watching from the palace roof, laughs aloud until the sky seems to split.
statements.evidence: HV 1.275: 'Hearing those proud words of Vāna Nārada so laughed aloud that as if the sky was sundered in twain'; later the same account places him 'sitting on the highest top of the palace'.

statements.claim: Krishna answers: 'Heroes do not vaunt. Come and fight.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.275: 'The heroes do not vaunt thus. What is the use of vaunting? Come and fight with me in the battle field.'

statements.claim: Bana covers Krishna with clubs, maces, spears and the rest, and when Krishna's arrows cut him to the quick he discharges the celestial astra that Brahma had long ago created for Hiranyakashipu.
statements.evidence: HV 1.275: Vāna 'covered Keshava' with parighas, clubs, tomaras, śaktis, maces and pattiśas; then 'discharged that celestial great weapon... which Brahmā, by his ascetic powers, had formerly created for Hiranyakashipu.'

statements.claim: The weapon shrouds everything in darkness and rains burning arrows; Krishna's Indra-given weapon dispels the darkness, quenches the fire, the gods laugh like lions and the Danavas lose heart.
statements.evidence: HV 1.275: 'all the quarters were enshrouded with darkness... A dreadful downpour of burning arrows was caused'; with Indra's weapon 'all the worlds were shorn of darkness, the fire was extinguished and the Dānavas completely lost their hearts... the gods began to laugh and roar like lions.'

statements.claim: Arrows from Krishna's great bow Sharnga shatter Bana's car with horses and standards, strip away his crown, mail, bow and shield, and a winged arrow strikes him on the breast, so that he swoons.
statements.evidence: HV 1.275: from the Śārṅga bow Keshava 'sundered Vāna's car, with horses and standards, into pieces', 'separated... his... crown, coat of mail, bow and shield', 'struck him on the breast with winged arrows', and 'Vāna lost his consciousness and swooned away.'

statements.claim: Bana rises and rushes at Krishna with all his thousand arms bearing every weapon; the Sudarshana discus severs the arms one by one, like a man pruning branches, until his terrible strength is gone.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.30-31: 'tato bāhu-sahasreṇa nānāyudha-dharo 'suraḥ... cakreṇa kṣura-neminā' (the Asura with his thousand arms bearing various weapons; [Krishna] with the razor-edged discus); pack summary: arms 'cut off... as if pruning branches'; HV 1.275: the discus 'gradually cutting off Vāna's thousand arms'.

statements.claim: Shiva — recovered from the yawning weapon — watches his devotee's arms fall, hymns Krishna as the primal person, the single source of all worlds, the sun hidden only by its own light, and pleads: 'This one is dear to me. He has followed me; I have given him freedom from fear.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.32-44: Rudra speaks while Bana's arms are cut (10.63.32-33), praising 'tvam eka ādyaḥ puruṣo 'dvitīyas' and 'yathaiva sūryaḥ pihitaś chāyayā svayā'; v.44: 'ayaṃ mameṣṭo dayito 'nuvartī mayābhayaṃ dattam amuṣya deva' — near-verbatim match.

statements.claim: Krishna spares Bana in honor of the boon given long ago to Prahlada: 'This Asura is not to be killed, even by me. His arms were cut to humble his pride.' He leaves Bana four arms, freedom from fear, and ageless, deathless life.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.46-48: 'avadhyo 'yaṃ mamāpy eṣa vairocani-suto 'suraḥ / darpopaśamanāyāsya pravṛkṇā bāhavo mayā / catvāro 'sya bhujāḥ śiṣṭā bhaviṣyaty ajarāmaraḥ'; pack summary confirms the sparing honors 'the boon given to Prahrada'. Variant noted in pack: HV/VP leave two arms; the story follows BP's four (its primary source).

statements.claim: Bana, who had imagined a million arms, stands humbled with four; the war for Aniruddha is over and the prince's release is imminent.
statements.evidence: Closing tableau and bridge to DKS_0347; consistent with BP 10.63.48-49 (four arms remain; fearlessness granted) but phrased as narration rather than a sourced event in this pack.

DKS_0346.notes: Blends HV 1.275 (boast, weapon-duel, swoon) with BP 10.63.20-48 (arm-cutting, Shiva's hymns, sparing) exactly as the pack presents both. Arms remaining: four per BP (primary) vs two per HV/VP — story correctly follows BP and the pack flags the variant.

statements.claim: Aniruddha had been carried off by magic to Shonitapura; Usha loved him, and Bana kept the young prince prisoner, bound with serpent-nooses, in the women's quarters.
statements.evidence: HV 1.276: Narada tells Krishna the prince 'is waiting, bound with serpents, in the female appartment'; the abduction-by-magic and serpent-bondage match BP 10.62/VP 5.33 (corpus chain: DKS_0343-0346).

statements.claim: Krishna's discus severed Bana's thousand arms one after another, until the demon king stood before his conqueror; yet Krishna spared him — at Shiva's plea, and because Bana, even in defeat, had bowed to him.
statements.evidence: Compressed recap of DKS_0346: the severing (BP 10.63.30-31) and sparing at Shiva's plea plus the Prahlada boon (BP 10.63.44-48) are supported, but two nuances are smoothed over: Bana was left four arms, not 'armless', and BP 10.63.49 has him bow his head only after receiving fearlessness — the bow did not motivate the mercy. The sentence is faithful in substance, loose in causal ordering; flagged as narration rather than error.

statements.claim: Krishna had pressed the sage Narada again and again for word of the boy: 'My mind is overpowered with affection... I wish to see even today Aniruddha, who has slain his enemies.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.276: 'O reverend sir, my mind is overpowered with affection... I wish to see even to-day Aniruddha who has his enemies slain.' Near-verbatim.

statements.claim: Granted fearlessness, Bana comes forward and touches his head to Krishna's feet.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.49: 'iti labdhvābhayaṃ kṛṣṇaṃ praṇamya śirasāsuraḥ' — obtaining fearlessness, the Asura bowed his head to Krishna.

statements.claim: Bana places Aniruddha and his bride Usha on a chariot, gives them an escort from his own army, and sends them home with the Yadavas.
statements.evidence: Pack's BP excerpt (10.63.49-52): 'Bana bowed to Krishna, placed Aniruddha and his bride Usha on a chariot, and sent them with an army'; BP 10.63.50 shows Aniruddha 'akṣauhiṇyā parivṛtaṃ su-vāsaḥ-samalaṅkṛtam' (surrounded by an akṣauhiṇī, well-dressed and adorned).

statements.claim: During Aniruddha's absence Dwaraka had been full of anxious talk, a son of the house spirited away with no one certain whether he lived.
statements.evidence: HV 1.276: 'The heroic Aniruddha being taken away stealthily the city of Dwārakā is filled with anxiety.'

statements.claim: Word runs ahead of the returning host and Dwaraka prepares as for a festival: banners on the walls, arches raised at the crossings, streets and squares swept and sprinkled.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.51: the capital is adorned 'dhvajaiḥ sa-toraṇair ukṣita-mārga-catvarām' — with flags, with arches, its streets and squares sprinkled; the story's 'swept and sprinkled' matches ukṣita.

statements.claim: Krishna enters his own capital to the blare of conches and roll of drums, greeted by citizens, friends and priests.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.51: 'viveśa śaṅkhānaka-dundubhi-svanair abhyudyataḥ paura-suhṛd-dvijātibhiḥ' — entered amid the sound of conches and dundubhi drums, welcomed by citizens, friends and brahmins.

statements.claim: At the heart of the procession ride Aniruddha with Usha beside him — the prince the city had feared lost and the bride who came back with him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.50 (Aniruddha returning adorned and escorted) and the pack summary placing the couple on a chariot sent with the army; the couple's return to Dwaraka is the episode's point. (Variant: HV 1.276 has Usha ride on a peacock with a goddess while the four heroes sit on Garuda; the story follows the BP reading.)

statements.claim: Long after the procession passed, the sound of the conches carried out over the water, telling the sea the house of Yadu had its prince back.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric closing image; Dwaraka is a coastal city in the corpus, but the detail is rhetorical, not a sourced fact.

DKS_0347.notes: One deliberate caution: the recap glosses the order of Bana's mercy (bow vs. four arms remaining) — see the RCN statement. Otherwise BP 10.63.49-52 and HV 1.276 both support the surrender, escort and triumphal return.

statements.claim: Shalva's army appears everywhere and nowhere at once — on the ground, in the sky, on mountain peaks, in the water — now a single host, now many, one form and many forms, seen and unseen.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.20-22: 'bahu-rūpaika-rūpaṃ tad dṛśyate na ca dṛśyate / kvacid bhūmau kvacid vyomni giri-mūrdhni jale kvacit' — many-formed and one-formed, seen and not seen, now on earth, now in the sky, on mountain tops, sometimes in water.

statements.claim: Shalva, an old enemy of the house of Yadu, had come against Dwaraka again with sorcery and numbers.
statements.evidence: Contextual framing: the pack places the engagement at Dwaraka (index location) within the ongoing Shalva war (BP 10.76), and Shalva's earlier enmity with the Yadus is established in earlier episodes of the corpus; the excerpt itself, however, begins mid-engagement and does not recount the siege or prior enmity.

statements.claim: Pradyumna, Krishna's son, rides out to meet him and in a single moment dispels the demon's illusions with his divine weapons, reading the false shapes in the air.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (BP 10.76.17-32): 'Pradyumna in a moment dispels the demon's illusions with divine weapons'; the illusory many-form/one-form army of vv.20-22 is what he reads through.

statements.claim: Pradyumna drives twenty-five iron-headed arrows with golden shafts into Shalva himself, strikes the king with a hundred more, and then fells his soldiers one arrow apiece.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.17-18: 'vivyādha pañca-viṃśatyā svarṇa-puṅkhair ayo-mukhaiḥ / śatenātāḍayac chālvam ekaikenāsya sainikān' — pierced [Shalva] with twenty-five gold-shafted, iron-tipped arrows; struck Shalva with a hundred; each soldier with one.

statements.claim: It was a wonderful deed, and warriors of both armies stopped to watch.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.19: 'tad adbhutaṃ mahat karma pradyumnasya mahātmanaḥ' (that wonderful great deed of the great-souled Pradyumna); pack summary: 'winning the admiration of both armies'.

statements.claim: Shalva's arrows — hot as fire and sun, unapproachable as serpent poison — fall in floods on the Vrishni heroes, and Pradyumna's own side is hard pressed.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.23-24: 'śarair agny-arka-saṃsparśair āśī-viṣa-durāsadaiḥ... vṛṣṇi-vīrā bhṛśārditāḥ' — with arrows of fire-sun touch, unapproachable like snake-venom, the Vrishni heroes were greatly afflicted.

statements.claim: Dyuman, Shalva's minister — himself wounded and pressed hard by Pradyumna earlier — seizes a mace and strikes the young warrior full on the chest; his armor gives way and the charioteer carries the senseless hero from the field.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.25-27: 'śālvāmātyo dyumān nāma pradyumnaṃ prak prapīḍitaḥ / pradyumnaṃ gadayā sīrṇa-vakṣaḥ-sthalam' — Dyuman, earlier oppressed by Pradyumna, shattered his chest with a mace; pack summary confirms the charioteer 'carries the senseless hero away'.

statements.claim: Regaining consciousness, Pradyumna rebukes his charioteer: 'No one born in the line of the Yadus is ever heard of as one who fled the field. What shall I say when I come before my two fathers, Rama and Keshava? My brothers' wives will laugh when they tell of this.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.27-30: 'labdha-samjño muhūrtena kārṣṇiḥ sārathim abravīt / na yadūnāṃ kule jātaḥ śrūyate raṇa-vicyutaḥ / kiṃ nu vakṣye 'bhisaṅgamya pitarau rāma-keśavau / vyaktaṃ me kathayiṣyanti hasantyo bhrātṛ-jāmayaḥ' — near-verbatim, including 'both fathers Rāma and Keśava'.

statements.claim: The charioteer answers: 'Knowing this, I carried you from the battle.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.31-32: 'sārathir uvāca / etad viditvā tu bhavān mayāpovāhito raṇāt' — 'Knowing this, you were carried away by me from the battle.'

statements.claim: Pradyumna, steadying himself on the rail of the chariot, looks back toward the battle.
statements.evidence: Closing tableau continuing from BP 10.76.27 (he recovers and speaks in the chariot); the specific posture is scene-setting, not a sourced event.

DKS_0348.notes: Very tight to BP 10.76.17-32; numbers, names (Dyuman as Shalva's minister, twenty-five/hundred arrows), quotes and sequence all match. Only the opening 'old enemy... against Dwaraka' framing relies on wider corpus context.

statements.claim: The passage opens with Krishna established in the highest duty of the householder, the one who keeps the home-fire.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.28: 'āsthitasya paraṃ dharmaṃ kṛṣṇasya gṛha-medhinām' — Krishna who had recourse to the supreme dharma of the householder (gṛhamedhin, keeper of the domestic fire).

statements.claim: Sixteen thousand and more than a hundred queens made their home in Dwaraka.
statements.evidence: Pack's rendered summary of BP 10.90.28-45: 'Krishna has sixteen thousand and more than a hundred queens' (the 16,000-plus-one-hundred-plus figure of the earlier enumeration).

statements.claim: Eight of the queens are named in an earlier passage as the chief jewel-women, Rukmini at their head; the rest pass as a crowd.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.29: 'tāsāṃ strī-ratna-bhūtānām aṣṭau yāḥ prāg udāhṛtāḥ' — of them, eight previously declared as the jewel-women; Rukmini heads the chief queens in the earlier enumeration (corpus's Rukmini episodes; pack character list includes Rukmini).

statements.claim: On every one of these queens Krishna begot ten sons; the arithmetic runs past a hundred and sixty thousand.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.30: 'ekaikasyāṃ daśa daśa kṛṣṇo 'jījanad ātmajān' (ten and ten sons on each one); 16,100+ × 10 exceeds 160,000 (16,108 wives × 10 = 161,080).

statements.claim: Among the sons a few names rise to the surface: Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Samba, Diptiman, Bhanu, Pushkara, Vedabahu, Shrutadeva, Sunandana.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.32-33 names Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Dīptimān, Bhānu, Puṣkara, Vedabāhu, Śrutadeva and Sunandana; Sāmba is added by the pack's own summary ('among the foremost are Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Samba and others') and is Krishna's son throughout the corpus.

statements.claim: No one born in this family was poor, and no one had few children; the men of the line of Yadu were famous for their deeds.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.38-39: 'na hy etasmin kule jātā adhanā abahu-prajāḥ / yadu-vaṃśa-prasūtānāṃ puṃsāṃ vikhyāta-karmaṇām' — near-verbatim.

statements.claim: Where the old reckoning attempts a total it runs into the crores and beyond, and the book asks: who could count the Yadavas?
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.40-41: 'tisraḥ koṭyaḥ sahasrāṇām aṣṭāśīti-śatāni ca / saṅkhyānaṃ yādavānāṃ kaḥ kariṣyati mahātmanām' — a count in the crores, then 'who will count the great-souled Yadavas?'

statements.claim: Pradyumna married the daughter of Rukmi, and their son Aniruddha married Rukmi's granddaughter — the same house joined twice over.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.35-36: 'sa rukmiṇo duhitaram upayeme mahā-rathaḥ / sa cāpi rukmiṇaḥ pautrīṃ dauhitro jagṛhe tataḥ' — the great warrior [Pradyumna] wed Rukmi's daughter; the daughter's son [Aniruddha] took Rukmi's granddaughter.

statements.claim: From Aniruddha came Pratibahu, and from Pratibahu, Subahu — names trailing into a line too long to follow.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.37: 'pratibāhur abhūt tasmāt subāhus tasya cātmajaḥ' — from him came Pratibāhu; Subāhu was his son.

statements.claim: Vajra, the grandson of Pradyumna through Aniruddha, alone would survive the destruction by the mace — the last days of Dwaraka, when the Yadava houses turned their weapons upon one another.
statements.evidence: Pack's rendered summary: 'Pradyumna's grandson through Aniruddha is Vajra, who alone would survive the destruction by the mace'. Note textual variance: v.37's immediate line runs Aniruddha→Pratibahu→Subahu, while the tradition (and this pack's summary) makes Vajra Aniruddha's son and sole survivor; the story follows the pack summary, its intended reading.

statements.claim: The text explains the family's size: in the war between gods and demons terrible demon-lords had been slain, and to hold such forces in check the gods themselves took birth in the line of Yadu, with Hari as their measure and master.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.42-44: 'devāsurāhava-hatā daiteyā ye su-dāruṇāḥ / tan-nigrahāya hariṇā proktā devā yadoḥ kule / teṣāṃ pramāṇaṃ bhagavān prabhutvenābhavad dhariḥ' — the fierce Daiteyas slain in the gods' war were to be checked by gods born in Yadu's line; Hari was their authority.

statements.claim: The book turns from counting to the smallest record — how Krishna slept, sat, walked, spoke, played and bathed among his family.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.45: 'śayyāsanāṭanālāpa-krīḍā-snānādi-karmasu' — sleeping, sitting, walking, conversing, playing, bathing and the like.

statements.claim: After millions upon millions, the truest measure of the man is an ordinary day in the middle of it all — a householder at the home-fire.
statements.evidence: Closing synthesis by the author, mirroring the passage's frame (v.28 householder dharma → v.45 daily acts); interpretive, not a sourced fact.

DKS_0349.notes: Textually dense but every enumeration, name and genealogy matches BP 10.90.28-45 or the pack summary. Flagged variance: Vajra's slot in the genealogy (v.37 lists Pratibahu/Subahu as Aniruddha's line; the summary names Vajra as the surviving grandson) — story follows the pack summary as instructed.

statements.claim: Krishna chose the ground himself, walking the edge of the forest at sunrise after his morning ablutions with the elders of the Yadu house following.
statements.evidence: HV 1.115: 'when the sun rose in the clear morning, Hrishikesha... having performed his morning ablution and sat for some time at the outskirt of the forest, began to survey it for finding out a site... The principal members of the Yudu race followed him.'

statements.claim: Krishna announces the site and its name: the city will be celebrated on earth as Dwaravati, like Indra's Amaravati; he is laying out courtyards, promenades, well-levelled roads and inner quarters, and bids the Yadavas take land, lay out gardens and crossings, survey roads and walls, and send for masons and artisans.
statements.evidence: HV 1.115 speech: 'I have also selected the name under which it will be celebrated on earth... this city of mine will be celebrated on earth by the name of Dwāravati like unto Indra's Amarāvti... I am laying out courtyards, promenades, well-levelled roads and inner appartments... Let all of you take lands for building houses; let gardens and crossings of four roads be laid out and let a survey of roads and walls be taken... masons be sent round the country.'

statements.claim: The Yadavas set about it that very day — some measuring plots with ropes, others honoring the tutelary deity with gifts to the brahmins — while the masons gather timber and stone and raise the gate and the boundary line.
statements.evidence: HV 1.115: Yadavas 'engaged in measuring their own lands with ropes' and 'began to worship the tutelary deity by adorning the Brahmanas'; the masons 'collected all the materials for building the fort and began to lay out the gate and the boundary line.'

statements.claim: Krishna calls on Vishwakarma, the celestial architect, and he comes and stands before Krishna, saying: 'You are adorable to me as grandfather Brahma and as the three-eyed Shiva; there is no difference among the three. Command me as you command the three worlds.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.115: 'Krishna thought of Viswakarmā... the celestial architect... came there and stood before Krishna'; his speech: 'thou art adorable unto me as the grand-father (Brahmā) and the three-eyed deity (Siva)... there is no difference amongst the three... do thou... issue command to me as thou dost order the three worlds.'

statements.claim: Krishna commands: 'Build me such a city that it may be celebrated on earth like Amaravati, so that mortals may see the beauty of this city and of the Yadu race.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.115: 'Build for me such a city that it may be celebrated on earth like Amarāvati... so that the mortals may see the beauty of my city and of the Yadu race.'

statements.claim: Vishwakarma agrees on one condition: the city must be so vast that even the four oceans might range within it, so Krishna asks the ocean — the lord of rivers — to withdraw twelve yojanas.
statements.evidence: HV 1.115: 'thy city will not sufficiently accommodate such a number of men. So very extensive should be thy city that even the four oceans, in their full forms, may range here'; Krishna to the ocean, 'lord of rivers': 'if you have any respect for me, then withdraw thy form in the water extending over twelve yojanas.'

statements.claim: Temples rise for Brahma, Indra and the gods of fire and water; four gates — Shudraksha, Aindra, Bhallata and Pushpadantaka — are set in the walls; the houses of the high-souled Yadavas go up street by street.
statements.evidence: HV 1.115: 'Temples... were built for Brahmā, the god of sacrifices, Indra, the presiding deities of fire and water and other gods. They then constructed the four gates... (namely Shudrāksha, Aindra, Bhallāta and Pushpadantāka)... the houses of the high-souled Yadavas were constructed.' (Dutt renders the four gates as gates 'of the temples'; the story sets them in the city walls — minor placement variance, same names.)

statements.claim: A few days after the founding, with Rishabha's consent, Balarama married Revati, the good-natured daughter of King Revata.
statements.evidence: HV 1.115 pack excerpt: 'A few days after with Reshava's consent Baladeva acquired the good-natured daughter of Revata, by name Revati.' Near-verbatim. (Variant in pack: VP 5.25 has Rāma sport two months in Vraja and marry Revatī, daughter of Raivata, on returning to Dwārakā; the story follows the HV reading, matching the pack's index summary.)

statements.claim: Balarama, Krishna's elder brother and the strong arm of the house, binds the Yadus by kinship to the line of Revata — the new city's first great household.
statements.evidence: Balarama's identity as Krishna's elder brother is corpus-wide fact, but the 'first great household' and kinship-significance of the match are the author's framing; HV gives the marriage only the single sentence the story itself quotes.

statements.claim: So Dwaraka began: the sea pushed back, the walls raised, and the elder brother married — a home complete only when someone begins a life inside it.
statements.evidence: Closing literary synthesis; rhetorical, not a sourced fact.

DKS_0350.notes: Very close paraphrase of HV 1.115 (the city-founding speech, Vishwakarma exchange, ocean's twelve-yojana withdrawal, gates and the closing Revati sentence). Story follows the HV chronology (marriage a few days after the founding) rather than the VP variant (after two months in Vraja), which the pack itself flags.

statements.claim: Uddhava, recalling the years at Dwaraka, remembered the host of Kala, the armies of Magadha led by Jarasandha, and Shalva coming against the city, and how each siege was broken when Krishna went out to meet the besiegers.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.9: 'kāla-māgadha-śālvādīn anīkai rundhataḥ puram' (the hosts of Kala, Magadha and Shalva that besieged the city he slew); pack excerpt: Uddhava recalls how Krishna destroyed these besieging hosts; Jarasandha as Magadha's king is the pack's listed character.

statements.claim: Jarasandha's hatred of the house of Yadu had followed Krishna from Mathura and could not be ended even by defeat.
statements.evidence: Not itemized in BP 3.3.9-10; connective characterization consistent with the corpus-wide Jarasandha-Yadu feud (Mathura sieges, Gomanta) and the pack's framing of Magadha as besieger.

statements.claim: Krishna slew Shambara, Dvivida, Bana, Mura, Balvala, Dantavakra and others; some he struck down himself, others he caused to be slain.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.10: 'śambaraṃ dvividaṃ bāṇaṃ muraṃ balvalam eva ca...' plus the pack's rendering 'he killed, or had killed' (Dantavakra among 'others like' the named); excerpt: 'slew Shambara, Dvivida, Bana, Mura, Balvala, Dantavakra and others.'

statements.claim: Shambara fought with illusion; Dvivida was the great ape of the mountains; Bana was the thousand-armed king of Sonitpura.
statements.evidence: One-line identifying epithets not expanded in BP 3.3.10 but matching the standard tradition used across this corpus (Dvivida as vānara in BP 10.67; Bana thousand-armed lord of Sonitpura; Shambara famed for māyā). Non-contradictory descriptors within a recalled name-litany.

statements.claim: Behind Krishna stood the strength of Dwaraka — Balarama with his plough and the warriors of the Yadu clan.
statements.evidence: Framing of the Yadava defence; consistent with the pack's arena (Dwaraka defences) and Balarama's role as Dwaraka's champion elsewhere in the corpus; not a specific sourceable assertion in 3.3.9-10.

statements.claim: Dwaraka stood whole after the sieges, and the women on the walls trusted their king, watching without weeping when he rode out.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric aftermath describing the city that would not fall; the pack states only that Krishna slew/defeated the besiegers, so the city's survival is the implied outcome.

DKS_0351.notes: Close rendering of BP 3.3.9-10 (Uddhava's recall). All names and the killed-or-caused-to-be-slain distinction match the verse. Epithets and siege atmosphere are connective and non-contradictory. No issues.

statements.claim: Balarama went to Vraja alone, with Krishna's consent.
statements.evidence: HV 1.102: 'Rāma, recollecting his friendship with Gopas, alone went to Vraja with Krishna's consent.'

statements.claim: On reaching Nanda's cow-pens he was embraced by the gopas and gopis, who were overjoyed at his return.
statements.evidence: BP 10.65.1: 'pariṣvaktaś cirotkaṇṭhair gopair gopībhir eva ca' (embraced by gopas and gopis who had long yearned for him).

statements.claim: The cowherd elders welcomed Balarama, saying they had heard of his deeds: destroying the great fish Panchajana in the ocean, fighting Jarasandha and the kings with him at Gomanta, and entering Mathura by which the earth was steadied.
statements.evidence: HV 1.102.12-15: 'We have heard of thy encounter, in the ocean, with Timi-like Panchajana, of his destruction and thy battle with Jarāsandha and other Kshatriyas on Gomanta... Thy entrance into the city of Mathura... By it the earth has been established.'

statements.claim: Balarama told the cowherds they were dearer than his own kin, that he and Krishna were reared in their houses, took meals with them, tended the cattle, and spent boyhood sporting there — they were firm friends.
statements.evidence: HV 1.102.17-19: 'You are our better friends than even the Yādavas. We had been reared by you and spent our boyhood in sporting here. We took our meals in your houses and tended the kine. You all are our firm friends.'

statements.claim: The gopis asked whether Krishna remembered his father, mother and friends, and complained that he had left them suddenly, cutting the thread of friendship; they wondered how the wise ladies of Dwaraka could trust the words of one so quick to charm and quick to leave.
statements.evidence: BP 10.65.9-12: 'kaccit smarati vā bandhūn pitaraṃ mātaraṃ ca saḥ... tā naḥ sadyaḥ parityajya gataḥ sañchinna-sauhṛdaḥ... kathaṃ nu gṛhṇanty anavasthitātmano vacaḥ kṛta-ghnasya budhāḥ pura-striyaḥ.'

statements.claim: When one gopi tried to turn the talk to other subjects the rest rejected it, saying their hearts were still with Krishna.
statements.evidence: BP 10.65.13: 'kiṃ nas tat-kathayā gopyaḥ kathāḥ kathayatāparāḥ' (what use to us, gopis, of other tales?).

statements.claim: Balarama consoled the gopis with Krishna's heart-felt messages, assuring them Krishna remembered his father, mother, boyhood friends and nights of song by the Yamuna.
statements.evidence: BP 10.65.15: 'saṅkarṣaṇas tāḥ kṛṣṇasya sandeśair hṛdayaṃ-gamaiḥ' (Balarama [consoled] them with Krishna's heart-reaching messages); the enumerated content mirrors the gopis' questions (10.65.9-11) and the pack summary ('consoled the gopis... with Krishna's heart-felt messages').

statements.claim: Balarama stayed in Vraja for two months, the spring months of Madhu and Madhava, sporting with the gopis in the Yamuna groves under the full moon with flower-scented winds.
statements.evidence: BP 10.65.16-17: 'dvau māsau tatra cāvātsīn madhuṃ mādhavaṃ eva ca / pūrṇa-candra-kalā-mṛṣṭe kaumudī-gandha-vāyunā'; pack summary: 'he stayed two months, sporting with them in the Yamuna groves.'

DKS_0352.notes: Faithful blend of BP 10.65.1-17 and HV 1.102; speeches (elders' praise, Balarama's reply) closely track HV's wording, gopis' questions and Krishna's messages track BP. No issues.

statements.claim: The goddess Varuni, sent by Varuna, flowed out of the hollow of a tree, and the fragrance of the honey-stream was carried to Balarama by the wind.
statements.evidence: BP 10.65.18-19: 'varuṇa-preṣitā devī vāruṇī vṛkṣa-koṭarāt / taṃ gandhaṃ madhu-dhārāyā vāyunopahṛtaṃ balaḥ.'

statements.claim: As he drank, gandharvas sang, drums sounded in the sky and flowers rained down; women sang his deeds.
statements.evidence: BP 10.65.20-22: 'upagīyamāno gandharvair vanitā-śobhi-maṇḍale / nedur dundubhayo vyomni vavṛṣuḥ kusumair mudā / upagīyamāna-carito vanitābhir halāyudha.'

statements.claim: Intoxicated, Balarama wore a single earring and a garland, his blue cloth loose, eyes rolling with pleasure — like the moon of an autumn night.
statements.evidence: BP 10.65.23: 'sragvy eka-kuṇḍalo matto vaijayantyā ca mālayā'; HV 1.102.22-29: 'Clad in an apparel dark-blue like a cloud... eyes rolling in intoxication... enjoy there like the moon in an autumnal night.'

statements.claim: Balarama summoned the Yamuna to come in bodily form and sport with him in her waters.
statements.evidence: BP 10.65.24: 'sa ājuhāva yamunāṃ jala-krīḍārtham īśvaraḥ'; HV 1.102.30: 'O great river, going to the ocean... come to me therefore in your bodily form.'

statements.claim: The Yamuna did not come — disregarding his words as the outcome of drunkenness — and he called again, 'Will you not come?'
statements.evidence: HV 1.102.31: 'Yamunā disregarded his words as being the out-come of drunkenness and did not come'; VP 5.25: 'calling out, Will you not come... will you not come?'

statements.claim: Enraged, Balarama drove the point of his plough into the river's bank and dragged her; the currents were upset and the fishes and water creatures grew bewildered as the river was forced from its course.
statements.evidence: BP 10.65.25: 'anāgatāṃ halāgrena kupito vicakarṣa ha'; HV 1.102.34-35: 'Bāma began to drag the bank... the currents of the river were upset and all the fishes and the aquatic animals grew bewildered'; VP 5.25: 'compelled the dark river to quit its ordinary course.'

statements.claim: Frightened, the Yamuna begged pardon: 'Rama, Rama, mighty-armed, I did not know your valour — forgive the river that did not know the glory of the Blessed One.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.65.26-28: 'evaṃ nirbhartsitā bhītā yamunā yadu-nandanam / rāma rāma mahā-bāho na jāne tava vikramam / paraṃ bhāvaṃ bhagavato bhagavan mām ajānatīm.'

statements.claim: His anger left him; he released the Yamuna, bathed and sported in her waters, and came out wearing blue garments and a golden garland.
statements.evidence: BP 10.65.29-31: 'tato vyamuñcad yamunāṃ yācito bhagavān balaḥ / kāmaṃ vihṛtya salilād uttīrṇāyā... vasitvā vāsasī nīle mālāṃ āmucya kāñcanīm.'

statements.claim: Long afterward the cowherds pointed to the path where the river had been dragged, and the night passed like a single moment.
statements.evidence: BP 10.65.32-33: 'adyāpi dṛśyate rājan yamunākṛṣṭa-vartmanā / evaṃ sarvā niśā yātā ekeva ramato vraje.'

DKS_0353.notes: Follows BP 10.65.18-33 with supporting color from HV 1.102 and VP 5.25; the summons, refusal, dragging, plea and release all track the sources. Vivid similes are connective. No issues.

statements.claim: Dvivida was an ape, the friend of Narakasura, who wrought destruction on the land in requital for his slain friend.
statements.evidence: BP 10.67.2-3: 'sakhyuḥ so 'pacitiṃ kurvan vānaro rāṣṭra-viplavam'; pack summary: 'Dvivida, the mighty ape and friend of Narakasura, seeking vengeance.'

statements.claim: Narakasura had been slain by Krishna.
statements.evidence: VP 5.36 (cross-ref in pack cluster): Dwivida 'vowed to revenge... the destruction of Naraka by Krishńa'; consistent with the corpus's Narakasura-slaying cluster.

statements.claim: Dvivida set fire to cities and villages.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (BP 10.67.1-8): 'set fire to cities and villages...'; VP 5.36: 'he set fire to the forests, to villages, and to towns.'

statements.claim: He tore up mountains by their roots and crushed the regions below, stood mid-ocean and flung up the sea with his arms so the coastal lands drowned.
statements.evidence: BP 10.67.3-4: 'kvacit sa śailān utpāṭya tair deśān samacūrṇayat / kvacit samudra-madhya-stho dorbhyām utkṣipya taj-jalam'; pack excerpt: 'uprooted mountains, drowned the coastal lands.'

statements.claim: He defiled the hermitages of the sages, breaking their trees and scattering their offerings and sacred fires, and hurled men and women into mountain caves.
statements.evidence: BP 10.67.5-6: 'āśramān ṛṣi-mukhyānāṃ kṛtvā bhagna-vanaspatīn / puruṣān yoṣito dṛptaḥ kṣmābhṛd-dronī-guhāsu saḥ'; pack excerpt adds 'defiled the sages' hermitages and sacred fires.' (Scattered offerings = connective gloss of defilement.)

statements.claim: He devastated the regions, defiling women of good families.
statements.evidence: BP 10.67.7: 'evaṃ deśān viprakurvan dūṣayaṃś ca kula-striyaḥ.'

statements.claim: The land he ravaged was Anarta, the country of the Yadavas.
statements.evidence: Pack index entry lists locations: Anarta for this event; BP 10.67.8 places Balarama, lord of the Yadus, at the scene of the devastation.

statements.claim: In the midst of the ruin Dvivida came upon Balarama, the lord of the Yadavas, standing with a garland of lotuses around his neck — not Krishna, who had slain his friend, but the other brother.
statements.evidence: BP 10.67.8: 'tatrāpaśyad yadu-patiṃ rāmaṃ puṣkara-mālinam' (there he saw Rama, the Yadu lord, garlanded with lotuses); Balarama as plough-bearer and Krishna as Narakasura's slayer are the pack's cluster facts.

DKS_0354.notes: Renders BP 10.67.1-8 accurately (event evt_0255); Dvivida's motive, ravages and the closing face-off with lotuses-garlanded Balarama all match. Terror-atmosphere sentences are connective. No issues.

statements.claim: Balarama was drinking varuni wine in the groves of Raivataka hill in the company of women, singing, when the ape Dvivida came and climbed onto a branch overhead.
statements.evidence: BP 10.67.9-10: 'gāyantaṃ vāruṇīṃ pītvā mada-vihvala-locanam / duṣṭaḥ śākhā-mṛgaḥ śākhām ārūḍhaḥ kampayan drumān'; VP 5.36: 'Halāyudha was drinking in the groves of Raivata, along with the illustrious Revatī and other beautiful females.'

statements.claim: Dvivida had been the dearest friend of Narakasura, whom Krishna slew, and in grief and fury had sworn to make the world pay.
statements.evidence: VP 5.36 (in pack): Naraka 'had a friend of exceeding prowess in the monkey named Dwivida... vowed to revenge... the destruction of Naraka by Krishńa.'

statements.claim: Dvivida had interrupted sacrifices, subverted rites, set fire to forests/villages/towns, hurled rocks on cities, cast mountains into the ocean, churned the sea over its shores, assumed shapes at will, enlarged himself to crush harvests, and deprived the land of peace and sacred study.
statements.evidence: VP 5.36 (in pack), recounting the ape's ravages verbatim: interrupted rites, 'set fire to the forests, to villages, and to towns,' overwhelmed cities with rocks, 'lifted up mountains... cast them into the ocean,' agitated the sea over its confines, 'could assume what shape he would, enlarged his bulk... crushed and spoiled the harvests,' and the world 'was deprived of sacred study and religious rites.'

statements.claim: The ape mocked Balarama and the women — grinning, rolling his eyes, flicking his brows and making faces at them until they drew back.
statements.evidence: BP 10.67.11-12: 'tā helayām āsa kapir bhrū-kṣepair sammukhādibhiḥ'; VP 5.36: 'grinned at and mocked him, and laughed at the women.'

statements.claim: Balarama hurled a stone at him; the ape caught it and laughed, mocking him further.
statements.evidence: BP 10.67.13-14: 'taṃ grāvṇā prāharat kruddho balaḥ... gṛhītvā helayām āsa dhūrtas taṃ kopayan hasan.'

statements.claim: Balarama took up his mace and plough; the ape struck him on the head, and the blow fell as harmlessly as red chalk flung at a mountain.
statements.evidence: BP 10.67.16-19: 'kruddho muṣalam ādatta halaṃ cāri-jighāṃsayā... tena balaṃ mūrdhany atāḍayat... girir yathā gairikayā prahāraṃ nānucintayan.'

statements.claim: Balarama struck him with the mace, blow after blow, until the ape's body was broken in a hundred places.
statements.evidence: BP 10.67.20: 'tenāhanat su-saṅkruddhas taṃ balaḥ śatadhācchinat.'

statements.claim: The ape kept fighting, hurling a rain of trees and rocks that fell harmlessly; Balarama cast aside his weapons and seized him with his bare arms, and when he brought him down the earth with its mountains and forests trembled.
statements.evidence: BP 10.67.22-25: 'tato 'muñcac chilā-varṣaṃ balasyopari... yādavendro 'pi taṃ dorbhyāṃ tyaktvā muṣala-lāṅgale / cakampe tena patatā sa-ṭaṅkaḥ sa-vanaspatiḥ'; pack excerpt adds 'after hurling trees and rocks in vain.'

statements.claim: The ape lay felled, vomiting blood, and did not rise; cries of victory and homage sounded in the sky and the gods rained flowers.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'was felled, vomiting blood, as gods rained flowers'; VP 5.36: 'felled him, vomiting blood, and lifeless'; BP 10.67.26: 'jaya-śabdo namaḥ-śabdaḥ sādhu sādhv iti cāmbare.'

statements.claim: Afterward the villages Dvivida had burned were at peace again, and the hill of Raivataka was said to carry a scar where the ape fell.
statements.evidence: The restored-land aftermath is implied by the slaying (BP 10.67.27 'nihatya dvividaṃ jagad-vyatikarāvaham' — slaying the ape who afflicted the world); the specific 'scar on the hill' is a folk-style close attributed to 'they said afterward,' not stated in the pack.

DKS_0355.notes: Accurate to BP 10.67.9-27, with the ravages-recap drawn from VP 5.36 as the pack intends; follows the BP variant (mace + bare-arm finish, per variant note 'BP: fells with mace') rather than VP's single fist-blow, which is the allowed variant choice. No issues.

statements.claim: Samba, a prince of the Yadava house, lay captive among the Kurus, and the young warriors of Dwaraka had girded for war; Balarama pacified them.
statements.evidence: BP 10.68.13: 'sāntvayitvā tu tān rāmaḥ sannaddhān vṛṣṇi-puṅgavān'; pack summary: the Kauravas hold and refuse to release Samba; HV 1.119 (cluster): 'Shāmva was confined by those princes in the city of Hastina.'

statements.claim: Balarama set out alone for Hastinapura in a chariot radiant as the sun and, arriving at the city of the elephants, stopped in the outer grove rather than riding in.
statements.evidence: BP 10.68.14-15: 'jagāma hāstina-puraṃ rathenāditya-varcasā / gatvā gajāhvayaṃ rāmo bāhyopavanam āsthitaḥ.'

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra (son of Ambika), Bhishma, Drona and Bahlika received him gladly with the cow of welcome and water of honor and asked after his kinsmen's welfare.
statements.evidence: BP 10.68.16-19: 'so 'bhivandyāmbikā-putraṃ bhīṣmaṃ droṇaṃ ca bāhlikam / te 'ti-prītās... gām arghyaṃ ca nyavedayan / bandhūn kuśalinaḥ śrutvā pṛṣṭvā śivam anāmayam.'

statements.claim: Balarama delivered the message of Ugrasena, king of the Yadavas: the Kurus had seized one righteous man by many, unjustly, and should release Samba.
statements.evidence: BP 10.68.20-21: 'ugrasenaḥ kṣiteśeśo yad va ājñāpayat prabhuḥ / yad yūyaṃ bahavas tv ekaṃ jitvādharmeṇa dhārmikam.'

statements.claim: The Kauravas, led by Duryodhana and his brothers, mocked the Yadavas as upstarts bound to the Kurus by marriage, eating at their tables and sleeping under their roofs, whose royal insignia were a gift not a right — 'enough of the Yadavas' kingship'; the claims, they said, fit them like nectar fits a serpent.
statements.evidence: BP 10.68.24-26: 'ete yaunena sambaddhāḥ saha-śayyāsanāśanāḥ / cāmara-vyajane śaṅkham ātapatraṃ ca pāṇḍuram / alaṃ yadūnāṃ naradeva-lāñchanair dātuḥ pratīpaiḥ phaṇinām ivāmṛtam'; pack summary: mocked them 'as cowherds who had risen above their station.'

statements.claim: The Kurus asked how even Indra could stand against them while Bhishma, Drona and Arjuna were their champions, and refused to release Samba.
statements.evidence: BP 10.68.27: 'katham indro 'pi kurubhir bhīṣma-droṇārjunādibhiḥ'; pack summary: 'the Kauravas... refused' to release Samba.

statements.claim: Balarama saw the Kurus' wickedness and understood that these evil ones, swollen with manifold pride, would not choose peace.
statements.evidence: BP 10.68.29-30: 'dṛṣṭvā kurūnāṃ dauḥśīlyaṃ śrutvāvācyāni cācyutaḥ / nūnaṃ nānā-madonnaddhāḥ śāntiṃ necchanty asādhavaḥ.'

statements.claim: Balarama reflected on the glory of Ugrasena — lord of the Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas, before whose feet fortune herself waits and on whose feet the guardians of the world set their crowns — and on the Kurus' taunt that 'the Vrishnis eat land given by the Kurus'; he thought: alas for men mad with wealth, stumbling like drunkards.
statements.evidence: BP 10.68.33-38: 'nograsenaḥ kila vibhur bhoja-vṛṣṇy-andhakeśvaraḥ... yasya pāda-yugaṃ sākṣāc chrīr upāste 'khileśvarī / yasyāṅghri-paṅkaja-rajo 'khila-loka-pālair mauly-uttamair dhṛtam... bhuñjate kurubhir dattaṃ bhū-khaṇḍaṃ vṛṣṇayaḥ kila / aho aiśvarya-mattānāṃ mattānām iva māninām.'

statements.claim: Balarama rose and walked out past the elders without another word, carrying his anger with him, unwilling to answer mockery with steel then.
statements.evidence: The packs record the embassy, the mockery and (next beat) Balarama's enraged plough-dragging of the city (BP 10.68.39+; VP 5.35); the silent departure is connective bridging between the two beats and contradicts no pack statement.

DKS_0356.notes: Faithful to BP 10.68.13-38; the Kauravas' mockery, the 'nectar to serpents' gibe, the Indra taunt and Balarama's reflections all track the verses, including the pāṇḍuram cāmara/chatra insignia detail folded into 'royal insignia... by gift.' Departure line is connective. No issues.

statements.claim: Still enraged after being mocked, Balarama drove the blade of his plough deep into the earth beneath the ramparts of Hastinapura and declared he would make the earth free of the Kauravas.
statements.evidence: BP 10.68.39-40: 'adya niṣkauravaṃ pṛthvīṃ kariṣyāmīty amarṣitaḥ / lāṅgalāgreṇa nagaram udvidārya gajāhvayam'; VP 5.35: 'plunged the blade of his ploughshare downwards, beneath the ramparts of the city.'

statements.claim: The city of Hastinapura — the city of the elephant — tilted, swayed and slid toward the Ganga like a boat torn loose, about to plunge into the river.
statements.evidence: BP 10.68.41: 'jala-yānam ivāghūrṇaṃ gaṅgāyāṃ nagaraṃ patat' (the city, whirled like a boat on the water, was about to fall into the Ganga).

statements.claim: The Kurus came out with their families, terrified, and took refuge at Balarama's feet, crying 'Rama, Rama, support of all, we did not know your power; you are the one cause of creation, preservation and destruction; you bear the earth on your head, O thousand-headed one; your anger is for the instruction of the world, not from hatred or envy; homage to you, soul of all beings.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.68.42-47: 'tam eva śaraṇaṃ jagmuḥ sa-kuṭumbā jijīviṣavaḥ / rāma rāmākhilādhāra prabhāvaṃ na vidāma te / sthity-utpatty-apyayānāṃ tvam eko hetur nirāśrayaḥ / tvam eva mūrdhnīdam ananta līlayā bhū-maṇḍalaṃ bibharṣi sahasra-mūrdhan / kopas te 'khila-śikṣārthaṃ na dveṣān na ca matsarāt / namas te sarva-bhūtātman.'

statements.claim: The Kauravas surrendered Samba and with him Lakshmana, the bride for whose sake the trouble had begun.
statements.evidence: Pack summary: 'the Kauravas, terrified, surrendered Samba and Lakshmana'; HV 1.119: Duryodhana 'sent Shamva with his wife'; VP 5.35: 'the Kauravas delivered Śámba and his bride'; HV 1.119: Samba was confined 'on account of his stealing away Duryodhana's daughter Lakshmanā.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana gave a herd of elephants every one sixty years old and six thousand golden chariots blazing like the sun.
statements.evidence: BP 10.68.49-50: 'duryodhanaḥ pāribarhaṃ kuñjarān ṣaṣṭi-hāyanān / rathānāṃ ṣaṭ-sahasrāṇi raukmāṇāṃ sūrya-varcasām.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana asked to be taken as Balarama's pupil in club-fighting, and Balarama accepted him.
statements.evidence: HV 1.119: Duryodhana 'presented himself for his discipleship. Rāma too accepted the Kuru king as his disciple in club fighting.'

statements.claim: Balarama accepted the gifts, released the city, returned to his own city, and in the assembly of the Yadus told his kinsmen the whole tale of what he had done among the Kurus.
statements.evidence: BP 10.68.51-52: 'pratigṛhya tu tat sarvaṃ bhagavān sātvatarṣabhaḥ / tataḥ praviṣṭaḥ sva-puraṃ halāyudhaḥ... sametya bandhūn anurakta-cetasaḥ... śaśaṃsa sarvaṃ yadu-puṅgavānāṃ madhye sabhāyāṃ kuruṣu sva-ceṣṭitam.'

statements.claim: Hastinapura was said to have leaned toward the river ever since, never standing quite straight again — a mark the city still shows.
statements.evidence: BP 10.68.53: 'adyāpi ca puraṃ hy etat sūcayad rāma-vikramam' (even today this city exhibits Rama's prowess); HV 1.119: 'from that time, this whirling city is seen bent towards the ocean.'

DKS_0357.notes: Accurate to BP 10.68.39-53 with HV 1.119 and VP 5.35 corroboration; the surrender speech, Duryodhana's gifts and discipleship, the assembly retelling and the still-leaning city all match. Tilted-streets panic detail is connective. No issues.

statements.claim: Hearing of the coming war between the Kurus and the Pandavas, Balarama bathed at Prabhasa, gratified the gods, seers and ancestors, and visited the holy waters Prithudaka, Bindu-saras, Tritakupa and Sudarshana and the tirthas along the Yamuna and Ganga.
statements.evidence: BP 10.78.16-19: 'śrutvā yuddhodyamaṃ rāmaḥ kurūṇāṃ saha pāṇḍavaiḥ / snātvā prabhāse santarpya devarṣi-pitṛ-mānavān / pṛthūdakaṃ bindu-saras tritakūpaṃ sudarśanam / yamunām anu yāny eva gaṅgām anu ca.'

statements.claim: He came to the Naimisha forest, where the sages were holding a long sacrifice that ran on season after season.
statements.evidence: BP 10.78.20: 'tam āgatam abhipretya munayo dīrgha-satriṇaḥ'; Naimisha per pack index/title.

statements.claim: The sages honored Balarama, seated him with his company, and made him welcome.
statements.evidence: BP 10.78.21: 'so 'rcitaḥ sa-parīvāraḥ kṛtāsana-parigrahaḥ.'

statements.claim: In the assembly sat Romaharshana, a suta of the charioteer line born of a mixed (pratiloma) union, seated among the brahmanas on a seat of honor; he did not rise nor offer folded hands, though he had been a pupil of the blessed seer Vyasa and had learned much.
statements.evidence: BP 10.78.22-24: 'apratyutthāyinaṃ sūtam akṛta-prahvaṇāñjalim / yasmād asāv imān viprān adhyāste pratiloma-jaḥ / ṛṣer bhagavato bhūtvā śiṣyo 'dhītya bahūni ca'; pack excerpt names him Romaharshana.

statements.claim: Balarama judged the suta untamed, undisciplined and vainly proud of his scholarship, seated above the brahmanas in the seat the sages had given him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.78.23-25: 'yasmād asāv imān viprān adhyāste... adāntasyāvinītasya vṛthā paṇḍita-māninaḥ'; the seat was the sages' gift per 10.78.29: 'asya brahmāsanaṃ dattam asmābhir.'

statements.claim: Balarama said, 'This is the very purpose for which I was born into this world,' plucked a single blade of kusha grass, and struck the suta down; Romaharshana fell and did not rise.
statements.evidence: BP 10.78.26-27: 'etad-artho hi loke 'sminn avatāro mayā kṛtaḥ / etāvad uktvā bhagavān nivṛtto 'sad-vadhād api'; pack excerpt: 'strikes him down with a blade of kusha grass.'

statements.claim: The sages cried out 'Ha! Ha!' in grief and told Balarama: 'We ourselves gave him this seat and raised him to the brahmana's seat; what you have done was done without knowledge — you have slain a brahmana; this is brahma-hatya.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.78.28-30: 'hāheti-vādinaḥ sarve munayaḥ khinna-mānasaḥ / asya brahmāsanaṃ dattam asmābhir yadu-nandana / ajānataivācaritas tvayā brahma-vadho yathā'; pack excerpt: 'the sages cry out that he has committed the sin of slaying a brahmana, saying this was done without knowledge and must be expiated.'

statements.claim: The sages asked Balarama, as purifier of the worlds, whether there is any purifier of this sin, and offered to show him the way to it.
