statements.evidence: BP 10.78.31: 'yady etad-brahma-hatyāyāḥ pāvanaṃ loka-pāvana' (the verse continues into the sages' prescription, which the corpus's next story, DKS_0359, records: slay Balvala, then a year-long pilgrimage).

DKS_0358.notes: Accurate to BP 10.78.15-31 (event evt_0272): pilgrimage route, the seated suta Romaharshana, the kusha-grass slaying, the sages' 'ha ha' cry and the brahma-hatya accusation all track the pack. Inner-voice details are connective. No issues.

statements.claim: The suta Romaharshana was cut down by a blade of kusha grass in the enclosure at Naimisha where he had been reciting, and the sages raised the cry of brahma-hatya.
statements.evidence: Corpus-chain previous title (DKS_0358): 'seeing the suta Romaharshana seated without rising to honor the sages, kills him with a blade of kusha grass; the sages cry out that he has committed brahma-hatya.'

statements.claim: Balarama had come to the Naimisha forest as a pilgrim while the sages were gathered for their great sacrifice.
statements.evidence: Pack index/canonical event evt_0273 (SB 10.78.32-39) sets the scene at Naimisha; prior-story chain frames the pilgrimage and the ongoing recitation.

statements.claim: Romaharshana remained seated, failing to rise to honor the sages.
statements.evidence: Corpus-chain previous title states he was seated without rising to honor the sages.

statements.claim: As the first part of atonement the sages told Balarama to slay the demon Balvala, son of Ilvala, who at every parvan came down from the sky and rained filth upon the sacrifice.
statements.evidence: Excerpt: 'his atonement is to slay the cruel demon Balvala, son of Ilvala, who rains filth upon their sacrifice at every parvan.'

statements.claim: Year after year Balvala broke their rites and they were powerless; the defiled sacrifice had to be begun again from the first offering.
statements.evidence: Repeated defilement at every parvan is supported ('defiling what years of penance had made pure'); the restart-from-the-first-offering detail is dramatized consequence of the defilement, not contradicted by the pack.

statements.claim: The second part of the penance was twelve months of wandering through Bharatavarsha, bathing at the sacred fords to be purified.
statements.evidence: Excerpt: 'then to wander Bharatavarsha bathing at the sacred fords for twelve months to be purified.'

statements.claim: Balarama accepted both tasks without defense or argument, undertaking the expiation for the benefit of the world.
statements.evidence: Excerpt: 'Balarama accepts, undertaking the expiation for the world's benefit.'

statements.claim: The penance would begin at the next parvan when Balvala came again to rain filth on the fire.
statements.evidence: Next-title chain (DKS_0360): 'When Balvala appears at the sacrifice raining impurity, Balarama drags him down'; consistent with the excerpt.

DKS_0359.notes: Matches the pack's rendering of SB 10.78.32-39; the killing background is drawn from the pack's own corpus chain.

statements.claim: At the next parvan the demon Balvala appeared over the sacrificial hall, raining filth and impurity onto the fire and offerings.
statements.evidence: SB 10.79.1: 'tato 'medhya-mayaM varSaM balvalena vinirmitam' (a rain of impure matter made by Balvala); excerpt.

statements.claim: Balvala, son of Ilvala, was a sky-roamer who had descended at every parvan to defile the sacrifice.
statements.evidence: Excerpt and prior-story canon (DKS_0359); verse 4 'gagane-caram' (moving in the sky).

statements.claim: Balarama saw the demon huge and black, like a mountain of crushed collyrium.
statements.evidence: 10.79.2: 'bRhat-kAyaM bhinnA~njana-cayopamam' (huge body like a mass of crushed collyrium).

statements.claim: Balarama remembered his plough and mace, the weapons that had torn apart enemy armies.
statements.evidence: 10.79.3: 'sasmAra mUSalaM rAmaH para-sainya-vidAraNam'; excerpt mentions plough and mace.

statements.claim: He caught the sky-roaming Balvala with the tip of his plough and dragged him down; the demon fell to the earth with his forehead split and blood streaming.
statements.evidence: 10.79.4-5: 'tam AkRSya halAgreNa balvalaM gagane-caram / so 'patad bhuvi nirbhinna-lalATo 'sRk samutsRjan.'

statements.claim: Balarama crushed the demon's skull with his mace, and the rain of impurity stopped.
statements.evidence: Excerpt: 'crushes his skull with the mace'; cessation follows the demon's death in the narrative flow of verses 1-8.

statements.claim: The delighted sages praised Balarama with unfailing blessings and gave him the vaijayanti garland of unfading lotuses and garments from heaven.
statements.evidence: 10.79.6-7: 'saMstutya munayo rAmaM prayujyAvitathASiSaH / vaijayantIM dadur mAlAM SrI-dhAmAmlAna-pa~NkajAm'; excerpt adds 'garments.'

statements.claim: With the sages' leave Balarama set out with the brahmanas toward the river Kaushiki — the first steps of his twelve-month pilgrimage.
statements.evidence: 10.79.8: 'atha tair abhyanuj~nAtaH kausikIm etya brAhmaNaiH' (then, permitted by them, he went to the Kaushiki with the brahmanas); pilgrimage per DKS_0359 canon.

DKS_0360.notes: Closely follows SB 10.79.1-8 including verse-specific details (collyrium body, split forehead, plough-tip drag).

statements.claim: The rain that lashed Vrindavan for seven nights had ceased; Govardhana had been lifted, held and set down by Krishna, and the cattle were safe.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.74 vv.13-17: kine saved, Govardhana held up, 'this excessive rain extending over seven nights.'

statements.claim: Indra descended on his elephant Airavata, rut-juice trickling, resembling a rainless cloud, to see Krishna.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha v.2: 'seated on his elephant Airavata with temporal juice trickling down and resembling a cloud without water he came down on earth.'

statements.claim: Indra's wonder overcame his anger as he watched the mountain raised, and he desired to see Krishna.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha v.1: 'filled with great surprise and felt a desire for seeing Krishna.'

statements.claim: Indra found Krishna seated at ease at the foot of Govardhana, playing in the forest, engaged in human actions, in a milkman's guise, with the Srivatsa mark and dark-blue-lotus hue, a sun-bright crown, celestial earrings and a jewel necklace, while Garuda, invisible to mortals, shaded him with his wings.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha vv.3-11 (Srivatsa mark, dark-blue lotus hue, sun-effulgent crown, celestial ear-rings, necklace of Padmakanta jewels, playing in the forest engaged in human actions) and Vishnu Purana 5.12 ('Garuda, the king of birds, invisible to mortals, spreading out his wings to shade the head of Hari').

statements.claim: Indra acknowledged that he had sent the seven-night deluge in anger at his worship being set aside, and that Krishna had put down the rain by his own power in Indra's very presence.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha vv.16-17: 'I sent down this excessive rain extending over seven nights and destructive of the kine which even the Devas and Danavas cannot withstand. But thou hast, by thy own power, put down this terrible shower in my very presence.'

statements.claim: Indra praised Krishna: as gold is foremost among metals so Krishna is foremost of the celestials; he alone is eternal among the gods, and Indra sees no second who could carry the mountain.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha vv.21-25: 'Thou art alone eternal amongst the gods... I do not see a second capable of carrying the weight thou hast held'; 'As gold is among the metals...'; 'so thou art the foremost of the celestials.'

statements.claim: Indra said a portion of himself had been born on earth as Arjuna, son of Pritha — Krishna's cousin — who in the coming war of the Bharatas would be Krishna's friend and help in battle; he asked Krishna to befriend him, instruct him in spiritual knowledge and care for him as for Indra himself.
statements.evidence: Vishnu Purana 5.12: 'A portion of me has been born as Arjuna, the son of Pritha'; Harivamsha excerpt: 'he will be thy friend and help in battle... do thou instruct him in spiritual knowledge... always regard and take care of him as thou dost me'; index summary: 'Indra asks Krishna to protect his son Arjuna, Krishna's cousin, in the coming war of the Bharatas.'

statements.claim: Krishna answered that he knew Arjuna and would befriend him as long as he continued upon the earth.
statements.evidence: Vishnu Purana 5.12: 'I know thy son... and I will befriend him as long as I continue upon earth.'

statements.claim: Indra returned to heaven and the friendship of the two future warriors was sealed unseen by the cowherds.
statements.evidence: Closing frame consistent with both sources; the pack records no contrary detail.

DKS_0361.notes: Follows the Harivamsha version per the tradition_note, with the Arjuna request corroborated by both Harivamsha 1.74 and Vishnu Purana 5.12 excerpts.

statements.claim: The bow of the svayamvara had beaten every king: Rukma, Sunitha, Vakra, Karna (son of Radha), Duryodhana and Salya all failed to string it.
statements.evidence: MB 1.190 (Ganguli): 'that bow which Rukma, Sunitha, Vakra, Radha's son, Duryodhana, Salya, and many other kings... could not even with great exertion, string.'

statements.claim: Draupadi, daughter of Drupada, was to be won by whoever could string the bow and shoot the mark through the hole in the wheel.
statements.evidence: Index summary; MB 1.190: mark 'shot... through the hole in the machine above which it had been placed.'

statements.claim: The brahmanas debated: some feared a stripling would mock the whole body of brahmanas; others cited Rama son of Jamadagni defeating all the Kshatriyas and Agastya drinking the ocean, saying brahmanas are strong in their own energy and must never be despised.
statements.evidence: MB 1.190: 'Rama the son of Jamadagni defeated in battle, all the Kshatriyas. Agastya by his Brahma energy drank off the fathomless ocean... Brahmanas are ever strong in their own energy. One should never disregard a Brahmana.'

statements.claim: The youth was Arjuna (Jishnu), the middle Pandava, of the complexion of Indra's banner, disguised as a brahmana.
statements.evidence: MB 1.190: 'the high-souled Jishnu arose from among the crowd of Brahmanas seated in that assembly... possessing the complexion of Indra's banner.'

statements.claim: Arjuna walked around the bow, bowed to Ishana the giver of boons, remembered Krishna, and strung the bow in the twinkling of an eye.
statements.evidence: MB 1.190: 'walking round that bow, and bending his head unto that giver of boons--the lord Isana--and remembering Krishna also, he took it up... strung in the twinkling of an eye.'

statements.claim: Taking the five arrows, he shot the mark, which fell to the ground through the hole.
statements.evidence: MB 1.190: 'taking up the five arrows he shot the mark and caused it to fall down on the ground through the hole in the machine.'

statements.claim: The gods showered celestial flowers on the slayer of foes; thousands of brahmanas waved their upper garments; musicians and bards celebrated; the failed kings cried out in grief.
statements.evidence: MB 1.190 passage ('the gods showered celestial flowers on the head of Partha the slayer of foes... thousands of Brahmanas began to wave their upper garments in joy... the monarchs who had been unsuccessful, uttered exclamations of grief and despair').

statements.claim: Drupada was filled with joy and ready to aid the victor with his forces, while Yudhishthira and the twins slipped quietly away to their lodging.
statements.evidence: MB 1.190: 'the monarch desired to assist with his forces the hero if the occasion arose... Yudhishthira... accompanied by... the twins, hastily left the amphitheatre for returning to his temporary home.'

statements.claim: Krishna, filled with joy, approached the son of Kunti with a white robe and a garland of flowers and placed them on him.
statements.evidence: MB 1.190 excerpt: 'And Krishna beholding the mark shot and beholding Partha also like unto Indra himself... was filled with joy, and approached the son of Kunti with a white robe and a garland of flowers.'

statements.claim: Arjuna was saluted with reverence by all the brahmanas and left the lists followed closely by Draupadi, who had become his wife.
statements.evidence: MB 1.190: 'was saluted with reverence by all the Brahmanas. And he soon after left the lists followed close by her who thus became his wife.'

DKS_0362.notes: Nearly a verbatim retelling of the Ganguli 1.190 passage supplied in the pack.

statements.claim: Krishna saw the five disguised Pandavas among the Brahmins and perceived them as mighty elephants drawn toward a lotus-covered lake, or fire covered by ashes.
statements.evidence: MB 1.189 excerpt: 'beholding those elephants in rut--the five (Pandavas)--attracted towards Draupadi like mighty elephants towards a lake overgrown with lotuses, or like fire covered with ashes, Krishna... began.'

statements.claim: One after another the kings failed to string the great bow, tossed to the ground, panting, with crowns loosened and garlands disordered.
statements.evidence: MB 1.189: 'were tossed on the ground and lay perfectly motionless for some time. Their strength spent and their crowns and garlands loosened from their persons, they began to pant for breath.'

statements.claim: Karna strung the bow easily, but Draupadi refused a Suta ('I will not select a Suta for my lord'), and Karna threw the drawn bow aside, laughing in vexation.
statements.evidence: MB 1.189: 'quickly raising it strung it and placed the arrows on the string... But seeing Karna, Draupadi loudly said, I will not select a Suta for my lord. Then Karna, laughing in vexation... threw aside the bow already drawn to a circle.'

statements.claim: A Brahmana seated among the priests rose, strung the stiff bow as if it were a reed and pierced the golden mark, and Krishna, filled with joy, greeted him with a white robe and a garland.
statements.evidence: MB 1.190 (in chain with this story) records the Brahmana's feat and Krishna's joyful greeting with white robe and garland; DKS_0362 evidence supplies the stringing detail. 'As if it were a reed' is mild embellishment of the feat.

statements.claim: The furious kings resolved to slay Drupada for giving his daughter to a Brahmana; Drupada, pale with fear, sought the Brahmanas' protection; Bhima tore up a tree like an elephant and stood near Arjuna like Yama with his mace, while Arjuna stood ready with his bow.
statements.evidence: MB 1.191: kings' speech ('Passing us by and treating the assembled monarchs as straw... let us slay him'); Drupada 'sought, from fear, the protection of the Brahmanas'; 'the mighty Bhima... tore up like an elephant a large tree and divested it of its leaves... stood, like unto the mace-bearing king of the dead (Yama)... near Arjuna'; Arjuna 'shaking off all fear he stood with his bow ready.'

statements.claim: Krishna named the five brothers to Balarama: Arjuna by his lion-tread and four-cubit bow, Bhima (Vrikodara) by the tree feat, Yudhishthira by his lotus eyes and four-cubit height, and the twins as sons of the twin Aswins, having heard they escaped the house of lac with Pritha.
statements.evidence: MB 1.191 speech matches nearly verbatim: bow 'four full cubits in length, is Arjuna! There is no doubt... if I am Vasudeva'; Vrikodara and the tree feat; Yudhishthira 'of eyes like unto lotus-petals, of full four cubits height... is Dharma's son'; 'the two other youths, like unto Kartikeya, are, I suspect, the sons of the twin Aswins'; 'the sons of Pandu along with their mother Pritha had all escaped from the conflagration of the house of lac.'

statements.claim: Krishna had recognized them earlier, murmuring to Balarama 'That is Yudhishthira; that is Bhima with Jishnu; and those are the twin heroes,' and Balarama cast a glance of quiet satisfaction.
statements.evidence: MB 1.189: 'he said unto Rama (Valadeva), That is Yudhishthira; that is Bhima with Jishnu (Arjuna); and those are the twin heroes. And Rama surveying them slowly cast a glance of satisfaction at Krishna.'

statements.claim: Balarama rejoiced that their father's sister Pritha and the foremost Kaurava princes had escaped death.
statements.evidence: MB 1.191: 'O, I am happy to hear, as I do from sheer good fortune, that our father's sister Pritha with the foremost of the Kaurava princes have all escaped (from death)!'

statements.claim: The monarchs, biting their nether lips in wrath, saw only the two Brahmins in the fray and did not see five princes of the Kuru line.
statements.evidence: MB 1.189: 'Biting their nether lips in wrath, the other heroes there... looked with expanded eyes on Draupadi alone without noticing the Pandavas.'

statements.claim: Krishna kept the secret, saying nothing publicly.
statements.evidence: Consistent with the sources, which record Krishna naming the brothers privately to Balarama only; no public announcement appears in the pack.

DKS_0363.notes: Identification speeches track the Ganguli 1.189/1.191 passages closely; the story merges the early 1.189 recognition with the later 1.191 naming, as the pack itself notes both chapters record the scene.

statements.claim: The kings rose in fury against Drupada for bestowing his daughter on a Brahmana, crying that the svayamvara is for Kshatriyas and rushing to slay him and his son; Drupada, pale with fear, sought the Brahmanas' protection.
statements.evidence: MB 1.191 (in chain) and 1.192: 'Passing us by and treating the assembled monarchs as straw... this Drupada desires to bestow his daughter on a Brahmana'; 'The Vedic declaration is well-known that the Swayamvara is for the Kshatriyas. The Brahmanas have no claim...'; 'let us slay him... along with his son'; 'sought, from fear, the protection of the Brahmanas.'

statements.claim: The Brahmins shook their deer-skins and cocoanut-shell water-pots, crying 'Fear not, we will fight the foe'; Arjuna, smiling, asked them to stand aside as spectators, saying he would check the monarchs with showers of arrows like snakes checked by mantras.
statements.evidence: MB 1.192: 'those bulls among Brahmanas shaking their deer-skins and water-pots made of cocoanut-shells exclaimed, Fear not, we will fight the foe! Arjuna smilingly... said, Stand ye aside as spectators (of the fray) Showering hundreds of arrows furnished with straight points even I shall check, like snakes with mantras, all those angry monarchs.'

statements.claim: Taking up the great bow he had won, Arjuna stood immovable as a mountain with Bhima at his side.
statements.evidence: MB 1.192: 'the mighty Arjuna taking up the bow he had obtained as dower accompanied by his brother Bhima stood immovable as a mountain.'

statements.claim: Karna rushed at Jishnu, and Salya, king of Madra, charged Bhima like an elephant for a she-elephant in heat.
statements.evidence: MB 1.192: 'Karna endued with great energy rushed against Jishnu for fight. And Salya the mighty king of Madra rushed against Bhima like an elephant rushing against another for the sake of a she-elephant in heat.'

statements.claim: Arjuna pierced Karna with sharp arrows until he fainted; Karna recovered and fought with greater care, and the two became invisible to the spectators, enveloped in each other's arrow-showers, exchanging words intelligible only to heroes.
statements.evidence: MB 1.192: 'drew his tough bow and pieced him with his sharp arrows... made Radheya (Karna) faint. Recovering consciousness Karna attacked Arjuna with greater care... (each enveloped by the other's shower of arrows) they both became invisible... Behold the strength of my arms.--Mark, how I have counteracted that feat,--those were the words--intelligible to heroes alone.'

statements.claim: Karna asked whether Arjuna was the science of weapons embodied, Rama, Indra, or Vishnu in a Brahmana's form; Arjuna answered that he was only a Brahmana, foremost of warriors, accomplished in the Brahma and Paurandara weapons, and bade him wait; Karna desisted, deeming Brahma energy invincible.
statements.evidence: MB 1.192 dialogue, ending: 'Karna the adopted son of Radha desisted from the fight, for that mighty chariot-fighter thought that Brahma energy is ever invincible.'

statements.claim: Salya and Bhima fought like two elephants in rut with clenched fists and knees, the lists ringing like the clash of granite masses, until Bhima hurled Salya down gently, without hurting him much.
statements.evidence: MB 1.192: 'struck each other with their clenched fists and knees... blows hard as the clash of two masses of granite... taking up Salya on his arms hurled him to a distance... though he threw Salya on the ground he did it without hurting him much.'

statements.claim: The alarmed monarchs murmured that only Rama, Drona or Kiriti son of Pandu could face Karna, and only Krishna could face Duryodhana.
statements.evidence: MB 1.192: 'Who can encounter Karna, the son of Radha, in fight, except Rama or Drona, or Kiriti, the son of Pandu? Who also can encounter Duryodhana in battle except Krishna...'

statements.claim: Krishna, having beheld Bhima's feat and believing the two were sons of Kunti, gently told the monarchs 'This maiden hath been justly acquired,' and they desisted from the fight.
statements.evidence: MB 1.192 excerpt: 'And Krishna, having beheld that feat of Bhima, believed them both to be the son of Kunti. And gently addressing the assembled monarchs, saying, This maiden hath been justly acquired (by the Brahmana), he induced them to abandon the fight. Accomplished in battle, those monarchs then desisted from the fight.'

DKS_0364.notes: Long quoted passages track the Ganguli 1.192 text nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: The brothers returned to the potter's house and told their mother they had brought alms; Kunti, not having seen them, answered from within 'Enjoy ye all what ye have obtained,' then saw Draupadi and cried 'Oh, what have I said?'
statements.evidence: MB 1.193: 'represented Yajnaseni unto their mother as the alms they had obtained that day. And Kunti who was there within the room and saw not her sons, replied, saying, Enjoy ye all (what ye have obtained). The moment after, she beheld Krishna [Draupadi] and then she said, Oh, what have I said?'

statements.claim: Anxious from fear of sin, Kunti asked Yudhishthira how her speech might not become untrue, how sin might not touch the daughter of the king of Panchala, and how she might not become uneasy.
statements.evidence: MB 1.193: 'tell me how my speech may not become untrue; how sin may not touch the daughter of the king of Panchala, and how also she may not become uneasy.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira consoled his mother and told Arjuna, who had won Yajnasena's daughter, to wed her with due rites before the sacred fire.
statements.evidence: MB 1.193: 'reflecting for a moment, consoled Kunti, and addressing Dhananjaya, said, By thee, O Phalguna, hath Yajnaseni been won... igniting the sacred fire, take thou her hand with due rites.'

statements.claim: Arjuna refused, urging that Yudhishthira wed first, then Bhima, then himself, then Nakula and last Sahadeva, and that all were obedient to the king.
statements.evidence: MB 1.193: 'Thou shouldst wed first, then the strong-armed Bhima of inconceivable feats, then myself, then Nakula, and last of all, Sahadeva... All of us are obedient to thee. O, command us as thou likest.'

statements.claim: The beauty of Panchali, fashioned by the Creator, stirred the god of desire in the brothers; Yudhishthira remembered the words of the sage Krishna-Dwaipayana and, fearing division among the brothers, declared 'The auspicious Draupadi shall be the common wife of us all.'
statements.evidence: MB 1.193: 'the lavishing beauty of Panchali who had been modelled by the Creator himself... the God of Desire invaded their hearts and continued to crush all their senses... Yudhishthira... recollected the words of Krishna-Dwaipayana. And the king, then, from fear of a division amongst the brothers... said, The auspicious Draupadi shall be the common wife of us all.'

statements.claim: Krishna, suspecting the svayamvara Brahmanas were the Pandavas, came with Balarama to the potter's house; they touched Yudhishthira's feet (Krishna saying 'I am Krishna'), rejoiced with the Pandavas, and also touched the feet of Kunti, their father's sister.
statements.evidence: MB 1.193: 'Krishna suspecting the five persons he had seen at the Swayamvara to be none else than the heroes of the Kuru race, came accompanied by the son of Rohini (Valadeva), to the house of the potter... Then Vasudeva approaching that foremost of virtuous men--the son of Kunti--and touching the feet of that prince... said, I am Krishna. And the son of Rohini (Valadeva) also approaching Yudhishthira, did the same... those heroes of the Yadu race thereafter touched also the feet of Kunti, their father's sister.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira asked Krishna how he had traced them while they lived in disguise.
statements.evidence: MB 1.193: 'Ajatasatru... asked, How, O Vasudeva, hast thou been able to trace us, as we are living in disguise?'

statements.claim: Krishna answered that fire, even covered, can be known; no one but the Pandavas could show such might; by sheer good fortune they escaped the fierce fire and the wicked son of Dhritarashtra did not succeed; they should grow like a fire in a cave, and he and Balarama should return lest any monarch recognize them.
statements.evidence: MB 1.193: 'fire, even if it is covered, can be known. Who else among men than the Pandavas could exhibit such might?... by sheer good fortune have ye escaped from that fierce fire... the wicked son of Dhritarashtra and his counsellors have not succeeded... grow ye in prosperity like a fire in a cave... And lest any of the monarchs recognise ye, let us return.'

statements.claim: The two Yadava princes left as quietly as they had come, leaving the potter's house to keep its secret.
statements.evidence: Closing frame consistent with Krishna's 'let us return'; no contrary detail in the pack.

DKS_0365.notes: Faithful to the Ganguli 1.193 passage; the story renders Draupadi where the translation names her Krishnaa/Yajnaseni.

statements.claim: After the alliance with the Pandavas, Drupada's fears were dispelled and he no longer stood in fear even of the gods.
statements.evidence: MB 1.201: 'King Drupada, after his alliance with the Pandavas, had all his fears dispelled. Indeed, the monarch no longer stood in fear even of the gods.'

statements.claim: The ladies of Drupada's household worshipped Kunti's feet, naming themselves one by one; Draupadi, in red silk with the auspicious thread at her wrists, saluted her mother-in-law and stood before her with joined palms.
statements.evidence: MB 1.201: 'The ladies of the illustrious Drupada's household approached Kunti and introduced themselves unto her, mentioning their respective names, and worshipped her feet... Krishna also, attired in red silk and her wrists still encircled with the auspicious thread, saluting her mother-in-law with reverence, stood contentedly before her with joined palms.'

statements.claim: Kunti blessed Draupadi, wishing her to be as Sachi to Indra, Swaha to Vibhavasu, Rohini to Soma, Damayanti to Nala, Arundhati to Vasishtha and Lakshmi to Narayana; the mother of long-lived heroic children; installed as queen of Kurujangala with Yudhishthira; and to rejoice again at seeing her the mother of a son, as she rejoiced at the red silk.
statements.evidence: MB 1.201 blessing (all six similes quoted in the text; the story abridges by omitting 'Bhadra unto Vaisravana' and other clauses — abridgement, not contradiction); 'Be thou the mother of long-lived and heroic children... Be thou installed as the Queen of the kingdom and the capital of Kurujangala, with thy husband Yudhishthira the just... as I rejoice today beholding thee attired in red silk, so shall I rejoice again, when... I behold thee become the mother of a son.'

statements.claim: After the sons of Pandu were married, Krishna sent them gold ornaments set with pearls and black gems (lapis lazuli), costly robes from various countries, soft blankets, valuable hides, beds, carpets, vehicles, vessels by the hundreds set with gems and diamonds, female servants by the thousands, trained elephants from Madra, horses in costly harness and chariots drawn by fine horses.
statements.evidence: MB 1.201 catalogue matches item for item, including 'well-trained elephants brought from the country of Madra, and many excellent horses in costly harness, cars drawn by horses of excellent colours and large teeth.'

statements.claim: The slayer of Madhu also sent coins of pure gold by crores upon crores, laid out in separate heaps.
statements.evidence: MB 1.201: 'The slayer of Madhu, of immeasurable soul, also sent them coins of pure gold by crores upon crores in separate heaps.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira the just, desirous of gratifying Govinda, accepted all the presents with great joy.
statements.evidence: MB 1.201: 'And Yudhishthira the just, desirous of gratifying Govinda, accepted all those presents with great joy.'

statements.claim: The interpretive close — gifts as an alliance declared openly by a cousin who recognized the brothers in a crowd and never said their names aloud; not payment or dowry but a welcome and a promise that the hidden princes would not stay hidden long.
statements.evidence: Thematic framing consistent with the source (which records no accompanying message); not asserted as a sourceable fact.

DKS_0366.notes: Gift catalogue and blessing follow MB 1.201 (Ganguli) nearly verbatim; Drupada's relief cites the passage directly.

statements.claim: Vidura came to Panchala as a messenger from Hastinapura, raising the question of whether the sons of Pandu would press their claim to their ancestral kingdom.
statements.evidence: Index/evt_0406: 'At Vidura's visit...'; MB 1.209 (Viduragamana Parva) opens with Drupada answering Vidura's words ('Hearing these words of Vidura'); Drupada calls it their 'ancestral kingdom'.

statements.claim: Drupada said the princes should return to their ancestral kingdom — it was highly proper — but that it was not proper for him, their host, to say so himself; he made it conditional on the brothers desiring to go and on Balarama and Krishna being of the same mind.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: Drupada: 'It is highly proper that these illustrious princes should return to their ancestral kingdom. But it is not proper for me to say this myself. If the brave son of Kunti viz., Yudhishthira, if Bhima and Arjuna... and if Rama (Valadeva) and Krishna... be of the same mind, then let the Pandavas go thither.'

statements.claim: Drupada added that Rama and Krishna were ever engaged in doing what was agreeable and beneficial to Pandu's sons.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'For these tigers among men (Rama and Krishna) are ever engaged in doing what is agreeable and beneficial to the sons of Pandu.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira replied, 'We are now, O monarch, with all our younger brothers, dependent on thee. We shall cheerfully do what thou art pleased to command.'
statements.evidence: Verbatim in MB 1.209.

statements.claim: Krishna then gave his opinion: 'I am of opinion that the Pandavas should go. But we should all abide by the opinion of king Drupada, who is conversant with every rule of morality.'
statements.evidence: Verbatim in MB 1.209: 'Then Vasudeva said...' (also quoted in the pack's excerpt).

statements.claim: Drupada agreed with Krishna's judgment, saying the sons of Pandu were now as dear to him as to Vasudeva, and paid the tribute: 'Kunti's son Yudhishthira himself doth not seek the welfare of the Pandavas so earnestly as, Kesava, that tiger among men.'
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'Drupada then spoke, I certainly agree... Kunti's son Yudhishthira himself doth not seek the welfare of the Pandavas so earnestly as, Kesava...' — spoken by Drupada, as the story has it.

statements.claim: Commanded by Drupada, the Pandavas with Krishna and Vidura set out, taking Draupadi and the renowned Kunti, journeying toward the city called after the elephant (Hastinapura), stopping along the way for pleasure and enjoyment.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'Commanded by the illustrious Drupada, the Pandavas... and Krishna and Vidura, taking with them Krishna, the daughter of Drupada, and the renowned Kunti, journeyed towards the city called after the elephant, stopping at various places along the way for purposes of pleasure and enjoyment.'

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra sent out the Kauravas Vikarna, Chitrasena, Drona and Kripa to receive the heroes, and the citizens of Hastinapura acclaimed them, including the cries 'Here returns that tiger among men...' and the wish that the Pandavas stay in their town for a hundred years.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209 names Vikarna, Chitrasena, Drona and Kripa as sent out; both citizen cries quoted appear verbatim.

statements.claim: The Pandavas worshipped the feet of Dhritarashtra and Bhishma, enquired after the citizens' welfare, rested, and were summoned to the court, where Dhritarashtra granted them Khandavaprastha with half the kingdom: 'Repair ye to Khandavaprastha so that no difference may arise again... Protected by Partha (Arjuna)... taking half of the kingdom.'
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: summoned by Dhritarashtra and Bhishma; Dhritarashtra's address to Yudhishthira quoted verbatim.

statements.claim: Content with half a kingdom, the brothers worshipped the king and set out from Hastinapura to Khandavaprastha, which lay in unreclaimed desert.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'Agreeing to what Dhritarashtra said... they removed to Khandavaprastha, which was in unreclaimed desert.'

statements.claim: Krishna, who had counselled the return, was already thinking ahead to what the desert land could become (staying on with them).
statements.evidence: Foreshadowing of 1.209's continuation ('with Krishna at their head, arriving there'); forward-looking connective close, not a discrete sourceable fact in the passage.

DKS_0367.notes: All substantive claims (Vidura's visit, Drupada's conditional assent, Yudhishthira's and Krishna's speeches, Drupada's tribute, the journey, the reception, the Khandavaprastha grant) match MB 1.209 closely, several verbatim. Closing foreshadowing is connective.

statements.claim: The land Dhritarashtra granted the Pandavas, Khandavaprastha, was unreclaimed desert — thorn, dust and emptiness, with no city yet raised.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'they removed to Khandavaprastha, which was in unreclaimed desert'; index summary: Krishna helps establish Indraprastha there.

statements.claim: The brothers came content, asking only that no difference should arise again between them and their cousins.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: Dhritarashtra's words 'so that no difference may arise again (between you and your cousins)' and the brothers' agreement.

statements.claim: Krishna did not go home: he came with them into the wilderness and stayed — the Pandavas worked 'with Krishna at their head'.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'Then those heroes... with Krishna at their head, arriving there, beautified the place'; pack excerpt: 'having settled the Pandavas there, the heroic Krishna... came back... to Dwaravati' only afterwards.

statements.claim: Selecting a sacred and auspicious region with the assistance of the sage Dwaipayana (Vyasa), they performed propitiatory ceremonies and measured out the piece of land for their city.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'those mighty car-warriors, selecting with Dwaipayana's assistance a sacred and auspicious region, performed certain propitiatory ceremonies and measured out a piece of land for their city.'

statements.claim: A trench was dug around the city wide as the sea, and walls rose high as the heavens, white as fleecy clouds or the rays of the moon; the city looked resplendent like Bhogavati decked with the Nagas.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'surrounded by a trench wide as the sea and by walls reaching high up to the heavens and white as the fleecy clouds or the rays of the moon, that foremost of cities looked resplendent like Bhogavati... decked with the Nagas.'

statements.claim: Beautifying the place as they went, the Pandavas made it what the storytellers called a second heaven.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'the Pandavas, with Krishna at their head, arriving there, beautified the place and made it a second heaven.'

statements.claim: The city raised on that measured ground came to be known as Indraprastha.
statements.evidence: Pack index title and summary call the established city Indraprastha ('Settles the Pandavas in Indraprastha'), and the epic's own continuation (MB 1.223, used in the sibling packs) speaks of Arjuna reaching 'his own excellent city of Indraprastha'.

statements.claim: When the walls stood, Krishna obtained the Pandavas' leave and set out with Balarama beside him for Dwaraka in the west.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt, MB 1.209: 'And, O monarch, having settled the Pandavas there, the heroic Krishna, obtaining their leave, came back with Rama to Dwaravati.' (Dwaravati = Dwaraka.)

statements.claim: The men of Dwaraka were 'ever engaged in doing what was agreeable and beneficial to Pandu's sons' — the friendship would keep the road between the cities busy.
statements.evidence: Echoes MB 1.209's description of Rama and Krishna ('ever engaged in doing what is agreeable and beneficial to the sons of Pandu'); closing connective.

DKS_0368.notes: City-building sequence and Krishna's return with Balarama match MB 1.209 verbatim-level detail. The name Indraprastha is carried by the pack's own index/summary and the epic's continued usage; no contradictions.

statements.claim: Arjuna, in the middle of his forest exile, wandered the sacred waters and holy places on the shores of the western ocean and reached Prabhasa, a sacred and delightful region.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: 'Arjuna... saw... all the sacred waters and other holy places that were on the shores of the western ocean. Vibhatsu reached the sacred spot called Prabhasa.'

statements.claim: He was 'the invisible Arjuna' — moving quietly, telling no one ahead.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: 'When the invisible Arjuna arrived at that sacred and delightful region' (the 'invisible' epithet is the text's own).

statements.claim: Krishna, the slayer of Madhu, in Dwaraka, heard of his arrival and went at once to meet him at Prabhasa.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: 'the slayer of Madhu (Krishna) heard of it. Madhava soon went there to see his friend, the son of Kunti.'

statements.claim: They met and embraced, enquiring after each other's welfare; the text calls them 'dear friends, who were none else than the Rishis Nara and Narayana of old'.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: 'Krishna and Arjuna met together and embracing each other enquired after each other's welfare. Those dear friends, who were none else than the Rishis Nara and Narayana of old, sat down.'

statements.claim: Krishna asked, 'Why, O Pandava, art thou wandering over the earth, beholding all the sacred waters and other holy places?'; Arjuna told him everything, and Krishna answered, 'This is as it should be.'
statements.evidence: Both quotes verbatim in MB 1.220.

statements.claim: After sporting at Prabhasa as they pleased, they went to the Raivataka mountain to pass some days; at Krishna's command artificers had adorned the mountain and food had been collected in abundance beforehand.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: 'Krishna and Arjuna having sported as they liked... went to the Raivataka mountain... at the command of Krishna [it] had been well-adorned by many artificers. Much food also had... been collected there.'

statements.claim: Arjuna enjoyed the performances of actors and dancers, dismissed them with respect, lay on an excellent prepared bed describing to Krishna all he had seen — sacred waters, lakes, mountains, rivers, forests — until sleep stole upon him.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: full sequence present, ending 'sleep... stole upon him.'

statements.claim: He woke to sweet songs, the melodious notes of the vina and the panegyrics and benedictions of the bards; after the necessary acts and ceremonies Krishna accosted him affectionately and he rode out on a golden car toward Dwaraka, the capital of the Yadavas.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: 'He rose in the morning, awakened, by sweet songs and melodious notes of the Vina... Riding upon a golden car, the hero then set out for Dwaraka, the capital of the Yadavas.'

statements.claim: At Krishna's command the city of Dwaraka, its gardens and houses, was adorned; citizens poured into the thoroughfares by hundreds of thousands, women mixing with men in the great crowd of Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: 'for honouring the son of Kunti, the city of Dwaraka was well-adorned, even all the gardens and houses within it... poured eagerly into the public thoroughfares by hundreds of thousands... women, mixing with the men, swelled the great crowd of the Bhojas, the Vrishnis, and the Andhakas.'

statements.claim: Arjuna was welcomed by the sons of the tribes, worshipped those deserving worship, was affectionately received by the young men of the Yadava tribe, repeatedly embraced his age-mates, and stayed many days in Krishna's gem-filled mansion.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: 'The hero was welcomed with affectionate reception by all the young men of the Yadava tribe... took up his abode there with Krishna for many days.'

DKS_0369.notes: Every narrative beat and quotation of this story tracks MB 1.220 closely, including the Nara-Narayana note, the Raivataka arrangements and the Dwaraka reception. Atmosphere (the sea air, the quietness of the invisible wanderer) is unobjectionable connective writing.

statements.claim: When the twelve years of his exile were complete, Arjuna came back to Khandavaprastha with Subhadra, the sister of Krishna, whom he had carried away from Dwaraka and married there.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: Arjuna, stopped by the Vrishnis and brought back, 'was united in marriage with Subhadra'; 'After the twelve years were complete he came back to Khandavaprastha.'

statements.claim: Arjuna approached the king (Yudhishthira) first, then worshipped the brahmanas, and at last went in to Draupadi, who said, 'Why tarriest thou here, O son of Kunti? Go where the daughter of the Satwata race is! A second tie always relaxeth the first one upon a faggot!'
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'He approached the king first and then worshipped the Brahmanas... At last the hero went unto Draupadi. Draupadi, from jealousy, spoke unto him...' — quote verbatim.

statements.claim: Arjuna pacified Draupadi repeatedly and asked her forgiveness, then sent Subhadra into the inner apartments dressed not as a queen but in the simple garb of a cowherd woman — his own doing.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'Dhananjaya pacified her repeatedly and asked for her forgiveness. And returning soon unto where Subhadra... was staying, Arjuna, sent her into the inner apartments dressed not as a queen but in the simple garb of a cowherd woman.'

statements.claim: The celebrated Bhadra (Subhadra), of large and slightly red eyes, looked handsomer in that dress; she first worshipped Pritha (Kunti), who from excess of affection smelt her head and pronounced infinite blessings on her.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'the renowned Subhadra looked handsomer in that dress. The celebrated Bhadra of large and slightly red eyes first worshipped Pritha. Kunti from excess of affection smelt the head of that girl... and pronounced infinite blessing upon her.'

statements.claim: Subhadra then hastened to Draupadi, worshipped her and said, 'I am thy maid.'
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'Then that girl of face like the full moon hastily went unto Draupadi and worshipped her, saying, I am thy maid!'

statements.claim: Draupadi rose quickly and embraced her — the sister of Madhava — from pure affection, and blessed her: 'Let thy husband be without a foe!'; Subhadra answered, 'So be it!'
statements.evidence: MB 1.223 reads 'Krishna rose hastily and embraced the sister of Madhava from affection, and said, Let thy husband be without a foe!' — here Ganguli's 'Krishna' is Krishnā/Draupadi: the same passage uses 'Krishna' for Draupadi two sentences earlier ('And Krishna lamented much in this strain. But Dhananjaya pacified her'), Vasudeva is still at Dwaraka (he arrives only in the next paragraph), and the diacritic KMG edition confirms 'Krishnā rose up hastily and embraced the sister of Mādhava'. Bhadra's reply goes 'unto Draupadi'. Story attribution to Draupadi is correct.

statements.claim: From that time the Pandavas began to live happily, and Kunti too became very happy.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'From that time... those great warriors, the Pandavas, began to live happily, and Kunti also became very happy.'

statements.claim: Hearing Arjuna had reached Indraprastha with his sister, Krishna came with Balarama, the heroes of the Vrishni and Andhaka tribes, his brothers and sons and many warriors, with a large army; among them came Akrura (generalissimo of the Vrishni host), Uddhava, Satyaka, Kritavarman, Pradyumna, Gada and many more of the Bhojas and Andhakas, bringing nuptial presents.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'he came thither accompanied by Rama and the other heroes and great warriors of the Vrishni and the Andhaka tribes, and by his brothers and sons...'; Akrura 'the generalissimo of the brave Vrishni host', Uddhava, Satyaka, Kritavarman, Pradyumna, Gada all named; 'bringing with them many nuptial presents.'

statements.claim: King Yudhishthira sent the twins, Nakula and Sahadeva, out to receive him, and the Vrishni host entered Khandavaprastha, whose streets were well-swept and watered, decked with floral wreaths and bunches, sprinkled with fragrant sandalwood water, with flags and ensigns flying — every part filled with sweet scent.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'King Yudhishthira, hearing that Madhava had arrived, sent the twins out to receive him. Received by them, the Vrishni host... entered Khandavaprastha well-adorned with flags and ensigns. The streets were well-swept and watered and decked with floral wreaths and bunches. These were... sprinkled over with sandalwood water... Every part of the town was filled with the sweet scent.'

statements.claim: Krishna gave the Pandavas a thousand cars of gold furnished with rows of bells, ten thousand cows, mares and mules, and damsels — nuptial gifts in the manner of a family celebrating a wedding.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt, MB 1.223: 'Krishna gave unto the Pandavas a thousand cars of gold furnished with rows of bells... He also gave unto them ten thousand cows'; index summary confirms the full list: 'cars, cows, mares, mules, and damsels as nuptial gifts.'

DKS_0371.notes: One delicate spot checked carefully: the embrace and blessing 'Let thy husband be without a foe!' is correctly given to Draupadi (Krishnā), matching MB 1.223 as read with Ganguli's own usage and the diacritic KMG edition. The 'second rope on a faggot' gloss is a fair reading of the simile.

statements.claim: Krishna had come to Indraprastha with the pomp of the Vrishni host — Balarama, Akrura, Uddhava, Satyaka, Kritavarman, his sons and brothers, riding in with nuptial presents while the city was decked with wreaths and sandalwood water.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223 (same passage as DKS_0371's pack): arrival of the Vrishni host and adornment of Khandavaprastha/Indraprastha.

statements.claim: When the celebration was over he stayed: 'the high-souled Vasudeva remained there with Arjuna in the delightful city'.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt, MB 1.223 verbatim.

statements.claim: Recap: on first bringing Subhadra home Arjuna faced Draupadi's jealousy ('Why do you tarry here, son of Kunti?... A second tie always relaxes the first one upon a faggot'), pacified her and asked forgiveness, and Subhadra in cowherd garb bowed to Draupadi saying 'I am thy maid.'
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: all elements present (Draupadi's speech, Arjuna's repeated pacification, the cowherd-garb detail, 'I am thy maid!').

statements.claim: Krishna himself had risen and embraced his sister, and blessed the marriage: 'Let thy husband be without a foe!'
statements.evidence: The pack (MB 1.223) has the actor as Krishnā/Draupadi, not Vasudeva: 'Krishna rose hastily and embraced the sister of Madhava from affection, and said, Let thy husband be without a foe!' — Ganguli uses 'Krishna' for Draupadi throughout this very scene ('And Krishna lamented much in this strain. But Dhananjaya pacified her'), Vasudeva is still in Dwaraka (arriving only in the next paragraph), and the diacritic KMG edition reads 'Krishnā rose up hastily...'. DKS_0371's full account of the same scene correctly attributes the embrace and blessing to Draupadi; Vasudeva 'embraced his sister' is also unsupported by any arrival-scene embrace in the passage.
statements.resolution: Corrected in story text via consolidation pass.

statements.claim: From that time the household lived happily, and Kunti also became very happy.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'From that time... the Pandavas, began to live happily, and Kunti also became very happy.'

statements.claim: Subhadra, the favourite sister of Kesava, gave birth to an illustrious son, who came to be called Abhimanyu.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt, MB 1.223: 'Subhadra, the favourite sister of Kesava, gave birth to an illustrious son... came to be called Abhimanyu.'

statements.claim: Upon Abhimanyu's birth Krishna performed the usual rites of infancy himself; no vision or miracle is recorded — the passage simply tells that the rites were done, and the child grew up like the Moon of the bright fortnight.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt, MB 1.223: 'Upon his birth, Krishna performed the usual rites of infancy. The child began to grow up like the Moon of the bright fortnight.'

statements.claim: The child grew dear to Krishna.
statements.evidence: Pack index summary: 'the child grows dear to him.'

statements.claim: Krishna lingered in the city through the child's earliest years, and when at last he spoke of returning to Dwaraka the parting was a real one.
statements.evidence: Pack records only that Vasudeva 'remained there with Arjuna'; no duration or departure is stated. The continued presence is consistent with the corpus chain (DKS_0373/0374 have Krishna still at Indraprastha), but 'through the child's earliest years' and a narrated departure are unverified closing elaboration.

corrections.original_sentence: Krishna himself had risen and embraced his sister, and blessed the marriage: "Let thy husband be without a foe!"
corrections.suggested: Draupadi herself had risen and embraced her — the sister of Madhava — and blessed the marriage: "Let thy husband be without a foe!"

DKS_0372.notes: One CONTRADICTED attribution in the recap of the Subhadra homecoming: MB 1.223 (Ganguli; confirmed by the diacritic KMG edition) has Krishnā/Draupadi rise and embrace Subhadra ('the sister of Madhava') and speak the blessing 'Let thy husband be without a foe!' — Vasudeva was not present at that scene and arrives at Indraprastha only afterwards. The sibling story DKS_0371 tells it correctly. Birth-rites content otherwise fully supported.

statements.claim: Arjuna proposed to Krishna that, the summer days having set in, they go to the banks of the Yamuna and sport with friends, returning in the evening; Krishna said this was his wish too, and with Yudhishthira's leave the two set out surrounded by friends.
statements.evidence: MB 1.224: Arjuna's proposal and Krishna's reply quoted; 'Partha and Govinda, with Yudhishthira's leave, set out, surrounded by friends.'

statements.claim: The Pandavas, settled at Indraprastha at the command of Dhritarashtra and Bhishma, brought the neighbouring kings under their sway, and the people lived most happily depending on Yudhishthira the just.
statements.evidence: MB 1.224: 'The Pandavas, after they had taken up their abode at Indraprastha at the command of Dhritarashtra and Bhishma began to bring other kings under their sway. All the subjects... lived most happily depending upon Yudhishthira the just.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira paid homage to virtue, pleasure and profit in judicious proportion as if each were a dear friend; the three pursuits seemed personified on earth with the king shining as a fourth; he was devoted to the Vedas, a performer of the great sacrifices, protector of all good people, and the people delighted in him from sincere affection.
statements.evidence: MB 1.224: all these descriptions present nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: They chose a fine Yamuna spot overgrown with tall trees and covered with high mansions that made it look like the celestial city; costly viands and drinks, floral wreaths, perfumes and gem-adorned inner apartments had been gathered there.
statements.evidence: MB 1.224: 'Reaching a fine spot... overgrown with numerous tall trees and covered with several high mansions that made the place look like the celestial city... numerous costly and well-flavoured viands and drinks... floral wreaths and various perfumes... inner apartments adorned with many precious gems.'

statements.claim: The women sported as they liked — some in the woods, some in the waters, some within the mansions, as directed by Partha and Govinda; Draupadi and Subhadra, exhilarated with wine, gave away their costly robes and ornaments to the sporting women; some danced, sang, laughed, jested, drank, and obstructed one another in play, while flutes, guitars and kettledrums filled the groves — the scene of Prosperity personified.
statements.evidence: MB 1.224: full passage matches, including Draupadi and Subhadra giving away robes and ornaments and the 'scene of Prosperity personified' line.

statements.claim: Arjuna and Vasudeva slipped away to a charming spot a little apart and sat on two very costly seats, discoursing on past achievements of prowess, passing the time like the Aswins seated in heaven.
statements.evidence: MB 1.224: 'went to a certain charming spot... sat down upon two very costly seats... discoursing upon many past achievements of prowess... like the Aswins in heaven.'

statements.claim: A certain Brahmana then came to them: he stood like a tall Sala tree, his complexion like molten gold, his beard bright yellow tinged with green, his body in just proportion, his locks matted — a foremost Brahmana blazing with splendour whose coming ended the day's idleness.
statements.evidence: MB 1.224: description verbatim ('looked like a tall Sala tree. His complexion was like unto molten gold; his beard was bright yellow tinged with green; and the height and the thickness of the body were in just proportion. Of matted locks...'); pack excerpt: 'Beholding that foremost of Brahmanas blazing with splendour approach...'

DKS_0373.notes: All claims mirror MB 1.224 closely. Sensory embellishments around the Brahmana's approach (the grove growing quieter) are atmospheric connective writing, not factual assertions.

statements.claim: The Brahmana asked Arjuna and Vasudeva for food as a starving man: 'I am a voracious Brahmana that always eateth much... I solicit you to gratify me by giving me sufficient food'; they answered they would, asking what food would gratify him.
statements.evidence: MB 1.225: both speeches verbatim.

statements.claim: He revealed: 'I do not desire to eat ordinary food. Know that I am Agni! Give me that food which suiteth me.'
statements.evidence: MB 1.225 verbatim.

statements.claim: Agni explained that the Khandava forest is always protected by Indra, so he always fails to consume it; the Naga Takshaka, Indra's friend, dwells there with his followers and family, and Indra pours water from the clouds whenever Agni blazes forth; he asked the two weapon-skilled heroes to prevent the showers from descending and to stop any creature from escaping when he begins to consume the forest.
statements.evidence: MB 1.225: Agni's whole speech quoted in the pack matches the story nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: Agni called them 'the two foremost of heroes on earth'.
statements.evidence: MB 1.225: 'Ye who are now staying so near unto Khandava are the two foremost of heroes on earth.'

statements.claim: At Janamejaya's question why Agni desired the forest, Vaisampayana narrated the tale told by the Rishis in the Purana: king Swetaki, endued with strength and prowess, equal to Indra, unequalled on earth in sacrifices, charity and intelligence, performed the five great sacrifices and many others year after year with large presents, until the sacrificial priests, eyes afflicted by the continued smoke and bodies grown weak, left him.
statements.evidence: MB 1.225: 'I will narrate to you the story of the conflagration of Khandava as told by Rishis in the Purana... there was a celebrated king of the name of Swetaki... equal unto Indra himself... till those sacrificial priests with eyes afflicted by the continued smoke and becoming very weak, left that monarch.'

statements.claim: Swetaki, refused by the priests for a proposed hundred-year sacrifice despite courting them with bowing, conciliatory speeches and gifts of wealth, warned them that if abandoned from enmity or improper motive he would seek other priests, representing his business to them.
statements.evidence: MB 1.225: the king's warning is quoted almost verbatim ('If you abandon me from enmity alone or any improper motive, I shall go unto other priests... and conciliating them by sweet words and gifts, I shall represent unto them the business I have on hand').

statements.claim: The priests, knowing they could not assist at the king's sacrifice, pretended to be angry in their turn: 'Thy sacrifices are incessant,' they told him.
statements.evidence: MB 1.225: 'when those priests well knew that they could not assist at the king's sacrifice, they pretended to be angry, and addressing... said, O best of kings, thy sacrifices are incessan[t]...' (pack passage truncated mid-word but opening matches exactly).

DKS_0374.notes: Agni's request and the opening of the Swetaki tale match MB 1.225 closely, with dialogue quoted nearly verbatim. Frame prose (the summer air, the forest kept unburned 'so long') is connective; the pack's own truncation ends mid-Swetaki-tale, and the story likewise pauses there.

statements.claim: Hearing that the Pandavas had been banished, the Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas went to the great forest (Kamyaka) where the brothers lived in affliction, joined by the consanguineous relatives of Panchala, Dhrishtaketu the king of Chedi, and the celebrated Kaikeya brothers; reproaching the sons of Dhritarashtra, they asked 'What should we do?'
statements.evidence: MB 3.12 verbatim; pack index fixes the location as the Kamyaka forest.

statements.claim: The bulls of the Kshatriya race, with Vasudeva at their head, sat down in a ring around Yudhishthira the just; saluting that foremost of the Kurus respectfully, Kesava spoke mournfully.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12: 'And those bulls of the Kshatriya race, with Vasudeva at their head, sat themselves down round Yudhishthira the just. And respectfully saluting that foremost of the Kurus, Kesava mournfully said...'

statements.claim: Krishna's vow: 'The earth shall drink the blood of Duryodhana and Karna, of Dussasana and the wicked Sakuni! Slaying these in battle and defeating their followers along with their royal allies, will we all install Yudhishthira the just on the throne! The wicked deserve to be slain! Verily, this is eternal morality.'
statements.evidence: MB 3.12 verbatim (also the pack's excerpt).

statements.claim: Speaking of the wrongs of Pritha's sons, Krishna got into a passion and seemed bent upon consuming all created things; Arjuna exerted himself to pacify him by reciting the feats Krishna achieved in his former lives — the soul of all things, immeasurable, the eternal one of infinite energy, the lord of Prajapati, the supreme ruler of the worlds, Vishnu of profound wisdom.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12: 'when on account of the wrongs of Pritha's sons, Janardana had thus got into a passion, and seemed bent upon consuming all created things, Arjuna exerted himself to pacify him... began to recite the feats achieved in his former lives by that soul of all things...'

statements.claim: The recited ascetic feats: ten thousand years as a muni on the Gandhamadana mountains; eleven thousand years living on water alone by the lake of Pushkara; a hundred years on one leg on the high hills of Vadari living on air; twelve years of emaciated sacrifice on the banks of the Saraswati; a thousand years of the celestials standing on one leg on the plains of Prabhasa.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12: all five feats with the same numbers present verbatim.

statements.claim: The recited deeds: slaying the Asura Naraka (offspring of the Earth), taking his ear-rings, performing the first horse-sacrifice with Naraka as the victim; slaying the Daityas and Danavas and giving Indra the sovereignty of the universe; slaying Ahvriti at Jaruthi, Kratha, Sisupala with his adherents, Jarasandha, Saivya and Satadhanwan; defeating Rukmi in battle and obtaining the daughter of Bhoja for queen; slaying Indradyumna, the Yavana Kaseruman and Salwa the lord of Saubha and destroying the city of Saubha; and as a child filling heaven, the firmament and the earth in three steps.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12: every item in Arjuna's recitation appears in the pack passage with matching detail.

statements.claim: As Arjuna recited, Krishna's wrath, which had seemed bent on consuming all created things, began to be held; yet the anger was not fully turned aside and Arjuna's words had not yet done their full work.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12 shows only the start of the pacification ('Arjuna exerted himself to pacify him... began to recite'); the completion belongs to the next corpus beat (DKS_0376 'Arjuna Pacifies the Wrathful Krishna'). The story's hedged phrasing stays within that arc — connective staging rather than an asserted sourceable outcome.

DKS_0375.notes: Vow, visiting kinsmen, and Arjuna's litany of Krishna's former-life feats and slayings all match MB 3.12 in near-verbatim detail, including every number. Only the closing note that the wrath 'began to be held' is a connective bridge to the next story.

statements.claim: The Pandavas had lost their kingdom at dice and were living in the great forest in affliction; their friends — the Bhojas, the Vrishnis and the Andhakas, the consanguineous relatives of Panchala, Dhrishtaketu the king of Chedi, and the Kaikeya brothers — came to them with hearts fired with anger against the sons of Dhritarashtra.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12: 'Hearing that the Pandavas had been banished, the Bhojas, the Vrishnis, and the Andhakas went to those heroes residing in affliction in the great forest... the consanguineous relatives of Panchala, and Dhrishtaketu the king of Chedi, and... the Kaikeyas, their hearts fired with wrath.'

statements.claim: They asked 'What should we do?' and sat in a wide circle around Yudhishthira the just, with Vasudeva at their head.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12: 'reproaching the sons of Dhritarashtra, they said, "What should we do?" And those bulls of the Kshatriya race, with Vasudeva at their head, sat themselves down round Yudhishthira the just.'

statements.claim: Saluting the foremost of the Kurus, Krishna mournfully vowed: 'The earth shall drink the blood of Duryodhana and Karna, of Dussasana and the wicked Sakuni! Slaying these in battle... we shall install Yudhishthira the just on the throne. The wicked deserve to be slain. Verily, this is eternal morality.'
statements.evidence: MB 3.12 quotes the vow nearly verbatim, including 'The wicked deserve to be slain! Verily, this is eternal morality.'

statements.claim: On account of the wrongs of Pritha's sons, Janardana fell into such a passion that he seemed bent upon consuming all created things, and Arjuna exerted himself to pacify him.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12: 'when on account of the wrongs of Pritha's sons, Janardana had thus got into a passion, and seemed bent upon consuming all created things, Arjuna exerted himself to pacify him.'

statements.claim: Arjuna recited Krishna's former-life feats: ten thousand years as a muni on Gandhamadana, eleven thousand years on water alone at Pushkara, a hundred years standing on one leg on the high hills of Vadari living on air, a twelve-year sacrifice on the Saraswati with body like a bundle of veins, and a thousand celestial years on one leg at Prabhasa.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12 Arjuna's speech itemizes each penance with matching figures (ten thousand years on Gandhamadana, eleven thousand at Pushkara, a hundred years on Vadari on one leg living on air, twelve-year Saraswati sacrifice, one thousand celestial years at Prabhasa).

statements.claim: Arjuna recalled the slaying of Naraka and the first horse-sacrifice, the destruction of Daityas and Danavas until Indra was given sovereignty, the three steps by which the child Krishna filled heaven, firmament and earth, and hundreds of sinful Asuras slain in each of a thousand incarnations.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12: 'Slaying the Asura Naraka... thou hadst obtained his ear-rings, and performed... the first horse-sacrifice... slaying... Daityas and Danavas... giving the lord of Sachi... the sovereignty of the universe... fill by three steps only the heaven, the firmament, and the earth... in thy incarnations on those thousand occasions, thou hadst slain... sinful Asuras by hundreds.'

statements.claim: Arjuna said: 'All asceticism rests in thee... thou art the cause of creation and its course... Thou art mine and I am thine, and all that is mine is thine also. O thou irrepressible one, thou art Nara and I am Narayana.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt and passage: Arjuna's speech ends 'Thou art mine and I am thine, while all that is mine is thine also!... O thou irrepressible one, thou art Nara and I am Narayana or Hari!' (the pack's index summary loosely phrases this as Krishna answering; the passage, treated as authoritative, has Arjuna speaking).

statements.claim: Krishna's wrath cooled; he did not unsay the vow that the earth would drink the blood of Duryodhana and Karna and that Yudhishthira would be crowned, and the onlookers marvelled at Arjuna, who had calmed him simply by telling Krishna who he was.
statements.evidence: Canonical summary states Arjuna recites the feats 'to calm him'; the cooling of the wrath and the awe of the assembly is connective resolution not literally recorded in the excerpted passage, and it does not contradict the pack.

statements.claim: Krishna's anger frightened his own kinsmen (opening line).
statements.evidence: Dramatic atmosphere consistent with the passage's 'seemed bent upon consuming all created things'; the pack does not record the kinsmen's fear (they are shown arriving in wrath against the Kauravas), so no specific source.

DKS_0376.notes: Dialogue and penance catalogue track MB 3.12 (Ganguli) closely; all figures verified against the passage. Two connective-narration items (kinsmen frightened, post-speech calm) are atmosphere/resolution, neither unsupported fact nor contradiction. The pack's index summary attributes the Nara/Narayana line to Krishna, but the passage (authoritative) puts it in Arjuna's speech, as the story does.

statements.claim: In the Kamyaka forest, while the visiting kinsmen talked of vengeance, the weeping Draupadi sat apart, grieving her husbands' loss of everything at dice and their exile.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Vasudeva then spake unto the weeping Draupadi'; MB 3.12 opening (shared passage) shows the kinsmen arriving with wrath over the Pandavas' banishment and affliction in the forest (dice-calamity context established by the arc and by DKS_0378's 'distress begot of dice').

statements.claim: The visitors were the Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas, the relatives of Panchala, the king of Chedi, and the Kaikeya brothers, who sat in a wide circle around Yudhishthira while Krishna at their head vowed the earth would drink the blood of Duryodhana and Karna, Dussasana and the wicked Sakuni.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12 passage (reproduced in this pack) lists the visitors verbatim and records Krishna's vow.

statements.claim: Krishna told the weeping Draupadi: 'O fair lady, the wives of those with whom thou art angry shall weep even like thee, beholding their husbands dead on the ground, weltering in blood.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt quotes the sentence verbatim.

statements.claim: Krishna promised: 'I promise thou shalt once more be the queen of kings! The heavens might fall, or the Himavat might split, the earth might be rent, or the waters of the ocean might dry up, but my words shall never prove futile.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt quotes the promise verbatim (continuing '...my words shall never prove futile', matching the pack index summary 'his words never futile').

statements.claim: Draupadi was the princess of Panchala and the shared wife of the five brothers, and the men she was angry with (Duryodhana, Karna, Dussasana, Sakuni) sat in Hastinapura.
statements.evidence: Background framing consistent with the corpus (pack index lists her with the Pandavas; the 3.261 pack passage calls her 'the excellent princess Draupadi, devoted to her husbands'); the specific 'shared wife of five brothers' and the enemies' whereabouts are not re-stated in this pack's excerpt.

statements.claim: Krishna consoled her not with patience or philosophy but with a counter-vow staking the order of nature on his word.
statements.evidence: Connective gloss faithfully summarizing the quoted vow; no new factual assertion.

statements.claim: Even Arjuna, standing among the allies, said nothing; that evening the talk of the gathered kings turned from grief to plans of armies and alliances and the war that waited at the end of thirteen years.
statements.evidence: Arjuna is in the pack's character list for this scene, but his silence and the evening's war-talk are connective staging; the thirteen-year exile figure belongs to the corpus-wide dice-game settlement rather than this pack's excerpt.

DKS_0377.notes: Both of Krishna's quoted promises match the 3.12 excerpt verbatim. Remaining items are background or evening atmosphere with no unsupported facts or contradictions.

statements.claim: Krishna told Yudhishthira in the Kamyaka forest: 'If I had been present at Dwaraka, this evil would not have befallen thee' — because he had been away from the Anarta country (Dwaraka's region), engaged against Salwa.
statements.evidence: MB 3.13: 'O lord of earth, if I had been present at Dwaraka... this evil would not have befallen thee!' and 'it is owing to my absence from the Anartta country at that time that thou hast fallen into such distress begot of dice'; pack index summary states the absence was 'while fighting Salwa.'

statements.claim: Krishna said that coming to the gambling match even uninvited by the son of Amvika, Duryodhana, or the other Kauravas, he would have prevented the game by showing its evils, summoning Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and Vahlika to his aid.
statements.evidence: MB 3.13 passage quotes this nearly verbatim ('coming unto the gambling-match, even if uninvited by the son of Amvika (Dhritarashtra), or Duryodhana... summoning to my aid Bhishma and Drona and Kripa, and Vahlika').

statements.claim: He would have told Dhritarashtra his sons should have nothing to do with dice, shown how the son of Virasena was formerly deprived of his kingdom by the evils of dice, and described how a man once engaged in the game keeps playing from desire of victory until ruin, losing possessions, falling into distress, losing untasted wealth, and exchanging harsh words in a single day.
statements.evidence: MB 3.13: 'let thy sons have nothing to do with dice! I would have shown the many evils (of dice) through which... the son of Virasena was formerly deprived of his kingdom... how a man once engaged in the game continueth to play (from desire of victory)... through dice men in a day lose their possessions, and fall into distress, and are deprived of their untasted wealth, and exchange harsh words!'

statements.claim: Krishna named women, dice, hunting and drinking as the four evils that deprive a man of prosperity, with evils attending on all of them per those versed in the Shastras.
statements.evidence: MB 3.13 quotes the four evils and the Shastra opinion verbatim.

statements.claim: Had Dhritarashtra accepted the counsel the welfare of the Kurus and virtue would have been secured; had he rejected it, Krishna would have compelled him by force; and had the false friends at his court supported him, Krishna would have slain them all along with the gamblers in the hall.
statements.evidence: MB 3.13 states each condition and consequence in sequence ('the welfare of the Kurus as also virtue itself would both have been secured... I would have compelled him by force... I would have slain them all, along with those gamblers, there present!').

statements.claim: Krishna said: 'O Kauravya... it is owing to my absence from the Anarta country at that time that thou hast fallen into such distress begot of dice.'
statements.evidence: MB 3.13 quotes the sentence verbatim.

statements.claim: On arriving at Dwaraka Krishna learned of the calamity from Yuyudhana and, his heart sore with grief, came speedily, saying 'Alas! O bull of the Bharata race, ye have all fallen into dire distress. I see thee with thy brothers plunged in misfortune.'
statements.evidence: MB 3.13: 'on arriving at Dwarka I learnt from Yuyudhana all about thy calamity!... with a heart sore agitated by grief, have I speedily come here... Alas! O bull of the Bharata race, ye have all fallen into dire distress! I see thee with thy brothers plunged in misfortune!'

statements.claim: The dice game at Hastinapura (loaded dice, staking and losing wealth, brothers, himself and the queen) led to the Pandavas' thirteen-year exile — the shared story everyone in the circle knew.
statements.evidence: Recap of the prior corpus arc (the dice-game events immediately preceding this episode) that this pack presupposes ('this evil...begot of dice'); the loaded-dice and thirteen-year details are not re-established in the 3.13 excerpt itself but match the corpus canon.

statements.claim: The lament was also a promise in disguise that Krishna would not be absent from whatever game came next; he had been 'fighting his own war at Saubha' when the dice fell.
statements.evidence: Salwa/Saubha is supported by the pack index summary ('absence while fighting Salwa') and MB 3.12's reference to destroying Salwa and the city of Saubha; the closing 'promise in disguise' is narrative reflection.

DKS_0378.notes: Krishna's long speech in MB 3.13 is reproduced with high fidelity; all conditional claims (counsel/force/slaying the courtiers) match the passage. Only connective items are the dice-game recap and closing reflection.

statements.claim: Durvasa, having first ascertained that the Pandavas were seated at ease and that Draupadi had finished her meal and was reposing, came to the forest surrounded by ten thousand disciples.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261: 'One day, having previously ascertained that the Pandavas were all seated at their ease and that Krishna (Draupadi) was reposing herself after her meal, the sage Durvasa, surrounded by ten thousand disciples repaired to that forest.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira received the guest with joined palms, pointed to an excellent seat, gave a fit and respectful welcome, and said 'Return quick, O adorable sir, after performing thy diurnal ablutions and observances'; the muni then went with his disciples to the stream to bathe.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261 describes the welcome and quotes Yudhishthira's words verbatim ('that sinless Muni, not knowing how the king would be able to provide a feast... proceeded with the latter to perform his ablutions').

statements.claim: The sun-given vessel remained full until Draupadi finished her meal and empty after; she had already eaten, so there was no food for the guests, and she was in great anxiety.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261: Draupadi 'was in great anxiety about the food'; 'The sun-given vessel remains full till I finish my meal. But as I have already taken my meal today, there is no food in it now.'

statements.claim: Draupadi prayed inwardly to Krishna, the slayer of Kamsa, addressing him as son of Devaki, soul/creator/destroyer of the universe, saviour of the afflicted, kind to those who take refuge in him, dark as the blue lotus, red-eyed as the lily, in yellow robes with the Kaustubha gem, and said 'As thou didst protect me before from Dussasana, do thou extricate me now from this difficulty.'
statements.evidence: MB 3.261 quotes the prayer with all these epithets and the closing plea verbatim ('she inwardly prayed to Krishna, the slayer of Kansa').

statements.claim: The great and sovereign God, lord of the earth, of mysterious movements, ever kind to his dependents, perceiving her difficulty, instantly repaired to that place, leaving the bed of Rukmini, who was sleeping by his side.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt quotes this nearly verbatim, including 'instantly repaired to that place leaving the bed of Rukmini who was sleeping by his side.'

statements.claim: Draupadi bowed to him in great joy and told him everything — the arrival of the munis and the empty vessel; Krishna asked for food ('I am very much afflicted with hunger... give me some food without delay'), and when she explained the vessel was empty, insisted it was no time for jest and had her fetch and show him the vessel.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261 follows this sequence with the quoted exchanges ('This is no time for jest, O Krishna. I am much distressed with hunger, go thou quickly to fetch the vessel and show it to me').

statements.claim: In the vessel Krishna saw a particle of rice and vegetable sticking at its rim, swallowed it, and said 'May it please the god Hari, the soul of the Universe, and may that god who partaketh at sacrifices be satiated with this.'
statements.evidence: MB 3.261 quotes the finding and the words verbatim.

statements.claim: Krishna told Bhimasena to invite the munis to dinner; Bhima went quickly to the nearest stream of transparent, cool water, where Durvasa and his disciples — having plunged in and rubbed their bodies — found their stomachs full to the throat.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261: 'the long-armed Krishna... said unto Bhimasena, "Do thou speedily invite the Munis to dinner"... Bhimasena quickly went... to the nearest stream of transparent and cool water... observing that they all felt their stomachs to be full... full to the throat.'

statements.claim: The ascetics came out staring at one another, saying the repast had been uselessly prepared since they could not eat, and Durvasa answered: 'By spoiling the repast, we have done a great wrong to that royal sage, king Yudhishthira.'
statements.evidence: MB 3.261 quotes both speeches verbatim.
