DKS_0379.notes: Very high fidelity: nearly every quoted line matches MB 3.261 (Ganguli) verbatim, including the correct disambiguation of the two 'Krishnas' (the princess Draupadi and the god). Minor glosses (Rukmini 'slept on unaware', atmosphere of Draupadi's despair) are connective only.

statements.claim: Durvasa's ten thousand disciples came out of the stream full — their stomachs heavy to the throat — unable to touch the promised feast.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261 (passage reproduced in this pack): the ascetics 'observing that they all felt their stomachs to be full... our stomachs seem to be full to the throat.'

statements.claim: Durvasa understood that they had done a great wrong to the royal sage Yudhishthira by spoiling the repast, and the company fled, fearing the king's wrath, without farewell.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261 has Durvasa say 'By spoiling the repast, we have done a great wrong to that royal sage, king Yudhishthira'; the pack's index summary confirms the outcome: 'the frightened Munis flee.' (The passage itself is truncated at this point in the pack, so the flight is per the pack summary.)

statements.claim: The Pandavas' sun-given vessel was empty because Draupadi had already eaten, so no feast could be made; Draupadi prayed to Krishna in Dwaraka, reminding him how he had protected her from Dussasana, and he left Rukmini's bed and came instantly.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261 (full passage in this pack) covers the empty vessel, the prayer ('As thou didst protect me before from Dussasana, do thou extricate me now from this difficulty'), and Krishna's instant arrival leaving Rukmini's bed.

statements.claim: Krishna found a single grain of rice and a leaf of vegetable clinging to the vessel's rim, ate it, and in that same hour the sages bathing in the stream felt their hunger die.
statements.evidence: MB 3.261: Krishna 'saw a particle of rice and vegetable sticking at its rim. And swallowing it...' while the ascetics 'having plunged into the river... felt their stomachs to be full.'

statements.claim: Krishna told the Pandavas he had been implored by Draupadi to come and so had come speedily; they need not fear Durvasa, who was gone; and 'Virtuous men never suffer.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt quotes Krishna's words verbatim: 'Knowing, ye sons of Pritha, your danger from that wrathful Rishi, I was implored by Draupadi to come, and (therefore) have I come here speedily. But now ye have not the least fear from the Rishi Durvasa... Virtuous men never suffer.'

statements.claim: Krishna asked the Pandavas' permission to return home, and they gave it freely and watched him go.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt ends Krishna's speech with 'I now ask your permission to let me return home'; pack index summary records that he 'returns home.'

statements.claim: The brothers found it strange comfort given their lives of suffering — the poisoned feast, the lost kingdom, the exile, their wife dragged before the assembly of enemies — yet believed him.
statements.evidence: Connective reflection listing prior corpus events (poisoning by the sons of Dhritarashtra is confirmed in the DKS_0383 pack passage 'gara-dana'; the dice/exile and Dussasana episode are established corpus events).

statements.claim: Yudhishthira, left alone, understood that the protection they had prayed for had been with them all along.
statements.evidence: Closing devotional reflection; no factual assertion requiring source.

DKS_0381.notes: Krishna's reassurance speech matches the pack excerpt verbatim. The munis' flight is supported by the pack's index summary (the passage is truncated mid-sentence in the pack file, so the summary is authoritative for that beat). Recap items match the shared 3.261 passage.

statements.claim: Krishna went to Akrura's house accompanied by Balarama (Rama) and Uddhava.
statements.evidence: SB 10.48.11: 'akrūra-bhavanaṃ kṛṣṇaḥ saha-rāmoddhavaḥ prabhuḥ' — Krishna went to Akrura's house together with Rama and Uddhava.

statements.claim: Akrura saw them from afar, bowed to Krishna and Balarama, and was greeted back by them; he held the water of their foot-washing on his head and, having worshipped them, rubbed their feet resting on his lap.
statements.evidence: SB 10.48.12-15: 'nanāma kṛṣṇaṃ rāmaṃ ca sa tair apy abhivāditaḥ / pādāvanejanīr āpo dhārayan śirasā... pādāv aṅka-gatau mṛjan.'

statements.claim: Akrura said: 'By fortune, the wicked Kamsa is slain with all his followers, and this family is yours' and 'Blessed are our dwellings, that the teacher of the world has entered them.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.48.16: 'diṣṭyā pāpo hataḥ kaṃsaḥ sānugo vām idaṃ kulam'; SB 10.48.24: 'adya... no vasatayaḥ... sa tvaṃ jagad-gurur adhokṣaja... praviṣṭaḥ.'

statements.claim: Akrura praised the two as foremost persons, cause and substance of the world; Krishna creates, sustains and dissolves the universe by his own powers; when the ancient Vedic path is lost he proclaims it for the world's good; and he has now descended into Vasudeva's house by his own portion to lighten the earth's burden, spreading glory over his family.
statements.evidence: SB 10.48.17, 20, 22-23: 'yuvāṃ pradhāna-puruṣau jagad-dhetū jagan-mayau... sṛjasy atho lumpasi pāsi viśvaṃ... sva-śaktibhiḥ... yadā yadā veda-pathaḥ purāṇaḥ... tvayodito 'yaṃ jagato hitāya... vasudeva-gṛhe 'vatīrṇaḥ svāṃśena bhāram apanetum ihāsi bhūmeḥ... kulasya yaśo vitanvan.'

statements.claim: Akrura said Krishna's way is hard to reach even for the kings of the gods, asked what wise man would seek refuge anywhere but in him (dear to devotees, true in speech, a grateful friend who grants every wish), and begged him to cut the bonds of son, wife, wealth, house and body.
statements.evidence: SB 10.48.25-26: 'kaḥ paṇḍitas tvad-aparaṃ śaraṇaṃ samīyād bhakta-priyād ṛta-giraḥ suhṛdaḥ kṛta-jñāt... sarvān dadāti suhṛdo bhajato 'bhikāmān... yogeśvarair api durāpa-gatiḥ sureśaiḥ... chindhy āśu naḥ suta-kalatrā-dhanāpta-geha-dehādi-moha-raśanāṃ.'

statements.claim: Krishna answered that great souls like Akrura are the ones to be served, the most worthy; holy places are not made of water, nor are the gods made of clay and stone — the true sacred presence lives in people, in a well-wishing friend and a heart bowed to the good.
statements.evidence: SB 10.48.29-31 (śrī-bhagavān uvāca): 'bhavad-vidhā mahā-bhāgā niṣevyā arha-sattamāḥ / na hy am-mayāni tīrthāni na devā mṛc-chilā-mayāḥ / sa bhavān suhṛdāṃ vai naḥ śreyān śreyaś-cikīrṣayā.' The last clause is the story's connective gloss of verse 31.

statements.claim: Krishna told Akrura that after Pandu's death his children were left with their mother in great sorrow, and the blind king of Hastinapura (son of Ambika), guided by his wicked son, dealt meanly with his brother's sons; the boys had been brought to the capital after their father's death, not by choice.
statements.evidence: SB 10.48.32-33: 'pitary uparate bālāḥ saha mātrā su-duḥkhitāḥ / teṣu rājāmbikā-putro bhrātṛ-putreṣu dīna-dhīḥ'; pack's rendered excerpt confirms 'the blind king follows his wicked son' and that the Pandavas were 'brought there with their mother after their father's death.'

statements.claim: Krishna commanded: 'Go to Hastinapura and learn how the Pandavas fare — whether things go well with them or ill'; having so commanded Akrura, he (with Rama and Uddhava) departed.
statements.evidence: SB 10.48.34-35: 'gaccha jānīhi tad-vṛttam adhunā sādhv asādhu vā / ity akrūraṃ samādiśya bhagavān harir īśvaraḥ.'

statements.claim: Akrura was the man who had once carried Kamsa's message and come back carrying Krishna's grace instead; he asked for no guard or retinue — a friend's eyes were his only credential.
statements.evidence: Backstory callback to the earlier corpus arc (Akrura's summons of Krishna to Mathura for Kamsa) plus connective staging of his departure; the pack presupposes Akrura's established devotion.

DKS_0382.notes: All episode content verifies verse-by-verse against SB 10.48.11-35 (Sanskrit, GRETIL) and the pack's rendered excerpt. Krishna's 'holy places are not made of water, nor gods of clay and stone' speech is correctly attributed to Krishna per the pack's śrī-bhagavān uvāca tag.

statements.claim: In Hastinapura, Kunti — widow of Pandu and mother of five sons the court had never wanted — lived watched on every side in the palace of the Kurus, until word came that her brother Akrura had arrived from Mathura.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49 context: Akrura was sent to Hastinapura (Gajasahvaya) by Krishna per SB 10.48.33-34 (previous pack); SB 10.49.6: 'pṛthā tu bhrātaraṃ prāptam akrūram' — Pritha (Kunti) approached her brother Akrura. Her widowhood/motherhood is the presupposed situation of the episode.

statements.claim: Akrura greeted the elders — Bahlika with his son, Bharadvaja, Gautama — as courtesy required, and then stayed for months, watching, to learn the king's conduct.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.1-3: 'saha-putraṃ ca bāhlīkaṃ bhāradvājaṃ sa-gautamam / yathāvad upasaṅgamya... uvāsa katicin māsān rājño vṛtta-vivitsayā.'

statements.claim: He marked the sons of Pandu's brilliance, energy, strength, courage, humility and other good qualities, and also what the sons of Dhritarashtra had done to them — the giving of poison and other unseemly deeds.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.4-5: 'teja ojo balaṃ vīryaṃ praśrayādīṃś ca sad-guṇān / kṛtaṃ ca dhārtarāṣṭrair yad gara-dānādy apeśalam.' (The 'poison mixed into food' wording is a slight elaboration of gara-dāna.)

statements.claim: Kunti came to Akrura weeping; among her rivals she was like a doe among wolves, and she asked whether her parents and brothers still remembered her.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.6-9: 'api smaranti naḥ saumya pitarau bhrātaraś ca me / ... sapatna-madhye śocantīṃ vṛkānāṃ hariṇīm iva'; pack excerpt: 'Weeping, Kunti said...'

statements.claim: Kunti said: 'The blessed Krishna, my brother's son, is the refuge, dear to his devotees. Krishna, Krishna, great yogin, soul of the universe, protector of all beings! I see no refuge for us but your lotus feet... Salutation to Krishna, the pure one, the supreme self.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.8-12: 'bhrātreyo bhagavān kṛṣṇaḥ śaraṇyo bhakta-vatsalaḥ / ... kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa mahā-yogin viśvātman viśva-bhāvana / nānyat tava padāmbhojāt paśyāmi śaraṇaṃ nṛṇām / namaḥ kṛṣṇāya śuddhāya brahmaṇe paramātmane.'

statements.claim: Akrura and Vidura stood with her, sharing her joy and sorrow; Vidura was the wise uncle of the Kurus who had always loved the Pandavas.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.14: 'sama-duḥkha-sukho 'krūro viduraś ca mahā-yaśāḥ'; Vidura's identity as the Kurus' wise, Pandava-loving uncle is corpus-canonical background.

statements.claim: Having spoken her grief aloud and been heard, Kunti's prayer reached its destination — answered in a friend's promise to carry her words back to Mathura; that night, perhaps, she slept more peacefully.
statements.evidence: Hedged, inward-looking closing ('perhaps... something in her knew'); consistent with Akrura's later report to Krishna in SB 10.49.30 (next story) but not a sourceable event in this pack.

DKS_0383.notes: Prayer and lament verified verse-by-verse against SB 10.49.1-14 (Sanskrit, GRETIL). The doe-among-wolves image is the pack's own (vṛkāṇāṃ hariṇīm iva). Only the closing is speculative inner state, clearly hedged.

statements.claim: Before leaving Hastinapura, Akrura — who had come to learn how the Pandavas fared and had learned of the poison and cruelties — asked to see the blind king Dhritarashtra, who sat on the throne his brother had left and loved his own sons with a crooked love.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.15: 'yāsyan rājānam abhyetya viṣamaṃ putra-lālasam' — as he was departing he approached the king who was intensely attached to his sons; Dhritarashtra's blindness and regency are presupposed (SB 10.48.33 'rājāmbikā-putro...').

statements.claim: Akrura counselled: 'Rule the earth by righteousness, and win your subjects by good conduct. Act otherwise, and you will be blamed in every mouth and walk into darkness.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.17-18: 'dharmeṇa pālayann urvīṃ prajāḥ śīlena rañjayan / anyathā tv ācaraṃl loke garhito yāsyase tamaḥ.'

statements.claim: He told the king no one dwells forever with anyone; a being is born alone and dies alone — no retinue follows a man out of the world, and guards cannot surround a grave.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.19-20: 'neha cātyanta-saṃvāsaḥ kasyacit kenacit saha / ekaḥ prasūyate jantur eka eva pralīyate.' The retinue/guards lines are rhetorical elaboration of 'born alone, dies alone.'

statements.claim: Wealth gathered by wrong means is carried off by others of little wit; the man who nourishes his sons on unrighteousness, thinking himself clever, takes the guilt onto his own shoulders and is finally abandoned by those very sons.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.21-23: 'adharmopacitaṃ vittaṃ haranty anye 'lpa-medhasaḥ / puṣṇāti yān adharmeṇa sva-buddhyā tam apaṇḍitam / svayaṃ kilbiṣam ādāya tais tyakto nārtha-kovidaḥ.'

statements.claim: Akrura concluded: 'Therefore this world, O king, is a dream, a waking illusion, a fantasy of the mind. Do not anchor your soul to it.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.24: 'tasmāl lokam imaṃ rājan svapna-māyā-manoratham.'

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra admitted: 'Even so, gentle one, your sweet words do not rest in my heart, because my heart is unsteady,' and asked 'What man can undo the ordinance of the Lord?' — the lord who, entering his own creation through his inscrutable power, sets in motion the wheel of the world.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.26-28: 'tathāpi sūnṛtā saumya hṛdi na sthīyate cale / īśvarasya vidhiṃ ko nu vidhunoty anyathā pumān / yo durvimarśa-pathayā nija-māyayedaṃ sṛṣṭvā guṇān vibhajate tad-anupraviṣṭaḥ... saṃsāra-cakra-gataye parameśvarāya.'

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra bowed to that unknowable power and fell silent; the counsel had been given but found no room in his heart.
statements.evidence: Verse 28's salutation ('tasmai namaḥ...') supports the bowing; the 'fell silent' and the closing verdict on the counsel are connective narration consistent with his confessed inability to act.

statements.claim: Back in Mathura, Akrura went straight to Krishna and Balarama and reported everything — the Pandavas' state, what the sons of Dhritarashtra had done, and the blind king's confession — without softening a word.
statements.evidence: SB 10.49.30: 'śaśaṃsa rāma-kṛṣṇābhyāṃ dhṛtarāṣṭra-viceṣṭitam' — he reported Dhritarashtra's conduct to Rama and Krishna; the fuller content (Pandavas' treatment and the king's reply) follows from his mission (10.48.34) and the pack summary 'reported all.'

statements.claim: The news did not surprise Krishna and Balarama; from that day a message had passed between Hastinapura and Mathura, and the road between them ran both ways.
statements.evidence: Closing connective imagery; no unsupported factual assertion.

DKS_0384.notes: Counsel and reply verify verse-by-verse against SB 10.49.15-30 (Sanskrit, GRETIL); Dhritarashtra's fatalistic reply is faithfully rendered. Elaborative lines (retinue/guards, falling silent) are rhetorical extensions of sourced verses.

statements.claim: Krishna, who ruled at Dwaraka, came to Indraprastha to see the Pandavas, arriving as a friend rather than with an army or a summons.
statements.evidence: SB 10.58.1-11 (pack excerpt): 'Krishna came to Indraprastha to see the Pandavas.' Nothing in 10.58.1-11 records an army or royal summons; the quiet visit is the episode's point.

statements.claim: The Pandavas were kings settled in the capital built on the Yamuna, and Yudhishthira's rule had made the kingdom prosperous.
statements.evidence: Contextual background consistent with the episode's setting (the Pandavas receive Krishna at Indraprastha as kings); prosperity is not asserted in this pack's passage, though MB 2.32 (companion episode) describes Yudhishthira's prosperous rule.

statements.claim: The five brothers received Krishna at once; Krishna paid his respects first to Yudhishthira and Bhima, then to the others, and Draupadi herself led him to the finest seat in the hall.
statements.evidence: SB 10.58.1-4: the Parthas embraced Acyuta (pariṣvajya), Krishna made obeisance to Yudhishthira and Bhima (yudhiṣṭhirasya bhīmasya kṛtvā pādābhivandanam), and the blameless Kṛṣṇā (Draupadi) seated him on the finest seat (paramāsana).

statements.claim: Satyaki, who had come from Dwaraka with Krishna, was honored and greeted by each of the brothers in turn.
statements.evidence: SB 10.58.5: sātyakiḥ pārthaiḥ pūjitaś cābhivanditaḥ — Satyaki was worshipped and greeted with obeisance by the Parthas.

statements.claim: Kunti, weeping with love, her voice choked, said to Krishna, 'Now we are safe, for you have remembered us.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.58.6-8: Kunti, eyes moist with deep affection, choked by love's agitation, said 'tadaiva kuśalaṁ no 'bhūt sa-nāthās te kṛtā vayam' (rendered in pack excerpt: 'now we are protected, for you remember us').

statements.claim: Kunti had been mother to the boys through wandering and want, when Krishna was the cousin who remembered them, came to them, and wrote to them in their exile.
statements.evidence: Emotional/relationship background framing Kunti's speech; the 'remembered us / protected us' substance is in SB 10.58.8, but the specific claim that Krishna 'wrote to them in exile' has no support in this pack's passage.

statements.claim: Yudhishthira asked Krishna to stay through the rains, and Krishna remained at Indraprastha for four months, delighting them all.
statements.evidence: SB 10.58.11: requested by the king he stayed happily through the rainy months (vārṣikān māsān ... abhyarthitaḥ sukham); pack summary: 'stayed four months, delighting all.'

statements.claim: During the stay Krishna lived among them at ease — long talks with Yudhishthira, grips with Bhima, garden walks with Arjuna, horse-and-sword arguments with the twins — and the palace became for a season only a house where someone beloved was staying.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric elaboration of the four-month stay; SB 10.58.11 records only that he stayed happily at the king's request, delighting them.

statements.claim: When at last he left, he took nothing with him but their goodbyes and left behind a household that had been, for a little while, whole.
statements.evidence: Poetic closing reflection; the pack records Krishna's departure only implicitly (verse 11 ends the stay) and asserts nothing of what he took or left.

DKS_0385.notes: No unsupported or contradicted claims. Story follows SB 10.58.1-11 faithfully (visit, embraces, Kunti's words, four-month rainy-season stay); the Kunti 'wrote to them in exile' line and the daily-life vignettes are connective narration.

statements.claim: Krishna came to Indraprastha for the Rajasuya, the great sacrifice through which Yudhishthira meant to be acknowledged a king of kings.
statements.evidence: MB 2.32: upon Krishna's arrival Yudhishthira seeks leave to perform the Rajasuya ('it is for thee that the whole earth is under my sway'); corpus index: 'Krishna Arrives at Indraprastha for the Rajasuya'. Variant note: MB frames the arrival as bringing treasure, SB as an emotional reunion — the story blends both without contradiction.

statements.claim: The city welcomed him as a festival: streets swept and sprinkled with water fragrant with elephant-musk, banners from the rooftops, golden arches at the crossings, full pitchers of welcome at the doorways.
statements.evidence: SB 10.71.30: saṁsikta-vartma kariṇāṁ mada-gandha-toyaiḥ ... citra-dhvajaiḥ kanaka-toraṇa-pūrṇa-kumbhaiḥ (roads sprinkled with rutting-elephant musk water, colorful banners, golden arches, full pitchers).

statements.claim: Yudhishthira came out with his preceptors and friends, the sound of music and Vedic chanting going before him; when Krishna stepped down the king's heart melted and he embraced him with both arms.
statements.evidence: SB 10.71.22-25: hearing of the arrival, Yudhishthira came out with preceptors and friends amid gīta-vāditra-ghoṣeṇa brahma-ghoṣeṇa; dṛṣṭvā viklinna-hṛdayaḥ ... dorbhyāṁ pariṣvajya (heart melted, embraced with both arms).

statements.claim: Bhima embraced him next, smiling through eyes blurred with love — Krishna was his mother's sister's son, his own cousin; Arjuna embraced him, and the twins Nakula and Sahadeva bowed and touched his feet.
statements.evidence: SB 10.71.26-27: Bhīma embraced his mātuleya (maternal uncle's son = cousin), smayan prema-jalākulendriyaḥ; arjunena pariṣvakto yamābhyām abhivāditaḥ (embraced by Arjuna, greeted with obeisance by the twins).

statements.claim: Bards and panegyrists sang his praises, and Krishna stood at the center of the welcome like the jewel crowning a hundred good reputations.
statements.evidence: SB 10.71.28-29: sūta-māgadha-gandharvā vandinaś copamantriṇaḥ ... puṇya-śloka-śikhāmaṇiḥ (bards/magadhas/gandharvas/panegyrists; he is the crest-jewel of the famously virtuous).

statements.claim: The city's women abandoned their household work the moment the news came and hurried down the king's road, braids loosening and garments slipping, to watch him pass; from the rooftops they showered flowers and embraced him in their minds.
statements.evidence: SB 10.71.32-33: women, hearing of his arrival, at once left housework, hair-knots and garment-bands loosened by eagerness, went to the king's road; women on the house-tops scattered flowers and embraced him mentally with smiling glances.

statements.claim: Women who caught sight of Krishna's queens — Rukmini, Satyabhama, Bhadra, Jambavati — murmured that the ladies of the Vrishni house moved among them like the stars around the moon, and asked what those women had done to be looked on by him.
statements.evidence: SB 10.71.34 (tārā yathoḍupa-sahāḥ ... kim akāry amūbhiḥ ... līlāvaloka-kalayotsavam ātanoti); the four queens are named in the pack's excerpt.

statements.claim: In the palace Kunti rose from her couch and went to meet her sister's son; Krishna bowed to his aunt and the elder women of the household, and Kunti brought Govinda home with her own hands, honoring him as the lord of the three worlds.
statements.evidence: SB 10.71.36-39: Pṛthā, seeing her nephew Krishna tri-bhuvaneśvaram, brought Govinda home herself (govindaṁ gṛham ānīya); Krishna made obeisance to his father's sister and the elder women (pitṛ-svasur guru-strīṇām ... abhivādanam).

statements.claim: At her mother-in-law's bidding, Draupadi welcomed each of Krishna's queens — Kalindi, Mitravinda, Saibya, Nagnajiti, and the rest — and settled them in the women's quarters with every honor.
statements.evidence: SB 10.71.40-41: śvaśṛvā sañcoditā kṛṣṇā kṛṣṇa-patnīś ca sarvaśaḥ ... kālindīṁ mitravindāṁ ca śaibyāṁ nāgnajitīṁ satīm. Note: the pack's own excerpt summary here names Rukmini/Satyabhama/Bhadra/Jambavati instead; the Sanskrit passage (authoritative per instructions) lists Kalindi, Mitravinda, Saibya, Nagnajiti — the story follows the passage.

statements.claim: Yudhishthira settled Janardana himself, giving him the best of the palace.
statements.evidence: SB 10.71.42: sukhaṁ nivāsayām āsa dharma-rājo janārdanam (Dharmaraja settled Janardana comfortably).

statements.claim: Seated at ease, Yudhishthira told Krishna: 'It is because of you that the whole earth is under my sway; through your grace I have gathered this wealth; I desire to give it away according to the ordinance to the brahmanas and to the fire. Grant me permission to perform the sacrifice with you and my brothers — install yourself at it, for if you perform it, I shall be cleansed of sin.'
statements.evidence: MB 2.32: Yudhishthira's address to Krishna, nearly verbatim ('O Krishna it is for thee that the whole earth is under my sway... I shall be cleansed of sin').

statements.claim: Krishna answered that Yudhishthira deserved imperial dignity; if he performed the great sacrifice and obtained its fruit they would all regard themselves as crowned with success; Krishna was always engaged in seeking his good and would obey whatever office he was given.
statements.evidence: MB 2.32: Krishna's reply, nearly verbatim ('Thou, O tiger among kings, deservest imperial dignity... Employ me also in some office... for I should obey all thy commands').

statements.claim: Yudhishthira replied that his resolve was already crowned with fruit since Krishna had arrived just as he wished, and with his brothers he set about gathering the materials for the Rajasuya.
statements.evidence: MB 2.32: 'my resolve is already crowned with fruit... when thou... hast arrived here agreeably to my wish'; 'Commanded by Krishna, the son of Pandu along with his brothers set himself upon collecting the materials.'

statements.claim: Closing simile: the king's city was gladdened by its truest friend 'like a dark region made bright by the sun.'
statements.evidence: MB 2.32: 'The capital of the Bharata was gladdened by Krishna's presence just as a dark region is rendered joyful by the sun.'

DKS_0387.notes: No unsupported or contradicted claims. SB 10.71.22-44 (embrace scene, queens' welcome, Kunti, Draupadi) and MB 2.32 (Rajasuya request dialogue) are both used faithfully. Discrepancy noted: pack's excerpt summary for 10.71.40-41 names Rukmini/Satyabhama/Bhadra/Jambavati, while the Sanskrit passage (followed by the story) names Kalindi/Mitravinda/Saibya/Nagnajiti — passage treated as authoritative.

statements.claim: The rumor reached Arjuna on the pilgrim road during his long exile from Indraprastha: at Dwaraka Balarama had decided to give their sister Subhadra in marriage to Duryodhana, a plan kept from everyone outside the house.
statements.evidence: SB 10.86.2: duryodhanāya rāmas tāṁ dāsyatīti na cāpare ('Rama would give her to Duryodhana — and no others [knew]'); pack excerpt: 'Arjuna, on pilgrimage, hears that Balarama intends to give their sister Subhadra to Duryodhana.' MB 1.223 (tail) confirms the episode falls in Arjuna's exile ending with his return to Khandavaprastha after twelve years.

statements.claim: Arjuna put aside the warrior's dress and went to Dwaraka as a wandering renunciant carrying the triple staff of a mendicant, where the Yadavas would not look for him.
statements.evidence: SB 10.86 (pack excerpt): Arjuna goes to Dwaraka 'disguised as a tridandi renunciant' (tridandi = bearer of the triple staff).

statements.claim: It was the rainy season and he stayed in Dwaraka through its months, accepted as a guest; one day, brought into a house and offered guest-offerings, he saw Subhadra, the great-hearted maiden, and she, seeing him, desired him — for he stole the hearts of women.
statements.evidence: SB 10.86.3-6: tatra vai vārṣitān māsān avātsīt (he stayed the rainy months); ekadā gṛham ānīya ātithyena nimantrya tam ... so 'paśyat tatra mahatīṁ kanyāṁ vīra-mano-harām; sāpi taṁ cakame vīkṣya nārīṇāṁ hṛdayaṁ-gamam.

statements.claim: On the day of a great festival procession, when the image of the gods was carried out of the city and Subhadra rode in a chariot, Arjuna seized his bow and carried her off, curbing the brave warriors who rushed to stop him.
statements.evidence: SB 10.86.8-9: mahatyāṁ deva-yātrāyāṁ ratha-sthāṁ durga-nirgatāṁ ... ratha-stho dhanur ādāya śūrāṁś cārundhato bhaṭān (during the great procession of the deities, she in a chariot that had left the fort; standing on the chariot, taking up his bow, he curbed the brave warriors).

statements.claim: Balarama's anger rose like the ocean at full moon — sudden and immense.
statements.evidence: SB 10.86.10: tac chrutvā kṣubhito rāmaḥ parvaṇīva mahārṇavaḥ (hearing it, Rama was agitated like the great ocean at the parvan/full moon).

statements.claim: Then Krishna spoke, and his father Vasudeva spoke with him, and between them they turned the storm.
statements.evidence: SB 10.86 (pack excerpt) records Krishna alone pacifying Balarama; MB 1.223 records a single conciliating speech delivered by 'Vasudeva' — the epic's own name for Krishna in this passage — and no source places Krishna's father Vasudeva in the scene or gives him any words. The story splits one counselor into two speakers.
statements.resolution: Corrected in story text via consolidation pass.

statements.claim: The counsel was that Arjuna's act was an honor, not an insult: the house of Vrishni was not for sale — no daughter was to be given in marriage like an animal, no one sold like goods, and a self-choice was a gamble no father should make; Arjuna had seen the faults in every gentler method and took the maiden by force according to the ordinance of warriors; he was the son of Kunti, born of the line of Bharata, and no one in all the worlds could vanquish Partha in battle except the three-eyed god.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'we of the Satwata race are never mercenary... accepting a bride in gift as if she were an animal?... Who... would sell his offspring?... Arjuna, seeing these faults in all the other methods took the maiden away by force, according to the ordinance... I do not see, in all the worlds... the person that can by force vanquish Partha in battle, except the three-eyed god Mahadeva.'

statements.claim: 'Go to him,' Krishna said, 'and by conciliation stop him and bring him back. If he rides home after defeating us, our fame is gone. There is no disgrace in friendship.'
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'go ye cheerfully after Dhananjaya and by conciliation stop him and bring him back. If Partha goes to his city after having vanquished us by force, our fame will be gone. There is no disgrace, however, in conciliation.' (Story's closing word 'friendship' for the source's 'conciliation' is a light paraphrase of the same idea.)

statements.claim: The Yadavas went out and stopped Arjuna with words, not weapons; he turned back to Dwaraka and, welcomed and honored by the sons of Vrishni, was united in marriage with Subhadra; appeased Balarama sent rich wedding gifts for the bride and the groom.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'Stopped by them, Arjuna returned to Dwaraka and was united in marriage with Subhadra. Worshipped by the sons of Vrishni's race...'; SB 10.86.11: prāhiṇot pāribarhāṇi vara-vadhvor mudā balaḥ (Balarama joyfully sent wedding-gifts for bride and groom).

statements.claim: When Arjuna brought his bride to Indraprastha, Draupadi's jealousy dissolved within the day: Subhadra said 'I am your maid,' Draupadi embraced her and answered 'Let your husband be without a foe,' and Kunti, from excess of affection, blessed the girl who had become her daughter; from that day the Pandavas' household lived happily.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: Subhadra worshipped Draupadi saying 'I am thy maid!'; Draupadi embraced her and said 'Let thy husband be without a foe!'; Kunti 'from excess of affection smelt the head of that girl... and pronounced infinite blessing upon her'; 'From that time... the Pandavas began to live happily.'

corrections.original_sentence: Then Krishna spoke, and his father Vasudeva spoke with him, and between them they turned the storm.
corrections.suggested: Then Krishna spoke — he whom the old telling also calls Vasudeva — and his words turned the storm.

DKS_0388.notes: One UNSUPPORTED claim: Krishna's father Vasudeva is introduced as a co-speaker, but SB 10.86 and MB 1.223 both present a single pacifier — Krishna (called Vasudeva in the MB passage). Everything else maps closely to SB 10.86.1-11 and MB 1.223.

statements.claim: On the last day of the Rajasuya, when the king himself was to be sprinkled with the consecrating waters, the great brahmana rishis entered the inner enclosure of the sacrificial compound along with the invited kings.
statements.evidence: MB 2.35: 'On the last day of the sacrifice when the king was to be sprinkled over with the sacred water, the great Brahmana Rishis... along with the invited kings, entered together the inner enclosure of the sacrificial compound.'

statements.claim: The rishis, with Narada at their head, sat at ease among the royal sages, arguing philosophy like hawks darting at meat; the enclosure, crowded with gods, brahmanas and great rishis, shone like the sky thick with stars, and no one without vows was near that platform.
statements.evidence: MB 2.35: 'those illustrious Rishis with Narada as their foremost... looked like the gods seated in the mansion of Brahma'; disputants fell on arguments 'like hawks darting at meat thrown up into the air'; 'that platform crowded with gods, Brahmanas and great Rishis looked... like the wide expanse of the firmament studded with stars'; 'there was then no Sudra near that platform... nor anybody that was without vows.'

statements.claim: Narada was glad at the king's prosperity born of the sacrifice, then grew thoughtful at the vast concourse of Kshatriyas; he recalled words heard of old in the mansion of Brahma — that the celestials had been commanded to be born on earth, to meet one another in war and to return — and knew this was a concourse of incarnate gods, with Narayana himself, born in the line of the Yadavas, moving among them as a man.
statements.evidence: MB 2.35: Narada 'began to recollect the words he had heard of old in the mansion of Brahma regarding the incarnation on earth of portions of every deity'; 'that was a concourse (of incarnate) gods'; Narayana 'had formerly commanded the celestials, saying,—Be ye born on earth and slay one another and come back to heaven'; 'had taken his birth in the race of Yadus... was then living in the world in human form.'

statements.claim: Krishna — himself the centre of all worlds, round whom every creature moved — was engaged at his own will in washing the feet of the brahmanas, taking up the menial office of the sacrifice, desirous of excellent fruits; no one had asked him.
statements.evidence: MB 2.35 (evidence excerpt): 'Krishna who was himself the centre of all worlds and round whom moved every creature, desirous of acquiring excellent fruits, was engaged at his own will in washing the feet of the Brahmanas.' The 'no one had asked/commanded him' clause renders 'at his own will' — connective import.

statements.claim: Bhishma then rose and advised Yudhishthira that the arghya be offered to the kings each as he deserved, naming the six worthy of arghya — the preceptor, the sacrificial priest, the relative, the Snataka, the friend, and the king — and that the first arghya be offered to the foremost among those present.
statements.evidence: MB 2.35: Bhishma's speech, nearly verbatim ('the preceptor, the sacrificial priest, the relative, the Snataka, the friend, and the king... are the six that deserve Arghya... let an Arghya be presented first of all unto him among those present who is the foremost').

statements.claim: Bhishma declared Krishna foremost — as the sun among all luminous objects in energy, strength and prowess — and said the sacrificial mansion was illuminated and gladdened by him as a sunless region is by the sun and still air by a breeze.
statements.evidence: MB 2.35: 'As is the sun among all luminous objects, so is the one (meaning Krishna)... in consequence of his energy, strength and prowess. And this our sacrificial mansion is illuminated and gladdened by him as a sunless region by the sun, or a region of still air by a gust of breeze.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira asked whom he meant; Bhishma judged by his intelligence and named Krishna; at the grandsire's command Sahadeva duly presented the first arghya of excellent ingredients to Krishna of the Vrishni race, who accepted it according to the forms of the ordinance.
statements.evidence: MB 2.35: 'Bhishma the son of Santanu judged it by his intelligence that on earth Krishna was the foremost of all... Sahadeva endued with great prowess duly presented the first Arghya of excellent ingredients unto Krishna of the Vrishni race. Krishna also accepted it according to the forms of the ordinance.'

statements.claim: Reflection: the hall had seen the lord of all worlds wash the feet of the priests and then saw him raised above all kings — the one who served all was fit to be honored by all — and that was the truest thing the Rajasuya showed that day.
statements.evidence: Interpretive gloss joining the two supported scenes (foot-washing and first arghya); asserts no new sourceable fact.

statements.claim: Among the seated kings, one had watched the first arghya with a face like a closed fist, his grievance older than the sacrifice — a hook for the following Shishupala episode.
statements.evidence: Transitional framing; Shishupala's grievance is the subject of the following story (MB 2.39+), not of this pack.

DKS_0389.notes: No unsupported or contradicted claims; MB 2.35 rendered closely, including Narada's vision, Krishna's voluntary foot-washing, and the arghya sequence. Interpretive reflections flagged as connective narration.

statements.claim: Krishna had received the first worship of the Rajasuya, and the kings of the earth, who had come from every direction to the sacrifice, felt the sting of it and the assembly grew agitated with wrath.
statements.evidence: MB 2.39 context: 'Beholding that vast assembly of kings agitated with wrath...'; the episode directly follows Krishna receiving the first arghya (per evidence excerpt: 'Upon Krishna having received the first worship...').

statements.claim: Shishupala, king of Chedi, rose and cried out: 'When I am here to head you all, what are you thinking of now? Arrayed, let us stand in battle against the assembled Vrishnis and the Pandavas!'
statements.evidence: MB 2.39 (evidence excerpt): Sunitha (Sisupala) said, 'When I am here to head ye all, what are ye thinking of now? Arrayed let us stand in battle against the assembled Vrishnis and the Pandavas?'

statements.claim: The vast assembly stirred like the terrific sea when whipped by the winds that blow at the time of universal dissolution.
statements.evidence: MB 2.39: assembly 'agitated with wrath, even like the terrific sea agitated by the winds that blow at the time of the universal dissolution.'

statements.claim: Krishna understood that the vast sea of monarchs, with its countless waves of troops, was preparing for a terrific rush, and he did not move — he neither rose nor reached for a weapon nor called for his chariot, waiting as a man who has already seen the end.
statements.evidence: MB 2.39 (evidence excerpt): 'Krishna then understood that the vast sea of monarchs with its countless waves of troops was preparing for a terrific rush.' The stillness/waiting is connective elaboration consistent with the passage (Krishna remains seated through the episode).

statements.claim: Yudhishthira leaned toward Bhishma and asked: 'This vast ocean of kings has been agitated by wrath. Tell me, O Grandsire, what I should do, so that my sacrifice may not be obstructed and my subjects may not be injured.'
statements.evidence: MB 2.39: Yudhishthira's words to Bhishma, nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: Bhishma answered: 'Fear not, O tiger of the Kurus. Can the dog slay the lion? As dogs in a pack approach the lion that is asleep and bark together, so are all these lords of earth... Achyuta now is like a lion asleep. Until he wakes, this chief of the Chedis makes these monarchs look like lions.'
statements.evidence: MB 2.39: Bhishma's reply, nearly verbatim ('Can the dog slay the lion?... Achyuta now is like a lion that is asleep...').

statements.claim: Bhishma continued: Shishupala, possessed of little intelligence, desires to take all these kings along with him, through the agency of the soul of the universe, to the regions of Yama; Vishnu has been desirous of taking back unto himself the energy that exists in Shishupala; the intelligence of this wicked-minded king and of all these monarchs has become perverse; Madhava is the progenitor as also the destroyer of all created beings of the four species in the three worlds.
statements.evidence: MB 2.39: Bhishma's continued speech, nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: The ruler of the Chedis heard every word and, not cooled, turned on the grandsire with words stern and rough — a man meaning to answer a prophecy with a war.
statements.evidence: MB 2.39 closing: 'Then the ruler of Chedis, having heard these words of Bhishma, addressed the latter... in words that were stern and rough.' The 'answer a prophecy with a war' clause is connective framing of the sequel.

DKS_0390.notes: No unsupported or contradicted claims; the story compresses MB 2.39 (Shishupala's war-cry, the sea simile, Krishna's perception, Yudhishthira's plea, Bhishma's dog-and-lion reply and his reading of Shishupala's perverse intelligence) in the source's own order. Krishna's stillness is connective narration, not contradicted by the pack.

statements.claim: Recap: Shishupala, king of Chedi, had called the assembled monarchs to war and the rage had gathered; Yudhishthira asked Bhishma, 'Tell me, O Grandsire, what I should do, so that my sacrifice may not be obstructed and my subjects may not be injured.'
statements.evidence: Continuation of the scene from MB 2.39 (Shishupala's call to arms and Yudhishthira's identical question are in the preceding chapter/pack DKS_0390); nothing in MB 2.40 contradicts the recap, which anchors the tirade that follows.

statements.claim: Bhishma answered without hesitation with the dog-and-lion speech: the monarchs are dogs barking in rage before the sleeping lion of the Vrishni race; Achyuta is like a lion asleep, and until he wakes this chief of the Chedis makes these monarchs look like lions.
statements.evidence: MB 2.40 (evidence excerpt for this pack quotes the lines): 'As dogs in a pack approaching the lion that is asleep bark together, so are all these lords of earth... Achyuta now is like a lion that is asleep.'

statements.claim: Then the grandsire spoke of what he truly saw: Shishupala, possessed of little intelligence, is desirous of taking all these kings along with him, through the agency of the soul of the universe, to the regions of Yama; assuredly Vishnu has been desirous of taking back unto himself the energy that exists in Shishupala; the intelligence of the wicked-minded king of the Chedis and of all these monarchs has become perverse; Madhava is the progenitor as also the destroyer of all created beings of the four species in the three worlds.
statements.evidence: MB 2.40 (evidence excerpt): 'Assuredly, O Bharata Vishnu hath been desirous of taking back unto himself the energy that existeth in this Sisupala...' plus the fuller speech in the passage.

statements.claim: Shishupala turned on Bhishma: 'Old and infamous wretch of your race, are you not ashamed of affrighting all these monarchs with these numerous false terrors? You are the foremost of the Kurus, and living as you do in the third state, celibacy, it is but fit for you to give counsel so wide of morality. Like a boat tied to another boat, like the blind following the blind, are the Kurus who have you for their guide.'
statements.evidence: MB 2.40: Shishupala's opening rebuke, nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: Shishupala mocked the recital of Krishna's deeds: slaying Putana (a vulture) in infancy; slaughtering Aswa and Vrishava, both unskilled in battle; throwing down by a kick an inanimate car; supporting the Govardhan mount for a week as if it were an anthill; eating a large quantity of food on a mountain-top; and — still more wrongful — the slaying of Kamsa, whose food he had eaten.
statements.evidence: MB 2.40: Shishupala's taunts, nearly verbatim ('If Krishna in his infancy slew a vulture... his slaughter of Aswa and Vrishava... threw down by a kick an inanimate piece of wood, viz., a car... supported for a week the Govardhan mount which is like an anthill... Kansa, whose food this one ate, hath been slain by him').

statements.claim: Shishupala accused Bhishma of throwing away the teaching that weapons must never descend on women, kine and Brahmanas, on those whose food has been taken and those whose shelter has been enjoyed: if at Bhishma's word one who has slain women (Putana) and kine is worshipped, what becomes of that great lesson?
statements.evidence: MB 2.40: 'The virtuous and the wise always instruct the honest that weapons must never be made to descend upon women and kine and Brahmanas and upon those whose food hath been taken, as also upon those whose shelter hath been enjoyed... If at thy word... one that hath slain women... and kine be worshipped, then what is to become of this great lesson?'

statements.claim: Shishupala taunted Bhishma's virtue: why was the virtuous girl Amva, who had set her heart upon another, carried off by him? Vichitravirya, knowing her condition, did not marry her though brought by him; in his very sight sons were begotten upon his brother's widow by another; his celibacy, led from ignorance or impotence, is fruitless; worship, gift, study and sacrifices distinguished by large gifts do not equal one-sixteenth part of what is obtained by a son; he is childless and old, the expounder of false morality.
statements.evidence: MB 2.40: Shishupala's charges against Bhishma, nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: Shishupala pronounced the sentence: 'Like the swan in the story, you shall now die at the hands of your relatives. Other men possessed of knowledge have said this of old, and I will presently recite it fully in your hearing' — and he began the tale of the old swan on the sea-coast, a bird forever preaching virtue to the feathery tribe while its own conduct fell short.
statements.evidence: MB 2.40: 'Like the swan in the story, thou shalt now die at the hands of thy relatives... I will presently recite it fully in thy hearing.' 'There lived of yore an old swan on the sea-coast. Ever speaking of morality, but otherwise in his conduct, he used to instruct the feathery tribe.'

DKS_0391.notes: No unsupported or contradicted claims; the opening recap reuses Bhishma's dog-and-lion speech already grounded in the scene (MB 2.39, pack DKS_0390) and quoted again in this pack's own evidence excerpt for 2.40. Shishupala's full tirade (deeds of Krishna, the women/kine/Brahmana rule, Amva and Vichitravirya, the swan-story curse) matches MB 2.40 closely.

statements.claim: Shishupala was born in the line of the king of Chedi with three eyes and four hands; as soon as he was born he screamed and brayed like an ass, striking fear into his father, mother and kin, and his parents resolved to abandon him.
statements.evidence: MB 2.42 (Bhishma's narration): 'This Sisupala was born in the line of the king of Chedi with three eyes and four hands. As soon as he was born, he screamed and brayed like an ass... his parents resolved to abandon him.'

statements.claim: An incorporeal voice told the king and his wife, with their ministers and priests, that the son would become both fortunate and superior in strength, that he should be cherished without anxiety — he would not die in childhood, his time was not yet come, and he that would slay him with weapons had also been born.
statements.evidence: MB 2.42: the incorporeal voice's words, nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: The anxious mother asked who would be the slayer of her son, and the voice answered: he upon whose lap the child, being placed, his superfluous arms fall down to the ground like a pair of five-headed snakes, and at the sight of whom the third eye on his forehead disappears — he will be his slayer.
statements.evidence: MB 2.42: the invisible Being's answer, nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: All the kings of the earth went to Chedi to behold the child; the king, worshipping each as he deserved, placed the child on their laps one after another, and though the child passed through the laps of a thousand kings the promised sign did not come to pass.
statements.evidence: MB 2.42: 'all the kings of the earth went to Chedi to behold him... the child was placed upon the laps of a thousand kings, one after another, yet that which the incorporeal voice had said came not to pass.'

statements.claim: Word of the wonder reached Dwaravati, and the mighty Yadava heroes Balarama and Krishna went to see their father's sister, the daughter of the Yadavas who was queen of Chedi; they saluted everyone according to rank, and after they had been worshipped the queen herself placed the child on Krishna's lap.
statements.evidence: MB 2.42: 'the mighty Yadava heroes Sankarshana and Janarddana also went to the capital of the Chedis, to see their father's sister—that daughter of the Yadavas (the queen of Chedi)... the queen with great pleasure herself placed the child on the lap of Damodara' (Sankarshana=Balarama, Janarddana/Damodara=Krishna).

statements.claim: As soon as the child was placed on Krishna's lap the superfluous arms fell to the ground and the eye on his forehead disappeared; the alarmed queen begged Krishna for a boon, calling him the assurer of all afflicted ones and the dispeller of everyone's fear.
statements.evidence: MB 2.42: 'As soon as the child was placed on his lap, those superfluous arms of his fell down and the eye on his forehead also disappeared. And beholding this, the queen in alarm and anxiety begged of Krishna a boon.'

statements.claim: Krishna answered: 'Fear not, O respected one. You are acquainted with morality; you need have no fear from me. What boon shall I give you? What shall I do, O aunt? Whether able or not, I shall do your bidding.'
statements.evidence: MB 2.42: Krishna's reply, nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: The queen asked that Krishna pardon the offences of Shishupala for her sake, and Krishna granted: 'O aunt, even when he will deserve to be slain, I will pardon a hundred offences of his. Grieve not.'
statements.evidence: MB 2.42: 'O aunt, even when he will deserve to be slain, I will pardon an hundred offences of his. Grieve thou not.' (This is the pack's evidence excerpt verbatim.)

statements.claim: Bhishma told the tale in the hall at Indraprastha while Shishupala stood before the assembly burning with pride in that very promise, and concluded: 'Even thus, O Bhima... is this wretch of a king, Shishupala of wicked heart, who, proud of the boon granted by Govinda, summons you to battle.'
statements.evidence: MB 2.42 closing: 'Even thus, O Bhima, is this wretch of a king—Sisupala of wicked heart, who, proud of the boon granted by Govinda, summons thee to battle!'

statements.claim: Closing reflection: the hundred offences had been counted out over the years in slights, mockeries and open insults, and the count was nearly spent.
statements.evidence: Forward-looking gloss consistent with the granted boon of a hundred pardons and Shishupala's insults at the Rajasuya, but the tallying itself is not in MB 2.42 (it belongs to the episode's continuation).

DKS_0392.notes: No unsupported or contradicted claims; MB 2.42 (Bhishma's narration of Shishupala's birth, the omens, the incorporeal voice, the thousand laps, the boon of a hundred pardons) is followed closely, including the direct dialogue.

statements.claim: The divine sage Narada appeared in Krishna's hall at Dwaraka, radiant, with matted locks the color of tawny flame, and the assembly stirred at his coming.
statements.evidence: SB 10.70.31-46 (pack excerpt): 'The divine sage Narada, radiant with matted tawny locks, appears in the assembly and is honored by Krishna.' Location Dwaraka is the chapter setting and the corpus index's location for this story.

statements.claim: Krishna rose and received him with the rites, had a seat set for him, and waited until the sage was at ease before he spoke.
statements.evidence: SB 10.70.33: sabhājayitvā vidhi-vat kṛtāsana-parigraham (he honored him according to rule, [the sage] having taken/provided a seat).

statements.claim: Krishna asked: 'Is there any fear today in the three worlds? For nothing is hidden from you among the worlds and those who rule them.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.70.34-35: api svid adya lokānāṁ trayāṇām akuto-bhayam / na hi te 'viditaṁ kiñcil lokeṣv īśvara-kartṛṣu (is there today for the three worlds freedom from fear from anywhere? — nothing is unknown to you among the worlds and their rulers).

statements.claim: Narada answered: 'Who is able to know your doings rightly? You create this world through your own power of illusion and draw it back again; you bring release to the soul that wanders, ignorant, through the body that carries it toward misfortune.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.70.37-38: tavehitaṁ ko 'rhati sādhu vedituṁ sva-māyayedaṁ sṛjato niyacchataḥ / jīvasya yaḥ saṁsarato vimokṣaṇaṁ na jānato 'nartha-vahāc charīrataḥ.

statements.claim: Narada announced: 'I will proclaim before the world this play within the world of mortals. The Pandava Yudhishthira, your cousin, desiring imperial sovereignty, will worship you with the Rajasuya, the sacrifice of emperors. In that best of rites even the gods and all who dwell near you are purified — by hearing of you, by chanting your name, by meditating upon you.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.70.39-42: athāpy āśrāvaye ... nara-loka-viḍambanam / yakṣyati tvāṁ makhendreṇa rājasūyena pāṇḍavaḥ / ... śravaṇāt kīrtanād dhyānāt pūyante 'nte-vasāyinaḥ; 'your cousin / desiring imperial sovereignty' per pack excerpt.

statements.claim: Narada praised Krishna's fame — spotless in heaven and spread through the lower worlds and upon the earth, a blessing to the worlds, a canopy over the quarters — and said the water that has washed his feet purifies the universe: in heaven it is called Mandakini, in the worlds below Bhogavati, and here upon the earth, Ganga.
statements.evidence: SB 10.70.43: yasyāmalaṁ divi yaśaḥ prathitaṁ rasāyāṁ bhūmau ca te bhuvana-maṅgala dig-vitānam / mandākinīti divi bhogavatīti cādho gaṅgeti ceha caraṇāmbu punāti viśvam.

statements.claim: Narada then delivered his request: Yudhishthira would perform the Rajasuya and Krishna should consent to it and come to the sacrifice, whose heart his presence would be.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt/index: Narada 'announces that Krishna's cousin Yudhishthira... will worship Krishna with the Rajasuya sacrifice, and that Krishna should consent', 'requesting Krishna's consent and presence.' The 'presence would be its heart' clause is connective elaboration of the same request.

statements.claim: Krishna, who knows everything before it is spoken, received the announcement as though it were news and, like one playfully seeking advice on a matter already decided, turned to Uddhava, his friend and minister, and asked him what he thought.
statements.evidence: SB 10.70.46: ity upāmantrito bhartrā sarva-jñenāpi mugdha-vat (though all-knowing, addressed as if bewildered); pack excerpt: 'Krishna then playfully asks Uddhava for his counsel.'

statements.claim: Closing: Uddhava would not be long in answering — Krishna's question was a decision already made, and the road from Dwaraka to Indraprastha would be traveled again, bearing the Yadavas and their lord to the sacrifice of emperors.
statements.evidence: Forward-looking closure consistent with SB 10.71 (Krishna's journey to Indraprastha with the Yadavas) and the corpus chain (DKS_0394), but not itself stated in SB 10.70.31-46.

DKS_0393.notes: No unsupported or contradicted claims; SB 10.70.31-46 rendered closely (Narada's visit, Krishna's question, Narada's praise and announcement of the Rajasuya, the Mandakini/Bhogavati/Ganga foot-water stanza, Krishna's playful question to Uddhava).

statements.claim: The treasury of Indraprastha had grown so heavy that no one imagined it could be emptied in a hundred years.
statements.evidence: MB 2.32: 'The large treasure room of the king became so much filled with hoards of wealth virtuously obtained that it could not be emptied even in a hundred years.'

statements.claim: In those days of Yudhishthira's rule, clouds poured exactly as much rain as the people wished, fields and herds and trade flourished, and the kingdom knew no drought, flood, plague, or fire.
statements.evidence: MB 2.32: 'clouds in his kingdom poured as much rain as the people desired, and the cities and the town became highly prosperous... cattle bleeding, agriculture and trade prospered highly... There were no droughts and floods and plagues and fires and premature deaths.'

statements.claim: Even thieves and cheats gave up lying when they dealt with each other, and foreign kings came to the court only to serve, to worship, or to offer tribute that would not impoverish them — never to fight.
statements.evidence: MB 2.32: 'even robbers and cheats never spoke lies amongst themselves... It was only for doing agreeable services, or for worshipping, or for offering tributes that would not impoverish, that other kings used to approach Yudhisthira (and not for hostility or battle).'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira's friends and ministers approached, each separately and all together, urging the sacrifice without delay, and Yudhishthira, weighing his treasury, fixed his heart on the Rajasuya.
statements.evidence: MB 2.32: 'His friends and officers, each separately and all together, approaching him said,--"The time hath come, O exalted one, for thy sacrifice. Let arrangements... be made without loss of time."' and 'the son of Kunti... fixed his heart upon the celebration of a sacrifice.'

statements.claim: The Rajasuya was a sacrifice that belonged to emperors, said to purify everything it touched.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.1-10 excerpt: Yudhishthira 'wishes to perform the purifying Rajasuya sacrifice'; MB 2.32: Krishna says 'Thou... deservest imperial dignity. Let, therefore, the great sacrifice be performed by thee.'

statements.claim: Krishna came to Indraprastha at the head of a great host, chariot wheels rattling, bringing a large mass of treasure — an inexhaustible ocean of gems — and leaving the Yadava army in Vasudeva's command.
statements.evidence: MB 2.32: 'having appointed Vasudeva to the command of the (Yadava) army, and bringing with him for the king Yudhishthira just a large mass of treasure... himself surrounded by a mighty host and filling the atmosphere with the rattle of his chariot-wheels... that inexhaustible ocean of gems he had brought.'

statements.claim: The capital was gladdened by his presence the way a dark region is gladdened by the sun, or still air by a gentle breeze.
statements.evidence: MB 2.32: 'The capital of the Bharata was gladdened by Krishna's presence just as a dark region is rendered joyful by the sun or a region of still air by a gentle breeze.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira stood before the seated Krishna with Dhaumya, Dwaipayana and the other sacrificial priests, and with Bhima, Arjuna and the twins.
statements.evidence: MB 2.32: 'the son of Pandu, with Dhaumya and Dwaipayana and the other sacrificial priests and with Bhima and Arjuna and the twins, addressed Krishna.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira told Krishna the whole earth was under his sway for Krishna's sake, that his wealth came through Krishna's grace, and asked permission to celebrate the sacrifice with his brothers, inviting Krishna to install himself at the rite or to permit Yudhishthira's own installation.
statements.evidence: MB 2.32: 'O Krishna it is for thee that the whole earth is under my sway... it is through thy grace that vast wealth had been got by me... I desire to devote that wealth according to the ordinance, unto superior Brahmanas and the carrier of sacrificial libations... grant me permission to celebrate a sacrifice... install thyself at that sacrifice... Or... permit me to be installed at the sacrifice along with these my younger brothers.'

statements.claim: Krishna answered that Yudhishthira deserved imperial dignity, that after conquering all the kings and gathering the requisites the sacrifice should be performed and none could surpass him in splendor, not even the gods, and asked to be employed in some office, saying he would obey all commands.
statements.evidence: MB 2.32: 'Thou... deservest imperial dignity. Let... the great sacrifice be performed by thee... Employ me also in some office... I should obey all thy commands.' BP 10.72.1-10 excerpt: 'after conquering all the kings and gathering the requisites the sacrifice should be performed, and... none can surpass Yudhishthira in splendor, not even the gods.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira replied that his resolve was already crowned with fruit since Krishna had arrived agreeably to his wish.
statements.evidence: MB 2.32: 'Yudhisthira replied--O Krishna, my resolve is already crowned with fruit, and success also is surely mine, when thou, O Harishikesa, hast arrived here agreeably to my wish!'

statements.claim: Commanded by Krishna, Yudhishthira and his brothers collected the materials for the Rajasuya, and the first order went to Sahadeva and all his ministers to appoint persons to gather the needed articles.
statements.evidence: MB 2.32: 'Commanded by Krishna, the son of Pandu along with his brothers set himself upon collecting the materials for the performance of the Rajasuya sacrifice... commanded Sahadeva... and all ministers also, saying,--Let persons be appointed to collect without loss of time, all those article[s].'

statements.claim: "Yet no one thought of that wealth as greed made visible" and the closing image of the brothers measuring what the world owed them.
statements.evidence: Moralizing/atmospheric framing of the kingdom's prosperity and the turn toward conquest; no specific source claim.

DKS_0394.notes: Blends MB 2.32 (prosperity, arrival, dialogue) with BP 10.72 (purifying Rajasuya, 'none can surpass even the gods'); both are cited in the pack. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: Yudhishthira sent Sahadeva to the south, Nakula to the west, Arjuna to the north, and Bhima to the east.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (BP 10.72.11-13): 'Sahadeva to the south, Nakula to the west, Arjuna to the north, and Bhima to the east'; Sanskrit v.12: 'sahadevaṃ dakṣiṇasyām ādiśat' (Sahadeva dispatched southwards).

statements.claim: Sahadeva, the youngest, was sent with the Srijnayas, his allied warriors.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.12: 'sahadevaṃ dakṣiṇasyām ādiśat saha sṛñjayaiḥ' (dispatched Sahadeva southwards together with the Srijnayas); Sahadeva being the youngest Pandava is standard within the corpus.

statements.claim: The brothers vanquished the kings of the four quarters and carried back abundant wealth for the sacrifice.
statements.evidence: BP 10.72.13: 'te vijitya nṛpān vīrā ājahrur digbhya ojasā' (those heroes, having conquered the kings, brought wealth from the directions); pack excerpt: 'They vanquish the kings and bring back abundant wealth for the sacrifice.'

statements.claim: From every direction the tribute moved toward Indraprastha, and the returning brothers' wealth poured into the treasury.
statements.evidence: Pack summary: 'they return laden with tribute for the sacrifice'; index excerpt: 'they return laden with tribute.'

statements.claim: Directional color — southern kings' 'ancient thrones,' western 'sea kingdoms and the sunset,' northern 'mountain kings' in their passes, eastern quarter 'of the rising sun' — and the homecoming descriptions (wagons heavy, wealth of sea/mountain lords).
statements.evidence: Atmospheric elaboration consistent with each brother's assigned quarter; the pack gives no per-direction campaign detail.

statements.claim: The priests rehearsed rites, craftsmen raised halls, and Indraprastha waited and questioned travelers for news while the brothers were away.
statements.evidence: Generic connective scene-setting for the interval of the campaigns; not contradicted by the pack.

DKS_0395.notes: Evidence pack is thin (only vv.12-13 in Sanskrit); the individual direction assignments for Nakula/Arjuna/Bhima rest on the pack's own excerpt and index summary, which the story follows exactly. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Shishupala, son of Damaghosha, king of Chedi, rose from his seat, raised his arm, and spoke harsh, fearless words, enraged by hearing Krishna's praises.
statements.evidence: BP 10.74.29: 'damaghoṣa-sutaḥ sva-pīṭhād utthāya kṛṣṇa-guṇa-varṇana-jāta-manyuḥ... utkṣipya bāhum... paruṣāṇy abhītaḥ' (son of Damaghosha rose from his seat, anger born of hearing Krishna's virtues described, raised his arm, spoke harsh words fearlessly).

statements.claim: Shishupala mocked the assembly for honoring a cowherd before men of austerity and learning whose sins were burned away by knowledge.
statements.evidence: BP 10.74.31-33: 'yūyaṃ pātra-vidāṃ śreṣṭhā mā mandhvaṃ bāla-bhāṣītam / tapo-vidyā-vrata-dharān jñāna-vidhvasta-kalmaṣān... gopālaḥ kula-pāṃsanaḥ' (do not take this for a child's babble... passing over the austerity/knowledge-bearing, sin-washed lords of the assembly, a cowherd, defiler of his family).

statements.claim: He accused Krishna of abandoning his order — cast out of every duty of caste and stage of life, stripped of all dharma — and spoke of the line of Yayati being cursed and driven out and of lost priestly splendor.
statements.evidence: BP 10.74.34-36: 'varṇāśrama-kulāpetaḥ sarva-dharma-bahiṣ-kṛtaḥ / yayātinaiṣāṃ hi kulaṃ śaptaṃ sadbhir bahiṣ-kṛtam / brahmarṣi-sevitān deśān hitvaite 'brahma-varcasam.'

statements.claim: Shishupala mocked Krishna's deeds — slaying a vulture in infancy was nothing remarkable, and holding up Govardhan for a week was like an anthill to a strong man.
statements.evidence: MB 2.41: 'If Krishna in his infancy slew a vulture, what is there remarkable in that... what is there remarkable in this one's having supported for a week the Govardhan mount which is like an anthill?'

statements.claim: He spoke of Jarasandha, the great king slain in his own city, calling the slayer a wretch of the Vrishni race who killed him unrighteously.
statements.evidence: MB 2.37: 'This wretch born in the race of the Vrishnis unrighteously slew of old the illustrious king Jarasandha.'

statements.claim: The sages in the hall stopped their ears at the blasphemy and cursed him; the angry Pandavas — Bhima blazing — rose with their allies the Matsyas, Kaikayas and Srijnayas to slay him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.74.38-40 (assembly hears the unbearable censure; 'tataḥ pāṇḍu-sutāḥ kruddhā matsya-kaikaya-sṛñjayāḥ'); pack index: 'The assembled sages stop their ears and curse him, and the enraged Pandavas and their allies rise with weapons to slay him'; MB 2.41: 'Bhimasena endued with energy became angry.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira pleaded with Shishupala that his words were scarcely proper, sinful and needlessly cruel, that he should not insult Bhishma, and that the older kings approved the worship of Krishna, whom Bhishma knows truly.
statements.evidence: MB 2.37, Yudhishthira's speech nearly verbatim: 'what thou hast said is scarcely proper for thee... highly sinful and needlessly cruel. Insult not Bhishma... these many kings, older than thou art, all approve of the worship offered unto Krishna... Bhishma knoweth Krishna truly. Thou knowest him not so well.'

statements.claim: Bhishma said that he who disapproves the worship of Krishna, the oldest one in the universe, deserves neither soft words nor conciliation; that every king in the assembly had been vanquished by Krishna's energy; that Krishna deserves worship by the three worlds; that the first worship was offered for his fame, heroism and success; and that Shishupala is a mere boy who does not know Krishna.
statements.evidence: MB 2.37, Bhishma's speech nearly verbatim: 'He that approveth not the worship offered unto Krishna, the oldest one in the universe, deserveth neither soft words nor conciliation... I do not behold in this assembly of kings even one ruler of men who hath not been vanquished in battle by the energy of this son of the Satwata race... he deserveth to be worshipped by the three worlds also... We have offered unto him the first worship because of his fame, his heroism, his success... This Sisupala is a mere boy and hence he knoweth not Krishna.'

statements.claim: The mighty-armed Bhishma caught hold of Shishupala, as Mahadeva seizes his own son.
statements.evidence: MB 2.41: 'the mighty-armed Bhishma caught him like Mahadeva seizing Mahasena.'

statements.claim: The king of Chedi stood unperturbed, seized sword and shield, and stood ready in the middle of the hall.
statements.evidence: BP 10.74.41: 'tataś caidyas tv asambhrānto jagṛhe khaḍga-carmaṇī' (then the Chedi king, unperturbed, seized sword and shield).

statements.claim: 'His face black with fury' and the closing metaphor of a storm gathered over one figure.
statements.evidence: Visual/atmospheric embellishment of the rage attested in BP 10.74.29; no specific sourceable fact.

DKS_0397.notes: Blends BP 10.74.29-41 (outburst, assembly reaction, sword-and-shield) with MB 2.37 (conciliation speeches) and MB 2.41 (mockery, Bhishma's seizure) — all listed as this story's sources. Follows the BP variant (Shishupala stays and seizes weapons) rather than MB 2.37's departure line; consistent with the pack's canonical event and the next story (Krishna Slays Shishupala). No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: It was Krishna — the lord of the lords of yoga, as the chronicle names him — who completed the great Rajasuya rite for the king.
statements.evidence: BP 10.74.47: 'sādhayitvā kratu rājñaḥ kṛṣṇo yogeśvareśvaraḥ' (Krishna, lord of the lords of yoga, having accomplished the sacrifice for the king).

statements.claim: Krishna bestowed ample gifts without stint on the officiating priests and all who had sat in the assembly; no one who served the rite went away empty-handed.
statements.evidence: BP 10.74.46: 'ṛtvigbhyaḥ sa-sadasyebhyo dakṣiṇāṃ vipulām adāt' (he gave ample dakshina to the priests together with the assembly members).

statements.claim: The avabhritha, the concluding bath, followed, and Yudhishthira bathed and was cleansed.
statements.evidence: BP 10.74.50: 'rājasūyāvabhṛthyena snāto rājā yudhiṣṭhiraḥ' (king Yudhishthira bathed with the Rajasuya's avabhritha).

statements.claim: Krishna stayed on in Indraprastha month after month and, when he asked leave, Yudhishthira was reluctant to give it; Krishna departed toward his own city (Dwaraka).
statements.evidence: BP 10.74.48: 'tato 'nujñāpya rājānam anicchantam apīśvaraḥ' (then, taking leave of the unwilling king, the Lord departed); pack excerpt: 'after some months takes leave of the reluctant Yudhishthira and returns to his own city.'

statements.claim: Gods, men and the beings of the air, every one of them honored by the king as they departed, carried away praise of Krishna and of the sacrifice.
statements.evidence: BP 10.74.51: 'rājñā sabhājitāḥ sarve sura-mānava-khecarāḥ' (all gods, men and sky-goers were honored by the king); pack excerpt: 'All the assembled guests depart praising Krishna and the sacrifice.'

statements.claim: One guest alone differed: Duryodhana — the wicked one, the strife itself, the disease of the Kuru line — could not endure the Pandavas' prosperity and carried his grievance toward Hastinapura.
statements.evidence: BP 10.74.52: 'duryodhanam ṛte pāpaṃ kaliṃ kuru-kulāmayam' (except wicked Duryodhana, the Kali [strife], the disease of the Kuru race); pack excerpt: 'except the wicked Duryodhana, who could not endure the Pandavas' prosperity'; return to Hastinapura/Gajahvaya consistent with BP 10.75.38 ('prayayau gajāhvayam').

statements.claim: Closing speculation that Duryodhana 'would spend the coming months trying to undo' the Pandavas' greatness, and that his grievance 'arrived before any of the praise did.'
statements.evidence: Foreshadowing/atmosphere consistent with the envy the pack attests; not a specific sourceable fact in 10.74.46-52.

DKS_0399.notes: All key claims map 1:1 onto BP 10.74.46-52 and the pack excerpt. The 'fires... allowed to grow quiet' and emperor-crowning imagery are atmospheric connective narration. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: The assembly hall in which Duryodhana was deceived was built by Maya, the great architect, for Yudhishthira.
statements.evidence: BP 10.75.33: 'sabhāyāṃ maya-kḷptāyāṃ' (in the hall fashioned by Maya).

statements.claim: Duryodhana came to Yudhishthira's sacrifice with his brothers and burned with envy at the splendor of the palace.
statements.evidence: BP 10.75.30-31: 'vīkṣya duryodhanaḥ śriyam... viṣakta-hṛdayaḥ kuru-rāḍ atapyat' (Duryodhana, seeing the splendor, the Kuru king burned, his heart poisoned); 10.75.35: 'tatra duryodhano mānī parīto bhrātṛbhir' (proud Duryodhana, surrounded by his brothers); presence at the Rajasuya established by DKS_0399 (BP 10.74.52) and the corpus chain.

statements.claim: The hall's splendor seemed gathered from the wealth of earthly kings, lords of demons, and Indra himself.
statements.evidence: BP 10.75.31: 'yasmiṃs narendra-ditijendra-surendra-lakṣmīr nānā vibhānti' (in which the glories of earthly kings, lord of the demons and lord of the gods shone variously).

statements.claim: Duryodhana, seeing crystal floor as water, gathered his garment to keep it dry and stepped forward onto hard, dry crystal.
statements.evidence: BP 10.75.36: 'sthale 'bhyagṛhṇād vastrāntaṃ jalaṃ matvā' (on dry ground he lifted the hem of his garment, taking it for water); pack excerpt: 'mistakes a crystal floor for water and lifts his garment.'

statements.claim: Then, before a real pool so clear it seemed to continue as floor, Duryodhana walked into the water and fell.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'then falls where he thought the floor was, deceived by the illusion'; index summary: 'mistakes water for floor and falls.'

statements.claim: Bhima laughed first and loudest, and the women of the court and the other kings laughed with him, though Yudhishthira made a sign for restraint.
statements.evidence: BP 10.75.37: 'jahāsa bhīmas taṃ dṛṣṭvā striyo nṛpatayo pare' (Bhima laughed seeing him; the women and the other kings too); pack excerpt: 'Bhima and the women laugh despite the king's restraint.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana, ashamed and blazing with rage, departed in silence and returned to Hastinapura.
statements.evidence: BP 10.75.38: 'sa vrīḍito 'vag-vadano ruṣā jvalan niṣkramya tūṣṇīṃ prayayau gajāhvayam' (he, ashamed, face downcast, blazing with rage, went out silently and departed to Gajahvaya [Hastinapura]).

statements.claim: Krishna watched in silence, intent on relieving the burden the earth carried, and let Duryodhana carry the humiliation home.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'while Krishna remains silent, intent on relieving the earth's burden'; Krishna is listed among the story's characters in the pack index.

statements.claim: 'Duryodhana, king of Hastinapura' — royal title applied to Duryodhana.
statements.evidence: The pack's own Sanskrit verses style him as ruler: BP 10.75.31 'kuru-rāḍ' and 10.75.35 'nṛpa'; the phrase is consistent with source usage.

statements.claim: Servants hiding smiles, the hall as 'a second heaven,' and the closing reflections on the slow work of the kings' pride.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric connective narration around the attested deception and laughter; no specific source claim.

DKS_0400.notes: The two-step illusion (crystal-as-water, then water-as-floor) follows the pack excerpt/index reading of BP 10.75.36 and the classic account. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Shalva was the friend of Shishupala, whom Krishna had struck down at the Rajasuya sacrifice.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.1: 'śiśupāla-sakhaḥ śālvo' (Shalva, friend of Shishupala); Shishupala's slaying at the Rajasuya is the prior corpus event (DKS_0398, BP 10.74.42-46) referenced by the pack's chain.

statements.claim: Shalva had been at Rukmini's wedding in the company that came to claim her and went away defeated; the Yadavas had humbled him once and now killed his friend.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.1: 'rukmiṇy-udvāha āgataḥ' (he had come to Rukmini's wedding); pack excerpt: 'who had been defeated at Rukmini's wedding.'

statements.claim: In the hearing of all the kings Shalva vowed to make the earth empty of Yadavas.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.2: 'śālvaḥ pratijñām akaroc chṛṇvatāṃ sarva-bhūbhujām' (Shalva made a vow in the hearing of all kings); pack excerpt: 'vows before the kings to make the earth devoid of Yadavas.'

statements.claim: Shalva went to the Himalayas and worshipped Shiva, the Pasupati, husband of Uma, eating nothing but a handful of dust each day for a year.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.3-4: 'devaṃ paśu-patiṃ prabhum... saṃvatsarānte bhagavān āśu-toṣa umā-patiḥ' (he [worshipped] the lord Pasupati; at year's end the quickly-contented Lord, husband of Uma); pack excerpt: 'eating a handful of dust each day, and after a year Shiva, easily pleased, offers him a boon'; Himalayas given as the location in the pack's index entry.

statements.claim: Shalva asked for a citadel that no god, demon, man, gandharva, serpent, or rakshasa could overcome — a city moving through the sky at its master's will.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.5: 'devāsura-manuṣyāṇāṃ gandharvoraga-rakṣasām' (of gods, demons, men, gandharvas, serpents, rakshasas — the list of powers named in the boon); BP 10.76.7: 'sa labdhvā kāma-gaṃ yānaṃ' (he obtained the will-moving vehicle).

statements.claim: Shiva consented and gave the making of the city to Maya, the architect called the conqueror of enemy cities, who built Saubha — dark, hard to assail, moving at its master's will.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.6-7: 'tatheti giriśādiṣṭo mayaḥ para-puraṃ-jayaḥ / sa labdhvā kāma-gaṃ yānaṃ tamo-dhāma durāsadam' ('so be it'; commanded by the mountain-lord, Maya the conqueror of enemy cities; he obtained the will-moving vehicle, the abode of darkness, difficult to assail).

statements.claim: The wise named it the abode of darkness, for it sailed wrapped in a gloom of its own.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.7: 'tamo-dhāma' (abode of darkness) is the source's own epithet for Saubha.

statements.claim: Shalva's purpose in obtaining Saubha was vengeance against Dwaraka and the house of the Yadavas.
statements.evidence: Vow to empty the earth of Yadavas (BP 10.76.2) plus the siege of Krishna's city that immediately follows in BP 10.76.8-11 and DKS_0402; Dwaraka listed as target in the pack index.

statements.claim: Growth thin as a shadow through a year of snows, and the 'easily pleased' gloss on Shiva.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric elaboration of the year-long austerity (BP 10.76.3-4); 'āśu-toṣa' (swiftly contented) supports the character gloss.

DKS_0401.notes: The 'iron' quality of Saubha is carried over from the corpus chain titles ('flying iron city'); nothing in the pack contradicts it (BP here stresses tamo-dhāma and durāsadam). No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Shalva came to Dwaraka in the self-moving, impenetrable flying city Saubha with a vast army and besieged the city.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.7-8: 'sa labdhvā kāma-gaṃ yānaṃ tamo-dhāma durāsadam / nirudhya senayā śālvo mahatyā' (having obtained the will-moving vehicle, the hard-to-assail abode of darkness, Shalva besieged with a great army); pack excerpt: 'Shalva flies to Dwaraka... and with a vast army.'

statements.claim: Shalva remembered the enmity of the Vrishnis — his friend Shishupala dead at the Rajasuya and his own defeat at Rukmini's wedding.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Shalva flies to Dwaraka remembering the enmity of the Vrishnis'; the specific grievances are established in DKS_0401's pack (BP 10.76.1-2).

statements.claim: From Saubha there rained weapons, stones, whole trees torn up by the roots, thunderbolts that split the towers, serpents, and showers of gravel.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.10: 'śilā-drumāś cāśanayaḥ sarpā āsāra-śarkarāḥ' (stones, trees, thunderbolts, serpents, showers of gravel).
