statements.claim: The gardens and famous groves were shredded; gates, walls, palaces, ramparts and upper terraces were shattered, dented and cracked.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.9: 'sa-gopurāṇi dvārāṇi prāsādāṭṭāla-tolikāḥ' (the gates with their towers, palaces, ramparts, upper terraces); pack excerpt: 'shatters its gardens and gates'; BP 10.76.11: 'ity ardyamānā saubhena kṛṣṇasya nagarī bhṛśam' (thus Krishna's city was severely afflicted by Saubha).

statements.claim: Pradyumna, Krishna's son by Rukmini, seeing his people afflicted, mounted his chariot and cried 'Do not fear,' rallying the city.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.12: 'pradyumno bhagavān vīkṣya bādhyamānā nijāḥ prajāḥ' (the blessed Pradyumna, seeing his own people afflicted); pack excerpt: 'mounts his chariot and cries "Do not fear"'; Rukmini's son per BP 10.76.16 ('rukmiṇī-sutaḥ').

statements.claim: Satyaki, Charudeshna, Samba, and Akrura with his younger brothers sallied forth, followed by the great archers and leaders of the chariot troops.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.13-14: 'sātyakiś cārudeṣṇaś ca sāmbo 'krūraḥ sahānujaḥ / apare ca maheṣv-āsā ratha-yūthapa-yūthapāḥ.'

statements.claim: A battle raged between Shalva's host and the Yadavas; Pradyumna countered the illusions of the lord of Saubha with divine weapons.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.15-16: 'tataḥ pravavṛte yuddhaṃ śālvānāṃ yadubhiḥ saha / tāś ca saubha-pater māyā divyāstrai rukmiṇī-sutaḥ.'

statements.claim: Krishna was not among the defenders: he had gone to Indraprastha, summoned by Yudhishthira for the sacrifice, and no news of the siege had reached him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.5: 'indraprasthaṃ gataḥ kṛṣṇa āhūto dharma-sūnunā' (Krishna had gone to Indraprastha, summoned by Dharma's son — cited in DKS_0403's pack and the corpus chain); DKS_0403's pack excerpt confirms he learned of the attack only by omens, i.e. not by news.

statements.claim: Terror as Shalva's real weapon — a siege from the sky that could not be answered — and the description of the city as 'golden... by the sea.'
statements.evidence: Interpretive framing of the terror the pack's summary attests ('terrifying its people'); Dwaraka's seaside setting is standard within the corpus.

DKS_0402.notes: Krishna's absence is grounded in the immediate successor passage (BP 10.77.5, in DKS_0403's pack) and the pack's variant note, since DKS_0402's own excerpt narrates only the siege. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Krishna had gone to Indraprastha, summoned by Yudhishthira for the Rajasuya.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.5: 'indraprasthaṃ gataḥ kṛṣṇa āhūto dharma-sūnunā' (Krishna had gone to Indraprastha, summoned by Dharma's son); pack excerpt: 'Krishna, summoned to Indraprastha for the Rajasuya.'

statements.claim: Krishna took leave of the elders of the Kurus, the sages, and Pritha his aunt with her sons.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.6: 'kuru-vṛddhān anujñāpya munīṃś ca sa-sutāṃ pṛthām' (taking leave of the Kuru elders, the sages, and Pritha with her sons); Pritha (Kunti) is Krishna's aunt, and the Pandavas are 'her sons.'

statements.claim: Krishna perceived dire omens that his own people were in danger and hurried back to Dwaraka.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'returns to Dwaraka perceiving dire omens'; BP 10.77.8: 'vīkṣya tat kadanaṃ svānāṃ' (seeing the slaughter of his own people).

statements.claim: On arrival Krishna saw the ruin of his own people and understood that the allies of the Chaidya — the friends of the slain Shishupala — had attacked his city while he was away.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'realizing the Chaidya's allies have attacked his city'; BP 10.77.8: 'vīkṣya tat kadanaṃ svānāṃ nirūpya pura-rakṣaṇam.'

statements.claim: Krishna ordered Daruka, his charioteer: 'Bring my chariot. Quickly. Straight to Shalva,' and Daruka drove the chariot out against Shalva.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.9-10: 'rathaṃ prāpaya me sūta śālvasyāntikam āśu vai... ity uktaś codayām āsa ratham āsthāya dārukaḥ' (Bring my chariot, O charioteer, quickly to Shalva; thus addressed, Daruka mounted and drove the chariot).

statements.claim: Shalva's army was already nearly broken by the Yadava princes when Krishna arrived.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.11: 'hata-prāya-baleśvaraḥ' (whose forces were nearly destroyed).

statements.claim: Shalva hurled a blazing spear at Daruka, the charioteer, which came down like a great meteor.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'hurls a blazing spear at Krishna's charioteer'; BP 10.77.12: 'tām āpatantīṃ nabhasi maholkām iva raṃhasā' (it fell from the sky with the speed of a great meteor).

statements.claim: Krishna's arrows met the spear in mid-air and cut it into a hundred pieces.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'which Krishna cuts to a hundred pieces with his arrows.'

statements.claim: Krishna pierced Shalva with sixteen shafts, and the flying city Saubha reeled through the sky.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.13: 'taṃ ca ṣoḍaśabhir viddhvā bānaiḥ saubhaṃ ca khe bhramat' (piercing him with sixteen arrows, and Saubha wandered in the sky).

statements.claim: Shalva's arrow struck Krishna's left arm — the arm holding Sharnga — and a great cry of lamentation went up from the beings watching.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.14-15: 'śālvaḥ śaures tu doḥ savyaṃ sa-śārṅgaṃ śārṅga-dhanvanaḥ / hāhā-kāro mahān āsīd bhūtānāṃ tatra paśyatām' (Shalva [struck] the left arm of Shauri together with Sharnga, of the bearer of the Sharnga bow; a great cry of lamentation arose from the beings watching there).

statements.claim: His people fought on without him while he was away, and the siege continued until Krishna's return.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.15 (battle of Shalva's host with the Yadus) narrated before Krishna's arrival in BP 10.77; consistent with DKS_0402.

statements.claim: The claim that the battle 'rose into the sky' and that Krishna 'brought the war its answer' by pressing on.
statements.evidence: Forward-looking connective narration consistent with Saubha reeling in the sky (BP 10.77.13) and the continuation of the duel in subsequent verses; not a specific sourceable assertion within 10.77.5-18.

statements.claim: 'In the middle of the honors and ceremonies of the Rajasuya' as the timing of Krishna's departure.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.5-6 places the summons at the Rajasuya visit; DKS_0399's pack had Krishna lingering in Indraprastha after the rite, so the exact phase of the ceremony is a connective gloss — the siege-during-the-Rajasuya-visit frame is what 10.77.5 supports.

DKS_0403.notes: Cross-story note: DKS_0399's pack (BP 10.74.48) has Krishna leave Indraprastha after the completed Rajasuya, while DKS_0402/0403 (BP 10.77.5) have the siege occur during his Rajasuya summons — a telescoping present in the source itself; each story is faithful to its own pack. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: A weeping man runs to Krishna's chariot crying 'Krishna, Krishna, mighty-armed one! Your father — you who love your father!' and reports that Shalva has broken into Dwaraka and carried off Vasudeva like an animal.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.21-22 (krsna krsna maha-baho pita te pitr-vatsala); pack excerpt: 'A man appears weeping and tells Krishna that Shalva has carried off his father Vasudeva like an animal.'

statements.claim: Krishna had hurried back from Indraprastha after omens of danger reached him during his cousin's great sacrifice, and found Shalva attacking with the flying city Saubha; since his return they had fought a running duel across the sea.
statements.evidence: Corpus chain (DKS_0403): 'Returning from Indraprastha and seeing evil omens, Krishna hurries to Dwaraka... and joins the fight'; MB 3.21 duel narrative in pack.

statements.claim: Shalva hurled iron javelins, flaming lances and heavy clubs, and Krishna cut each into two or three pieces so the sea rained splinters.
statements.evidence: MB 3.21 (pack): 'that wicked one hurled at me Sataghnis, and mighty maces, and flaming lances, and stout clubs... I speedily resisted them with my swift arrows, and cut them in two or three pieces.'

statements.claim: Krishna hurled his mace at Shalva; when it came spinning back, the sky where Shalva had stood was empty and his war-cries came from everywhere.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.19-20: struck Shalva with his mace of terrible velocity; when the mace returned (gadayam sannivrttayam) Shalva disappeared (salvas tv antaradhīyata).

statements.claim: Shalva then appeared holding an old man in Vasudeva's robes, taunted 'Here is your father!... Save him, if you can!', and beheaded the old man before Krishna.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.25-26: 'esa te janita tato yad-artham iha jivasi' and Shalva (mayavi) strikes with his sword; pack excerpt: 'Shalva then seems to behead Vasudeva before Krishna, taunting him to save him if he can.'

statements.claim: For a moment Krishna took on the human mood and was grief-stricken, thinking only of the fallen father.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.22,27: nisamya vipriyam krsno manusim prakrtim gatah; 'tato muhurtam prakrtav upaplutah sva-bodha aste sva-jananusangatah' — for a moment overwhelmed by attachment, he remained absorbed in his own awareness.

statements.claim: Looking again, Krishna saw no messenger, no body, no head, no blood — only the sky with Saubha — and perceived it was the demon's sorcery, Maya; the father he had mourned was safe and the death had never happened.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.28: 'na tatra dutam na pituh kalevaram prabuddha ajau samapasyad acyutah' (no messenger, no father's corpse); pack excerpt: 'perceives it to be the demon's sorcery wrought by Maya.'

statements.claim: Krishna raised his bow again and the real battle resumed.
statements.evidence: MB 3.21 (pack): 'recovering my senses, I again began to discharge arrows by hundreds.'

DKS_0404.notes: Battlefield recap (Indraprastha omens, sea duel, Dwaraka 'undefended') is connective recap of the DKS_0403 chain; 'every man in that host knew the report was possible' is inner-state atmosphere, not a factual assertion contradicted by the pack.

statements.claim: Shalva came down one final time rushing at Krishna, and Krishna met him with arrows that pierced his guard, cut through his armor, snapped his bow, and tore the jewel from his crest.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.32 (pack excerpt): 'Krishna pierces the rushing Shalva with arrows, cuts through his armor, bow and crest-jewel.'

statements.claim: Krishna's own horses and charioteer Daruka had earlier stood thick with shafts; the pierced and enfeebled Daruka confessed he could barely hold the reins, and Krishna cheered him, telling him the driver's duty was to stay at the reins.
statements.evidence: MB 3.21 (full text quoted in the DKS_0404 evidence pack of the same Shalva battle): 'Salwa covered Daruka, and my steeds, and my car... with hundreds of straight shafts'; Daruka: 'My body hath become weak!'; 'seeing the charioteer... pierced and enfeebled by the shafts of Salwa... I cheered him up.' Detail belongs to the same duel narrative; not present in DKS_0405's own excerpted passages.

statements.claim: Krishna took up his mace and turned it on the city; Saubha came apart and fell into the water in a thousand fragments, swallowed by the sea.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.33 (pack): 'tat krsna-hasteritaya vicurnitam papata toye gadaya sahasradha' — shattered by the mace hurled from Krishna's hand it fell into the water in a thousand fragments; pack excerpt agrees.

statements.claim: Men would say Saubha went down as Tripura had gone down of old, the triple city shaken from the sky by the great god's shafts.
statements.evidence: MB excerpt in pack: 'it fell like the city of Tripura shaken by the shafts of Maheswara.'

statements.claim: With the city gone, Shalva came at Krishna on foot, mace in hand, and as he rushed in Krishna severed the arm that held the mace.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.34: 'adhavatah sa-gadam tasya bahum bhallena chittva' — severing the arm of the rushing, mace-bearing Shalva.

statements.claim: Krishna raised the discus, which blazed like the sun at the end of the world, and it cut off Shalva's crowned head; where it passed, the enemy burned.
statements.evidence: BP 10.77.35 (pack excerpt): 'wielding his wondrous discus blazing like the sun at world's end, cuts off his crowned head'; MB excerpt: 'with its energy it set the foe ablaze.'

statements.claim: The war was over: the sea smoothed over the scattered stones of Saubha and the sky above Dwaraka was only sky again.
statements.evidence: Closing imagery consistent with the pack's account of Saubha's destruction; phrasing is atmospheric, not a discrete sourceable event.

DKS_0405.notes: Two pack quirks noted: (1) the MB 'passage' quoted under DKS_0405 (3.23) is forest-departure text, but the pack's MB excerpt lines correctly describe the discus cutting Saubha and cleaving Salwa — story follows the BP variant (mace shatters city), matching the pack's own summary; (2) the Daruka anecdote is supported by MB 3.21, quoted in full in the adjacent DKS_0404 evidence pack for the same battle.

statements.claim: On the road home from the war with Shalva, the ground began to shake and a single figure — Dantavakra, mace in hand — approached on foot.
statements.evidence: BP 10.78.1: 'ekah padatih sankruddho gada-panih prakampayan' — alone, on foot, angry, mace in hand, making the earth tremble; pack excerpt: Dantavakra 'rushes at Krishna on foot.'

statements.claim: Dantavakra, kin to the slain Shishupala and friend to the slain Shalva, had come from his kingdom of Karusha to settle the debt of his slain friends, alone and on foot.
statements.evidence: BP 10.78.3 (kārūṣaḥ = king of Karusha) and excerpt: 'Dantavakra, eager to repay his slain friends'; pack summary: attacks 'to avenge Shishupala and Shalva'; verse 4 'tvam matuleyo nah' makes both cousins of Krishna.

statements.claim: Krishna took up his own mace, Kaumodaki, and waited.
statements.evidence: BP 10.78.2 ('gadam adaya satvarah'); pack excerpt names 'his mace Kaumodaki.'

statements.claim: Dantavakra taunted Krishna as a betrayer of friends and kinsman-killer — 'You are our own cousin... you turn on your own kin... I owe my friends a debt... I have come to pay it with your head.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.78.4-6: 'tvam matuleyo nah krsna mitra-dhrung mam jighamsasi / tarhy anrnyam upaimy ajna mitranam mitra-vatsalah' — cousin, betrayer of friends, repaying his debt to friends; killing Shishupala (at the rajasuya) and Shalva is chain-supported context (DKS_0401-0405).

statements.claim: His words were harsh as goads on an elephant, and Krishna heard them without a word.
statements.evidence: BP 10.78.6: 'evam ruksais tudan vakyaih krsnam totrair iva dvipam' — goading Krishna with harsh words like goads on an elephant.

statements.claim: Dantavakra's mace came down on Krishna's head, but Krishna did not move, as though the blow had fallen on a mountain.
statements.evidence: BP 10.78.7: 'gadayabhihato 'py ajau na cacala yadudvahah' — though struck by the mace in battle the Yadu chief did not stir; pack excerpt: 'strikes him on the head with his mace. Unshaken, Krishna...'

statements.claim: Kaumodaki struck Dantavakra square in the chest and crushed it; he staggered, blood pouring from his mouth, and fell, and a subtle, wonderful light rose out of him and entered Krishna.
statements.evidence: BP 10.78.8-9: 'gada-nirbhinna-hrdaya udvaman rudhiram mukhat' (heart shattered by the mace, vomiting blood from the mouth); 'tatah suksmataram jyotih krsnam avisad adbhutam' (then a most subtle light wonderfully entered Krishna).

statements.claim: Viduratha, Dantavakra's brother, grief-stricken, rushed at Krishna, who severed his crowned head with the razor-edged discus.
statements.evidence: BP 10.78.10-11: 'vidurathas tu tad-bhrata bhratr-soka-pariplutah'; 'krsnas cakrena ksura-nemina' — Krishna cut off his head with the razor-edged discus; pack excerpt: 'severs his crowned head with the discus.'

DKS_0406.notes: Setting details ('Dwaraka's walls still a day's march ahead', 'no one on the road') are connective; closing reflections on the light and on vengeance are interpretive, not sourceable facts asserted as events.

statements.claim: In the hall of the Kurus at Hastinapura, Yudhishthira staked his wealth, kingdom, brothers one by one, then himself, and finally Draupadi, losing her too.
statements.evidence: MB 2.66 (pack): herald tells Draupadi 'The king had first staked his brothers, then himself, and then thee.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana commanded the herald (Pratikamin): 'Go, bring Draupadi here. You have nothing to fear from the sons of Pandu.'
statements.evidence: MB 2.66 (pack): 'Go Pratikamin, and bring thou Draupadi hither. Thou hast no fear from the sons of Pandu.'

statements.claim: The herald went unwillingly, like a dog entering a lion's den, and told Draupadi she had been won and must come to Dhritarashtra's house for menial work.
statements.evidence: MB 2.66 (pack): 'like a dog in a lion's den'; 'Yudhishthira having been intoxicated with dice, Duryodhana, O Draupadi, hath won thee... put thee in some menial work.'

statements.claim: Draupadi asked what prince stakes his wife, and sent the herald back to ask the gambler whom he lost first — himself or her.
statements.evidence: MB 2.66 (pack): 'What prince is there who playeth staking his wife?... ask that gambler... whom he hath lost first, himself, or me.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira sat like one demented, deprived of reason, and gave no answer good or ill.
statements.evidence: MB 2.66 (pack): 'Yudhishthira, however sat there like one demented and deprived of reason and gave no answer good or ill to the Suta.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana summoned Draupadi to put her question in the assembly; on the herald's second visit she answered that morality is the one highest object in the world and she would obey whatever the virtuous elders decided.
statements.evidence: MB 2.66 (pack): Duryodhana: 'Let the princess of Panchala come hither and put her question'; Draupadi: 'Morality, however, it hath been said, is the one highest object in the world... I am ready to do what those elderly and virtuous persons... will definitely tell me.'

statements.claim: The kings and elders sat with faces downward, none speaking, knowing the eagerness and resolution of Dhritarashtra's son; Yudhishthira sent word that she should go before her father-in-law and weep.
statements.evidence: MB 2.66 (pack): 'all sat with faces downwards, uttering not a word, knowing the eagerness and resolution of Dhritarashtra's son'; Yudhishthira 'sent a trusted messenger unto Draupadi, directing... she should come before her father-in-law weeping bitterly.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana then sent Dussasana — 'this herald fears Bhima. Go yourself, and bring the daughter of Yajnasena here by force' — and Dussasana, eyes red as blood, told her 'you have been won by us, and won rightly. Accept the Kurus for your lords.'
statements.evidence: MB 2.66 (pack): Duryodhana: 'this son of my Suta... feareth Vrikodara. Therefore, go thou thyself and forcibly bring hither the daughter of Yajnasena'; Dussasana 'rose with blood-red eyes... 'Come, come, O Krishna... thou hast been won by us... come now and accept the Kurus for thy lords.''

statements.claim: When she would not come, Dussasana seized her and dragged her into the hall before the gathered kings and began to strip her in the sight of all.
statements.evidence: Pack index summary and canonical event (evt_0400): 'As Dussasana drags her before the assembly and strips her, Draupadi cries out...'; MB passage shows Dussasana entering her abode and forcing her before the assembly.

statements.claim: Draupadi cried out to Govinda dwelling in Dwaraka, Krishna fond of the cowherds of Vrindavan, Kesava, husband of Lakshmi, lord of Vraja, destroyer of afflictions, Janardana — to rescue her from the Kaurava ocean.
statements.evidence: MB excerpt in pack: 'O Govinda, O thou who dwellest in Dwaraka, O Krishna, O thou who art fond of cow-herdesses... O Kesava, seest thou not that the Kauravas are humiliating me... O Janarddana, rescue me who am sinking in the Kaurava Ocean.'

statements.claim: She called past the assembly and her bound husbands, to the one name that could cross the distance toward the city by the sea.
statements.evidence: Poetic framing of the prayer; no discrete factual assertion beyond the supported cry itself.

DKS_0407.notes: The interpretive sentence on the legal hinge of Draupadi's question ('a man who does not own himself cannot stake his wife') is framing consistent with the passage; closing paragraph is connective atmosphere.

statements.claim: In the Pandava camp at Upaplavya before the war, Yudhishthira spoke for peace; Sahadeva and the mighty car-warrior Satyaki approved, and Bhima too declared for peace; then Draupadi rose to address Krishna.
statements.evidence: MB 5.82 (pack): 'king Drupada's daughter Krishna... applauding Sahadeva and that mighty car-warrior Satyaki, addressed Madhava seated by his side. And beholding Bhimasena declare for peace, that intelligent lady... said.'

statements.claim: Draupadi spoke holding her dishevelled tresses, her black lotus-leaf eyes wet with tears.
statements.evidence: Pack index summary: 'Draupadi, clutching her dishevelled hair'; MB 5.82 (pack): 'of eyes that were black in hue and large like lotus leaves, bathed in tears'; excerpt: 'call to thy mind these tresses of mine seized by Dussasana's rude hands.'

statements.claim: She recalled that the Pandavas had asked only for five villages — Avishthala, Vrikasthala, Makandi, Varanavata, and any fifth — via the message privately delivered to Sanjaya, and Duryodhana would not grant even that.
statements.evidence: MB 5.82 (pack), near-verbatim list of the five villages and the private message to Sanjaya; 'Suyodhana hath not acted according to them.'

statements.claim: She argued that if Duryodhana wanted peace only with the kingdom surrendered there was no need for Krishna to travel to Hastinapura; the Pandavas with the Srinjayas could withstand the Dhritarashtra host, and men unwinnable by conciliation or gifts must be met with severity.
statements.evidence: MB 5.82 (pack): 'there is no necessity of going thither for making such a peace. The Pandavas with the Srinjayas... are quite able to withstand the fierce Dhritarashtra host'; 'should be treated with severity.'

statements.claim: She urged that a Kshatriya true to his order must strike the covetous, with only a Brahmana excepted as preceptor of all orders, and that there is as much sin in sparing one who deserves death as in slaying one who does not.
statements.evidence: MB 5.82 (pack): 'He that is covetous... ought surely to be slain by a Kshatriya... The exception in the case of a Brahmana...'; 'there is equal sin in not slaying one that deserveth to be slain.'

statements.claim: She recounted her identity — daughter of Drupada risen from the sacrificial altar, sister of Dhrishtadyumna, daughter-in-law of Pandu, queen of his five sons, mother of five sons bound to Krishna as Abhimanyu was — and how she was seized by the hair, dragged into the assembly and treated as a slave in Krishna's own lifetime.
statements.evidence: MB 5.82 (pack), matching the identity catalogue and 'I was seized by the hair, dragged into the assembly and insulted in the very sight of the sons of Pandu and in thy life-time... treated as a slave.'

statements.claim: She reminded him how the brothers sat silent while she called on him in her heart ('Save me, O save me!'), how Dhritarashtra offered a boon and she asked only that the Pandavas be freed with cars and weapons, and how they were freed only to be exiled to the woods.
statements.evidence: MB 5.82 (pack): 'in my heart I called upon thee, O Govinda... Save me, O save me!'; 'Let the Pandavas be free men with their cars and weapons'; 'were freed but only to be exiled into the woods.'

statements.claim: She cried 'Fie to Arjuna's bowmanship and fie to Bhima's might, since Duryodhana lives even for a moment,' and asked that his wrath be directed at the sons of Dhritarashtra.
statements.evidence: MB 5.82 (pack): 'Fie to Partha's bowmanship, oh, fie to Bhimasena's might since Duryodhana, O Krishna, liveth for even a moment... let thy wrath, O Krishna, be directed towards the sons of Dhritarashtra.'

statements.claim: Weeping, walking like a cow-elephant, she came and stood before Krishna, waiting for his answer.
statements.evidence: MB 5.82 (pack): 'bathed in tears, and walking like a cow-elephant, approached the lotus-eyed [Krishna].'

DKS_0409.notes: Her plea to inflict punishment 'with the Pandavas and the Srinjayas' and the 'son of Pritha' glory clause are direct paraphrases of the passage; no unsupported or contradicted factual claims found.

statements.claim: Krishna comforted the weeping Draupadi at Upaplavya, telling her she would soon behold the ladies of Bharata's race weeping as she wept, with their husbands and kinsmen slain.
statements.evidence: MB excerpt in pack: 'Soon wilt thou, O Krishna, behold the ladies of Bharata's race weep as thou dost'; index summary: 'swears that the women of the Kuru race will soon weep as she does, with their kinsmen slain.'

statements.claim: He swore that the mountains of Himavat might shift, the earth might split into a hundred fragments, but his words could never be futile.
statements.evidence: MB excerpt in pack: 'The mountains of Himavat might shift their site, the Earth herself might split into a hundred fragments... still my words can never be futile.'

statements.claim: He told her to dry her tears and swore she would soon see her husbands with their enemies slain.
statements.evidence: MB excerpt in pack: 'Stop thy tears, I swear to thee, O Krishna, soon wilt thou see thy husbands, with their enemies slain.'

statements.claim: Her appeal recapped the five villages refused, the seizure by the hair and dragging into the assembly, her cry 'save me, O save me', and freedom that ended in exile.
statements.evidence: Recap of the preceding DKS_0409 episode; every element matches MB 5.82 passage quoted in the pack.

statements.claim: The promise would be answered in the fate of the whole Kuru line: the men who wagered her would fall and their wives would weep as she had.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Krishna: Kuru ladies 'weep as thou dost... with their enemies slain') and index summary; story's elaboration is faithful paraphrase.

statements.claim: The men present recalled that his word had held before in that assembly hall, when her robes streamed out endlessly and no hand could strip her.
statements.evidence: Corpus chain reference to DKS_0408 'Krishna Protects Draupadi with Endless Robes'; allusion, consistent with the corpus narrative.

DKS_0410.notes: MB 5.82 passage displayed in the pack is Draupadi's preceding speech; Krishna's comforting vow is carried by the pack's excerpt of the same chapter. Metaphors ('the two were of the same fabric', 'settled like a stone') are connective.

statements.claim: At Upaplavya the brothers gathered around Krishna and pressed him to carry their cause to Hastinapura; Bhima and Nakula each spoke entrusting the family's hope to him before Arjuna rose.
statements.evidence: Pack index summary: 'Bhima, Arjuna and Nakula each address Krishna, urging him to seek peace with the Kauravas and entrusting their cause to him.' (No speeches of Bhima/Nakula are quoted in the pack passage, which contains only Arjuna's words; the story gives them no quoted content either.)

statements.claim: Arjuna said Yudhishthira had already said what should be said, but that Krishna seemed not to think peace easily obtainable — whether from Dhritarashtra's covetousness or the Pandavas' present weakness — and that nothing should be regarded as impracticable.
statements.evidence: MB 5.78 (pack), close paraphrase of Arjuna's opening.

statements.claim: Arjuna urged Krishna to strive for peace, as the foremost friend of both Pandavas and Kurus, even as Prajapati is friend of both gods and Asuras; 'as soon as thou goest thither, it will be accomplished.'
statements.evidence: MB 5.78 (pack), verbatim: 'foremost of all friends of both the Pandavas and the Kurus, even as Prajapati is of both the gods and the Asuras... As soon as thou goest thither, it will be accomplished.'

statements.claim: Arjuna said whatever Krishna wished — peace or war — the Pandavas would honour, and recalled that Duryodhana, unable to bear Yudhishthira's prosperity, had deprived them of their kingdom by deceitful dice.
statements.evidence: MB 5.78 (pack): 'Whether it be peace or war with the foe that thou wishest, any wish, O Krishna, that thou mayest entertain, will certainly be honoured by us'; 'deprived us of our kingdom by the sinful expedient of deceitful dice.'

statements.claim: Arjuna asked what bowman born in the Kshatriya order, invited to combat, would turn from the fight even if sure to die, and said he had thought Suyodhana deserved death since their sinful defeat and banishment to the woods.
statements.evidence: MB 5.78 (pack), verbatim: 'What bowman is there, who, born in the Kshatriya order, and invited to combat, turneth away from the fight even if he is sure to die?... even then... I thought that Suyodhana deserved death at my hands.'

statements.claim: If Krishna judged the Kauravas' immediate destruction preferable, let it be done soon; Krishna alone could walk the road of peace, related to both houses and trusted in both courts.
statements.evidence: MB 5.78 (pack): 'if thou deemest their immediate destruction to be preferable, let it be effected soon'; 5.78: Krishna is 'foremost of all friends of both the Pandavas and the Kurus' (kinship/trust gloss is consistent with 5.83's 'Related with both the parties').

statements.claim: Arjuna recalled how Draupadi was insulted in the assembly by Duryodhana and borne with patience, said wise counsels would be lost on Duryodhana like seed in barren soil, and asked Krishna to do without delay what he thought proper.
statements.evidence: MB 5.78 (pack), verbatim: 'how Draupadi was insulted in the midst of the assembly... Wise counsels will be lost on him like seed sown in a barren soil. Therefore, do without delay what thou... thinkest to be proper.'

DKS_0411.notes: Pack evidence covers Arjuna's speech only (MB 5.78); the story's claim that Bhima and Nakula also spoke rests on the pack's own index summary and is left unquoted, so no fabricated content is asserted. 'For days the tent had argued' and the closing atmosphere are connective.

statements.claim: Arjuna told Krishna he was the best friend of all the Kurus, related to both parties, and competent to bring about peace and reconciliation between the Pandavas and Dhritarashtra's sons.
statements.evidence: MB 5.83 (pack): 'Thou art now, O Kesava, the best friend of all the Kurus. Related with both the parties... it behoveth thee to bring about peace between the Pandavas and the sons of Dhritarashtra.'

statements.claim: Arjuna asked Krishna to tell Suyodhana that if the foolish Duryodhana did not accept his auspicious counsels he would be the victim of his fate.
statements.evidence: MB 5.83 (pack), verbatim: 'say unto our ever-wrathful brother Suyodhana... If the foolish Duryodhana doth not accept thy auspicious and beneficial counsels... he will surely then be the victim of his fate.'

statements.claim: Krishna answered: 'Yes, I will go to king Dhritarashtra, desirous of accomplishing what is consistent with righteousness, what may be beneficial to us, and what also is for the good of the Kurus.'
statements.evidence: MB 5.83 (pack), verbatim quote; also the pack excerpt.

statements.claim: The next morning was bright with the Maitra hour, the month Kartika under the constellation Revati, the season of dew after autumn, the earth covered with abundant crops.
statements.evidence: MB 5.83 (pack): 'a bright sun arose in the east. The hour called Maitra set in... The month was (Kaumuda Kartika) under the constellation Revati. It was the season of dew... The earth was covered with abundant crops.'

statements.claim: Krishna performed the morning rites — bath, unguents and ornaments, worship of Sun and Fire, touching a bull's tail, bowing to Brahmanas, walking round the sacred fire, viewing auspicious articles.
statements.evidence: MB 5.83 (pack): 'purified himself by a bath, and decked his person with unguents and ornaments, worshipped both the Sun and Fire. And having touched the tail of a bull and reverently bowed to the Brahmanas, walked round the sacred fire, and cast his eyes on the auspicious articles.'

statements.claim: Recollecting Yudhishthira's words, Krishna ordered Satyaki to ready his car with conch, discus, mace, quivers, darts and all weapons, since Duryodhana, Karna and Suvala's son were wicked and even contemptible foes should not be disregarded.
statements.evidence: MB 5.83 (pack), verbatim: 'Janardana recollected Yudhishthira's word and addressed... Satyaki... 'Let my car be made ready and let my conch and discus along with my mace, and quivers and darts and all kinds of weapons... be placed on it, for Duryodhana and Karna and Suvala's son are all of wicked souls.''

statements.claim: The chariot blazed like the fire of universal dissolution, matched the rider's speed, had wheels like sun and moon, emblazonments of moons/fishes/animals/birds, garlands, pearls and gems, a tall flagstaff with pennons and tiger-skins, and was yoked with Saivya, Sugriva, Meghapushpa and Valahaka; Garuda perched on the flagstaff with a terrible rattle.
statements.evidence: MB 5.83 (pack), detailed description matching all elements including the four named steeds and Garuda on the flagstaff.

statements.claim: Krishna mounted the car, high as Meru's summit and loud as kettle-drum or thunder, took Satyaki up beside him, and set out amid cloudless sky, auspicious winds, right-whirling auspicious animals and birds, cranes/peacocks/swans, and right-leaning homa-fed flames.
statements.evidence: MB 5.83 (pack), matching omens and portents descriptions.

statements.claim: Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, the twins, Chekitana, Dhrishtaketu of the Chedis, Drupada and the king of Kasi followed the car as Krishna set out for the residence of the Kurus.
statements.evidence: MB 5.83 (pack): 'Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, followed him, as also Bhima and Arjuna and... the twin sons of Madri. And the valiant Chekitana and Dhrishtaketu, the ruler of the Chedis, and Drupada and the king of Kasi...' (list continues in the truncated passage; 'Yudhishthira followed his cousin' is accurate — Yudhishthira and Krishna are cousins through Kunti/Vasudeva).

DKS_0412.notes: Story extends through the departure narrative that the corpus's next story (DKS_0413, 'Krishna Prepares His Chariot and Sets Out for Hastinapura') is titled to cover — an editorial overlap, not a fidelity issue; every element is verbatim-grounded in MB 5.83. Closing 'accompanied... for a little way and then let it go' is connective.

statements.claim: It was the month of Kartika under the star Revati; autumn had gone and the season of dew had come, and the earth around Upaplavya lay covered with abundant crops.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'The month was (Kaumuda Kartika) under the constellation Revati. It was the season of dew, Autumn having departed. The earth was covered with abundant crops all around.'

statements.claim: The night had passed and a bright sun rose in the east on the morning Krishna set out.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'The night having passed away, a bright sun arose in the east. The hour called Maitra set in, and the rays of the sun were still mild.'

statements.claim: Krishna had promised to ride to Hastinapura and ask for peace; Arjuna had begged him to go, and Krishna gave his word to the Kurus that he would come.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: Arjuna's plea to bring about peace and Krishna's reply, 'Yes, I will go to king Dhritarashtra, desirous of accomplishing what is consistent with righteousness...'

statements.claim: 'For months the Pandavas had lived on borrowed hope, and all of that hope now rested on a single journey.'
statements.evidence: Non-factual emotional framing of the stakes of the peace mission; no specific sourceable event asserted.

statements.claim: Before the sun was high Krishna finished his morning rites: bathed and anointed, he worshipped both the Sun and Fire, touched the tail of a bull, bowed to the brahmanas, walked round the sacred fire, and cast his eyes on the auspicious articles.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'purified himself by a bath, and decked his person with unguents and ornaments, worshipped both the Sun and Fire... touched the tail of a bull and reverently bowed to the Brahmanas, walked round the sacred fire, and cast his eyes on the (usual) auspicious articles placed in view.'

statements.claim: Krishna remembered Yudhishthira's request and called to Satyaki, Sini's grandson, who sat near him, ordering his car made ready with conch, discus, mace, quivers, darts and all weapons, because Duryodhana, Karna and Suvala's son are wicked-souled and even a contemptible foe should not be disregarded.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'Janardana recollected Yudhishthira's word and addressed Sini's grandson Satyaki, seated near, saying, "Let my car be made ready..."' — speech quoted near-verbatim.

statements.claim: His attendants understood the wishes of Kesava and yoked the marvellous car: wheels like the sun and moon, emblazoned with crescent and full moons, fishes, beasts and birds, garlands of flowers, pearls and gems, gold, a flagstaff with bright pennons, tiger-skins; the sight raised the hearts of the Yadavas.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083 detailed description of the car ('two wheels that resembled the sun and the moon... emblazonments of moons... fishes, animals, and birds... garlands of diverse flowers... pearls and gems... variegated with gems and gold... flag-staff bearing beautiful pennons... covered with tiger-skins... enhanced the joy of the Yadavas').

statements.claim: The four great horses Saivya, Sugriva, Meghapushpa and Valahaka, bathed and in beautiful harness, were yoked to the car.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'they yoked unto it those excellent steeds named Saivya and Sugriva and Meghapushpa and Valahaka, after these had been bathed and attired in beautiful harness.'

statements.claim: Garuda, lord of winged creatures, came down and perched on the flagstaff, making it rattle terribly; Krishna mounted the chariot high as the summit of Meru, its sound deep as a kettle-drum and loud as thunder, took Satyaki up, and set out filling the earth and sky with the rattle of his wheels.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'Garuda, the lord of the feathery creation, came and perched on the flag-staff of that car producing a terrible rattle... Saurin then mounted on that car, high as the summit of the Meru... And taking Satyaki also upon it, that best of male beings set out, filling the earth and the welkin with the rattle of his chariot-wheels.'

statements.claim: The sky became cloudless, auspicious winds blew, the air freed of dust grew pure; auspicious beasts and birds wheeled on his right, cranes, peacocks and swans cried good omens, and the altar fire blazed up toward the right free of smoke.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'the sky became cloudless, and auspicious winds began to blow around... auspicious animals and birds, whirling by the right side, began to follow him, and cranes and peacocks and swans all followed the slayer of Madhu, uttering cries of good omens. The very fire... freed from smoke blazed up cheerfully, sending forth its flames towards the right.'

statements.claim: On Krishna's right side stood the great sages Vasishtha, Vamadeva, Bhuridyumna, Gaya, Kratha, Sukra, Kusika and Bhrigu with other brahmarishis and celestial rishis.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'Vasishtha and Vamadeva, and Bhuridyumna and Gaya, and Kratha and Sukra and Kusika and Bhrigu, and other Brahmarshis and celestial Rishis... all stood on the right side of Krishna.'

statements.claim: Behind the chariot came the Pandavas — Yudhishthira son of Kunti, Bhima, Arjuna, the twin sons of Madri — with Chekitana, Dhrishtaketu ruler of the Chedis, Drupada, the king of Kasi and the mighty car-warrior Sikhandin.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, followed him, as also Bhima and Arjuna and those other Pandavas, viz., the twin sons of Madri. And the valiant Chekitana and Dhrishtaketu, the ruler of the Chedis, and Drupada and the king of Kasi and that mighty car-warrior Sikhandin' (list continues in pack excerpt).

statements.claim: It seemed the whole earth was moving with that one chariot, its sound rolling ahead like a promise toward the gates of Hastinapura.
statements.evidence: Figurative close to the departure scene; atmosphere rather than a factual assertion.

DKS_0413.notes: Clean adaptation of MBh 5.083 (Ganguli). Every event, name and detail — rites, chariot, horses, Garuda, omens, sages, followers — maps directly to the passage. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: Yudhishthira followed Krishna some distance on foot after the chariot set out and came up beside it to give his messages.
statements.evidence: Index summary: 'Yudhishthira, following Krishna some distance, asks him to salute and comfort his grieving mother Kunti...'; MBh 5.083: 'And while Krishna was proceeding, Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, followed him.'

statements.claim: The whole company — Bhima, Arjuna, the twins of Madri and the allied kings Chekitana, Dhrishtaketu, Drupada, the king of Kasi and Sikhandin — had come out with the chariot and fallen back one by one, until only the eldest Pandava remained walking after it.
statements.evidence: Pack confirms these figures followed the chariot (5.083 list); the 'fallen back one by one, only Yudhishthira left' staging is narrative arrangement to set up his private words, not contradicted by the pack.

statements.claim: Yudhishthira asked Krishna to ask after Kunti's welfare, salute her, embrace her and comfort her over and over, for she was overwhelmed with grief on account of her sons.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083): 'That lady who hath brought us from our infancy... should be asked about her welfare--Salute and embrace, and, oh, comfort her over and over, overwhelmed with grief as she is on account of her sons.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira sent salutations to the Kuru king Dhritarashtra, to Bhishma, to Drona, to Kripa, and to Vidura, 'endued with great wisdom'.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083): 'Salute her for me, the Kuru king Dhritarashtra also... and Bhishma, and Drona, and Kripa... and also Vidura endued with great wisdom.'

statements.claim: Background glosses on the elders: Dhritarashtra the blind father who watched his son swallow a kingdom and did nothing; Bhishma who taught them arms and is bound to the other side by his vow; Drona and Kripa the teachers who shaped them; Vidura the wise uncle who stood by the Pandavas when no one else dared.
statements.evidence: Identifying character glosses attached to the pack-supported salutation list; canonical background framing rather than new sourceable claims, and nothing contradicts the pack.

statements.claim: Krishna took the messages into his keeping and promised each would be delivered exactly as given — the embrace for the mother, salutations for the king, honours for the elders, warm regard for Vidura.
statements.evidence: Krishna's accepting reply falls beyond the pack excerpt's cutoff; the promise is continuity narration consistent with his undertaking the errand. Index summary does not record Krishna's reply.

statements.claim: Nothing was asked for himself: Yudhishthira sent no demand, no warning and no word of his own rights — only his mother's grief and courtesy owed to the old.
statements.evidence: Non-factual framing summarizing the message content, which the pack excerpt bears out (greetings and salutations only).

statements.claim: Krishna also carried his own word to Arjuna: he would go to king Dhritarashtra desirous of accomplishing what is consistent with righteousness, what may be beneficial (to the Pandavas) and what is for the good of the Kurus.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'Yes, I will go to king Dhritarashtra, desirous of accomplishing what is consistent with righteousness, what may be beneficial to us, and what also is for the good of the Kurus.' (Story renders 'us' as 'the Pandavas', matching the speaker's party.)

statements.claim: Closing imagery: Yudhishthira watching the chariot shrink toward the horizon, the messages riding ahead 'like a small, careful map of everything the coming days might break'.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric close; interpretive commentary on the pack-supported parting scene.

DKS_0414.notes: Supported by pack excerpt + index summary (MBh 5.083). Note: the pack's primary passage is truncated mid-list ('...the mighty car-warrior Sik'), so the message dialogue is carried by the verbatim excerpt and index. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: Arjuna walked a few more steps beside the chariot and spoke again while the morning was still early and the chariot had not yet cleared the camp.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083): 'Then Arjuna, proceeding a few steps, further said...' The early-morning setting matches 5.083's 'The night having passed away, a bright sun arose in the east.'

statements.claim: Recap of Arjuna's earlier plea: he had called Krishna the best friend of both houses, begged him to bring peace between the Pandavas and the sons of Dhritarashtra, and asked him to tell Suyodhana that refusing counsels fraught with virtue and profit would make him the victim of his own fate.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083 opening: Arjuna's full plea, including 'say unto our ever-wrathful brother Suyodhana... "If the foolish Duryodhana doth not accept thy auspicious and beneficial counsels fraught with virtue and profit, he will surely then be the victim of his fate."'

statements.claim: Arjuna's parting warning: 'If Dhritarashtra's son, who always adopts improper means, acts otherwise, then I shall surely, O Janardana, annihilate the whole race of the Kshatriyas.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083): 'If, however, Dhritarashtra's son, who always adopts improper means, acts otherwise, then I shall surely, O Janardana, annihilate the Kshatriya race.'

statements.claim: Krishna had already accepted the errand, having answered that he would go to king Dhritarashtra desirous of righteousness, benefit and the good of the Kurus; the warning did not change the errand.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: Krishna's acceptance quote; the story's reading that the warning accompanies rather than alters the mission is sound framing.

statements.claim: Hearing this, Bhima set his feet on the earth and set forth a terrible shout.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083): '...he set forth a terrible shout.' Index summary: 'Bhima, hearing this, sets forth a terrible shout that makes all bowmen tremble.'

statements.claim: The bowmen who heard the shout trembled, and the steeds and elephants lost all control of their bodies in fear.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083): 'And hearing that shout of his, all the bowmen trembled in fear and steeds and elephants were seen to pass urine and excreta.' The story's 'lost all control of their bodies' is a decorous rendering of the same detail.

statements.claim: Atmosphere of the shout: some nearby felt the very ground tremble, the birds of omen that had followed the chariot scattered, and the camp fell silent after.
statements.evidence: Hyperbolic scene-setting extending the pack-supported terror of the shout; no independent sourceable fact, and nothing contradicts the pack.

statements.claim: Interpretive close: the shout was 'the war itself announcing its presence', and Duryodhana, when he chose, would be choosing in the hearing of that shout.
statements.evidence: Explicitly interpretive framing of the warning + roar, consistent with the pack's account of the mission's stakes.

DKS_0415.notes: Clean. Arjuna's warning, the Bhima roar, and the bowmen/steeds/elephants reaction all match the pack excerpt verbatim (MBh 5.083). No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: On the road Krishna met a company of rishis blazing with Brahmic lustre, the radiance of men who had worn away worldly desires in austerity.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083): 'on his way Kesava of mighty arms met with some Rishis blazing with Brahmic lustre.'

statements.claim: Krishna reined in, alighted from the chariot and went to worship the sages — as an envoy of kings he bows first before sages.
statements.evidence: Index summary: 'On the road Krishna alights to worship a band of celestial Rishis.' The envoy-bows-first clause is connective framing.

statements.claim: Among the sages Krishna recognised Narada, the tireless traveller of the three worlds, whose presence meant whatever happened there would be known everywhere.
statements.evidence: Pack index lists Narada among the story's characters (Krishna, Parashurama, Narada) for this event; Narada's role as celestial reporter is a canonical characterization. The character gloss is connective.

statements.claim: Parashurama, Jamadagni's son, came forward, approached Govinda the slayer of Madhu and embraced him.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083): 'Jamadagni's son... approached Govinda the slayer of Madhu, embraced him, and said...'

statements.claim: Parashurama said: 'We are desirous of beholding all the Kshatriyas of the earth assembled from every side... And we are anxious to listen to those words fraught with virtue and profit, which will be spoken by you unto the Kurus, in the presence of all.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083) quotes these words near-verbatim (final clause clipped at the pack's truncation point).

statements.claim: The sages had renounced the world yet journeyed to hear Krishna's speech about peace; they would not take sides but came to witness where the fate of the earth would be spoken aloud.
statements.evidence: Interpretive gloss on the pack-quoted motive ('desirous of beholding all the Kshatriyas... anxious to listen to those words fraught with virtue and profit'), presented as the story's reading of the meeting.

statements.claim: Parashurama is described as the ancient sage feared by warriors since before the fathers of the men now gathering.
statements.evidence: Canonical background on Parashurama (the Kshatriya-destroying avatar) identifying him for readers; not stated in the pack excerpt but uncontradicted.

statements.claim: Krishna received the blessing and embrace, remounted the chariot and rolled on toward Hastinapura, leaving the rishis as witnesses behind him.
statements.evidence: Continuation consistent with the meeting occurring on Krishna's road to Hastinapura (pack: 'on his way'); the 'company of witnesses in the dust' imagery is connective close.

DKS_0416.notes: Meeting, embrace and Parashurama's quoted words all match the pack excerpt (MBh 5.083); Narada's presence is supported by the pack's character index. Primary passage in the pack is truncated, so the excerpt + index carry the evidence. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: When Krishna set out from Upaplavya, ten mighty car-warriors capable of slaying hostile heroes, fully armed, rode behind his chariot, with a thousand foot-soldiers and a thousand horsemen and attendants by the hundred carrying provisions in abundance.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: 'ten mighty car-warriors, capable of slaying hostile heroes, fully armed, followed in his train. And a thousand foot-soldiers, and a thousand horsemen, and attendants by hundreds, also formed his train, carrying... provisions in abundance.'

statements.claim: Janamejaya, the king to whom the tale was told, asked how Krishna journeyed and what omens were seen at his setting out.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: Janamejaya asks 'How did the illustrious slayer of Madhu... proceed on his journey? And what omens were seen when that hero set out?'

statements.claim: Dread omens at Krishna's departure: thunder and lightning with no clouds, fleecy clouds raining in his rear, the seven great rivers (Sindhu among them) flowing backwards, reversed directions, fires blazing from the earth, repeated earth-tremors, wells and water-vessels swelling over, universal darkness and dust hiding the points of the horizon, and loud roars with no visible source.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084 narrates each omen near-verbatim: 'Though there were no clouds in the sky, yet the roll of thunder accompanied by flashes of lightning was heard... The seven large rivers including the Sindhu (Indus) though flowing eastwards then flowed in opposite directions... wells and water-vessels by hundreds swelled up and ran out... Loud roars were heard in the sky without any being being visible...'

statements.claim: A south-westerly wind, harsh with thunder, uprooting trees by the thousands, crushed the city of Hastinapura.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: 'A south-westerly wind, with the harsh rattle of the thunder, uprooting trees by the thousands, crushed the city of Hastinapura.'

statements.claim: In the places through which Krishna passed the world turned gentle: delicious breezes, showers of lotuses and fragrant flowers, a road free of prickly grass and thorns.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: 'In those places... through which he of Vrishni's race passed, delicious breezes blew and everything became auspicious. Showers of lotuses and fragrant flowers fell there. The very road became delightful, being free from prickly grass and thorns.'

statements.claim: Wherever he stayed, Brahmanas by the thousand glorified the giver of wealth and worshipped him with dishes of curds, ghee and honey and presents of wealth; women came out and strewed fragrant wild flowers on him.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: 'Brahmanas by thousands glorified that giver of wealth... and worshipped him with dishes of curds, ghee, honey, and presents of wealth. The very women, coming out on the road, strewed wild flowers of great fragrance on the person of that illustrious hero.'

statements.claim: He passed villages abounding in bees and diverse cities and kingdoms and came to Salibhavana, filled with every kind of crop, delicious and sacred.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: 'He then came upon a delightful spot called Salibhavana which was filled with every kind of crops... after having... seen various villages abounding in bees... and after having passed through diverse cities and kingdoms.'

statements.claim: The cheerful citizens of Upaplavya, well-protected by the Bharatas and free from anxiety about invaders, came out of their town and stood on the way to behold Krishna, and worshipped him with all the honours of a guest.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: 'Always cheerful and of good hearts, well-protected by the Bharatas and therefore free from all anxieties on account of the designs of invaders... many of the citizens of Upaplavya, coming out of their town, stood together on the way, desirous of beholding Krishna... worshipped him... with all the honours of a guest.'

statements.claim: When Kesava came to Vrikasthala the sun reddened the sky with straggling rays; alighting, he performed purificatory rites, had the steeds unharnessed and said his evening prayers; Daruka tended the horses according to the rules of equine science, removing yokes and traces and letting them loose.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: 'the sun seemed to redden the sky by his straggling rays of light. Alighting from his car, he duly went through the usual purificatory rites, and ordering the steeds to be unharnessed, he set himself to say his evening prayers. And Daruka also, setting the steeds free, tended them according to the rules of equine science, and taking off the yokes and traces, let them loose.'

statements.claim: Krishna said, 'Here we must pass the night, for the sake of Yudhishthira's mission,' and the attendants raised a temporary abode and prepared excellent food and drink.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: 'the slayer of Madhu said, "Here must we pass the night for the sake of Yudhishthira's mission."... the attendants soon set a temporary abode and prepared in a trice excellent food and drink.'

statements.claim: The noble, high-born, modest, Veda-obedient Brahmanas of the village honoured him with benedictions and auspicious speeches and placed their wealthy houses at his disposal; saying 'Enough', Krishna paid them homage each according to rank, went with them to their houses, returned in their company to his own tent, fed all the Brahmanas with sweetmeats and took his meals with them, passing the night happily.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084 narrates the whole exchange, including 'Saying unto them--"Enough"--the illustrious Krishna paid them proper homage, each according to his rank... And feeding all the Brahmanas with sweet-meats and himself taking his meals with them, Kesava passed the night happily there.'

statements.claim: Closing line — Krishna passed the night 'at the threshold of the city whose sky had darkened at his coming'.
statements.evidence: Connective close recalling the pack-supported omens that crushed/darkened Hastinapura.

DKS_0417.notes: Near-complete faithful rendering of MBh 5.084 (Ganguli): retinue, both omen catalogues (ruin for Hastinapura, auspiciousness on Krishna's route), Salibhavana, Upaplavya citizens, and the Vrikasthala night all match the passage. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: Learning from his spies that the slayer of Madhu had set out, Dhritarashtra's hair stood on end; he addressed Bhishma, Drona, Sanjaya and Vidura, and spoke to Duryodhana and his counsellors about honouring Krishna.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.085: 'understanding from his spies that the slayer of Madhu had set out, Dhritarashtra, with his hair standing erect, respectfully addressing the mighty-armed Bhishma and Drona and Sanjaya and the illustrious Vidura, said these words unto Duryodhana and his counsellors.'

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra's speech: men, women and children everywhere talk of Dasarha of great prowess coming for the Pandavas' sake; he is the Lord of all creatures on whom rests everything, full of intelligence, prowess, wisdom and energy, eternal Virtue itself, whose worship brings happiness and neglect misery.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.085 quotes the speech near-verbatim ('strange and wonderful is the news that we hear... He is the Lord of all creatures, and on him resteth the course of every thing in the universe... eternal Virtue. If worshipped he is sure to bestow happiness; and if not worshipped he is sure to inflict misery.').

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra ordered pavilions furnished with every object of enjoyment set up on the road and asked what Bhishma thought; Bhishma and the others applauded the words, saying 'Excellent'.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.085: 'Let pavilions be set up on the road, furnished with every object of enjoyment... What doth Bhishma think in this matter?' ... 'Bhishma and others, all applauding those words of king Dhritarashtra, said,--"Excellent."'

statements.claim: Duryodhana ordered delightful sites chosen for pavilions abounding with gems of every kind at proper intervals; he sent handsome seats, beautiful girls, scents and ornaments, fine robes, excellent viands, drinks of diverse qualities and fragrant garlands.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.085: 'King Duryodhana then... ordered delightful sites to be chosen for the erection of pavilions. Many pavilions were thereupon constructed abounding with gems of every kind... And the king sent thither handsome seats... beautiful girls, and scents and ornaments, and fine robes, and excellent viands, and drink of diverse qualities, and fragrant garlands of many kinds.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana took especial care to erect a highly beautiful pavilion full of precious gems at Vrikasthala for Krishna's reception, and once the godlike arrangements (far above human capacity) were done, he informed Dhritarashtra.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.085: 'the king of the Kurus took especial care to erect, for the reception of Krishna, a highly beautiful pavilion at Vrikasthala, full of precious gems. And having made all these arrangements that were god-like and much above the capacity of human beings... informed Dhritarashtra of the same.'

statements.claim: The road from Vrikasthala to the capital became a pageant; travellers and citizens slowed to look, and talk was all of the wealth being spent for one man.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric expansion of the pack-supported display; the specific bystander reactions are invented observers, not contradicted by the pack.

statements.claim: Kesava arrived at the capital of the Kurus and passed all the gem-studded pavilions, seats, garlands and viands by without casting a single glance at them; no gem drew his eyes.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.085: 'Kesava, however, of Dasarha's race, arrived at the capital of the Kurus, without casting a single glance at all those pavilions and all those gems of diverse kinds.'

statements.claim: Interpretive close: Duryodhana built as though magnificence could dazzle Krishna into alliance, but Krishna, who needed nothing, made the whole architecture of the welcome irrelevant.
statements.evidence: Explicitly interpretive contrast of the lavish reception with Krishna's disregard; consistent with the pack, not asserted by it.

DKS_0418.notes: Faithful rendering of MBh 5.085 (Ganguli) — Dhritarashtra's speech, the 'Excellent' response, Duryodhana's pavilions/gifts and the Vrikasthala pavilion, and Krishna passing all by without a glance are all in the passage. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: Scene framing: Dhritarashtra, planning lavish gifts for Krishna, spoke of heaping wealth on him and most of the assembly took it for wisdom, until Vidura answered with the truth.
statements.evidence: Vidura's speech in the pack (5.087) presupposes Dhritarashtra's wish to give ('It is much, O king, that thou wishes to give unto Kesava as thy guest'); the assembly's reaction is connective staging. Dhritarashtra is blind — canonical epithet used throughout the corpus.

statements.claim: Vidura's opening: Dhritarashtra is respected by the three worlds, loved and regarded by everybody, and at his age can never speak against scripture or well-directed reason; virtue resides in him permanently like characters on stone, light in the sun, billows in the ocean.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.087: 'thou art respected by three worlds... Venerable in year as thou art, what thou wilt say at this age can never be against the dictates of the scriptures... virtue resideth in thee permanently' — with the same similes.

statements.claim: Vidura urged him to strive with friends and kinsmen to retain his virtues, adopt sincerity of behaviour, and not from folly cause the wholesale destruction of his sons, grandsons, friends, kinsmen and all that are dear to him.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.087: 'Strive, therefore, with thy friends and kinsmen to retain those virtues of thine. Oh, adopt sincerity of behaviour. Do not from folly, cause a wholesale destruction of thy sons, grandsons, friends, kinsmen, and all that are dear to thee.'

statements.claim: Vidura said Kesava deserves all the offered gifts and much more — the whole earth itself — but swore by his own soul that Dhritarashtra did not wish to give them from virtue or to please Krishna: all of it betrays deception, falsehood and insincerity.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.087: 'Know, however, that Kesava deserves all this and much more, aye, the whole earth itself. I truly swear by my own soul that thou dost not wish to give all this unto Krishna either from motives of virtue or for the object of doing what is agreeable to him... all this betrays only deception, falsehood, and insincerity.'

statements.claim: Vidura exposed the secret purpose: the five Pandavas desire only five villages and Dhritarashtra will not give even that, so he is unwilling to make peace and seeks to win Krishna by wealth and separate Kesava from the Pandavas.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.087: 'By the external acts, O king, I know thy secret purpose. The five Pandavas, O king, desire only five villages. Thou, however, dost not wish to give them even that. Thou art, therefore, unwilling to make peace. Thou seekest to make the mighty-armed hero of Vrishni's race thy own by means of thy wealth... thou seekest to separate Kesava from the Pandavas.'

statements.claim: Vidura declared Dhritarashtra unable by wealth, attention or worship to separate Krishna from Dhananjaya, knowing Krishna's magnanimity, Arjuna's firm devotion, and that Dhananjaya, Kesava's very life, can never be given up.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.087: 'I tell thee, however, that thou art unable, by wealth, or attention, or worship, to separate Krishna from Dhananjaya. I know the magnanimity of Krishna; I know the firm devotion of Arjuna towards him, I know that Dhananjaya, who is Kesava's life, is incapable of being given up by the latter.'

statements.claim: Vidura said Janardana will accept nothing but a vessel of water, the washing of his feet and the usual enquiries after the welfare of those he will see; Dhritarashtra should offer the hospitality most agreeable to him, for no respect may not be offered to Janardana.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.087: 'Save only a vessel of water, save only the washing of his feet, save only the (usual) enquiries after the welfare (of those he will see), Janardana will not accept any other hospitality or set his eyes on any other thing... there is no respect that may not be offered to Janardana.'

statements.claim: Vidura urged the king to give Kesava the object he comes for — peace between Dhritarashtra and Duryodhana on one side and the Pandavas on the other — to follow his counsels and behave as a father toward the Pandavas, who are children to him in years and disposed to pay him filial regard.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.087: 'Give unto Kesava... that object in expectation of which... he cometh to the Kurus. Kesava desires peace to be established between thee and Duryodhana on one side and the Pandavas on the other... Thou art their father, O king, and the Pandavas are thy sons... behave as father towards them, that are disposed to pay thee filial regard.'

statements.claim: Interpretive close: the gifts were a strategy to prise Krishna loose from the Pandavas, the peace Krishna offered was real, and the question hanging over the hall was whether anyone would hear it.
statements.evidence: Summary reading of Vidura's speech, directly grounded in the pack-quoted content.

DKS_0419.notes: Vidura's entire admonition is carried near-verbatim from MBh 5.087 (Ganguli); all named points — five villages, inability to separate Krishna from Dhananjaya, the water/feet-washing-only hospitality, the plea for peace — match. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: Duryodhana agreed with Vidura that all said about Krishna was truly said: Janardana is greatly devoted to the Pandavas and can never be separated from them.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.088: 'All that Vidura hath said about Krishna, hath indeed, been truly said; for Janardana is greatly devoted to the Pandavas and can never be separated from them.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana argued the proposed wealth ought never to be bestowed: Kesava is not unworthy of worship but time and place are against it, for he would think he was being worshipped out of fear, and an intelligent Kshatriya must not do what brings disgrace.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.088: 'All the diverse kinds of wealth... ought never to be bestowed upon him. Kesava is, of course, not unworthy of our worship, but both time and place are against it, for he... will very likely think that we are worshipping him out of fear... an intelligent Kshatriya must not do that which may bring disgrace upon him.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana concluded it was out of place to give Krishna anything now, for war having been decided upon should never be put off by hospitality — though the large-eyed Krishna deserves the most reverential worship of the three worlds.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.088: 'the large-eyed Krishna deserveth the most reverential worship of the three worlds. It is quite out of place, therefore... to give him anything now, for war having been decided upon, it should never be put off by hospitality.'

statements.claim: Bhishma answered: worshipped or not, Janardana never becomes angry; none can treat him with disrespect for he is not contemptible; whatever he purposes cannot be frustrated; so do without hesitation what Krishna says, bring about peace with the Pandavas through Vasudeva, and tell him only what is agreeable.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.088 quotes Bhishma's reply to Duryodhana near-verbatim, including 'Do without hesitation what Krishna of mighty arms sayeth and bring about peace with the Pandavas through Vasudeva as the means.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana declared he could by no means live sharing his swelling prosperity with the Pandavas and formed a great resolution: to imprison Janardana, the refuge of the Pandavas, when he comes the next morning, so that the Vrishnis, the Pandavas and the whole earth would submit to him; he asked Bhishma for the means so Krishna would not guess the purpose.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.088: 'I will imprison Janardana who is the refuge of the Pandavas. He will come here tomorrow morning; and when he is confined, the Vrishnis and the Pandavas, aye, the whole earth, will submit to me. What may be the means for accomplishing it, so that Janardana may not guess our purpose... it behoveth thee to say.'

statements.claim: Hearing these fearful words about imprisoning Krishna, Dhritarashtra and all his counsellors were very much pained and deeply afflicted; the king protested that it is not immemorial custom — Hrishikesa comes as an ambassador, is related to them and dear to them, has done no wrong, and does not deserve imprisonment.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.088: 'Dhritarashtra, with all his counsellors, was very much pained and became deeply afflicted... "O ruler of men, never say this again, this is not immemorial custom. Hrishikesa cometh here as an ambassador. He is, besides, related to and is dear to us. He hath done us no wrong; how then doth he deserves imprisonment?"'

statements.claim: Bhishma denounced the plan: this wicked son's hour has come, he chooses evil though entreated by well-wishers, Dhritarashtra follows in the wake of a wicked wretch who treads a thorny path, and the wicked son with his counsellors, coming in contact with Krishna of unstained acts, will be destroyed in a moment; Bhishma declared he dared not listen to such words.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.088: 'This wicked son of thine... hath his hour come... will be destroyed in a moment. I dare not listen to the words of this sinful and wicked wretch that hath abandoned all virtue.'

statements.claim: Bhishma, inflamed with rage, rose and left the assembly.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.088: 'Having said this, that aged chief of the Bharata race, Bhishma of unbaffled prowess, inflamed with rage rose and left that place.'

statements.claim: Closing tableau — the assembly staring after him, the blind king stricken, the prince unmoved, and the plan to imprison the ambassador left standing in the hall like a storm not yet broken.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric close consistent with the pack; 'blind king' is the canonical epithet for Dhritarashtra used throughout the corpus.

DKS_0420.notes: Faithful rendering of MBh 5.088 (Ganguli): Duryodhana's refusal of gifts, his imprison-Krishna resolution, Dhritarashtra's pained protest and Bhishma's denunciation and departure all match the passage near-verbatim and in order. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: Every street of Hastinapura was adorned as though for a festival when Krishna came; the principal avenues were decorated with jewels and gems, and no one, man, woman or child, remained indoors, so eager were the citizens to see him.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'in honour of Krishna, the city was beautifully adorned, and the principal streets were decorated with diverse jewels and gems. And, O king, ... on that occasion no one,--man, woman, or child,--remained in doors, so eager were the citizens for beholding Vasudeva.'

statements.claim: Before he reached the gates the welcome had begun: all the Dhartarashtras except Duryodhana, attired in their finest robes, had gone out to meet him together with Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and the other elders, and the people followed by thousands, on cars of diverse kinds and many on foot.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'And all the Dhartarashtras except Duryodhana, attired in excellent robes, and with Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, and others, went out to meet him. And the citizens by thousands, O king, on cars of diverse kinds, and many on foot, also came out, desirous of beholding Hrishikesa.'

statements.claim: Krishna had risen at day-dawn, gone through his morning rites, and taken leave of the Bharatas before setting out for the city of the Kurus; the inhabitants of Vrikasthala came out to bid him farewell and only returned to their homes when he was gone.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'Rising up (from his bed) at day-dawn, Krishna went through his morning rites, and taking leave of the Bharatas, set out for the city (of the Kurus). And all the inhabitants of Vrikasthala, bidding farewell unto that mighty one of long arms while he was about to depart, all returned to their homes.'

statements.claim: Meeting Bhishma of spotless deed, Drona and Dhritarashtra's sons on the way, Krishna entered the city surrounded by them all; citizens lined the streets, bent their heads down to the ground and sang eulogies in his honour as he passed through.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'meeting on the way Bhishma of spotless deed, and Drona, and Dhritarashtra's sons, he entered the city, surrounded by them all... And all the citizens came out and lined the streets and bent their heads down to the ground singing eulogies in his honour.'

statements.claim: Substantial mansions, filled with high-born ladies, seemed about to fall down under their living weight, and Krishna's steeds, endued with great speed, moved very slowly through that dense mass of human beings.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'substantial mansions, filled with high-born ladies, seemed to be on the point of falling down on the ground in consequence of their living weight. And although Vasudeva's steeds were endued with great speed, yet they moved very slowly through that dense mass of human beings.' The women leaning thickly from the windows is a light visual elaboration of this, not contradicted by the pack.

statements.claim: Krishna came at last to Dhritarashtra's ash-coloured palace, enriched with numerous buildings, passed through the first three chambers, and came upon the royal son of Vichitravirya, the blind king Dhritarashtra.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'that lotus-eyed grinder of foes then entered Dhritarashtra's ash-coloured palace which was enriched with numerous buildings. And having passed through the first three chambers of the palace... Kesava, came upon the royal son of Vichitravirya.'

statements.claim: At Krishna's approach the blind monarch of great fame stood up, and with him rose Drona and Bhishma, Kripa and Somadatta, and king Vahlika also — all of them stood up to honour him.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'the blind monarch of great fame stood up along with Drona and Bhishma, Kripa and Somadatta, and king Vahlika also,--all stood up for honouring Janardana.'

statements.claim: Krishna worshipped Dhritarashtra and Bhishma with proper words and without losing any time, then greeted the other kings according to their seniority in years and accosted Drona and his son, Vahlika, Kripa and Somadatta.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'the Vrishni hero... worshipped him and Bhishma with proper words and without losing any time... greeted the other kings according to their seniority in years. And Janardana then accosted the illustrious Drona and his son, and Vahlika, and Kripa, and Somadatta.'

statements.claim: In the chamber lay a spacious seat of beautiful workmanship, made of gold and set with jewels; at Dhritarashtra's request Krishna took it, and the king's priests duly offered him a cow, honey and curds and water.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'there in that chamber lay a spacious seat of beautiful workmanship, made of gold and set with jewels. And at Dhritarashtra's request, Achyuta took that seat; and the priests of Dhritarashtra duly offered Janardana a cow, honey and curds and water.'

statements.claim: After the rites of hospitality Krishna remained a while among the Kurus, laughing and jesting with them according to his relationship with each, and came out with the king's permission; having duly greeted all the Kurus in their assembly, he went to the delightful abode of Vidura, who worshipped him with every auspicious and desirable offering.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'Govinda remained there for a while, surrounded by the Kurus, laughing and jesting with them according to their relationship with him... came out with the king's permission. And Madhava having duly greeted all the Kurus in their assembly, then went to the delightful abode of Vidura; and Vidura... worshipped him with every auspicious and desirable offering.'

statements.claim: Vidura asked what use in telling Krishna of the joy he felt at this advent, for Krishna was the inner Soul of all embodied creatures; when the reception was over he enquired about the welfare of the Pandavas, and Krishna, to whom the past and the future were as the present, told him everything in detail about the doings of the sons of Pandu.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: Vidura's words 'for thou art the inner Soul of all embodied creatures'; 'after the hospitable reception was over, Vidura... enquired of Govinda... about the welfare of Pandavas'; 'that scion of Dasarha's race... unto whom the past and the future were as the present... began to tell him everything in detail about the doings of the sons of Pandu.'

statements.claim: Closing frame: the day that began with the whole city pouring out of doors to see Krishna ended with him speaking of his cousins in the lamplight of Vidura's quiet house, while the errand of peace still waited to be spoken aloud.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric summary of 5.089's own sequence (street welcome → palace → Vidura's abode, where he reports on the Pandavas); no new sourceable fact asserted.

DKS_0421.notes: Entire story closely follows MBh 5.089. Story title/summary and the 'women leaning from windows' flourish are visual elaboration consistent with the 'living weight' detail.

statements.claim: After his meeting with Vidura, Krishna went in the afternoon to his paternal aunt Pritha (Kunti), whose countenance... he had not seen in a long time; beholding him, whose countenance beamed like the radiant sun, she encircled his neck with her arms and poured forth lamentations remembering her sons, and the tears of Pritha flowed fast.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.090: 'Janardana... after his meeting with Vidura, went then in the afternoon to his paternal aunt, Pritha.
