statements.claim: Gandiva would not brace, the string stayed slack, the incantations of the superhuman weapons would not return, the shafts merely scratched skin, even the arrows given by Agni were destroyed, and the barbarians carried off the women of the Vrishni and Andhaka tribes
statements.evidence: VP 5.38 (pack): 'Arjuna began to brace his heavenly bow Gandiva... but it was in vain; for... it continued flaccid: neither could he call to recollection the incantations of the superhuman weapons... those shot from Gandiva merely scratched the skin. The arrows given him by Agni... now were themselves destroyed... he beat the banditti with the horn of his bow; but they only laughed... and the barbarians, in the sight of Arjuna, carried off all the women of the Vrishni and Andhaka tribes.'

statements.claim: Arjuna lamented 'Alas! I am deserted by my lord!' and in that instant Gandiva, the heavenly weapons, his chariot and horses perished before his eyes; he declared himself overcome by peasants without that righteous aid
statements.evidence: VP 5.38 (pack): 'Alas! alas! I am deserted by my lord!... and in that instant the bow and heavenly arms, his car and steeds, perished entirely... These two arms are mine; mine is this fist... I am Arjuna: but without that righteous aid all these are pithless... without him I am overcome by peasants.'

statements.claim: Arjuna went to Mathura, installed the Yadava prince Vajra as its king, and there in a wood found Vyasa and prostrated himself at his feet
statements.evidence: VP 5.38 (pack): 'Arjuna went to the city of Mathura, and there installed the Yadava prince, Vajra, as its king. There he beheld Vyasa, who was living in a wood... saluted him respectfully.'

statements.claim: Vyasa asked how Arjuna was shorn of his lustre and whether he had been beaten by his inferiors in battle
statements.evidence: VP 5.38 (pack): 'How is it that I see you thus shorn of your lustre?... Or, what is, most probably, the case, have you been beaten by your inferiors in battle?'

statements.claim: Arjuna sighed deeply and told him that Hari who was their strength and brightness had left them; Gandiva famed through the three worlds was foiled by peasants' sticks and Krishna's households carried off; it was a wonder that he lived
statements.evidence: VP 5.38 (verified against full Wilson text, pack passage truncated here): 'Arjuna, having sighed deeply, related to Vyasa all the circumstances... Hari, who was our strength, our might... has left us... The bow Gandiva, that was famed throughout the three worlds, has been foiled... by the sticks of peasants... the whole households of Krishna... carried away by peasants... it is wonderful that I live.'

statements.claim: Vyasa told him to think no more of his disgrace, that time subjects all beings to similar vicissitudes, and that rivers, seas, mountains, gods, men, trees and insects are all created and destroyed by time
statements.evidence: VP 5.38 (pack excerpt + full text): 'Think no more, my son, of your disgrace... Know that time subjects all beings to similar vicissitude... Rivers, seas, mountains, the whole earth, gods, men, animals, trees, insects are, all, created, and, all, will be destroyed, by time.'

statements.claim: Krishna came down to lift the earth's burden; that object is accomplished - all the kings are slain, the Vrishni race destroyed, nothing remained for him to do, so the lord departed with his ends fulfilled; at creation he creates, in duration preserves, at the end destroys
statements.evidence: VP 5.38 (full text): 'These mighty works of Krishna... have been performed to relieve earth of its burthens: for this he has come down... This object has been, now, accomplished. All the kings (of the earth) are slain; the race of Vrishni and Andhaka is destroyed: no more remained for him to accomplish. Therefore has the lord departed... his ends being, all, fulfilled... At the period of creation, the god of gods creates; in that of duration, he preserves; and, at the end (of all), he is mighty to annihilate.'

statements.claim: Arjuna's defeat by miserable thieves was as much time's work as his victories; it is only the sport of the universal Hari
statements.evidence: VP 5.38 (full text): 'In like manner as, through thy devotion to Vishnu, these were overthrown by thee, so, at last, has thy defeat by miserable thieves been wrought by time... Be assured, son of Pritha, that it is (but) the sport of the universal Hari.'

statements.claim: Ashtavakra story: a brahman crooked in eight places stood in water meditating for years; after the Asuras were overthrown the nymphs passed to a festival on Meru, praised him, and at his offer some asked for the best of men and sovereign of the Brahmans as husband; when he rose from the water they laughed at his crookedness and he cursed them to fall into the hands of thieves after obtaining the first of males, later softening that they would return to the sphere of the gods
statements.evidence: VP 5.38 (full text): 'a Brahman, named Ashtavakra, was pursuing his religious penances, standing in water... for many years. In consequence of the overthrow of the Asuras, there was a great festival on the summit of Meru... they praised and hymned him... Whatever you wish for, ask of me... grant us a husband, the best of men, and sovereign of the Brahmans. So be it, replied Ashtavakra, and, thereupon, came up from the waters. When the nymphs beheld him... crooked in eight places, they could not restrain their merriment, but laughed aloud... you shall obtain the first of males for your husband; but... you shall (afterwards) fall into the hands of thieves... they should finally return to the sphere of the gods.'

statements.claim: It is because of that curse that the wives of Kesava have fallen into the hands of the barbarians; all this destruction was effected by the lord of all and Arjuna's end too is near, since he has withdrawn his strength and splendour
statements.evidence: VP 5.38 (full text): 'It is in consequence, then, of the curse of the Muni Ashtavakra, that these females, who were, at first, the wives of Kesava, have, now, fallen into the hands of the barbarians... All this destruction has been effected by the lord of all; and your end is, also, nigh at hand, since he has withdrawn from you strength, splendour, valour, and preeminence.'

statements.claim: Death is the doom of everyone born, fall the end of exaltation, union terminates in separation, growth tends to decay; knowing this, wise men feel neither grief nor joy
statements.evidence: VP 5.38 (full text): 'Death is the doom of every one who is born; fall is the end of exaltation; union terminates in separation; and growth tends but to decay. Knowing (all this), wise men are susceptible of neither grief nor joy.'

statements.claim: Vyasa told him to relinquish everything and repair to the holy forest, and to tell Yudhishthira that tomorrow, with his brothers, he must tread the path of heroes; Arjuna went back and told his brothers, and the sons of Pandu placed Parikshit on the throne and went to the forest
statements.evidence: VP 5.38 (full text + pack excerpt): 'along with your brothers, relinquish everything, and repair to the holy forest. Go, now, and say, from me, to Yudhishthira, that he, to-morrow, with his brethren, tread the path of heroes... Thus instructed by Vyasa, Arjuna went and related to the other sons of Pritha all that he had seen... the sons of Pandu placed Parikshit on the throne, and went to the forest.'

DKS_0490.notes: Pack passage truncates mid-dialogue (~'...or of the deat[h]'), so the second half (Vyasa's consolation, Ashtavakra tale, enthronement) was verified against the full Wilson VP 5.38 text that the pack cites; story tracks it almost verbatim. 'Arjuna went alone' is connective framing - VP has Daruka conduct Arjuna to Dwaraka and the text later stresses the wealth/women were 'in the possession of Arjuna alone.'

statements.claim: A great solar eclipse occurs, and the Yadavas journey to Samanta-panchaka to bathe and give cows and gifts.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (BP 10.82.1-15): 'A great solar eclipse occurs, and the Yadavas, together with Vasudeva, Akrura and others, journey to Samanta-panchaka ... to bathe and give cows and gifts.'

statements.claim: Samanta-panchaka is the field of the Kurus where Rama, best of weapon-bearers, once made the earth free of the kings (made lakes of kings' blood).
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.2: 'niḥkṣatriyāṃ mahīṃ kurvan rāmaḥ śastra-bhṛtāṃ varaḥ' — Rama, best of weapon-bearers, making the earth free of kshatriyas; index: 'the field where Rama had once made lakes of the kings' blood'.

statements.claim: The blessed Rama hallowed the field with his great sacrifice, though untouched by any deed's stain.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.3: 'īje ca bhagavān rāmo yatrāspṛṣṭo 'pi karmaṇā' — Lord Rama performed the sacrifice there, untouched by karma.

statements.claim: Krishna went, with Balarama, Vasudeva, Akrura and the chief men of the Yadava houses.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'the Yadavas, together with Vasudeva, Akrura and others, journey to Samanta-panchaka'; BP 10.82.10: 'vṛṣṇayaḥ kṛṣṇa-devatāḥ' (the Vrishnis whose deity is Krishna).

statements.claim: The road filled with chariots gleaming like the dwellings of the gods, drawn by swift horses and hung with garlands of gold.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.6-7: 'te rathair deva-dhiṣṇyābhair hayaiś ca tarala-plavaiḥ / vyarocanta mahā-tejāḥ pathi kāñcana-mālinaḥ'.

statements.claim: It seemed all the people of the land were on the road, each hoping to leave his sins behind in the sacred water.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.4-5: 'mahatyāṃ tīrtha-yātrāyāṃ tatrāgan bhāratīḥ prajāḥ / yayur bhārata tat kṣetraṃ svam aghaṃ kṣapayiṣṇavaḥ' — Bharata's people came to that field to destroy their own sin.

statements.claim: At the tirtha they bathed in Rama's pools, fasting with minds gathered close, and then bathed a second time as the rite required; they gave cows and gifts.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.8-9: 'tatra snātvā mahā-bhāgā upoṣya su-samāhitāḥ / rāma-hradeṣu vidhi-vat punar āplutya vṛṣṇayaḥ'. The 'five pools' phrasing glosses the place-name Samanta-panchaka (the five lakes of Rama); the verse itself says 'Rama's pools' without the numeral.

statements.claim: Kings had come from Kamboja, Kaikaya, Madra, Kunti, Anarta and Kerala.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.12: 'kāmboja-kaikayān madrān kuntīn ānarta-keralān'.

statements.claim: Long-separated kinsmen embraced one another with joy, hearts and faces opening like lotuses, tears flowing.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.13: 'anyonya-sandarśana-harṣa-raṃhasā protphulla-hṛd-vaktra-saroruha-śriyaḥ'; verse 11: 'suhṛt-sambandhino nṛpān'.

statements.claim: The women of the two houses embraced, kumkuma-marked, with tears of love in their eyes.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.14: 'striyaś ca ... kuṅkuma-paṅka-rūṣitān ... praṇayāśru-locanāḥ'. Story relocates the kumkuma mark from breasts (verse) to shoulders — a modest rendering of the same detail, not a contradiction.

statements.claim: The youngest saluted the elders and were blessed in return.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.15: 'tato 'bhivādya te vṛddhān yaviṣṭhair abhivāditāḥ'.

statements.claim: Toward the end of the day a caravan of cowherds arrived — Nanda, Yashoda and the cowherds of Gokula.
statements.evidence: Corpus-chain continuity with DKS_0492 (BP 10.82.30-37, the Nanda-arrival event); the eclipse gathering ends as the next event's caravan arrives.

statements.claim: The Yadavas read the eclipse not as a bad omen but as an occasion for pilgrimage; tents, campfires and an evening reunion followed.
statements.evidence: The eclipse-as-summons framing and the evening camp atmosphere (tents, news exchanged, children shown to relatives) are scene-setting connective narration; the underlying reunion of friends and kin is verse-supported.

DKS_0491.notes: Fully grounded in BP 10.82.1-15 (+ chain to 10.82.30-37 for Nanda's arrival). 'Middle of the day', 'five pools' count, and the tented-evening scene are connective/inferential; kumkuma moved from breasts to shoulders is a modest adaptation of verse 14.

statements.claim: Nanda arrived with the cowherds, and the Vrishnis rejoiced to see him as bodies revive when life returns.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.31: 'taṃ dṛṣṭvā vṛṣṇayo hṛṣṭās tanvaḥ prāṇam ivotthitāḥ'.

statements.claim: Vasudeva was the first to reach him, embracing his old friend, pleased past words, overwhelmed with love.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.32: 'vasudevaḥ pariṣvajya samprītaḥ prema-vihvalaḥ'; verse 31 context places Vasudeva's embrace immediately on Nanda's arrival.

statements.claim: Krishna and Balarama came forward, bowed to Nanda and Yashoda, seated them on the seats of honor, and embraced them, speechless with love.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.33-34: 'kṛṣṇa-rāmau pariṣvajya pitarāv abhivādya ca / tāv ātmāsanam āropya bāhubhyāṃ parirabhya ca'; pack excerpt: 'speechless with love'.

statements.claim: Yashoda took her two sons onto her lap.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Yashoda takes her two sons on her lap'; BP 10.82.37 ('nyastau' — placed/resting).

statements.claim: Devaki and Rohini embraced Yashoda and spoke of the love she had shown the boys in Gokula: 'Who could forget that friendship, queen of Vraja?'
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.36: 'rohiṇī devakī cātha pariṣvajya vrajeśvarīm / kā vismareta vāṃ maitrīm anivṛttāṃ vrajeśvari'; verse 37 credits Yashoda (and Nanda) with the boys' affection, prosperity, nourishment and protection.

statements.claim: The boys, who had never known their parents' care, rested in her hands as the eyelash rests on the eye — safe and afraid of nothing.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.37: 'etāv adṛṣṭa-pitarau ... bhavati pakṣma ha yadvad akṣṇor nyastāv akutra ca bhayau'.

statements.claim: The cowherds of Gokula stood around smiling and wiping their eyes, as if they too had come home; Yashoda gave Devaki and Rohini back their sons, whole and grown.
statements.evidence: Emotional scene-setting and interpretive gloss of the embrace (verse 36-37); the mothers' mutual consolation is not spelled out in the verses but follows naturally from them.

statements.claim: Vasudeva watched from a little way off, carrying an unnameable debt he would have to speak of before the gathering ended.
statements.evidence: Internal monologue (connective narration) foreshadowing Vasudeva's confession, which the pack records in the following event (DKS_0494 / BP 10.84.58-69).

DKS_0492.notes: Grounded in BP 10.82.30-37. Vasudeva's silent 'debt' is connective foreshadowing of his remorse speech (BP 10.84) in DKS_0494; no unsupported facts.

statements.claim: The gopis, who had not seen Krishna for a long time, came to him at Samanta-panchaka.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.38: 'gopyaś ca kṛṣṇam upalabhya cirād abhīṣṭaṃ' — obtaining Krishna, longed-for after a long time; pack index places the meeting at Samanta-panchaka.

statements.claim: They embraced him in their hearts and thereby attained a state that even the ever-yoked (nitya-yujām) can hardly reach.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.38: 'dṛgbhir hṛdī-kṛtam alaṃ parirabhya sarvās / tad-bhāvam āpur api nitya-yujāṃ durāpam'.

statements.claim: Their eyes had once cursed their own eyelids for blinking and stealing him from sight.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.38: 'yat-prekṣaṇe dṛśiṣu pakṣma-kṛtaṃ śapanti'.

statements.claim: Krishna came to them in a quiet place apart from the crowds.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.39: 'bhagavāṃs tās tathā-bhūtā vivikta upasaṅgataḥ' — the Lord approached them, thus situated, in a secluded spot.

statements.claim: He asked whether they remembered their friendship, and whether they suspected him of ingratitude.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.40-41: 'api smaratha naḥ sakhyaḥ ... / apy avadhyāyathāsmān svid akṛta-jñāviśaṅkayā'.

statements.claim: As the wind gathers clouds, grass, cotton and dust and scatters them, so the Lord brings beings together and carries them apart.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.42: 'vāyur yathā ghanānīkaṃ tṛṇaṃ tūlaṃ rajāṃsi ca'.

statements.claim: Devotion to him grants immortality to beings; he is the beginning and end of all beings, inside them and outside them.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.43-44: 'mayi bhaktir hi bhūtānām amṛtatvāya kalpate / ahaṃ hi sarva-bhūtānām ādir anto 'ntaraṃ bahiḥ'.

statements.claim: The gopis prayed that his lotus feet — contemplated in the heart by the lords of yoga, the one support for those fallen into the well of the world — would always rise in their minds, even for them who dwelt at home.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.47: 'nalina-nābha padāravindaṃ yogeśvarair hṛdi vicintyam agādha-bodhaiḥ / saṃsāra-kūpa-patitottaraṇāvalambaṃ gehaṃ juṣām api manasy udiyāt sadā naḥ'.

statements.claim: By this instruction the gopis' bondage dissolved and they attained him.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'by which instruction the gopis, their bondage dissolved, attained him'.

statements.claim: The gopis had grown older in his absence and measured the days by his absence, counting the waiting itself as keeping him near.
statements.evidence: Interior framing of the gopis' longing (verse 38 'cirāt' supports only that much time had passed since they had seen him).

DKS_0493.notes: Grounded in BP 10.82.38-47. The paraphrase of Krishna's teaching (wind/cloud simile, devotion as immortality, immanence) and the gopis' final prayer track the verses closely; longing-interiority is connective.

statements.claim: Nanda stayed three months, honored with great worship by the Yadavas, and the farewell lasted all that time.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Nanda stays three months, honored by the Yadavas'; BP 10.84.58: 'nandas tu saha gopālair bṛhatyā pūjayārcitaḥ'.

statements.claim: Vasudeva, weeping as he recalled the friendship, told Nanda that the snare called affection is hard to cast off, and that blinded by royal splendor he had neglected his oldest friend.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Vasudeva, weeping as he recalls the friendship, tells Nanda that the snare called affection is hard to cast off, and that blinded by royal splendor he neglected his old friend'; BP 10.84.61-62 ('prāg akalpāc ca kuśalaṃ bhrātar vo nācarāma hi').

statements.claim: In the years when it had been in his power he had done nothing for Nanda, while Nanda had done everything for his sons.
statements.evidence: BP 10.84.62 + pack excerpt ('neglected his old friend, in whose house his sons grew up'); the balance of Vasudeva's debt to Nanda is the substance of the 10.84 speech as rendered in the excerpt.

statements.claim: Vasudeva said: 'May royal splendor never befall a man who desires his own good,' for it blinds the eyes.
statements.evidence: BP 10.84.63: 'mā rājya-śrīr abhūt puṃsaḥ śreyas-kāmasya māna-da'; the 'steals the eyes' gloss matches the excerpt's 'blinded by royal splendor'.

statements.claim: For Vasudeva the great ocean of his longing had at last been crossed.
statements.evidence: BP 10.84.59: 'vasudevo 'ñjasottīrya manoratha-mahārṇavam' — Vasudeva easily crossed the great ocean of his desire.

statements.claim: Nanda's carts were loaded with gifts from Vasudeva, Ugrasena, Krishna, Uddhava and Balarama.
statements.evidence: BP 10.84.67: 'vasudevograsenābhyāṃ kṛṣṇoddhava-balādibhiḥ'; verse 66: 'kāmaiḥ pūryamāṇaḥ' (filled with objects of desire).

statements.claim: Nanda departed with the cowherds and cowherdesses of Vraja, his heart fixed on Govinda's lotus feet.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'departs with the cowherds, his heart fixed on Krishna's lotus feet'; BP 10.84.68 ('govinda-caraṇāmbuje').

statements.claim: When the kinsmen had gone, the Vrishnis, whose deity is Krishna, turned homeward.
statements.evidence: BP 10.84.69: 'bandhuṣu pratiyāteṣu vṛṣṇayaḥ kṛṣṇa-devatāḥ'.

statements.claim: The caravan moved off down the road to Mathura, with Krishna walking beside Nanda's cart to the edge of the camp and Balarama and Krishna watching until the carts were small against the sky.
statements.evidence: Departure staging not verbatim in the pack (which gives no destination); Nanda's home Vraja lies in the Mathura region, and the honor Krishna/Balarama show him is verse-supported (10.84.65 'premṇā govinda-rāmayoḥ'), so this is reasonable connective narration.

statements.claim: Nanda answered Vasudeva not with a speech but with an embrace, having done what a friend does.
statements.evidence: BP 10.84.65 ('nandas tu sakhyuḥ priya-kṛt premṇā govinda-rāmayoḥ' — Nanda did what was dear to his friends through love of Govinda and Rama) supports the substance; the 'no speech' framing is connective.

DKS_0494.notes: Grounded in BP 10.84.58-69. Note pack carries canonical event_id evt_0495 (internal id quirk; content matches the DKS_0494 farewell event). Mathura road and cart-side farewell are connective staging only.

statements.claim: Krishna delighted in Dwaraka, sporting in the lakes as the single beloved of his sixteen thousand wives.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.4-6: 'reme ṣoḍaśa-sāhasra-patnīnāṃ eka-vallabhaḥ' ... 'vijahāra vigāhyāmbho hradinīṣu mahodayaḥ'; pack index note: same scene in HV 1.235 and BP 10.90.

statements.claim: The queens surrounded him and the water-sport was mutual splashing, he sprinkling them and being sprinkled.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.8-10: 'sicyamāno 'cyutas tābhir hasantībhiḥ ... siñcan muhur yuvatibhiḥ pratiṣicyamāno'.

statements.claim: He stood among them as an elephant-lord among his cows (female elephants).
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.10: 'reme kareṇubhir ivebha-patiḥ parītaḥ'.

statements.claim: Musicians played on the bank with drums and other instruments.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.7: 'upagīyamāno gandharvair mṛdaṅga-paṇavānakān' (flutes and cymbals are connective extrapolation of the drum list).

statements.claim: Each of the sixteen thousand was certain he was sporting only with her, and there was no jealousy among them, their minds and eyes being fixed on one man.
statements.evidence: HV 1.235: 'amongst the women of Keshava every one thought: "I am the most favourite of Keshava: he is sporting only with me"'; 'those women, having their minds and eyes fixed on one man, did not cherish jealousy against one another'; BP 10.90.13 ('mukundaika-dhiyo').

statements.claim: Some queens cried out 'O Hari, I am being drowned — save me!' and clung to him.
statements.evidence: HV 1.235: 'Some of them, having eyes like a deer, held Hari by the neck, and said: "O Hari, I am being drowned, save me"'.

statements.claim: Some rowed small boats shaped like herons, serpents and sea-monsters; some swam by their own strength and some with water jars.
statements.evidence: HV 1.235: 'began to row in wooden boats of the shape of herons and serpents ... Makara-shaped boats'; 'some swam depending on their own breast and some on water jars'.

statements.claim: The water stood at the knee of one, the thigh of another, the breast of a third, each met exactly as she came.
statements.evidence: HV 1.235: 'The ocean yielded its water to whatever extent the women wanted, either up to their knees, thighs or breast' (rendered here as playful water in the Dwaraka lakes, per the pack's treatment of BP 10.90 + HV 1.235 as the same scene).

statements.claim: His garland was streaked with saffron and his hair fell loose about his face from the play.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.10: 'tat-stana-viṣajjita-kuṅkuma-srak / krīḍābhiṣaṅga-dhuta-kuntala-vṛnda-bandhaḥ'.

statements.claim: The queens sang songs of longing to the osprey, the shelduck, the waning moon, the southern breeze, the rain-clouds and a swan, asking it of Shauri the Unconquered One and of his fickle friendship.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.14-23: songs to the kurari (v.14), cakravākī (v.15), moon (v.17), malayānila/southern breeze (v.18), megha/clouds (v.19), and the haṃsa/swan (v.23: 'haṃsa svāgatam ... brūhy aṅga śaureḥ kathāṃ ... kaccid ajitaḥ svasty āsta ... kiṃ vā naś cala-sauhṛdaḥ smarati').

statements.claim: By such constant, single-hearted love the queens attained the supreme state.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'by such constant love attain the supreme state' (BP 10.90 context).

statements.claim: The city had settled back into pleasure after the long years of exile and war, with elephants in the streets, heavy gardens and music.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.1-3 describes the flower-laden, elephant-thronged city; the 'after exile and war' timeline and 'music never quite stopped' are connective framing.

DKS_0495.notes: Grounded in BP 10.90.1-24 + HV 1.235 (pack treats both as the same water-sport scene, each-queen-believes-she-is-favoured motif). Water-at-knee/thigh/breast and boats come from HV; songs from BP.

statements.claim: King Dhritarashtra, whose hundred sons had been slain, set out from Hastinapura (the city called after the elephant) in grief to meet the Pandavas.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12 (Ganguli): 'king Yudhishthira the just heard that his uncle Dhritarashtra had set out from the city called after the elephant. Afflicted with grief on account of the death of his sons.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira went out to meet him with his brothers, Krishna of Dasharha's race, Yuyudhana and Yuyutsu; Draupadi, burning with grief, followed her lord.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12: 'The son of Kunti was followed by the high-souled and heroic Krishna of Dasharha's race, and by Yuyudhana, as also by Yuyutsu. The princess Draupadi also, burning with grief ... sorrowfully followed her lord.'

statements.claim: On the banks of the Ganga the Bharata ladies wept like a flight of ospreys, arms raised, asking where was the righteousness of the king who had slain sires, brothers, preceptors, sons and friends.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12: 'the crowd of Bharata ladies afflicted with woe and crying like a flight of she-ospreys ... with arms raised aloft in grief ... "Where, indeed, is that righteousness of the king ... since he has slain sires and brothers and preceptors and sons and friends?"'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira saluted his uncle's feet and the brothers announced themselves, each giving his own name.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12: 'Yudhishthira the just saluted the feet of his eldest uncle. Having saluted their sire according to custom ... the Pandavas, announced themselves to him, each uttering his own name.'

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra reluctantly embraced Yudhishthira with a few words of comfort, then sought Bhima, his wrath a fire fanned by the wind of grief, ready to consume the Bhima-forest.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12: 'reluctantly embraced the eldest son of Pandu ... Having embraced Yudhishthira the just and spoken a few words of comfort ... the wicked-souled Dhritarashtra sought for Bhima, like a blazing fire ... that fire of his wrath, fanned by the wind of his grief, seemed then to be ready to consume the Bhima-forest.'

statements.claim: Krishna, who had understood Dhritarashtra's intentions from the very outset and kept ready an iron statue of Bhima made at Duryodhana's order, drew the real Bhima away and set the statue in the king's embrace.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12: 'Ascertaining the evil intentions cherished by him towards Bhima, Krishna, dragging away the real Bhima, presented an iron statue of the second son of Pandu to the old king. Possessed of great intelligence, Krishna had, at the very outset, understood the intentions ... and had, therefore, kept such a contrivance ready' ... 'that iron statue of Bhima, which had been caused to be made by thy son, had been kept ready for thee.'

statements.claim: The blind king, endued with the strength of ten thousand elephants, crushed the iron statue as if it were a reed; his own breast was bruised, he vomited blood and fell like a parijata tree topped with its flowery burden.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12: 'Endued with might equal to that of 10,000 elephants, the king reduced that statue into fragments. His own breast, however, became considerably bruised and he began to vomit blood. Covered with blood, the king fell down on the ground like a parijata tree topped with its flowery burden.'

statements.claim: Sanjaya, son of Gavalgana, raised and steadied him, saying 'Do not act so,' and the king, his wrath spent, wept 'Alas, oh Bhima, alas, oh Bhima!'
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12: 'His learned charioteer Sanjaya, the son of Gavalgana, raised the monarch and soothing and comforting him, said, "Do not act so." The king then ... began to weep aloud, saying, "Alas, oh Bhima, alas, oh Bhima!"'

statements.claim: Krishna revealed that the king had broken only an iron statue, that no one can escape the pressure of his arms as no one escapes the Destroyer, and that the slaughter of Bhima would not revive his sons — bidding him approve what was done for peace and not set his heart on grief.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12: Krishna's speech — 'Do not grieve, O Dhritarashtra, for thou hast not slain Bhimasena! That is an iron statue ... there is none equal to thee in strength of body ... as no one can escape with life from an encounter with the Destroyer himself, even so no body can come out safe from within thy embrace ... The slaughter of Bhima ... would do thee no good. Thy sons ... would not be revived by it. Therefore, do thou approve of what has been by us with a view to secure peace and do not set thy heart on grief!'

statements.claim: The whole court watched the approach with dread no one spoke aloud, and the meeting 'should have been a simple one — a nephew comforting an uncle'.
statements.evidence: Connective tension-building framing around the supported events (the king's murderous intent is itself verse-supported).

DKS_0496.notes: Very close rendering of MBh 11.12 (Ganguli), including the iron statue, the 10,000-elephant strength, and Krishna's full speech. 'He wanted the man who had killed Duryodhana' relies on the war-arc canon that Bhima slew Duryodhana (corpus chain).

statements.claim: Maid-servants came and washed the king after he had been bloodied, and then Krishna addressed him again.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'Certain maid-servants then came to the king for washing him. After he had been duly washed, the slayer of Madhu again addressed him.' ('Dressed his wounds' is a small connective extension of the washing scene.)

statements.claim: Krishna told the king he had read the Vedas and scriptures, heard the old histories and everything about the duties of kings, and was learned, wise and indifferent to strength and weakness — so why cherish wrath when all that overtook him was his own fault?
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'Thou hast, O king, read the Vedas and diverse scriptures. Thou hast heard all old histories, and everything about the duties of kings. Thou art learned, possessed of great wisdom, and indifferent to strength and weakness. Why then dost thou cherish such wrath when all that has overtaken thee is the result of thy own fault?'

statements.claim: Krishna, Bhishma, Drona, Vidura and Sanjaya had counselled him before the war, telling him the Pandavas were superior to his sons in strength and courage, but he had not followed their advice.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'I spoke to thee before the battle. Both Bhishma and Drona ... did the same, as also Vidura and Sanjaya. Thou didst not, however, then follow our advice ... knowing that the Pandavas were superior to thee and thine ... in strength and courage.'

statements.claim: A king who can see his own faults and knows the distinctions of place and time obtains great prosperity; one who rejects the counsel of well-wishers meets distress and grieves over the policy he chose.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'That king who is capable of seeing his own faults and knows the distinctions of place and time, obtains great prosperity. That person, however, who, though counselled by well-wishers, does not accept their words, good or bad, meets with distress and is obliged to grieve in consequence of the evil policy he pursues.'

statements.claim: The king had not kept his soul under restraint but let Duryodhana rule him; Krishna urged him to observe a different course, recollect his own faults and govern his wrath.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'Thou didst not keep thy soul under restraint, but suffered thyself to be ruled by Duryodhana. That which has come upon thee is due to thy own fault. Why then dost thou seek to slay Bhima? Recollecting thy own faults, govern thy wrath now.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana had, from pride, caused the princess of Pancala to be brought into the assembly, and that mean wretch had been slain by Bhimasena in just revenge.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'That mean wretch who had, from pride, caused the princess of Pancala to be brought into the assembly has been slain by Bhimasena in just revenge.'

statements.claim: Krishna declared the sons of Pandu perfectly innocent yet treated most cruelly by the king and his son.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'The sons of Pandu are perfectly innocent. Yet have they been treated most cruelly by thee and him.'

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra acknowledged it was parental affection for his own sons that made him fall away from righteousness, that by good luck Bhima had never come within his embrace, and that, free of wrath and fever, he now desired to embrace Bhima, on the Pandavas depending his welfare and happiness.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'It is parental affection ... that caused me to fall away from righteousness ... By good luck, that tiger among men, the mighty Bhima of true prowess, protected by thee, came not within my embrace. Now, however, I am free from wrath and fever. I desire eagerly ... to embrace that hero ... When all the kings have been dead, when my children are no more, upon the sons of Pandu depend my welfare and happiness.'

statements.claim: The old king then embraced Bhima, Dhananjaya and the two sons of Madri, weeping over them, comforting them and pronouncing blessings upon them.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'the old king then embraced those princes of excellent frames, Bhima and Dhananjaya, and those two foremost of men, the two sons of Madri, and wept, and comforted and pronounced blessings upon them.'

statements.claim: An hour earlier he had crushed what he believed was Bhima in his arms — an iron statue Krishna had substituted.
statements.evidence: Recap of the immediately preceding canonical event, supported by MBh 11.12 in the DKS_0496 pack ('Krishna ... presented an iron statue of the second son of Pandu to the old king'); 'an hour earlier' is connective timing.

DKS_0497.notes: Faithful rendering of MBh 11.13 (Ganguli); Krishna's admonition and Dhritarashtra's reply track the passage nearly sentence by sentence. 'Dressed his wounds' is a mild extension of the washing scene.

statements.claim: Gandhari had just cursed Krishna — that he would die, as her sons had died, by the hands of his own kinsmen — and he had accepted the curse with a smile.
statements.evidence: Continuity with the immediately preceding canonical event (corpus-chain previous story DKS_0498, 'Gandhari Curses Krishna; He Accepts with a Smile'); the MBh 11.26 passage has Krishna answer Gandhari's grief right after the curse.

statements.claim: Krishna told Gandhari to arise and not set her heart on grief, for through her own fault the vast carnage had taken place.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'Arise, arise, O Gandhari, do not set thy heart on grief! Through thy fault, this vast carnage has taken place!'

statements.claim: Duryodhana was wicked-souled, envious and exceedingly arrogant; Gandhari applauded his wicked acts and regarded them as good; he was cruel, the embodiment of hostilities, and disobedient to the counsel of the elders.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'Thy son Duryodhana was wicked-souled, envious, and exceedingly arrogant. Applauding his wicked acts, thou regardest them to be good. Exceedingly cruel, he was the embodiment of hostilities, and disobedient to the injunctions of the old.'

statements.claim: Krishna asked Gandhari why she wished to ascribe her own faults to him.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'Why dost thou wish to ascribe thy own faults to me?'

statements.claim: One who grieves for what has already occurred obtains more grief; by indulging in grief one increases it two-fold.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'Dead or lost, the person that grieves for what has already occurred, obtaineth more grief. By indulging in grief, one increases it two-fold.'

statements.claim: The woman of the priestly class bears sons for austerities, the cow for burdens, the mare for speed, the servant-woman for servitors, the herdsman's wife for keepers of cattle — but a princess bears sons for being slaughtered.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'A woman of the regenerate class bears children for the practice of austerities; the cow brings forth offspring for bearing burdens; the mare brings forth her young for acquiring speed of motion; the Shudra woman bears a child for adding to the number of servitors; the Vaishya woman for adding to the number of keepers of cattle. A princess, however, like thee, brings forth sons for being slaughtered!'

statements.claim: Gandhari remained silent, her heart exceedingly agitated by grief.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'Gandhari, with heart exceedingly agitated by grief, remained silent.'

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra asked Yudhishthira how many had fallen and how many had escaped; Yudhishthira answered one billion, six hundred and sixty million and twenty thousand fallen, and two hundred and forty thousand one hundred and sixty-five escaped.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'One billion 660 million and 20,000 men have fallen in this battle. Of the heroes that have escaped, the number is 240,165.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira told where the fallen had gone: those who cast off their bodies gladly in fierce battle reached regions like Indra's; those who died without joy found the company of the celestial musicians (Gandharvas); those who fell turning away or begging quarter reached the world of the hidden ones (guhyakas); the high-souled who advanced unarmed against armed foes attained the bright regions of Brahman; the rest attained the region of the Uttara-Kurus.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'Those warriors of true prowess that have cheerfully cast off their bodies in fierce battle have all attained regions like those of Indra ... they that have encountered it cheerlessly have attained the companionship of the Gandharvas. Those warriors that have fallen ... while turning away from the field or begging for quarter, have attained the world of the guhyakas. Those high-souled warriors ... advancing unarmed against fighting foes, have all assumed bright forms and attained the regions of Brahman. The remaining warriors ... have attained the region of the Uttara-Kurus.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira had received the gift of spiritual sight from the sage Lomasa during his years of wandering.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'While at thy command I wandered in the forest, I obtained this boon ... I met with the celestial rishi Lomasa and obtained from him the boon of spiritual vision.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira commanded that the funeral rites of the slain be duly performed so that nobody might perish for want of someone to care for them.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'Cause the funeral rites of the slain, numbering by thousands, to be duly performed, so that nobody may perish for want of persons to take care of them!'

statements.claim: Pyres were built of sandalwood, aloe and gathered wood, with ghee, oil, perfumes, silken robes, broken chariots and heaps of weapons, and were lit; Duryodhana and his hundred brothers, Shalya, Jayadratha, Abhimanyu, Duhshasana's son, Bhurishrava, Drupada, Virata, Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna and the thousands of Srinjayas were burned with due rites.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'procuring sandal, aloe and other kinds of wood ... clarified butter and oil and perfumes and costly silken robes ... large heaps of dry wood, and broken cars and diverse kinds of weapons, caused funeral pyres to be duly made and lighted and then without haste burnt, with due rites the slain kings ... the bodies of Duryodhana and his hundred brothers, of Shalya, and king Bhurishrava; of king Jayadratha and Abhimanyu ... of Duhshasana's son ... of Virata and Drupada; of Shikhandi ... and Dhrishtadyumna ... and the hundreds of Srinjayas.'

statements.claim: Krishna spoke 'with the pyres not yet built', and Dhritarashtra had been listening at Gandhari's side.
statements.evidence: Timing/staging connective narration; the passage order (rebuke, numbers, then the funeral command) supports the sequence, and Dhritarashtra's presence is implied by his immediately following question.

DKS_0499.notes: Faithful rendering of MBh 11.26 (Ganguli) — the rebuke, the grief teaching, the classes of women, the casualty numbers (1,660,020,000 fallen; 240,165 escaped), the ends of the fallen, and the funeral of the named kings all track the passage. Curse recap relies on chain continuity with DKS_0498.

statements.claim: Years later, when people asked what Krishna and Arjuna spoke of after the war, the answer began with a confession: everything Krishna had told him on the battlefield, Arjuna had forgotten.
statements.evidence: MBh 14.16 (Ganguli): Janamejaya asks what conversation took place between Kesava and Arjuna in the assembly rooms; Arjuna: 'What thy holy self said unto me at that time, O Kesava, through affection, has all been forgotten by me, O chief of men, in consequence of the fickleness of my mind.'

statements.claim: Arjuna, having recovered his kingdom, spent his days in joy in Krishna's company in the palace at Hastinapura, in rooms that seemed a piece of heaven, surrounded by relatives and attendants.
statements.evidence: MBh 14.16 (Ganguli): 'The son of Pritha (Arjuna), having recovered his own kingdom, joyously spent his time... in the company of Krishna... in that palace of celestial beauty' in rooms that 'looked... like a veritable portion of Heaven... surrounded by their relatives and attendants.'

statements.claim: Arjuna said Krishna's greatness and his form as the Lord of the universe had become known to him on the approach of battle, and that Krishna would soon be leaving for Dwaraka.
statements.evidence: MBh 14.16: 'thy greatness became known to me upon the approach of the battle... thy form also, as the Lord of the universe, then became known to me... Thou again, O Madhava, wilt repair to Dwaraka soon.'

statements.claim: Krishna embraced Arjuna and answered that it was exceedingly disagreeable to him to learn that Arjuna had not, from folly, received what was imparted; the recollection of all he had told him would not come to him now; the teaching was more than sufficient for understanding Brahma; he could not discourse on it again in detail, for he had spoken of Supreme Brahma while concentrated in yoga.
statements.evidence: MBh 14.16 (Ganguli), Krishna's reply: 'embraced Phalguna and replied... It is exceedingly disagreeable to me to learn that thou didst not, from folly, receive what I imparted. The recollection of all that I told thee on that occasion will not come to me now... That religion... is more than sufficient for understanding Brahma. I cannot discourse on it again in detail. I discoursed to thee on Supreme Brahma, having concentrated myself in Yoga.'

statements.claim: Krishna promised to recite an old history upon the same topic, by which Arjuna, listening with an understanding adapted to the teaching, might attain the highest end.
statements.evidence: MBh 14.16: 'I shalt now, however, recite to thee an old history upon the same topic... so that, with an understanding adapted to my teaching, thou mayst succeed in attaining to the highest end.'

statements.claim: In the old history, a Brahmana of irresistible energy had come to Krishna and Arjuna from the regions of Heaven, from the presence of the Grandsire, and was reverenced duly; asked about the religion of Emancipation — out of compassion for all creatures and not for his own good — he agreed to speak, asking that they listen with concentrated attention.
statements.evidence: MBh 14.16: 'a Brahmana came to us from the regions of Heaven. Of irresistible energy, he came from the regions of the Grandsire. He was duly reverenced by us... That which thou askest me, O Krishna, connected with the religion of Moksha (Emancipation), led by thy compassion for all creatures (and not for thy own good)... I shall now tell thee duly... Do thou listen with concentrated attention.'

statements.claim: The old history concerned a Brahmana named Kasyapa, foremost of all persons conversant with duties, who had heard of another Brahmana who had mastered the scriptures on the departure and reappearance of beings, possessed the direct knowledge yoga gives, knew the truths of the world, pleasure and pain, merit and demerit, beheld the ends attained by embodied creatures, lived like one emancipated, had his senses under control, seemed to blaze with the resplendence of Brahma, could go everywhere at will, knew the science of disappearing at will, roved with invisible Siddhas and celestial musicians, and was unattached as the wind.
statements.evidence: MBh 14.16 (Ganguli), the Brahmana's narration: 'A Brahmana of the name of Kasyapa, possessed of penances and the foremost of all persons conversant with duties, came to a certain other Brahmana who had become conversant with all the mysteries of religion...' — followed by the full catalogue of the sage's attainments as rendered in the story.

statements.claim: Kasyapa, having heard of him, desired to see him; approaching the sage and seeing those wonderful attributes, he fell with a rapt heart at his feet and began to wait upon him with dutiful reverence.
statements.evidence: MBh 14.16: 'Kasyapa having heard of him truly, desired to see him... Kasyapa, moved by the desire of acquiring merit, fell, with a rapt heart, at the feet of the sage when he had seen all those wonderful attributes. Filled with wonder... Kasyapa began to wait upon that foremost of all Brahmanas, with the dutiful reverence.'

statements.claim: The old history Krishna promised would unroll through the days that followed into the teaching known as the Anugita; it is the tale of Kasyapa as told by the Brahmana of Heaven.
statements.evidence: Index/chain confirm Krishna 'instead narrates an old history (the Anugita)' and the MBh 14.16 passage places the Brahmana of Heaven's narration in answer to Krishna's enquiries (the inner tale is of Kasyapa approaching the sage). The closing sentence slightly compresses the nesting (the Brahmana of Heaven narrates to Krishna; within that narration the sage teaches Kasyapa), but 'told to Kasyapa' is a defensible shorthand for where the narration is headed and is connective framing, not a correction-worthy factual error.

DKS_0500.notes: No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims; prose tracks MBh 14.16 (Ganguli) nearly clause-for-clause. One minor nesting compression in the closing frame (see last statement).

statements.claim: By the time the Yadava clan had all but destroyed itself, there was almost no one left at Krishna's side; he had watched the course of his own maya run out to its end.
statements.evidence: SB 3.4 index: 'Uddhava recalls how, as the Yadavas destroyed themselves, Krishna sat at the foot of an ashvattha tree...'; SB 3.4.2: 'bhagavān svātma-māyāyā gatiṃ tām avalokya saḥ' — the Lord, seeing that course of his own maya.

statements.claim: Krishna walked to the bank of the Sarasvati, sipped the water, and sat down at the foot of an ashvattha tree.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (SB 3.4.2-10 rendered): 'The Lord... sipped the Sarasvati and sat at the foot of a tree'; index location: 'the bank of the Sarasvati, at the foot of an ashvattha tree.'

statements.claim: There Krishna told Uddhava to go to Badari, the hermitage in the north; Uddhava, unable to leave his feet, lingered and followed at a distance; Krishna found him there and said: I know your heart's desire; I grant you what is hard for others to attain.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (SB 3.4.2-10): 'he said to me, go to Badari. Yet, unable to leave his feet, I followed; and he, finding me there, told me: I know your heart's desire; I grant you what is hard for others to attain.' (Badari as the northern hermitage is standard identification consistent with the pack.)

statements.claim: Uddhava saw his Lord seated alone, contemplating — dark and radiant, free of all passion, eyes peaceful and touched with red, right foot resting on his left thigh.
statements.evidence: SB 3.4.5-7: 'adrākṣam ekam āsīnaṃ vicinvan dayitaṃ patim' (I saw my beloved Lord seated alone, contemplating); 'śyāmāvadātaṃ virajaṃ praśāntāruṇa-locanam' (dark-and-radiant, passionless, tranquil reddish eyes); 'vāma ūrāv adhiśritya dakṣiṇāṅghri-saroruham' (right lotus foot resting on the left thigh).

statements.claim: Uddhava is the great devotee, the friend of Vyasa (Dvaipayana) himself, and bowed with joy, his head bent low.
statements.evidence: SB 3.4.8-9: 'tasmin mahā-bhāgavato dvaipāyana-suhṛt-sakhā... pramoda-bhāvānata-kandharasya' — the great devotee, friend of Dvaipayana, neck bent with joyful emotion.

statements.claim: Krishna told Uddhava: This is the last of your births; my grace has come to you; what I spoke long ago to Brahma, seated on the lotus born from my navel at the beginning of creation, is what I give you now.
statements.evidence: SB 3.4.11-12: 'sa eṣa sādho caramo bhavānām āsāditas te mad-anugraho yat' (this is the last of your births — my grace has been obtained by you); 'purā mayā proktam ajāya nābhye padme niṣaṇṇāya mamādi-sarge' (spoken by me long ago to the unborn Brahma seated on the lotus of my navel at the beginning of creation).

statements.claim: Uddhava praised Krishna — the one who acts without desire, whose birth and non-birth are beyond telling, the refuge of the distressed whom the frightened reach by fleeing from every fear, the one invoked in mantras, whose knowledge of the self is unbroken, complete and eternal.
statements.evidence: SB 3.4.15-16: 'karmāṇy anīhasya bhavo 'bhavasya te durgāśrayo 'thāri-bhayāt palāyanam / mantreṣu māṃ vā upahūya yat tvam akuṇṭhitākhaṇḍa-sadātma-bodhaḥ' — desireless acts, birth and non-birth inconceivable, refuge of the distressed, invoked in mantras, unbroken complete eternal self-knowledge.

statements.claim: Krishna taught Uddhava the supreme knowledge that illuminates the secret of the self, and granted him the state hard for others to attain; the account in SB 3 is Uddhava's own recollection.
statements.evidence: SB 3.4.17-18: 'jñānaṃ paraṃ svātma-rahaḥ-prakāśaṃ provāca kasmai bhagavān samagram' (the supreme knowledge revealing the secret of the self, taught completely); pack index: 'granted him the ancient teaching and the supreme state'; the passage is Uddhava speaking (śrī-uddhava uvāca), matching the story's 'Uddhava has left us his own account of that hour.'

DKS_0501.notes: No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims. Dense Sanskrit pack (SB 3.4.2-18) maps cleanly onto the story's details; final 'whisper by a river' line is poetic atmosphere.

statements.claim: In the palace at Mathura, when Krishna wanted comfort carried to the people of his boyhood, he looked to Uddhava, his beloved devotee, his friend whose heart was fixed on him alone.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.1: 'tam āha bhagavān preṣṭhaṃ bhaktam ekāntinaṃ kvacit' — the Lord spoke to his dearest devotee, wholly fixed on him alone; index sets the episode in Mathura.

statements.claim: Krishna sent Uddhava with a message: 'Go to Vraja... Bring joy to my parents' — Nanda and Yashoda who had raised him; the summons of Kamsa's court had carried him away to Mathura.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.2: 'gacchoddhava vrajaṃ saumya pitror nau prītim āvaha' — go to Vraja, bring joy to our parents. (Nanda/Yashoda as his Vraja parents and Kamsa's summons as the cause of his removal to Mathura are canonical SB background consistent with the pack; not stated in the six excerpted verses but uncontested context.)

statements.claim: The women of Gokula had their minds fixed on Krishna; their very lives were given up for his sake; for his sake they had abandoned comfort, standing, even their own bodies; to them he was the dearest of all dear ones, and he was far away; they were keeping themselves alive only with great difficulty.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.3-5: 'tā man-manaskā tṛṣṭ-prāṇā mad-arthe tyakta-daihikāḥ / mayi tāḥ preyasāṃ preṣṭhe dūra-sthe gokula-striyaḥ / dhārayanty ati-kṛcchreṇa prāyaḥ prāṇān kathañcana' — minds fixed on me, lives given up, bodies abandoned for my sake; the Gokula women to whom I am dearest of the dear, far away, barely sustaining their lives with great difficulty.

statements.claim: Uddhava, who held no office, had been at Krishna's side through the long years in Mathura and had seen how Krishna grew quiet whenever the talk turned to Vrindavan — a single mention of the village could stop him mid-sentence.
statements.evidence: Not in the pack's six excerpted verses; invented-but-plausible connective backstory dramatizing the affection that 10.46.1-5 implies (Krishna's tender message to Vrindavan). No pack source contradicts it.

statements.claim: Uddhava accepted the charge, promising to tell Nanda and Yashoda of their son, carry Krishna's love to the women of Gokula, and not rest until he had consoled them; he made ready and set out for Vrindavan.
statements.evidence: The mission's substance is supported (SB 10.46.1-6 + chain to DKS_0503 where Uddhava arrives in Vrindavan); Uddhava's spoken acceptance and the travel details are connective narration not present in the excerpted verses.

DKS_0502.notes: No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims. The gopis' message is rendered near-verbatim from SB 10.46.3-5; the opening paragraphs (Uddhava's rank, Krishna's demeanor) are acceptable connective backstory.

statements.claim: Uddhava reached Nanda's Vraja as the sun went down.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.7: 'prāpto nanda-vrajaṃ śrīmān nimlocati vibhāvasau' — he reached Nanda's Vraja as the sun was setting.

statements.claim: The village at dusk was alive: bulls scenting the cows bellowed and fought in the lanes, white calves leaped about so the settlement seemed dressed in them, and the women sang the auspicious deeds of Bala and Krishna.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.8-10: bulls fighting for the scent of cows ('vāsitārthe 'bhiyudhyadbhir... vṛṣaiḥ'), white calves leaping everywhere ('vilaṅghadbhir go-vatsair maṇḍitaṃ sitaiḥ'), women singing the auspicious deeds of Bala and Krishna ('gāyantībhiś ca karmāṇi śubhāni bala-kṛṣṇayoḥ').

statements.claim: Every home bore marks of worship of the fire, the sun, the guest, the cow, the Brahmana, the ancestors and the gods, and the forests around stood in full flower, loud with the calling of birds.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.11-12: 'agny-arkātithi-go-vipra-pitṛ-devārcanānvitaiḥ' and 'sarvataḥ puṣpita-vanaṃ dvijāli-kula-nāditam.'

statements.claim: Nanda hurried to meet Uddhava, Krishna's own companion and beloved attendant, embraced him and honored him as he would have honored Vasudeva himself, pressed the finest food upon him and seated him comfortably on a couch; only then did he begin his questions.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.13-14: Nanda approached Uddhava, 'kṛṣṇasyānucaraṃ priyam', fed him 'paramānnena' and seated him 'kaśipau sukham'; pack excerpt: 'was embraced by Nanda and honored as Vasudeva himself'; Nanda's questions follow at vv. 15+.

statements.claim: Nanda asked whether his friend, the son of Shura, was well; said that by good fortune the sinner Kamsa had been killed with all his followers by the very evil he had done; asked whether Krishna remembered his mother, friends and playmates, and whether Govinda would ever come back to look upon his own people.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.15-18: 'kaccid aṅga mahā-bhāga sakhā naḥ śūra-nandanaḥ' (15); 'diṣṭyā kaṃso hataḥ pāpaḥ sānugaḥ svena pāpmanā' (16); 'api smarati naḥ kṛṣṇo mātaraṃ suhṛdaḥ sakhīn' (17); 'apy āyāsyati govindaḥ sva-janān sakṛd īkṣitum' (18).

statements.claim: Nanda remembered how Krishna had sheltered them from the forest fire, from wind and rain, from the great bull and from the serpent; his heroic deeds and playful sidelong glance; and the rivers, mountains and forests adorned by the touch of Krishna's feet.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.19-21: 'dāvāgner vāta-varṣāc ca vṛṣa-sarpāc ca rakṣitāḥ / smaratāṃ kṛṣṇa-vīryāṇi līlāpāṅga-nirīkṣitam / saric-chaila-vanoddeśān mukunda-pada-bhūṣitān.'

statements.claim: Nanda mused that Krishna and Rama must be the best of the gods come down among men: who else could have broken the great bow tall as three palm trees as an elephant king snaps a staff, or brought down Kamsa — strong as ten thousand elephants — together with the two wrestlers and the royal elephant?
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.22-24: 'manye kṛṣṇaṃ ca rāmaṃ ca prāptāv iha surottamau / kaṃsaṃ nāgāyuta-prāṇaṃ mallau gaja-patiṃ yathā / tāla-trayaṃ mahā-sāraṃ dhanur yaṣṭim ivebha-rāṭ.'

statements.claim: The demons of Krishna's boyhood — Pralamba, Dhenuka, Arishta, Trinavarta, Baka — had fallen to the two brothers one after another.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.25: 'pralambo dhenuko 'riṣṭas tṛṇāvarto bakādayaḥ.'

statements.claim: Yashoda listened and wept as Nanda recounted Krishna's deeds.
statements.evidence: SB 10.46.27-28 (pack): Yashoda, as her son's deeds were narrated, wept; pack excerpt: 'and Yashoda wept as she listened.'

DKS_0503.notes: No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims. Nearly every sentence maps to SB 10.46.7-28 verse-by-verse; only sensory connective color (Uddhava walking the lanes, 'the old man's questions spilling out') is added.

statements.claim: The omens had begun to appear in Dwaraka — a strange bird on a rooftop, a vessel of milk soured before its time — and then signs that made the city speak in low voices; Krishna read them all and grew quiet.
statements.evidence: Index confirms 'fearful omens in Dwaraka' preceding Krishna's departure, and SB 11.6.39 ('tan nirīkṣya...') has Uddhava 'seeing those [omens]'; the specific examples (bird on a rooftop, soured milk) are generic utpāta flavor not in the excerpted verses — acceptable atmosphere.

statements.claim: Uddhava had lately returned from Vrindavan, carrying Krishna's message to the cowherds and bringing back their longing; Nanda's grief, the gopis' tears and the villagers' devotion were fresh with him.
statements.evidence: Supported by the corpus chain (DKS_0502/DKS_0503 and the canonical Uddhava mission of SB 10.46-47); pack index places this episode after the Vrindavan return arc.

statements.claim: Dwaraka had grown rich and proud; its pride worked like a slow fever — long feasts, quarrels over a look, young Yadu clansmen who had forgotten fear; elders whispered the family had grown too great for the earth to hold it.
statements.evidence: Not in the excerpted verses (SB 11.6.39-49), which begin at Uddhava's plea; the decadence of the Yadavas is standard Bhagavata background for their destruction, and 'the omens seemed to say the same thing' ties it to the pack's omens. Atmosphere, not a contested fact.

statements.claim: Uddhava found Krishna alone and fell at his feet, saying: 'Even for half a moment, Keshava, I cannot bear to leave your lotus feet. Wherever you go, carry me also to your abode.'
statements.evidence: SB 11.6.39-42: Uddhava approached the Lord of lords in a secluded place ('vivikta upasaṅgamya jagatām īśvareśvaram'); pack excerpt (vv. 41-42): 'Lord, even for half a moment I cannot bear to leave your lotus feet; carry me also to your abode.'

statements.claim: Uddhava declared Krishna's pastimes the supreme good fortune of human beings, with nothing in the three worlds beside them, and that he had treasured everything Krishna touched — the bed, the seat, the roads, the river pools, his games, his meals, his garlands, scents, clothes and ornaments.
statements.evidence: SB 11.6.43-45: 'tava vikrīḍitaṃ kṛṣṇa nṛnāṃ parama-maṅgalam / śayyāsanāṭana-sthāna-snāna-krīḍāśanādiṣu / tvayopabhukta-srag-gandha-vāso-'laṅkāra-carcitāḥ.'

statements.claim: Even the ascetics who renounce everything and wear only the wind for clothing wander the paths of action remembering and singing Krishna's deeds; they never touched his hand, and they cannot let him go.
statements.evidence: SB 11.6.46-48: 'vāta-vasanā ya ṛṣayaḥ śramaṇā ūrdhra-manthinaḥ / vayaṃ tv iha mahā-yogin bhramantaḥ karma-vartmasu / smarantaḥ kīrtayantas te kṛtāni gaditāni ca.'

statements.claim: Krishna raised Uddhava up and answered: 'What you have said is exactly my own intent. Brahma, Shiva, and the guardians of the worlds long for my return to heaven. The time has come.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (vv. 49-50): Krishna, addressed by his devoted servant, answered: 'What you have said is exactly my own intent; Brahma, Shiva and the world-guardians long for my return to heaven.' ('Raised him up' and 'the time has come' are minor connective gestures consistent with the reply's content.)

statements.claim: Krishna granted Uddhava his prayer — he would not be left behind — and then began to instruct him, as a teacher to a beloved disciple, about the self, the world and the way to freedom.
statements.evidence: Index summary: 'Krishna, granting his wish, begins to instruct him'; the instruction proper unfolds in the following SB chapters (11.7+), matching the corpus chain to DKS_0505.

DKS_0504.notes: No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims. The core dialogue (Uddhava's plea, Krishna's reply) is rendered almost verbatim from SB 11.6.39-49; opening omen-and-city mood is connective atmosphere.

statements.claim: Krishna tells Uddhava the story of King Yadu and the avadhuta: 'Listen... I will tell you what freedom looks like.'
statements.evidence: SB 11.7 is Krishna's instruction to Uddhava; 11.7.23: 'atrāpy udāharantīmam itihāsaṃ purātanam' — here they cite this ancient history — introducing the avadhuta narrative; the pack excerpt quotes the frame.

statements.claim: There was a king named Yadu, of the line of Nahusha, and one day a wandering brahmin — an avadhuta who had put aside everything — came down the road where his party had halted in a forest.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.24: 'avadhūtaṃ dvi-jaṃ kañcic carantam akuto-bhayam' (a certain twice-born avadhuta wandering fearlessly); Yadu is named ('śrī-yadur uvāca') and addressed as 'nāhuṣātmaja' (son of Nahusha); index location: 'a forest road.'

statements.claim: The avadhuta owned nothing and feared nothing, and there was a serenity in him unlike anything Yadu had seen at court.
statements.evidence: Fearlessness is supported ('akuto-bhayam', 'afraid of no one' in Yadu's later speech); the contrast with Yadu's court is interpretive connective color building on verses 26-29.

statements.claim: Yadu spoke of people burning in the fire of desire and greed, and asked the avadhuta: 'Men spend their lives in dharma, wealth, pleasure, and the itch of curiosity... But you are capable, wise, skilled, fortunate; your speech is like nectar; for those who ask, you are the very cause of joy. You act like a child, a madman, a ghost — and yet you are a sage. How did you gain such wisdom?'
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.26-29: 'prāyo dharmārtha-kāmeṣu vivitsāyāṃ ca mānavāḥ / tvaṃ tu kalpaḥ kavir dakṣaḥ su-bhago 'mṛta-bhāṣaṇaḥ / janeṣu dahyamāneṣu kāma-lobha-davāgninā / tvaṃ hi naḥ pṛcchatāṃ brahmann ātmany ānanda-kāraṇam'; pack excerpt: Yadu asked, 'You act like a child, a madman, a ghost, and yet you are a sage; how did you gain such wisdom?'

statements.claim: The avadhuta answered that he has twenty-four gurus, naming them: earth, wind, sky, water, fire, the moon, the sun; the pigeon, the python, the ocean; the moth, the bee, the elephant, the honey-gatherer; the deer, the fish, Pingala, the osprey; the child, the maiden, the arrow-maker, the serpent, the spider, the cricket.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.32-35: 'pṛthivī vāyur ākāśam āpo 'gniś candramā raviḥ... ete me guravo rājan catur-viṃśatir āśritāḥ / yato yad anuśikṣāmi'; the pack's rendered excerpt lists the identical twenty-four, in the same order, including Pingala, the osprey (kurara) and the cricket (peśaskṛt).

statements.claim: Yadu's inner reaction — surprise that his teachers include a python, a fish, a maiden, and a woman named Pingala — and his request 'Then teach me.'
statements.evidence: Pingalā is indeed feminine (SB 11.8's famous courtesan), but Yadu's musings and his explicit 'teach me' request are connective narration; the lessons follow directly in the text (11.7.36+) in response to his question.

statements.claim: The avadhuta began with the first of his teachers: the earth itself.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.36ff opens the sequence of lessons with the earth; chain to DKS_0506 ('The earth taught me forbearance').

DKS_0505.notes: No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims. The 24-guru list matches the pack's list exactly and in order; the court-burden color in the opening is generic connective framing.

statements.claim: The earth taught forbearance: every being tramples her — beasts and men, armies, cattle, cart-wheels — morning and evening, yet she never strays from her course; so the wise one, though the world treads on him, does not leave his path.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.36: 'bhūtair ākramyamāṇo 'pi dhīro daiva-vaśānugaiḥ' — though pressed upon by beings, the steadfast one does not deviate; pack index: earth = forbearance.

statements.claim: The wind taught detachment: it moves everywhere — through palaces, market streets and every corner of every house — and clings to nothing it touches; so the yogi moves among the objects of the senses and remains unattached.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.39: 'viṣayeṣv āviśan yogī nānā-dharmeṣu sarvataḥ' — the yogi entering among sense objects everywhere; pack excerpt: 'Moving among the objects of sense, the yogi remains unattached like the wind.'

statements.claim: The sky taught him to remain unaffected: clouds, rain, smoke and birds cross it and leave no mark; so the wise one dwells among all the bodies of the world, moving and unmoving, hidden in each and touched by none, seeing the one self in all things.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.40-42: 'pārthiveṣv iha deheṣu praviṣṭas tad-guṇāśrayaḥ / antarhitaś ca sthira-jaṅgameṣu brahmātma-bhāvena samanvayena' (hidden in moving and unmoving beings through identity of Brahman and self) and 'tejo-'b-anna-mayair bhāvair meghādyair vāyuneritaiḥ' (clouds driven by wind); pack index: sky = unaffectedness.

statements.claim: The water taught purity: clear by nature, sweet to the taste, wherever it flows it becomes a holy place (a tirtha) for men to bathe in; so the sage, pure in himself, makes everything around him sacred and men's dirt falls from them in his presence.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.43: 'svacchaḥ prakṛtitaḥ snigdho mādhuryas tīrtha-bhūr nṛṇām' — naturally clear, soft, sweet, a tirtha for men; pack excerpt: 'pure and sweet like water.'

statements.claim: The fire taught him to be untainted: whatever it is given — wood, refuse, offerings, filth — it burns and takes no stain; it shines by its own heat and is hard to approach; so the sage is not polluted by what he consumes.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.44: 'tejasvī tapasā dīpto durdharṣodara-bhājanaḥ' — radiant, shining by tapas, hard to approach, an undecaying vessel; pack excerpt: 'untainted by what he consumes, like fire.'

statements.claim: The moon taught waxing and waning: it swells to fullness and thins to a sliver, and both are its own nature; the body's states — birth, youth, age, death, up to the cremation ground — belong to the body, not the self, and the wise one watches them as the moon watches its phases.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.45-49: 'kvacic channaḥ kvacit spaṣṭaḥ...' (the moon sometimes hidden, sometimes visible) and 'visargādyāḥ śmaśānāntā bhāvā dehasya nātmanaḥ' (states from creation to the cremation ground belong to the body, not the self); 'guṇair guṇān upādatte yathā-kālaṃ vimuñcati' (takes up and lets go qualities with time); pack index: moon = waxing and waning.

statements.claim: The sun taught the one soul in many bodies: one sun rises on palace and hut, king and beggar, illumining all; the one self appears in every body, and when a body ends nothing of the light is lost.
statements.evidence: SB 11.7.50: 'budhyate sve na bhedena vyakti-stha iva tad-gataḥ' — he awakens in himself without distinction, standing in the many like the one sun; pack excerpt: 'one soul appearing in many bodies, like the sun.'

statements.claim: Yadu's interjections — that the first lesson found its mark, that he had filled his court with the learned and none had told him anything so simply — and that the avadhuta then went on to the eighth teacher, the pigeon.
statements.evidence: The lesson content is fully supported; Yadu's inner reactions are invented psychological connective framing, and the transition to the pigeon as the next guru matches the canonical order (SB 11.7.51ff / chain to DKS_0507).

DKS_0506.notes: No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims. All seven element-lessons track SB 11.7.36-50 in pack order (earth, wind, sky, water, fire, moon, sun); only Yadu's reflective interludes are connective.

statements.claim: The python taught contentment: he lies where he happens to be and takes whatever comes within reach — fine food or foul, much or little; if nothing comes he lies still for days without effort, pursuit or complaint; so the sage accepts what chance brings and does not run after more.
statements.evidence: SB 11.8.1-2: 'grāsaṃ su-mṛṣṭaṃ virasaṃ mahāntaṃ stokam eva vā / ... śayītāhāni bhūrīṇi nirāhāro 'nupakramaḥ' — the python takes food fine or foul, great or small (that chance brings), and lies for many days without food, without enterprise.

statements.claim: The sage bears a body full of vigor and strength yet does not spend it on striving; his hands do what needs doing but his acts leave no trace on him because they are not born of desire.
statements.evidence: SB 11.8.3: 'ojaḥ-saho-bala-yutaṃ bibhrad deham akarmakam' — bearing a body full of ojas, strength and power, yet actionless (free from karma-driven acts).

statements.claim: The ocean taught depth: the rivers pour into it and it does not swell; the rivers dry up and it does not sink; it is so deep none can fathom it and so still none can stir it; whatever pours in or is withheld, its fullness is its own.
statements.evidence: SB 11.8.4: 'muniḥ prasanna-gambhīro durvigāhyo duratyayaḥ' — the sage serene, deep, unfathomable, hard to cross — the ocean simile of the pack excerpt: 'which neither swells when rivers pour in nor dries when they do not.'

statements.claim: The sage remains the same whether the world pours gifts on him or leaves him empty-handed; whether his desires are fulfilled or he is left destitute, he is fixed on Narayana alone, and his fullness does not rise or fall with fortune.
statements.evidence: SB 11.8.5: 'samṛddha-kāmo hīno vā nārāyaṇa-paro muniḥ' — whether his desires are fulfilled or he is deprived, the sage is fixed on Narayana.

statements.claim: Yadu understood the python's stillness and the ocean's depth as one teaching — freedom comes not from having enough but from not needing anything — and the avadhuta, seeing the lesson had landed, spoke next of the moth and the flame.
statements.evidence: Yadu's synthesis is interpretive connective narration consistent with verses 3-5; the moth as the next guru matches the canonical sequence (SB 11.8.6ff) and the chain to DKS_0509 ('The Moth and the Bee').

DKS_0508.notes: No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims. Both lessons render SB 11.8.1-5 closely; only Yadu's reflective closing is connective.

statements.claim: The avadhuta watched a moth circle a lamp flame and fall into it, at night, by a lamp in a wayside rest-house, and counted the moth among his teachers.
statements.evidence: The moth-into-flame exemplum is the source's own simile (BP 11.8.6-7: the uncontrolled man falls like the moth into the flame), and the moth is one of the avadhuta's named gurus (BP 11.7.33-34, corpus chain DKS_0505); but the specific witnessed scene (wayside rest-house, night lamp) is dramatized setting not present in the pack.

statements.claim: Bewitched by a woman's beauty — the gold of her ornaments, the fine weave of her clothes — the man not master of his senses falls into blinding darkness, as the moth into the flame.
statements.evidence: BP 11.8.6-7: dṛṣṭvā striyaṃ deva-māyāṃ tad-bhāvair ajitendriyaḥ / yoṣid-dhiraṇyābharaṇāmbarādi-dravyeṣu māyā-raciteṣu mūḍhaḥ — seeing woman, the uncontrolled man falls into blinding darkness; the gold ornaments and garments are in the verse.

statements.claim: The wandering teacher was an avadhuta — a brahmin who had put aside home, name and belongings — who walked the forest roads taking lessons from everything he met, with no guru but the world.
statements.evidence: Corpus chain: BP 11.7.24 (avadhūta brahmin wandering fearlessly), 11.7.33-34 (list of his gurus incl. the moth), established in DKS_0505/0506; consistent with this pack.

statements.claim: He learned to read the smallest things — a drop of water, a bent blade of grass, a sparrow's quarrel — each a page of some teaching; nothing was too small to teach him, and nothing too small to destroy a man.
statements.evidence: Generic illustration of the avadhuta's practice of taking gurus from earth, water, creatures etc. (BP 11.7.33, chain DKS_0505-0506); the specific instances are atmospheric, not asserted by this pack.

statements.claim: The moth's lesson was desire: the flame asks nothing, the moth gives everything; so a man who is not master of his senses follows beauty's brightness and falls — and the avadhuta had seen it happen to men he knew.
statements.evidence: The teaching itself is supported (BP 11.8.6-7); 'he had seen it happen to men he knew — sensible men undone by a face' is invented personal history used as connective rhetoric, asserting no sourceable canonical event.

statements.claim: It is not that beauty is false; it is that desire cannot stop at looking — it must draw nearer until the lovely light is the fire that burns.
statements.evidence: Interpretive gloss on the moth simile consistent with the verse's point; not itself a sourceable claim.

statements.claim: The bee taught the other way: the sage gathers the essence from great and small teachings as the bee gathers from flowers, and stores nothing up.
statements.evidence: BP 11.8.9 (aṇubhyaś ca mahadbhyaś ca śāstrebhyaḥ kuśalo naraḥ — the wise man [gathers essence] from small and great scriptures) with the bee simile; pack excerpt: 'the sage gathers the essence from great and small teachings, like the bee from flowers, but stores nothing for tomorrow.'

statements.claim: The bee visits many flowers and takes from each only a little, carrying nothing away to hoard; each blossom is left able to bloom again.
statements.evidence: Naturalistic elaboration of the bee simile from the pack excerpt; description of how bees work, not a canonical event claim.

statements.claim: He eats a little at a time, just enough to keep the body alive, and what is begged for the day is used that same day; he never lays it up for the evening or the morning.
statements.evidence: BP 11.8.8 (stokaṃ stokaṃ grased grāsaṃ deho varteta yāvatā) and 11.8.10-11 (sāyantanaṃ śvastanaṃ vā na saṅgṛhṇīta bhikṣitam / bhikṣukaḥ).

statements.claim: The avadhuta said he had made himself the bee — tasting sweetness without owning it, listening to great and small teachings without serving any, sleeping with empty hands, free of the need that makes men hold on.
statements.evidence: First-person dramatization of the teaching in 11.8.8-11; consistent but the 'he had made himself the bee' claim is connective.

statements.claim: The moth and the bee together are one complete teaching: the moth shows what appetite costs, the bee what appetite is for.
statements.evidence: Closing synthesis of the two supported lessons; non-factual framing.

DKS_0509.notes: Faithful to BP 11.8.6-11. Scene-setting (rest-house, watching the moth, 'men he knew') is dramatized connective narration around the source's similes; no UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims. Avadhuta/guru-list identity supported via corpus chain (DKS_0505, BP 11.7).

statements.claim: The elephant — the strongest thing in the forest, able to uproot a tree — is caught by a she-elephant: hunters send the cow out as a decoy and the great male follows her into the clearing where rope and stake wait; he is not conquered but led.
statements.evidence: The pack supports the core image — 'bound like the elephant caught by the she-elephant' (BP 11.8.12) — but the hunters-decoy/rope-and-stake mechanism is a dramatized naturalistic gloss of how such capture happens; the source records no specific capture scene.

statements.claim: If desire can bind an elephant, what will it do to a man; strength counts for nothing against desire — the elephant could have broken every rope and instead stood quietly while it was tied.
statements.evidence: Expansion of the 11.8.12 simile (the ascetic bound like the elephant caught by the she-elephant); rhetorical elaboration, consistent with the pack.

statements.claim: A renunciate should not touch a woman even of wood; the wise do not go near what brings the death of the self.
statements.evidence: BP 11.8.12-13: padāpi yuvatīṃ bhikṣur na spṛśed dāravīm api / nādhigacchet striyaṃ prājñaḥ karhicin mṛtyum ātmanaḥ.

statements.claim: The honey-gatherer climbs to the wild hive in the rocks, is swarmed and stung for every comb he takes, and comes down aching and half-blinded carrying honey — which others eat; he keeps only the scars, and climbs again next season.
statements.evidence: Dramatization of the pack's honey-gatherer exemplum ('the wealth painfully hoarded is enjoyed by others, as the honey-gatherer steals the bees' honey'; BP 11.8.14-15: wealth painfully amassed by the greedy is enjoyed by others). Scene details are connective inference.

statements.claim: So it is with wealth painfully hoarded: a man gathers it in sleeplessness and worry and in the end others enjoy it; the sage does not pile up what was gathered in suffering.
statements.evidence: BP 11.8.14-15 (na deyaṃ nopabhogyaṃ ca lubdhair yad duḥkha-sañcitam / su-duḥkhopārjitair vittair āśāsānāṃ gṛhāśiṣaḥ) and the pack's honey-gatherer rendering.

statements.claim: The deer — swift and watchful, uncatchable in a run — is caught by song: hunters lure it with a flute and it stops, ears turned to the music, forgetting what kept it safe.
statements.evidence: Pack supports 'the deer is snared by song' (BP 11.8.16-17, where the point is the renunciate not listening to village music/dancing/songs of women); the flute-lure hunting scene is dramatized connective detail.

statements.claim: A wandering renunciate should not listen to the music and dancing of the village, the songs that please the senses; the sweetest sound can be the snare.
statements.evidence: BP 11.8.16-17: grāmya-gītaṃ na śṛṇuyād yatir vana-caraḥ kvacit / nṛtya-vāditra-gītāni juṣan grāmyāṇi yoṣitām.

statements.claim: The fish is caught by the mouth and hooked through the tongue; the taste of the bait undoes it.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'the fish, allured by the tongue's bait, meets death on the hook' (BP 11.8.18: jihvayāti-pramāthinyā jano rasa-vimohitaḥ).
