statements.claim: Of all the senses the tongue is the hardest to master: a man may close his eyes and stop his ears, but the craving for taste follows him everywhere — a man may refuse cup and plate and still be undone by the memory of a taste.
statements.evidence: The tongue's power to delude is in BP 11.8.18 (ati-pramāthinī, rasa-vimohitaḥ); 'hardest to master' and the closable-eyes/ears and memory-of-taste elaborations are interpretive connective glosses.

statements.claim: The senses are conquered quickly when they are not fed — the secret is to stop feeding them.
statements.evidence: BP 11.8.19: indriyāṇi jayanty āśu nirāhārā manīṣiṇaḥ.

statements.claim: It must be all the senses together: a man who has mastered one sense while another rules him is not yet master of anything.
statements.evidence: BP 11.8.20: tāvaj jitendriyo na syād vijitānyendriyaḥ pumān.

statements.claim: The avadhuta walked on past the village music and the markets' sweets, having seen where each road ended — in the rope, in the stings, in the bow, in the hook.
statements.evidence: Closing connective recap of the four exempla; 'in the bow' alludes to the deer's end, not stated in the pack.

DKS_0510.notes: Faithful to BP 11.8.12-20 (elephant/wooden-woman, hoarded wealth, village music, tongue, fasting the senses, all-senses-together). All scene mechanics (decoy cow, hive in rocks, flute lure) are connective dramatizations of pack-supported exempla — no UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: The osprey, carrying prey, was mobbed from every side by stronger birds; it let the meat fall, the attackers wheeled away after it, and the osprey flew on free and unhurt.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.1 (sāmiṣaṃ kuraraṃ jaghnur balino 'nye nirāmiṣāḥ — other strong, meatless birds struck the osprey holding prey) and pack index summary ('letting go of prey seized by stronger birds'); the letting-go outcome is the point of the exemplum.

statements.claim: The birds that took the meat were no stronger in the wing than the osprey — only more numerous, and more hungry.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.1 says the attackers WERE the strong ones (balino 'nye nirāmiṣāḥ — 'other strong birds without prey'; standard translations: 'a hawk carrying meat was attacked by stronger hawks'), the pack's index summary says the prey was 'seized by stronger birds', and the story's own opening paragraph says 'the stronger birds came'. The story's later claim that they were only more numerous contradicts the verse, the index, and itself.
statements.resolution: Corrected in story text via consolidation pass.

statements.claim: The lesson was in the letting go: it was not hunger that endangered the bird but the prize; so it is with a man who grips what he cannot keep.
statements.evidence: Consistent with the exemplum's point (attachment to prey brings the attack; the unattached are unassailed — gitabase on SB 11.9: 'attachment creates misery, but the person who is unattached... is qualified'); framed as connective commentary.

statements.claim: The avadhuta said he had made himself like the osprey: for him there was neither honor nor disgrace, and none of the cares that keep householders wakeful, because he had let them all go.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.2: na me mānāpamānau sto na cintā geha-putriṇām (I have neither honor nor disgrace, nor the anxiety of householders with sons).

statements.claim: Only two beings are free of care — the child, who has nothing and wants nothing, absorbed in its own joy, and the sage; from the child he learned to be glad without possessions.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.3 (dvāv eva cintayā muktau paramānanda āplutau — two alone are free of care, immersed in supreme bliss; the child and the sage, per the pack index 'the child (freedom from care)'); the child-at-play description is connective color.

statements.claim: A maiden, alone in the house husking grain, heard her bangles clink at every stroke, minded the noise as unbecoming, and broke them off one by one until a single bangle remained — and a single bangle makes no sound.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.4-8 (kumārī alone husking rice in private; her two wristlets' clink judged unbecoming (jugupsita); she broke them one by one until one remained — with one there is no sound); pack excerpt: 'a maiden, alone, husking grain, heard her bangles clink and broke them one by one until only one remained, and it was silent.'

statements.claim: So should the sage dwell: alone; where many live together there is quarreling, and even two voices make a noise; strip away what clinks and there is silence.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.9: vāse bahūnāṃ kalaho bhaved vārtā dvayor api (in the dwelling of many there is quarrel; even of two, talk/noise).

statements.claim: The arrow-maker sat straightening and smoothing a shaft with his whole attention, and a king's procession passed on the road behind him with music and banners — it was said the king himself rode in it — and the man never saw it.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'like the arrow-maker so absorbed in straightening his shaft that he did not see the king pass by, the mind should be fixed on one point' (BP 11.9.10-12); the procession details are connective elaboration.

statements.claim: From that man the avadhuta learned to fix his own mind on a single point until nothing could pull it away — such absorption is the whole of the mind kept in one place, not laziness or dreaming.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.10-12 (mana ekatra saṃyuñjyāj jita-śvāso jitāsanaḥ ... ātmany avaruddha-citto na veda kiñcid bahir antaraṃ vā — with the mind thus fixed in the self he knows nothing outside or within); the 'not laziness' gloss is connective.

statements.claim: Solitude and one-pointedness — the maiden's silence and the arrow-maker's absorption — are one discipline: empty the room until nothing clinks, then give the whole mind to the one thing that matters.
statements.evidence: Closing synthesis of the two supported lessons; non-factual framing.

corrections.original_sentence: The birds that took the meat were no stronger in the wing than the osprey — only more numerous, and more hungry.
corrections.suggested: The birds that took the meat were the stronger ones — strong, and hungry, with no prey of their own — and the osprey, burdened by its prize, could not defend it against them.

DKS_0512.notes: One CONTRADICTED: BP 11.9.1 (balino 'nye nirāmiṣāḥ) has the attacking birds as the STRONGER ones — the pack index ('seized by stronger birds'), all translations, and the story's own opening agree — but the story later asserts the attackers were 'no stronger in the wing... only more numerous, and more hungry.' Everything else (osprey letting go, honor/disgrace, child, maiden's bangles, arrow-maker) is faithful to BP 11.9.1-12.

statements.claim: The serpent owns nothing — it enters a burrow another creature has abandoned, lies there without care, and moves on homeless; the avadhuta made its way his own, wandering alone and living in no house he had built.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.13 (eka-cāry aniketaḥ syād apramatto guhāśayaḥ — wandering alone, homeless, dwelling in a cave) and pack excerpt ('the serpent enters another's abandoned home and thrives'); the burrow was never its own, so nothing could be taken from it is connective.

statements.claim: Building a house brings only sorrow: the labor of raising the walls, the worry of keeping them, the grief of leaving them — all for a body that will not last.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.14: gṛhārambho hi duḥkhāya viphalaś cādhruvātmanaḥ (undertaking a house is for sorrow, fruitless, for the impermanent self); the labor/worry/grief triad is connective elaboration.

statements.claim: As the spider sends the thread forth from its own heart, plays with it, and draws it back into itself, so the one Lord Narayana — who alone is — spins out the world by his own power, sustains it, and in time withdraws it; the web is not supported by anything outside the spider.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.15-20 (eko nārāyaṇo devaḥ ... sva-māyayā ...; yathorṇanābhir hṛdayād ūrṇāṃ santatya vaktrataḥ) and pack excerpt: 'as the spider sends forth the thread from its own heart, plays with it and draws it back, so the Lord creates, sustains and withdraws the world.'

statements.claim: The wasp takes a living creature and seals it into the mud of a wall; the creature, helpless, broods on the wasp until it becomes like what it contemplates, and in time is a wasp itself.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.22: kīṭaḥ peśaskṛtaṃ dhyāyan kuḍyāṃ tena praveśitaḥ (the insect, meditating on the wasp, is placed by it into the wall) and pack excerpt: 'as the wasp, meditating on its captor, becomes like it.'

statements.claim: So it is with the mind: it becomes what it dwells upon — a mind on the world becomes worldly, a mind on the Lord becomes like the Lord; most men are exactly what they have been thinking of.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.21-22 (yatra yatra mano dehī dhārayet sakalaṃ dhiyā ... kīṭaḥ peśaskṛtaṃ dhyāyan) and pack excerpt: 'the mind becomes what it dwells upon.' The 'most men... rarely choose' tail is connective.

statements.claim: This was the avadhuta's last and deepest teaching; he had counted twenty-four teachers in all — earth, wind and water, the pigeon and the python, the moth and the bee, the elephant and the deer, the maiden and the arrow-maker — and with the serpent, the spider and the wasp the count was complete.
statements.evidence: The count of twenty-four gurus and the list order (ending in serpent, spider, peśaskṛt) are established in BP 11.7.33-34 (ete me guravo rājan catur-viṃśatir āśritāḥ), quoted in the corpus chain pack DKS_0505; the serpent/spider/wasp are the final three teachers of BP 11.9 (13-22), which closes the avadhuta's enumeration.

statements.claim: All of them, he said, pointed to the same place — past the creatures, to the one who spins them out and draws them back; a strange end to a list that began with the earth underfoot.
statements.evidence: Theistic synthesis consistent with the spider teaching (11.9.15-20) and the corpus arc; non-factual closing framing.

DKS_0513.notes: Faithful to BP 11.9.13-22 (serpent's borrowed hole, house-building sorrow, spider/ūrṇanābhi creation-withdrawal, wasp/peśaskṛt meditation). The 'twenty-four teachers... count complete' claim is supported via the corpus chain (DKS_0505 pack, BP 11.7.34 catur-viṃśatir), whose list ends with the serpent, spider and peśaskṛt. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Sanaka and his brothers — the mind-born sons of Brahma, the oldest minds in creation — asked Brahma for the subtle goal of yoga; no one, not even their father, could answer.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'The mind-born sons of Brahma asked him the subtle goal of yoga'; index summary: 'unable to get an answer from Brahma, were taught by Krishna himself appearing as a swan.' 'Oldest minds in creation' is connective color consistent with the mind-born Kumaras.

statements.claim: Brahma did not answer from his own knowledge but turned inward and meditated on Krishna; and Krishna, seeing what was needed, appeared before the sages in the form of a swan.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.18 (sa mām acintayad devaḥ praśna-pāra-titīrṣayā — that god, wishing to cross the question, thought of me) and pack excerpt: 'pondering their question, Brahma meditated on me, and I appeared to them in the form of a swan.'

statements.claim: A great white hamsa glided into that assembly; the sages rose, walked up to it, bowed at its feet, and asked who it was that they should be answered by a bird.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.19-20 (dṛṣṭvā mām ta upavrajya kṛtvā pādābhivandanam / ity ahaṃ munibhiḥ pṛṣṭas tattva-jijñāsubhis) and pack excerpt: 'They asked who I was.' The 'that we should be answered by a bird' irony and 'calm as the water it had crossed' are connective.

statements.claim: The swan's reply turned the question back on them: if in truth there is no difference in the self, their question had no ground — know that I alone am, and nothing apart from me.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.21-22 (vastuno yady anānātva ātmanaḥ praśna īdṛśaḥ ...) and pack excerpt: 'if in truth there is no difference in the self, their very question has no ground — know that I alone am, and nothing apart from me.'

statements.claim: The mind runs into the qualities of nature and they into it; the more it serves them the deeper it sinks; waking, dreaming and dreamless sleep are only states of the intellect spun out of those qualities.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.24-26: guṇeṣv āviśate ceto guṇāś cetasi ca ... abhīkṣṇaṃ guṇa-sevayā / jāgrat svapnaḥ suṣuptaṃ ca guṇato buddhi-vṛttayaḥ.

statements.claim: Bondage is the self forgetting itself and seeing many where there is one; so long as the sense of difference does not turn back, the knot holds — yet the one who enjoys waking objects, recollects them in dream, and withdraws in deep sleep is the same throughout, the knower behind the senses.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.27-31 (ahaṅkāra-kṛtaṃ bandham ... yāvan nānārtha-dhīḥ puṃso na nivarteta; yo jāgare bahir ... bhuṅkte ... svapne suṣupta upasaṃharate sa ekaḥ ... indriyeśaḥ).

statements.claim: Cut the knot in the heart with the sword of knowledge: the world is the play of the mind, like the circle of fire a whirled burning brand traces — one light, and the eye believes a ring of flame.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.32-33 (sañchidya hārdam ... jñānāsinā; īkṣeta vibhramam idaṃ manaso vilāsaṃ ... alāta-cakram).

statements.claim: Withdraw the gaze, turn from thirst, sit in silence and taste the bliss that is your own self; the body is perishable, put on and taken off like a garment — the awakened man watches the exchange without confusion, as a drunken man hardly notices a change of clothes.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.34-35 (dṛṣṭim pratinivartya nivṛtta-tṛṣṇas tūṣṇīṃ bhaven nija-sukhānubhavo nirīhaḥ; vāso yathā parikṛtaṃ madirā-madāndhaḥ).

statements.claim: Even the body's comings and goings are governed by the acts that set it in motion, and the one established in awareness does not return to the dream once the reality is seen.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.36: deho 'pi daiva-vaśa-gaḥ khalu karma yāvat ... svāpnaṃ punar na bhajate pratibuddha-vastuḥ.

statements.claim: This is the secret of sankhya and yoga, the two great paths; the swan declared: I am the essence of yoga, of sankhya, of truth, of the right, of radiance; all the qualities of nature serve me, who am beyond them, wanting nothing.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.37-39: mayaitad uktaṃ vo viprā guhyaṃ yat sāṅkhya-yogayoḥ / ahaṃ yogasya sāṅkhyasya satyasyartasya tejasaḥ / māṃ bhajanti guṇāḥ sarve nirguṇaṃ nirapekṣakam.

statements.claim: The sages Sanaka and his brothers felt their doubt fall away and worshipped and praised the swan.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.40-41: iti me chinna-sandehā munayaḥ sanakādayaḥ / tair ahaṃ pūjitaḥ saṃyak saṃstutaḥ paramarṣibhiḥ.

statements.claim: Krishna told all this to Uddhava long afterward; the question the Kumaras had carried dissolved not in an answer but in seeing who it was that asked, and the swan, having done its work, was gone, leaving only the stillness it had pointed to.
statements.evidence: Krishna-to-Uddhava frame is supported (the chapter is Krishna's discourse to Uddhava; pack index: 'Asked by his disciples about the swan form, Krishna recounts...'). The swan's departure is not in the quoted verses (15-41, which end with the Kumaras' worship) — closing connective coda consistent with the appearance-form.

DKS_0514.notes: Highly faithful to BP 11.13.15-41: nearly every doctrinal claim maps to its verse (mind-qualities, three states, knot of difference, firebrand circle, withdrawal/bliss, garment body, karma-governed body, sankhya-yoga secret, essence of yoga/sankhya/truth/right/radiance, doubt cut, worship). The closing 'swan was gone' and scene touches are connective; no UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: In the city of Avanti lived a brahmin who owned more than anyone and gave away less than anyone; his wealth was a hoard kept like a yaksha's treasure, and his relatives and guests were not honored even with a word; he was miserly by habit and cruel in manner, and his sons and kinsmen turned against him.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.5-8: avantiṣu dvijaḥ kaścid āsīd āḍhyatamaḥ śriyā (a brahmin richest in wealth); vāṅ-mātreṇāpi nārcitāḥ (not honored even with a word); duhśīlasya kadaryasya druhyante putra-bāndhavāḥ; yakṣa-vittasya.

statements.claim: His relatives took part of his wealth and thieves carried off the rest, and he who had been the richest man in Avanti sat looking at his empty rooms; he had lost both worlds — this one's comforts and the merit the next would have counted, worn away by the contempt he had earned.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.8-10: cyutasyobhaya-lokataḥ / tad-avadhyāna-visrasta-puṇya-skandhasya; jñātyo jagṛhuḥ kiñcit kiñcid dasyavaḥ. 'Sat looking at empty rooms' is connective.

statements.claim: For a long time he brooded over the ruin, then the grief turned and he spoke to himself: what calamity is this, that I tormented myself for nothing?
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.12-13: dhyāyato dīrghaṃ naṣṭa-rāyas ... aho kaṣṭaṃ vṛthātmā me 'nutāpitaḥ.

statements.claim: Wealth never gives happiness to a miser — not once, not ever; it brings theft, violence, falsehood, deceit, desire, anger, pride and intoxication — fifteen evils grow from a single root of gold.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.14, 16-18: prāyeṇāthāḥ kadaryāṇāṃ na sukhāya kadācana; steyaṃ hiṃsānṛtaṃ dambhaḥ kāmaḥ krodhaḥ smayo madaḥ / ete pañcadaśānarthā hy artha-mūlā matā nṛṇām.

statements.claim: Brothers break with brothers over the smallest amount; fathers, wives and friends all split apart where money is.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.19-20: bhidyante bhrātaro dārāḥ pitaraḥ suhṛdas tathā / arthenālpīyasā.

statements.claim: He had been given a human birth, which even the immortals pray for, and the highest station of a brahmin — the very door to heaven and to freedom — and spent it chasing a hoard; what use are riches or the givers of riches, desires or the givers of desires?
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.21-26: labdhvā janmāmara-prārthyaṃ mānuṣyaṃ tad dvijāgryatām / svargāpavargayor dvāraṃ ...; kiṃ dhanair dhana-dair vā kiṃ kāmair vā kāma-dair uta.

statements.claim: Surely the Lord Hari, who contains all the gods, is pleased with me, to have stripped all this away; with what life is left I will dry up this body, and the gods of the three worlds will rejoice in me.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.27-29: nūnaṃ me bhagavāṃs tuṣṭaḥ sarva-deva-mayo hariḥ / so 'haṃ kālāvaśeṣeṇa śoṣayiṣye 'ṅgam ātmanaḥ / tatra mām anumoderan devās tri-bhuvaneśvarāḥ.

statements.claim: He left everything, became a silent wandering mendicant with his senses and breath under control, and walked the roads and villages begging his bread.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.31-32: sa cacāra mahīm etāṃ saṃyatātmendriyānilaḥ / taṃ vai pravayasaṃ bhikṣum avadhūtam asaj-janāḥ (he walked the earth, controlled in self, senses and breath; the aged mendicant).

statements.claim: The townspeople tormented him — some snatched his triple staff, some his bowl and water pot, some took the food from his hands on the riverbank; they tried to make the silent man speak and struck him when he would not; they called him a cheat wearing the flag of religion, a fraud; some laughed, some spat insults, and here and there one muttered that he bore it like a mountain.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.32-38: kecit tri-veṇuṃ jagṛhur eke pātraṃ kamaṇḍalum; annaṃ ... bhuñjānasya sarit-taṭe; yata-vācaṃ vācayanti tāḍayanti na vakti cet; eṣa dharma-dhvajaḥ śaṭhaḥ; aho eṣa mahā-sāro dhṛtimān giri-rāḍ iva; vihasanty / durvātayanti.

statements.claim: Mocked and beaten by the base, enduring the pains that come from the world, from the body and from the gods themselves, he lifted his voice and sang a song that has been sung ever since.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.39-41: evaṃ sa bhautikaṃ duḥkhaṃ daivikaṃ daihikaṃ ca yat / paribhūta imāṃ gāthām agāyata narādhamaiḥ. 'A song sung ever since' is connective.

statements.claim: The song: the mind alone creates the qualities of nature and from them all the varied works of men; the self does nothing — it only watches, golden and still, while the mind chases and suffers and calls itself the doer.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.42-43: mano guṇān vai sṛjate ...; anīha ātmā manasā samīhatā hiraṇ-mayo mat-sakha udvicaṣṭe.

statements.claim: For a man whose mind is calm and collected, what need is there of gifts, rites, vows or learning? The gods themselves fell under the mind's sway, and the mind bows to nothing else; it is an unconquerable enemy, unbearable in force, a thorn in the heart, and few master it.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.44-47: samāhitaṃ yasya manaḥ praśāntaṃ dānādibhiḥ kiṃ vada tasya kṛtyam; mano-vaśe 'nye hy abhavan sma devā ...; tam durjayaṃ śatrum asahya-vegam arun-tudaṃ tan na vijitya kecit.

statements.claim: Foolish men look at this body, which is only mind-stuff, and cry I and mine; but neither people, nor gods, nor planets, nor karma, nor time tinges the self with joy or grief — no one outside, anywhere, at any time; the mind alone turns the wheel of existence, and the man who knows this stands on the ground the great seers of old stood on.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.48-56: dehaṃ mano-mātram imaṃ gṛhītvā mamāham ity andha-dhiyo manuṣyāḥ; janas tu hetuḥ ... devatās ... grahā ... karma ... kālaḥ (the five rejected causes); na kenacit kvāpi kathañcanāsya dvandvoparāgaḥ parataḥ parasya; etāṃ ... adhyāsitāṃ pūrvatamair maharṣibhiḥ.

statements.claim: Krishna ended the story with a single sentence: no one gives a person joy or sorrow except his own confusion; therefore, my son, restrain the mind with discernment — with all your strength, restrain it.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.58-59: sukha-duḥkha-prado nānyaḥ puruṣasyātma-vibhramaḥ / tasmāt sarvātmanā tāta nigṛhāṇa mano dhiyā.

DKS_0515.notes: Very faithful to BP 11.23.5-60 — nearly every claim tracks a verse (yaksha-treasure hoard, both worlds lost, fifteen evils from wealth, the five rejected causes of joy/sorrow, Krishna's closing command). No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: King Pururava, son of Ila (Aila), far-famed and once lord of the whole earth, ran through a forest naked and weeping after the nymph Urvashi, who had left him — mad with grief, unsatisfied, chasing her through years and nights.
statements.evidence: BP 11.26.3-5: ailaḥ samrāḍ imāṃ gāthām agāyata bṛhac-chravāḥ / tyaktvātmānaṃ vrayantīṃ tāṃ nagna unmatta-van nṛpaḥ / kāmān atṛpto 'nujuṣan kṣullakān varṣa-yāminīḥ; pack index summary ('pursues her naked and weeping'); name Pururava/Aila per index. Forest setting per index locations.

statements.claim: Krishna told Uddhava this story as a mirror for every man who hands his mind to another and calls it love.
statements.evidence: The story is part of Krishna's discourse to Uddhava (11.26, śrī-bhagavān uvāca frame); the 'mirror held up' purpose is framing.

statements.claim: After long running, in the depth of the forest, the madness broke and he sang the song remembered as the song of Aila: he no longer knew whether the sun had risen or set — he knew only that she was not there.
statements.evidence: BP 11.26.3, 7: ailaḥ ... agāyata; nāhaṃ vedābhinirmuktaḥ sūryo vābhyudito 'muyā.

statements.claim: What delusion seized me, that I, a self, made myself the plaything of a woman! I was the lord of the world and threw away my own majesty like a straw to run after her; where is her power, her brilliance, her sovereignty? All of it existed only in my own mind.
statements.evidence: BP 11.26.8-10: aho me ātma-sammoho yenātmā yoṣitāṃ kṛtaḥ; sa-paricchadam ātmānaṃ hitvā tṛṇam iveśvaram; kutas tasyānubhāvaḥ syāt teja īśatvam eva vā. 'All of it existed in my own mind' is a connective gloss of the rhetorical question.

statements.claim: What use is learning, austerity, renunciation or scripture to a man who does not know his own good? Shame on me — a fool who thought himself wise; for years I served the nectar of her lips, and the mind she stole from me — what power could have freed it? Even when she spoke well-chosen words to warn me, I was too dull to hear.
statements.evidence: BP 11.26.11-15: kiṃ vidyayā kiṃ tapasā kiṃ tyāgena śrutena vā; dhiṅ māṃ mūrkhaṃ paṇḍita-māninam; sevato varṣa-pūgān me urvaśyā adharāsavam; puṃścalyāpahṛtaṃ cittaṃ ko nv anyo mocituṃ prabhuḥ; bodhitasyāpi devyā me sūkta-vākyena durmateḥ.

statements.claim: What harm has she done me? A man sees a snake in a rope and screams — the rope never harmed him; the terror was in the seeing.
statements.evidence: BP 11.26.16: kim etayā no 'pakṛtaṃ rajjvā vā sarpa-cetasaḥ.

statements.claim: What is this body I adorned and grieved over — a foul sack of flesh and bone, impure, made of bad smells? Whose is it: my parents', my wife's, my master's, the fire's that will take it, the dogs' and jackals' that will feed on it?
statements.evidence: BP 11.26.17-18: kvāyaṃ malīmasaḥ kāyo daurgandhyādy-ātmako 'śuciḥ; pitroḥ kiṃ svaṃ nu bhāryāyāḥ svāmino 'gneḥ śva-gṛdhrayoḥ.

statements.claim: In this worthless corpse the mind fastens itself, in this heap of skin, flesh, blood, sinew, marrow and bone; let a man who knows his good not cling to women or to anything of the world of women with his senses leashed to desire — attachment is born of contact, of seeing and longing, never from what is unseen and unheard; therefore let there be no contact, no clinging.
statements.evidence: BP 11.26.19-23: tasmin kalevare 'medhye tuccha-niṣṭhe viṣajjate; tvaṅ-māṃsa-rudhira-snāyu-medo-majjāsthi-saṃhatau; athāpi nopasajjeta strīṣu straiṇeṣu cārtha-vit; adṛṣṭād aśrutād bhāvān na bhāva upajāyate; tasmāt saṅgo na kartavyaḥ strīṣu straiṇeṣu cendriyaiḥ.

statements.claim: As he sang, the delusion left him; the emperor who had run naked and weeping rose up clothed in his own understanding, and the peace he had chased settled over him where he stood.
statements.evidence: Pack index summary: 'realizing his delusion, he sings the song of Aila on the futility of attachment to women, and attains peace.' The 'clothed in his own understanding' figure is connective.

statements.claim: Krishna ended the tale: if even Pururava, far-famed lord of the whole earth, was brought so low by a mind fastened on an object of desire, then let anyone who hears the song of Aila look to his own heart.
statements.evidence: The passage closes with the Bhagavan's continuing words (bhp_11.26.025 śrī-bhagavān uvāca in the pack's own text); the moral drawn matches the chapter's purpose in Krishna's instruction to Uddhava.

DKS_0516.notes: Faithful to BP 11.26.3-24 (Aila's gāthā: sun-without-her, plaything of a woman, straw-cast majesty, useless learning, body's foul constituents, rope-snake, no-contact doctrine, peace attained). Glosses are connective; no UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: The final teaching had been given — the long instruction of the Uddhava Gita, spoken by Krishna to Uddhava in Dwaraka — and now Krishna commanded: Go to my hermitage called Badari, far in the north, by the celestial route, as the blessed go.
statements.evidence: BP 11.29.40-43 (Krishna's command to Uddhava; pack excerpt: 'Go, Uddhava, as I have commanded, to my hermitage called Badari'); Vishnu Purana 5.37: 'Do you go by a celestial route... to the holy place Badarikāśrama.' Dwaraka setting per pack index locations.

statements.claim: He was to go to the hermitage on the bank of the Alakananda, where the very sight of the river washes away every stain; there, in the solitude sanctified by the long austerities of Narayana and Nara, patient with the pairs of opposites, gentle in conduct, senses under control, he should abide in the teaching; meditating on Krishna he would come to him beyond the three paths.
statements.evidence: BP 11.29.41-43: īkṣayālakanandāyā vidhūtāśeṣa-kalmaṣaḥ / titikṣur dvandva-mātrāṇāṃ suśīlaḥ saṃyatendriyaḥ / matto 'nuśikṣitaṃ yat te viviktam anubhāvayan; pack excerpt ('you will come to me beyond the three paths'); VP 5.37 (the spot sanctified by Narayana and Nara; meditating, he obtains perfection).

statements.claim: Uddhava heard the command and could not move — separation from Krishna was the one thing his heart refused, and the friend who had been trusted with more than any other man in Dwaraka stood stricken, unable to leave him.
statements.evidence: BP 11.29.45: su-dustyaja-sneha-viyoga-kātaro na śaknuvaṃs taṃ parihātum āturaḥ (tormented by separation from hard-to-give-up affection, unable to leave him). Uddhava's unmatched trust is established through the whole arc (Krishna's final instruction to him, BP 11.6-11.29; corpus DKS_0501-0504).

statements.claim: Uddhava was 'the friend who had carried messages between Krishna and the Pandavas.'
statements.evidence: Characterization padding: Uddhava's role as Krishna's trusted emissary is well established (he delivered Krishna's message to the gopis of Vrindavan, BP 10.46 / corpus DKS_0110-0111, and moved in Krishna's party to Indraprastha, DKS_0371), but no message-carrying specifically between Krishna and the Pandavas appears in this pack or the corpus chain; not contradicted, treated as connective biography.

statements.claim: He walked around Krishna again and again, then knelt, took Krishna's feet and placed them on his own head — and, bearing Krishna's sandals in his hands, went forth.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (BP 11.29.40-45 rendering): 'Uddhava, unable to leave him, walked around him again and again, placed Krishna's feet on his head, and, bearing his sandals, at last went forth.'

statements.claim: He placed the Lord within his own heart and set his face north.
statements.evidence: BP 11.29.46: tatas tam antar hṛdi sanniveśya gato mahā-bhāgavato viśālām (the great devotee, placing him within his heart, went to Viśālā [the Badari region, in the north]).

statements.claim: On the way he paused at Hastinapura, where Vidura, the wise uncle of the Pandavas, drew the story from him.
statements.evidence: No support in the pack (BP 11.29.40-47, BP 3.4.19-21, VP 5.37, MBh 16.3) for a stop at Hastinapura: the pack's index summary for this story has Uddhava departing directly for Badari (locations: 'Dwaraka, the road to Badarikashrama'), the Vidura-Uddhava dialogue from which BP 3.4.19-21 is drawn took place on the bank of the Yamuna (SB 3.1-3.4; corpus's own account of that meeting, DKS_0527, BP 3.2.1-20, places it on the Yamuna bank after the news of Prabhasa), and the pack's MBh 16.3 instead has Uddhava's leave-taking with the Pandavas at the sea-coast. The place and the mid-journey 'pause' framing are invented.
statements.resolution: Corrected in story text via consolidation pass.

statements.claim: The story Vidura drew from him — how Uddhava had worshipped the sanctity of Krishna's feet, learned the path of self-knowledge, bowed and come away heart-torn with separation, and would go on to the hermitage of Badari where Narayana and the sage Nara once performed their long austerities.
statements.evidence: BP 3.4.19-21 (pack excerpt): 'having worshipped his feet and received the path of self-knowledge, I bowed to the Lord and came away, heart-torn with separation; I will go to the hermitage of Badari, where Narayana and Nara performed their long austerities.'

statements.claim: Then Uddhava went on, north along the road that climbs toward the mountains, carrying Krishna's sandals and the teaching; Dwaraka and the life he had known there fell behind him.
statements.evidence: BP 11.29.46 (going to Viśālā with Krishna placed in his heart) and the pack's sandals detail; Badari lies north in the Himalayas (VP 5.37). Journey color is connective.

statements.claim: They say the road was long and the hermitage was high, and the man who walked it had left behind himself — the self that clings and grieves — until the walking itself became the teaching.
statements.evidence: Closing devotional reflection; no sourceable factual assertion.

corrections.original_sentence: On the way he paused at Hastinapura, where Vidura, the wise uncle of the Pandavas, drew the story from him: how he had worshipped the sanctity of Krishna's feet, how he had learned the path of self-knowledge, how he had bowed and come away heart-torn with separation, and how he would go on to the hermitage of Badari, where Narayana and the sage Nara once performed their long austerities.
corrections.suggested: And Vidura, the wise uncle of the Pandavas, drew the story from him: how he had worshipped the sanctity of Krishna's feet, how he had learned the path of self-knowledge, how he had bowed and come away heart-torn with separation, and how he would go on to the hermitage of Badari, where Narayana and the sage Nara once performed their long austerities.

DKS_0517.notes: One UNSUPPORTED: the 'paused at Hastinapura' stop. The pack (11.29.40-47, VP 5.37, MBh 16.3) has Uddhava depart directly for Badari; the Vidura dialogue quoted from BP 3.4.19-21 belongs to the Yamuna-bank meeting (SB 3.1-3.4, per corpus DKS_0527), and MBh 16.3 places Uddhava's leave-taking with the Pandavas at the sea-coast — no source puts him at Hastinapura. Correction drops the location/timing claim while keeping the BP 3.4.19-21 content (Vidura asking, Uddhava telling of the farewell and his Badari plan). The 'carried messages between Krishna and the Pandavas' clause is connective biography (his messenger role to the gopis and presence in the Pandava wedding party are corpus facts).

statements.claim: Narada, standing in Dwaraka before his departure, recites Krishna's deeds one by one as if taking dictation.
statements.evidence: Pack index: 'Narada Prophesies the Ocean Will Swallow Dwarka || Before departing, Narada prophesies...' and Harivamsha 1.249 is Narada's recital of the same deeds.

statements.claim: The nooses made by Mura were cut; Nisumva and Naraka slain; the road to Pragyotish freed from dangers.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249 (Dutt): 'the nooses made by Mura have been cut, Nisumva and Naraka have been slain and the road to the city of Pragyotish has been freed from all dangers.'

statements.claim: The kings of the world were frightened by the twang of Krishna's bow and the sound of the conch Panchajanya.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'the proud kings of the world have been frightened in battle by this descendant of Shura... with the twang of his bow and the sound of his conch-shell Panchajanya.'

statements.claim: Rukmi, protected by his Deccan chariot-warriors, was vanquished and Rukmini carried away in a car blazing like the sun and rumbling like a cloud.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'Having vanquished easily the highly powerful Rukshmi well protected by the Decean car-warriors resembling clouds... carried away Rukshmini... in a car effulgent like the sun and producing a rattle like unto the muttering of clouds.'

statements.claim: In Jaruthi, Ahdriti, Kratha and Shishupala fell; Dantavakra and Shatadhanwa with all their soldiers; Shalwa of the city Shoubha struck down; Dyumutsena struck by the discus.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'In the city of Jāruthi he defeated Ahdriti, Kratha and Shishupala and vanquished Dantavakra and Shatadhanwā with all their soldiers... the beautiful lord of Shoubha killed Shālwa... struck Dyumutsena with his discus.' The 'dashed from the sky' phrasing is atmospheric colour over the discus stroke.

statements.claim: Gopati and Talaketu, followers of Ravana on the summit of Mahendra, were killed in a twinkling; Hansa and Dimvaka slain after them.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'In the city of Irāvati on the summit of the mount Mahendra there lived two followers of Rāvana Gopati and Tālaketu... killed them both, within the twinkling of an eye, the Dānavas Hansa and Dimvaka have been also slain by Krishna with their followers.'

statements.claim: Varanasi was burnt down; Maya killed with knotty arrows; the son of Indrasena released.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'Vārānashi (Benares) has been burnt down by the high souled Keshava... Having killed Maya in battle with knotty arrows Krishna... has released the son of Indrasena.'

statements.claim: Varuna was defeated beneath the sea at Lohitakuta; the Parijata tree was carried off from Indra's palace though the celestials could not prevent it.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'The highly powerful Varuna... has been defeated in battle by Krishna repairing to Lohitakuta (under water)'; 'Having gone to Indra's palace, he, although prevented by the highly powerful celestials, disregarding their king, carried away the Pārijāta tree.' Minor nuance: the pack has the celestials actively trying to prevent the taking, not passively 'forbidden to interfere' as the story phrases it; outcome is unchanged.

statements.claim: The kings of Pandya, Poundrya, Kalinga, Matsa and Banga were slain; Kaliya was despatched from the river to the sea; Yama was vanquished and restored the dead son of Sandipani.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'The intelligent Janārddana has slain the kings of Pandya, Poundrya, Kalinga, Matsa and Banga'; 'defeated in water the highly powerful Nāga king Kālya... despatched him to the sea'; 'Having vanquished Vivaswān's son Yama, Hari... has restored to life the dead son of Sāndipani.'

statements.claim: In his dwarf form Krishna took the three worlds from Bali; Kamsa's courtiers Peetha, Paithika and Asitoma were killed; the Daityas Jambha, Airavata and Virupa were slain while he wore the semblance of a man.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'in his pristine dwarfish form Mādhava stole away from Bali the three worlds'; 'killed Peetha, Paithika and Asitomā the courtiers of the long-armed Kansa'; 'killed the Daityas Jambha, Airāvata and Virupa, assuming the semblance of a man.'

statements.claim: Arjuna was crowned with success and Drona, Bhishma, Karna and Suyodhana were defeated; the daughter of the king of Suveera was carried away to please Vabhru.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'the Lord Madhusudana has crowned the foremost of Bharatas, Arjuna... with success'; 'defeated, in battle, Drona, Drauni, Karna, Bhishma, Suyodhana and other warriors'; 'For pleasing Vabhru the powerful Hari... carried away by force the daughter of the king of Suveera.' Naming the field 'Kurukshetra' is contextual gloss beyond the chapter text but consistent with the war described.

statements.claim: Having established virtue among mortals through sacrifices and accomplished the work of the gods, Krishna would return to his own region, and the ocean would devour Bhogavati and Dwaraka.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'Having established virtue amongst the mortals by performing various sacrifices and accomplished the great work of the gods he will return to his own region. Then the highly illustrious Krishna will make the ocean devour the cities Bhogavati, a favourite resort of the Rishis, and Dwārakā.'

statements.claim: The city of jewels and sacrificial grounds would sink with its gardens into Varuna's abode; none among gods, Asuras or men except the slayer of Madhu would be able to live there.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'This city of Dwārakā, filled with various jewels and sacrificial grounds, will enter, with its gardens, into the abode (sea) of Varuna... constructed by Vāsudeva and resembling the residence of the sun. There is none amongst the gods, Asuras, and men and none will be, except the slayer of Madhu, who will be able to live here.'

statements.claim: Having instituted his regulations among the Dasharhas, Vishnu would be united with Narayana, Soma and Surya.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.249: 'Having thus instituted many excellent regulations amongst the Dāshārhas Vishnu himself will be united with Nārāyana, Shoma and Surya.' ('As fire returns to fire' is figurative imagery.)

statements.claim: Krishna heard the prophecy without arguing, and Narada took his leave while Dwaraka continued its day above the waiting sea.
statements.evidence: Scene-setting around the recital/prophecy; matches the pack's 'before departing' frame. Krishna's silent reception and the waiting-sea imagery are atmosphere, not pack-asserted facts.

DKS_0518.notes: Close, largely verbatim rendering of the Harivamsha 1.249 recital; every named deed, list and prophecy detail maps to the passage. Two micro-nuances only: 'forbidden to interfere' (pack says the celestials tried to prevent the Parijata removal but were disregarded) and 'at Kurukshetra' as a locational gloss not named in the chapter. Neither rises to UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: The Yadu boys, giddy and reckless, dressed Samba, son of Jambavati, in women's clothes and led him to the visiting sages claiming the veiled boy was pregnant.
statements.evidence: BP 11.1.13-15 and VP 5.37: boys disguised 'Samba, the son of Jambavatī, as a woman' (BP 11.1.13: sāmbaṃ jāmbavatī-sutam); VP (Wilson): 'they dressed and adorned Sumba, the son of Jámbavatí, as a damsel.' Pack excerpt: boys asked 'This dark-eyed one is pregnant; what will she give birth to?'

statements.claim: The sages, undeceived, answered in anger that 'she' would bear an iron mace that would destroy the clan.
statements.evidence: BP 11.1.15 (kupitā: angered): pack excerpt 'The angry sages answered: She will bear an iron mace, the destroyer of your clan.' VP 5.37: 'She will bring forth a club, that shall crush the whole of the Yádava race.'

statements.claim: The mace came forth from Samba's belly on the spot, and the terrified boys cried 'What have we done, ill-fated as we are? What will people say of us now?'
statements.evidence: BP 11.1.16-17: 'te 'ti-santrastā vimucya sahasodaram / kiṃ kṛtaṃ manda-bhāgyair naḥ kiṃ vadiṣyanti no janāḥ' — terrified, they released it from the belly and lamented exactly that. VP 5.37 confirms a club 'was produced from the belly of Śámba.'

statements.claim: The boys carried the mace to the assembly; Ugrasena, the Yadava king, had it ground to powder and the powder cast into the sea.
statements.evidence: BP 11.1.18-20: 'tac copanīya sadasi... yadu-rājaḥ sa āhukaḥ' — carried it to the assembly; Ahuka (Ugrasena) the Yadu king ground the mace to powder and had it thrown into the water. VP 5.37: Ugrasena had the iron club ground to dust and thrown into the sea.

statements.claim: A fish swallowed a scrap of the iron among the powder in the sea; the fish was caught by fishermen, and the iron was eventually worked into the arrow that waited in a hunter's quiver.
statements.evidence: BP 11.1.21-22: 'kaścin matsyo 'grasīl lohaṃ cūrṇāṇi taralaiḥ tataḥ / matsyo gṛhīto matsya-ghnair jālenānyaiḥ sahārṇave' — a fish swallowed the iron with the powder in the waters and was caught by fishermen with nets. Pack index excerpt: the last bit of iron 'in the hunter's hands became the arrow.' (The working through later hands is the standard BP continuation of the same episode; pack summary supports the fish-to-arrow chain.)

statements.claim: Krishna was not surprised when the news reached him: the sages had pronounced the curse knowing the mind of the Lord, and holy anger was an instrument of a design already made.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.23: the sages, angered by the Yadu and Bhoja boys at play, cursed them 'knowing the mind of the Lord' (bhagavan-mata-kovidāḥ). MB 16.1 excerpt (in pack): 'The slayer of Madhu, informed of what had taken place, summoned all the Vrishnis...' — Krishna is informed and does not overturn the sentence.

statements.claim: He gathered the Vrishnis to him so that when the curse ripened they would be found together; the clan kept its city while the curse settled over the house.
statements.evidence: Krishna's summoning of the Vrishnis is in the pack (MB 16.1 excerpt); the motive gloss ('so that when it arrives, they will be found together') and the closing 'curse settled over the house' imagery are the story's interpretive framing, not pack statements.

DKS_0519.notes: Faithful composite of BP 11.1.13-23 (joke, curse, mace birth, lament, assembly, grinding, fish) with VP 5.37 (Samba as Jambavati's son) and BP 3.3.23 (sages knowing the Lord's mind). All characters, sequence and outcome match the pack; no UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: Uddhava recalls Krishna's deliberation after the great war: with Drona, Bhishma, Arjuna and Bhima gone, the remaining burden of the earth was the unbearable host of the Yadavas.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.13: 'kiyān bhuvo 'yaṃ kṣapitoru-bhāro yad droṇa-bhīṣmārjuna-bhīma-mūlaiḥ' — what burden of earth remained when Drona, Bhishma, Arjuna and Bhima (its roots) were gone; pack excerpt: 'the unbearable host of the Yadavas.'

statements.claim: The Yadava host numbered eighteen akshauhinis and could be destroyed by no enemy.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.13 (Sanskrit): 'aṣṭādaśākṣauhiṇiko mad-aṃśair āste balaṃ durviṣahaṃ yadūnām' — the invincible Yadava army of eighteen akshauhinis. Pack summary: 'could be destroyed in no other way than by their own quarrel.'

statements.claim: Krishna's words: 'When they quarrel among themselves, eyes red with wine, there is no other way to destroy them' and 'When I act, they will vanish of themselves.'
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.14: 'mitho yadaiṣāṃ bhavitā vivādo madhv-āmadātāmra-vilocanānām / naiṣāṃ vadhopāya iyān ato 'nyo mayy udyate 'ntardadhate svayaṃ sma' — matches the pack's rendered excerpt verbatim in substance.

statements.claim: The destruction would come through their own quarrel under the pretext of the brahmins' curse on Samba — the iron mace — which Krishna recognised as the door.
statements.evidence: Pack variant note cross-refs vp5_037_03 (extermination of the Yadava race 'by the pretext of an imprecation denounced by Brahmans' — the Samba/iron-mace episode, VP 5.37); BP 3.3's own continuation (v.23, in the corpus chain) has the sages curse the boys. The curse-as-pretext reading is the pack's canonical event (evt_0285, recall of the self-destruction).

statements.claim: No war could be fought against the Yadavas and won; the only way to lighten the earth of them was to let them destroy themselves, wine in their eyes, at Prabhasa.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.13-14 and pack summary ('the Yadu warriors... could be destroyed in no other way than by their own quarrel, and that when he acted, they would destroy themselves'); the festive ride to Prabhasa is the follow-on in the same Uddhava recollection (BP 3.3.24) and the corpus chain.

statements.claim: Staging: Krishna spoke these words aloud to Uddhava in Dwaraka, and Uddhava remembered them for the rest of his life.
statements.evidence: The pack presents the deliberation as Uddhava's recollection of Krishna's reflection (uddhava uvāca; 'evam sañcintya bhagavān...'); rendering it as a direct conversation is a dramatisation of that recall, faithful in content.

DKS_0520.notes: Substantive claims (burden analysis, 18 akshauhinis, wine-reddened quarrel, self-removal, curse pretext, Prabhasa) all match BP 3.3.13-14 and the pack's canonical cross-ref. Only the framing as a spoken dialogue with Uddhava is dramatised recall. No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: After the Yadavas perished at Prabhasa, Krishna set the aftermath in motion: he sent Daruka to the Kurus to summon Arjuna and dispatched Vabhru to guard the women, then entered Dwaraka, touched his father's feet, and asked him to protect the ladies until Arjuna/Dhananjaya came.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4 (in pack): 'Krishna commanded Daruka, saying, Going to the Kurus, inform Partha of this great slaughter of the Yadus...'; 'Do thou go quickly for protecting the ladies...'; 'Entering the city of Dwaravati, Janardana said these words unto his father, Do thou protect all the ladies of our house, till Dhananjaya comes'; 'Krishna touched the feet of his father with his head.' (Errand order is compressed; MB 16.4 has them find Rama first, then send Daruka/Vabhru, then visit the city, then return to find the serpent issuing.)

statements.claim: Krishna found Balarama sitting in a solitary spot with his back against a tree, absorbed in Yoga.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Keshava beheld Rama sitting in a solitary spot thereof. He also saw that Rama had set himself to Yoga'; 'reclining his back against a tree, in a solitary spot of earth.'

statements.claim: A great serpent issued from Balarama's mouth: white as snow, huge as a mountain, crowned with a thousand hoods, red-eyed — Sesha, leaving the human body it had dwelt in.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'from out his mouth was issuing a mighty snake. The colour of that snake was white. Leaving the human body (in which he had dwelt so long), that high-souled naga of a 1,000 heads and having a form as large as that of a mountain, endued besides with red eyes, proceeded along that way which led to the ocean.' VP 5.37 (pack index): 'The great serpent Śesha issues from the mouth of Ráma.'

statements.claim: The ocean came forth to receive Sesha, with the kings of the serpents (Karkotaka, Vasuki, Takshaka, Prithusravas, Sankha, Kumuda, Pundarika, Dhritarashtra, Hrada, Kratha, Sitikantha, Chakramanda, Atishanda, Durmukha, Amvarisha), the sacred rivers and Varuna at their head.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Ocean himself, and many celestial snakes, and many sacred Rivers were there... There were Karkotaka and Vasuki and Takshaka and Prithusravas and Varuna and Kunjara, and Misri and Sankha and Kumuda and Pundarika, and the high-souled Dhritarashtra, and Hrada and Kratha and Sitikantha... and Chakramanda and Atishanda, and that foremost of Nagas called Durmukha, and Amvarisha, and king Varuna himself.' (Story omits Kunjara and Misri — abridgement, not error.)

statements.claim: They offered Arghya and water for his feet, performed the rites of honour and saluted him with the customary enquiries; saints and serpents hymned him as the white form passed into the deep.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'offering him the Arghya and water to wash his feet, and with diverse other rites, they all worshipped the mighty Naga and saluted him by making the usual enquiries'; VP: the snake 'entered into the waters of the deep'; pack index summary: 'enters the ocean, hymned by saints and serpents.'

statements.claim: Krishna watched, then wandered thoughtfully in the forest, recollecting Gandhari's words, the brahmin's imprecation, the iron bolt, the quarrel at Prabhasa, and Durvasas' words over the remnant of the payasa he had eaten as Krishna's guest.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'he had thought before this of everything that had been fore-shadowed by the words uttered by Gandhari in former days. He also recollected the words that Durvasas had spoken at the time his body was smeared by that Rishi with the remnant of the Payasa he had eaten (while a guest at Krishna's house).' The curse/bolt/quarrel items are the same recollection (MB 16.4: 'thinking of the destruction of the Vrishnis and the Andhakas').

statements.claim: Krishna then sat down on the bare earth, the forest keeping watch — Balarama's remaining body like a tree with its spirit departed.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4 confirms Krishna 'sat down on the bare earth' after wandering thoughtfully; the tree-with-spirit-departed simile and 'forest kept watch' are atmospheric framing of the departure scene.

DKS_0521.notes: Very close to MB 16.4 (Ganguli), with the full serpent-name catalogue and honours scene intact; VP 5.37 supplies the naming of Sesha. The single structural liberty is compressing the errands (Daruka/Vabhru/Dwaraka visit) into one continuous pre-forest sequence — MB has Krishna find Rama first, do the errands, then return to see the serpent — an ordering compression, not a contradiction. No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Dreadful omens rose in Dwaraka — birds wheeling in unfamiliar circles, the sea holding its breath — and the city felt something coming.
statements.evidence: BP 11.30 has Krishna call the portents 'dreadful omens... the banners of death' (pack excerpt); the specific imagery (birds' circles, the sea's stillness) is atmospheric expansion of 'the omens reached Dwaraka,' not pack text.

statements.claim: Krishna told the Yadava elders: 'These dreadful omens are the banners of death. Not for a moment should we remain here. Let the women, the children, and the old ones go to Shankhoddhara. We will go to Prabhasa, where the Sarasvati flows westward, and worship there.'
statements.evidence: BP 11.30.4-9 (pack excerpt): 'These dreadful omens are the banners of death; not for a moment should we remain here. Let the women, children and elders go to Shankhoddhara, and let us go to Prabhasa where the Sarasvati flows westward.' Elders answered 'so be it' (iti sarve samākarṇya yadu-vṛddhāḥ, v.9).

statements.claim: The elders of the Yadus answered 'So be it' and the great departure began; the women, children and old turned toward Shankhoddhara at the parting of the ways while the rest pressed on to the mouth of the Sarasvati.
statements.evidence: BP 11.30.5 and 9: women/children/elders to Śaṅkhoddhāra; the Yadu elders assent. BP 3.3.24: after some months the Vrishnis, Bhojas and Andhakas went to Prabhasa; crossing to the mainland from the island city is the canonical setting of the tirtha journey.

statements.claim: Krishna linked the omens to Gandhari's curse: at the close of the great war the bereaved queen had cried out against him, promising ruin to his race as ruin had come to hers.
statements.evidence: MB 16.2 (pack excerpt) confirms the operative frame: Krishna 'endeavoured to bring about those occurrences which would make Gandhari's words true.' The one-line gloss of what Gandhari had said at the war's end summarises that earlier curse scene (canonical in the corpus chain) rather than restating this pack's text.

statements.claim: Krishna said: 'The fourteenth lunation has been made the fifteenth by Rahu once more... It has once more appeared, it seems, for our destruction.'
statements.evidence: MB 16.2 (pack excerpt): 'The fourteenth lunation has been made the fifteenth by Rahu once more... It has once more appeared, it seems, for our destruction.'

statements.claim: The Mahabharata says plainly that Krishna moved to bring about what Gandhari's words foretold, commanding the Vrishnis to make a pilgrimage to a sacred water.
statements.evidence: MB 16.2 (pack excerpt): 'Vasudeva, having said so, endeavoured to bring about those occurrences which would make Gandhari's words true. That chastiser of foes commanded the Vrishnis to make a pilgrimage to some sacred water.'

statements.claim: Months passed before the great gathering assembled; the camp spread along the western shore with boats beached in rows and smoke of ten thousand cooking fires.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.24: 'after some months' the clans went joyfully to Prabhasa (katipayair māsaiḥ). The scale of the camp and cooking-fire imagery is descriptive colour consistent with a multi-clan assembly at the shore; the beached boats follow from the sea crossing.

statements.claim: Uddhava remembered that they went joyfully, deluded by fate: they bathed in the sacred waters, honoured the gods and rishis, and gave the brahmins cows, gold, silver, beds, garments, chariots, elephants and lands.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.24-27 (pack excerpt and Sanskrit): 'saṃhṛṣṭā rathair deva-vimohitāḥ' — joyful, deluded by fate; v.25-26: they bathed, honoured the gods and rishis and gave cows, gold, silver, beds, garments, chariots, elephants (ibhān), maidens and land. Pack excerpt: 'gave the brahmins cows, gold, silver, beds, garments, chariots, elephants and lands.'

statements.claim: Krishna went with them, bathed and gave with them, letting them have their last happy days at Prabhasa since the curse would ripen wherever they stood.
statements.evidence: Interpretive framing of Krishna's known foreknowledge and acceptance (BP 3.3.13-14 deliberation, MB 16.2 'endeavoured to bring about...'); the emotional reading of the final good days is the story's commentary, not a pack statement.

DKS_0522.notes: Two source strands are combined cleanly (BP 11.30.4-10 for the command/Shankhoddhara split; BP 3.3.24-27 for the joyful, fate-deluded journey and gifts; MB 16.2 for Rahu and Gandhari's words). Krishna's speeches are near-verbatim. Omens imagery and the Gandhari backstory gloss are connective; the Gandhari curse scene itself is the referenced antecedent (MB 16.2 'make Gandhari's words true'). No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: One day the sages Vishvamitra, Kanwa and Narada arrived in Dwaraka, and Vrishni heroes, Samva among them, decided to sport with them — already afflicted by the deities' rod of chastisement.
statements.evidence: MB 16.1: 'the Vrishni heroes numbering Samva amongst them, saw Vishvamitra and Kanwa and Narada arrived at Dwaraka. Afflicted by the rod of chastisement wielded by the deities, those heroes, causing Samva to be disguised like a woman, approached those ascetics.'

statements.claim: They presented the disguised Samva (heir of Vasudeva) as the wife of Vabhru, desirous of a son, and asked what she would bring forth.
statements.evidence: MB 16.1: 'This one is the wife of Vabhru of immeasurable energy who is desirous of having a son. Ye Rishis, do you know for certain what this one will bring forth?'

statements.claim: The rishis, eyes red with wrath, answered that Samva, heir of Vasudeva, would bring forth a fierce iron bolt for the destruction of the Vrishnis and Andhakas; the wicked, pride-intoxicated boys would through it become the exterminators of their own race, with the exception of Rama and Janardana.
statements.evidence: MB 16.1: 'with eyes red in wrath... This heir of Vasudeva, by name Samva, will bring forth a fierce iron bolt for the destruction of the Vrishnis and the Andhakas. Ye wicked and cruel ones, intoxicated with pride, through that iron bolt ye will become the exterminators of your race with the exception of Rama and Janarddana.'

statements.claim: The sages added that the plough-armed hero would cast off his body and enter the ocean, and a hunter named Jara would pierce the high-souled Krishna as he lay on the ground.
statements.evidence: MB 16.1: 'The blessed hero armed with the plough will enter the ocean, casting off his body, while a hunter of the name of Jara will pierce the high-souled Krishna while lying on the ground.'

statements.claim: The three sages then went to see Keshava; Krishna heard them, summoned all the Vrishnis, told them of it, said 'That which is destined will surely happen', and entered his mansion, not wishing to ordain otherwise.
statements.evidence: MB 16.1: 'Having said so they then proceeded to see Keshava. The slayer of Madhu, informed of what had taken place, summoned all the Vrishnis and told them of it... he simply said that that which was destined would surely happen. Hrishikesa having said so, entered his mansion. The Lord of the universe did not wish to ordain otherwise.'

statements.claim: The next day Samva brought forth the iron bolt, fierce and like a gigantic messenger of death; through it all the individuals of the Vrishni and Andhaka races were to be consumed into ashes. The fact was reported to the king.
statements.evidence: MB 16.1: 'When the next day came, Samva actually brought forth an iron bolt through which all the individuals in the race of the Vrishnis and the Andhakas became consumed into ashes... a fierce iron bolt that looked like a gigantic messenger of death. The fact was duly reported to the king.'

statements.claim: Ugrasena, in great distress, had the bolt ground to fine powder and men cast the powder into the sea.
statements.evidence: MB 16.1: 'In great distress of mind, the king (Ugrasena) caused that iron bolt to be reduced into fine powder. Men were employed, O king, to cast that powder into the sea.'

statements.claim: At the command of Ugrasena (Ahuka), Krishna, Rama and the high-souled Vabhru it was proclaimed that no Vrishni or Andhaka might manufacture wine or intoxicating spirits, on pain of being impaled alive with all his kinsmen; through fear of the king and of Rama's word the people obeyed.
statements.evidence: MB 16.1: 'At the command of Ahuka, of Janarddana, of Rama, and of the high-souled Vabhru, it was, again, proclaimed throughout the city that from that day, among all the Vrishnis and the Andhakas no one should manufacture wines and intoxicating spirits of any kind, and that whoever would secretly manufacture wines and spirits should be impaled alive with all his kinsmen. Through fear of the king, and knowing that it was the command of Rama also of unimpeachable [authority]... the people obeyed.'

statements.claim: Closing gloss: the powder had only been hidden, not recalled — 'the words of rishis, once spoken, do not dissolve in salt water' — and Dwaraka went dry overnight while the curse kept its own time.
statements.evidence: The ban and the sea-casting are pack-supported; the sea-keeping-its-secret reflection and 'emptied their jars' imagery are the story's ominous commentary on the unspent curse, not pack assertions.

DKS_0524.notes: Nearly verbatim MB 16.1 (Ganguli): disguise, triple curse, sages' visit to Keshava, Krishna's 'destined' acceptance, next-day bolt, Ugrasena's grinding, and the wine prohibition with its impalement penalty all track the passage exactly. The 'sat down at the city's edge' and closing reflections are connective. No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: After the slaughter at Prabhasa, Krishna walked out with his charioteer Daruka and Vabhru, following in the wake of Rama to discover his retreat; they found him sitting thoughtfully in a solitary spot, his back against a tree.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Then Daruka and Keshava and Vabhru left that spot, following in the wake of Rama (for discovering his retreat). They beheld that hero of infinite energy sitting thoughtfully, reclining his back against a tree, in a solitary spot of earth.' (Folded arms and 'strength gone out of him' are descriptive colour.)

statements.claim: Krishna commanded Daruka: 'Go to the Kurus. Inform Partha of this great slaughter of the Yadus. Let Arjuna come here quickly, hearing of the destruction of the Yadavas through the brahmin's curse.'
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Krishna commanded Daruka, saying, Going to the Kurus, inform Partha of this great slaughter of the Yadus. Let Arjuna come here quickly, hearing of the destruction of the Yadavas through the Brahmana's curse.'

statements.claim: Daruka, deprived of his senses by grief, climbed onto his car and drove toward Hastinapura, the capital of the Kurus.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Thus addressed, Daruka, deprived of his senses by grief, proceeded on a car to the (capital of the) Kurus.' Hastinapura is the Kuru capital named throughout the MB's framing of this errand; 'climbed onto his car' is faithful rendering.

statements.claim: Krishna commanded Vabhru to go quickly and protect the ladies, letting no robbers injure them, tempted by the wealth with them.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Do thou go quickly for protecting the ladies. Let not robbers do them any injury, tempted by the wealth (that is with them).'

statements.claim: Vabhru — still helpless with wine but cheerless at the slaughter of his kinsmen — departed; once he had gone a little distance, the iron bolt attached itself to a mallet in a hunter's hands and sprang of itself upon that solitary survivor of the Yadava race and slew him, for he too was named in the brahmins' curse.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Vabhru, still helpless with wine but cheerless at the slaughter of his kinsmen, departed. He had rested for a while by the side of Keshava, but as soon as he had proceeded to a distance, the iron-bolt, attaching itself to a mallet in the hands of a hunter, suddenly sprang of itself upon that solitary survivor of the Yadava race and slew him, who also had been included in the curse of the Brahmanas.'

statements.claim: Krishna beheld Vabhru's death and did not move; he told Balarama: 'Wait for me here till I place the ladies under the care of kinsmen.'
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Beholding Vabhru slain, Keshava of great energy addressed his elder brother and said, Do thou, O Rama wait for me here till I place the ladies under the care of kinsmen.'

statements.claim: Entering Dwaravati, Krishna told his father to protect all the ladies of the house till Dhananjaya came, saying he would meet Rama that day, that he had beheld this carnage as he had beheld the Kuru carnage, that he could not see the city without the Yadavas, and that he would practise penances in the woods with Rama.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Janardana said these words unto his father, Do thou protect all the ladies of our house, till Dhananjaya comes. At the skirts of the forest Rama is waiting for me. I shall meet him today. This great carnage of the Yadus has been beheld by me even as I beheld before the carnage of those Kshatriyas who were the foremost ones of Kuru's race. It is impossible for me to see this city of the Yadavas without the Yadus beside me. Know that proceeding to the woods I shall practise penances with Rama in my company.' Krishna then 'touched the feet of his father with his head, and quickly left his presence.'

statements.claim: The ladies and children wailed; Krishna retraced his steps and said: 'Arjuna will come here. That foremost of men will relieve you of your grief.' Then he walked out of Dwaraka toward the forest.
statements.evidence: MB 16.4: 'Then a loud wail of sorrow arose from the ladies and children of his house... Keshava retraced his foot-steps and said unto them, Arjuna will come here. That foremost of men will relieve you of your grief.' The closing image of the yellow robe against the trees anticipates Jara's sight of the man 'dressed in yellow robes' (same chapter, in pack).

DKS_0525.notes: Verbatim-faithful MB 16.4 (Ganguli): Daruka's errand, Vabhru's command and iron-bolt death, Krishna's speech to his father, the wailing and the consolation all match the passage sentence-for-sentence. Minor descriptive colour (folded arms, robe growing small) is connective. No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Arjuna returned from Dwaraka to Hastinapura broken and weeping — face withered with grief — and wiped his eyes with his hand as he stood before Yudhishthira.
statements.evidence: BP 1.15.1-2 (Sanskrit): 'śokena śuṣyadvadana' (face withered by grief), 'pāṇinā... āmṛjya netrayoḥ' (wiping his eyes with his hand); pack index: 'Arjuna returns from Dwaraka broken and weeping and tells Yudhishthira.'

statements.claim: He remembered the friendship, affection and intimacy of the years when Krishna was his charioteer — at Draupadi's svayamvara when the kings burned with envy, and at the burning of Khandava when he fought the gods themselves.
statements.evidence: BP 1.15.3, 6-7: 'sakhyaṃ maitrīṃ sauhṛdaṃ ca sārathyādiṣu saṃsmaran' (recalling friendship, affection and the charioteering); v.6 the svayamvara at Drupada's house before kings maddened with desire; v.7 'aham u khāṇḍavam agnaye 'dām indraṃ ca sāmaragaṇaṃ tarasā vijitya' (I gave Khandava to Agni, conquering Indra with his hosts).

statements.claim: He remembered the sage Durvasa whose terrible hunger had once threatened the Pandava house, and how Krishna had come to them in the forest and turned the danger aside.
statements.evidence: BP 1.15.10: 'yo no jugopa vana etya durantakṛcchrād durvāsaso' — Krishna protected them in the forest from the great calamity of Durvasa.

statements.claim: He remembered the Gandiva bow and every campaign it had won at Krishna's side, and Krishna's voice calling across the chariot — 'O Partha, O Arjuna, my friend, son of Kuru's race'.
statements.evidence: BP 1.15.11-12 (Gandiva and its victories, won with Krishna) and v.17: 'narmāṇy... he pārtha he 'rjuna sakhe kurunandana' — the jests, 'O Partha, O Arjuna, friend, son of Kuru'; v.18 the shared laughter at play.

statements.claim: He told the king that the Yadavas, deluded by the curse of the brahmins, drank the varuni, the madira wine, until their minds were churned and they were beside themselves, and in that madness slew one another with their bare fists, brother against brother, until the seashore of Prabhasa ran with their blood; of the whole race only four or five were left.
statements.evidence: BP 1.15.21-22 and pack excerpt: 'In the city of our friends, the Yadavas, deluded by the curse of the brahmins, drinking the madira wine and beside themselves, slew one another with their bare fists; but four or five were left.' Sanskrit v.22: 'vāruṇīṃ madirāṃ pītvā madonmathitacetasām' (drinking varuni/madira, minds churned). Prabhasa as the location of the fratricide is the same Uddhava recollection's setting (BP 3.3.24) and the corpus chain (DKS_0523 'The Yadava Fratricide at Prabhasa').

statements.claim: Krishna had taken up that body the way an actor takes up a costume and cast it off when the earth's burden was lightened — leaving the world at his own hour.
statements.evidence: BP 1.15.33-34: 'yayāharad bhuvo bhāraṃ tāṃ tanuṃ vijahāv ajaḥ / yathā matsyādirūpāṇi dhatte jahyād yathā naṭaḥ' — the Unborn cast off the body that had borne the earth's burden, as an actor (naṭaḥ) takes up and drops forms like the fish-avatars. The 'own hour' framing reflects the same departure by the Lord's will.

statements.claim: In the very moment Mukunda abandoned the earth, the Kali age entered — the age of quarrel, the cause of all evil for the unawakened.
statements.evidence: BP 1.15.35 and pack excerpt: 'when Mukunda abandoned this earth, in that very moment the Kali age, the cause of all evil for the unawakened, entered.'

statements.claim: Kunti too heard of the destruction of the Yadavas and the Lord's going, and took the measure of it in silence.
statements.evidence: BP 1.15.31-32: 'pṛthāpy anuśrutya dhanañjayoditaṃ nāśaṃ yadūnāṃ bhagavadgatiṃ ca tām' — Pritha (Kunti) also heard, from Arjuna's words, of the destruction of the Yadavas and of the Lord's going. Her silent reckoning is connective rendering of her listening.

statements.claim: Closing scene: the sun rose over Hastinapura as always, the walls stood and the river ran, and only the wise could feel that the age itself had changed.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric epilogue to the Kali-age entry; the ordinary-day imagery is the story's closing reflection, not pack text.

DKS_0526.notes: Faithful to BP 1.15 (Arjuna's grief and recollections, the varuni-madira fratricide report, 'four or five left', the actor simile, Kali age at Mukunda's departure, Kunti's hearing). Every memory (svayamvara, Khandava, Durvasa, Gandiva, Krishna's call) maps to a specific verse of the chapter. Prabhasa in the slaughter sentence is the canonical location from the same Uddhava account (BP 3.3.24) and the corpus chain. No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Uddhava had served Krishna since he was five years old and had grown old in that service.
statements.evidence: BP 3.2.1-2: 'yaḥ pañca-hāyano mātrā prātar-āśāya yācitaḥ / sa kathaṃ sevayā tasya kālena jarasaṃ gataḥ' (serving him, he grew old in time).

statements.claim: Vidura asked Uddhava to speak of Krishna, and Uddhava sat for a moment silent, sunk in the sweetness of Krishna's feet, limbs trembling, tears falling, then wiped his eyes and smiled.
statements.evidence: BP 3.2.3-5: 'sa muhūrtam abhūt tūṣṇīṃ kṛṣṇāṅghri-sudhayā... pulakodbhinna-sarvāṅgo muñcan mīlad-dṛśā śucaḥ / śanakair... punar āgataḥ'; pack excerpt: wiping his eyes he smiled.

statements.claim: Uddhava lamented that the sun (Krishna) had set, that he had no good news for houses stripped of fortune, and that the world was wretched, more so the Yadavas who dwelt with Hari and never knew him.
statements.evidence: BP 3.2.6-7 pack rendering: 'The sun Krishna has set; what good news can I tell in homes bereft of fortune? Wretched is this world, and more so the Yadavas, who dwelt with Hari and knew him not.' Sanskrit: 'durbhago bata loko 'yaṃ yadavo nitarām api'.

statements.claim: The Yadavas were masters at reading a glance, mature in counsel, devoted to Krishna alone, yet the Lord's own maya had closed their eyes.
statements.evidence: BP 3.2.8-9: 'iṅgita-jñāḥ puru-prauḍhā ekārāmāś ca sātvatāḥ / devasya māyayā spṛṣṭāḥ'.

statements.claim: At the Rajasuya of Yudhishthira the three worlds looked upon Krishna and their eyes were blessed.
statements.evidence: BP 3.2.12: 'yad dharma-sūnor bata rājasūye nirīkṣya dṛk-svastyayanaṃ tri-lokaḥ' (dharma-sūnu = Yudhishthira).

statements.claim: Krishna's loving laughing glance in the rasa play gave worth to all it fell on.
statements.evidence: BP 3.2.13: 'yasyānurāga-pluta-hāsa-rāsa-līlāvaloka-pratilabdha-mānāḥ'.

statements.claim: At that same Rajasuya even Shishupala, who hated Krishna all his life, reached perfection through that hatred.
statements.evidence: BP 3.2.18: 'dṛṣṭā bhavadbhir nanu rājasūye caidyasya kṛṣṇaṃ dviṣato 'pi siddhiḥ'; 'fixed gazing' gloss is traditional (Shishupala's meditation on Krishna in enmity).

statements.claim: In the great battles, heroes of the earth fell gazing on the lotus of Krishna's face.
statements.evidence: BP 3.2.19: 'tathaiva cānye nara-loka-vīrā ya āhave kṛṣṇa-mukhāravindam'.

statements.claim: Uddhava spoke of the Unborn Lord's birth-play in Vasudeva's house and of how Krishna, bowing at his parents' feet, had spoken to them.
statements.evidence: BP 3.2.15-16: 'ajasya janma-viḍambanaṃ yad vasudeva-gehe' and 'yad āha pādāv abhivandya pitroḥ'.

statements.claim: Uddhava told Vidura he was no ordinary minister but one without equal, a lord of the three worlds whose every desire was fulfilled by the fortune of his own sovereignty.
statements.evidence: BP 3.2.20: 'svayaṃ tv asāmyātiśayas tryadhīśaḥ svārājya-lakṣmy-āpta-samasta-kāmaḥ'.

statements.claim: Vidura had come to the bank of the Yamuna to learn from Uddhava the deeds of Krishna.
statements.evidence: Pack index entry: characters Uddhava/Vidura, location 'the bank of the Yamuna'; canonical event evt_0537 frames Vidura hearing Uddhava's lament.

statements.claim: The river that flowed past them was the same water that had once carried the little boat of the cowherd boy's infancy.
statements.evidence: Closing lyrical image tying the Yamuna to Krishna's infancy; the pack's BP 3.2.1-20 contains no infancy-boat motif (the Yamuna infancy crossing belongs to the earlier Vasudeva episode of the corpus), so the concrete 'boat' image is an atmospheric flourish rather than a pack-supported event.

DKS_0527.notes: No UNSUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED. One connective-narration question: the final image of the Yamuna having 'carried the little boat of the cowherd boy's infancy' is an invented concrete detail (no boat motif in the infancy tradition the pack draws on); kept as atmosphere, flagged for possible rewrite to the pack-grounded crossing image.

statements.claim: Arjuna found the bodies of Krishna and Balarama and performed the funeral rites for them and for all the slain.
statements.evidence: VP 5.38: 'ARJUNA having found the bodies of Krishńa and of Ráma, performed for them, and the rest of the slain, the obsequial rites.'

statements.claim: The eight queens of Krishna, Rukmini at their head, embraced the body of Hari and entered the funeral fire; Revati held the corpse of Rama on the blazing pile, which was cool to her.
statements.evidence: VP 5.38: 'The eight queens of Krishńa... with Rukminí at their head, embraced the body of Hari, and entered the funeral fire. Revatí also, embracing the corpse of Ráma, entered the blazing pile, which was cool to her, happy in contact with her lord.'

statements.claim: Ugrasena, and Vasudeva with Devaki and Rohini, gave themselves to the flames.
statements.evidence: VP 5.38: 'Ugrasena and Anakadundubhi [Vasudeva], with Devakí and Rohiní, committed themselves to the flames.'

statements.claim: Arjuna made the people leave the city, took Vajra, and led the thousands of Krishna's widowed wives out of Dwaraka slowly and with tenderness, the city following.
statements.evidence: VP 5.38: 'Arjuna... made all the people leave the city, and took Vajra with him... conducted the thousands of the wives of Krishńa, with Vajra, and all the people, from Dwáraká, with tenderness and care, and travelled slowly away.'

statements.claim: Behind them the sea rose and swallowed Dwaraka, leaving only the dwelling of the deity of the Yadu race; the ocean has never washed it away, Kesava still abides there, and whoever visits that holy shrine is freed of his sins.
statements.evidence: VP 5.38: 'The ocean rose, and submerged the whole of Dwáraká, except alone the dwelling of the deity of the race of Yadu. The sea has not yet been able to wash that temple away, and there Keśava constantly abides... Whoever visits that holy shrine... is liberated from all his sins.'

statements.claim: On the same day Hari departed from the earth, the dark-bodied Kali age descended.
statements.evidence: VP 5.38: 'on the same day that Hari departed from the earth the powerful dark-bodied Kali age descended.'

statements.claim: The Sudharman palace and the Parijata tree, which Krishna had brought down from heaven, went back to heaven.
statements.evidence: VP 5.38: 'The Sudharman palace and the Párijáta tree, which had been brought to earth by Krishńa, both proceeded to heaven.'

statements.claim: Arjuna halted the column in the country of Panchanada, a rich and fertile spot, and robbers, coveting the widowed women and wealth, assembled the villainous Abhiras.
statements.evidence: VP 5.38: 'Arjuna, halted the people... in the Panchanada country, in a rich and fertile spot; but the desires of the robbers... were excited, when they observed so many widowed females, also such great riches... they assembled the villainous Ábhiras.'

statements.claim: The robbers taunted that Arjuna, rich and guarded only by husband-slain women, was a disgrace to brave men, his pride swollen from slaying Bhishma, Drona, Jayadratha and Karna, and urged the villagers to take their long thick staves.
statements.evidence: VP 5.38: 'Here is this Arjuna, immensely rich, and having numerous women, whose husbands have been slain... His pride is raised by the death of Bhíshma, Drońa, Jayadratha, Karńa... Up, up; take your long thick staves.'

statements.claim: They rushed with cudgels and clods of earth; Arjuna derided them — 'Retire, wretches, ignorant of what is right, unless you are eager to die' — but they seized his treasure and his women.
statements.evidence: VP 5.38: 'they rushed, armed with cudgels and clods of earth... Arjuna... said to them in derision, "Retire, wretches, ignorant of what is right, unless ye are desirous of dying." But they disregarded his menaces, and seized his treasures and his women.'

statements.claim: Gandiva would not tighten — the string stayed slack — the incantations of the superhuman weapons would not return, his arrows only scratched the herdsmen, Agni's arrows were themselves destroyed and fatal to him, and the might of Krishna could not be recalled, so arrows flew at random or were brushed aside.
statements.evidence: VP 5.38: 'he began to brace his heavenly bow Gándíva... it continued flaccid: neither could he call to recollection the incantations of the superhuman weapons... merely scratched the skin. The arrows given him by Agni to carry certain destruction now were themselves destroyed, and were fatal to Arjuna... now they were put aside by the peasants, or they flew at random.' Khandava provenance of Agni's gift is the standard context for the Agni-given arrows.
